Through these things, it is clear they do not live a human or animal life burning with senses and impulse, but a divine one, as if their soul were at rest and God were there in place of the soul, moving them as if He were a more excellent soul.

There are various types of those divinely inspired, both due to the variety of the gods—who inspire in different ways—and due to the difference in the modes of inspiration. These modes are as follows: for either the god himself possesses us, or we devote ourselves to him and become entirely his, or we perform an action in common with the god. Also, we either become masters of the lowest divine powers, or the middle, or the highest. Likewise, sometimes it is the bare presence of the god, sometimes beyond presence there is a communion, and interdum beyond this a union is achieved. Again, regarding the inspiration, either the soul alone becomes a partaker, or even the body immediately becomes a participant in some way, or even the "common animal" <note>the composite of soul and body</note> becomes equally a partaker. According to the diversity of these differences, there are different signs, effects, and works of the inspired. According to the aforementioned diversity of the inspirers or the inspiration, some of the inspired are moved either in their whole body or in certain limbs, or on the contrary, they remain still. Likewise, they perform dances and harmonious songs, or the opposite. Again, their body seems either to grow in height or in breadth, or to be carried through the air <note>referring to levitation</note>, and the opposite. Likewise, they utter voices, either uniform and continuous, or uneven and interrupted by silence. And then

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...they relax their tones and then tighten them. The inspired person is free from his own action and holds the god in place of his own soul.

<margin>m</margin> The **greatest** sign of divine inspiration is that he who draws down and introduces the deity beholds the spirit descending, and discerns how great and of what sort it is, and is mystically taught and guided by it. Furthermore, those who receive the deity see a certain appearance of fire before the reception. Sometimes this is even seen by those present, either when the god arrives or when he departs. From this sign, those skilled in these matters most truly discern the power of the deity, its rank, and concerning what things it speaks truly and what it accomplishes. But those who secretly introduce spirits without such visions, as if hiding in darkness, are shaken. Nor do they understand what they are doing, except for certain small things—that is, some signs in the body of the inspired person itself. Therefore, when the excellence of the divine fire and a certain ineffable appearance of light rests upon the one who is possessed from without, and fills him entirely and dominates him deeply, and embraces him on all sides within itself, so that he cannot perform any action of his own—what sense-perception or self-awareness can remain in a soul receiving divine fire? Or what human motion, passion, distortion, imagination, or alienation <note>original: "alienatio"; here meaning a loss of self or mental derangement</note> can be present, such as some people suspect?

Porphyry defines divine inspiration thus: "a motion of the mind together with demonic inspiration." Iamblichus says, however, that in a soul divinely inspired, neither human mind nor thought is carried along, if it is indeed truly contained by the god. Nor is it an inspiration of demons, but of gods; nor again should it be defined as a "departure" or "alienation." For these terms signify a fall into a worse state, but rather it should be called a "reductio" <note>a leading back or restoration</note> and a return to a better state. Therefore, inspiration is nothing other <gloss>than</gloss> the minds being entirely occupied and contained by God. From this, indeed, ecstasy follows afterward—that is, a certain departure or alienation—as a side effect following the inspiration. 

Plato in the *Phaedrus* says that the ancients called prophecy "mania," that is, madness <note>This refers to the Greek word *mania* (μαινία)</note>. This is because only those seized by divine madness truly prophesy. Later people, however, by adding the letter 't', called it "mantia" <note>original: "mantiam"; referring to *manteia* (μαντεία), the Greek word for divination. Plato suggests the 't' was added by those who didn't understand the sacred madness of the ancients</note>. Likewise, priests, sibyls, and prophets, as long as they are "prudent" <note>meaning: in their right, rational mind</note>, foresee either very little and obscurely or nothing at all; but when they are carried away by God, they truly prophesy. Hence they have foreseen, among many nations, dangers imminently threatening by divine will, warned the peoples, and through sacrifices appeased divine Nemesis <note>The goddess of divine retribution</note>. 

Likewise, he says that a presage made by human art is called a <term>conjectural calculation</term> <note>original: "putatiónem coniecturalem"; this refers to "technical" divination like reading bird flights or entrails, which Iamblichus considers inferior to direct inspiration</note> and is of <gloss>no</gloss> weight if compared with divine inspiration and prophecy. Iamblichus says that divine inspiration and prophecy are not in the mind or soul, whether as a quality in a subject or as an action in an agent...

# IAMBLICHUS:

...but that it is entirely the act of God himself, depending simply upon God. I call it an act performed by God in the mind or soul simply, as if in instruments vacant of all their own motion; and thus true foretellings are given. But if motion from the body or soul, or some such quality, is meanwhile introduced or precedes it, the visions are confounded. Nor will there be true prophecies, nor can there be legitimate divine inspiration there where anything human is mixed in.

There were generally three opinions concerning inspiration and divine prophecy. The first traced its cause to the soul. The second to the body. The third to the composite <note>The "composite" refers to the human being as a joined entity of both body and soul.</note>. The first places it in that state in which the whole soul is led back into its own divine part, or into the mind; or when its action has become more vehement or fuller; or when thought has become sharp and most swift in motion; or when the mind has grown hot. 

The second places its cause in the body, when it has a certain complexion <term>complexion: in medieval and Renaissance medicine, the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within a person</term>, namely either melancholic or temperate, or a certain elemental quality, or furthermore a special one, or a certain spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; here referring to "pneuma," a thin, vapor-like substance thought to circulate through the body to facilitate sensation and movement</note>. 

The third says its cause is a certain proportion by which the body and soul are joined together. 

Iamblichus says it is not the work of the soul or the body, or the composite, nor does it have its cause in them. For that prophetic inspiration acts, both in foretelling and in effecting, beyond every custom of human nature. But a man, or anything of a man, cannot progress beyond his own boundaries toward divine boundaries. Nor can superior things be generated from inferior ones. Therefore, the cause of this is solely divinity itself: namely, when lights descend from the gods into us, and spirits are handed down by them. And there is present with us a dominion and absolute power from that place, encompassing all things that are in us, and completely banishing our own awareness and motion, and bringing forth speeches—through the man, indeed, but not with the man's own thought. Rather, [divinity] itself pronounces through the mouth of the one raving <note>original: "furentis"; this refers to "divine frenzy" or *theia mania*, a state of being "filled with the god" rather than being mentally ill</note> who is placed outside of himself. While, clearly, whatever things are in us serve the divinity entirely, and yield to the sole dominant divine action. 

Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and an occasional critic of Iamblichus's more ritualistic approach to magic and theurgy</note> says that music brings passions to the soul, and likewise calms them, and that different sounds suit different souls and characters. Likewise, he says music changes the complexions and affections of the body, stirs up fury, or restrains fury. Iamblichus concedes these things. But he denies that these are the causes of divine inspiration. Since they are human—partly natural, partly artificial—and they have nothing divine in themselves. Porphyry seems to suspect this when he says some are inspired when they hear flutes <note>original: "tybias"; likely the *aulos*, a Greek double-reed instrument associated with the ecstatic rites of Dionysus</note>, or cymbals, or drums, while others when they hear other melodies. These correspond to various orders of the gods...

<summary>Iamblichus rejects psychological and biological explanations for prophecy, arguing that divine inspiration is a purely supernatural event where the human mind is bypassed and replaced by the action of a god. He distinguishes between the natural emotional effects of music and the truly divine possession that occurs during sacred rites.</summary>

<keywords>Iamblichus, Porphyry, divine inspiration, prophecy, Neoplatonism, divine frenzy, humoral theory, music therapy, theurgy</keywords>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...into the world <note>This completes the thought from the previous page: that divine proportions are introduced into the world.</note> there are various types of motions, and specific motions are assigned to specific things. From these, various melodies flow forth, which correspond through their own movements to certain divine principles of motion in a fixed order. Since these divinities are everywhere and impart their own special qualities to those who belong to them, they are especially present in those melodies that most closely correspond to them. They introduce themselves into our spirits, which are affected by these sounds, and they take possession of the person, soon filling them entirely with their own essence and power. The cause of this inspiration <term>inspiration: original "afflatio," literally a "breathing upon" or divine blowing into the soul</term> is not so much a human emotion excited by music, but rather the inherent congruence of music to God, for God is naturally present where such harmony exists. 

Things that come to our sight are too much like images <note>original: "imaginaria," referring to things that are mere shadows or representations</note> and they point toward intellectual things instead. Things perceived by the senses lower than hearing are too material. However, things perceived by hearing are intermediate; they correspond to the soul and, when introduced into the spirit along with motion, emotion, and meaning, they powerfully affect the soul on one hand and the body on the other. 

Thus, the whole person, according to the specific properties of the melodies, becomes a vessel <note>original: "susceptaculum," a receiver or container</note> for this or that divinity. Those who are inspired behave differently—some in motion, some in stillness, and in other states—according to the diversity of the divinities by whom they are inspired, and even more so according to the differences in the music. For this emotional reaction to sound ceases at the moment when God begins to act. The soul, while in the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" is the Neoplatonic realm of pure thought and divine forms, the soul's true home before birth.</note>, heard the divine harmony; it remembers this harmony here on earth when it hears melodies that contain a trace of the divine. Upon remembering it, the soul is powerfully moved, provided it is one of those souls that especially contemplated the "Idea of Harmony" itself in its homeland <note>original: "patria," meaning the divine realm from which the soul descended.</note>. 

Having become familiar with God through this kind of affection, the soul is then inspired by a singular presence of God, from which it performs wonders. Therefore, the cause of this inspiration and miracle is not a passion brought on by sounds, nor is it because the soul's nature is composed of harmony, but rather it is due to a likeness to God and God's actual presence. 

Furthermore, it should certainly not be said that inspiration consists of this: that through music and the inspiration itself, certain "superfluous" things encrusted in the soul and body are purged. The right of prophecy <term>prophecy: original "vaticinium," the gift of divining the future or speaking for a deity</term> does not arise from a specific physical temperament. For divine gifts are not breathed into us in varying ways according to our bodily variety. The divine gift is "impassible" <note>original: "impatibile," meaning it cannot be affected or changed by external physical forces</note>, and it is given beyond the power of nature through God’s own direct action. 

Neither water, nor air, nor any other physical element provides prophecy; rather, it is the sacred rites performed involving these things—or more accurately, the purification of the mind together with the purification of the vehicle <note>The "vehicle" (vehiculum) refers to the "astral body" or the subtle spirit that carries the soul between the material and divine worlds.</note> and a focused intention toward God—that receives the divine power, which is everywhere and always most ready. When the inspired mind speaks and acts above and against the habit of nature, the cause of such inspiration is not natural—it is not from our body, nor the quality of a location, nor the celestial alignment at the person's birth—but these things happen solely because of God's presence. Hence, the various types of inspired people do not follow the natural physical variations found within us.

<summary>Iamblichus argues that divine inspiration via music is not a psychological or medical reaction, but a supernatural event where the soul remembers divine harmony and becomes a vessel for God. He rejects the idea that prophecy is caused by physical elements or biological temperaments, insisting it requires spiritual purification.</summary>
<keywords>music, harmony, divine inspiration, prophecy, soul, purification, intelligible world, vehicle of the soul, Iamblichus</keywords>

# IAMBLICHUS

...but different species, both of divine inspiration and of the manner by which we share in the divine presence. Therefore, the fact that some men who are divinely inspired remain calm while others are excited, and some seek out mountains and deserts while others behave differently, does not arise from differences in the natural causes within us—such as our location, or the music <note>Referring back to the discussion of musical harmony on the previous page.</note> they might have recently heard or are currently hearing. Instead, it comes from the various properties of the gods by whom the inspired are governed, and from the various modes of inspiration. **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre was a Neoplatonist philosopher and critic whose "Letter to Anebo" prompted Iamblichus to write this defense of ritual and mystery.</note> brings forward three oracles from among many: one at **Colophon**, where prophecy came by drinking water; another at **Delphi**, where one prophesied while sitting at the mouth of a cave; and a third at **Branchidae**, where they prophesied by drawing up vapor from the water. Each one acts according to the manner of its own nature to produce effects and works. Therefore, the spirits themselves, depending upon the gods, arouse and excite men, and in this very work, they exceed all natural and human movement. This action of theirs is in no way similar to the usual actions known to men.

In **Colophon**, there was a subterranean place in which there was a spring. The priest, therefore, would sacrifice on appointed nights and then taste the water. Finally, he would prophesy there, having become invisible to those present. It might seem to someone that the divine spirit <term>spirit: original "spiritus," here referring to a subtle, breath-like essence or "pneuma" that bridges the soul and body</term> passed through the water into the priest. However, this is not actually the case. For the divine does not pass through the things that participate in it according to distance or division; rather, it encompasses from without and illuminates and fills the water from within with a certain power contributing to prophecy—namely, a <gloss>purifying</gloss> power. Thus, when the priest drinks, it purifies the **luminous spirit** <note>In Neoplatonism, the "luminous spirit" is a subtle "vehicle" (ochema) of the soul that allows it to interact with the physical world and perceive divine light.</note> implanted within us and adapts it to God. Through this purification and adaptation, we are able to receive God. But there exists, moreover, another presence of God beyond the power infused into the water, one that is prior, above, around, and illuminating from within. This presence is absent from no one, provided they can reach it through congruity. Thus, it is present suddenly and uses the prophet as an instrument; meanwhile, the prophet is neither in control of himself nor aware of what he speaks. He does not even know where he is, so that even after giving the response, he hardly recovers himself. Indeed, even before drinking the water, he abstains from food for a day and a night and withdraws himself for certain sacred rites inaccessible to the common people. Therefore, because of this sequestration from human affairs, he renders himself pure and fit for receiving God. From these things, it is gathered that a man is prepared here for God in two ways: one through the purifying water made such by God to purify the spirit; the other through sobriety, solitude, the separation of the mind from the body, and the focusing of the intention toward God. 

The **Sibyl** <note>The Sibyl here refers to the Pythia, the priestess of Apollo at Delphi.</note> in **Delphi** received God in two ways: either through a certain thin and fiery spirit that broke out somewhere from the mouth of a certain cave, or while sitting in the inner sanctuary on a bronze seat having three or four feet <note>A reference to the famous Delphic tripod.</note> and dedicated to God; and in both ways, she exposed herself

->to the divine spirit<-

<summary>Iamblichus explains that prophetic ecstasy is not caused by nature or music alone, but by the specific ways gods inhabit sacred sites like Colophon and Delphi. He describes how ritual purification and sacred elements (water and vapors) prepare the priest's "luminous spirit" to be used as a divine instrument.</summary>

...by the divine spirit, from which she was illuminated by a ray of divine fire. And so, sometimes a great burst of fire flies out all at once from the cave, surrounds her on all sides, and fills her with divine splendor. At other times, while she remains seated upon the seat sacred to the god, through which she is made ready for the god, she is joined to the stable prophecy of the god. In both ways, through these things, the **Sibyl** <note>The Sibyl was a title for various ancient prophetesses, most famously the Pythia at the Oracle of Delphi, who sat upon a tripod over a chasm in the earth.</note> becomes entirely belonging to the god. Thus, the god is suddenly present, yet in the meantime remains distinct—being something other than the fire, the spirit, the seat, and all the physical or natural equipment of that place.

The prophetess at **Branchidae** <note>An ancient Greek sanctuary and oracle of Apollo located near Miletus (modern-day Turkey).</note>, when she either sits upon the axle <note>original: "axe" - likely referring to the tripod or a symbolic chariot seat.</note> or holds in her hand a wand given by some god, or dips her feet or the hem of her garment in the water, or breathes in the vapor from certain waters, she is filled in these ways with divine splendor. Having obtained the god, she prophesies. For by all these means she is made ready for the god, whom she receives from the outside.

However, it is clear that prophecy does not arise from any physical power, nor from the soul’s own nature, nor from the tools of the locations, but from the presence of the god coming from without. This is evident from the fact that the priest himself, before he delivers the oracles, must perform many sacrifices according to the rite, observe **sanctity** <term>sanctimonia: a state of ritual purity and holiness required to approach the divine</term>, wash himself, and abstain entirely from food for three days. He stays in seclusion and then begins, little by little, to be illuminated and to rejoice marvelously. Through these things, it is clear that the god is called from the outside to arrive, and that he does arrive from without.

Even before the priest comes to the place of the water, he is in a way inspired; and while in that place a certain spirit <note>original: "spiritus" - here meaning a physical vapor or breath that acts as a medium for the divine.</note> flies out from the water of the spring, it is certain that the god is something else besides these things—separate from them all, the cause of the place, the spring, and the entire prophecy.

The power which inspires **prophecy** <term>vaticinium: the act of foretelling or the divine message itself</term> in us is absolute and free from places and times. Otherwise, it would not be able to express all places and times at once. For if it were inseparably attached to the nature of places or materials, or if it proceeded according to a movement determined by numbers, it could not foreknow those things which are everywhere and always, nor would it be everywhere and always itself. But if it is absolute from these things—as being superior to those things which occur in time or are contained in a place—then it is present to all waters wherever they may be, and it is present to all things that happen in time simultaneously from all sides. Thus, in one moment, it comprehends the truth of all things because of its essence, which is entirely separate and surpasses all things.

The divine power, the origin of prophecy, is everywhere whole and always whole. This power is not from the body, nor from the soul that is devoted to the body, but from the "absolutes"—that is, from the **angels** <note>In Neoplatonism, "angels" (angelis) are divine messengers or intermediaries that exist between the supreme gods and the human world.</note> and the god who are everywhere, or at least the power itself is wherever there is any angel through whom they are everywhere. This power, being separate from all bodily things, is present to all things. It is not contained by place, or body, or the soul, which is restricted to some particular species. Rather, this prophetic power belongs to the god and is separate from all things; therefore, it is present everywhere at once to those who are able to participate in it. It illuminates from the outside, fills all things, and runs through all the **elements** <term>elementa: the four basic constituents of the physical world (earth, air, fire, water)</term>. It leaves no living creature or nature behind into which it does not impress something of itself, according to that creature's capacity, contributing to the **presage** <term>praesagium: a foreboding or divine sign of the future</term>. Indeed, it is able to fill all things equally because it is equally absolute from all things.

## IAMBLICHUS

Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus who questioned the efficacy and morality of certain ritual practices.</note>, besides the publicly celebrated prophecies, mentions a certain private type: namely, those of people who claim they can attract spirits to prophesy through certain characters <note>original: "characteres" — these refer to magical sigils, symbols, or "seal-letters" believed to have inherent power to compel or summon spirits.</note>, which Iamblichus rejects. This is because they neglect all religion and holiness while trusting only in the characters; thus, they are unable to obtain the actual presence of any god or good spirit. This presence is how true prophecies are usually given, but these people are deceived because, although they use characters agreeable to the gods and focused intention, they only receive a small, obscure, and imaginary apparition from the higher powers. And since they meanwhile neglect holiness, they fall under the power of evil spirits <note>original: "daemonum" — in this context, referring to lower, deceptive entities rather than benevolent divine beings.</note> who lie and deceive, and who pervert and confuse whatever small signs or appearances might have occurred from the gods.

But those who are granted the true presence of the gods receive a prophecy that is true and unchangeable, which cannot be disturbed by evil spirits. For just as darkness cannot withstand the presence of the sun when it arrives, but suddenly flees away without hindering the sun at all, so too when the power of the gods shines from every direction—filling all things with good—every disturbance that usually occurs from evil spirits has no place, but is suddenly destroyed. For when the good spirits are fully present, the evil spirits vanish; they are neither able to move themselves nor to cloud the divine splendor.

He condemns those who neglect all religious contemplation and holiness, trusting only in characters through which they hope they will enclose the very substance of some god so they may prophesy in his presence. Porphyry also used to reject the confidence of such people.

He also relates that, besides these, there are others in whom the imagination <note>original: "phantasia" — the mental faculty that creates and perceives images, which Neoplatonists believed could be influenced by the divine.</note> is sometimes stirred up when they apply certain things, even if in other matters their minds are sound, while they are in a ritual frenzy of the imagination. For example, when they have hidden in the darkness, or drunk certain potions, or used songs <note>original: "catibus" — likely a scribal error for "cantibus," meaning incantations or ritual chants.</note> or certain constructions. Then, while in a frenzy, they imagine hidden and future things—some seeing them in water, others on a wall, others in the open air <note>original: "sub diuo" — literally "under the god," a phrase meaning in the clear, open air.</note> (that is, in the clear air), others in the sun, and others in the stars.

This divine light enters into the imagination specifically; and if we see anything marvelous from the outside, it happens through the sight following the imagination like a servant. The gods move the mind without any medium through their presence alone whenever they find it ready, or they pour a certain light from themselves into the ethereal vehicle of the soul <note>original: "aethereum animæ uehiculum" — the "spirit-body" or "astral body," a subtle intermediate layer between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>, by which images are moved in the imagination as they themselves wish. In both cases, the divinity is never "enclosed." When the aforementioned things suitable for prophecy are applied, the attention of the mind and thought notices what happens, though the divine light does not specifically reach as far as these, namely to the rational

He explains that while lower rituals attract deceptive spirits, the true presence of a god dispels all darkness and falsehood.</summary>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...rational powers, but meanwhile the imagination has been alienated <note>meaning the imagination is "set apart" or "transformed" from its usual human state</note>, because it is incited from above beyond the human custom. Sometimes it holds a person in darkness for the purpose of prophesying, for nothing in those shadows resists the coming light. At other times they are held in the light when they are being prepared, so that there may be a greater likeness to the divine light. This is then received in the light of the sun, or the moon, or a clear night, or in water prepared as a transparent medium <note>original: "per diaphanon" — a term for a clear or translucent material used in scrying</note>, or on a wall prepared with sacred characters <note>original: "characteribus" — mystical symbols or sigils believed to have the power to anchor divine energy</note>. Here, indeed, because of the solidity of the surface, that which is once received from the divine is retained for a longer time.

Furthermore, they bring forward certain things related to the gods that are to be introduced, and they provide the one about to prophesy with potions, and certain compositions and songs or incantations suitable for preparing the receptacle <note>the "receptacle" refers to the human body or soul ready to receive the god</note> and for accommodating the presence and appearance of the gods—specifically, so that their hidden light may be revealed somewhere to the senses, though always according to the will of the gods, whether it be drawn from the ether, the air, the sun, the moon, or some other celestial sphere. Insofar as it pleases the gods, who give freely as the principal authors, they move the imagination; through the imagination, they sometimes move the senses when objects are appropriately placed, and sometimes they move the imagination through the senses. Magical images made from solid matter preserve this power for a longer time. The higher powers give gifts to those who are prepared, not only through nature but through the intellect and the free will of the gods themselves.

The gods give signs of future things in entrails <term>entrails</term> <note>original: "extis" — the internal organs (liver, heart, etc.) of a sacrificial animal, which were inspected by priests called haruspices to predict the future</note>, in birds, and in new portents of the stars. From these, human sagacity conjectures events through the proportion of the signs of their coming: just as from the fall of a bird one might predict the fall of a man, or from a defect of the members in the entrails one predicts a failure, or from a small thing falling, their own downfall. The gods imprint signs of the future in things by the ministry of universal nature and specific natures, or by the obedience of spirits <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "daemonum" — here referring to intermediary spirits who serve the gods and govern the physical elements</note> who serve the gods and rule over the elements, animals, and all similar things, which act easily according to the will of the gods. And if they symbolically declare the will of the distinguished god and future events, as Heraclitus says <note>Heraclitus was a Greek philosopher who famously stated that the divine "neither speaks nor hides, but gives a sign"</note>, they meanwhile represent the manner of the divine workmanship. For just as they make things through stable images and pre-signify events, so too do they act through new portents and signs of any kind; and meanwhile, they sharpen our sagacity from that same cause and occasion.

The internal organs in these portents are changed against nature within the animals by their own soul, and by the spirit presiding over them, and by the motion of the air and the motion of the heavens—contrary to nature and according to the will of the gods to warn men. That this happens by divine power is clear, because often certain principal members necessary for life are not found in the animals. These are suddenly taken away by a miracle, though it is certain they could not have been missing just moments before. In the catching of auguries <term>auguries</term> <note>original: "auguriis" — the practice of interpreting the will of the gods by observing the flight or behavior of birds</note>, the birds are miraculously moved by their own soul, by the presiding spirit, and by the motion of the air and heaven. From that heaven, power descends through all the air, shaping and moving it toward the gods...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's defense of divination. It transitions from discussing how the soul is prepared for prophecy to explaining the objective mechanisms by which gods produce signs in the physical world, such as the movements of birds and celestial phenomena.</meta>

<margin>ci</margin>

# IAMBLICHUS

...the opinion of those who believe signs are produced for their own sake. I speak of a judgment pre-determined and decreed from the beginning; thus birds often cast themselves down, or dash themselves against objects, or kill themselves in other ways while they contribute to signifying. They do not do this voluntarily, but are drawn by divine power. Certain flames, made like stars by divine power, are sometimes created very easily in the air as signs of future events at the nod of the celestial gods. The upper air is ignited there, which is very easy to lead and shape—especially by the gods—into fire. Meanwhile, certain influences of the celestial bodies descend into this air, leading to the creation and movement of stars similar to celestial lights in power and motion. 

The **World Animal** <note>original: "Mundanum animal" — the Neoplatonic concept of the universe as a single, living organism with interconnected parts</note> is so united within itself that its members feel together <term>sympathy|resonance</term> <note>original: "compassio" — the philosophical idea that one part of the universe reacts to another because they share the same life-force</note>; even parts that seem remote from one another are moved together as if they were close, just like members of the same animal. And this union and sympathy allows the gods to show signs to humans, first through the heavens, and then through the air. The gods do not do this immediately, but through intermediate instruments: namely <term>daemons|spirits</term> <note>original: "dæmones" — in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but mediating spirits between gods and mortals</note>, souls, natures, and all things depending on them. They begin according to one principle, and from there they spread the movement descending from them wherever they wish. Therefore, without being tied to or coordinated with things that are born and die, the gods rule each of these things. Just as in craftsmanship and providence, their intellect is not turned toward our affairs, but while it remains within itself, it turns all signs and prophecy toward itself, and perceives them as proceeding from itself.

All prophets confess that they obtain prophecy through gods or daemons, because none can see the future except those who are the causes and masters of future things, through whom others may see. **Porphyry** <note>A philosopher who wrote a famous "Letter to Anebo" questioning the logic of religious rituals</note> wonders why the gods would serve humans so much that prophets might even prophesy by means of flour <note>original: "per farinam" — a reference to aleuromancy, or divination using flour</note>. **Iamblichus** responds that the gods do not provide this out of obedience, but from an excess of power and goodness. And since they contain all causes within themselves, while remaining in themselves without turning toward lower things, they bestow gifts and signs according to the level of the recipient's preparation—just as the sun gives light to transparent things and to the eyes, and gives heat as well. Because we see that humans care for subjects by turning toward their work and being distracted by different tasks, and are drawn away from themselves and labor, we suspect that the gods provide in a similar way. On the contrary, insofar as they turn toward themselves and their one form—which is the cause of lower things—they act, move, and rule all things. They are not distracted by various things, but vibrate all things from one principle and a simple nod, with a certain succession of events depending on it; they do not bend themselves toward the subjects, but through their own state, they most fully render all things like themselves. God supplies different modes of prophecy; he is not distracted himself, but suggests them all with an indivisible nod and a simple form. He suggests different ones at different times, yet he is not varied through time, but inspires all things with the same eternal strike of mind and will, even though these are unfolded at different times.

<summary>Iamblichus explains that divination works through the "sympathy" of the universe as a living organism and argues that gods provide signs through an overflow of their power, not out of servitude to humanity.</summary>
<keywords>Iamblichus, Porphyry, divination, World Animal, cosmic sympathy, daemons, providence, signs, celestial influence</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on how the gods communicate through physical signs and begins a new section on the necessity of divine presence in religious rituals. # ON THE MYSTERIES

...[the divine] is not confined or distracted by these omens, but embracing all signs in its single form, it expresses them from itself while remaining consistent within itself, transmitting everything by a single act of will. Such is the abundance of **providence** <note>original: "prouidentiæ" — the divine care and foresight of the gods for the world</note> in showing us signs that it provides indications of the future even in pebbles, rods, wood, stones, grain, and flour. In these, it wonderfully seems to grant a soul to the inanimate, motion to the motionless, and a certain intelligence to those lacking reason, as if these objects seem to know the future events they portend to us. 

And just as God often speaks wisdom through fools—declaring that it is not the man speaking there, but God—so too does He portend future events through the most common things. He remains far above these objects, yet through all of them He instructs our intellect. God reveals certain matters of higher knowledge through the lowest things that lack knowledge themselves; in this, He testifies that He far transcends nature. While He offers diverse signs, He is not constrained by them, nor is He distracted by them. Rather, standing in His one and indivisible form, He encompasses all signs there; from that state, by a single and simple nod, He unfolds all things and provides us with evidence of the past, present, and future everywhere.

->No work of any efficacy occurs in sacred rites except through the power and indeed the presence of some divinity.<-

In religion, no work of any miraculous efficacy can occur unless one of the higher beings is present as an observer and fulfiller of the work. The gods lead the perfect works, the angels lead the middle ones, and the <term>daemons|spirits</term> <note>original: "dæmones" — in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil, who bridge the gap between gods and humanity</note> lead the third. Human nature cannot even sustain a rational thought or a prayer concerning the gods without the gods, much less be capable of performing divine works without them. 

For human nature is so weak and dull that it has no remedy for its own <term>insignificance|nothingness</term> <note>original: "nullitatis" — the state of being nothing or having no power on one's own</note> except for a certain portion of divine light descending from above, without which we can do nothing divine. Just as those are deceived who trust they can create a soul from inanimate things or a mind from the mindless, so too are those who believe they can create divine things from non-divine ones. They wrongly think they can perform the proper works of the gods without the gods—such as prophecies, miracles, and similar acts like divine apparitions and <term>expiations|purifications</term> <note>original: "expiationes" — rituals intended to cleanse a person or community of spiritual impurity or "miasma"</note>.

->The divinities, when invoked, are present with us, not by compulsion but of their own will.<-

It is admitted that the works of religious efficacy are perfected by the presence of gods, angels, and daemons. **Porphyry** <note>A Phoenician Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who questioned many of the ritual practices defended here by Iamblichus</note> indeed suspects that the divinities...

<sig>c ii</sig>

<summary>Iamblichus explains that the gods use even the lowliest inanimate objects to signal the future and argues that no religious ritual has power without the voluntary presence and aid of divine beings.</summary>

# IAMBLICHUS.

...to be drawn to these things by a certain necessity of invocation. Iamblichus denies that any necessity is imposed either by man or by the world upon the deities, who, since they are immaterial, do not accept an order coming from elsewhere. Likewise, invocation and sacred ritual bring the priests toward the deities through a certain assimilation and familiarity, rather than through violence inflicted upon the priests, much less upon the deities themselves. God and the entire chorus of deities joined to God are above every necessity coming from the outside.

Prophecy <term>vaticinium: the art of foretelling the future through divine inspiration</term> is perfected while the priest performs sacred rites; at that time, no "passion" <note>original: "passio" — here meaning an external state of being acted upon or overwhelmed by emotion</note> falls upon the priest or the diviner when they are divinely inspired. Much less does it fall upon the deities, who do not enter into souls unless they are empty of passion. Nor should it be said that the prophetic mind is a middle or effective instrument of divine matters, nor that the priest who invokes is the effective cause of divine works. On the contrary, God is all things and can do all things. He fills all things with Himself, while human nature has no efficacy in these matters. For compared to divinity, human effort is a mere plaything <note>original: "ludus" — implying that human rituals are like children's games compared to the vast power of the gods</note>. We laugh at those who say that God happens to be present to some people because of the power of a celestial configuration in their birth-chart <note>original: "genesi" — referring to an astrological horoscope or the alignment of stars at birth</note>. For it is not fitting for uncreated and universal causes to be enslaved to anyone through their birth, or its cycle, or through external causes. 

Some people, because they were unwilling to honor God with their cares and did not perceive any mode of providence and handiwork other than that which arises from human anxiety, denied that the gods act or provide. Similarly, those who do not see the excellent way in which gods are present—without labor and without changing themselves—would deny that gods take part in prophecies and miracles. The manner in which all these things occur is proper to the gods and is known only to them. Porphyry <note>A scholar and rival philosopher to Iamblichus who sought rational or psychological explanations for spiritual phenomena</note> says that divine works, such as prophecies and miracles, are sometimes certain "passions" of the soul excited by small sparks, and that the soul can imagine, speak, and do these things by its own power. Iamblichus says that a divine work happens neither by chance (since it is ordered) nor by man (who is far inferior). For it is necessary that a divine work be performed by divinity. Therefore, all works similar to divinity do not sprout from human nature, but from divine nature.

->The works of miracles and prophecy are not performed by any power<-
->of the stars, the body, or the soul, but by the pure and free power of God.<-

The human soul is both contained within a single species and is too much overshadowed by a decaying body. Therefore, it has no effective power for a divine work. If ever we seem [to be able to do] such a thing in some way...

# ON THE MYSTERIES

<margin>c iii</margin>

...to be able to do. We only perform these things through divine illumination flowing down from above, through which we seem to be participants in divine action. If divine works were performed by the soul by the soul's own nature and its own power, the soul would be the master of power and prudence, or indeed every soul would perform such things. But now, in truth, the soul does not perform all these things, and even the soul that appears perfect is still imperfect compared to divine matters. Therefore, it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works. Otherwise, religion would not be necessary for us to achieve these things; rather, we would be masters of divine works through our own practice without God, if these things were performed by the power of the soul itself. 

Finally, if the soul performed divine things by its own power, either every soul would do so, or at least those which possessed the soul's own specific power and perfection: namely, knowledge, art, prudence, and the moral virtues acquired through prudence. But now, it is not such people who perform these works, but rather those who are "inspired" <term>concitati: literally "stirred up," referring to those in a state of religious ecstasy</term> and "withdrawn" <term>abstracti: those whose minds are pulled away from physical senses toward the divine</term>. 

**Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who questioned many traditional religious practices</note> had proposed three theories concerning divine works: 
1. That the soul is the instrumental cause <note>An "instrumental cause" is like a tool used by a craftsman; it does the work, but is not the source of the idea</note> of these acts.
2. That the soul is sometimes the principal cause. 
3. That the soul can be an equal co-cause, so that from the soul and the divine spirit combined, a third kind of substance or existence is created. 

**Iamblichus** <note>The presumed author of this text, responding to Porphyry's doubts</note> says that whenever one thing is made from several, those several things must be both related and changeable, so that because they are in flux, they can be mixed together into a single "fifth" thing—just as the four elements mix <note>The four elements of earth, air, fire, and water were thought to combine to form all physical matter</note>. He admits that many souls might merge into one whole—perhaps into the vegetative, sensory, and motive parts within us—and be reduced to the act of the intellect, or perhaps a vital harmony results from all of them in the body, or perhaps souls in their heavenly home <note>original: "in patria" — the spiritual homeland of the soul</note> conspire into a single Idea of all souls. 

However, divinity, like an archetype far removed from everything else, does not merge into a unity with others. Regarding the third theory: it is impossible, especially since the soul has already fallen from its original state, and because divinity is so vastly different that it cannot fall into a mixture. And since divinity is immutable, it is not changed into something else that is common to both. 

It was said earlier that divine "forms" <note>original: "species" — the spiritual essences or images of divine things</note> are awakened in the soul by tiny sparks. Granted; but these would not be translated into purely divine forms if they were merely physical and natural. Finally, where it is said that the soul joins with divinity into a third new thing, the soul is being made equal to God. It would imply that God is changed there and receives something from the soul, just as the soul is changed and receives something from God. This is absurd, especially because it would admit that the gods, like mere elements, would merge in their effects into a single form created in time, and that eternal beings would be contained within a temporary thing. This happens whenever it is said that from the soul and God (or from the gods) one single temporal thing is produced. We must ask whether something new results beyond the things that came together, or not. If nothing results...

<summary>This page argues that divine miracles are caused by God alone, not the human soul. Iamblichus refutes Porphyry’s idea that the soul could be a "co-cause" or "instrument" of divinity, asserting that the eternal, immutable divine cannot mix with the changing, fallen nature of the human soul.</summary>

<keywords>theurgy, Porphyry, Iamblichus, divine illumination, soul, divinity, instrumental cause, principal cause, divine forms, elements, immutability</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical debate between Porphyry and Iamblichus regarding the nature of spiritual entities. # IAMBLICHUS :

<meta>catchword: Concerning so...</meta>

...then a true union will not occur, nor will there be a true unity, just as in a craft that depends solely on the skill. If eternal things fall from their state to become something temporal, they would result in something else. Unless they are changed, a third thing does not result, but it is entirely absurd to claim that something which comes to be through a temporal birth <note>original: "generatione," referring to the process of coming into existence</note> is itself eternal. Nor is it fitting to claim it is temporal, lest eternal things serve the temporal. Nor is it fitting to claim this thing can be dissolved, even if made from eternal things. And yet, through a new birth, it seems it would be dissolvable. That opinion, therefore, is absurd.

**Porphyry** says that the soul sometimes generates a demonic power and essence which imagines future events through such motions. I say "generates" in the sense that it brings together certain materials that possess such powers within themselves, especially materials taken from living animals.

**Iamblichus** denies that demons are born or perish. For he denies that demons—which are superior to bodies and the soul—are generated by the soul from bodily powers. He also denies that the actions of an individual soul, enclosed in a body, can result in essences <note>the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note> that exist independently outside the soul. He denies that the powers of bodies, which are entirely tied to matter, can be released from them to generate demons. Furthermore, he asks: what power is it that releases material forces from matter and then fuses them into one to generate a demon? In that case, this power itself would seem to be demonic, and thus the demon would already exist even before it is supposedly "generated."

A soul, especially one that speaks for the divine <note>original: "uaticinio," relating to prophecy or divine oracles</note>, cannot be generated from things lacking a soul or prophecy. A superior thing cannot be procreated from an inferior thing. No essence or substance can be established from the motions of the soul and bodily powers, which are neither substances nor essences. Likewise, nothing that is sown through birth has any greater quality than what is handed down to it by its principal generating cause. Therefore, since neither the body nor the soul possesses prophecy of itself, the soul cannot procreate a prophetic demon from its own motions or from bodies.

Perhaps someone will say that demons are not generated by us, but that they preside over living things in an orderly way; and so, when materials from animals entrusted to this demon are applied at the right time, this demon is drawn here to such things as if through "compassion" <term>compatientem: from the Greek "sympatheia," the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and react to one another's movements</term>. 

**Iamblichus** says that demons who are "compassionate" <note>original: "compatiantur"; here meaning "affected by" or "sharing the feelings of" the material world</note> to such an extent cannot prophesy the truth. For true prophecy does not belong to a nature that is "passible" <term>passibilis: capable of feeling, suffering, or being changed by external forces</term> or enclosed by a specific body, place, or time. Instead, it must be set free from all these things, so that it may

->foresee things done in any place or time equally and<-
->simply.<-

c iiii

### On divine and human dreams.

<margin>Porphyry</margin> Porphyry says that the foretellings of dreams are partly from ourselves and partly from an external source. Iamblichus, however, says they arrive solely from the outside. He argues that we often study and perform various actions to "hunt" for such a foretelling, yet it is not granted; conversely, it is often given to those who are not seeking it at all. If the effect of a dream arose from our own nature and human will, it would occur when we planned for it. Instead, it is sent by the gods according to their own judgment—specifically, when and how they wish to show the future through a certain kindness. The Orphic hymn <note>A collection of ancient Greek hymns attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus, often used in Neoplatonic ritual and philosophy</note> declares the same thing.

Porphyry says that the cause of prophecy <note>original: "vaticinii," referring to the act of foretelling the future</note> is a certain "passion" <note>original: "passionem," here meaning a state of being acted upon or an "affection" of the soul, rather than just an emotion</note> of the mind. Iamblichus denies this, saying that a passion is, by its very nature, unstable, disordered, and disturbed. True prophecy, however, must be entirely stable and orderly. Therefore, it cannot reside in a "passion." Likewise, when the soul is prudent and constant, acting according to its more excellent powers—namely the intellectual and rational ones—it does not foresee the future. How, then, would it achieve this foresight when it is suffering under disordered and disturbed motions? Furthermore, passion has no inherent quality for the contemplation of beings and truth, but instead brings an impediment.

In addition, if the things of the world were themselves constituted by "passions," then a passion in the soul might reach them through a certain similarity. But since they are actually constituted and governed by formal reasons <note>original: "rationibus," referring to the underlying logical or divine principles of things</note> and forms <note>original: "speciebus," the Platonic Ideas or archetypes</note>, surely this foreknowledge must be something else entirely, alien to all passions. Again, passion only senses present things. Since prophecy also reaches into the future, it does not deal in passion.

Porphyry says that prophecy is a certain passion arising in the imagination <term>phantasia: the faculty of the soul that forms and stores mental images</term>, emerging either from our own thoughts, or by the instinct of the bodily nature within us, or falling upon us in a similar way to how those in a "frenetic" <note>meaning a state of delirium or temporary madness</note> state happen to prophesy. To support this, he points to several signs: first, that in the state of prophecy, the imagination acts vehemently while the senses are meanwhile occupied and restrained. Second, that "suffumigations" <note>the burning of incense or herbs to produce vapors</note> are used by the one about to divine, clearly to affect the imagination. Third, that invocations are used to incite that same affection. Finally, he notes that not everyone, but only the young and the more simple-minded, are suitable for this.

Iamblichus responds that the "occupation" or closing off of the senses is actually a sign that no *human* image <note>original: "phantasma"</note> is then present. Vapors are used to create a "congruity" or harmony with God, not to affect the soul of the observer. Invocations do not excite either thoughts or bodily passions in us; for these remain unknown to us and are known only to the God who is being called upon. As for the "simple" people, they are merely more exposed to the divine spirit coming from the outside. Regarding what Porphyry says—that prophecy is a passion of the imagination such as often happens to the melancholic <note>In ancient medicine, those with an excess of "black bile," believed to be prone to both depression and flashes of inspiration</note> and the foolish who often speak of the future—he [Porphyry] misuses...

<summary>This page outlines a disagreement on the origin of prophecy: Porphyry argues it is a psychological state (passion) of the imagination, while Iamblichus insists it is a stable, external gift from the gods that transcends human emotion.</summary>

-> IAMBLICHUS <-

C 3

...with the divine gift of prophecy <note>original: "vaticinii munere," referring to the gift of prophetic insight</note>, while he compares the alienation <note>In this context, alienation (original: "alienatio") refers to "ecstasy" or the state of the soul being outside its normal human consciousness. It is not social isolation, but a "standing apart" from the physical self.</note> caused divinely for a better purpose to the alienation caused by diseases, drunkenness, or madness occurring for the worse. Alienation of the soul arising from our own passions <note>original: "passionibus," meaning states of being acted upon by external or internal emotions</note>, which happens below the human state, casts the soul down; but that which is made by God lifts the human being above the human level and joins them to God. The former makes the soul unstable and drowns it entirely in matter, whereas the latter makes it constant and master of order, and releases it from matter.

In no way should it be said that divine inspiration has anything in common with the alienation caused by the humors <note>original: "humoribus," referring to the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which ancient medicine believed controlled health and temperament.</note>, drunkenness, or madness. For these are distant from God beyond what can be thought. Therefore, such insanity is just as far removed from divine inspiration; they have nothing similar or in common. Alienation arising from bodily causes is a depravity of the mind resulting from weakness. But that which is done divinely is the salvation of the soul resulting from a fullness of power. In the former, while the soul undertakes its own operations, it produces them in a perverted and turbulent manner. In the latter, however, while it is free from its own life and intellect, it exposes itself to be used by a power superior to itself.

Finally, just as divine things are distant from the lowest natural things, so too are their actions and effects distant from natural effects. Thus, the alienation induced divinely has nothing in common with that which occurs by human means. Therefore, when you think of the former, separate from it entirely all the defects and accidents of the latter. Furthermore, when you meditate on the sacred sobriety and vigilance received divinely, do not compare it with human sobriety. And in both cases, remove from the mind whatever is in any way similar to those imaginations which humors and similar causes stir up, keeping them separate from divinely applied imaginations.

Likewise, do not think that the ambiguous state of a man—the middle ground between a sober mind and an alienated one—is similar to the state of a sacred mind looking at God with a single gaze; nor should you believe that the most certain gazes of divine things are similar to imaginations stirred up by the art of sorcery <note>original: "arte venefica," literally "poisonous art," referring to deceptive magic or witchcraft.</note>. For the things we imagine when fascinated have no truth of action or essence beyond the mere images. For the end of such magic is not to simply do something, but to extend images only to the point of appearing. 

It must not be thought that the divine prophet hits upon the truth by chance, as the insane sometimes do, nor by some natural passion, just as animals often react to certain forces of the world that are beginning to bring about something in the future—acting in the air, in a sense, before they do on the earth. And so by being affected in this way, animals sometimes foresee future earthquakes and storms, especially those animals that are either easily affected or perceive things keenly. For foreknowledge coming either by chance or by such a natural reaction is rare, disordered, not continuous, and entirely obscure. But divine prophecy [observes] the order of the universe in a continuous...

<summary>Iamblichus distinguishes divine "ecstasy" or prophecy from medical madness and animal instinct, arguing that true divine inspiration is an orderly, superior state of being joined to God rather than a bodily sickness or a random accident.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical distinction between divine inspiration and human mental states, specifically focusing on how true prophecy differs from natural intuition or "hunches."</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

<meta>catchword: auditis</meta>

-> ...and beholds it with a firm and connected reason. <-

If some innate faculty for perceiving the future exists within us, it is not, for that reason, true prophecy. For such a faculty is not always truthful, but only occasionally; nor does it apply to all things, but only to some. True prophecy, however, is truthful both always and in all things. Likewise, a foreknowledge produced by skill <note>original: "prenotio arte facta," referring to technical divination like reading entrails or bird flight</note> hunts for the future from signs that are not entirely reliable, because they do not always have the outcome joined to them. But that which is performed by divine providence beholds the effects directly from their causes with a firm and present gaze. In a completely continuous way, it connects all things—even those that are changeable, temporary, and distant from one another—anticipating future events as if they were already present. 

Someone might say that the future can be foretold by combining four gifts: namely, from a person's specific nature, from a skill applied to that nature, from the common sympathy <note>original: "compassione," referring to the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected like a single living organism</note> of all things among themselves as parts of the same living being, and from the physical arrangement of bodies, through which some things provide signs to others. 

But in truth, even when these factors coincide and signs are clearly perceived, such a perception only has something similar to prophecy. While the universe contains "footprints" of prophecy everywhere, they are not clear everywhere. Just as the image of the Good itself manifests God in all things, so there is some trace of prophecy in all things. 

Yet, the one divine and unmixed kind of <term>prophecy<gloss>vaticinium</gloss></term> must not be defined by these mere likenesses sent down into the world of becoming <note>original: "generationem," the physical realm of birth, change, and decay</note>, and much less should it be defined by the imaginings of those who are delirious. For all these things are deceptive. **Prophecy** itself must be defined by a single principle and a single order, and by a single divine form and a single intelligible and immutable truth. On the other hand, every changeable perception must be separated from it as something indefinite, which in no way fits the gods and divine things. 

When we perform a task that is natural to us, the seeds and preparations for it are certainly granted to us from the beginning by nature itself, which is the cause of such work. However, no such preparations or seeds are given by nature—whether universal nature or human nature—for that prophecy which is above nature and human custom. For nature lacks intellect. Nature is not the primary author of what happens, especially insofar as nature exists within us. But prophecy is more than intellectual; it reaches the very causes of events and, in a single and sudden gaze, embraces the order of the entire universe. A work of this kind belongs properly to God, who performs this within us while we are then vacant <note>original: "vacantibus," meaning a state where the human mind is quiet or still to allow divine action</note> from our own actions. 

If any foreboding <note>original: "Præsagiũ," a lesser form of hunch or natural intuition</note> happens to us by natural instinct or is produced by a skill, it can certainly have a preparation and aptitude in our nature. But this kind of foreboding is very narrow and obscure, and it merely looks up toward true prophecy. Divine prophecy, however, is most ample, certain, and stable; it holds the highest rank everywhere. Therefore, it could not have been implanted in us by nature. 

<margin>Porphyrius</margin>

<meta>This page transitions from the general nature of prophecy to a specific debate between Porphyry and Iamblichus regarding the use of material objects (herbs, stones, and "idols") in divine communication.</meta>

## IAMBLICHUS

He <note>Referring to Porphyry, Iamblichus's predecessor and intellectual rival</note> conjectured that a certain disposition of our nature, whether physical or mental, contributes primarily to prophecy. This was based on the observation that those who summon prophecy into a human being often carried certain little stones and herbs, tied sacred knots, and then untied what had been bound. They also changed the circumstances of those who received such things from them, turning bad situations into better ones. But **Iamblichus** turns these observations and effects back into a different argument: that the inspiration of prophecy comes from the outside and from above. For when things consistent with certain divinities are employed, they adapt us to receive their inspiration.

<term>Porphyry</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was often skeptical of the more "magical" elements of religion</note> says that we should not despise the art which, using certain vapors over a fire under the favorable influence of the stars, creates "idols" of the gods that immediately appear in the air. These are somewhat similar to the gods and possess a similar kind of efficacy. <term>Iamblichus</term> replies that these idols are held in low regard by the priests who have seen the true forms of the gods. No excellent good can be found in something that springs forth from matter and the forms within it, or from the powers of such forms combined with human art. For that which is made by a human is inferior to the human, and that which is made as an "idol" is a kind of shadow—appearing rather than truly existing—and vanishing as soon as it is made. It is not produced by a master craft which creates true essences, but rather by an imitative art that merely renders images of essences.

Certainly, the <term>God who is the maker of the world</term> <note>original: "deus mundi opifex," often called the Demiurge</note> does not create all things through celestial motions, nor through particular matter, nor through divided powers. Instead, he produces worlds through his intellect, his will, and through immaterial forms, as well as through an eternal soul that is both above the world and within it. The maker of these "idols," however, is said to produce them through the stars, yet not in the way it might seem. For while there are innumerable powers in the celestial gods, the lowest of all is their natural power. Within this natural power of the celestial gods are the **reasons**, specifically the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes seminales," the generative principles or "seeds" that determine how physical things grow and take shape</note> (which generate forms) and certain other immobile principles that precede the seminal ones—namely, the coordinators of forms. 

Therefore, the authority of both types of principles precedes all generation. After them, in the celestial bodies, there are qualities, powers, motions, and the "effluxes" or "outflows" emanating from them, which dominate the entire orderly arrangement of worldly things according to these principles. The lowest power of the celestials leads the generation of earthly things. Many arts, such as medicine, gymnastics, and agriculture—which clearly cooperate with the operation of nature in their work—use these qualities and powers transmitted to lower things through celestial outflows. Even the <term>idol-maker</term> <note>original: "idoloficus," one who creates artificial divine manifestations or magical images</note> himself draws some generative portion from these celestial outflows, however small and weak it may be. For he does not utilize the actual motions or powers of the heavens themselves...

<summary>This page presents Iamblichus's rebuttal to Porphyry regarding theurgy, arguing that true divine inspiration comes from above, whereas human-made "idols" or magical images are mere shadows of reality. It explains the hierarchy of divine creation, from the Demiurge's intellect down to the "seminal reasons" that govern the physical world.</summary>

-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...by the very powers inherent in them, or by powers naturally established around celestial motions; nor can it <note>Referring to this lower form of magic</note> reach them. Instead, it is occupied with certain powers which have flowed down from the nature of those celestial bodies to the very end, falling to the lowest place in the world. He <note>The magician or "idol-maker"</note> certainly employs a specific art, but it is neither pious nor divine. Indeed, these lowest powers of the heavens, working together upon a specific piece of matter, are able to transmute, transfigure, and transform it in various ways. Furthermore, they even receive a transposition from one to another of those powers which reside in specific things.

When someone fashions idols <note>original: "Idola"; here meaning magical constructs or temporary images rather than permanent statues</note> of this kind from many materials and under celestial influences, then the variety of celestial actions on one hand, and the gathered material powers on the other, does indeed produce something. But this action falls far short not only of divine craftsmanship <note>original: "opificio diuino"</note>, but even of natural production. For Nature carries out its own work with a single, steady course and simple action.

Therefore, this making of idols is an artificial mixture concerning the final emanation <note>original: "defluxum"</note> of the celestials, and concerning those things which are moved and recede from celestial nature at the very last. Since man is a better being, and created from better things, he ought not to devote himself to making idols. These things are not truly alive, but are merely inflated with a certain outward show of life. Nor are they held together by an internal and true harmony, but by an external and feigned one, destined to last only a short time. Nor do they possess anything true or legitimate, since they are concocted solely by human art. In fact, only that which is simple and uniform in action or composition prevails within them. For this reason, they are greatly deficient, because they are heaped together from qualities that are far different and contrary, and they do not possess any perfected power.

Since a multitude of such emanations is caught from many sources and mixed into something external, utterly meager, and weak, these idols have no stability; indeed, they vanish more quickly than the images that appear in mirrors. For when a <term>fumigation</term> <note>The ritual burning of incense or herbs to create smoke</note> is applied with exhaling vapors, they are immediately formed; but when the smoke and vapor spread through the entire air, they suddenly dissolve.

The making of idols for such wonders is altogether unworthy of a seeker of truth. For he who schemes these things—whether he delights in them while recognizing their utility (and thus becomes like them), or whether he worships them as gods—is guilty of an unspeakable sin in deed and word. No divine light shines into a soul occupied with the dark phantasms of idols. <term>Porphyry</term> says that the makers of idols observe the course of the celestial bodies in their construction, stating at which point especially the celestial bodies run...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that creating magical "idols" via astrology and vapors is a low, unstable art that captures only the weakest "leavings" of divine power. He warns that such practices are unworthy of the soul and lack the stability of true divine work.</summary>

<keywords>Iamblichus, Porphyry, idol-making, emanations, theurgy, fumigation, celestial influence, phantasms</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section where Iamblichus critiques the "manufacture of idols." He argues that artificial magical images made of earthly materials are mere shadows or "phantasms" and lack the true substance of the divine or even the demonic.</meta>

### IAMBLICHUS

...you, and by the concurrence of what things true or false prophecies will come forth. Likewise, regarding what occurs there: whether they are significant, or effective, or on the contrary, void of significance and efficacy. Although men construct **idols** <note>original: "idola"; here referring to artificial magical images or apparitions rather than holy statues</note> from selected materials through the observation of the stars, these things nevertheless possess nothing divine within them. For the materials moved here from the heavens are the very last in the process of generation, and they are subject to the final flows <note>original: "defluxus"; the weakened remnants of celestial energy as they reach the earth</note> from heaven. For such **phantoms** <note>original: "phantasmata"</note> are so easily changed that at the slightest nod they are either inert or, on the contrary, prophetic, significant, or effective. Certainly, such easy passivity and rapid mutability declare that they have nothing of divine power. 

There are no powers in these materials that serve as the "elements" of spirits <term>demons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "demons" (daemones) are intermediary spirits between gods and men, not necessarily evil beings</note>, nor can these spirits be generated from particular bodies; rather, it is by the spirits that these bodies are generated and preserved. Nor can man, by his own machinations, create the forms of the spirits themselves; on the contrary, we have been formed with a fertile body by the spirits. It must not be thought that some multitude or composition flows together from the union of elements that has a power proper to spirits in itself. For the spirit itself—simple, uniform, and subsisting in itself—gathers diverse elements into one, generates composites from them, and grants whatever permanence exists within them. 

Nor is it fitting to call these idols "demons." For the author of idols is one thing, and the great spirit—the leader of spirits—is another; and the very substance of spirits is different from the phantoms of idols. And you yourself, Porphyry, admit that neither a god nor any spirit is "drawn down" <note>An ancient magical concept where a deity was forced to descend into an object</note> from above. Therefore, this manufacture of idols, being devoid of both god and spirit, brings about neither prophecy nor any sacred work.

->Mysteries of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian sages</note> concerning the priesthood, God, and good and evil spirits.<-

<margin>P</margin>
Porphyry records the opinion of those who say that all prophecies are infused into us by **evil spirits**. Their nature is said to be deceitful, taking every form, and versatile; they simulate gods, sublime spirits, and the souls of the deceased, and by meeting us with this fallacy, they provide omens. Even if Porphyry does not approve of this opinion, he nonetheless mentions it to the Egyptian <note>Referring to Anebo, the Egyptian priest to whom Porphyry wrote his questioning letter</note> for consultation. Iamblichus also condemns this practice of mentioning profane things during sacred matters; and he immediately recounts the mysteries which the Egyptian heard from the prophets of the **Chaldeans** and such things. The true gods give good things to the good...
