## ON THE MYSTERIES

...souls <note>The OCR "bōis" likely refers to "nobis" (us) or "animis" (souls) in this context</note> being purified through sacrifices, with whom they [the gods] are present, and by their communion they drive far away from them all wickedness and passion. By their own splendor, they also ward off those dark spirits. For evil spirits, when the light of the gods enters, flee just as shadows flee before the sun; nor can they further disturb the pious sacrificer, who is liberated from all wickedness, perversity, and passion. 

However, those who are destructive and who sometimes insolently invade the holy rites against the proper order and rituals—these, surely, because of the weakness of their action and their lack of power, are unable to reach the gods. But because of certain defilements, they are both driven away from the gods and become suited to evil <term>demons</term> <note>In this Platonic context, demons are intermediary spirits. "Evil" demons are those that lead the soul toward matter and away from the divine</note>, by whose most foul breath they are completely filled. From this, they emerge as most wicked, namely as profane, dissolute, and equally unjust, possessing a desire unlike that of the gods and in all things most similar to the wicked demons with whom they are constantly involved. 

These men, therefore, being full of passions and wickedness, draw evil spirits to themselves through their very kinship. Having soon been occupied by these spirits, they are then further incited toward every kind of iniquity, where one helps and strengthens the other in turn toward this very end—just as a circle joins the beginning to the end, producing an equal cycle. 

Thus far the **Chaldeans** <note>original: "caldei"; referring to the ancient Babylonian priest-sages whose "Oracles" Iamblichus considered divinely inspired</note>. When the profane perform holy rites against the proper ritual, the outcome is frustrated; for in place of the gods, others [demons] are celebrated, and in place of good spirits, evil ones are introduced. Their errors, therefore, ought not to be mentioned when discussing legitimate sacrifices, nor should what happens to them be considered a law. 

Just as sacrilege is the opposite of divine worship, so too are those occupied by evil demons—the authors of intemperance and deception—the opposite of legitimate priests. From these priests, every unjust spirit, wickedness, and passion is far removed; rather, the presence of good deities is at hand, and from above they are filled with truth by the **divine fire** <note>original: "ignis divinus"; a central concept in theurgy representing the pure, purifying energy of the highest gods</note>. To these men, evil spirits bring no hindrance to the goods of the soul; nor is the smoke of pride or soft flattery suggested from that source, nor are they deceived by any fumigation, nor disturbed by any force. 

On the contrary, all these evils are then dispersed and vanish instantly by the presence of a good deity, as if struck by a lightning bolt. For such men, there comes forth a truthful **prophecy** <note>original: "vaticinium"</note>, with which no other thing can be compared in any part, and which must be studied properly with that holiness we have described. For by this method alone is unshakable truth acquired in prophesying and absolute virtue within the soul. By these two things, surely, the priest ascends to the **intelligible fire** <note>original: "ignem intelligibilem"; the highest realm of divine intellect</note>, which ought to be the goal proposed for every prophecy and sacrifice. 

You have thought it necessary, O **Porphyry** <note>The student/colleague to whom Iamblichus is responding</note>, to mention far too rashly the opinion of those who [believe]...

<summary>Iamblichus explains that proper sacrifice purifies the soul and drives away evil spirits through divine light, while "profane" practitioners who ignore ritual order attract wicked demons. He concludes that true theurgy leads the priest to the "intelligible fire" of divine truth.</summary>

# IAMBLICHVS.

...lest they think that prophecy is granted by an evil <term>demon</term> <note>In this Neoplatonic context, a demon is an intermediary spirit between gods and humans, not necessarily "demonic" in the modern sense</note>. For these spirits, having dwelled in darkness from the beginning and always, can neither discern the true from the false, nor understand the principles to which these things belong.

->Invocations and the commands of men toward spirits.<-

**P**orphyry wonders why we sometimes humbly invoke spirits as if they were our superiors, and at other times we seem to compel them by commanding them as if they were inferiors. Iamblichus distinguishes them in this way: The Gods, certainly—and all who are superior to our nature—bestow, out of the fullness of their goodness, the will for good things, and a certain kindness fitting for worthy souls. They cherish the religious as their own offspring, nurslings, and disciples, and they take pity on those who labor. There are, moreover, certain intermediate kinds of divinities who are the <term>ephors</term> <note>original: "ephori"; these are overseers or celestial magistrates who maintain cosmic order</note> and presiding officers of discernment and judgment; they provide counsel on what things ought to be done and what avoided. They certainly assist with just causes; they call men back from unjust ones, and they often justly hurl back upon wicked men the injuries they try to inflict, so that they themselves suffer the very things they were striving to do. There is, again, another class of spirits surrounding us that is indiscriminate and unreflective, which has been allotted one single power according to the distribution from the individual parts of the universe. Whence one is devoted only to one single task. For just as a sword only divides and performs no other action, so it is with the spirits distributed throughout the world on account of the divisible necessity of nature itself. This one, indeed, only divides; that one, however, only gathers the things that are made and generated. Therefore, certain hidden spirits, having each been allotted a different power, perform only that single thing for which they were ordained. If anyone, therefore, receiving those things which contribute to the whole in a distributed order, should deflect them elsewhere and carry out something as if by transgression, that which follows is the harm of the one who uses it wrongly. But let us return to the question. To answer the question: orders and violent commands are directed toward spirits that neither use their own reason nor possess the principle of judgment and discernment. Since our thought possesses a nature for reasoning and discerning the condition in which things exist, and also embraces many powers of life within itself, it is accustomed to command those spirits who do not use reason and who are determined toward only a single action. Invoke them, therefore, as superiors, since they attempt to draw from the universal world that contains us those things which contribute to the whole, concerning certain things contained in particulars and divided things. On the other hand, the soul commands them as inferiors, because our intellectual nature is more excellent than that which lacks intellect; and even if those [spirits] occupy a broader [place] in the world...

<summary>Iamblichus explains the hierarchy of spirits, justifying why theurgists "supplicate" higher gods while "commanding" lower, irrational spirits who lack the human power of reason and judgment.</summary>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...should have an action. Likewise, there is a double <term>persona</term> <note>original: "figura, siue præteſta"; the Latin refers to both a "figure" and the "toga praetexta" worn by Roman magistrates and priests, symbolizing a specific role or status</note> in the priest: one is human, the other divine. He puts on the divine persona through the sacred rites in which divine power is hidden, lifting his mind upward toward divinity and joining it to God. Therefore, by applying this divine character to his soul, he is able—clothed as he is under the <term>authority</term> <note>original: "præteſtu"; here meaning both the "cover" of a garment and the representative power of God</note> of God—to command spirits of this kind as their superior. This is true even if, as a man, he is accustomed to pray, invoking them as superiors insofar as he calls upon powers from the universe.

But we may solve the question more truly in this way: a certain common bond of harmonious benevolence and a connection of indissoluble unity contains the whole administration of sacred things, so that this execution is divine and exceeds every mode of human administration. Therefore, we must remove all human elements from this process. The priest does not summon a spirit as if it were absent, nor does he command a separate being to perform a task, as men usually do among themselves. Rather, a certain single and identical action of <term>divine fire</term> <note>A common Neoplatonic metaphor for the pure, energetic presence of the divine that permeates reality</note>, ready and present of its own accord and acting from itself, shines forth and operates. It does so in the same way through all things simultaneously: both through those things which are then passed on to others, and through those which are capable of receiving something from it.

Therefore, divine works fulfilled in sacred rites are not done through the opposition of one thing to another, as is the case with things that are born and die. They are not transformed through a difference between the one calling or moving and the one called and moved, as human affairs usually are; instead, the whole is fulfilled through identity, union, and consensus. Once any discrepancy is removed, the actor and the power by which the act is done are a single, simple, and universal thing.

<margin>Divine Justice</margin>
Porphyry asks why the higher beings often command their worshippers to be just, yet sometimes, when entreated, they appear to inflict injury. Iamblichus responds that they do not inflict injuries, but rather just punishments; and if by chance the acts seem unjust, they are not from gods, but from wicked <term>demons</term>. The Gods do not behold only a small part of this life, but the whole of it; and not this life alone, but the soul's universal life from age to age. And so, because of merits <note>original: "promeritis"; the rewards or punishments earned by the soul's conduct</note> contracted in a previous life, they often punish in a following one, whether they are asked to punish or not.

Meanwhile, we who see nothing beyond the present believe that misfortunes sometimes happen to us without merit. Yet we often suffer in this life for what we inflicted in another, and what we do now, we will suffer eventually. Furthermore, many sins of men are hidden from us, but they are not at all hidden from the gods. Likewise, we define justice as each person doing their duty according to the current laws of their country. The gods, however, define it much more broadly, looking to the whole order of the universe and focusing especially on the way souls are led back to the gods; from that perspective, they carry out their judgment. And so great a diversity exists between divine judgment...

<summary>Iamblichus explains that a priest acts through a divine persona rather than human effort, and argues that seemingly "unjust" divine acts are actually punishments for sins committed in previous lives.</summary>

# IAMBLICHVS.

...about justice itself and our own, such that we cannot fully grasp it. Now indeed, the gods themselves weigh what is just in one way when looking at a single soul, and in another way when looking at the entire kinship of souls. For if there exists a communion of the same nature among souls—both those living in the body and those placed outside the body—it produces a certain shared embrace for all, which is the same for the entire life of the world and the cosmic order; thus, it is necessary to require the execution of judgment from the whole, <note>The author suggests that justice is not merely individual but must be understood within the context of the entire "Universal Order."</note> that is, from the universal order and the necessity required by the souls among themselves. Especially where the magnitude of crimes committed by a single soul exceeds the punishment following from those sins. Therefore, the gods, when invoked, never inflict punishments unless they are just. For since they possess **goodness** according to their very essence, they cannot be the cause of evil or injustice. But if someone should happen to prove from imprecations made to the high gods that certain adversities happen to some people unjustly, we shall be compelled to seek other causes besides the gods and the good <term>numina</term> <note>original: "numina"; divine powers or spirits that preside over specific places or things</note>. Even if we happen not to find those causes, we should not, because of this, suspect anything of the gods that is unworthy of the divine nature, nor of that certain knowledge regarding the goodness of the gods which is innate in our intelligences. In this, without a doubt, all Greeks and barbarians agree. Consequently, since there are different types of evils, and since they are discordant, they must be referred not to one cause, but to various causes.

If what we were saying about <term>idols</term> <note>original: "idolis"; here referring to "eidola" or phantom-images that can deceive the senses</note> and wicked demons is true, from this there certainly arises a manifold origin of evils. For they simulate the presence of the gods and of good demons. Therefore, they command their worshiper to be just, so that they themselves may seem to be good, just like the gods. However, since they are evil by nature, when they are asked to inflict evil, they do so willingly, and they lead us toward unjust things. These are the ones who lie and deceive in <term>oracles</term> <note>Prophetic messages or the sites where they are delivered, which Iamblichus warns can be hijacked by lesser, deceptive spirits</note>, and who advise and perform shameful deeds. But the gods and good demons never deceive, nor do they contribute to iniquitous things. Furthermore, the nature of evil demons is inconsistent with itself, unstable and self-discordant, persuading one thing at one time and another at another; but the nature of the higher beings is constantly consistent with itself and always preserves the same tenor in action. The corporeal parts of the world are not void of **virtue**, but insofar as they are larger, more beautiful, and more perfect than our bodies, to that extent they possess greater powers and actions. Therefore, each one of them has powers that differ individually and produces diverse actions. Likewise, by a certain relationship to one another, they can accomplish much more. Indeed, from the whole parts of the world, a certain multiform action descends into the individual parts; and it descends most easily because of the likeness of their powers. Namely, to the extent that the powers following in step correspond to those that preceded them. Especially where...

# ON THE MYSTERIES.
<center>d</center>

...moreover, the one undergoing the action is adapted to the agent. Therefore, due to the necessities of the body, there arise from the "wholes" <note>The "wholes" (tota) refer to the universal systems or the cosmos as a complete organism, as opposed to "parts" (particulae), which are individual beings or objects.</note> into certain parts things that are evil and destructive; yet these same things are beneficial to the whole and in harmony with the **universal symphony**, even if they are meanwhile harmful to the parts. This happens either because the parts cannot sustain the powerful actions of the whole, or because of the degradation that occurs when forces mix with the lower realms—a weakness natural to the lowest things—or because certain parts are simply not in proportion with other parts.

Furthermore, the nature of the world itself is capable of many things beyond the mere physical body of the world. For the concord of similar things and the discord of dissimilar things produce many effects. Indeed, the coming together of many elements into one "universal animal" <note>Neoplatonists viewed the entire universe as a single, living, breathing creature.</note> and the powers flourishing in the world—however many and of whatever kind they may be—act one way in the whole and another way in the parts. This is due to the inherent weakness of the parts, which are ultimately distributed and divided. Friendship, love, and contention <note>Iamblichus is likely referring to the Empedoclean forces of Love and Strife that move the elements.</note> within the wholes themselves are active **operations**; however, in the individual parts, these same forces are experienced as **passions** <note>In this context, "passions" (passiones) refers to things that are "undergone" or suffered passively, rather than actions taken by choice.</note>.

Likewise, those forms and pure reasons that exist in the divine intellect participate in a certain material deficiency when they enter the nature of the universe. In individual things, they eventually encounter formlessness. Those things which are united in the wholes become divided in the parts. Moreover, certain parts are corrupted so that the "wholes," established according to nature, may be preserved; parts are crushed and pressed while the wholes remain the same, continuing to be born without suffering.

When some sorcerer <note>original: "veneficus"; a maker of potions or a dealer in dark magic</note> by his imprecations brings down a calamity upon someone from above—namely by using certain natural and corporeal powers of the universe—the transmission of such an action indeed comes from above without any choice or inherent wickedness. However, the sorcerer <note>original: "maleficus"</note>, while using this very thing, deflects the transmission toward entirely contrary and evil ends. This transmission and action descending from above is moved by a certain "sympathy" because of the similarity between things, even under the influence of contrary passions. 

The sorcerer, however, by his own choice, draws that which has been transmitted toward evil, contrary to what is just. Yet the transmission itself operates according to the single <term>harmonia mundi</term> <note>original: "harmonia mundi"; the "harmony of the world," the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected like notes in a song.</note>, so that even the most distant things cooperate. If someone, perceiving this, attempts to lead certain strong parts of the whole against other parts unjustly—thus causing harm—the universe is not the cause of such damage. Rather, the cause is **human abuse**, which transgresses the order of the universe and perverts what is lawful. 

Therefore, the gods do not bring evil upon us, but rather the natural forces and bodies that depend on the divine. And even these do not send down their influences as evil, but as good and salutary outpourings to the lowest parts of the world. It is those who receive them who, by their own mixture and perversity, transform them; thus, what was given in one way is received in a contrary condition.

After this, you ask: why is it that those superior by nature do not hear one who invokes them unless he is chaste, yet meanwhile, when entreated, they assist in illicit unions? Nor are they ashamed to incite their worshippers to foul lusts. When...

He then pivots to a new question regarding the apparent contradiction between divine requirements for priestly chastity and the gods' alleged involvement in immoral human desires.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's explanation of how universal forces, which are inherently good and harmonious in the cosmic "whole," can produce "evil" or disordered effects when they are filtered through the weak and divided "parts" of the material world. It specifically addresses the origin of illicit sexual desire.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

We are incited to intercourse that is "illicit"—unlawful according to human laws—by hidden causes. Perhaps it is "lawful" according to the laws of the cosmos <note>Iamblichus distinguishes between "human laws," which govern social behavior, and "mundane/cosmic laws," which govern the necessity of procreation and the survival of the species.</note> when, for instance, the birth of a necessary person is required. Truly, the instinct for love <note>original: "venerem," referring to Venus or sexual desire</note> in the universe tends toward friendship and harmony. However, in the "parts" <note>In Neoplatonism, "the parts" refers to individual beings or specific material bodies, as opposed to the "whole" of the cosmos.</note> it becomes more violent, because these individual parts, due to their <term>complexion</term> <note>A technical term referring to the specific physical and temperamental makeup of an individual.</note>, easily fall into excessive sympathy with one another and with the whole. Finally, what descends from heaven for a good purpose is here on earth often turned toward evil. The world is a **single living creature** in which the parts, though distant in location, are nevertheless drawn toward one another because of their shared nature. 

And yet, this reconciling force of the world and the common cause of all mixing draws the parts together by its very nature. Such attraction and appetite can be increased beyond the normal order by a certain <term>Art</term> <note>Iamblichus is referring to the "theurgic" or magical art, which can manipulate natural sympathies.</note>. This reconciling force, infused in all things, is good; it is everywhere the cause of fulfillment, communion, harmony, mutual love, and a worldly union which exists under the command of the Ruler. However, in the parts—due to their distance from one another and from the whole, and because of their weak and needy nature—it produces a mutual union through "compassion" <note>In this context, "compassion" refers to "sympathy" (sympatheia), the natural resonance or attraction between things with similar properties.</note>. From this, a sharper appetite is born in many people. 

Therefore, the <term>Art</term>, detecting this "coagulating" force dispersed throughout nature, draws it in from all sides, collects it, and directs it toward a single point. In this way, through its various "engines," it makes a naturally moderate appetite for necessary union become unbridled. It does this by applying matter that specifically aids procreation and by mixing together different natural forces; by this mixture, the practitioner governs and produces unions for procreation at his will. Furthermore, since there are forces in herbs and stones that can either dissolve or bring things together—and these forces are much greater in larger natural things—it is possible to intensify the urge for intercourse by using such things; even without the work of the <term>Art</term>, love can be ignited and attraction created by these objects themselves. 

We have discovered that **wicked demons** <note>original: "dæmones improbos." In this era, "demons" were often seen as intermediary spirits, some of whom were "bad" because they were too attached to the material world.</note> have a great deal of power over procreation and earthly or human affairs. Therefore, it should not seem strange that the fire for illicit intercourse is frequently lit in us by them. Certain souls can also contribute to this: some still living in the body (which have a wonderful power of attraction) and others that have been released from the body but are still wrapped in a "turbid and moist spirit" <note>Neoplatonists believed that impure souls remained weighed down by a "misty" or "moist" spiritual envelope, keeping them tied to the physical realm and its desires.</note>, wandering around places of procreation and committing such acts. Therefore, let no one say that the gods, or the demons who follow them, are the causes of illicit love and intercourse. Rather, blame our own depraved natural instincts, or the art of sorcery, or evil demons, or souls that are not yet pure.

->ON THE MYSTERIES<-

## On sacrifices: from where they derive power and what they contribute.

The question is asked: by what reason are sacrifices appropriate to the higher beings, how do they benefit men, and what do they do in the world? **Porphyry** says that not only prophets, but <term>hypophets</term> <note>These are "interpreters" or assistants to the primary prophets who relayed divine messages to the people.</note>—that is, all priests who deliver a prophecy received from others—must abstain from animals, lest they be contaminated by the divine vapors <note>original: "divaporibus," likely referring to the subtle spiritual exhalations or "fumes" associated with the ritual act.</note> exhaling from them. However, contrary to this opinion is the common saying that the gods are greatly soothed by the smell <note>original: "nidoribus," the fatty odor of roasting meat in a sacrifice.</note> of animals as if by food, and are captured by it. **Iamblichus** condemns both ideas: namely, that the gods are either stained by the smell of meat or ensnared and baited by it. 

The **World-Soul** and the heavenly beings, by the fact that they are present in their bodies, neither receive passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to being affected or changed by external physical stimuli.</note> from them nor are distracted from the higher intellects. But individual souls <note>Referring to human souls, which are "parts" rather than the "whole."</note> suffer both. One would err greatly to attribute similar defects to the higher souls; for the condition of universal things and individual things, or of causes and effects, is not equal. Indeed, feeding on bodies once joined to a soul undoubtedly brings upon us a burden and a stain; it creates a downward tendency in the soul, through which it melts away into pleasures, succumbs to them, and breeds many other diseases in the soul. 

But the vapor exhaling from animals and the sacred <term>suffumigation</term> <note>The ritual burning of incense or sacrificial offerings to create aromatic smoke.</note> properly performed does not harm the gods, the mundane causes, or the universal causes. For the vapor does not contain or order the higher beings toward itself, but it is contained by them and coordinated with the universe and the gods. And so, by their command, it can be fitted to the higher beings and harmoniously agree with them. 

Therefore, the religious abstain from animals—not because the gods could be defiled by animal vapors, for the power of the gods, before anything material touches it, scatters the material without even physical contact. Not only does this power destroy and delete these bodily things without needing proximity, before they even get close, but the celestial bodies themselves do not receive any material element into themselves. They do not let anything foreign in, nor do they lose what is their own. 

Furthermore, the vapors of earthly things, having progressed barely five <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of distance; five stadia is roughly 925 meters or a bit over half a mile.</note>, flow back; they do not stain or nourish the material and revolving [celestial] body. That body has no power of change in itself, nor does it have anything contrary to itself; it is not carried from the center or toward the center, but must either remain at rest or revolve. Therefore, the bodies beneath the moon—being composed of disagreeing powers and movements, and being entirely changeable and carried up or down—have nothing in common with heaven: neither nature, nor power, nor action. Thus neither vapor nor anything else from them reaches the heaven, which is entirely separate from them, and rightly [considered] unbegotten.

<summary>Iamblichus argues that religious sacrifices do not affect or "feed" the gods, as the divine and celestial realms are immune to material contamination and earthly vapors. He distinguishes between the purity of the World-Soul and the vulnerability of individual human souls to the "stain" of eating meat.</summary>

...they take no change from things that are generated. How then can the nature of the gods be defiled by vapors of this kind? For that divine nature repels material vapors with a single (so to speak) strike. Therefore, such things are not harmful to the beings above, but to us; for these divisible and material things, being kindred to us, share something in common regarding suffering or action toward similar things. But against celestial and divine things—which are placed in another kind of essence, endowed with different natures and powers, and surpassing them entirely—they can neither act nor communicate anything.

### What is the reason for sacrifices? What is their utility?

**Porphyry** thinks that sacrifices are offered to the gods for this reason: so that we might worship them with gifts of this kind, as we often do for our elders, and also so that we may return thanks for the good things received from the divine, rendering good for good. **Iamblichus** says that a cause of this kind is drawn from common human custom and is not appropriate to the nature of the gods, which exceeds human manners beyond measure. However, such modes and declarations of sacrifice do not fully demonstrate the greatest efficacy <term>efficacy</term> <note>The power of the ritual to actually produce a result, rather than just being a symbolic gesture.</note> of sacrifices. I mean that efficacy without which we are not freed from plague, hunger, or lack; nor do we obtain timely winter rains; rather, it is through this that we also achieve the purification and perfection of our souls, and freedom from this realm of generation <note>In Neoplatonism, "generation" refers to the physical world of birth, decay, and constant change, from which the soul seeks to escape.</note>. 

Therefore, one will not much approve of these modes based on your assignment, as if you had assigned a worthy cause for their effects. And if perhaps he does approve, he will certainly accept them in the second place as consequences and as something adapted in a secondary way to the first and most ancient causes of such works. We desire, therefore, the reason why sacrifices have efficacy for bringing things about, and from where they are adapted to the principal gods, who are the causes and principles of what happens.

Someone will say that because the world is a single living being <note>original: "animal unum," reflecting the Stoic and Platonic concept of the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, where the entire universe is treated as one biological and spiritual organism.</note>, and has one and the same life everywhere, therefore the communion of similar powers, or even the distance of dissimilar ones, or certainly a certain fitness of the agent to the patient, moves similar things in the same way; while it runs, evidently, according to a single sympathy <note>original: "compassionem," used here in the philosophical sense of *sympatheia*—the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" for one another.</note> even from the most remote point to the most remote point, as if these too were close. For among these also, the communion of life itself is an equal assignment of this kind; he speaks the truth indeed, and it follows necessarily regarding sacrifices. Yet the true mode of sacrifice is not shown in this way. For the very essence of the gods is placed neither in nature nor in natural necessities, through which a binding obligation might be stirred up by natural passions <note>In this context, "passions" means being affected by external forces or physical needs.</note>, or extended through the whole of nature...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that sacrifices are not merely social gifts to the gods (as Porphyry suggested), but are essential spiritual tools for purifying the soul and influencing the physical world. He rejects the idea that gods are moved by physical needs, suggesting instead that sacrifice works through a higher, divine logic beyond simple cosmic sympathy.</summary>

d iii

...by extended powers. Rather, outside of these things, the divine essence is determined according to itself, having nothing in common with them, whether in essence, power, or in action and passion <note>In philosophical terms, "passion" refers to being acted upon or affected by an external force.</note> simultaneously. To the aforementioned explanation, some add that there is a certain correspondence in lower things to those above, and thus a contribution to the **efficacy of sacrifices**. For example: they suggest that in the crocodile, the **number six** <note>original: "hexagonarius numerus". The number six was often associated with the Sun in ancient numerology because of its mathematical properties.</note> corresponds with the Sun. Again, in the dog and the **cynocephalus** <term>cynocephalus</term> <note>Literally "dog-head," referring to the baboons sacred to the Egyptian god Thoth, which were believed to have a mystical relationship with the phases of the moon.</note>, they suggest certain physical patterns and powers are shared with the Moon. Likewise in other things, certain material species—such as in sacred animals: colors, shapes, and forms—may suit some of the higher beings, or even a specific limb of an animal, such as the **heart of a rooster**.

These and other similar natural things used in sacrifices are said to be the causes of miraculous works. However, from this specific assignment of causes, the **divine cause**—which is entirely supernatural and not moved by natural motions—is not truly identified. Instead, what is described is a certain natural power contained within matter and bodies, which is excited by corporeal motions and material things, and then calmed again; I mean naturally, and along with those things that pertain to nature.

If, indeed, such a result follows a sacrifice, it is adapted to the preceding causes as a "co-cause," without which the work might not occur. It is better, therefore, to say that the miraculous effects of sacrifices proceed—as if from a cause—from a certain **friendship**, accommodation, and conciliating relationship, much like that of craftsmen to their crafts, or parents to their offspring. 

Therefore, when we are led and guided by this common principle and we take some animal (or other living thing born of the earth) that preserves the will and purpose of the Creator sincerely and exactly, we then move the specific cause of the "craft-work" <note>The "craft-work" or *opificiam* refers to the divine act of creation or theurgy.</note> that presides over and is mixed into this creature. 

Since there are many such causes—some presiding intimately and without a mediator, such as **daemons** <note>In this context, daemons are not "demons" but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>, while others are ordered higher than these, such as divine causes—and since one most ancient cause presides over all of them, certainly in a **perfect sacrifice**, all these causes are moved in their proper order. 

According to the order which each has been allotted, they are familiarly accommodated and (so to speak) appropriated to the sacrifice by a certain kindred condition. But if the sacrifice is **imperfect**, it ascends only to a certain degree and does not transcend further. For this reason, many believe that sacrifices are made only to "good daemons." Many others believe they are made to the lowest powers of the gods. Still others believe they are made to the worldly or earthly powers of daemons or gods. While these people explain a real part of sacrifices, they are ignorant of their **total power** and all the "goods" that extend themselves deep into everything divine. We, however, admit all these things at once and comprehend the natural elements as well...

<summary>Iamblichus explains that while natural correspondences (like the sacredness of baboons or specific numbers) play a role in ritual, the true power of sacrifice comes from a divine "friendship" or kinship between the Creator and the created. He argues that rituals must engage the entire celestial hierarchy, from local spirits to the highest gods, to be truly effective.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s explanation of how sacrifices function within the cosmic hierarchy. Having previously discussed natural correspondences (sympathies), he now argues that while material elements are involved, the true power of a sacrifice comes from higher, "demiurgic" or creative causes that act through an unchanging divine intellect rather than being "fed" by human offerings.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

Indeed, we accept those things which, as if in a single living creature, are moved together according to suitability, sympathy, or reciprocal affection, simply as subordinate elements and consequences serving the effective cause that appears in sacrifices. However, we accept the **spirits** <term>Dæmonia</term> <note>In this context, "daemons" are not evil "demons" but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note> and the divine powers that oversee the earthly world as being the authorities placed closest to our own rank. Yet we judge that the most powerful causes of effective sacrifices belong to the most perfect and **demiurgic powers** <term>opificiífque poteftatibus</term> <note>These are the "craftsman" or "creator" powers responsible for shaping the cosmos.</note>. Since those supreme demiurgic powers encompass all the subordinate causes within their own order, we believe that all effective causes are moved together simultaneously, in a single stroke, along with them. Since in a perfect sacrifice the subordinate causes are moved along with the supreme and demiurgic causes, a common benefit then proceeds from all of them into the whole of creation. Sometimes these benefits reach cities, peoples, and all kinds of nations—whether greater or smaller groupings—and sometimes they reach households or each individual man. These goods come through an abundantly beneficent will, for the higher beings grant their distribution not through **passion** <note>Here meaning "emotion" or "being affected by external influence."</note>, but by judging that they should give according to the propriety, familiarity, and kinship of things, using an **impassible mind** <term>impaffibili mente</term>. A certain internal friendship, which contains all things, brings about this binding together through an ineffable communion. These things are surely truer and participate more in the essence and power of the gods than what you suspect—namely, that the higher beings are primarily **lured** <note>original: "inefcari," meaning to be enticed as if with bait.</note> by the **smell of fat** <term>nidoribus</term> from animal sacrifices. For if spirits are enveloped in some kind of body—which some think is nourished by sacrifices—that body is certainly immutable, impassible, and radiant, and it lacks for nothing; thus, nothing flows out from it and nothing needs to flow in. And even if there were some need, why would it be necessary for it to flow in through sacrifices? For the world and the air within it have an inexhaustible supply of earthly exhalations surrounding them on all sides. Furthermore, even if the bodies of spirits did lose substance, sacrifices would not restore it in equal measure, nor would they preserve the balance between excess and deficiency natural to spirits, or maintain a similar proportion. Finally, since the **Architect of the World** <note>The Creator or Demiurge.</note> provided abundant and ready nourishment for all earthly and sea-dwelling animals, would he have left those beings superior to man without nourishment? And while he established that the daily food for other living things should be copiously prepared by their own efforts, why would he want an accidental food to be supplied to spirits by humans? Truly, if we were to neglect such nutrition, the bodies of the higher beings would surely burn out and perish. Therefore, if we were the ones who nourished the spirits, we would also be the **creators** <note>original: "generatoremus," following the catchword "remus." The author is arguing the absurdity of humans being the source of existence for spirits.</note>...

<summary>Iamblichus refutes the idea that gods or spirits are "fed" by the smoke of sacrifices, arguing instead that sacrifices trigger a chain of divine and creative causes that bring benefits to humanity through a spiritual "friendship" or kinship.</summary>

...we would be providing for them, and we would be their superiors. On the contrary, the truth is quite different. For it is they who nourish us; everywhere, higher things nourish the lower, just as celestial things nourish the earthly. Indeed, the **soul** is perfected and sustained by the **intellect** <term>intellectus</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "Intellect" is the realm of pure, eternal forms that exists above the "Soul."</note>, while the soul itself perfects nature. Furthermore, the offering of sacrifices through fire consumes the material substance and assimilates it entirely to itself; the fire does not make itself like the matter. Instead, it leads the offering back toward the divine, celestial, and immaterial fire, and does not descend in any way toward matter or the realm of **generation** <note>The physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note>. 

If the exhalation of vapors from sacrifices were intended to be material nourishment, then the matter would necessarily have to remain intact. In that case, a greater influx of nourishment would flow from the materials received. However, in reality, all the matter is burned and consumed, and it is utterly transformed into the very purity and subtlety of fire. This actually signifies the opposite of what you were saying. For the **Higher Beings** <term>Superi</term> <note>A general term for gods and superior spirits.</note> are entirely free from **passion** <note>In this context, "passion" means being affected or changed by something external, like hunger or emotion.</note>, since it pleases them for matter to be dispersed and consumed by fire. They render us, too, strangers to such passions, and they make whatever is within us like the gods—just as fire makes all hard and dark things similar to subtle and luminous bodies. Through sacrifices, the gods elevate us—along with the consumption of the offerings by fire—toward the divine fire. Just as fire rises toward fire, this process lifts and leads even heavy and hard things up toward the divine and celestial realms.

The bodily **vehicle** <note>The "astral body" or energetic shell that allows a spirit to interact with the physical world.</note> provided to the **spirits** <term>dæmonibus</term> does not consist of matter, nor of the elements, nor of any body known to us. Therefore, an elemental essence—which is entirely foreign to them—cannot become nourishment for these spirits. Rather, just as the gods, through their lightning-like fire, divide matter and separate from it those things that are immaterial by essence but bound to matter (rendering them impassible instead of subject to change), so too does our fire. By imitating the action of the divine fire, our fire destroys whatever material remains in the sacrifice; it purifies the items offered, releases them from the bonds of matter, and—on account of the purity of its nature—renders them fit for communion with the gods. In the same way, it releases us from the bonds of **generation**, makes us like the gods, and fits us for their friendship, lifting our material nature toward the immaterial. 

This general reasoning regarding sacrifices is sufficient, I believe, for those of a clever nature to sagaciously investigate the specific nature of each sacrifice based on this common rule. Nevertheless, indulging even those with slower intellects, we shall add some specific points to these, bringing clearer evidence into the open. The best starting point for all these matters is that which explains the context of sacrifices as being linked, in proper order, to the hierarchy of the gods. We posit that some gods are **material**, while others are **immaterial**. The **material gods** are those who encompass and organize matter within themselves. The **immaterial gods** are those entirely segregated from matter. According to the **priestly art** <note>Original: "sacerdotiã arté," referring to theurgy or divine ritual work.</note>, it is proper to begin sacrifices with the material gods; for otherwise, one cannot reach the immaterial gods...

<summary>Iamblichus explains that sacrificial fire does not "feed" the gods but rather purifies matter and elevates the human soul toward the divine. He introduces a distinction between material gods, who govern the physical world, and immaterial gods, who exist beyond it.</summary>

# IAMBLICHVS.

The ascent is open. These deities, therefore, possess a certain communion with matter insofar as they preside over it and dwell within it. They also dominate those things that occur within matter, such as division, impact and rebound, change, **generation** <note>In Neoplatonism, "generation" refers to the constant process of physical birth and becoming in the material world.</note>, decay, and all material bodies. If, therefore, anyone wishes to worship these gods rightly, he must surely offer a cult according to their nature and their rank—that is, a material worship for material beings. In this way, our whole selves will be brought into proper familiarity with their whole selves through all things, and we will offer a kinship in worship that is suitable for them. 

Thus, bodies deprived of life, the slaughter of animals, the destruction of bodies, and multiform change—along with decay and the total casting away of the preceding matter—are fitting for the material gods. This is not because of who they are in themselves, but because of the matter over which they preside. For even if they are highly separated from it, they are nevertheless present to it; even if they hold matter in an immaterial power, they nevertheless exist along with it. 

Now, things governed are not alien to their governors; likewise, things adorned are not alien to their adorners. Furthermore, the things that provide service are easily adapted to their users as instruments in due proportions. Therefore, it is indeed alien to employ matter in sacrifices for the immaterial gods, but for all the material gods, it is entirely appropriate. 

It is worthwhile, moreover, to consider the dual condition of our own life. At one time, we become entirely **soul** <term>anima</term>, positioned outside the body and elevated by the **mind** <term>mens</term> <note>In this context, the "mind" refers to the highest intuitive faculty that connects a human to the divine realm.</note>; we are raised up through the heights along with the whole company of immaterial gods. At another time, however, we are bound by the earthly body and are corporeal, being constrained by matter. Similarly, there will be a twofold method of divine worship: one will be simple, incorporeal, and pure from all generation, suiting pure souls. The other will be full of bodies and material action, suiting those souls that are not yet pure, nor yet purged from all generation. 

There are, then, two types of sacrifices. The purest sacrifices belong to men who are highly purified. This rarely happens to one person, or to very few indeed, as **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his ideas on the unity of opposites and the ever-changing nature of the universe.</note> says. But material sacrifices, which involve change, are suitable for souls still occupied with the body. Therefore, unless you offer sacrifices of this kind to cities not yet purified from their physical and bodily association, you will wander away from both the immaterial and the material goods alike. The former [the immaterial] cannot receive them, and for the latter [the material], one does not offer what is proper and consistent. 

Added to this is the fact that each person ought to care for their **essence** <term>essentia</term> according to what they are, not according to what they are not. Therefore, one must not violate the proper measure and nature of the worshiper. I judge that a properly adapted relationship between the humans who care for the gods and the powers being cared for will choose a mode of worship suitable for itself. For a relationship of this kind, tempered in an immaterial way...

<summary>Iamblichus distinguishes between material and immaterial gods, arguing that material sacrifices are appropriate for the former and for humans still bound to their physical bodies. He emphasizes that worship must match both the nature of the deity and the spiritual purity of the practitioner.</summary>

...chooses the immaterial insofar as it is coupled with the incorporeal beings themselves by the powers of pure incorporeality. A connection of that sort, bodily joined to bodies, chooses a similar worship for the essences presiding over bodies. We often make vows and perform tasks for the sake of the body's necessary needs toward the gods who govern the body and toward good spirits <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmonēsq; bonos". In this context, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humanity.</note>, while we clearly strive to purge the body of certain stains and ancient filth, or to release it from diseases, and to apply health, or to remove heaviness and sluggishness, and to apply lightness and efficacy, or to provide some other good for the body. Then, therefore, we will not treat the body rightly through some intellectual and incorporeal reasoning. For the body is not so natured that it can be cured in these ways; rather, when it finds things akin to itself, then the body is cured and purged by bodies.

Therefore, the rite of sacrifice for such a purpose will necessarily be bodily. In this way, it will purge the excesses of the body, supply those things that are lacking according to necessity, and bring whatever has been distributed back into proportion and order. We often sacrifice asking for things from those above that are suited to human life—namely, those things necessary for food or pertaining to those things we desire for the sake of the body. What then will fall to our lot from the gods themselves, who are entirely separated from all human generation <note>In Neoplatonism, "generation" refers to the constant cycle of birth and change in the material world.</note>? What might contribute to us the banishing of poverty or sterility, or the bringing of abundance, or lead to other necessities of life? Nothing indeed. For those who are released from all things do not handle gifts of this kind. 

If, however, anyone says that those immaterial gods encompass within themselves the entirely immaterial gods, and says that they embrace their gifts according to one primary cause, certainly a certain abundance of divine gift descends from there to the lower realms. But it should be granted to no one to say that those who handle these things carry out human life and actions in a proximate way. For the management <term>dispensatio</term> of such things as are here is divided and particular, and it is carried out with a certain turning toward these things; it is neither entirely separated from bodies, nor can it admit a pure and sincere governance and prefecture. 

Therefore, the mode of sacrificing for such things is appropriate which has commerce with bodies and generation—not that which is entirely separated from matter and the body. For he who is entirely pure <note>The "pure" worshipper or the highest class of deity.</note> transcends such things, nor does he have any proportion to them. But he who uses bodies and their powers is most akin to all such things, capable of supplying certain prosperities of life, and avoiding the adversities threatening us, and providing a moderate temperament for the human race. The vast multitude of men is subject to universal nature and is governed by natural powers, and it tends lower toward the works of nature, fulfilling...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that material sacrifices are necessary for physical needs because the body requires physical remedies and is governed by deities who oversee the material realm. He distinguishes these lower, practical rites from the purely intellectual worship of the highest, immaterial gods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between the human soul, nature, and the appropriate forms of divine worship. The previous page concluded by discussing how physical rites are necessary for those whose lives are still bound to the needs and nature of the body.</meta>

# IAMBLICHVS:

...which takes up the administration of fate and the order of fated works, and exercises practical reason only regarding natural things. Very few, relying on the supernatural power of the mind <note>The author uses 'supernatural' here to mean 'above the physical laws of nature' rather than the modern spiritualist sense.</note>, depart from nature and betake themselves to the separate and unmixed intellect. Consequently, they emerge superior to natural powers. Some, however, hold a middle ground between pure intellect and nature; of these, some follow both in turn, while others lead a life mixed from both. Others are released from the lower things and transfer themselves to higher things.

Therefore, those who are governed by universal nature and themselves lead a life enslaved to their own nature, and who enjoy the powers of nature, will perform worship suitable to nature and consistent with bodies moved by nature. For this purpose, they choose locations, qualities of the air, matter, the powers of matter, bodies, the qualities and habits of bodies, suitable movements, and the changes of those things involved in generation <term>generation</term> <note>original: "generatione". In Neoplatonic philosophy, 'generation' refers to the physical world of constant change, birth, and decay, as opposed to the eternal, unchanging world of the intellect.</note>, as well as similar things in other parts of divine worship and in the ritual of sacrificing.

But those who live by the mind alone, released from the bonds of nature, will contemplate an intellectual rule of worship, free from the physical body, in every part of religion. Those who lead a middle life between intellect and nature will also follow a middle way of religion, and according to the differences of their middle lives, they will seek different ways of worshiping through middle means. For they will either deal with both in turn, or they will lean from one to the other, or they will touch upon lower things in order to attain higher things through them, believing they cannot otherwise reach the more sublime.

In the class of divine essences and powers, some have the soul and nature subject to them—namely, serving their crafts <term>crafts</term> <note>original: "opificiis". This refers to the creative or demiurgic work of the gods in shaping the material world.</note> as much as they wish. Others, however, are entirely separate from soul and nature—I do not just mean from the worldly and generative soul, but also from the divine soul and its nature. Finally, others hold a middle place and bring together a connection between the extremes, either according to one unbreakable bond, or according to an overflowing tradition of the greater ones, or according to the unimpeded reception of the lesser ones, or according to a linked agreement of both.

When we worship the gods who rule over the soul and nature, it is not out of place to offer natural powers to them and to consecrate to such gods the bodies that are governed by nature. For all the works of nature both obey them and contribute something to their administration. But when we desire to venerate gods who are far secluded and collected in their own unity, we must worship them with honors entirely released from matter. For intellectual gifts are owed to these: an incorporeal life, perfect virtue, consummate wisdom, and their respective duties. But for the middle gods, who are the leaders of middle goods, middle things are appropriate, as we have said.

Starting therefore from another principle—namely from the world—by the distribution to the worldly gods <term>mundane gods</term> <note>original: "diis mundanis". These are deities associated with the physical cosmos and the planets.</note> of the four elements in the world, assigned from a common lot according to the measurements made of the elements, from the circumference...

...[intellectu]al centers revolved in order, we have easy access to the truth of sacrifices. For if we are in the world and are contained in it as parts, and are first generated by it, and are perfected by its total powers, and are composed of its four elements, and possess a certain portion of life and nature obtained from it, indeed, we ought not to omit the world and the worldly <note>original: "mundanos". In Neoplatonic thought, "mundane" refers to anything belonging to the cosmos/physical universe.</note> orders in divine worship. 

Let us suppose, therefore, that around any part of the world there is indeed some body, as we see; and that, furthermore, incorporeal powers are present within these bodies, distributed in order. Thus, the law of sacred rites rightly distributes like to like, and proceeds from the highest to the lowest through all the intermediaries, applying bodies to corporeal things and incorporeal to incorporeal things—rendering to each, clearly, its own. 

However, if any religious person attains the supramundane <term>supramundane</term> <note>original: "super mundanum". This refers to a divinity that exists "above the world," outside the physical laws and celestial spheres of the universe.</note> divinity—though this happens very rarely—this person, positioned entirely apart from bodies and matter, surely follows such a worship, united with supramundane gods by supramundane power. But what happens barely at last to one person at the peak of the priesthood is not suitable to establish as a common law for everyone, neither at the beginning nor in the middle of the religious state. For these people [the majority] perform corporeal worship in some manner. 

Therefore, anyone <term>skilled</term> <note>Text uses 'pitus' with a crossed 'p', a standard Latin abbreviation for "peritus".</note> in the priesthood will confess that one must offer worship to the higher powers that is neither partial nor imperfect, but fitting and whole. Since, therefore, before the gods are present and descend to earth, all the powers underlying them are set in motion, and precede them like forerunners and a ceremonial procession, surely he who does not distribute to all what is suitable to each, nor honors each with their own specific honor, does not attain the presence of the gods itself. 

But he who makes all the divinities favorable to himself, offering pleasing and very similar gifts to each, is certainly not frustrated by the outcome, but receives the divine choir with a whole and full presence. Since these things are so, the rite of religion ought not to be simple or composed of few things, but multiform, and consisting of every harmony, and constituted from all worldly things everywhere (as we have said). 

For if that which is called upon in the priesthood and moved toward us were something simple and of only one order, then surely a simple mode of sacrificing would suffice. But in truth, it is known to none how great a multitude of powers is usually aroused when the gods descend and are moved, except to those priests who have already experienced it through the work itself. Therefore, they alone know what constitutes the perfect fullness of worship, and how much the outcome frustrates us if even a few things are omitted. Just as in a harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly becomes dissonant; so, if one divinity is omitted—without whom the ritual is incomplete—religion itself does not achieve its desired end. For while this one element is lacking, the sacred work [weakens] its structure...

-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...and does not have wholeness <note>original: "integritatem". In this context, it refers to the spiritual completeness of a soul that has fully transcended the material world.</note>. When divine powers are about to descend openly to our senses, a manifest loss occurs for us if we neglect any of the higher beings and do not honor them. Similarly, when they come secretly in the sacred work <note>original: "opere sacro", likely referring to theurgy, the ritual practice of "divine work."</note>, it is dangerous if you honor one but do not honor another according to their dignity and order. For he who cheats anyone of their proper honor throws the entire work of religion into confusion, as he dissipates the one and whole arrangement. Nor, as someone might think, is only the work of receiving the deity then imperfect, but the structure of the whole perishes. 

What truly? Does not the very summit of sanctity return to the highest principle itself—the "One"—of the whole multitude of deities? And does it not worship all divine essences and lordships together in it? Without a doubt. But a summit of this kind arrives quite late, and to very few; and we should think it goes best with us if such things happen at the very end of life. 

But the present discussion does not set down laws for a man of that kind. For he is superior to the law; instead, it establishes these laws of sacred rites for those in need of some law. The multitude of deities is like a world <note>original: "mundus", meaning an ordered universe.</note>, having many orders acting in harmony <note>original: "conspirantes", literally "breathing together."</note> into one order. Similarly, sacrifices ought to have a number and order equally acting in harmony into one order, so that individual things rightly correspond to individual deities. 

Similarly, those things which are around us and within us are multiple; they ought not to correspond only from some part, but from all parts congruently to the divine causes of our affairs, and thus ascend to the supreme leaders. Therefore, religious observance performs various things around us and within us. For it either perfects by propagation, or cuts away, or cleanses, or orders things lacking order, or separates us further from mortal error. Finally, it reconciles all things with all the celestial beings in familiarity. 

And yet, when both meet as one—divine causes on that side, and human preparations on this side in equal measure—then perfect religion accomplishes all things and brings back immense benefits from the sacrifices. Indeed, the abundance of power in the highest causes of the universe is such that, just as it surpasses lower things in other respects, so too does it greatly surpass them in this: namely, in the very magnitude of its presence. Thus, the causes of all things are most present of all to all things, to such an extent that the very power of each cause is present everywhere, whole and always, apart from any hindrance. 

By this reasoning, therefore, the first principles of all things shine through <note>original: "subrutilant".</note> even to the last things. And immaterial principles are present in material things in an immaterial way. Let no one wonder if we say that some matter is pure and divine. For since matter itself was made by the <term>Craftsman</term> <note>original: "opifex". This refers to the Demiurge, the divine figure who shaped the physical universe in Platonic thought.</note> and father of all, it can rightly acquire a certain perfection of its own, suitable for receiving the gods. ->1<-

[Nothing] prohibits the higher beings from spreading their light to the lower ones. Therefore, they do not allow matter to be devoid of higher beings. For this reason, whatever part of matter is perfect, pure, and god-like is not unfit for receiving the gods. Since it was necessary that even earthly things should in no way be excluded from divine communion, the earth itself also received a certain divine portion within it, sufficient to receive the gods. Therefore, the wisdom of the sacred rites <note>original: "sacrorum sapientia". This refers to the knowledge of theurgy, or "god-working," which uses physical materials as tools for spiritual ascent.</note>, having contemplated these things and diligently finding suitable receptacles for each of the gods according to their harmony, often combines stones, herbs, animals, spices, and other similar things that are sacred, perfect, and god-like. And from all these, it then builds a pure and complete receptacle <note>original: "susceptaculum". In theurgic practice, a receptacle is a physical object or person prepared to hold or "house" a divine presence.</note>. For it is not right to despise all matter, but only that which is alien to the gods. It is proper to choose matter suited to them, as that which can harmonize and contribute to the dwellings of the gods, the foundations of statues, and the works of sacrifices. For otherwise, no possession or portion of divine things can reach earthly places and the humans living here, unless such a foundation has first been laid.

We must believe the secret discourses <note>original: "Archanis sermonibus". These are the hidden or oral teachings of the mystery schools or the "Chaldean Oracles" which Iamblichus followed.</note> which bear witness that a certain matter was handed down from the gods through blessed visions; this matter is therefore kindred to those very gods who handed it down. The sacrifice of such matter rouses the gods to manifest themselves; it immediately calls them to be understood, captures their presence, and demonstrates them perfectly. One can learn these same things from the very distribution of the divine throughout different places, and from the supervision that is divided among individual things. Whatever has obtained its place across various orders—whether greater or lesser—follows this rule. For it is clear to the gods who are rulers of certain places that a sacrifice made of the very things born there will be most fitting; such things will please the governors, the governed, and all that pertains to them. Their own works are always especially pleasing to those who created them. And those who first bring things into being naturally find those things most acceptable in return. Whether animals, plants, or other things seen as distributed by the higher powers, they have at the same time obtained a supervision under them and they procure for us an inseparable communion with those higher beings. Therefore, some of these things, as long as they are preserved and held, increase a familiar bond <note>original: "familiarem proprietatem". A technical term in theurgy referring to a natural affinity or "sympathy" between a physical object and a specific deity.</note> with the gods for those who hold them—at least those which, by remaining whole, preserve the power of communion between men and gods. Such are certain animals among the Egyptians and the "sacred man" <note>original: "sacer homo". This likely refers to a consecrated priest or a theurgist whose life has been dedicated to divine service.</note> everywhere; but others, when sacrificed and burned, create a clearer intimacy, namely those which effect a more kindred resolution into the principles of the primary elements and the causes of the higher beings.

# IAMBLICHVS

...and according to a more sacred rite. For everywhere, the more that appropriateness and familiarity are perfected, the more perfect blessings descend to us from that source. These are not merely human inventions, nor have they gained their authority through human customs; rather, the god himself, when duly called upon during the sacred rites, is the author of such laws <note>original: "auctor est eiusmodi legum". Iamblichus argues that the rules of religion are revealed by the divine, not made up by people.</note>. Surrounding this god are many gods and angels, under whom every nation on earth has been allotted a specific deity as its governor and shared provincial guardian.

From that same source, a specific deity is also assigned to every temple. Likewise, for the sacred acts we perform for the gods, some god acts as an observer and director. For those performed for angels, an angel; for those for daemons <term>daemons: in this Neoplatonic context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediate spirits that act as messengers between gods and humans</term>, a daemon; and in other cases in the same manner, a perfected being has been allotted a kindred guardianship according to its own kind. 

Therefore, since we handle sacrifices under the watchful eyes of the deities who authored these sacred things, we must revere the laws of divine holiness and the legitimate ways of sacrificing. We must hope for results in these rites because we sacrifice under the sovereignty of the deities and gods. Meanwhile, we must take the greatest care not to offer anything unworthy of the higher beings, or anything alien to them. 

Finally, in summary, we advise that we should diligently look around at every single thing within us and concerning us, as well as the things in the world, and likewise the gods, angels, and daemons distributed among the nations. In this way, we should similarly offer a "friendly" sacrifice <note>original: "amicum sacrificium". This refers to a sacrifice that is harmoniously "tuned" to the nature of the specific spirit being addressed.</note> to each one. For only by this method is the holiness and religion worthy of each deity preserved.

A vow, or adoration and prayer, completes every work of sacrifice; it contributes primarily to the whole of religion and forges a sacred and indissoluble communion between souls and the gods. Of this prayer, there are three species:
1.  The first gathers us together and provides us with contact and knowledge of the divinity.
2.  The second binds us in a harmonious communion with the divine and calls down gifts sent from the heavens, which complete our every work even before we speak or think.
3.  The third effects an **ineffable unity** <note>original: "ineffabilem unitatem". This is the "henosis" or mystical union that is the ultimate goal of theurgic practice.</note> and places all authority within the gods, perfectly positioning and confirming our soul within them. 

Indeed, in these three boundaries—by which all divine things are measured—prayer forges a friendship for us with the gods and brings us a threefold sacred benefit from them. One pertains to **illumination**, another to the **common execution of works**, and another to a **perfect fullness from the divine fire**. Likewise, adoration and its power sometimes precede the sacrifices themselves, are sometimes inserted in the middle of sacrifices, and sometimes complete the end of the sacrificing. Indeed, no work in the sacred rites is ever performed without the supplications of adoration. Finally, adoration, when practiced for a very long time, nourishes and perfects our intellect. It makes the soul far more spacious for receiving the divine...

...[divi]ne things to men. It habituates us to receive the splendors of divine light. It gradually perfects those faculties within us for grasping the deities <note>original: "numina contingenda"</note>, until it leads us to the very summit. Moreover, it gradually withdraws the human habits of our thought and introduces divine habits; it also creates a persuasion, communion, and friendship that is perpetual and far from interruption. It increases divine love, and kindles and elevates whatever is divine within the soul, purging whatever is contrary and adverse to the spirit. And from that ethereal and splendid spirit <note>original: "spiritu æthereo splendidoque." Neoplatonists believed the soul possessed a "luminous vehicle" or astral body that required purification through ritual.</note> which is wrapped around the soul, it shakes off whatever leans toward the world of generation <term>generation: the physical realm of birth, change, and decay</term>. Finally (to speak briefly), the power of prayer <term>prayer: the Latin "adoratio" here refers to theurgic prayer, which Iamblichus views as a ritual act of union rather than mere petition</term> makes those who pray frequently the familiar companions and disciples of the gods.

Since prayer is of such a nature and has such a connection with sacrifices, it is clear that the goal of sacrifices participates in the touch of the Creator <note>original: "opificii contactus." This refers to the Demiurge, the divine intelligence that crafts the cosmos.</note>. Inasmuch as through these works, one is adapted to the gods. Therefore, the benefit of sacrifice is as great as that which is sent from the primary causes and the creators to the human race. From this, the power of prayer again appears as something that leads us back, fulfills us, and is effective in producing union, holding a common bond from the gods. And how prayer and sacrifice mutually confirm each other, and in turn confer a power for the wonderful effects of religion. From this, it also appears that the priestly discipline <note>theurgy</note> and its operation possess a harmony <note>original: "conspirationem," literally a "breathing together" or sympathy.</note> among its parts no less than the limbs of a living animal, and no part of it can complete its work without the whole.

### De sacrificiis animalium.
### On the sacrifices of animals.

<margin>P</margin> Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a philosopher who wrote a letter to Anebo questioning the logic and morality of theurgical practices.</note> wonders why it is necessary by the law of sacred rites that one who is to inspect divine things must not touch a dead body at that time. Nevertheless, invocations and the attainment of divine things are frequently performed through the bodies of dead animals. Iamblichus resolves the matter thus: the prophets <note>original: "uates," referring to those who speak for the gods or lead rituals.</note> command the spectator of divine things not to touch a dead body that has not been consecrated. But they permit touching what is consecrated. Furthermore, they forbid even looking at or touching human bodies that the soul has already departed. For some trace, image, or demonstration of divine life is extinguished in the body by death. However, no religious law forbids touching the dead bodies of other animals, since they did not participate in a more divine life while living. Moreover, insofar as we rise toward the immaterial gods, it is expedient not to have touched such a body; but insofar as we strive to approach the material gods, touching is fre...

...will be frequently expedited. For we are accustomed to call upon gods of such a kind through animals. Namely, those who preside over such animals, especially those who govern them closely and, as it were, through a certain kindred condition. Likewise, for men who are confined in matter, bodies deprived of life <note>referring to carcasses or sacrificed remains</note> bring a certain stain—that is, the non-living upon the living, the filthy upon the pure, and the private upon that which possesses a settled disposition. Such things bring the power of dying to those who possess the dead, because of a certain common relationship between them. But for a daemon <term>daemon: in Neoplatonism, these are intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</term> who is entirely incorporeal and incapable of suffering, such bodies are not at all harmful. For the daemon greatly transcends that which is perishable.

->On prophecies through animals<-

<margin>q</margin> When prophecy is conducted through the bodies of sacred animals—as when predicting the future—it should not be thought that the gods themselves approach these things. One must not think that the universal providers stoop to a divided, particular, material, and proportional care concerning individual animals. Rather, it is the daemons—and those who are indeed highly divided and assigned individually to each species of animal—who have obtained the immediate care and presidency over animals. For these spirits have obtained a lordship that is not entirely sufficient nor free from matter. Therefore, they are appropriately accustomed to touch such instruments <note>original: "instrumenta" - referring to the animal bodies used in ritual</note>. To this end, so that we may obtain this kind of prophecy from daemons through animals, it is necessary to prepare a seat <note>or "receptacle"</note> for them, through which they can dwell among men and interact with us. This seat must be incorporeal, so that incorporeal daemons may be present to us through it. This seat, then, will be the soul of such animals, now set free from the body. For insofar as that soul is itself now separated from the body, it is compatible with the daemons; yet it is also compatible with us through a certain kinship of life. Therefore, acting as a medium, it serves its presiding daemon by suggesting foreknowledge to man and declaring the daemon’s commands, thereby reconciling us with the daemon. A soul using such prophecies does not merely hear or receive the prophecy; it also contributes no small amount from itself toward its execution in the work. For the soul is moved and cooperates, and at the same time foresees through a certain sympathetic <note>original: "compassionem," referring to the Neoplatonic concept of "sympathy," where all parts of the universe resonate with one another</note> necessity. But prophecy of this kind stands at a very great distance from the divine and the true. It deals with small and fleeting matters—things placed in a divided nature. These are the things carried along within the realm of generation <term>generation: the physical world of change, birth, and decay</term>, which exhibit motions toward those capable of receiving them and bring about various passions <term>passions: the state of being acted upon or changed by external forces</term> in those things naturally exposed to sympathy. Therefore, through such sympathy, this kind of foreknowledge arises. However, perfect foreknowledge cannot occur through passion. For that which is immutable and pure—
