### How those who offer prayers used to threaten daemons.

Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a philosopher who questioned the logic of threatening the gods</note> relates that priests were accustomed to use certain violent threats against the higher powers, such as: "unless you do this," or "on the contrary, if you do something else, I will shatter the heavens," or "I will reveal the secrets of Isis," or "I will divulge the mystery <note>original: "archanum"</note> hidden in the abyss." Or "I will stop the *baris*"—that is, a certain sacred boat among the Egyptians—"or I will scatter the limbs of Osiris to Typhon" <note>In Egyptian mythology, Typhon (Set) murdered Osiris and scattered his body; here, the priest threatens to repeat this cosmic disaster</note> and other similar things. Iamblichus <note>The author of this work, defending theurgical practices</note> adds that those who utter these curses were not accustomed to direct such threats, as Porphyry thinks, toward the sun and the moon or other celestial beings. Instead, there is a certain class of powers in the world that is highly divided, lacking in discernment, and inconsiderate. This class indeed receives reason <note>original: "rationem"</note> from another, or hears speech, but possesses no intelligence of its own. It distinguishes neither truth from falsehood, nor the possible from the impossible. Therefore, this class, when provoked by threats, is immediately stirred up and stunned, as it is naturally moved by more vehement words, and it leads or drags other things along through a certain dull and unstable imagination. Furthermore, the priest often commands and threatens the worldly divinities not by human virtue, but by the divine power of ineffable sacraments <term>sacraments: here meaning "theurgic symbols" or "divine tokens" (synthemata) that grant the priest authority</term>. He is then established in the order of the higher gods, and therefore by his own nature he employs greater commands and threats. Yet, he does not do this as if he were actually going to do what he then asserts, but rather to declare how much power he has obtained through his union with the gods—a power acquired, clearly, from the knowledge and possession of ineffable symbols or seals which we call sacraments. Likewise, daemons <term>daemons: intermediate spirits that manage the material world</term> are divided by provinces and parts, guarding sections of the world. Individually, they have such great care for the parts entrusted to them that they cannot tolerate even a word contrary to that order and dispensation. Indeed, they zealously guard the perpetual and immutable persistence of worldly things. They have undertaken their own immutable order because the order of the gods remains immobile in the same state. Therefore, in the place where the daemons—whether ethereal or distributed around the earth—have their being, they cannot even bear to hear themselves being assailed by threats. Consequently, daemons diligently provide for the guardianship of ineffable and secret mysteries. They do so with such great observance because they understand that the order and dispensation of the universe is chiefly contained in such mysteries. To the extent that, clearly, through these words, the divinities are designated allegorically—

<meta>This page continues the defense of theurgical practices by Iamblichus. The previous page discussed the seemingly impious practice of threatening the gods or daemons during rituals. Iamblichus here explains that these threats are not directed at the high gods, but at lower, terrestrial daemons who are moved by such words, and then transitions into how Egyptian symbols represent higher spiritual truths.</meta>

<header>IAMBLICHUS:</header>

...[desig]nated, and the worldly orders. For this reason, the parts of the world remain in order, because the beneficial power of Osiris <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and rebirth, representing the stabilizing divine principle</note> remains pure and untouched, and they are not mixed with contrary tumult and error. Furthermore, the very life of all things remains pure and uncorrupted insofar as the life-giving and beautiful reasons <note>original: "rationes" — the governing principles or ratios of the universe</note> which are hidden in Isis <note>The Egyptian goddess of magic and wisdom, often associated here with the hidden forms of nature</note> remain in that same place. While the world is driven from that source, those reasons do not descend into this body that is visible to our eyes. 

And yet all things remain immobile and simultaneously eternal—namely, by the succession of generation—since nothing can ever stop the course of the sun. They persevere, moreover, as a whole, because those things which are hidden in the abyss <note>original: "abysso" — referring to the primordial depths or the hidden spiritual source of life</note>—that is, in the deep—are never revealed. In these depths, therefore, all things together and the entire universe find their salvation; specifically, in the fact that those things which are naturally hidden are preserved as hidden, and the most secret essence of the gods never undergoes a contrary fate, nor is it mixed with opposites. 

I say that the terrestrial daemons <note>lower spiritual entities that dwell near the earth and are more subject to passion than the gods</note> cannot endure to hear this, nor can they withstand being affected by these words and having the secrets profaned. And therefore, against daemons of this kind, the use of such words has some power. However, no one serves these threats anywhere else. Nor are such pleas established for the gods themselves. For this reason, the Chaldean priests <note>Sages of ancient Babylon, known for their "pure" star-based theology</note>—among whom the speech addressed to the gods alone is judged and decreed as pure—never use threats. But the Egyptians, who mix the language of daemons with divine sacraments, sometimes turn themselves to threats of this kind.

### Explanation of the symbols of Egyptian theology.

The Egyptians, imitating the very nature of the universe and the craftsmanship <note>original: "fabricam"</note> of the gods, also display certain images of mystical and hidden notions by creating symbols. Just as nature expresses hidden principles in apparent forms as if through symbols, and the gods explain the truth of Ideas <note>The perfect, divine archetypes of all things</note> through manifest images. 

Since they perceive that all higher things delight in being likened to lower things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness from those higher powers (to the extent that they can be imitated), they rightly offer a mode of action consistent with the higher powers. They do this when they clothe hidden mysteries in manifest symbols. In interpreting these, leave behind the words and receive the meanings. 

Therefore, when they mention "mud" <note>original: "lutum"</note> in sacred rites, as they often do, understand this to be the "body" of the world: the matter and the generative power inserted into it, which is equally agitated and flowing. Or, it can be understood as the principal cause, placed as a sort of foundation for the elements and the elemental powers. Since this is the nature of mud, God himself, as the author of generation and of all the powers of nature...

<summary>Iamblichus explains that ritual threats are only used against lower daemons to maintain cosmic order and begins an explanation of Egyptian symbols, such as "mud," representing primordial matter.</summary>

...of all things that are inherent in the elements, being the cause as one who towers over all these things, himself immaterial, undivided, immobile, and unbegotten, existing entirely from himself and entirely within himself. But because he towers above all, he shines forth as one separated from all worldly things, proceeding alone by himself through the heights. 

This is also confirmed by the symbol that follows, where the god is presented sitting upon an aquatic lotus <note>The lotus was a primary symbol in Egyptian theology for the sun and the emergence of the world from the waters of Nun</note>, that is, a plant where it is signified that the god, by his own sovereignty, transcends worldly mud <note>original: "lutū" — symbolic of the chaotic, material, and changing nature of the physical world</note> and does not touch it while governing, but holds a sovereignty that is entirely intellectual <note>pertaining to the "Nous" or Divine Mind</note> and empyrean <term>empyrean: referring to the highest, most spiritual part of heaven, characterized by pure light and fire</term>. 

For all things in the lotus are round—both the fruits and the leaves—by which is signified the circular action of the mind, which always stays the same and acts in the same manner. Therefore, the god himself remains within himself above even this action, surpassing such sovereignty as holy and venerable, and resting entirely within himself—which is indeed signified by the act of sitting. 

Furthermore, where they introduce the god as the pilot of a ship, they signify his sovereignty as the governor of the world. For just as a pilot, separated from the ship and the rudder, moves, rules, and directs the ship in an instant with a certain ease, so the god himself governs the world from above—namely, from the first principles of nature—providing the primary causes of motions. 

Now, since all the parts of the sky and the celestial living beings <note>original: "animalia cælestia" — likely referring to the constellations of the Zodiac</note>, and the entire motion of the universe and time itself according to which the world moves—in short, everything contained in the whole—receive powers descending from the sun, some of which are mixed within them while others surpass any mixture, the symbolic mode of expression also introduces these things. In words, it designates the sun as being figured according to the celestial animals, and changing forms in turn through the hours <note>original: "oras" — referring to the seasons or the hours of the day</note>. Meanwhile, it demonstrates his unchanging and at the same time total transmission throughout the whole world. 

But since those things which look up toward him are carried about the indivisible transmission of the god in different ways, and they receive many-formed powers from the sun according to the diversity of their own natures and motions, for this reason, symbolic tradition teaches that one god enters through a multitude of gifts, and that one power of the god is present through many-formed powers. Therefore, he says that the one and the same god remains constant, but asserts that the changes of forms and transformations result in the recipients <note>Iamblichus is explaining that the "changes" we see in the gods are actually just changes in how we, as limited beings, perceive or receive their power</note>. This is why he says the god is changed according to the animals and according to the hours, as if such mutations varied around the god according to the different receptacles of the god. The Egyptians use such prayers <note>original: "uotis"</note> not only in the case of the gods...

### On divine names.

<margin>Porphyry</margin> Porphyry asks why priests use certain names that signify nothing. Iamblichus responds that all such names signify something among the gods, even if in some cases the meaning is unknown to us; yet certain ones are known, the interpretation of which we have received from a divine source. In truth, the mode of signification within them is ineffable <term>ineffable: beyond human expression or description</term>. It is not according to human imaginations, but according to the intellect <note>In Neoplatonism, the "Intellect" or *Nous* refers to the highest level of the human mind that can commune with the Divine Mind</note> which is divine within us, or rather, in a simpler and more excellent way, according to the intellect united to the gods. Therefore, one must remove from divine names all clever inventions, rational discourses, and natural comparisons innate to the voice itself relative to things placed in nature. 

Just as the symbolic character of divine likeness is intellectual within itself and divine, so we ought to suppose and accept this very same character in all things. What is present here for us is the very thing most to be venerated in it; for it is more excellent than can be divided into our understanding. Indeed, in those divine names where we have received their explanation <note>original: "resolutionem" — the unfolding or decoding of a name's hidden meaning</note> from a divine source, we have the entire knowledge of the divine essence, power, and order encompassed in the name itself. 

Furthermore, let us guard the mystical and ineffable image of the gods entirely in the soul, and through these names, we raise the soul to the gods and, being elevated, join it to them according to our strength. Hence the question is asked why we prefer "barbarian" <note>original: "barbara" — In this context, it refers to non-Greek languages, specifically those of the ancient Near East and Egypt, which were considered more primordial</note> names over others among divine names. It is because the gods have approved the entire speech of sacred nations—such as the Egyptians and Assyrians—as being most suitable for sacred rites. For this reason, we judge that these common expressions and ways of speaking should be applied to the language and speech related to the gods, especially because this way of speaking existed as the oldest and first. 

And since they received the first names from a divine source, when they mixed them with their own language as with something familiar, tempering them with a voice agreeable to them, they thus handed them down to us to be preserved forever. We, likewise, must duly preserve the rule of tradition hereafter. For if anything else is fitting for the gods, that which is eternal and immutable is most akin to the gods above all else. 

In the midst of this, Porphyry says that one who hears the sound of divine names looks toward what they signify, and therefore the concept itself—remaining the same everywhere regardless of the wording—is sufficient. Iamblichus responds in this manner: "However, it is not as you think; for if names..."

...if these names had been established by human agreement or convention, it would not matter if one were exchanged for another. But if they were adapted to the very nature of things, then those names which most closely harmonize with that nature are also most beloved by the gods. From this, it is clearly evident that the language of the sacred nations is, with good reason, preferred over all others. For names translated into another language do not preserve exactly the same meaning <note>original: "mentem" — literally 'mind' or 'intent'</note>. Rather, there are certain properties belonging to individual nations that cannot be expressed to other nations through speech. Furthermore, even if we were able to translate the specific qualities of these meanings into another language, they still do not preserve the same power once they have been changed.

Moreover, foreign <term>barbara: In the ancient world, "barbaric" simply referred to non-Greek cultures, specifically the Egyptians and Assyrians, whom Iamblichus viewed as more ancient and spiritually pure</term> names possess a great deal of emphasis—that is, an effectiveness in suggestion and demonstration. They also possess a concise brevity. Because they contain the minimum of ambiguity, variety, and wordiness, they are most suitable for the celestial beings.

Therefore, set aside those suspicions that fall away from the truth—suspicions by which you wonder if the Egyptian language is used only because the speaker is Egyptian, or because the use of the Egyptian tongue was required by the one being invoked. Rather, consider this: since the Egyptians were the first of all people to be granted the presence and participation of the gods <note>Iamblichus believed the Egyptians were the original "priestly nation" who received direct revelation</note>, the gods especially approve when they are called upon according to the Egyptian rite. Nor should it be said that these obscure, foreign names of divine things are merely the devices of tricksters or sorcerers. For how could things that are most closely joined to the gods—and which join us to them, possessing a power almost equal to the heavens—be mere imaginary fictions? Without these names, no work is accomplished in the sacred rites.

Neither are these "veils" or "coverings" produced by our own human passions and attributed to the divine based on mere rumor. For we do not start from our own human experiences; on the contrary, we attribute words to the gods that are suitable to them according to their own nature. Nor do we hold notions about the divine that are contrary to how they truly are. But just as nature itself is, and just as the first people to hand down the laws of religious sanctity attained the truth about the divine, so we persevere in those same ways. For if anything else in sacred laws and rites pleases God, stability itself pleases him most and is especially fitting. It is necessary, therefore, to preserve the ancient rites of adoration forever intact as sacred things, neither taking anything away nor adding anything from elsewhere. For this has recently become a cause of decline: all names and prayers have been weakened because, through this very transgression <note>original: "praevaricationem"</note> and the desire for innovation, they are constantly being changed, and they never cease to be changed.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For the Greeks are by nature fond of new things and are carried headlong in every direction, like a ship lacking ballast <note>ballast: heavy material used to stabilize a ship; here, a metaphor for the lack of tradition</note>, possessing no stability, nor do they preserve what they have received from others. But this was also quickly said...

## The opinion of the Egyptians concerning God and the gods.

<margin>question</margin> Thereupon, Porphyry asks what the Egyptians intend the first cause to be. Whether it is Intellect <note>original: "intellectum" — The divine Mind</note> or something above Intellect. Likewise, whether it is one single thing alone or together with something else, or others. Again, whether it is incorporeal, or perhaps corporeal. Furthermore, whether it is the same as the Creator <term>opifice: The Demiurge, or world-maker</term> of the world or if it is superior to the Creator; and whether all things flow forth from one or from many. And whether they intend the first foundation of all to be matter that is entirely formless, or bodies of some kind; and whether matter itself is unbegotten or begotten. To these things Iamblichus responded thus: 

Truly, I will first tell you the reason why the sacred and ancient writers of the Egyptians have held various views on these matters. And moreover, why the wise men of this age do not speak of them in the same way. Since there are many essences in the universe, and they differ from one another in many ways, it is rightfully so that many principles of theirs have been handed down, having different ranks, and different principles by different priests. Indeed, Seleucus <note>An ancient writer on Egyptian theology</note> recounts the universal principles in their entirety. Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius" — referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> himself has handed them down in twenty thousand volumes, or as Meneteus chronicles, he handed them down in thirty thousand volumes—and likewise in six thousand five hundred and twenty-five—and in these, he has demonstrated all things perfectly. 

However, other ancients have introduced various specific principles of particular essences here and there. It is necessary, therefore, to briefly declare the truth concerning all these things, and first that which you asked first. The first God is before that-which-is <term>ens: Being, or the state of existence</term>, and alone; He is the father of the first god, whom he begets while remaining in his own solitary unity; and this is above the intelligible <note>Beyond the reach of human thought or intellectual categorization</note>. It is the exemplar of himself, who is called "father of himself," "son of himself," "father to the one," and "truly good God." For He is greater and first, and the fountain of all things, and the root of those things which are first understood and which understand—namely, the Ideas <term>idearum: The archetypal forms or blueprints of reality</term>. 

From this One, certainly, the self-sufficient god unfolded himself. And therefore he is called self-sufficient, father of himself, and prince through himself. For this is the principle, the god of gods, a unity from the One, above essence, the principle of essence. For from him comes essence; therefore, he is named the father of essence. For he himself is the "super-existently existent" <note>original: "superenter ens" — Iamblichus's term for that which exists beyond the normal category of Being</note> principle of intelligible things. These are the most ancient principles of all, which Hermes places before the ethereal, empyrean, and celestial gods.

<summary>Iamblichus begins his explanation of Egyptian theology, responding to Porphyry's questions about the First Cause. He describes a hierarchy of divine unity where a solitary, supreme God precedes all existence and begets a self-sufficient secondary deity who acts as the source of all essence and archetypal Ideas.</summary>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...composing a hundred books on the empyrean <note>The highest, "fiery" heaven</note> realms, and just as many on the ethereal, and a thousand on the celestial. According to another order, he places the god **Emeph** <note>An Egyptian deity often identified by Neoplatonists as the "leader" of the celestial gods</note> before the celestial gods as a leader, whom he says is an intellect understanding itself and turning its thoughts back into itself. Before this one, he places one indivisible being, which he calls the first exemplar, or expression, or image, and which he names **Icthon**. In this being is the first understanding subject and the first understood object, which is worshipped by silence alone. 

Beyond these, however, other leaders preside over the craftsmanship of visible things. For the creative intellect <note>original: "opifex intellectus" — The Demiurge, or world-shaper</note>, who is both the master of truth and wisdom, insofar as it proceeds into the realm of generation <note>The world of birth, death, and change</note> and brings the hidden power of latent principles into the light, is called **Amun** in the Egyptian tongue. Insofar as it completes all things without falsehood and with craftsmanship alongside truth, it is named **Phtha**; the Greeks, however, call him **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus, the god of the forge and craftsmanship</note>, considering only his technical skill. Insofar as he is the bringer of good things, he is called **Osiris**, and he has other names according to his different powers and actions. 

There is also another lordship among them over the whole of the elements involved in generation, and over their powers; four of these are masculine and four are feminine. They attribute this lordship to the **Sun**. Likewise, another lordship over all of nature that is involved in generation is attributed to the **Moon**. 

**Marsilio:** <note>This is an interjection by Marsilio Ficino, the translator and commentator, clarifying the hierarchy using the philosophy of Proclus</note> You can arrange a consistent order here according to Proclus <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in this way: 
1. The first is the **One** itself, above being and above the whole intelligible realm. 
2. The second is the **One-Being**, or the unity of being, in which its unity is placed before its own being; it can also be called the "intelligible intellect" and its own father. 
3. The third is the **Intelligible-Intellectual Intellect**, which is at once the united intellect and expression, the first **Icthon**. 
4. The fourth is the **Intellectual Intellect** already unfolded, the leader of the celestial gods, **Emeph**. 
5. The fifth is the **Creative Intellect**, the nearest leader of the worldly craftsmen, who are the celestial, empyrean, and ethereal gods; this perhaps is the intellect of the world-soul, which is named **Amun**, **Phtha**, **Vulcan**, and **Osiris**. 

**Iamblichus:** Truly, whether they divide the heaven into two parts, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six, or doubles of these, or in whatever other way, they also establish lordships for these divisions, whether fewer or more. Again, they place one leader before these; and thus the Egyptian treatise on principles, proceeding from the highest things to the last, descends from the one into the multitude. It is clearly governed from the one by God everywhere, so that indefinite nature is held under a certain definite limit by His command—and especially by that high unity which is the cause of all things. God truly produced matter from materiality <note>original: "materialitate" — The abstract principle or essence of matter</note>, namely...

...from the derived essentiality which the Craftsman <note>original: "opifex" — the Demiurge or world-shaper</note>, assuming it as vital, made into simple and impassible spheres. But the last part of this he took for the making of generable and corruptible bodies <note>The physical world of birth and decay</note>. With these things thus distinguished, the doubts are easily resolved which you say you conceived from the Egyptian books you read. For those which are circulated under the title of Mercury <note>original: "mercurii" — Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note> contain Mercurial opinions, even if they often speak in the style of Greek philosophers. For they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unlearned in philosophy.

I would wish, indeed, that whoever touches upon the primary causes of worldly things would also declare the ultimate principles. Likewise, let whoever treats of the planets, the zodiac, the decans <note>divisions of the zodiacal signs into ten-degree segments</note>, the horoscopes, and the stars as powerful leaders, hand down the particular distributions of the principles. Consequently, the dogmas which are in the *Salmeschoiniaka* <note>original: "salaminiacis" — a collection of ancient Egyptian astrological and ritual texts</note> contain only a very brief part of the Mercurial arrangements. Likewise, those things treated regarding the appearances or occultations of stars, or the waxing or waning of the moon, have their assignment of causes among the last things for the Egyptians. Indeed, the Egyptians do not think all things are natural, but they distinguish life—both intellectual and animal—from nature. Not only in the world, but also in humans. And since they have placed intellect and reason as existing by themselves at the head, they judge that whatever happens, happens accordingly; and of those things involved in generation, they assert the Craftsman to be the first principle or father. They also recognize a vital power, both that which is in heaven and that which exists above heaven.

Likewise, they place pure intellect above the world, and one indivisible intellect in the whole world, and another distributed through all the circles.

Now truly, they are not accustomed to contemplate these things with speech and naked reason alone, but they further advise and teach that our nature should proceed to higher and more universal things, and things superior to fate, even to God himself, the Craftsman of the world. Provided that the soul carries neither matter with it, nor anything else except the observation of the opportune time; and they teach that we attain this through sacred works <note>original: "sacrorum opera" — the practice of theurgy, or ritual to connect with the divine</note>, and they effect this at the same time. Hermes himself handed down this way to us. But he interpreted it for King Ammon <note>A legendary Egyptian king often paired with Hermes in wisdom dialogues</note>, having found it in the inner sanctuaries of the temple in the city of Sais <note>original: "Sayn" — an ancient capital of Egypt</note>, inscribed in sacred Egyptian letters, and he also provided it to us. The name of God runs through the universe. There are also many other orders regarding these same things. Therefore, you do not seem to me to be right to reduce all the things of the Egyptians to natural causes alone. For among them, there are more things and more essences; there are also super-worldly powers which they have worshipped through religious principles and holiness.

# ON THE MYSTERIES.

->On free will and how we are released from fate.<-

<margin>P</margin> After these things, Porphyry says that many of the Egyptians also subject our very will to the movement of the stars. Iamblichus responds from the Mercurial <note>original: "mercurialibus" — referring to the teachings of Hermes Trismegistus, known to the Egyptians as Thoth</note> opinions in this manner: man has two souls, as the Mercurial writings teach. One indeed is from the first intelligible <note>the realm of pure, divine thought</note>, and partakes of the power of the Creator <note>original: "opificis" — the Demiurge or world-shaper</note> himself. The other is truly instilled in us from the circuit of the heavens, into which the soul that contemplates divine things creeps. The soul descending into us from the worlds, therefore, follows the circuits of those worlds. But that soul which comes from the intelligible exists in an intelligible manner and stands above the circuit of generation <note>the cycle of birth and physical existence</note>; and through it, we are both released from fate and ascend to the intelligible gods. We possess a religion that tends toward the eternal.

Therefore, it must not be thought—as you were doubting—that all things are bound by the unbreakable chains of necessity, which they call fate. For the soul has a principle proper to itself, by which it may commit itself to the intelligible, and indeed depart from those things which are born <note>the material world of change</note>, and approach Being itself and the divine. Nor, again, do we apply fate to the gods, whom we worship in temples, with sacrifices, and with statues as those who release us from fate. The gods themselves dissolve fate. However, the lower natures descending from them, which are already entangled in the generation, the body, and the world, carry out fate.

Rightly, therefore, do we offer all sanctity to the gods, so that they alone, ruling through intellectual persuasion, may dissolve the evils threatening us from fate. For not everything is bound within the nature of fate; rather, there is another principle of the soul, superior both in nature and in generation, through which we can be joined to the gods, surpass the worldly order, and participate in the eternal life and action of the supracelestial gods. Through this, therefore, we are able to exempt ourselves from fate. For when the more excellent parts of those things within us are active, and the soul is recalled to the more excellent parts of itself, then it is entirely segregated from those things which bind it in generation, and it departs from the inferior things. It exchanges one life for another and places itself in a different order while completely deserting the prior order.

What then? Is it possible to release oneself from fate through the gods who move in the heavens? And yet, at the same time, to consider those same gods the leaders and authors of fates, binding lives entirely with unbreakable chains? Perhaps, indeed, nothing prevents it from being so. For since the gods embrace many essences and powers within themselves, what prevents there being in them other differences and contrarieties which are inestimable to us? Indeed, it is also permitted to say this: that in each of the gods—even the visible ones—there are certain intelligible principles of essence, through which the souls may achieve flight and freedom from the generation of the worlds. If anyone considers the two orders of gods...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that humans possess a dual soul—one bound to the stars and fate, and another capable of transcending them through divine contemplation and the help of the gods.</summary>

# IAMBLICHUS

...does not admit the duty of absolution. That is, concerning both mundane <note>earthly or cosmic</note> and supramundane <note>beyond the physical universe</note> beings, a release will eventually occur, at least through the supramundane ones. These truths are declared more carefully in the treatise on the gods: which gods especially are those who lead us back to the heights, how they recall souls and with what powers, by what reasoning they dissolve fate, and through which specific returns achieved by sacred operations <note>original: "sacrorum operatione" — referring to theurgy, or "god-work"</note> this is accomplished. It also explains what the order of mundane nature is, and how perfected intellectual action rules over this order. 

For this reason, regarding what you cited from the verses of Homer—namely, that the "gods are flexible" <note>original: "deos esse flexibiles" — a reference to Iliad 9.497, suggesting gods can be swayed by human offerings</note>—we judge it a wickedness to say such a thing. For the holy works of religion have long been defined by pure and intellectual laws; by a greater order and power, the inferior things are dissolved. Insofar as we are translated into a better lot, to 그 degree does a departure from inferior things occur. Nor, for that reason, does anything happen contrary to the rule established from the beginning, as if the gods were swayed because of a sacrifice or worship performed afterward. Rather, from the first descent, God sent down souls on the condition that they might return to him again. Nor do the ascents and descents of souls contradict each other. For just as in the intellectual universe, generation <note>the process of coming-into-being</note> exists together with essence—indeed, this whole system is rightly connected—so too in the disposition of souls, their release from generation agrees with their care for generation.

### On the personal guardian spirit of each person.

<margin>q</margin> After these things, Porphyry asked many questions about each person's own guardian spirit <term>daimon<gloss>In this context, a "daimon" is not an evil demon, but a personal protective spirit or "genius" that guides an individual's life.</gloss></term>. Iamblichus responds to these as follows: There are two ways of treating the guardian spirit proper to each individual. One is sacred, or god-making <note>original: "deificus"</note>; the other is technical. The former invokes the guardian spirit from higher, divine causes. The latter invokes it from the circuits of the stars that revolve in the realm of generation <note>the physical world of birth and death</note>. The former does not use an investigation of each person’s nativity <note>original: "geniturae" — an astrological birth chart</note>, while the latter explores such things diligently. The former is universal and stands above nature; the latter cultivates and cares for the guardian spirit more particularly according to the laws of nature. 

Since these things are so, you seem to me to have absurdly transferred the more perfect worship to a merely human manner, and to have exercised your questions only within this lower method. Moreover, where you seek or worship the guardian spirit only by the natural way, you seem to have accepted only a very small part of that path. For those who inquire and operate technically concerning nature are accustomed to call upon the guardian spirit in an orderly way from the decans <note>the thirty-six 10-degree divisions of the zodiac</note>—that is, the "makers"—and from the dispensers of influences, the images of heaven, the stars, the sun, and the moon; likewise from the poles and all the elements and the world. But you, not rightly selecting the briefest part of these—namely the lord of the birth chart <note>original: "genitalis figurae dominum"</note> itself—bring in questions only about this. In this part, having assumed this one thing, you investigate in what way the lord of the astrological figure itself grants the guardian spirit, and according to what kind of life, power, or influence flows into us from it. Here you delay entirely in the exploration of the horoscope...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that gods are not "swayed" by prayer but follow eternal laws that allow souls to rise above fate. He then begins a critique of Porphyry’s astrological approach to finding one's personal guardian spirit, distinguishing between divine and technical methods.</summary>

...doubting <note>The Latin "tans" is likely the end of "dubitans," meaning "doubting" or "questioning."</note> whether the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "daemon" — in Neoplatonism, this refers to a personal guardian spirit or intermediary being, not an evil "demon."</note> exists or not, and whether the master of the birth configuration <note>original: "figurae dominum" — the planet that rules one's natal chart.</note> can be found or perhaps cannot. And if, through the spirit, we drive away things that were necessary for us, do you also affirm that these things were destined for us through fate together with the spirit?

### On the judgments of astrologers and the spirit.

**P**orphyry says that if someone were to know the configuration of their birth and the master of that configuration, they would find their own spirit, and through it, they would be released from the fate of their birth. But he adds that it is impossible to know those things, and to find this spirit, and that the rules of astronomy and astrology <note>In this period, the terms for astronomy and astrology were often used interchangeably to describe the study of celestial influence.</note> are incomprehensible and uncertain, even according to the testimony of <term>Chaeremon</term> <note>An Egyptian priest and philosopher who wrote on the influence of the stars.</note>. Iamblichus says that the spirit is neither known through nor given by that configuration and its influence. Otherwise, it would not release us from the fate of our birth. Rather, it is given from a more ancient and higher principle—namely, from the superior gods—and at the very moment when the soul first inclines toward sensible <note>perceivable through the senses</note> things before conception. He also says we are released from fate not so much through the spirit as through the worship of a higher divinity. Indeed, those words of Porphyry not only disagree with themselves but also with the truth. For the spirit is not assigned to each person solely by the specific configuration of their birth, but there is also a more ancient beginning. Likewise, if the spirit were recognized only here, one would not for that reason be happy just by knowing their natal spirit. And who, then, would receive this guide to escape the things of fate if the spirit himself were assigned to fulfill these very things? You completely overlook the primary questions regarding the essence and order of the spirit, and only touch upon the last ones concerning whence it descends.

You inquire, furthermore, why innumerable rules of astrology are circulated and why there are doubts about the birth chart, from which it appears that knowledge of these things cannot be had. I, however, think first that the most certain truth about the stars can indeed be held through divine prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium" — referring to divine inspiration or oracles.</note>. We do not entirely need the counting of rules or artificial predictions. Moreover, I add that you have not demonstrated that knowledge from that source is entirely impossible regarding what pertains to mathematical science, simply because diverse opinions are held among them, or because Chaeremon or anyone else speaks against it. For in that way, we would be forced to say there is no science in any field of knowledge or art because of conflicting opinions. But surely, everywhere, not only do false things disagree with each other, but the false also disagrees with the true, so that everywhere, beyond the false, the truth can be found. -># IAMBLICHVS<-

...[comprehending] <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the limits of human knowledge.</note> even astronomy is not possible, let alone astrology, and that there are many disagreements among practitioners, and it is attacked by many. Iamblichus responds that divine **divination** <note>original: "vaticinium"</note> can teach the nature and effect of the stars without the technical art of astrology. **Astronomy** and other arts once given by the gods are, over a long period of time, confused by human opinions and finally retain very little of divinity and truth. In astronomy there is something of the truth, though it is a small amount which is evident through the effects of the stars upon one another, proceeding from their measurements in the heavens, just as was said before concerning the eclipse of the sun and moon and the aspects of the planets. The rules of measurements, magnitudes, distances, progressions, comets, and similar things observed for a long time among the **Chaldeans** <note>The Chaldeans were ancient Mesopotamian people renowned as the founders of astronomy and astrology.</note> and among us, testify that the science of astronomy is true. 

Porphyry says that the master of the **birth configuration** <note>original: "dominum figurae" — the specific planet that "rules" or has the most influence over a person's natal astrological chart.</note>, or the masters if there are many, cannot be grasped even by the judgment of astronomers and astrologers, but from that source the personal **spirit** <note>original: "daemonem" — in this context, a personal guardian spirit or guiding intelligence assigned to an individual at birth, not an evil entity.</note> must be sought. Iamblichus says that astrologers provide rules—some five, others fewer, others more—for finding or discerning the masters of the birth configurations. I do not say, he declares, that rules are truly held, found, and discerned, but rather that it is so *thought* and handed down by them, contrary to what Porphyry stated. What prevents the master of the chart and the spirit from being found through astrology with great difficulty, but most easily through divine divination and sacrifices? 

Nor should it be thought that the spirit is assigned by the master of the natal chart alone. For there are more and older principles than this. Nor can we find our own personal spirit through human arts, but only through divine ones. Each person's own spirit is not distributed by a particular disposition of the heavens or the elements, but by the whole disposition of the world, at the moment the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> descends; then the spirit himself reigns and provides a certain executor for the life which the soul has chosen. This spirit joins the soul to the body and cares for the life communicated to the body. He directs the soul's own life, constantly provides the principles for thought, and we act in such ways as he brings to our minds; he governs us to the extent that, once we are perfected by sacred rites, we exchange this master for God. Then the spirit, yielding to God, either ceases from his work or leads toward the same end. One’s own **lot** <note>original: "sors"</note> is assigned to the soul as it descends from the whole body of the world, and life is as it then stands in relation to that soul, and that lot is guided and fulfilled by a certain spirit. Therefore, it is impossible to judge certain outcomes since we cannot comprehend the convergence of all causes, unless we attain that knowledge through divine inspiration.

### Whence the personal spirit comes, what it does, and whether it is unique.

The personal spirit is not assigned from a certain part of the sky or the elements, but rather from the whole world, and from the multiform life within it, and from the multiform bodies through which the soul passes as it descends into **generation** <note>original: "generationem" — the process of becoming physical or being born into the material world.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the defense of theurgic doctrine by Iamblichus. Having previously discussed how the "lord of the birth" is identified through astrology, he now moves to define the nature and function of the personal guardian spirit (daemon) and rebuts Porphyry’s suggestions that we might have multiple spirits or that the spirit is simply a part of our own mind.</meta>

-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

For is there not a specific **lot** <note>original: "sors" — a predestined portion or destiny assigned to an individual at birth.</note> properly set apart and decreed for us, distributed according to its own particular governance? This certainly existed first in the **exemplar** <note>The divine model or archetype of the soul that exists in the intelligible realm before the soul is born into a physical body.</note> before souls descended into the cycle of birth. As soon as the soul receives its leader, the **spirit** <note>original: "daemon" — in this Neoplatonic context, a guardian spirit or guiding intelligence assigned to a person, not a "demon" in the modern malevolent sense.</note> himself stands ready, the subsequent fulfiller of our lives. This spirit, as I have said, binds the descending soul to the body. He personally looks after the combined nature of the living being. He directs the soul's own life. Whatever we reason, he provides the principles of our logic, and we act according to the thoughts he brings into our minds. He governs us until, purified by **sacred rites** <note>original: "sacris opibus" — refers to theurgic rituals intended to elevate and purify the soul.</note>, we receive a **god** as our leader in place of the spirit. To this god the spirit then yields, so that he either withdraws in the god's presence or serves the same divine purpose. 

You were asking then whether several spirits are present to each individual, with different spirits governing different parts of the human being. To this we reply that the spirit does not merely preside over a single part of us, but is present to the whole at once and leads the entire being, just as he is assigned by the universal orders of the world. You conjectured that multiple spirits are present to us, corresponding to the number of our various parts. Furthermore, you suggested that even within the body itself there are different spirits: one for health, another for beauty, and others for specific physical conditions, and that one spirit might preside over all these in the body. Likewise, you thought that one spirit rules the body, another the soul, and another the intellect. 

Yet such a conjecture actually proves the opposite: that the body, the soul, and the intellect are all governed by one and the same spirit. Therefore, do not divide them so that there is one spirit for the body, another for the soul, and another for the intellect. For it is absurd to think that while the living being itself is one, the spirit set over that being is multiform. For those who hold sovereignty are always simpler than those they rule. It is even more absurd if many ruling spirits, like parts of a spiritual group, were not united into one but were disconnected from each other. You even introduce conflict among them, as if some ruling spirits were good and others were evil. However, evil spirits nowhere hold a lot of governance, nor are they distributed with equal authority or number in opposition to the good. 

After this, you suspect that the personal spirit is actually a certain part of the soul—namely, the intellect—and that a man is **blessed** <gloss>original Greek: εὐδαίμονα (*eudaemona*) — literally "having a good spirit," this is the root of the word for happiness or flourishing.</gloss> who possesses a wise intellect. If this were true, there would no longer be any order higher than man set over man. Instead, among the divided parts of the soul, the higher would dominate the lower. Yet there, all parts are of the same kind; none of them rules over subjects as an absolute authority. Next, you introduce the worship of the spirit as if it were directed toward many: sometimes toward two spirits, sometimes toward three. Truly, it is a sacrilege to divide the causes that preside over us or to fail to trace the governance back to a single source, since unity rules in all things. Furthermore, even those who [think] the spirit [is determined] according to the body...

# IAMBLICHUS

...and the administration of the body, you divide his sovereignty and reduce it to a very narrow part of the same. Therefore, it is not fitting to consider the religious worship concerning the **spirit** <note>original: "daemonium" — refers here to the nature or activity of the guardian spirit.</note> as divided in such a way, since the very opinion upon which it is founded wavers with weakness.

**T**herefore, there is one proper spirit for each of us as our governor. It is not right to consider a spirit as entirely common and the same for all men—specifically, as being common in himself but joined to each person by a particular condition. For the division according to each species and the very otherness of matter does not admit the fellowship and identity of things that are incorporeal in themselves.

### Invocation of the spirit.

<margin>q</margin>**Y**ou then ask why we are accustomed to call upon the spirit with a certain common invocation among everyone, since clearly the invocation is conducted through the one Lord of the spirits, who from the beginning assigned to each his own spirit, and in sacrifices reveals to each his own according to His will. For in the order of **sacred operations** <note>original: "sacrarum operationum" — theurgy, or rituals designed to communicate with or ascend to the divine.</note>, the lower powers are always called through the superior deities. Therefore, among the spirits, a certain leader of those who hold sovereignty over **generation** <note>original: "generationem" — the realm of physical birth, change, and becoming, as opposed to the eternal realm of the gods.</note> sends down his own spirit to each individual. After his own is present to each person, he then reveals the worship appropriate for him, and makes known his name and the proper mode of his invocation. And this is the appropriate order of spirits: for one order is akin to those invoking; another proceeds from more ancient causes; another produces a harmony among them, contributing commonly to the same end. Do not, therefore, think divine invocations are similar to human ones, nor compare the **ineffable** <note>original: "ineffabiles" — things that are beyond the power of words to describe or which are too sacred to be spoken.</note> to the effable, nor compare those things which surpass every limit and every indeterminate mode to human commands and mandates, whether these be defined or entirely undefined. For those things among us have nothing in common with the whole **genus** <note>The category or class of higher spiritual beings.</note>, nor with those things which exceed us according to the entire order and surpass our whole essence and nature. Indeed, it is from this point that the greatest errors happen to men: when, out of human weakness, they are accustomed to reason about the daemonic dominations and weigh vast, significant, and perfect things by small, worthless, and divided ones.

### On happiness.

**Y**ou suspect whether perhaps some other way to **happiness** <note>original: "felicitate" — in this context, "eudaimonia" or the highest state of human well-being and spiritual fulfillment.</note> lies hidden besides divine worship, and you ask which one this might especially be. But truly, if the essence and perfection of all goods is contained in the gods, as well as the primary power and the first principle of goods there, then it is rightly only we priests, and those who have similarly dedicated themselves to the higher beings and [attain] a lawful union with them...

2 (11)

...having followed them, we studiously pursue the beginning and end of all good things. In this state, certainly, both the contemplation of truth is present, and the consummation of **intellectual knowledge** <note>original: "intellectualis scientiæ" — in Neoplatonism, this refers to 'Noesis,' a direct, intuitive grasp of divine reality higher than mere logical reasoning.</note>. And along with the knowledge of the gods, a conversion toward ourselves and the recognition of our own nature also follows. Indeed, you suspect in vain that perhaps the religious man depends on human opinions and favors. For what leisure can there be for a soul dedicated to the gods to listen to human praises?

-> That Religion is True. <-

<margin>f</margin>
Nor do you rightly doubt what follows, lest perhaps the religious man himself be deceived, where you say the soul often fabricates great things from chance events. What beginning for fictions can there be in things that truly exist? Is it not the **imaginative power** <note>original: "potentia phantastica" — the faculty of the soul that creates mental images; Iamblichus argues that when the mind is focused on higher truths, this lower "dream-making" faculty is silent.</note> within us that fashions and transforms images? And when the intellectual life acts perfectly, no imagination arises. Is not truth itself present with the gods according to their essence? Is it not much more the case that truth is founded upon the harmony found in intelligible things? Therefore, such things are spread by you and others in vain. Furthermore, where you and others slander religious people as charlatans, empty, and boastful, you depart further from the truth. For just as in other arts, so too in religion there are those who falsely profess it. Such a profession departs further from religion than anything else; for evil is more contrary to good than it is to the "non-good."

-> On natural, artificial, and divine foreknowledge. <-

<margin>f</margin>
If some natural aptitude for foretelling the future exists within us—just as animals have a natural foreknowledge of earthquakes, storms, and cold—such a "pre-notion" does not seem to have anything venerable about it. For such a natural inkling follows from the sharpness of the senses, or a kind of empathy, or some other commotion of the natural powers. Nor, again, if someone predicts according to the discourse of reason or the observation of signs preceding certain effects—as doctors are accustomed to foresee a fever from a contraction of the pulse and shivering—does such a presence seem to be particularly worthy of honor. For it proceeds from a human, suspect, and bodily condition. 

Therefore, only the **prophecy** <note>original: "vaticinium" — specifically refers to divinely inspired oracles or predictions.</note> that comes from the divine truly exhibits the divine life to us, while it possesses both foresight and divine intelligences. It renders us truly divine and brings to us a legitimate good; for the most blessed intelligence of the gods is abundantly filled with all good things. You might suspect, perhaps, that prophets inspired by the divine foresee what is to come, yet are not happy because of it. For they are able to foresee, yet they do not know the future...

...to use [reasoning], but on the contrary, it must be said that every foreknowledge is divinely inspired for the good and is filled with goodness, and it is possessed of order and decorum. And it brings utility to us; for the gods, along with the omen, also suggest a faculty for avoiding and shunning the inconveniences naturally looming over us. And when it is necessary to exercise virtue, and for this the ignorance of the future contributes, they themselves hide the future so that the soul might become better as a result. But when this is of no consequence, and it is beneficial for the soul to foresee so that they might return safely to higher realms, then they instill prophecy deep within the middle essences of the souls.

### The Way to Happiness

<margin>q</margin> Next, you asked what is the way to happiness, and in what thing happiness itself consists. Listen then to this: the man who is an intellect <note>original: "intellectus homo" — in Neoplatonism, this refers to the true, spiritual man whose essence is pure thought.</note>, capable of contemplation within himself, was once joined to the contemplation of the gods. But then he entered another kind of soul, adapted to the human form, and because of this, he is bound within the chains of necessity and fate. Therefore, it is fitting to consider by what principle especially one can be released from such chains. There is, however, no release except the knowledge of the gods themselves. For the very idea of happiness is to know the Good itself. Just as the idea of evils is the forgetfulness of good things and a deception regarding evil, so that knowledge [of the gods] meets with the divine. But this forgetfulness and deception is inseparable from that which is transient <note>original: "à caduco" — literally "the falling," referring to the perishable material world.</note>. Likewise, the former [knowledge] rightly measures the essences of the intelligible through the sacred paths of holiness. The latter, however, falling from the first principles and rejected, casts itself down to measure the material form. The former is again the recognition of its own parent; the latter is a departure, along with forgetfulness, far removed from God the Father himself, who is above all things and self-sufficient. The former preserves true life, calling it back to the Father. The latter leads man, the master of generation <note>original: "principem genituræ" — the soul’s role in bringing life into the physical world.</note>, down to that which never remains, but is turned in a perpetual flux. Let this, then, be your first way to happiness, possessing the intellectual fullness of divine union within souls. The sacred and deifying tradition of happiness is called the gate to the God who is the maker <note>original: "opificem" — the Demiurge or creator of the cosmos.</note> of all, or the place, or the court of the Good. It possesses as its first power a chaste and sober holiness of the soul, which is far more useful than a sober chastity of the body. Then, it possesses the adaptation of thought toward the participation and vision of the Good, and at the same time, the expulsion of opposites. Thirdly, it offers union with the gods, the givers of all good things. After which, individually and specifically, both to the parts of the world and to the di... <note>original: "di-" — likely "diuinis" (divine), completed on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page concludes the treatise by Iamblichus. It follows the discussion on how the soul is released from the "chains of necessity" through the knowledge of the gods. <meta>Significant bleed-through from the reverse side of the page makes some letters difficult to distinguish, but the context of the Neoplatonic closing is clear.</meta>

...with the divine powers diffused through the parts of the world, it joins the soul to them, and then it joins the soul to the entire Creator <note>original: "opifici" — refers to the Demiurge or the divine Craftsman who shaped the universe</note>. It offers on all sides a consensus with Him, and places the soul outside of all matter, joined now with the sole eternal Reason of the universe. For example: it places the soul in the very power of the Creator—which is self-generated, self-moving, sustaining all things completely, elevating, and intellectual—and which likewise adorns all things. Item: the soul is recalled to the intelligible <term>intelligible: that which can be understood by the mind/intellect alone, rather than the physical senses</term> truth, and is again made perfect by that which is self-perfect and productive; and by the other powers of God the Creator, it is gradually adapted according to the property of each, so that in their actions, thoughts, and creative faculties, the purified and sacred soul is perfectly established. And then at last, it places the soul within God the Creator in His entirety.

### Conclusion on Religion and Happiness among the Egyptians.

**AND** here, among the Egyptians, is the end of the religious and sacred elevation. They consider the "Good" itself to be one thing in the divine realm—namely, the God who is understood prior to all things—and another in the human realm: specifically, the union with the Lord Himself. As Bytis the prophet <note>Bytis is a legendary Egyptian priest mentioned in Hermetic literature as having translated the teachings of Thoth/Hermes</note> explained from the Hermetic books <note>original: "libris mercurialib’" — referring to the books of Hermes Trismegistus, identified with the Roman Mercury</note>. This part of wisdom, therefore, has not been omitted among the Egyptians, as you suspect, but has been duly handed down to us according to the rites of holiness. Nor do the priests trouble the divine Intelligence regarding trivial matters, but rather concerning those things which pertain to the purification, liberation, and salvation of the soul. They do not meditate on difficult things that are useless to men, but rather on the most useful matters of all for the soul. Nor do the priests hallucinate, clouded by some deceitful and seductive demon <note>original: "dæmone" — in this context, a lesser spiritual being that could mislead the unworthy</note>; they completely transcend the deceptive and demonic nature in all things and ascend to the intelligible and the divine.

These matters having been thus treated, I pray to the gods that they may grant to me and to you the true protection and observance of these understandings, which shall never fail at any time, and that they may provide the truth of eternal things throughout all eternity. And may they make us participants in the more perfect understandings concerning the gods, in which the most blessed end of all good things is set before us, and the entire authority and foundation of friendship and harmony among ourselves.

# PROCLUS

### Excerpts by Marsilio Ficino from the Greek commentaries of
### Proclus on Plato’s first *Alcibiades*.

The starting point of the Platonic dialogues and of all philosophy—the most important and firmest foundation—is considered to be the **knowledge of our nature**. For if this is correctly understood, we will be able to know more perfectly what "good" is consistent with us, or what "evil" is at odds with us. Nature is arranged such that just as the essences of things differ from one another, so do their specific perfections. Therefore, to find what the perfection of our nature is and how it is obtained, we must first recognize our essence. This is indeed what is proposed in the *Alcibiades*, and it is the goal of all of Plato’s teaching.

When we consider the essences of things, we must investigate whether the essence of a thing is among those which are **indivisible**, or of the kind that are **divided** around bodies, or of those which are placed **in the middle**. Likewise, we must ask whether the essence is **eternal**, or existing through time, or created in some part of time. Again, is it **simple** and existing before composition, or is it **composite**—and if so, is it joined by unbreakable bonds, or can it be resolved back into the parts from which it was composed? If we consider each thing in this way, we can then more easily judge what kind of "good" it possesses. It is clear that for a completely indivisible essence, the good is eternal; but for a divisible essence, the good is found in time and motion. Finally, for the middle essence <note>original: "mediæ... substantiæ" — in Neoplatonic thought, the human soul is the "middle" between the eternal divine realm and the temporal physical realm</note>, perfection is weighed according to the measures of its own substance; such a perfection requires time, but **primary time**, which can be aptly measured in the circuits of the heavens. We are ignorant of ourselves because we are occupied by a "birth-producing" oblivion <note>original: "oblivione genefica" — the Platonic concept that entering a physical body causes the soul to forget its divine origin</note> and are struck by the disturbance of life among rational forms. Meanwhile, we think we know many things that we actually do not, because we possess the innate reasons <term>reasons: "rationes" or "logoi," the internal blueprints or principles of things that the soul inherently contains</term> of things within our essence. There are **three types of conversion** <note>original: "conuersionis" — the "turning" or movement of the soul's attention</note>: for whatever turns, it either turns toward something worse than itself (when it falls from its own perfection), or it rises toward something better (due to the vigor of its own life and natural action), or it reflects back upon itself (due to a knowledge that is compatible with it and a middle type of motion). The turning toward the worse is a kind of "suffering" of the soul as it sheds its wings and is placed in forgetfulness of itself and of higher things. But turning toward oneself and toward the better belongs not only to souls, but also to the divine beings themselves, as **Parmenides** <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue *Parmenides*, which deals with the nature of the "One" and existence</note> teaches us.

Plato signifies in the introduction, among other things, that a mind fond of truth produces knowledge that is compatible with the things to be known. It does not produce a changing knowledge of unchanging things, nor an ambiguous and wavering knowledge of necessary and stable things. Rather, as he taught **Socrates** in the *Republic*, knowledge should be simple and uniform...

<summary>This page introduces Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Alcibiades, arguing that self-knowledge is the essential starting point for all philosophy. It describes the soul as a "middle" essence and explains the three ways the soul can turn: downward into forgetfulness, upward toward the divine, or inward toward itself.</summary>

## ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

<note>original: "De Anima et Daemone"</note>

...to know all intellectual things joined in a uniform intellectual power; <note>This refers to the highest form of intuition where the mind perceives truths all at once rather than through step-by-step logic.</note> then, through scientific and cogitative knowledge, to contemplate the "middle reasons" of things by the unfolding and composition of species. Thirdly, returning from the truth, to judge sensible things by the power of the senses through their own proper instruments of knowledge. Finally, by the power of imagination, to apprehend the images of sensible things. 

Now, <term>Timaeus</term><note>A character in Plato’s dialogue of the same name who describes the creation of the universe.</note> distinguishes types of cognition according to their proportion to the things being known; he commands us to judge **beings** <note>In this context, "beings" refers to eternal, unchanging realities like mathematical truths or divine laws.</note> by intelligence and reason, but to judge those things which are not truly "beings"—but are instead constantly becoming and perishing—by opinion and sense. He argues that the "reasons" <note>The underlying principles or logic (Latin: *rationes*).</note> of those things that truly exist are fixed and stable, while the reasons of things flowing in the world of generation are merely imaginary and contingent. For everywhere, reasons and speech imitate the very things they explain. 

Furthermore, **Socrates** says in the <term>Cratylus</term><note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the origins of names and language.</note> that regarding eternal things, names more closely touch the nature of the thing; but regarding changeable things, names also often change and depend more on convention. 

Everywhere among the gods, various properties exist. For some are the **craftsmen of the universe**, giving substance to the species of beings and their adornment. Others propagate life and generate various vital energies. Others preserve the unchangeable order of things and keep the bonds of the universe unbreakable. Finally, others, having been allotted different powers, preserve all things through their own specific beneficence. 

Similarly, the entire **amatory order** <note>The "order of Love." In Neoplatonism, Love is a cosmic force of attraction that pulls lower things back toward the divine.</note> is the cause of **conversion** <note>The process by which a soul or thing "turns back" toward its divine source.</note> for all things toward divine beauty and form. It leads all subsequent things back to that beauty, joining them to it, and strengthening them once joined; it then fills the things that follow from there, radiating the gifts of the divine light proceeding from that source through all things. 

For this reason, it is taught in the <term>Symposium</term><note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the nature of Love (*Eros*).</note> that **Love is a great daemon**, <note>The word *daemon* here refers to a mediating spirit or "power," not an evil entity. It acts as a bridge between the human and the divine.</note> since Love is the first of all to demonstrate this kind of middle power in itself. Love is the intermediary between the "desirable" (the object of love) and the "desirer" (the one who loves), and it is the cause of the conversion of lower things into higher ones. 

Therefore, the entire "amatory cohort," stationed in the vestibule of the Cause of Beauty, calls all things to it and creates a middle path between that which is lovable and those things which are called back by love. Because of this, Love declares itself the archetype of the entire <term>daemonic order</term>, holding this "middle state" among divine things, just as daemons hold the middle ground between the divine and the mortal. 

Since every amatory cohort possesses this property among the gods, we conceive of its summit as unique and hidden, coupled with the first and **intelligible beauty** among the supreme gods. We see its middle progression among the super-mundane gods, shining with intellectual character. Its third progression is distributed multifariously around the world, producing many orders and powers from itself and distributing these gifts to the various parts of the world. For after the unique and first principle of Love, and after the tripartite substance proceeding from there...

...variety, a crowd now shines with love. From this source, the choirs of angels are filled with love. Even the crowds of **daemons** <note>In Neoplatonism, "daemons" are not necessarily evil; they are mediating spirits between gods and humans.</note>, full of this god, follow the gods, having been recalled toward **intelligible beauty** <note>The ultimate form of beauty that can only be perceived by the mind, not the eyes.</note>. The army of heroes, together with daemons and angels, revel wildly around this beauty. Finally, all things are awakened, live again, grow green, and grow warm around the influx of beauty itself. 

Now, indeed, the souls of humans—touched by an inspiration of this kind and naturally related to God—move constantly around the beautiful. They descend into the province of <term>generation</term> <note>The physical world of birth, change, and death.</note> to offer benefit to imperfect souls and to provide for those who seem to need salvation. The gods themselves, and the followers of the gods, remain in their own proper state while benefiting those who follow them and converting them to themselves. However, the souls of men, having fallen downward and touching the world of generation, display the beneficial providence of the gods as far as their strength allows. 

Therefore, just as some souls are established according to one god and others according to another, they sincerely oversee these falling provinces and the souls wandering here. Some benefit the more imperfect souls through prophecy, others through expiations and sacrifices, and others through the divine help of healing. So too, the souls who have chosen the **amatory life** <note>A life dedicated to the pursuit of higher Love and Beauty.</note> are moved toward the care of talented souls under the leadership of God and the Beautiful. From the beauty appearing to the senses, they are led back to divine beauty, and they call those they love to join them. 

But those souls who fall away from this heavenly gift because of a perverse education—even if they otherwise possess a nature inclined toward love—stumble upon mere shadows of beauty. Because of their ignorance of true beauty, they admire and love bodily forms, remaining ignorant of their own true passion. For just as according to **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who heavily influenced Ficino.</note> a downward flow of the mind creates mere cunning, and a fallen portion of wisdom creates <term>sophistry</term> <note>The use of clever but false arguments.</note>, so too the gift of love, when it falls into an impure vessel, produces a life of intemperance and tyranny.

...and pulling the soul toward that [materiality], away from the contemplation of true beings, down toward the imagination familiar with things that fall away; thus, in the elevation of love, the crowd of common lovers is an obstacle, pretending to be a true lover and twisting the soul of the youth away from heavenly goods toward earthly and dark things. Similarly, in the most holy expiations <note>Rituals of purification or atonement meant to prepare the soul for divine encounter.</note> and sacred rites, before the god himself is clearly present, the attacks of certain earthly daemons <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, mediating spirits that inhabit the sublunary or material realm; they can be distracting or helpful depending on their nature.</note> suddenly occur, appearing in strange forms and disturbing those who are being purified and perfected, deflecting them from pure goods toward matter. For this reason, the gods command that you should not look upon them until you have shielded your eyes through sacred power. For so, they say, do the divine oracles <note>original: "divina eloquia"; likely a reference to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a text central to Neoplatonism.</note> speak: *It is not profitable for you to look upon them before you have purified and hallowed the body. For they, by soothing the souls, deflect them from the sacrifices everywhere.* Therefore, just as in the sacred rites the divine first appears only when we have driven out all this demonic force that drags souls into matter, so too the divine lover meets the beloved after the common lovers have been repulsed. Likewise, just as a good daemon guards each person from childhood and examines all their actions and words, and provides for them even before their parents, and stands by after the parents as a constant governor of the whole life, and is a guide for us to the judges after death—in the same way, Socrates conducts himself toward Alcibiades. Finally, just as a good daemon is present to us mostly in secret, providing for us without our knowledge, counseling in silence, and correcting us ineffably <note>Beyond the power of words to describe.</note>, so does Socrates act toward Alcibiades.

<margin>i</margin> **THE** Intellect itself indeed always acts within us and always offers the light of understanding. For then the intellect shines upon us, then it speaks as if with us, then it communicates its voice to us, which before was present in silence.
