man in himself, and now man as a pilot, and not simply man but the charioteer. In general, that which is unparticipated <note>original: "imparticibabile"; a technical term for a principle that remains pure and transcendent, rather than being "shared" or "divided" into lower things.</note> differs from that which is participated. And that which exists in itself differs from that which is already reckoned together with something else. And finally, that which is exempt <note>meaning transcendent or set apart</note> differs from that which has obtained a coordination with another. Since, therefore, Alcibiades is understood in two ways—both as a soul simply, and as a soul using a body—in the respect where he is simply a certain soul, Socrates acts as a Mind <note>original: "mentis"; the higher intellect that guides the soul.</note> toward him; but in the respect where he is a soul using a body, Socrates plays the part of a good daemon. <term>daemon</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, a *daemon* is not an evil spirit, but a mediating spiritual guide or guardian that connects the human and divine realms.</note> And he himself is both a daemon in relation to the man, and intellect in relation to the soul. Now truly, when we consider the demonic mediation, we place it between gods and men. But when we consider the intellect, we suspend the soul from the intellect at the summit, and the body from the soul. Indeed, you have another division in the *Symposium* <note>Plato's dialogue on the nature of love.</note>, where it is taught that daemons exist as a medium between gods and men; you have another in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> which says that the soul occupies a middle position between intellect and body. Therefore, the intellect and the daemon are the same thing: toward the soul [as a pure essence] it is considered intellect, but toward the human soul [in the body] it is considered a daemon.

### How love as a god is neither first nor last, and how in divine things there is the good, the wise, the beautiful; likewise faith, truth, and love.

<margin>a</margin> We ought to place the nature of Love <note>The OCR reads "Morem" (Manner), but contextually this is almost certainly "Amorem" (Love).</note> neither among the first of beings, nor among the last. Not among the first, because the "lovable" object <note>original: "amabile"; that which is worthy of being loved, namely the Good or the Beautiful.</note> is higher than love itself. Not among the last, because the lover is a participant in love. It is necessary, therefore, to establish Love between the lovable and the lover, and to assert that it is lower than Beauty itself, but prior to all other things that love. Where then did it emerge from the beginning? In what way does it proceed through the universe, and with which unities did it come forth? Since, then, there are three substances among the intelligible and hidden gods: the first is marked by the Good—namely the Good itself understanding from itself—where, as the sacred oracles <note>original: "sacra eloquia"; likely the *Chaldean Oracles*, which Proclus regarded as divine revelation.</note> teach, the unity is Fatherly. The second is designated by the Wise, where the first intelligence flourishes. The third is defined by the Beautiful, where the most beautiful of the intelligibles exists, as the *Timaeus* says. Doubtless, three unities also exist according to these intelligible causes: consisting uniformly in the intelligibles according to their cause, but first shining forth in the ineffable order of the gods, namely: Faith, Truth, and Love. Faith <note>original: "Fides"</note> indeed firms all things in the Good. Truth <note>original: "Veritas"</note> unfolds all knowledge in beings. Finally, Love <note>original: "amor"</note> turns all things and gathers them into the nature of Beauty itself. Truly, a trinity of this kind proceeds from here through all [ranks] of the gods.

In another way, however, it declares itself through other orders, everywhere enfolding its powers with God and his properties. In one place, indeed, it exists ineffably, unknownly, and uniquely. In another, by reason of containment and connection. In another, as if perfecting and forming; here again intellectually and paternally. There, it is entirely motive and life-giving and effective. It is the converter of subsequent things toward the prior ones, and truly the restorer and perfecter.

**Providence** runs through every single thing, even to the smallest, and is meanwhile subject to none. <margin>which</margin> Those who are more diligent in assigning the reasons for things hand down these two most powerful elements of divine and demonic providence: First, that providence proceeds from above through all things to the very last, and omits nothing, even of the smallest, from its reach. Second, that it receives absolutely nothing from those things it governs, nor is it filled by their nature, nor is it mixed with them anywhere. For it is not mixed with the things governed simply because it preserves and disposes all things. For the nature of the divine and of <term>daemons</term> <note>In this philosophical context, a *daemon* is a benevolent spiritual intermediary, not an evil spirit.</note> is not subject to the passions of particular souls. Nor yet, while it remains transcendent and separate from the things that follow it, does it leave anything among the lower things disordered or neglected. Rather, for this very reason, it adorns all things fittingly and is set free from those things it has dispensed. It is at once beneficent and pure, the adorner of all things, and meanwhile unencumbered by the things it has cultivated. It runs through all things, especially because it is nowhere restrained. Moreover, divine men provide for lower things most diligently and, at the same time, tranquilly. What, therefore, is to be said of the gods themselves and the good daemons? Are they not present to all things, yet free from all things? Filling all things with themselves, they are nowhere mixed with anything; running through the universe, they have nowhere surrendered their own life. Shall we not confess that the gods love their own offspring? Just as the poets imagine that Jupiter loves a girl, or Venus herself; surely because love of this kind is a provider, a preserver, a perfecter, and a sustainer.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON

## ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON

It is a certain union, yet one involving much distinction. For this reason, the **sacred utterances** <note>original: "eloqa [eloquia] sacra"; likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles, a text Proclus considered divinely inspired.</note> are accustomed to call the fire of this love "the joiner." For proceeding from the **intelligible intellect** <note>The highest realm of pure thought and being, which contains the "blueprints" of reality.</note>, it binds all subsequent things to one another and to that source.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, Love reconciles all the gods to intelligible beauty; it reconciles the **daemons** <note>In this context, daemons are not "demons" but intermediate spirits that act as messengers or guardians between gods and humans.</note> to the gods; and it joins us to both the daemons and the gods. In the gods, Love exists in the first degree, **above essence** <note>The Neoplatonic idea that the highest divine principles are "beyond being" or essence.</note>; for every race of the gods is of this kind. In the daemons, however, it exists by way of **essence**. Finally, in souls, it exists through the effect of **illumination**. This threefold order seems similar to the threefold power of the Intellect. For indeed, one Intellect exists as **unparticipated** <note>A source of intelligence that remains pure and independent, not divided among the things that think.</note>, set apart from all particular kinds. Another is **participated**, in which the souls of the gods share as something superior. Yet another is **infused** into souls from this one, which is truly the perfection of the souls themselves.

Plato himself indicates these three types of Intellect in the *Timaeus*. Therefore, understand that the love implanted in the gods is consistent with the **unparticipated intellect**; for that love is absolute, both from all things that receive it and from those illuminated by it. Compare **daemonic love** to the **participated intellect**. For that love is essential and perfected by itself, like a pre-participated intellect dwelling most closely to souls. Finally, you must assign the third kind of love—infused into souls by illumination—to the intellect that is possessed as a **habit** <note>Intellect "according to habit" refers to the human capacity for reasoning that must be practiced and developed.</note>. Not without reason do we consider Love to be joined to the entire intellectual difference. For Love has its primary and hidden substance in the **intelligible intellect**. For if it proceeded from there, it is also established there through its cause. And it seems to me that Plato found this god in the writings of **Orpheus** <note>Proclus frequently links Plato’s philosophy to the mystical poems attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus.</note>, where the same being is called both Love and a **Great Daemon**; Plato himself seems to have been content with this hymn. Justly, therefore, does **Diotima** <note>The priestess in Plato's *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about the ladder of Love.</note> call Love a "Great Daemon." And Socrates, when he disputes concerning Love, also disputes concerning daemons.

->First, concerning daemons in general. Second, concerning familiar<-
->daemons. Third, concerning the daemon of Socrates.<-

<margin>d</margin> We must next speak first in general about daemons, then about those who, having been allotted to us, govern us, and thirdly about the daemon of Socrates. Daemons, having been allotted their substance from the first **life-giving goddess** <note>Likely referring to Rhea or Hecate, who in Neoplatonism represents the source of soul and life.</note>, and flowing from there as if from a fountain, obtained an **animal essence** <note>An "animated" or soul-based existence.</note>. Those who possess a greater and more perfect substance have a more intellectual essence; those who hold the middle rank have an essence that is less intellectual and more **rational**. Those holding the last parts of the third and daemonic order have a varied and more rational... <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("ma-"), likely continuing to "material" or "matter" on the next page.</note>

# PROCLUS

<meta>Catchword: public (refers to the *Republic* of Plato)</meta>

...and material nature. Therefore, beings of this kind of substance are divided according to the division of the gods, inasmuch as they perform the role of ministers to the gods. For they respond and serve in different ways: some serve the entirely absolute gods, who began and led all things before the world existed; others serve the mundane <term>mundane: gods that belong to and govern the physical universe</term> gods who immediately preside over the parts of the world, and who are distributed according to the twelve celestial gods. These daemons are distributed according to all the properties of the mundane gods; for every mundane god commands some order of daemons, to which he imparts his own power as to a neighbor.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Indeed, a god who is a **maker** <note>original: "opifex"; refers to the Demiurge or creator-god role in Platonic thought.</note> bestows the power of making. A god who is **unchangeable** provides an uncontaminated faculty, and likewise a god who is a **perfector** provides a perfecting power. Around each and every god is an innumerable multitude of daemons, who carry the same names as their divine leaders. They are surely delighted when they are called **Apollos**, **Mercuries**, or **Joves** <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, since they express the property of their own gods within themselves. Consequently, mortal things obtain divine influences through these daemons; thus plants and animals are produced, some reflecting the images of one set of gods, and others reflecting another. From close at hand, the daemons bestow the gifts of their leaders upon these things, while from a higher position, the gods preside over the daemons from above.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, the last things agree with the first in their experience. For the marks of the first things are found in the last, and the causes of the last things are contained in the first. Truly, the middle genera <note>The "daemonic" rank of beings.</note> of daemons fill all things and connect them at once; they themselves contain the communion of all things, while they are participants in the gods and are themselves participated in by falling <note>mortal or decaying</note> things. Thus, if anyone should say that the **Maker of the universe** established this order among the daemons to hold the whole together, he will not wander from the truth. For indeed, **Diotima** <note>A wise woman in Plato's *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about the nature of Love and daemons.</note> attributes this order to them—connecting divine and mortal things together, channeling the waters flowing from above, referring all following things back to the gods, and finally filling the universe according to the connection of this middle state.

->He refutes two opinions: the first, saying there are no other daemons except<-
->our souls released from the solid body; the second, that of **Amelius**, who<-
->thinks that daemons are certain wandering gods.<-

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**W**e shall not, therefore, admit those who say that daemons are our souls which have already finished this life and been translated into another. For it is not proper to bring a being considered a daemon by its condition <note>i.e., a human soul acting like a daemon</note> into the same category as a daemon by its very essence, nor to establish the eternal middle-ground of all mundane things from a life that is manifold and self-changing. For the daemonic guardianship itself always stands in the same way, continuing the universe. But the soul does not retain its order in such a way, as **Socrates** says in the ***Republic***...

-># ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.<-
<meta>catchword: hi</meta>

...Republic <note>original: "publica"; this completes the word "Respublica" from the previous page's catchword</note>. For at other times the soul chooses other lives. Nor will we again approve of those who judge certain gods to be daemons, as if they were "wandering gods," as Amelius <note>Amelius Gentilianus (3rd century AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> thinks. Instead, we shall follow Plato himself, who calls the gods the masters of the universe, but subjects the flocks of daemons to the gods; and in every instance, we shall approve the reasoning of Diotima <note>The wise woman in Plato's *Symposium* who describes Love as a "great daemon"</note>, who assigns to daemons a middle rank between gods and mortals.

## Concerning familiar daemons. He also lists five types of daemons and their various duties.

<margin>c</margin> Since, therefore, daemons are established in the middle, as we have said, the first and highest among them are the divine daemons. These frequently appear as gods on account of their excellent similarity to the gods. Indeed, in every order, the first rank reflects the form of the order above it. For the intellect <note>the higher, spiritual mind</note> presents itself from itself as a god, and the most ancient part of souls is intellectual in its existence; therefore, the highest genus of daemons, being closest to the gods, is uniform and divine. 

The second after these are daemons already endowed with an "intellectual property," who preside over the ascents and descents <note>the movement of souls between the spiritual and material realms</note>, declaring and handing down the disposition of the gods to all. 

The third are the daemons who distribute the influences of divine souls to those that follow, and they complete the bond of those who look upward, providing the flow from the gods down to them. 

The fourth transmit the effective powers of universal natures into things capable of being generated <note>the physical world of birth and decay</note>, and they inspire life, order, and ratios into particular natures, as well as the entire production of mortal things. 

The fifth are in some way corporeal, and they bind together the outer extremities of bodies.

For in what way will eternal bodies agree with those that are perishable? How will the causes agree with the effects, unless a middle rank of this kind binds them together? For a nature of this middle kind rules over corporeal goods and provides for all natural abundances. Most of their number, however, are occupied with matter; they contain and weave together the powers descending from above from celestial matter into [physical] matter. They guard this matter immediately and preserve the variety and the "painting" of forms within it.

## The five duties of daemons: the first daemons join souls to their own gods.

<margin>c</margin> Since, therefore, daemons are many and multiform, as Diotima says, the highest indeed join the souls proceeding from the Father <note>likely referring to the Demiurge or the First Principle</note> to the gods who are their leaders. For every god leads first the daemons, and then the particular souls. For just as Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> says, the god who is the maker <note>original: "opifex"; the Demiurge/Creator</note> of these beings sowed some souls in the sun, others in the moon, and others in other gods...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the hierarchy of daemons from Proclus’s commentary on Plato. It specifically addresses the relationship between the soul and its guiding daemon, refuting the idea that the rational soul itself is a daemon, and classifying daemons into three types: by essence, by comparison, and by disposition.</meta>

# PROCLUS
<meta>catchword: Hac arbi</meta>

Indeed, there are divine daemons <note>original: "dii sunt dæmones"; Proclus refers to the highest class of daemons who are god-like in their nature</note> who have obtained souls according to their essence and join them to their own leaders. Every soul, even if it revolves around its own god, needs the benefit of such a daemon. Truly, the second class of daemons manages the ascents and descents of souls, and through these, many choices are made for the souls. Certainly, the most perfect of souls, which lead a life in the realm of generation <note>the material, changing world</note> without being entangled in earthly commerce—just as they have chosen a life agreeable to their own god—so too do they live according to a divine daemon. This daemon, while they formerly remained among the higher beings, had joined them to their own god. For this reason, that Egyptian marveled at Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; an Egyptian priest reportedly attempted to summon Plotinus's guardian daemon at the Temple of Isis, only to find a god appeared instead</note> as if he were governed by a certain divine daemon. Therefore, concerning souls who live their lives here as if they are soon to return to the heights, this daemon is the same here as it is above. But concerning less perfect souls, the daemon according to essence is one thing, and the one that accompanies the newly brought-forth life is another.

A daemon is spoken of in three ways: either by **essence**, or by **comparison**, or by a certain **disposition** <note>original: "habitudine"; referring to the soul’s state or orientation</note>.

<margin>s</margin>
If these things are correctly established, no one will now agree with those who say that our rational soul is itself a daemon. For a daemon is something other than a human, as Diotima <note>The wise woman in Plato's *Symposium* who explains the nature of Love as a daemon</note> teaches, placing daemons between gods and humans. Socrates himself signifies this here, where he distinguishes between human causes and daemonic causes, saying: "not indeed for a human cause, but a daemonic obstacle <note>original: "dæmonicum obstaculum"; referring to Socrates' "daimonion," the inner voice that warned him against certain actions</note> held me back." Since a human is a soul using a body, a daemon and a rational soul should not be thought of as the same thing. Now indeed, this is also clear where Plato, in the *Timaeus*, says that the daemon is the reason <note>the rational part</note> established within us. However, we must admit this only in the sense of a certain **comparison**. For a daemon by **essence** is one thing, a daemon by **comparison** is another, and a daemon by **habit** or **disposition** is another. For everywhere, authorities are accustomed to call "daemon" that which stands nearest in a certain daemonic order to that which is lower. By this usage, Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> in the works of Orpheus <note>The legendary poet; Proclus frequently cites Orphic hymns</note> called his father Saturn <note>Cronus</note> a "daemon," and Plato himself in the *Timaeus* gave the name "daemons" to those gods who arrange the world of generation from nearby. There he says: "to treat of the other daemons and to bring their generation into the light is a task greater than human genius can bear." Certainly, a daemon by **comparison** is of this kind: one which provides for each individual from nearby, even if it is a god, or even if it is inferior to a god. But a soul is called a daemon by a certain **disposition** when, through some more marvelous similarity to the daemonic genus than is typical for a human, it performs its actions and hangs its entire life upon a daemon.

<summary>Proclus argues that the rational soul is distinct from its guardian daemon, classifying daemons into three categories—essential, comparative, and dispositional—to explain why even gods or rational faculties are sometimes called "daemons."</summary>

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

## ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

By this reasoning, I believe, Socrates in the *Republic* <note>original: "i re publica"; referring to Plato's dialogue on justice and the soul</note> called those souls "daemons" <note>In Greek philosophy, a 'daemon' is not an evil spirit, but a tutelary deity or a being intermediate between gods and men</note> who have spent their lives well, have been transferred to a better lot, and now inhabit more venerable places. Finally, the daemon according to its own essence is not called a daemon because of its relationship to lower things, nor because of some similarity to something else; rather, it has obtained this name by its own inherent property, and it is distinguished in its existence by its own powers and different modes of action. To be sure, in the *Timaeus* <note>another of Plato's dialogues</note>, the rational soul is indeed called a "soul-daemon" <note>original: "dæmō aīalis"</note>. However, we are investigating the daemon of the human being itself, not the soul-daemon; we seek the one that directs the rational soul, and which is not merely its instrument. We seek, moreover, the one who eventually leads the soul, once released from the living body, to the judges. This is as Socrates asserts in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul</note>: when the living being is no more, the daemon leads each person to the judge—the very same daemon, he says, that had been allotted to the person while they were living. For if the daemon was obtained by that person while living, and it is the same one who presents them for judgment after death, then surely it had obtained the person himself, and not just the living body. Furthermore, starting from above and commanding, it governs our entire constitution.

<insert>Those who argue against the idea that the daemon is either an operating part of the soul or a part set over it.</insert>

But those people are not to be approved of who, having dismissed the rational soul, say that the daemon is that which operates within the soul—as if in the living, reason itself were the daemon; or in the angry, the irascible part <note>the "thumos" or spirited part of the soul</note>; or in the desiring, the concupiscible part <note>the "epithumia" or part of the soul driven by physical appetite</note>. Nor, again, should we listen to those who say that the daemon is that which immediately presides over whatever part is operating in our life—as if reason presided over the angry, or the power of anger over the lustful. In the first place, to say that daemons are parts of the human soul is the view of those who admire human life too much. Such people do not approve of Socrates in the *Republic*, who arranges the heroic and human race after the gods and daemons, and who rebukes the poets for introducing heroes who are no better than men, but are instead enslaved to similar passions. Socrates, therefore, in rebuking such things, would be far from the opinion of placing daemons (who are superior to heroes) among the parts and powers of the soul. For from this, it would follow that things which are better by their very essence would be placed inside to complete things that are worse. Furthermore, changes in our lives would lead to various changes in the daemons. For a greedy man is often changed into an ambitious life, and an ambitious man into a life lived according to right opinion, and this man into one endowed with scientific knowledge. Thus, one daemon would exist at one time, and another at another. For the very part acting in the soul is sometimes one, sometimes another. If, therefore, either this operating part itself or the part presiding closely over it were the daemon, the daemons would surely change along with the mutations of human life, and there would be many daemons in a single life.

<summary>Proclus argues that the 'daemon' is a distinct, superior entity that governs the soul, rather than being a mere psychological faculty or part of the soul itself. He cites Plato's Republic, Timaeus, and Phaedo to show that the daemon serves as a lifelong guide and a post-mortem judge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the "daemon" (the guiding spirit or tutelary genius), focusing on why the daemon remains constant throughout a person's life and how it differs from the "Intellect" (the higher mind). It specifically references the teachings of Plato and the personal "daemon" of Socrates.</meta>

->PROCLUS<-

The same soul would [otherwise] obtain different daemons, which can in no way happen. For the soul never changes the daemon's leadership within the same course of life; instead, the same daemon governs us from our very birth until we stand before the judge of life. This is exactly what Socrates asserts in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul; here it refers to the "allotted spirit" that leads the soul to judgment</note>.

The daemon is not a particular intellect <term>intellectus</term> <note>In this philosophical context, "Intellect" refers to the highest part of the mind that perceives divine truths directly, rather than through reasoning</note>, but a substance differing from the intellect, positioned within the "breadth of souls" <note>original: "latitudine animarum"; this refers to the hierarchy or category of beings that exist between pure divinity and physical matter</note>. Therefore, those who think that the particular intellect is the same thing as the daemon allotted to us do not seem to me to be correct; they confuse the properties of the mind with the nature of the daemon. For all daemons are contained within the rank of souls and exist as secondary to the divine souls. The intellectual order, however, is something different from the soul; these things have not obtained the same essence, nor the same power, nor the same action. 

Furthermore, souls enjoy the Intellect only when they have turned toward it, received light from it, and joined their own actions to it. By contrast, they are under the daemon's leadership through their entire life, through all their conduct, and through everything—whether those things proceed from fate or from providence. For it is the daemon itself that rules our entire life, fulfills the choices we made before birth, and delivers the gifts of fate and the rewards granted by the gods who lead fate. It even suggests and measures out the illuminations that come from providence. 

Now, insofar as we are certain kinds of souls, we depend on the Intellect alone; but insofar as we are souls using a body, we also need a daemon. For this reason, Plato called the Intellect the "governor of the soul" in the *Phaedrus*, but everywhere else he called the daemon the "observer and caretaker of men." Indeed, no one who considers this rightly will find any other single providence so near to us, and so concerned with all our affairs, as this daemonic providence and care. For the Intellect is shared in by the rational soul (as we have said), but not at all by the body. Nature is shared in by the body, but not at all by the Intellect. 

The rational soul masters anger and desire; however, it does not have power over accidental or lucky events. The daemon alone moves all things, governs all, and cultivates and arranges all our affairs. Indeed, it perfects our reason, tempers our disturbances, inspires our nature, sustains the physical body, supplies us with chance occurrences, fulfills the requirements of fate, and grants the gifts of providence. This daemon exists as the unique ruler of the whole person, holding the rudders of our entire life and governing all things within us and around us.

> Three things to note concerning the daemon of Socrates: first, that it is also called a god; second, that it appears through a voice; third, that it calls him back but does not drive him forward.

**CONCERNING** the daemon of Socrates, we must consider three things. First, that he calls it a "god," as is evident here and in the *Apology* <note>The dialogue recording Socrates' trial</note>. Second, that it gave a sign to Socrates by means of a voice, which appears in the *Theages* and the *Phaedrus* <note>Other Platonic dialogues where Socrates discusses his "divine sign" (daimonion)</note>. Third, that it used to call Socrates back [from an action], but did not provoke <note>original: "prouoca[bat]"; the text cuts off, indicating the daemon typically warned Socrates *against* doing something rather than commanding him to start something</note>...

<summary>Proclus argues that the daemon is a constant, lifelong guardian distinct from the human intellect, acting as the primary intermediary between the individual and the forces of fate and providence. He begins a specific analysis of Socrates' famous "divine sign" or daemon, noting its god-like status and its vocal, cautionary nature.</summary>

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

...as the *Apology* <note>Plato’s *Apology of Socrates*, the famous account of his trial and defense</note> testifies. At the source of divine souls—those which have chosen a life of the intellect—daemons are divine, being the highest in the genus of daemons. They participate in the gods before all others; for just as there is a "daemon" within the gods, so too there is a "god" within the daemons. But there [in the gods], the substance <term>substantia</term> is divine, while the proportion <term>proportio</term> <note>Meaning the relational role or the way the entity manifests within the cosmic order</note> is daemonic. In daemons, however, the property is daemonic, while the proportion declares a divine essence. Indeed, they so far excel all other daemons that they frequently appear as gods. 

Rightly, therefore, Socrates calls his daemon both a "daemon" and a "god," as it is the highest of the daemonic order. For this reason, Socrates was perfected, being governed by such a daemon and directing himself toward the standard set by that daemon. Therefore, pay attention to what concerns that "voice" of the daemon. Socrates truly first enjoyed the daemon's inspiration through his intellect and his knowledge of separate things <note>Meaning abstract spiritual realities or the Platonic "Forms," which exist separately from physical matter</note>, which continually recalled him to divine love. Secondly, he directed his providence <term>providentia</term> <note>Here used to mean careful foresight and management of his duties on earth</note> toward lesser matters in the business of life. According to the action of the daemon itself, he received light proceeding from it—not merely by intelligence or thought, nor by the powers of opinion alone, but also in his very spirit <term>spiritus</term>, as that daemonic inspiration would suddenly go forth throughout his whole life and move his physical senses.

For it is clear that from the same action hanging over us from above, the reason <term>ratio</term> enjoys the gift in one way, the imagination in another, and the sense in another; each of the faculties within us is moved and acted upon by the daemon according to its own specific condition. Therefore, the voice did not fall upon Socrates passively from the outside; rather, it was an inspiration proceeding from his innermost parts through the whole soul. Advancing even to the instruments of the senses, it finally emerged as a voice, coming into his awareness not so much by any physical sense as by a "con-sense" <note>original: "consensu"; this implies a shared internal perception or a harmony between the spiritual inspiration and the physical hearing</note>. For such illuminations from good daemons and gods are accustomed to happen in this way.

->Other daemons, ordered under various gods, have diverse offices among themselves.<-

<margin>q</margin> As for what was said about the daemon of Socrates—namely, that it restrained him rather than urged him on—this is not a benefit common to all our daemons. Therefore, because Socrates' character was full of natural talent and love toward men, and was already inclined toward good deeds of its own accord, he did not need daemonic exhortation. Yet the daemon would dissuade him whenever he approached those who were unsuitable or unready for his teaching; clearly, he was one who needed the bridle rather than the spurs <note>A metaphor suggesting Socrates was already so self-motivated to do good that he only required restraint from errors, not a push to act</note>.

Furthermore, some daemons possess a purifying and untainted power; others possess a generative power, others a perfecting one, others a creative one, and they are divided entirely according to the properties and powers of the gods under whom they are ordered. Now, according to their substance, each daemon sponsors their clients toward a blessed life: some indeed moving us toward the care of lesser things, while others pull us back from external actions.

<summary>This page explores the hierarchy of daemons, explaining how Socrates' personal daemon acted as a divine inspiration that moved his soul and senses from within. It highlights that Socrates' daemon primarily functioned to restrain him because his own virtuous character already inclined him toward the good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary by Proclus on the nature of Socrates' "daemon" (divine spirit), specifically focusing on its purifying role and its place in the cosmic hierarchy between humans and gods.</meta>

-># PROCLUS<-

It seems, therefore, that the daemon of Socrates obtained a cleansing <term>purgatory</term> <note>original: "purgatoriam"; referring to the process of purifying the soul from material distractions</note> property of this kind, being the cause of an untainted life. It is ordained under the power of **Apollo**, who presides over all universal purification with a uniform virtue. By this virtue, the daemon separates Socrates from excessive commerce with the common crowd and draws him back to the inner sanctuary of the soul, toward actions set apart from lower things. Indeed, just as in the teachings of **Orpheus**, **Apollo** presides over **Bacchus**, recalling him from his dispersion into the "Titanic" multitude <note>In Orphic myth, Bacchus/Dionysus was torn apart by Titans; Apollo represents the force that restores unity and order</note>, so too does this daemon act for Socrates, being a follower of Apollo. For our intellect is the offspring of the Apollonian divinity.

To know the substances of gods and souls is the task of a perfectly purified intellect. Generally, however, we recognize their powers through their actions, and through these actions, we divine their essences.

<margin>d</margin>
Among these matters, Socrates promises **Alcibiades** <note>The young Athenian statesman who was a student of Socrates</note> that the daemon’s *power* will be known, rather than its *substance*. For the divine **Iamblichus** <note>A hugely influential Neoplatonist philosopher who lived c. 245–325 AD</note> says that to contemplate the substances of daemons—and generally of all beings superior to us—is extremely difficult for us unless we possess a perfectly purified intellect. Since even the essence of the soul is not easily known to everyone, only **Timaeus** <note>The speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus* who explains the creation of the soul and the universe</note> declared its entire essence. For its nature is entirely divine and requires a long exposition to be explained, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*. However, it is easy to explain the *powers* of the divinities; for we perceive those very powers from the actions of which those forces are the immediate mothers. Indeed, **Power** is the medium between **Action** and **Essence**, being produced by the essence while in turn producing the action. Furthermore, power itself has the greatest familiarity with daemons. For everywhere, the power of a daemon occupies a middle position. In the realm of intelligible things, it joins the "Father" and the "Intellect." For Power exists simultaneously with the Father, while the Intellect exists from the Father. In the realm of intellectual things, it couples actions with essences; for action is the offspring of power, while essence gives birth to powers from itself. Therefore, the divinities that are the media between us and the gods are properly designated by the name of **Power**, possessing the middle place everywhere. For true essence and true being exist among the gods. Power, duly ministering to the gods, has its place in daemons. Finally, action and effect, having progressed outward through their power, are turned toward us.

...to divide the things to be known according to the differences of those who know them. Thus, that which is eternal and divine by its very essence knows all things in an eternal and divine way; that which is human knows in a human way. That which is truly indivisible <note>original: "individuum"; referring to unified, non-material realities</note> surely knows in an indivisible way, or rather, it anticipates those things which are divisible. Because it is eternal, it knows even temporal things beyond the constraints of time. Because it is rational, it knows rational things in a rational manner. From these points, it is clear that gods and **daemons** <note>In this context, daemons are not "demons" but intermediary divine spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans</note> know the indefinite in a definite way, and the unstable in a stable and firm manner. Do we not see that many things unknown to those beings lower than us are, in the meantime, known to us? For those without reason <note>original: "In rationalia"; referring to animals or non-rational life</note> are unable to grasp the nature of the universal itself, yet we are able to gather such knowledge. Why then should we wonder further that those things which we only guess at through ambiguous and deceptive cognition are firmly grasped by the higher beings? For our weakness is no judge of their power, just as the irrational creature below us cannot judge our reason—even if that which is irrational within us or outside of us might stir our own intelligence. Why would it not be absurd if a mere conjectural foresight of the future were found in some places, but a stable, determined, and certain foresight were found nowhere? For the very nature of things cannot take its beginning from imperfect, impure, or contradictory things. If the guessing of the future partakes in ignorance and is not certain, where then is the actual knowledge of the future in itself? Where is that pure source from which that which comes later—and which desires that source—has drawn its substance, if not among the higher powers?

->The higher powers consult for our good, even if they foresee that we will not obey them.<-

<margin>a</margin> The **Pythian Apollo** <note>Apollo in his role as the source of the Oracles at Delphi</note> responded to **Laius** <note>The King of Thebes and father of Oedipus</note>, advising him not to father a son, otherwise he would be subject to the violence of the daemons. He foresaw, meanwhile, that Laius would not obey the oracle. But **Phoebus** <note>Another name for Apollo, meaning "the bright one"</note>, acting as a good provider, proposed the choice of a better life to him. And Laius certainly did not cause the god to err, but rather, because of his own ignorance, he was ensnared by future dangers. Indeed, the actions of all virtuous men tend toward their own innermost depths. Therefore, if a man has acted beneficently and divinely, he already possesses his goal within his own proper action, even if nothing is perfected externally as a result. In a similar way, daemons often act regarding us. Consequently, divine things frequently seem to meet and run ahead of lower things; meanwhile, they do not depart from their own seats, but while they remain within themselves, they seem to approach us because of the "aptitude" of the person receiving them. For in the invocations of the gods, and in encounters that happen spontaneously, divinity itself seems to approach us in a certain way, even though it is we who have traveled toward it.

## A dialectical rule concerning necessary and contingent propositions.

Masters of dialectic <note>The art of logical argument and investigation</note> are accustomed to saying that even if one has used ten thousand necessary <note>original: "necessariis"; propositions that must be true by logical necessity</note> propositions, but has introduced a single contingent one <note>original: "contingentem"; propositions that might be true or false depending on circumstances</note>, the conclusion will altogether turn out like the weaker part. <margin>a</margin> Similarly, if the very thing we seek to know has something of a material and unstable nature mixed within it, it undoubtedly causes our knowledge of this very thing to be indefinite and ambiguous. For cognitions of unstable things are not secure from refutation, but such things are hardly grasped except through a kind of likeness. Such also is natural virtue, because everywhere that which is imperfect, being related to matter, is most easily changed. Self-sufficiency itself primarily belongs to the gods; for the gods are the Good, being certain super-essential <note>original: "super essentiales"; existing beyond the level of mere being or essence</note> goodnesses and the fullness of all beings. Through them, self-sufficiency belongs to all others—to intellects, divine souls, daemons, and to us. These others are self-sufficient by a certain participation, but the gods are so by their very substance. Wherefore, the common and immutable opinion designates happiness by self-sufficiency; for to those whom it belongs to fare well, it is fitting for them to possess self-sufficiency.

<insert>The rational soul is from the first maker of the world; the irrational soul is from the younger gods. Therefore, the former is nobler than the latter.</insert>

We say that the rational soul within us is nobler than the irrational soul, because the first maker of the world <note>original: "primus mundi opifex"; often called the Demiurge in Platonic philosophy</note> procreated the former, while the younger gods <note>original: "dii iuuenes"; subordinate deities who, in Plato’s *Timaeus*, fashion the mortal parts of the soul</note> produced the latter. Indeed, the nobility of human families is an image of this "generosity" <note>original: "generositatis"; here used in the sense of noble lineage or high birth</note>, yet it has ignobility mixed in and changes in turn. However, the stable and eternal nobility of souls is derived from the gods, around whom they are said to have once been placed, and from the divine powers under which they were ordered. For those souls are nobler which are followers <note>original: "pedissequæ"; literally "foot-followers" or handmaidens</note> of the more sublime gods, depending on greater powers according to the distribution arranged in the universe. I assert the same thing also regarding cities. For from above, according to...

### ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

...while the strong difference descends even unto souls. And we say that some gods are indeed fiery, others ethereal, others celestial, and finally others are terrestrial. Again, of souls, some are from the solar sphere, others from the mercurial, and others indeed from the lunar. And this distribution of souls according to their location is such that one can truly take pride in it. Nobility is not measured according to earthly parents and cities.

More perfect souls have been matched to the more sublime gods and daemons <note>original: "daemonibus"; in this Neoplatonic context, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, serving as guardians rather than evil "demons"</note> who are around them, and vice versa.

<margin>s</margin>
Among these points, Socrates designates the difference of the good daemons who preside over us according to their essence, and the powers which they have been allotted in the world. Likewise, the more perfect souls are subject to more powerful daemons, and are preserved by them, and are directed everywhere as is expedient; however, the less perfect souls are subject to lower daemons. For just as souls are fated to be around the gods according to their dignity, so also are they rightly ordered under the daemons. And just as the gods are leaders, so also that Father and Creator of the world <note>Referring to the Demiurge, the divine architect of the universe in Platonic thought</note> is said to have set daemons as curators <term>curatores</term> <note>original: "curatores"; spiritual guardians or caretakers assigned to watch over an individual</note> over souls. Wherefore Socrates calls the daemon and god assigned to him his curator. He clearly asserts to Alcibiades that this is the only true curator of a human being. He is also the author of happiness <note>original: "beatitudinis"; a state of blessedness or supreme well-being</note> because of his wonderful power, which surely no man is able to provide for us.

**The order of things requires that after the ideal cause there are things that are always participants in the ideas, and entirely stable, then things that are ordered and always changeable.**

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s Neoplatonic commentary on Plato’s dialogue "Alcibiades I." Having previously discussed the hierarchy of souls and their divine origins, Proclus here explores why divine qualities (like Justice) must flow downward through the universe and how "Opportunity" (the right timing) acts as a bridge between the divine and the human, illustrated by Socrates’s inner voice.</meta>

# PROCLUS

For it was not right that Justice itself should remain sterile, imparting absolutely nothing of its own property to any other thing. Indeed, none of the primary principles are of such a kind; rather, sterility itself belongs only to matter, as it is the lowest of all things. Nor, again, was it right that what was first intended to be shared with others should be shared directly by those things which only participate in it occasionally. For from that which remains entirely simple and immutable, that which is composite and changeable is certainly too far removed. Therefore, it requires a certain middle bond to make contact with that higher reality. Nor, again, should that which is shared by things that can always be illuminated from above have its gift stop only at those things, lest this very thing—which is always suspended from the first principles—be the absolute end of the universe. It is necessary, therefore, to establish a threefold order, as we have said, not only concerning Justice, but concerning the Beautiful, the Equal, the Similar, and finally all the **Forms** <note>original: "species"; in Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in the physical world</note> of things.

Just as the gods bring benefit to souls by applying cures for diseases—that is, for sins—and providing fruits at the appropriate times, so also divine men seek the right **opportunity** <term>opportunitas</term> <note>original: "opportunitatem"; translating the Greek *Kairos*, meaning the "opportune" or "right" moment that transcends linear time</note> for instruction. But while the gods themselves determine the measures of these opportunities through their intellectual and divine form, men pursue them through science and knowledge. There are also those among men who hunt for these moments through the inspiration of a **daemon** <note>original: "daemonica"; referring to a personal guardian spirit or guiding inner voice</note>. For the presence and familiarity of good daemons has a special power within us to infallibly seize the right opportunity everywhere, which is exactly what happened to Socrates. Now, just as a specific place is properly destined for every body by nature itself, so also certain parts of time are suited to certain actions. And just as certain circuits of the whole world are the causes of fertility or sterility for animals and plants, so too a specific time is suitable for individual actions, and another for completing this or that task. Such a time is the "opportunity" of any action, bringing a sense of the "Good" and a successful end both to those performing the action and to the results themselves. For this reason, the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who emphasized the mathematical and harmonious structure of the universe</note> also named the very first cause—from which the Good is present to all things—"Opportunity" itself, since it grants to all things the ability to be perfect. On such an occasion, Socrates relied on his daemon regarding **Alcibiades** <note>A prominent and ambitious Athenian statesman who was a student of Socrates</note>, approaching him to say certain things at the very moment Alcibiades was thinking of coming to him to ask those very same things. For all things are joined together in this way, and thus a communion of goods is perfected everywhere, provided that the perfecting causes are most ready to hand them down.

<sig>g iii</sig>

## ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT. <note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE"; the word "daemon" here refers to a guiding spirit or intermediary divinity, not an evil entity.</note>

Those things that are destined to receive participation are awakened to it; and those higher powers, in turn, extend their perfecting power. The former have received the power of "fitness" from nature. For **power** <term>potentia</term> is twofold: one belongs to the agent (the doer), and the other to the patient (the receiver). The first is the mother of action, while the latter is the vessel for perfection. It is necessary that whatever is to act must be overflowing within itself and so ready to act that, even if no receiver is present, it remains perfect in itself and is moved to give of its own accord. Likewise, whatever is to be acted upon must long for participation and move itself toward that perfecting power; even if that power is not yet present, the receiver must be awakened to participation through its own supreme fitness. 

Since there are two kinds of causes—some being immobile and present to everyone everywhere, and others being mobile and present only sometimes to the things they perfect, and at other times distant—the **intelligible** <note>In Platonic thought, "intelligible" refers to the higher realm of pure ideas and truths that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses.</note> things are certainly present everywhere in the same way, always bestowing their gifts in the same manner. However, **sensible** <note>Things perceived by the five senses.</note> things may be present to those participating in them at one moment and absent the next, just as the sun is present now, filling things with light, and then departs. When things are thus, and when a fitness for one of the immobile causes exists within the one who is to participate, then that cause is simultaneously present and the work of the efficient cause is completed. In such cases, only the unfitness of the subjects usually prevents the gifts from being received. For those things which are destined to give always give, and are always present everywhere in the same way. Therefore, whatever has become "fit" suddenly becomes a participant in the cause. 

But when something is prepared for one of the mobile causes, even if the subject is ready, that which was to give is often absent. For it is necessary that this cause also be recently present, since it requires a specific place and time to give. In general, as we have said, it is necessary through all communions of good things that these two precede: both the perfecting power of the giver and the completed fitness of the receiver. The perfection of the giver must concur with the preparation of the receiver, and together with such a meeting, the efficient cause itself is carried to the patient according to its essence. 

Furthermore, a meeting of this kind is not accidental, nor does anything orderly usually arise from disordered or uncoordinated things, like things that flow together by mere chance. Instead, it is necessary that such a **harmony** <note>original: "conspirationé"; literally a "breathing together," referring to the cosmic sympathy between different levels of reality.</note> happen in some cases through nature, and in others through intellect. Likewise, it may arise from a certain **daemonic** <note>spirit-led</note> cause, or rather from a divine one. Indeed, it was under this condition that Socrates met with Alcibiades at the opportune moment for the same purpose; the "good spirit" was the cause of this timely meeting, determining the **opportunity** <term>opportunitas</term> <note>referring to *Kairos*, the "right time" or "god-given moment."</note> for Socrates to meet him. For opportunity itself, beginning from above among the divine, proceeds all the way to the extremes; and some opportunities...

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic theory of participation, arguing that for a divine gift to be received, there must be both a perfect giver and a "fit" receiver, brought together by a spiritual or divine "opportunity." This metaphysical framework justifies why Socrates waited for the "right moment" (determined by his divine sign) to approach Alcibiades.</summary>

# PROCLUS

[...divi]nity is determined by the gods. Another kind of life is guided by spirits; another by fate; and another by chance. For Fortune, as it is said, and Opportunity govern all human affairs.

->*Those images which you saw more closely in your homeland, you follow here above all others.*<-

<margin>a</margin> Our souls wander here among the images of those things they saw in their first home <note>The "homeland" of the soul is the intelligible or divine realm from which it descended.</note>, and they are more deeply affected by those images whose archetypes <term>exemplaria</term> they had contemplated more attentively there. For different souls are suited to different spectacles. Therefore, some dwell upon certain images and others upon different ones. For they love the likenesses of those things they had looked upon there.

Whoever indeed were the followers of great Jupiter <note>original: "Iovis"; the Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods.</note>, and lived together with him—having a leading rank among the twelve princes of the universe <note>Refers to the twelve Olympian gods who govern the spheres of the cosmos.</note>—these certainly, having come here according to the form of their god, seek a commanding kind of life. And though they are truly ignorant of what is genuinely imperial, they pursue the appearance of leadership among these images. If they happen upon wise teachers, such a passion leads them toward salvation through a certain return to the celestial realms. But if they linger too long among the images, they decline into tyranny. 

Hence, Socrates says in the *Republic* that souls recently departed from the heavens primarily choose commanding lives. For since a little while before they traveled together with the celestial gods and saw their power dominating all things, they themselves also desire a life similar to theirs, ruling over others. And most indeed abuse such a desire; very few use it rightly. Plato places the **Contemplative** life as the most excellent. The second is the **Ambitious**. The third is the **Voluptuous** or the **Greedy**. Those souls coming from heaven who were raised most correctly choose the contemplative life. Those also coming from heaven but who were raised poorly choose the ambitious life; the rest, coming from the earth, choose the others.

->*It is a natural belief in all people that the gods know the hidden secrets of souls.*<-

<margin>o</margin> All people naturally speak their innermost thoughts, passions, and desires to the gods, being persuaded by certain innate anticipations <term>anticipationes</term> <note>These are "prolepses," or basic concepts that the mind possesses naturally before any formal learning.</note> that the divinity itself knows all things, even the hidden movements of souls. Certainly every bond and community formed by reason requires the presence of a god. For what else unites many things and gathers together what is separated, if not divinity?

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.

### God by His providence confirms our free choice.

The gods set forth various lives before the souls, and for those same souls—after they have made their choice—they determine certain lots <note>original: "fortes"; refers to the "lots" or destinies assigned by the Fates.</note> which are suited to the chosen life. Thus, freedom of choice <term>arbitrium</term> <note>The capacity of the soul to choose its own moral and spiritual path.</note> is contained within the midst of providence; it is moved and determined from that source, and it turns within that center. These things are clearly described in the *Republic* <note>original: "re. pu."; referring to Plato's *Republic*, specifically the Myth of Er in Book X.</note>, where the prophet <note>The spokesperson for the Fates who addresses the souls before they choose their next lives.</note> sets forth lives before the souls, receiving the lots from the knees of Lachesis <note>One of the three Fates in Greek mythology, responsible for measuring the thread of life.</note>. And crying out among the souls, he says: "O ephemeral souls" <note>original: "o animae diurnae"; a translation of the Greek "ephemeroi," meaning creatures that live only for a day.</note> and so forth. Indeed, the presentation of lives is made by Lachesis through the intermediary of the prophet. But the actual choice regarding the lives proposed there belongs to the souls themselves. Now, the prophet there, anticipating all the souls' choices within himself, finally casts the lots. Surely, the thing itself which seems unstable and indefinite is always understood beforehand by higher and more perfect beings according to a single limit, and in a stable and orderly fashion.

### Three opinions of Plato.

From the words of Plato, we gather three things here: first, that being evil is to be judged altogether worse than not being at all; second, that the separation of the soul from the body frees us from the evils that dwell in this perishable region <note>The material world, which is subject to decay and "falling."</note>, and from the obstacles which here hinder the attainment of a fitting goal; third, that the very desires of souls have the greatest power over the forms of life they take, and that we are not such beings as are formed and moved merely by external things. For we bring forth choices from our own selves, through which we live our lives.

### Higher beings hold with certainty those things which are uncertain in reality.

You will receive from this an admirable opinion: namely, that those things which are superior and uniform everywhere anticipate the inferior; yet the inferior things are not equal to the power of the superior. Likewise, the knowledge of higher beings firmly encompasses the actions of the inferior within itself. However, the knowledge of inferior beings can never encompass the entire action of the superior. That which is higher receives nothing from the inferior into itself—just as the heavens do not receive any suffering from the changes of the lower air <note>original: "sublimarium passionem"; referring to meteorological phenomena like storms or heat which were thought not to affect the celestial spheres.</note>. Nor does an immovable cause introduce anything worldly into itself from the movement of worldly things. Nor do eternal things admit anything into themselves from things acting in time. Finally, this is a necessity: while the divine mind knows all things, it does not undergo change even when it is knowing that which is subject to change <note>original: "contingens"; refers to things that might or might not happen, or things that change.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic exploration of the soul’s nature, shifting from the theme of divine providence and the choice of lives (the Myth of Er) to the logical methods of the soul and the hierarchical descent of "the Good" into the material world.</meta>

# PROCLUS.

Argumentation is twofold: it resolves through negation and composes through affirmation. The former takes things apart, the latter puts them together, and both methods harmonize with the very nature of the soul.

Alcibiades <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue *Alcibiades I*, where Socrates questions the young, ambitious Alcibiades about the nature of justice and knowledge.</note> is unable to assign a time in which he thought he did not know those things about which he now deliberates; certainly he never sought them out at any time, nor did he ever learn them from teachers. But if he neither sought them nor received them from others, he surely neither learned them nor discovered them. If he neither learned nor discovered them, he rightly does not know them. If he does not know them, he is not a good judge in those matters for which he cannot assign a time when he thought himself ignorant. You see, indeed, how if a dispute is conducted in this way, we proceed sometimes by **composition** <term>compositio</term> <note>The process of building up complex ideas from simpler ones, or the soul "clothing" itself in layers as it descends into the material world.</note> and sometimes by **resolution** <term>resolutio</term> <note>The process of breaking down complex things into their primary principles, or the soul stripping away material attachments to return to its source.</note>. We speak by composition through affirmation, but by resolution through negation. Moreover, this composition and resolution entirely suit the nature of the soul, which indeed glides down from more perfect things to lesser ones through the composition of reasons and the adding on of certain *alien garments* <note>original: "alienorum quorumdam indumentorum"; a Neoplatonic metaphor for the physical body and the irrational passions that "clothe" the pure soul as it descends into matter.</note>, until it is enclosed in this thick and solid bond <note>The physical body.</note>. Conversely, however, it rises again to the heights through resolution and the casting off of those things which disagree with its own nature, until—escaping **naked**, as the sacred utterances <note>Possibly a reference to the Chaldean Oracles or other mystical texts favored by Neoplatonists.</note> hand down—it is joined to the Forms which are entirely separated from matter. For this reason, argumentation proceeding through affirmation descends from more perfect to more imperfect things, while that proceeding through negation conversely ascends.

->The Good itself, though it towers over intellectual essence, nevertheless extends itself even to the lowest depth.<-

<margin>i</margin>
<note>Space left for an initial 'I' which was not printed.</note>
**T**he Good itself, as if subsisting in itself above intellectual nature—if it is permitted to say so—descends even to the last things, illuminating and preserving all, adorning them, and in the meantime turning them back toward itself. First, indeed, it is present to those things that truly exist <note>The eternal Forms or Ideas.</note>. Second, to divine souls. Third, to the deities <term>numinibus</term> <note>Specifically the "daemons" or guardian spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and men.</note> presiding over the human race. Fourth, to our souls, and then to animals and plants, and to all bodies. Finally, even in the formless matter of the lowest dregs of things <note>original: "feci"; literally the dregs or sediment at the bottom of a liquid, here meaning the most degraded level of material existence.</note>, the Good itself secretly and ineffably performs its own duty before every order of being. All things, however, participate in it everywhere, each in its own different order. And so far as each is naturally fit, they report back to the Good. Some do so more weakly, others more effectively; some more uniformly, others more according to a divisible condition; some, moreover, eternally, others changeably. For just as more divine things have an indivisible essence, so they possess a Good that is indivisible and united. But those things which have departed further from the principles, being placed now in a certain distance and division, obtain their own Good. For this reason, such things, in a certain assembly striving toward the same goal and by a mutual conspiracy...

<summary>Proclus explains the soul's two logical paths—composition (descent into matter) and resolution (ascent to the divine)—and describes how "the Good" permeates every level of reality, from the highest Forms to the lowest matter.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Neoplatonism, Alcibiades, composition, resolution, hierarchy of being, The Good, emanation, soul's ascent, purification</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of the soul's journey. Having established how the soul "clothes" itself in material reasons during its descent, Proclus now explains how individual beings—lacking total self-sufficiency—must find harmony through the "One," and how the god Mercury assists the soul in recovering its lost knowledge through the processes of learning and discovery.</meta>

### ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT <note>original: *daemon*, referring here to a guiding spirit or intermediary being between gods and men.</note>

They completely require harmony <note>original: *conspiratione*, literally "breathing together" or concord.</note>. For since each individual thing does not possess the self-sufficiency that constitutes the element of the Good, it must at least supplement the defect of its nature through mutual communion. Thus, it strengthens its own weakness, which was caused by its division, through this harmony. Indeed, for this very reason, individual men—who are weak on their own—gather together for common counsel, thus joining their divided minds to one another; they strive to light a single light, as if from many sparks. Truly, the multitude never appears to provide for itself collectively unless it is organized around some "one" prevailing thing within it. This can be observed across the entire order of things: namely, that the "Multitude" is everywhere born from the "One" <term>uni congenitam</term>, and must be called back to that utterly absolute Unity through a related "one." The Divine Good has therefore inserted a desire for itself in all things, so that through this longing it might be able to impart its gifts to us.

->Mercury is the author of discovery and learning for us.<-

<margin>m</margin> Mercury, as the messenger of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, unfolds the fatherly will to our souls and thus presents us with **learning** <term>disciplina</term>. Furthermore, as he is the author of inquiry, he grants **discovery** <term>inventio</term> to his followers. Now, when learning comes into our souls from the powers above, it is more excellent than discovery. However, when it comes from our equals—such as from men who merely awaken the cognitive power within us—it is inferior to discovery. Therefore, discovery is a middle ground, suited to the nature of the soul which is "self-moving" <note>A core Platonic definition of the soul: that which moves itself.</note>. For through discovery, the very power living and operating within us by itself is most clearly revealed. Learning, however, has a dual nature: according to its better part, it fills the soul from its superior causes; according to its lesser part, it awakens the vital power within us from things outside of us, under the condition of being moved from elsewhere. Furthermore, the gods themselves often enough declare, through their manifest presence and expositions, that a certain knowledge of things is born in us from the higher powers; they show the order of the universe to our souls and precede us like leaders on the journey toward the divine, hanging lanterns <note>original: *faces phanales*, like processional torches or beacons.</note> as a signal for the path.

**Because of the innate notions of things, we think we know everything.**

<margin>a</margin> Our souls are weighed down by a **double ignorance** <note>A concept from Plato’s *Sophist*: not only not knowing, but being ignorant of one's own ignorance.</note>. We think we know many things because of the notions of things that were born in us from the beginning, yet we are ignorant because of "forgetfulness" <note>original: *oblivionem*, the Neoplatonic idea that the soul forgets its divine origins when it enters a body.</note>. He who is weighed down by this double ignorance seeks nothing further, just as the wise man himself does not seek. In this very respect, the ignorant person is in a way "similar" to the wise man—just as **Matter** <term>materia</term> is similar to **God** through a certain "dissimilar similarity" <note>Proclus argues that both God (the One) and Prime Matter are "indefinite," but God is above all form while Matter is below all form.</note>. For as one authority rightly handed down: just as Matter is formless, so too is God; and both are utterly infinite and unknown.

<summary>Proclus explains how the soul overcomes its inherent weakness and "double ignorance" through the mediation of Mercury, who provides both external instruction and the internal spark of discovery. He concludes with a paradoxical comparison between the formlessness of God and the formlessness of Matter.</summary>

<keywords>Proclus, Neoplatonism, Mercury, Hermes, discovery, learning, double ignorance, the One and the Many, self-sufficiency, divine guidance, matter vs. god</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic exploration of the soul’s ascent and descent. Following the previous discussion on how Mercury aids the soul in recovering its lost knowledge through learning, Proclus now contrasts the soul's two states: its likeness to the Divine Intellect through knowledge, and its likeness to formless matter through ignorance. He then aligns the seven stages of human life with the seven planetary spheres.</meta>

ON THE SOUL: PROCLUS.
<meta>Catchword: of the lower things</meta>

# PROCLUS.

Although all these things correspond to God according to what is better, they belong to matter according to what is worse.

> Through acquired knowledge the soul becomes like the Intellect; through **double ignorance**, it becomes like matter. <note>Double ignorance (original: *duplicem ignorantiam*) is a Platonic concept where a person is not only ignorant of the truth, but is also ignorant of their own ignorance—mistakenly believing they possess knowledge they do not have.</note>

<margin>a</margin><insert>A</insert>soul, through the possession of knowledge, turns out to be like the **Intellect** <term>intellectus / nous</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the Intellect is the divine realm of pure, eternal thought, above the level of the individual soul.</note> by comprehending the knowable itself according to its actualization, just as the Intellect understands the intelligible. However, according to double ignorance, the soul becomes like matter; for just as matter seems to possess all things while in reality it possesses nothing, so too the soul suffering from double ignorance seems to itself to have what it does not. Furthermore, there is a twofold cognition of souls: one is indistinct, occurring through a simple and naked understanding; the other is articulated, possessing certain knowledge and free from ambiguity. For we seem, as he says, to know all things as if in a dream, yet to be ignorant of those same things while awake. This is because we possess the **rational principles** <term>rationes / logoi</term> <note>The "logoi" are the inner blueprints or essential reasons of all things, which Neoplatonists believed were "implanted" in the soul from its divine origin.</note> through our very essence, and we "breathe out" our cognitions of them from this source; yet, according to our outward activity and production, we do not possess them sufficiently. Therefore, time does not precede the notion of the **Forms** <note>original: *specierum*, referring to the Platonic Ideas or archetypes.</note> that are implanted and constant within us through our essence; for we have held these from **eternity** <note>original: *aevum*, distinct from linear time; it refers to the duration of eternal things.</note>. But time *does* precede the knowledge that is produced through the distinction and application of these rational principles. Thus, we are capable only at the time when we first receive this articulated knowledge. For example: I knew what a circle itself is [essentially], but I learned what it is in *this* specific time; or I learned what the Form of justice is in *another* time, and similarly for other things of which we possess knowledge through actual practice. Therefore, regarding the thing itself which we remember, we do not sufficiently recall the specific time of its origin; but of the act of **recollection** <note>original: *reminiscentiæ*, referring to the Platonic theory of *anamnesis*, where learning is actually the soul "remembering" truths it knew before birth.</note> itself, there is certainly a determined time.

### The seven ages of man, corresponding to the seven planets.

<margin>b</margin><insert>A</insert>lthough the order of the human ages follows the order of the universe:
The **first age** follows the power of the **Moon**. For then we live according to the nutritive and vegetative faculty <note>Focusing on physical growth and survival, like a plant.</note>.
The **second** follows **Mercury**, when we apply ourselves to the study of letters, the lyre, wrestling, and similar games.
The **third** follows **Venus**, when the limbs swell with seed and we are immediately incited to procreation.
The **fourth** follows the **Sun**; for then vigor reigns, the perfection of age hastens, and it is the middle of life.
The **fifth** follows **Mars**, in which we strive for power and victories.
The **sixth** follows **Jupiter**, which desires prudence and an active, civic life.
The **seventh** follows **Saturn**. In this age, it is consistent with nature to desist from procreation, to separate oneself from bodily concerns, and to transfer oneself to another, incorporeal life. The higher things are everywhere.

<summary>Proclus explains that the soul possesses innate divine knowledge (recollection) but suffers from 'double ignorance' when tied to matter, and he maps the seven stages of human life to the governing influence of the seven planets.</summary>
