<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of how higher forms of knowledge encompass lower ones. It transitions from the individual soul's cognitive states to the cosmic "guardian daemon" and the universal harmony that governs everything from the celestial spheres down to plants and animals.</meta>

->ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.<-

## ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

...encompass the knowledge of lower things uniquely, and more excellently. For whatever the sense perceives under material conditions, the imagination perceives the same thing immaterially. What opinion reckons without a known cause, knowledge <note>original: *scientia*</note> comprehends through the cause; and so forth, higher things always contain within themselves, through absolute eminence, all the knowledge belonging to lower things. Thus, nothing of ours is hidden from the **guardian daemon** <term>daemonem praefectum / personal spirit</term> set over us—neither the movements of the mind, nor natural power, nor accidental change. Rather, he alone surveys and governs all things. In this universe, all the ends <note>Here "ends" refers to the final purpose or goal (*telos*) of a thing.</note> of everything arranged within it lead toward the very end and purpose of the world. For so that the world might be perfect, as **Timaeus** says, all animals—both divine and fleeting—were created. <note>Timaeus is the narrator of Plato's famous dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world; here, "animals" refers to all living beings, including stars and humans.</note> Similarly, in a well-ordered city, the ends of all parts serve the goal of civic skill. Likewise, just as each thing involved in the process of becoming possesses existence according to a single form, and is therefore not infinite. But the intelligible itself is all things, since it possesses the causes of sensible things; so too, any private craftsman is largely ignorant, once skilled, but the civil leader is absolutely prudent. For he knows both his own end and the ends of others, and directs the other arts toward the single life of the city.

Through the harmony reigning in heaven, the higher beings temper all other things harmoniously.

<margin>c</margin>
Heaven is full of concord and the fitness of its motions. Furthermore, the deities superior to us are participants in the harmony proceeding from heaven. After this, the well-ordered life of men adopts a consonance of character and a fitness of actions; from there, the gift of those same superior beings descends even to brute animals and plants. For these too are naturally participants in harmony. For the superior beings contain and perfect all mundane things by a **harmonic ratio** <term>harmonica ratione</term>, and they accommodate them to one another and to the world. Indeed, they harmonize the body to the **Intellect** by means of the soul as a mediator through harmonic reason. They join the circuit of **identity** <note>The "Circle of the Same" (identity) and "Circle of the Other" (alterity) are Platonic concepts from the *Timaeus* describing the movements of the heavens and the structure of the soul.</note> to the process of becoming through the circuit of **alterity** (as I might call it), which is assigned to the middle. Finally, they join fire to earth through intermediate bonds. Moreover, they cultivate every soul with harmonic ratios. And they couple every body with similar measures. And they perform every movement everywhere with musical measures. Therefore, the musical disposition within us is a gift of the **Muses**, although it is the final reflection of them. For the artful and contemplative dispositions within us have gods as their presiding guardians and derive their origin from them.

<summary>This page describes how higher beings and the "guardian daemon" possess a total knowledge of human affairs and how celestial harmony organizes the entire physical world. It explains that human virtues and artistic skills are gifts from the gods and Muses, mirrored from the divine order.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the "guardian daemon" and universal order to the philosophical importance of the "final cause" (the purpose or goal of a thing). It draws heavily on Plato's *Sophist* and *Timaeus*, as well as Pythagorean and Aristotelian ethics, to explain how the soul finds truth and how harmony is achieved in both the human and physical worlds.</meta>

->PROCLUS<-

## He who is ignorant of the final cause, is ignorant of every cause.

**I**gnorance of the **final cause** <note>The "final cause" (telos) refers to the ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists or is made.</note> regarding any matter results in the other causes pertaining to that same thing being similarly ignored. Since the "end" or goal is the first, chief, and most powerful of causes, it is for the sake of this goal that efficient causes <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note> act, and for this that things being made are completed. For this reason, **Timaeus** <note>Timaeus is the speaker in Plato’s dialogue of the same name, which discusses the creation of the universe.</note> considers this type of cause to be held as the best among the wise. **Plato**, in his work *The Sophist*, teaches that there is a twofold depravity of the soul. One of these is ignorance, which falls upon the reason; the other is discord, occurring between the rational part and the irrational part. This kind of discord is a disease of the soul, while ignorance is a deformity. For since reason holds the order of "form" within the whole soul, the depravity of reason is rightly called the soul's ugliness, just as the virtue of reason is the soul's beauty. Indeed, ignorance arises because of the dominance of the irrational power, whereas knowledge arises because of the command of the rational part. This deformity of the soul happens when reason is overcome—specifically when the soul produces actions that are unharmonious, inconsistent, ineffective, and ill-suited to its goal. In cultivating the soul, once impediments are removed, one must move the soul entirely toward royal contemplation. For the knowledge of truth is innate within us; however, we are prevented from perceiving it because of the passions that block us, which arise from the process of physical birth. These passions include forgetfulness, narrow-minded opinion, false imaginations, and immoderate desires. Once these are driven out, the mind must be turned back into itself, and in this way, it suddenly enjoys the truth.

---

## The goal of war is justice. The goal of peace is friendship, which is more desirable than justice.

**T**he goal of war is indeed justice. But the goal of peace is another, more excellent good: namely, friendship and union. For the goal of all virtue, as the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who emphasized harmony, numbers, and the soul.</note> teach and **Aristotle** confirms, is that once everyone has been made friends, we would have no further need for justice—specifically when "mine" and "not mine" have been abolished. Yet, even if all people were just, there would still be a need for friendship to gather men together. That injustice is the beginning of wars is declared by war itself, which **material forms** <note>In Neoplatonism, "material forms" are the qualities like heat or cold as they exist in physical matter, rather than as pure, abstract ideas.</note> wage against one another. For heat fights against cold—not when they are separated in space, but when one strives to occupy the place of the other. Since a form lacks its own seat, it rightly resists that which comes from the outside and tries to push it out of its place. Because of this, the principles <note>original: *rationes*</note> implanted in nature run together without rebellion, for each one stands firm within itself. However, because material forms cannot remain separate from matter, they rightly struggle against each other for a "common lodging." This is because matter cannot receive two contrary forms at the same time without confusion.

<meta>The text ends mid-argument, preparing to explain how matter's limitations necessitate conflict, unlike the realm of pure ideas. Catchword: "How" (Quomodo).</meta>

<summary>Proclus explains that understanding a thing's purpose (final cause) is essential for all knowledge and links the soul's virtue to the dominance of reason over passion. He further argues that while justice resolves conflict, friendship is a higher state of social and cosmic union that transcends the need for law.</summary>

->DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE<-
<note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE" - On the Soul and the Spirit/Daemon</note>

## ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

### How the soul is variously clothed while descending, and in turn is purged and returns.

<margin>d</margin>The descent of the soul into the body has indeed separated it from the divine souls, from which it was once filled with intelligence, power, and purity. Instead, it has joined with the realm of generation, nature, and material things, by which it has been imbued with oblivion, error, and ignorance. For as the soul descends, multiform lives and various "garments" <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "garments" (vestes) represent the layers of irrationality or material attachment the soul acquires as it falls from the heavens into a physical body.</note> are attached to it from the world, dragging it into a fleeting composition and standing in the way of the contemplation of separate things <note>The "separate things" are the immaterial, divine realities that exist apart from the physical world.</note>. Therefore, the soul must be led back from here toward that ever-watchful and upright nature; it must prune away those secondary and tertiary powers that grew during the descent—just as seaweed, grass, rocks, and shells cling to the sea-god **Glaucus** <note>Glaucus was a mythical fisherman who became an immortal sea god; his body became so encrusted with marine growth that he no longer looked like himself. Plato used this as a metaphor for the soul obscured by bodily passions.</note>. It must restrain those impulses that carry it outward and remember again the essence of separate things and the divine nature from which the descent began, and toward which it is proper for all life to strive.

The soul is self-moving by its own nature; the body is moved by something else; but because of their mutual interaction, each takes on the condition of the other.

<margin>a</margin>The soul is, by its very essence, self-moving. However, when joined to the body, it has in a certain way also become "moved from without." For just as the soul’s own presence gives to the body the final trace of the ability to move itself, so too has the soul, because of its partnership with the body, taken on the mark of being moved by external forces. Therefore, by virtue of its self-moving power, the soul is fertile and more inclined toward discovery; it gives birth to reasons and sciences. But because of its "moved-from-without" condition, it frequently needs to be stirred by others. Now, more perfect souls are more ready for discovery, while more imperfect souls stand in greater need of external supports. For the former are more self-moving and share less in a lower nature. The latter move themselves less, suffering more strongly from the corporeal <note>Relating to the physical body.</note> influence. Nevertheless, when these souls make progress—rising up from the body and collecting themselves out of matter—they immediately become more fertile and inventive regarding those things in which they were previously barren and wavering due to the clumsy laziness of a life touching matter and the filthy lethargy contracted from the realm of generation. We, therefore, by observing the <term>mean <gloss>The "mean" (mediocritas) is the balanced middle state or proportional center between two extremes.</gloss></term>, assign the causes of rational nature and its condition, pertaining especially to its more imperfect and more perfect states, and we judge these to be the paths toward their perfection. Whoever assigns reasons for these things without observing the mean—either rising too high or sinking too low—wanders far from the truth of the soul. For we do not approve of those who...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic exploration of the soul's journey. Having established the importance of the "final cause" (the ultimate purpose) on the previous page, the text now moves to the "descent" of the soul from the divine realm into the material body, and how it must recover its self-moving nature to regain its original purity. # PROCLUS

...[They claim] that the soul, having fallen into a moist body and being hindered by its obstacle, is mindless from the start. However, as the moisture gradually evaporates due to innate heat and becomes better balanced, the wise power of the soul grows stronger. This type of perfection must be judged as physical and material, for it assumes that the soul's perfection comes from the balancing of the body’s humors <note>In ancient medicine and philosophy, the "humors" or fluids of the body were thought to dictate temperament and mental clarity.</note>. Yet the soul possesses its own essence prior to the elements and the entire realm of generation <note>In Platonic philosophy, "generation" refers to the world of constant change and physical birth, as opposed to the eternal realm of "being."</note>; it is a kind of life that is mixed neither with the body nor with nature.

Furthermore, we do not agree with those who believe the soul is a literal part of the divine essence, and that this "part" remains identical to the divine whole and is always perfect. [They claim] that any chaos or disturbance only affects the "animal" part within us. Those who hold this view imagine the soul to be eternally perfect, always knowing, never in need of recollection <note>original: "reminiscentia" – This refers to Plato’s theory of *anamnesis*, the idea that learning is actually the soul "remembering" truths it knew before it was born.</note>, always free from passion, and never corrupted.

However, in the **Timaeus**, it is said that the essence of our soul is not composed of the primary ingredients, as the superior souls are, but is made of second or third-tier mixtures. And **Socrates**, in the **Phaedrus**, says that our powers are mixed with their opposite—the lack of good—and are full of internal conflict. For this reason, the better parts are sometimes victorious, and at other times the worse parts prevail. What more is there to say? Does he not say himself that our charioteer <note>A reference to Plato’s famous allegory in the *Phaedrus*, where the soul is depicted as a charioteer driving two horses—one noble and one unruly.</note> is sometimes corrupted, writing that many souls "go lame" because of the charioteer’s failings? And many more lose their wings.

Yet, there is a power within us more ancient than the charioteer’s power. This is the part that remembers divine things and uses the secondary and tertiary powers as its servants. We are clearly taught this in the **Phaedrus**. Indeed, as we have said, we must preserve the measures <note>original: "mensuras" – the specific proportions or ratios that define the soul's harmony.</note> of the soul, assigning it a rational perfection and growth; we must not derive this growth from physical things, nor from purely divine ones, if we are to be true interpreters of **Plato**. We must not twist the philosopher’s words to fit our own preconceived opinions.

Since the soul is sometimes imperfect and later perfected, and since it suffers the forgetting of divine things only to remember them again, it is clear that *time* also plays a role in its perfection. For how could it be moved from ignorance to wisdom, or from vice to virtue, unless it underwent these changes through time? Every change occurs within a span of time.

Let these things be said regarding the perfection of souls in general. From this, we should understand that one who knows what is just must have passed from ignorance into the knowledge <meta>catchword: cognitionem</meta> of it at some point; they do not always have the reasoning of justice ready at hand. Unlike those beings who are superior to us, we are born imperfect from the beginning. Nor is this simply because of the body’s physical changes...

<summary>Proclus argues that the human soul is not eternally perfect like divine souls, but must undergo a process of "recollection" and improvement through time. He refutes the idea that the soul's wisdom is merely a result of bodily health, insisting instead on its distinct, though fallen, essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic exploration of the soul’s essence. The previous page discussed the soul’s pre-existence and its independence from the physical body's "humors." Here, the author examines how the soul experiences time and how it must ascend from the chaotic multiplicity of the material world back toward the simplicity of the "One."</meta>

-># ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.<-

<margin>•</margin>...[that] we also attain a knowledge of what is just. For our essence is not bodily, nor is it made of material things. It is necessary for all changes of the soul to be measured by time. Thus also <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was a foundational Greek philosopher; the text here refers to his theories on how the soul acquires "habits" or states of being through time.</note> places the change in the soul according to its active state and its habits—and their opposites—within the realm of time. Therefore, no one doubts that when the soul is joined to a body and passes from wickedness and ignorance to their opposites <note>The opposites here are virtue and knowledge.</note>, it requires an interval of time. 

However, some believe that the soul, while remaining apart in itself, does not need time to act; instead, they think that time is created from the soul itself. I believe this view requires some explanation. For time is twofold: one kind is born together with natural life and the bodily motion of the universe. But the other proceeds through the incorporeal life. This [second type of time] measures the cycles of divine souls as well. Again, it completes the actions of our own souls even when they are separated <note>Meaning the soul when it is not currently inhabiting a physical body.</note>; whereas time stretched out alongside natural life measures our life lived together with the body. But it in no way measures the life of the soul as it lives by itself. Yet there is some knowledge within us that exists before all time. Some knowledge also comes to be within time. 

<term>Socrates</term> <note>The teacher of Plato; he often appears in these texts as the ideal seeker of wisdom.</note>, therefore, looking at knowledge expressed in action, asks what time existed before this. But <term>Alcibiades</term> <note>A brilliant but wayward student of Socrates in Plato's dialogues; here he represents someone possessing innate but unexamined knowledge.</note>, possessing at least that knowledge situated in his essence—because of which he thinks he knows even what he does not [actively] know—cannot assign a time when he first received it; for we have had this knowledge from eternity <note>original: "ab aevo" — a philosophical term for time that is eternal or outside of the linear progression of human events.</note>. Wherefore, if one speaks of one type of knowledge and the other of another, both are true: namely, that time preceded knowledge, and that you cannot readily point to a time which you can affirm preceded knowledge. For before knowledge that is not yet completed, there is no time; but before knowledge made perfect in action, time existed.

->Many steps by which we ascend from the "many" to the "one" by contemplation.<-

<term>Plato</term> and <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>Pythagoras was an earlier philosopher who greatly influenced Plato; both taught that the soul must find "Unity" to find truth.</note> command us to flee from the "many" <note>The "many" or "multiplicity" refers to the chaotic, distracting variety of the material world.</note> so that we may <margin>**P**</margin> attain the simplest truth. Indeed, we must flee the "many" of the external crowd, which distracts and deceives us in many ways. But much more so must we flee the "many" of the internal crowd; for this distracts and deceives even more. 

First, therefore, flee the varied crowd of the passions. Second, that of the senses. Third, of the imaginations. Fourth, of independent opinions. For all the "many" just mentioned are so diverse in themselves that some are contrary to others in every respect. Whence it is better to devote oneself to the sciences. In these, the "many" no longer holds any contradiction. For even if passions are contrary to passions, senses to senses, imaginations to imaginations, and opinions to opinions, yet no science is contrary to science...

It also outlines the Neoplatonic "ascent," urging the soul to move away from the distractions of the senses and passions toward the unified truth of the sciences.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s discourse on the soul’s journey. Having previously discussed the soul's relationship with time and its inherent divinity, the text now moves into the practical and philosophical "ascent"—how the soul moves from the many complicated facts of the world back to a singular, divine unity.</meta>

-># PROCLUS.<-

<meta>Catchword: deris</meta>

...is found. Therefore, in this multitude of propositions and notions, let us gather them into one and connect the total number of sciences with a certain single bond. For so far is it from these things being contrary to one another, that even one notion serves another, and all the lower sciences serve the superior one, having their points of departure from them. Here, moreover, it is necessary to move from the many sciences that presuppose a single one toward that very "One" which presupposes nothing further, and to rightly refer all things to this primary source. 

After attaining science <note>In this context, "science" (scientia) refers to structured, discursive knowledge or academic study.</note> and its study, it is now beneficial to set aside complex compositions, divisions, and multifaceted arguments, and from there ascend to the intellectual life and its simple intuitions and perceptions. For science is not the highest peak of knowledge. Rather, above it is the **intellect** <term>intellectus</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "intellect" (or *Nous*) is higher than "reason." It is the faculty of direct, immediate spiritual vision rather than step-by-step logic.</note>—and I do not mean only the intellect separated from the soul, but also that very illumination infused into the soul from above. Regarding this, **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE); the author refers here to Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*, where he argues that the "intellect" is the source of our knowledge of first principles.</note> also says that the intellect is that by which we know the ultimate terms or principles. And **Timaeus** <note>The main speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus*; he describes how the soul is the only place where true understanding can be realized.</note> says that this very thing occurs in nothing else except the soul. Ascending, therefore, to this intellect, let us contemplate the intelligible essence together with it; namely, by looking upon the indivisible and simple kinds of beings through indivisible and simple perceptions.

But indeed, after the venerable intellect, it is right to awaken finally the very summit of the soul's existence (so to speak), through which we are **one**, and under which our internal multitude is united. For just as we touch the divine intellect through our own intellect, so also we may reach the **First One** <note>The "One" is the ultimate Neoplatonic God, the source of all existence which is beyond even being or mind.</note>—from whom all things receive their unity—through our own inner unity, which is like the flower of our essence. Indeed, it is through our own "one" that we are most closely joined to the Divine. For everywhere, like can be understood by like: knowable things by science, things of the mind by the intellect, and the most unified measures of beings by the unity of the soul. 

Now, this unity, through which we act, is the summit of our actions; through it, we are made divine. This happens when, fleeing all multitude <note>The "multitude" refers to the chaotic distractions of the material world and the fragmented nature of lower thoughts.</note>, we take refuge in our own unity and become one, acting with singleness of purpose. Thus far, we have advised that multitude must be fled by proceeding through the ordered steps of knowledge. Next, let us proceed similarly through the levels of things that can be known to prove the same point. Flee all sensible things <note>Sensible things are those perceived by the five senses, such as physical objects.</note>; for they are crowded together, divisible, and utterly changeable. Therefore, they cannot be held by pure knowledge. Transfer yourself, therefore, from these things to the incorporeal essence. For every sensible thing has a unity that is merely accidental; it is dispersed through itself, full of infinity, and for that reason its "good" is divisible, accidental, distant from itself, departing and residing in a place not its own. When you have ascended...

<summary>Proclus describes the soul's ascent from the multiplicity of sensory experience and scientific reasoning to the simple, intuitive grasp of the Intellect, and finally to a mystical union with "the One." This process relies on the principle that the soul can only understand the divine through its own internal unity, which mirrors the First Principle of the universe.</summary>

-># ON THE SOUL AND THE DEMON.<-

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DEMON.

...[consi]dered <note>Original: "deris", likely the end of a verb such as *consideraveris* (if you have considered).</note> there and have been placed among **incorporeal things** <term>incorporea</term>, you will behold that order of the **soul** <term>anima</term> which moves above bodies—acting by itself and through itself, possessing its own substance in itself and from itself. Yet it is also multiplied, and it anticipates within itself a certain appearance of **essence** <term>essentia</term> <note>In this context, "essence" refers to the fundamental nature of a thing that exists before it takes physical form.</note> that is to be divided among bodies. There, indeed, you will see many relationships of reasons, various proportions, and many bonds. Likewise, you will see certain "wholes," as well as the parts and circles of the soul, and a multiform variety of powers. Furthermore, you will see that the perfection of souls is not eternal, nor does it consist entirely as a fixed whole all at once; rather, it is unfolded in time and engaged in discursive movements <note>Discursive movement refers to step-by-step reasoning, moving from one thought to the next, rather than knowing everything instantly.</note>. For such is the nature of the soul.

But after you have witnessed the multitude belonging to souls, betake yourself to the **intellect** <term>intellectus</term> and the intellectual realms, so that you may possess the unity of things. There, become a contemplator of that higher nature. Behold a nature remaining in eternity, a vigorous life, and an awake intelligence to which nothing of life is lacking—a state that does not require the cycles of time for its perfection. 

When you have inspected these things and seen how much better they are than souls, ask next whether there is any "multitude" there; and since the intellect is one, ask whether it is also universal. Likewise, since it is uniform, ask whether it is moreover multiform. You will find that it is indeed so. Therefore, when you have perceived that intellectual multitude—which is nevertheless entirely indivisible and united—transfer yourself again to another principle. Look above intellectual essences and consider their **unities** <term>unitates</term>. And finally, behold the **Unity** that is absolute and set apart from all things. Having progressed this far, you will have left behind all multitude and reached the very **fountain of the Good** <term>boni fons</term> itself. 

Since these things make it clear that the perfection of the soul is obtained specifically by fleeing all multitude—both external and internal—as well as the multitude of the universe itself, we can also conclude this: our souls do not merely gather knowledge <term>cognitio</term> from things perceived by the senses. They do not find the "Whole" or the "One" by looking at particular and divided things. Instead, they bring forth **instruction** <term>disciplina</term> from their own innermost depths, and they correct what is imperfect in the things that appear to us. 

For it is not fitting to think that those things which truly "are not" <note>Neoplatonists often referred to the material, changing world as "non-being" because it lacks the permanent reality of the spiritual world.</note> are the primary causes of the knowledge existing in the soul. It is not fitting that things which disagree among themselves, and which require the soul’s reasons and arguments because they are ambiguous, should come before a knowledge that remains eternally the same. Nor can changing things generate reasons that consist in unity. Nor can indeterminate things be the causes of a determinate intelligence. Therefore, it is not fitting to receive the truth of eternal things from the "many," nor to take the judgment and distinction of universals from sensible things, nor to seek the judgment and definition of good things from things that lack reason. Instead, it is necessary for the soul to enter into itself.

It argues that true knowledge is not gathered from the outside world but is brought forth from within the soul itself.</summary>

# PROCLUS

...[unpolluted] being <note>The text begins mid-word, completing the Latin *intaminatam* (unpolluted or untarnished) from the previous page's catchword.</note>, there to search thoroughly for the **true** and the **good**, and the true reasons for all things. For the **essence** <term>essentia</term> <note>In this context, the fundamental reality or "soul-stuff" that makes the soul what it is.</note> of the soul itself is full of these things. Yet they are hidden because of the **forgetfulness of birth** <note>Original: "oblivione genetica." Neoplatonists believed that entering a physical body caused the soul to forget the divine truths it once knew.</note>. Therefore, the soul seeks the truth by looking at external things, even while it possesses that truth within its own essence; it explores the good outside itself, having deserted its own inner life. 

From here, therefore, everyone ought to begin the knowledge of themselves. For if we distract our gaze into the multitude of men, we shall never discern the one **species** <term>specie</term> <note>Meaning the "Form" or ideal blueprint of humanity, as opposed to individual people.</note> belonging to them, obscured as it is by the multitude, the division, the discord, and the manifold changes of those who participate in that species. But if we turn our sharp gaze inward upon ourselves, here indeed we shall behold both the one **reason** and the one **nature** of men, removed from all disturbance. Rightly, therefore, **Socrates** separates the soul far from the sight of the multitude so that it may learn what man truly is, and he refutes opinions which are impediments to this contemplation. For the multitude is an impediment to us in the soul’s conversion into itself and in the knowledge of the one species. Here, variety overshadows the **One**. Otherness obscures **Identity**. Dissimilarity clouds **Similitude**. For in the realm of matter, the species are confused, and better things are mixed with the worse.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The properly natural life of the soul is not in an earthly body, but in a sublime one; therefore all forms here are sick and delirious.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;No one ought to wonder if—when we say that what is **natural** <term>naturale</term> occurs more frequently than what is contrary to nature, and while the latter is contracted into a narrow space, the natural is amplified throughout the universe—we nevertheless confess that the majority of men are ignorant and evil, while those who are the opposite are very few. For it is not natural for souls to lead their lives together with bodies and to be engaged in **generation** <term>generatio</term> <note>The cycle of birth, death, and physical change.</note>. On the contrary, a separate, immaterial, and incorporeal life is rather what is in harmony with souls. Therefore, when they are engaged in the realm of generation, they are like men inhabiting a **plague-ridden region**. But when they live outside of generation, as **Plato** says, they are like those who dwell in the **meadows** <note>A reference to the "Plain of Truth" or the celestial meadows described in Plato's *Phaedrus*.</note>. Just as, therefore, it is not to be wondered at that among those who inhabit plague-ridden places, the vast majority are sickly while very few preserve their natural health, so too you should not wonder that many souls placed in the realm of generation are subject to passions and are wicked. On the contrary, it would be amazing if souls involved in such bodies, bound by these knots, and surrounded by such great change, were sometimes found to be sober, pure, and undisturbed. Is it not amazing for the soul to live immaterially in material things, and to remain unchang[ing] in fleeting things... <note>The text cuts off mid-word: *incon[stans]* or *incon[cussa]*.</note>

<summary>Proclus argues that truth is found by looking inward at the soul’s essence rather than at the external world, comparing the soul's life in the physical body to living in a plague-ridden region.</summary>

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT
<note>Original Latin: *De Anima et Daemone*. In this context, "daemon" refers to a guiding spirit or a divine intermediary rather than an evil entity.</note>

->h ii<-

...[un]polluted to preserve itself somewhere. And since it has already drunk from those cups, it has not been lulled to sleep by these drugs. For in truth, **forgetfulness**, **error**, and **ignorance** are like a certain drug <term>pharmaco</term> that turns souls toward the **region of dissimilarity** <note>Original: *locum dissimilitudinis*. A Platonic concept describing the material world, which is "dissimilar" or unlike the perfect, unified realm of the divine.</note>. Why then do you wonder that many, according to their way of life, are **wolves**, many are **pigs**, and many others are wrapped in some other beastly form? Since this earthly place is the dwelling-place of **Circe** herself <note>In Homer's *Odyssey*, the sorceress Circe turned men into animals using a magical potion. Here, she represents the physical world’s power to degrade the human soul into animalistic passions.</note>. Many souls, because of immoderate desire, have been baited by these poisonous cups. Rather, you should wonder if any among mortals are found anywhere who are neither charmed nor ensnared by such potions—those who, relying on the gift of **Mercury** <note>Original: *Mercurii*. Mercury (Hermes) gave Odysseus the herb "moly" to resist Circe’s magic; here, Mercury represents Reason or divine Intellect.</note>, betake themselves to reason and knowledge. For just as you should not wonder if you look into **Tartarus** <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld in Greek mythology, used here to represent a state of spiritual punishment.</note> and see tortured souls—for that is the place for such things—so also you should not wonder if many souls living in the realm of **generation** <term>generatio</term> <note>The physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note> are disturbed, ignorant, and mindless. For the world of generation requires such souls. Therefore, just as in **Heaven** all are good, and in Tartarus all are wicked, so in the world of birth many are indeed depraved, and few are upright. For the world of birth does not incline toward the better and more divine extremes, but toward the worse.

## The wicked man agrees neither with others nor with himself.

<margin>i</margin> The wicked man cannot agree with himself. For it is necessary, on account of his **rational nature**, that he sees the truth in some way; yet, on account of his **disturbed imagination**, he is mostly ignorant and at odds with himself. This is shown by **repentance** <term>penitentia</term> which arrives when his disturbances are calmed. The intemperate man, therefore, because of an **intelligence** <term>intelligentia</term> related to the divine, sometimes thinks and speaks of divine things. But because of his desire and disturbed imagination, he departs far from divine **temperance**. And since he is always at war with himself, it is no wonder that he cannot agree with others.

## Those who know something agree entirely upon it.

<margin>o</margin> It is necessary for those who know something to be in **concord** <term>concordia</term> regarding it. The first cause of this concord is the determined nature of the things themselves. The second is that the judging functions of **cognition** <term>cognitionis</term> are the same in everyone. The third is that in the **first principles**, the intellect is united to itself. Therefore, whatever possesses intelligence is a sharer in this **union**. **Knowledge** <term>scientia</term> is a certain illumination depending on the intellect; concord, however, is an illumination proceeding from **unity**. For concord is the union of different things. It is necessary, therefore, that those who share the same knowledge agree with one another.

# PROCLUS

Each of us is a soul, and it possesses within itself all forms, both divine and natural.

<note>The initial letter 'T' for 'Totum' is missing from the original Latin text, likely left for a specialized artist (rubricator) to paint in later.</note>
The whole of Plato's purpose in this book is to recall us to the knowledge of ourselves, and to demonstrate that our essence consists in **forms** <term>species: the ideal, eternal blueprints of reality</term> and **reasons** <term>rationibus: the logical principles underlying existence</term>. It aims to show that the soul produces all sciences from within itself, and recognizes within itself all forms, both divine and natural. A perfect knowledge of ourselves would be to judge our powers from our essence, and our actions from those powers. However, we usually obtain a more common knowledge of ourselves by knowing our powers from our actions, and the essence of the soul from its powers. These three—essence, power, and action—flow together within the soul. For its essence exists in act, and its action is essential. For the soul becomes intellectual according to its act, and it becomes akin to its essence according to its own perfection.

The soul leads itself by free motion; it provides good for itself, purges itself, and instructs itself, even when it seems to be instructed from elsewhere.

<note>The initial letter 'A' for 'Animalia' is missing from the original Latin text.</note>
**Living creatures** deprived of reason are governed by external impulses and are cared for from the outside, specifically in that condition where the mover itself moves them; they are, of course, deprived of that faculty by which a thing is able to lead and preserve itself. However, the **rational soul**, because of its property of being self-moving and self-operating, can by its own nature act upon itself, move itself, and provide good for itself. Now, indeed, purification does not happen to us from external things, but takes its origin from the innermost parts of the soul. For every evil happens from external things and is foreign to the soul, but good comes from within. For the soul is naturally **good-form** <note>Original: *boniformis*. Having the shape or nature of the Good.</note>. And the more perfect it becomes, the more it claims for itself a life that is self-moving. This is because it only becomes "movable from elsewhere" due to its commerce and involvement with the body. Therefore, whatever it receives from external sources remains placed outside itself, like sensory objects and things perceived by the imagination. Only those things are truly *in* the soul which are made by the soul within itself and are produced by it. It is therefore purged by itself, since reason, beginning from itself, ends in itself. For this reason, what **Socrates** says is rightly understood: "Among those disputing, the one who answers is properly the speaker." <note>This refers to a Socratic principle where the person answering questions is the one actually producing the truth from their own mind.</note> If this person is refuted, and through refutation is purged, then certainly while he is being purged, he purges himself and frees himself from ignorance, applying the refutation to himself. This is consistent with the nature of a self-moving soul. This saying also confirms that **learning is recollection** <note>Original: *disciplinas esse reminiscentias*. This refers to the Platonic theory of *anamnesis*, suggesting we don't "learn" new things, but remember truths our souls knew before birth.</note>. For the fact that those who answer speak all things from themselves is the greatest sign of recollection—namely, that souls bring forth reasons and discourses from themselves. They only need someone to awaken them. They are not **blank tablets** <note>Original: *tabellas uacuas*. A reference to the "tabula rasa" or a wax tablet without writing; Proclus argues the soul is born already "written" with knowledge.</note> which receive shapes from the outside. For they are...

<meta>Catchword: enim (for)</meta>

<summary>Proclus argues that the soul is a self-moving entity containing all universal knowledge within itself, asserting that learning is actually a process of internal "recollection" rather than receiving external information.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of the soul's inherent knowledge. Having established that the soul contains the "forms" or blueprints of reality, the text now explains why this knowledge is often hidden and how the soul returns to harmony through the guidance of the "daemon" and the intellect.</meta>

->### ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.<-
<sig>h iii</sig>

For these forms are always inscribed within, and the scribe himself is inside. Yet not everyone can read what is inscribed, or even recognize that they have been written. This is because, due to the **oblivion of birth** <note>original: "geneſicam obliuionē" — the Neoplatonic idea that the soul forgets its divine origins when entering a physical body</note>, the eye of the soul is covered with filth, and from that very oblivion, people fall into passions. The only task, therefore, is to remove the obstacle that has been placed in the way. Knowledge brought in from the outside is not necessary. For souls have the doors of truth within themselves, but they are closed off by earthly and material appearances. If, therefore, one demonstrates things with great care, the souls—though prompted from elsewhere—bring forth the decreed answers from within themselves. By this very fact, they declare that the Platonic doctrine is true: that the soul knows all things, and merely requires something from the outside to prompt it to respond. Furthermore, when someone is being educated, that they should purge themselves is the work of a **daemonic power** <term>daemon: in this context, a protective spirit or higher guiding principle of the soul, not a "demon" in the modern sense</term>. For daemons do not act upon us from the outside, but they direct and govern us from within, as if from the **stern of a ship** <note>original: "ex puppi" — a classic metaphor for the pilot or governor of the soul</note>. Nor do they purge us as if we were bodies that received our capacity for movement from elsewhere. Instead, they care for us as beings who move by our own power. In this way, they both provide good things and purge away the passions. Socrates, therefore, acting in the role of a "good daemon," showed that a youth is refuted not so much by another person, but by himself.

## Why the wicked and ignorant man is at odds with himself and others, and why the good man is in agreement, and the knowing are in harmony with one another.

<margin>C</margin>ontingent upon this, a frequent discord within themselves rightly happens to most people. This is because they take some things in from the senses, some again from the imagination, others frequently from opinion, some from anger, and many from lust. For such passions are moved in men not only from opinions—as the **Stoics** <note>The Stoics believed that emotions (passions) were the result of incorrect cognitive judgments or "opinions."</note> teach—but also, conversely, they often change their opinions because of certain passions and impulses; they often bring back the worst opinions in place of the best. These people, receiving multiform motions within themselves from many principles and powers—and indeed from the lower ones—undoubtedly possess a soul that is at odds and discordant. But those endowed with knowledge receive their entire cognition from a single higher principle. For the **Intellect** <term>intellectus: the higher, intuitive mind that grasps truth directly</term> provides them with principles. Now, indeed, all true judgments are the daughters of the intellect. Since, therefore, they all proceed from such a principle of simplicity, it is only right that they are all in harmony with one another.

## Those who think man is composed of soul and body consequently separate the useful from the just; but those who hold that man is the soul join them together.

<margin>W</margin>hether the just and the useful are the same is a point on which others disagree. The Platonists, however, judge them to be the same. For the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus, who generally prioritized pleasure (defined as the absence of pain) as the highest good.</note> certainly, and some of the Stoics, when they place our ultimate end in that which is according to nature...

<summary>This page discusses the Platonic theory of "recollection," asserting that the soul contains all truth but is blinded by the physical world. It also explains how the "daemon" guides the soul from within and argues that true knowledge leads to internal and social harmony.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a Neoplatonic commentary by Proclus on the nature of justice, the soul's relationship to the body, and the nature of knowledge. It follows the previous discussion regarding the soul's internal "forms" and the role of the daemon in purging the soul's vision.</meta>

# PROCLUS

->...to live, and the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who taught that the "good life" required certain external and physical necessities.</note> who fulfill our "good" from necessary things.<-

They cannot easily confirm that the **just** and the **useful** are the same thing. Similarly, this is true for whoever says that a human being is an animated body, or is composed of both soul and body. For such a person will flee from wounds and slaughter—even if it is unjust to do so—so that the "animal" [the living creature] might be preserved. This is because the "good" of any animal is to behave according to its nature and to be preserved in that state. In this view, therefore, the useful is separated from the just. 

However, those who place the "end" <note>original: "finem" — the ultimate goal or purpose of life (the *telos*).</note> itself in the soul, needing nothing from the body, and who believe that the human being is actually the soul using the body as a tool—these people certainly judge the **just** and the **useful** to be the same. For they place both within the soul, and they understand that the passions of the instruments <note>original: "passiones instrumentorum" — the suffering or experiences of the body, which the soul uses as an instrument.</note> are separate from those who use them. Indeed, the argument proving that the just is the useful proceeds in this way:

*   Everything **just** is beautiful. <note>original: "pulchrum" — in Platonic thought, this refers to moral beauty or nobility.</note>
*   Everything **beautiful** is good.
*   Therefore, everything **just** is good.
*   And since the **good** and the **useful** are the same, everything **just** is useful.

<margin>The soul draws into itself the form of the thing to which it adheres; likewise concerning the "vehicles" of divine souls and our own.</margin>

Souls also draw into themselves the "species" <note>The essential form or appearance.</note> of those things with which they join themselves. Surely, when they liken themselves to the **intellect**, they soon claim for themselves an immutability in their opinions and their life. But when they couple themselves to **generation** <term>generation: the realm of physical birth, change, and decay, as opposed to the eternal realm of the forms.</term>, they follow novelty everywhere, and are carried now into these opinions, and now into those. In such a state, they hardly perceive the stable reasons of the soul itself. 

In this way, Plato indicates that the more noble and gifted souls—those possessing the intelligence of the inviolable purity of the gods and inserting this very purity into their own **idol** <note>original: "idolo" — likely referring to the *eidolon*, the lower reflection or "image" of the soul that interacts with the material world.</note>—are also accustomed to being occupied in some way with apparent purity. Since the essence of the divine garments is inviolable and their purity is immaterial, it is certainly necessary for souls to put on their own kindred garments by purifying them, keeping their "robes" uncontaminated by the world of generation, and not placing all their focus on the purity of external clothes.

<margin>Knowledge, remaining one within itself, fills many without being diminished; from this we infer that the soul is separate from the body.</margin>

It is indeed indivisible, resting in itself, and meanwhile it perfects all things participating in it, just like...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s nature, specifically how the soul acts as a middle point in the metaphysical hierarchy where the transcendental "trinities"—the Good, the Beautiful, and the Just, as well as Being, Life, and Intellect—converge into a single essence.</meta>

# PROCLUS.

<meta>catchword: truly</meta>

...even if something exists, it is nonetheless shameful and deformed if it participates in the "One" <note>original: "unius particeps"; in Neoplatonism, the "One" is the ultimate source of all, but without "Form," things in the lower world remain chaotic.</note> but lacks **Form** <term>speciei: here meaning the Platonic Form or Idea that gives a thing its specific nature</term>. That which is perceived by the senses possesses traces of beauty, but not of justice. For this reason, Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* <note>Referring to Plato's *Phaedrus* 250d: "But beauty, as I said before, beamed in bright light amongst those other visions... of justice and temperance there is no luster in their earthly copies."</note> that among fleeting images, there is no splendor of justice or temperance; only beauty has the privilege of being most clearly evident everywhere and most desirable. Therefore, where there is the **just**, there is the **beautiful**. Where the **beautiful** is, there is the **good**, whether you choose to look at the first principles or at the manifestations of those principles extended to the furthest reaches of reality.

All things participate in the **Good** itself, for it is the beginning of all. Only things that possess a Form participate in the **Beautiful**. Finally, only souls participate in **Justice**. Now, in the very center of all things—which is the soul—all these are connected to one another: the Good, the Just, and the Beautiful. That which is "good" within the soul is also its "beautiful" and its "just." Likewise, the Just is simultaneously beautiful and good, and the Beautiful is similarly good and just.

Nor is this statement true only regarding this specific trinity; it is true in many other cases as well. Just as among the first principles, **Being** itself precedes **Life**, and **Life** precedes **Mind** <term>mente/intellectus: the higher intellect or intuitive understanding</term>. Similarly, in their effects, not every being that possesses "being" also possesses "life," nor is every living thing immediately endowed with a "mind." But conversely, all intelligent things also live and exist; and all living things exist by the very fact of their living.

However, while there is such a distinction among the lowest levels of reality, these three flow together within the soul through this kind of trinity. In the soul, Being, Life, and Intellect exist as one; Life is both Intellect and Essence. Intellect is similarly both Essence and Life. For there is one simplicity in the soul and one substance; neither being, nor living, nor understanding is an accidental addition there. Rather, its **Intellect** is essential and alive; its **Life** is intellectual through its essence; and finally, its **Essence** is intellectual and living.

Therefore, everything is everywhere, and from all these, a "one" is formed in a similar way: its "good" prevails through beauty and justice, and its "beautiful" is both good and just. Again, the "just" is filled with the good and the beautiful. The subject is certainly one, though the definitions are diverse. Here, we do not consider these three to be identical in their definitions, nor do we think they are different in their subject; rather, we preserve their different definitions while maintaining that the subject is one. For this reason, these qualities concur with one another throughout the actions of the soul. Just as the definitions of the virtues are different, yet there is one possessor of them all; it is impossible to participate in **Justice** while being void of **Temperance**, or to have these two while lacking the others...

-> He proves that everything just is, by its very nature, beautiful and good. <-

<margin>Therefore</margin> We shall confirm that everything just is beautiful by the following arguments: since the soul is a certain "multitude" <note>In Neoplatonism, the soul is a "multitude" because it contains different faculties and parts, unlike the "One," which is perfectly simple.</note>, and within it there is a first part, a middle part, and a final part. Tell me, when do we say justice is created within the soul? Is it when the middle or the final part tries to dominate those above them? Or rather, is it when the first part commands the middle, and the middle commands the last? 

But if justice occurred when the inferior parts prevailed over the superior, those parts would no longer be "inferior" by nature. For that which is fit to be called "better" is more honorable by nature. If, therefore, it is impossible for the same thing to be naturally better and naturally worse at the same time, justice must be found in the soul when that which is best within it <note>This "best part" refers to Reason or Intellect.</note> holds the command over the whole of one's life. In this state, the middle part is subject to the better part, yet prevails over the last part. For then each part of the soul has what is appropriate to it: the first part reigning, the second part supporting <note>original: *stipans*, literally meaning to attend as a guard or to crowd around in support.</note>, and the last part serving the better. 

Thus, the "just" itself is by nature the distributor of what is appropriate to each part of the soul. It is the cause of preserving each part's own duty and of distributing its proper dignity; it is, in this way, the preservation of the entire internal order. Moreover, an order and moderation of this kind, being fitting to nature, is naturally beautiful. Therefore, justice is the cause of beauty and is itself beautiful. 

Now, the "just" is twofold. One type is found in contracts, which preserves **arithmetic equality** <term>arithmeticam aequalitatem: a simple 1:1 ratio where everyone receives an identical amount, regardless of status or merit</term>. The other type is concerned with distribution, consisting of **geometric equality** <term>geometrica aequalitate: proportional justice where rewards are given based on a person's merit, worth, or "dignity"</term>. In the first case, the soul preserves arithmetic equality so that we do not defraud a partner in contracts by receiving more than we gave. In the second case, it distributes unequal things to unequal people according to each person's dignity, following geometric proportion; so that just as the persons differ among themselves, so too the things distributed to them differ. Therefore, every just thing, as we have said, is equal.

### PROCLUS

...moreover, everything that is equal is beautiful, for the unequal is uncomposed and ugly. 

Therefore, every just thing is beautiful. Furthermore, beauty exists in bodies when **form** <note>original: "forma." In this philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that gives shape and identity to chaotic matter.</note> overcomes **matter**. For matter itself is formless and ugly; when form is overcome by matter, the form is filled with a certain shapelessness and deformity, and it becomes something of a formless thing, having been made similar to the underlying nature of matter. 

If, therefore, the intellectual part within us acts as form, and the irrational part acts as matter—for the intellect and reason are counted in the order of the **limit** <note>original: "terminus." The Neoplatonic concept of *Peras*, the principle of order and definition.</note>, while the irrational is located in the genus of the **infinite** <note>original: "infinitum." The principle of *Apeiron*, representing lack of limit, chaos, or raw potential.</note>, as it is by nature indeterminate and devoid of measure—it is necessary that beauty also shines forth in the soul when reason reigns, and the parts of life lacking reason are subjected to reason. 

But justice itself gives the command to reason and assigns servitude to the irrational. It attributes to each what is fitting for it: leadership to the principal part, and obedience to the inferior part. Just as in the craftsmanship of the world the irrational is subject to us, so too is the irrational subjected to our innate reason as a vehicle <note>original: "vehiculum." This refers to the "astral body" or the soul's chariot mentioned in Platonic thought.</note>. Thus, justice is naturally beautiful and is the cause of beauty in the soul. 

Likewise, justice is something perfect and defined, for injustice is judged to be imperfect and undefined; it wanders infinitely and never stays its step, transgressing the boundary of justice. Therefore, justice itself imposes measure and limit upon whatever it is present in, and thus makes all things perfect. Since it is such a thing, it deservedly makes the soul beautiful. For beauty naturally follows that which is perfect and measured, just as deformity accompanies the unmeasured and the indeterminate. 

Justice, therefore, is beautiful by nature. Finally, the maker of the world himself adorned this entire universe through justice. He bound the world with the most beautiful knot of all knots, and made it indissoluble because of the power of <term>analogical proportion</term> <note>The mathematical harmony (analogia) that binds the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—into a unified cosmos.</note>, which contains the world and makes it a friend to itself on every side. That which is similar to the world—the most beautiful of all visible things—is surely itself also beautiful. Therefore, that which is just is necessarily also beautiful.

<margin>f</margin> Many others think that wounds and death are evils. But which of these is truly an evil for us? Certainly, such a thing does not pass into the soul, which is who we ourselves are. For the sufferings of the instruments do not change the virtues of those who use them; thus, a blacksmith does not lose his art of cutting simply because his axe <note>original: "seca," likely a contraction or error for "securi" (axe).</note> is sometimes blunt. Nor, even if our happiness consisted in the craft of smithing, would we think the blacksmith unhappy because he lacked an axe. Indeed, just as the soul has the body as its instrument, so also the body has certain instruments through which it moves external things. A defect in these does not harm a healthy state <term>habitudinem (habitudo)</term> of the body; similarly, the passions of the body do not pass through into the soul. 

Therefore, even if death is an evil of the body, it is nonetheless not an evil of the soul. If, then, a beautiful action belongs to the soul, while an evil might meanwhile exist in something else, it has not yet been shown that the same thing is sometimes beautiful and simultaneously evil. It is also possible to distinguish by dialectical reason <note>Logic-based reasoning used to find truth through the exchange of arguments.</note> that one thing is something **according to itself** <term>per se</term>, while another is **according to accident** <term>per accidens</term>. For a brave action is beautiful according to itself. Yet it is evil (if it ever be evil) only by accident, since it happens that the one acting bravely dies; let us grant, if you wish, that death is among the number of evils. Therefore, a brave duty—according to the very fact that it is brave, and thus also beautiful—is not also an evil; rather, it is brave by its own nature, but involves an "evil" only by accident due to the occurrence of death. 

Furthermore, anyone who separates the **good** from the **beautiful** is ignorant of the essence of man, placing one in one thing and the other in another: the good in the body, and the beautiful in the actions of the soul. But in truth, the man himself is the mind itself, an essence segregated from the body, in which whatever exists is both beautiful and good.

### How these two differ, namely "according to itself" and "as itself"
Terms of this kind—namely **according to itself** and **as itself**—are distinguished even in the works of Aristotle. For what belongs to something "according to itself" may not belong to it primarily. However, what is appropriate to something "as itself," in addition to being appropriate, also belongs to it primarily and equally. 

Therefore, if the **Beautiful** is the cause of the soul's balance <note>original: "commensurationis," referring to the internal harmony or "right proportion" of the soul's faculties.</note>, and is called beautiful for this very reason, it ensures that the better part of the soul rules over the worse; it perfects us and purges the soul's deformity. By this very reasoning, it is **Good**—not indeed by accident, but because it is Beautiful. For if that which is beautiful is balanced, then insofar as it is balanced, it is also good. Since the Good is the ultimate measure, certainly that which is beautiful exists as the good. 

Similarly, the **Ugly**, insofar as it is ugly, is **Evil**. For insofar as it is ugly, it is formless, undetermined, and disordered; and by this very reasoning, it is evil. Therefore, that which is ugly is certainly evil. Consequently, the same thing is always both beautiful and good, and conversely, the ugly is equally evil. Keep this rule in mind, which Aristotle also used later: **If any two things are interchangeable, their opposites are also interchangeable.** <note>This is a fundamental rule of Platonic and Aristotelian logic used here to prove that ethics (Good/Evil) and aesthetics (Beautiful/Ugly) are two sides of the same coin.</note> If, therefore, the Beautiful and the Good are interchangeable with one another, it follows that their opposites—namely Evil and the Ugly—are similarly interchangeable.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Latin translation of Proclus's "On Sacrifice and Magic." # PROCLUS

...no. For why else do we think those plants which they call **heliotropes**, that is, **sun-followers**, move toward the movement of the sun? Or that **selinetropes**, that is, **moon-followers**, turn toward the moon? Indeed, all things pray and sing hymns to the leaders of their own order <note>The "order" refers to the Neoplatonic "Chain of Being," where everything in the universe belongs to a specific divine series, such as the solar or lunar series, led by a particular god.</note>. But some do so in an **intellectual** way, others in a **rational** way, others **naturally**, and others still in a **sensible** <note>Meaning "perceptible by the senses."</note> way. 

Thus the sun-follower moves toward the sun in whatever way it can. And if anyone could hear the vibration made by it in the air's circuit, they would surely perceive it as a kind of sound composed for its king—the sort of song a plant is capable of making. For this reason, one may see the sun and moon on earth, but in an earthly quality. In heaven, however, one may see all plants, stones, and animals living an **intellectual life** according to their heavenly nature. 

The ancients, having contemplated these things, applied some of the heavenly things to the earthly ones; from this, they drew down divine powers into a lower place because of a certain **similarity**. Truly, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. For if someone heats hemp <note>original: "canabim"</note> or papyrus and then brings it close to a nearby lamp—even if it does not touch it—he will see the hemp suddenly ignited. Even though it did not touch the fire, the ignition descends from above to the lower parts. 

Let us therefore compare the heated hemp or papyrus to a certain kinship of lower things to higher ones. Its approach to the lamp represents the opportune use of things according to time, place, and matter. The movement of the fire into the hemp represents the presence of **divine light** to that which is capable of receiving it. Finally, the catching of the hemp represents the **deification of mortals** and the illumination of material things, which are then carried upward like ignited hemp because of a certain participation in the **divine seed**. 

What shall I say of the **Lotus**? The Lotus folds its leaves before the sun rises, but as the sun rises, it unfolds them little by little. As the sun ascends to the mid-point of the sky, the plant spreads its leaves wide; but as the sun moves from the midpoint toward its setting, the plant gradually contracts its leaves. It seems to honor the sun through this expansion and contraction of leaves no less than humans do with the gestures of their cheeks and the movement of their lips. 

Not only in plants, which have a trace of life, but also in stones one may see an imitation and participation in the lights above. Just as the **helitis** stone <note>A term for various "sun-stones" like sun-jasper or certain types of quartz believed to trap solar light.</note> imitates solar rays with its own golden rays. The stone called the **Eye of Heaven** or **Eye of the Sun** has a shape like the pupil of an eye, and a ray flashes from the center of the pupil. Also, the **selenite** stone—that is, the **lunar** stone—is shaped like a horned moon and follows the lunar motion with its own changes...

# ON SACRIFICE AND MAGIC

...it. Then there is the stone **helioselenus** <note>original: "helioselenus," a stone believed to contain the properties of both the sun (helios) and the moon (selene)</note>, that is, the **solar-lunar** stone, which in a certain way imitates the meeting of the sun and the moon, representing it through its color. Thus, all things are full of divine beings: earthly things are full of celestial things, and celestial things are full of **super-celestial** things. Every order of things proceeds down to the very last. 

For those things which are gathered together as one above the order of things are subsequently expanded as they descend. There, different souls are arranged under different deities. Furthermore, there are many **solar** animals, such as **lions** and **roosters**, which participate in a certain solar deity according to their own nature. From this, it is marvelous how much inferior things in the same order yield to superior ones, even if they do not yield in size or physical power. 

Hence they say that the rooster is greatly feared by the lion and is almost revered. We cannot assign the cause of this to physical matter or the senses, but only to the contemplation of the higher order. For it is clear that the presence of **solar power** belongs more to the rooster than to the lion. This is evident because the rooster applauds the rising sun with certain hymns, as it were, and calls out to it when it turns toward us from the mid-heaven of the **antipodes** <note>The "antipodes" refers to the side of the earth opposite to the observer.</note>. At times, certain solar **angels** <note>In this Neoplatonic context, "angels" and "demons" are spiritual intermediaries between gods and humans, not necessarily the figures found in Judeo-Christian tradition.</note> have appeared endowed with such forms; though they themselves are formless, they appear in form to us, who are composed of form. Sometimes, too, solar **demons** have been seen with the faces of lions. When a rooster was presented to them, they suddenly vanished. This proceeds from the fact that things lower down in the same order always revere those that are higher—just as many people, when gazing upon images of divine men, are accustomed by that very sight to fear committing anything shameful. 

To speak briefly: some things turn themselves toward the revolutions of the sun, like the plants we mentioned; others imitate the shape of the solar rays in a certain way, like the **palm** or the **date** <note>original: "dactylus"</note>; others possess the fiery nature of the sun, like the **laurel**; and others have other qualities. One can certainly see the properties gathered in the sun distributed everywhere among those following in the solar order—namely, among angels, demons, souls, animals, plants, and stones. 

Therefore, the authors of the ancient priestly rites discovered the worship of higher powers from visible things. While they mixed some things, they purified others. They mixed many things together because they saw that simple elements had some property of a deity, but not enough on their own to summon that deity. Therefore, by this very mixing of many things, they attracted heavenly **influences** <note>original: "influxus," the "flowing in" of divine or celestial power into the material world</note>. Since they created one thing out of many through composition, they made it like the **One** <note>The "One" is the ultimate, absolute principle in Neoplatonic philosophy, from which all reality emanates.</note> which is above the many. They also fashioned statues from many mixed materials and combined scents into a single artful composition, gathering divine **symbols** <note>original: "symbola," meaning material tokens or signatures that resonate with a specific god</note> into a unity, rendering a single thing that reflects the divine as it exists in its essence...

...grasping, as it were, as many powers as possible. Sometimes, a single herb or stone is sufficient for the divine work. For purification, sulfur and sea water are required. 

Therefore, the priests, through the mutual kinship and **sympathy** <note>original: "compassionem," the Neoplatonic concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" for one another</note> of things, brought them together into one, and through their natural opposition, they cast out [unwanted forces]. They purified with sulfur and **asphalt** (that is, **bitumen**) when necessary, and sprinkled with sea water. For sulfur purifies because of its sharp scent, and sea water purifies because of its **fiery portion** <note>Ancient philosophers believed salt and sea water contained a hidden heat or fire</note>. They applied other things suitable for the worship of the gods, and other things in a like manner. 

Wherefore, by receiving from these and similar things, they first recognized the powers of **spirits** <note>original: "dæmonum," referring to intermediary beings or "daimons," not necessarily evil entities</note>; they saw that these spirits are very close to natural things and actions. Through these natural objects to which the spirits are drawn, the priests summoned them into their presence. Then, from the spirits, they proceeded to the powers and actions of the gods themselves. This happened partly by the spirits teaching those who were learning, and partly by the priests, through their own effort, interpreting fitting **symbols** <note>theurgical "tokens" or "signatures" found in nature</note> and ascending into the proper understanding of the gods. And finally, having set aside natural things and actions—and for the most part the spirits as well—they were received into the fellowship of the gods.

# Porphyry on the occasions, or the causes leading us to intelligible things. Translated by Marsilio Ficino.

## On the nature of corporeal and incorporeal things.

Every **body** <note>original: "corpus," meaning a physical, material object</note> exists in a place. However, none of those things which are **incorporeal** <note>original: "incorporea," things without physical bodies, like souls or thoughts</note> in themselves, nor anything of that kind, exists in a place. 

Those things which are incorporeal in themselves are everywhere, for the very reason that they are more excellent than every body and place. They are not spread out through space, but exist in a certain **indivisible condition**. Those things which are incorporeal in themselves are present to bodies not by location, but are present to them whenever they wish, by turning toward them and inclining themselves insofar as they naturally turn and incline toward those bodies. But since they are not present to bodies by a local condition, they are present to them by a certain **disposition** <note>original: "habitudine," a relationship or state of being</note>.

# ON THE OCCASIONS.
<note>original: "De Occasionibus." This is Ficino’s title for Porphyry’s *Sententiae ad intelligibilia ducentes*, a collection of short philosophical aphorisms.</note>

Those things which are **incorporeal** <note>having no physical body or matter</note> in themselves are certainly not present to bodies through substance or through essence. For they do not mix with bodies; nevertheless, from a certain inclination, as if in a single moment, a certain power subsists in them, communicated to those things already near the bodies. For that very inclination, following a certain power, establishes a presence near the bodies.

### On the nature, binding, and loosing of the soul.

The soul is a certain middle ground between **indivisible essence** <note>a reality that cannot be broken into parts, like pure thought</note> and the essence that is divisible among true bodies. The **Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus," referring to the divine mind or the realm of pure forms</note>, however, is an indivisible essence alone. But qualities and material forms are divisible according to the bodies they inhabit. Not everything that acts upon another does so through proximity and touch; even those things that do something by approaching and touching according to accident do not use proximity as their primary means. The soul is bound to the body by a certain turning toward the **passions** <note>physical sensations or emotions that "happen" to the body</note> arising from the body. And again, it is released insofar as it suffers nothing from the body. What nature has bound, nature herself looses. Again, what the soul has united, the soul herself separates. Nature indeed binds the body in the soul. But the soul binds itself in the body. Therefore, nature separates the body from the soul, but the soul separates itself from the body.

All things are in all things in a certain way, according to the condition of those things in which they exist.
<note>This is a fundamental Neoplatonic principle: the entire universe is interconnected, and every level of reality contains a version of every other level.</note>

We do not understand all things to be in all things in the same way; rather, the essence of each individual thing relates to all things in its own specific manner. In the Intellect, things exist **intellectually**; in the soul, **rationally**; in plants, through **seeds**; in bodies, through **images**. And in that which is above all these (the One), they exist in a way that is beyond the intellectual and beyond essence.

In the highest things, there is **unity** with power; in the lowest things, there is **multitude** with weakness.

Incorporeal substances, when descending, are indeed distinguished and multiplied into individual parts through a lack of power; when ascending, however, they are unified and return together into one through an abundance of power.

### On the kinds of life.

Not only in bodies is the condition ambiguous, but **life** itself is spoken of in many ways. For the life of a plant is one thing, and that of an animal another. Another still is the life of an intellectual essence, another of a higher nature; one belongs to the soul, another to the intellect. For those higher things also live, even if none of the things that exist because of them can attain a life similar to theirs.

Those things that generate partim turn toward what they have generated, and some not at all.

Everything that generates by its own essence generates something lesser than itself, and...
