->Sense, imagination, memory, intelligence.<-

Memory is not a certain preservation of imaginations, <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ τὸ μελετηθέντων προβαλέσθαι ἐκ νέας προβλήματα"</note> but rather the bringing forth again of problems previously meditated upon; it is the very propositions or productions into act of those things which the mind has meditated upon, bringing them newly into action.

The soul indeed possesses the **rational principles** <term>rationes: the blueprints or logical structures of all things</term> of all things. It acts according to them, either provoked to such an expedition by another, or turning itself inward toward these principles. And when it is provoked by another, it undertakes to introduce senses as if toward external things; but when it enters into itself, it reaches toward the **intelligences** <note>acts of pure, divine thought</note>. Therefore, senses are not outside of imagination, nor—as someone might say—are the intelligences, insofar as they belong to the living being. Nor again are the senses without the **passion** <note>the state of being acted upon or experiencing a physical sensation</note> of the sensory instruments. Thus, intelligences are also not without imagination, unless there is an analogous condition; just as a physical shape is a certain consequence of a sentient animal, so a **phantasm** <term>phantasma: a mental image or representation</term> is something that follows the intelligence of the soul that understands within a living being.

->The soul is immortal.<-

The soul is an unextended, immaterial essence, immortal in a life that possesses its living and being from itself, and possesses them in the same way.

The **passion** of the soul and the body is vastly different. For in the body, it occurs through transformation <note>a physical change in state, like heating or cooling</note>. But the passion of the soul is a certain adaptation and affection toward the thing itself, and a certain action, in no way similar to the heating and cooling of bodies. Therefore, if the passion of bodies occurs through transformation, it must be said that all **incorporeal** <note>existing without a physical body</note> things are devoid of such passion. For those things which are separated from matter and bodies in their activity remain the same; but those which approach matter and bodies are not themselves passive, but rather those things in which they appear are what "suffer" the passion. For when a living being perceives, the soul seems to be like a certain separate **harmony** <note>a musical metaphor common in Neoplatonism; the soul is the order that governs the instrument</note> moving the tempered strings by its own power. The body, however, is like the harmony which exists inseparably within the strings. But the cause of movement appears to be the living being, because it is **animated** <note>endowed with "anima" or soul</note>. This is similar to a musician, who causes harmony by being himself harmonious. The bodies which are struck through sensory passion appear similar to the tempered strings. For there...

### On the differences between incorporeal things.

The very name "incorporeal" is not used to describe a single, shared category of things in the way that the word "bodies" is. Instead, it is used simply to describe a lack of a body. For this reason, nothing prevents some incorporeal things from being **essence** <note>fundamental reality or being</note>, while others are not essence. Some exist before bodies, while others exist together with bodies. Likewise, some are separate from bodies, while others are not separate. Furthermore, some exist through themselves, while others need other things in order to exist. Finally, some are identical to their own self-moving actions and lives, while others are lives and actions that are changed in some way—namely, they are defined by the **negation** <note>defining something by what it is not</note> of those things which they are not, rather than by the presence of those things which they are.

### Passions assigned to primary matter in a similar way by Plotinus.
<note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; Porphyry was his student and editor.</note>

For the ancients, the specific properties of **primary matter** <term>materia prima: the fundamental, formless "stuff" that underlies all physical objects but has no qualities of its own</term> are indeed incorporeal. For matter is different from bodies; furthermore, it is devoid of life, and is neither intellect, nor soul, nor anything living by itself. Likewise, it is formless, changeable, infinite, and powerless. Therefore, it is not "being," but truly "non-being," a soft, appearing image. For that which is first in physical bulk is itself powerless; likewise, it is a longing for existence, "standing" but not in a stable state. Furthermore, it is always appearing within itself, now small, now large, now less, now more, now deficient, now exceeding; it is something that is always "becoming," but never truly "is," and yet it is not able to escape. Indeed, it is the total lack of "being." For this reason, whatever it promises, it lies. Even if it appears large, it immediately turns out small. It is like a sort of play or mockery, fleeing into non-existence. Its flight does not happen in physical space, but rather occurs as it falls away from "being." For this reason, the images that are within it are, in turn, within an even worse image—just as in a **mirror**, where that which is located elsewhere appears in another place; the mirror itself seems to be full, yet it possesses nothing while it seems to possess everything.

### What is acted upon, and what is not.

**Passions** <note>original: "passiones." In this context, it refers not to emotions, but to the state of being "acted upon" or undergoing change/suffering from an external force</note> are all centered around that which is subject to chance and destruction. For the path to destruction is the admission of a "passion," and it is the nature of a thing that "suffers" to perish. But no incorporeal thing perishes. Rather, certain things among them either exist or do not exist; for this reason, none of them "suffers." For that which is "suffering" (or being acted upon) ought not to remain exactly as it is, but must be of such a nature that it can be altered by the qualities of the things that enter it, which thus bring about a "passion."

<summary>This page defines "incorporeal" as a category of privation and describes primary matter as a deceptive, "non-being" mirror of reality. It concludes by arguing that only physical things can "suffer" or be acted upon, because incorporeal essences are not subject to decay.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Latin translation of Porphyry's "Sententiae" (Points of Departure to the Intelligible) by Marsilio Ficino. The previous page established that "incorporeal" things are not a single class but a diverse group of realities defined by their lack of physical body. This section moves into the specific metaphysics of how the soul and intellect remain unchanged even when the physical "composite" (the body) undergoes change or death.</meta>

# PORPHYRY:

For the alteration that occurs does not arise from just anything. Therefore, **matter** <note>the underlying "stuff" of the universe which has no qualities of its own</note> itself does not suffer. For in its own nature, matter is devoid of quality. Nor do the **forms** <note>the ideal patterns or blueprints</note> that enter into it and subsequently depart from it suffer change. Instead, the **passion** <term>passio</term> <note>Latin: "passio" here refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing a change, rather than "passion" in the sense of strong emotion</note> occurs regarding the **composite** <note>the physical object made of both matter and form, like a statue made of bronze and the shape of a man</note>. The "being" of a thing consists in this composition; for it is in the opposing forces and qualities of the things entering and bringing about the "passion" that the thing seems to persist in its existence. For this reason, those things whose life comes from external sources and not from themselves can, of course, suffer both "living" and "non-living." But for those things whose existence consists in life, it is necessary that they remain according to life, just as it is appropriate for the "absence of life" to not suffer change insofar as it is an absence of life. 

And so, just as it happens that the composite of matter and form—that is, the **body**—is changed and suffers, yet this does not happen to the matter itself; so too, living, perishing, and suffering in this very way is seen in the composite of **soul and body**. Yet this does not happen to the soul. For the soul is not something fused together from life and non-life, but consists of life alone; indeed, it is a **simple essence** <note>a basic, indivisible reality</note> and the very definition of the soul is a nature that moves itself.

### Every intellect is of all forms.
Intellectual essence is so similar in its parts that beings exist both in any particular intellect and in the universal intellect. But in the **universal intellect** <note>the cosmic mind or "Nous"</note>, even particular beings exist by a universal principle. In a **particular intellect**, however, even universal things exist simultaneously with particular things through a certain particular condition.

### The soul does not die, because its essence is life.
Concerning an essence whose being consists in life, and whose "passions" (experiences) are certainly forms of life, even "death" involves a certain kind of life. It is not a total deprivation of life all at once. Since the "passion" or life there is not entirely directed toward "not-living," it is the loss of the physical connection that occurs there.

### Every incorporeal life remains immortal, no matter how it is changed.
In **incorporeal lives** <note>realities that exist without physical bodies, such as souls or spirits</note>, progressions are produced while the prior stages remain firm within themselves, losing nothing of their own. Nor do they change in order to provide substance to lower things. Therefore, the things that exist because of them do not exist through any loss or transformation of the source. Nor is this produced like a "generation" <note>the birth or creation of physical things</note> which participates in perishing and change. Therefore, they are **unbegotten and incorruptible**; indeed, they are made unbegotten and incorruptible according to this very principle.

### How that which is above the intellect is understood.
Concerning that which is superior to the mind <note>Referring to "The One," the ultimate source in Neoplatonism which is beyond thought</note>, many things are said through the intelligence; however, it is contemplated through a certain **emptiness of intelligence** <note>often called "divine ignorance" or "darkness," where one stops thinking to experience the source directly</note> which is a better kind of understanding.

But through sleep itself, the knowledge and experience of it are held. For like is usually known by like; since all knowledge is a kind of **assimilation** <note>the process of becoming similar to the object of study</note> toward the very thing that is known.

## Non-being is either superior to being, like God, or inferior, along with matter.

What is called **non-being** <term>non ens</term> is either something we devise for ourselves by being separated from being itself, or something we "super-understand" <note>conceive of as a higher reality</note> while we possess being. Therefore, if we are separated from being, we do not conceive of non-being as something above being itself; instead, we conceive of non-being as a false **passion** <note>a state of being acted upon or a delusion</note>. This happens to the person who departs from their own true self. For just as anyone—as a truly existing being (that is, truly and through themselves)—can be led back to that non-being which is superior to being <note>the "One" or God in Neoplatonic thought, which is so perfect it is "beyond being"</note>, so too the person departing from being and from themselves is led down to the non-being which is the fall and ruin of being itself <note>matter or nothingness</note>.

## Incorporeal substance is wherever it wishes.

The nature of the body does not hinder that which is **incorporeal** <note>having no physical body, like a soul or intellect</note> from being wherever and however it chooses. For just as what is lacking in mass is incomprehensible to the physical body (since nothing of it pertains to the body), so the body—which is stretched out in mass—does not become an obstacle to the incorporeal; it lies there as if it were non-being. Nor does that which is incorporeal travel to where it wishes by the conditions of physical location, for **place** <note>Latin: "locus"</note> exists only together with mass. Nor, again, is it constrained by the limits of bodies. For whatever lies within a mass in any way can be confined in a narrow space and undergo change in its local condition. But that which is entirely exempt from mass and magnitude cannot be contained by those things which are in a mass, and it remains free from local movement. Therefore, it is found there by a certain and specific disposition, wherever it is disposed to be. It exists both **everywhere** and **nowhere** at the same time. For this reason, it is perceived by a certain specific state, either above the heavens or in some part of the world; yet when it is held in some part of the world, it is not seen with the eyes, but its presence is made manifest to humans through its works.

## Incorporeal substance is not confined by any body, but produces its essence in the body through which it applies itself to the body.

If that which is incorporeal is ever understood to be "in" a body, it is not necessary for it to be enclosed like animals shut in a **park** <note>original: "parco", meaning a fenced enclosure or preserve</note>. For no body can so confine it within itself, nor can it be held like a **wineskin** <note>original: "uter", a leather bottle</note> draws in and contains some liquid or air. Rather, the incorporeal must substitute powers flowing outward from its own internal unity, by which it descends and applies itself to the body. Thus, its link to the body is fulfilled through a certain ineffable extension of itself. For which reason, no other...

# PORPHYRY

...[The body] <note>completing the sense from the previous page</note> does not indeed bind the soul, but the soul certainly binds itself. Therefore, the soul does not unbind itself when the body is broken or perishes; rather, the soul unravels itself when it turns away from its familiar affection toward the subject <note>the material body it inhabits</note>.

Universal causes are not turned toward their effects; rather, they turn those effects toward themselves.

No substance among those that are universal and perfect turns toward its own offspring <note>original: *genituram*, referring to the things it brings into being</note>. Instead, all perfect substances are led back to their generators, and this continues all the way down to the world-body. Because the world-body is perfect, it is led back to the soul—I mean the intellectual soul—and for that reason, it revolves in a circle. The soul of the world, however, is raised toward the **Intellect** <term>intellectus</term> <note>the divine, cosmic Mind</note>. The Intellect is further raised to the **Principle** <note>the First Principle or the "One"</note>. Thus, all things reach this very point, starting from the furthest extremes and moving as far as the capacity of each allows, as they are elevated toward the First. This process is usually achieved either from nearby or from a distance. Thus, these things can be said not only to desire God, but also to reach Him according to their powers. 

In particular substances, however—which are capable of falling into many things—there is a downward leaning toward the world of change <note>original: *genituras*, the realm of birth and decay</note>. Therefore, in these, "sin" is said to have occurred, and in these, unfaithfulness is condemned. Matter itself contaminates these substances simply because they are capable of leaning toward it. Yet, they remain capable of turning back to the Divine without error. Thus, **perfection** consists in a secondary thing remaining preserved by turning back toward what came before it. **Defect**, on the other hand, turns higher things toward lower ones and makes them love these very things, while they turn away from the superior in the meantime.

->How God, the Intellect, and the Soul are differently everywhere.<-

God is everywhere because He is nowhere; the Intellect is everywhere because it is nowhere; and the Soul is everywhere because it is nowhere. Finally, [the Soul] is everywhere because it exists and is nowhere. But regarding the fact that God is "everywhere and nowhere," He is this in relation to all things that exist after Him. Regarding Himself, however, He is only as He is and as He wills. 

The Intellect, however, is in God, who is everywhere; but in those things that exist after it, the Intellect exists "nowhere and everywhere" alike. Finally, the Soul is in the Intellect and in God; it is similarly everywhere, but in the body, it is everywhere and nowhere at the same time. 

The body, however, is in the soul, and in the intellect, and in God. Indeed, all things—both beings and non-beings—are from God. And yet, God Himself is not these beings and non-beings, nor does He exist in them. For if He were only "everywhere," He would be all things and in all things. But since He is also "nowhere," all things are certainly made through Him; and again, they are made *in* Him because He exists everywhere, yet they remain distinct from Him because He is "nowhere." 

Similarly, the Intellect, existing everywhere and nowhere, is the cause of the soul and the things following the soul. It is neither the soul itself, nor the things after the soul, nor does it exist in them, because it is not only "everywhere" in relation to things after it, but also "nowhere." Again, the soul is neither the body, nor is it in the body, but it is the cause of the body. Since it is everywhere through the body at once, it is also nowhere in the body. Finally, the progression of the universe ends in that which is unable to be both "everywhere and nowhere" at the same time, but participates in each in alternating turns.

->From Porphyry<-

# From Porphyry’s *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, as interpreted by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine.

## The soul sleeps in this body.

We prescribe abstinence from animals not indeed for all people, but only for those who intend to contemplate the divine. Such a person truly observes the sorceries <note>original: *veneficia*; here referring to the "poisons" or distracting enchantments of physical existence</note> of this dwelling in which we live; indeed, they recognize that the soul's true nature is to be naturally and perpetually awake, and they perceive the "sleep" by which the soul is oppressed here in the body. To this soul, we shall provide an education and nourishment that is consistent both with the nature of this physical realm and with its own self-knowledge.

## Happiness is not the knowledge of divine things, but a divine life.

## For us, blessed contemplation is not an accumulation of words and a multitude of academic disciplines, as someone might perhaps think; for it is not composed in that way. Nor does it increase according to the quantity of arguments and words. Otherwise, nothing would prevent those who have gathered all the disciplines from being happy. Yet, no mere academic discipline can fill a person with happy contemplation, nor do those who teach true doctrines ever achieve that goal unless those teachings are accompanied by a life translated into the very nature of divine things. Truly, the end goal of contemplation is **Being** <term>ens</term> <note>Reality itself in its highest, most stable form</note> itself, and attaining the truth to such an extent that this state of mind unites the contemplator—according to the strength of their nature—into one with that which they contemplate. For the return is not to something else, but to one’s true self; it is not a union with another, but a true harmony with oneself. That true self is the **Intellect** <term>intellectus</term> <note>The higher, intuitive mind that perceives spiritual truths beyond mere logic</note>. Therefore, the goal is to live by the Intellect. To this end, the speeches and disciplines applied from the outside provide us with a "purification," but they are not the actual means by which our happiness is fulfilled. For if happiness itself consisted in a heap of words and arguments, it would be possible for people who simply maintain a certain education and perform certain duties to reach that happy end. But since it is necessary to exchange this life for another—purging the soul through words, arguments, and actions—tell me: what kind of words and what kind of works will best instruct us? Surely only those words and duties by which we are separated from the things that stir the senses and the passions? Thus, we may finally be led back to the intellectual life, which is above the imagination and, as far as we are able, free from passion.

## On the soul’s descent and ascent.

If we are to fly back to those things that are truly our own, we must entirely cast off these things which we have taken on from our mortal nature, along with the affection that leans toward them, through which our descent into the body occurred. Furthermore, we must remember our blessed and eternal substance; and while we strive to ascend to the incorporeal realm, we must meditate on two things especially: by what reasoning we may cast off the material and the perishable...

->PORPHYRY.<-

It is necessary to consider by what path we may especially return; namely, by returning along a path contrary to the one by which we descended to these present conditions of ours. For we were, and still are, intellectual essences, pure from all sense-perception and living [originally] apart from the irrational nature. But we have been coupled to a sensible nature, partly through the weakness of our soul's eternal connection to our intelligible source, and partly through a power that leans toward lower things. For all those powers that act in concert with the senses and the body only begin to flourish and take effect when the mind fails to persevere in the intelligible <term>intelligibile</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms, accessible only to the intellect</note> realm itself. We become like a degraded soil which, though it has often received wheat, eventually yields only darnel <note>original: *lolium*; a weed often found in grain fields, used here as a metaphor for the "weeds" of the irrational mind</note>. 

And this happens through a certain depravity of the soul, which indeed does not lose its own essence while the irrational sprout grows, but through this very growth, the soul is joined to mortality as it is drawn away from its own nature toward what is foreign. Therefore, if we ever strive with all our strength to return to our pristine state, it is necessary to segregate the mind entirely from sense, from imagination, and from every irrational condition and passion that follows from them, as far as the necessity of nature permits. We must duly arrange and piece together, part by part, those things which pertain to the mind, establishing tranquility and peace by means of this war against the irrational; thus, we may not only hear about the intelligible things of the intellect, but also experience the great power we possess when enjoying the contemplation of the mind, having been restored to an incorporeal nature. 

And so, truly living through the intellect, we shall no longer live falsely alongside natures related to the perishable. Therefore, we must loosen many of our garments <note>A famous Neoplatonic metaphor: the "garments" are the layers of the physical body and the irrational soul that "clothe" the pure spirit</note>—both this visible garment and those inner robes still applied to us. For we ought not only to avoid vicious effects, but we must pull up those effects by the very roots. Indeed, the departure from the body can happen through violence, or it can happen through a kind of persuasion; and it is performed rightly through a certain thinning out, and, as one might say, through the forgetting and "death" of the passions. This is indeed the best departure, since the soul drags nothing of that from which it is being torn away along with it. For as we have discovered in things manifest to the senses, whatever is pulled out by violence usually drags something with it—either a part or a trace of the uprooting itself and of that from which it is eradicated.

### On the release of the soul.

The ancient sages diligently avoided everything that could bind them to the body. Thus, the Pythagoreans and similar wise men partly withdrew into solitude; and partly, even when living among the crowd, they lived in temples and sacred groves where they would be far removed from the entire throng. Plato, however, chose the Academy as his dwelling—a field not only solitary and set apart from the city, but even (so it is said) unhealthy <note>Ancient sources suggest Plato chose an "unhealthy" spot so that the body's vigor would be kept in check, preventing it from distracting the soul</note>. Others did not even spare their own eyes, so that they might preserve an inner contemplation, uninterrupted and perpetual. The philosopher indeed [does] not [extrude] <note>The sentence concludes on the following page: "...does not extrude the soul from the body through violence."</note> the soul from the body through violence...

# ON ABSTINENCE

...expels it. For if one inflicts force <note>referring to a violent or forced separation of soul and body, such as suicide, which Neoplatonists generally argued against because it left the soul still tethered to the passions</note>, it will nevertheless remain in that same place from which it tried to compel it to depart. Nor will he think it matters little if, by fattening the body, he strengthens a harder prison for himself. For he will take care lest the senses and their pleasure, if they grow strong, submerge the soul deeper into the body. Indeed, if the actions of the senses did not impede the pure action of the mind, what would be so burdensome about being in the body, provided that you were not affected by the motions that occur through the body? For how would you judge or say what you have suffered, unless you both suffered and were present to those things you were suffering? 

The Intellect <term>Intellectus</term> <note>original: *Intellectus*; in this context, the highest faculty of the soul that perceives divine truths directly</note> should certainly remain within itself, even if we are not at all within it; but whoever departs from the intellect is already in that place to which he has crossed over, wandering up and down with the focused effort of a certain perception. He is already present there where the perception itself is performed. Much less can someone who descends to the experience of sensible things and acts through the irrational faculty <term>facultas irrationalis</term> <note>The part of the soul responsible for basic instincts and emotions, as opposed to reason</note> be able, in the meantime, to sincerely contemplate those things which belong to the mind. 

Neither do those who attribute two souls to us <note>A reference to the Platonic theory that we have a rational, immortal soul and an irrational, mortal one</note> permit us to have twin attentions at the same time. Otherwise, they would have created two joined animals. It might be possible for one to be intent on some things while the other did not claim the works of its partner for itself. But why would it be necessary to weaken the bodily passions, to die to them, and to meditate on this daily, if we were able to act according to the intellect while joined to mortals without the inspection of the intellect, as someone once declared? 

For "the intellect sees, the intellect hears." <note>A famous ancient maxim attributed to Epicharmus: "Mind sees and mind hears; all else is deaf and blind"</note> But if, while eating luxuriously and guzzling the sweetest wine, you can meanwhile apply yourself to divine things, why are you not frequently in divine things while you cling to human ones and perform those acts in your dealings which are not even honorable to speak of? For the disturbances of the "child" <note>original: *pueri*; a metaphor for the undisciplined or infantile part of the soul that craves physical pleasure</note> within us are everywhere; and because they are foul, the contemplator cannot be distracted by them and contemplate at the same time. For where sense and such awareness are present, the intelligible <term>intelligibile</term> <note>the realm of pure thought and divine forms</note> is absent; and the more the faculty lacking reason is excited, the further away intelligence is. For it is impossible for someone carried here and there to be here and there at the same time. For we do not produce our attentions with a part of ourselves, but with our whole being.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument in *On Abstinence*, moving from the general theory of how the soul is distracted by the senses to the specific benefits of a meatless diet for both physical health and spiritual clarity. It concludes the first book and introduces the second, which focuses on the nature of sacrifices and divinity.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

The body is struck by external things, and this "striking" reaches our perception. For perception itself—and the act of paying attention—is the very essence of sound. Yet it is impossible for the soul to "sound" <note>original: *sonet*; Porphyry uses the metaphor of the soul vibrating or resonating with sensory input</note> unless it is entirely turned toward that sound and has directed its presiding eye toward that very thing.

However, once the cause of our many physical needs is removed, and we have been freed from the abundance of things brought into the body, we are lightened of their weight. Then, the eye of the soul flashes out from the smoke and the physical flood; it no longer requires reminders or logical demonstrations because of its natural, tireless ingenuity.

Furthermore, the consumption of meat does not contribute to health at all; rather, it hinders health. For health is preserved by the same means through which it is recovered. It is recovered through a very thin diet and by abstaining from meat; therefore, health is also maintained by these practices. If it is argued that abstaining from animal food contributes less to the strength of a Milo <note>Milo of Croton was a famous ancient Greek wrestler known for his prodigious strength and for supposedly eating enormous quantities of meat</note>, certainly a philosopher has no need for such an increase in bulk. If he intends to be contemplative, rather than devoting himself to physical exploits and lack of restraint, it is surely fitting for him to maintain his health—not out of a fear of death, but rather so that he is not barred from the benefits that come from contemplation.

Nothing preserves health more than a tranquil state of mind and a disposition of thought directed toward that which Truly Is <term>Truly Is</term> <note>original: *vere est*; a Platonic term referring to the eternal, unchanging reality of the divine forms as opposed to the shifting physical world</note>. For much vigor flows from the soul into the body, as our own associates have proven through experience. They reached a point where they expelled the most bitter pains of the joints in their feet and hands—pains that had lasted eight whole years and forced them to be carried by others—at the same moment they abandoned their obsession with money and public affairs and turned their study toward the divine. Thus, they cast out their cares and their physical disease at the same time. 

From this it is apparent that much—indeed, everything—contributes to health when a certain state and habit of the mind is adopted; a thin and frugal diet also contributes greatly to the same end. If it is necessary for us to confess the truth freely without fear, there is no other way to reach our ultimate goal unless we attach ourselves to God (if it is permitted to say so) and tear ourselves away from the body and bodily pleasures. Since our salvation is not won through the mere hearing of words and theories, but through our actual deeds, I say we cannot be joined to God except through the purest abstinence. This applies not only to some specific lesser god, but even to the God who presides over all things, who exists simply beyond even incorporeal nature. Just as He is simpler, purer, more self-sufficient, and more distant from matter than all others, so too must the soul be pure if it is ever to enjoy His presence.

<meta>This page continues from the end of Book 1 of Porphyry’s *On Abstinence*, transitioning into Book 2. ->ON THE OCCASIONS<-

# ON THE OCCASIONS.

The first sacrificers offered not animals but herbs and flowers first, then trees, and they burned spices as incense. Those who first began to eat animals were driven to attack living creatures by a scarcity of crops; for previously they fed upon the fruits of the earth.

There are three reasons why one must sacrifice to the gods: that we may venerate them, that we may return thanks, and that we may ask for necessities from them and ward off evils. To obtain these things, however, the vow of the mind <note>original: *votum animi*; the inward intention or spiritual promise</note> is sufficient, to which certain small gifts from the crops may be added. Truly, it is a sin <term>nefas</term> <note>nefas: a violation of divine law or a "forbidden act"</note> to slaughter animals.

Indeed, we too shall dedicate sacred things to the gods, but we shall offer different sacrifices, just as is fitting; we shall also sacrifice to the various powers according to their differences. To the god himself who reigns over all things—as a certain wise man <note>likely referring to the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana</note> said—we shall offer nothing sensible <note>meaning nothing perceptible by the senses, such as physical objects or incense</note>; neither burning incense nor even naming him. For there is nothing material that is not immediately impure to him who is entirely immaterial. Therefore, neither is spoken word suited to him, nor even the inner word of the mind when it is stained by some passion of the soul.

Instead, we shall worship him rightly with pure silence and pure thoughts <term>intelligentiae</term> <note>original: *intelligentiis*; refers to noetic or purely intellectual perceptions</note> concerning him. It is necessary, therefore, that having been joined to and made like god, we dedicate this elevation of our own souls toward him as if it were a sacred victim. This very thing is both divine praise and our salvation. In this contemplation of god, then—which is free from all passion—this sacrifice is fulfilled.

But to his children, who are the intelligible gods <note>spiritual beings or lesser deities perceived by the intellect rather than the eyes</note>, we ought to offer praise even through speech. For to each of the divinities <term>numina</term>, a just offering of first-fruits is made from those things which they bestow, and by which they nourish us and preserve us in being, for the purpose of sacrifice. Therefore, just as farmers bring first-fruits from what they gather—namely, handfuls of crops and the fruits of trees—to the divinities, so we shall dedicate to them the first-fruits of our intellect and the thanks for similar excellent gifts.

That is, we give thanks for those things which they have bestowed upon us: namely, the contemplation of the divinities themselves and the order <note>original: *numerum*; referring to the mathematical or hierarchical arrangement of the gods</note> of their being. This is especially true since, through that very inspection of them, they truly nourish us, being present everywhere to us and appearing, and happily breathing upon our salvation.

But now, it even wearies many students of philosophy to labor at this; they, worshiping glory rather than divinity, revolve around statues. They neither consider whether or how such things should be approached, nor do they strive to learn from those who excel in divine wisdom how far and to what extent one should participate in these rites. We, however, will not contend with these people at all, nor will we strive to judge such things; rather, we will mostly imitate the holy and ancient ones, dedicating as first-fruits to the divinities that very contemplation which the higher beings have granted us, and the use of which is absolutely necessary for our true salvation.

Thus the Pythagoreans, being engaged with numbers and lines, dedicated much from these to the gods: naming one number Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, often associated with the Monad or the number Seven</note>, another Diana, another Apollo; and again, one justice, another temperance, and similarly at the end...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animal sacrifice is a late and "sinful" corruption of original plant-based offerings. He posits that the highest God requires only silent, intellectual worship, while lesser deities should be honored with the "first-fruits" of thought and mathematical contemplation.</summary>

...figures and such similar sacrifices, they pleased the gods by means of the gods themselves, so that they might call upon each of the gods with their own offerings and frequently use their favor for prophecy, or if they lacked anything for an investigation. For the gods who are within the heavens, whether they are in some way wandering <note>original: *errantibus*; referring to the planets</note> or non-wandering <note>referring to the "fixed" stars</note>—whose leader we must consider to be the Sun first, then the Moon—we can properly consecrate fire as if it were already a kinsman. And we must observe what the theologian <note>original: *theologus*; likely referring to Pythagoras or the Orphic tradition, whom Porphyry considers divine authorities on ritual</note> commands. He says, moreover, that no living being is to be sacrificed, but he recognized only flour and honey and the fruits of the earth and flowers; for he knew the man who is a worshiper of true piety. To the gods, indeed, no living thing was ever to be sacrificed, but rather to demons and others, whether good or evil. But let us set these matters aside. To me, indeed, those things which most of the Platonists have made public seem now to be brought forward for the ingenious. They pass down this much: that the first god, since he is incorporeal <term>incorporeus</term> <note>incorporeus: existing without a physical body or material form</note>, immobile, and indivisible, is contained in nothing, not even in himself; he needs nothing external, nor does even the soul of the world <term>Anima Mundi</term> <note>Anima Mundi: the "World Soul," a philosophical concept of an intrinsic spirit that connects all living things in the universe</note> need external things. For it possesses and contains that very thing which is stretched out in three dimensions, and a power that moves naturally; and by its own nature it has decreed to be moved in a well-ordered way, and to move the body of the world according to the highest reasons. Moreover, it received the body into itself and embraced it, although it is incorporeal and free from every passion. To the remaining gods, however—to the world and to the wandering and non-wandering stars which consist of soul and body and are manifest to our eyes—we must sacrifice with inanimate <note>original: *inanimatis*; meaning bloodless offerings like plants or incense rather than animals</note> sacrifices for the reason we have stated.

### On the kinds of good and evil demons.

There remains the multitude of invisible beings, whom Plato called "undifferentiated demons" <term>dæmones</term> <note>dæmones: in Greek philosophy, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediate spirits or "guides" that sit between gods and humans</note>. Some of these, indeed, named by men, have obtained honors equal to the gods and other forms of worship among individuals. Others, however, being of many forms, are not named; but from certain people throughout villages or cities, they receive a name and worship secretly in some way. The remaining crowd is thus commonly called by the name of demons. Moreover, a firm belief exists among all people: that these spirits will certainly harm the human race if they become angry because they are neglected or do not receive their lawful worship. And conversely, they will do good to those men who have won them over for themselves with vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other things that follow. Since, therefore, this opinion about demons is confused and carries much potential for false accusation, it is necessary to distinguish their nature by reason. For perhaps it is necessary, they say, to declare from where the error concerning them has fallen upon men. It must be distinguished, therefore, in this manner:

Whichever souls, sprouting from the "Total Soul," govern the great parts of the regions below the moon <gloss>and remaining in the spirit</gloss> <note>original gloss: *& in peridũ μένωι*; likely a corruption of the Greek *en pneumati menōn*, meaning "dwelling in the breath/spirit"</note>, whether leaning upon or adhering to or placed upon the spirit, but surpassing it according to reason—these are certainly to be judged as good demons, and they provide all things for the utility of those things which occur, whether for certain people...

<summary>Porphyry distinguishes between the highest God, who requires no physical sacrifice, the celestial gods who receive bloodless offerings, and demons who are often wrongly appeased with blood. He begins a systematic classification of demons, defining "good" demons as those who govern the sublunary realm according to reason.</summary>

# ON CIRCUMSTANCES #

<warning>The bottom of the page is faded and partially illegible.</warning>

...[they] preside over animals, or over certain fruits, or over other things ordered for their sake, such as rains and temperate winds, clear skies, the tempering of the seasons, and everything else contributing to these. Among us, they likewise preside over the arts, the discipline of music, medicine, gymnastics, and similar things. It is impossible for those who provide for the utility and convenience of things to inflict harm in return; among these are to be numbered the demons <note>original: *dæmones*; in Greek philosophy, these are 'daimones,' intermediary spirits that can be good or bad, distinct from the 'demons' of later Christian tradition.</note> who <term>Plato</term> <note>Plato explains the role of demons as messengers in his dialogue, the *Symposium*.</note> says transmit and report human matters to the gods and divine matters to humans. They carry our prayers to the gods as if to judges, and they bring down the gods' commands and warnings to us along with prophecy <term>vaticinium</term> <note>original: *vaticinio*; the art of delivering oracles or divine messages.</note>.

However, any souls that are not at all ruled by the spirit <term>spiritus</term> <note>original: *spiritui*; here referring to the 'pneuma' or 'spirit-body,' a thin, vaporous substance that Porphyry believed connects the immaterial soul to the physical body.</note> they are joined to, but instead yield for the most part, are said to be excessively carried away when the spirit of anger and lust grows strong. These souls are indeed themselves demons, but they are rightly named evildoers <term>malefici</term> <note>original: *malefici*; literally 'evil-doers,' referring here to harmful or malicious spirits driven by passion.</note>. Both these and those we called different from them are invisible and not at all manifest to human senses, for they are not clothed in a solid body. Moreover, they do not all have a single form, but are marked by many figures. And the forms that seal their spirit appear at some times, but at others not at all. Sometimes those who are worse even change their forms. 

Their spirit, insofar as it is something corporeal, is subject to passion and is dissolvable; but insofar as it is so bound by souls, its appearance can endure for a long time, yet it is not eternal. It is consistent that something always flows out from it and it is nourished. The body of good demons consists in symmetry <note>original: *commensuratione*; referring to a balanced, harmonious physical state.</note>, just like the bodies of things manifest to us, but the bodies of the evil-doers are disproportionate. They inhabit a place near the earth because of their passive affection. Therefore, there is no evil they do not dare to commit; for they have an entirely violent and insane character, being abandoned by the guardianship of the better demons. For this reason, they mostly plot and rush into fierce and sudden ambushes. And while they carry out their incursions, they partly try to hide and partly inflict violence. 

Therefore, the sufferings inflicted by them are sharp and swift. Healings and corrections from the better demons seem to be slower. For every good thing is easy and steady in its governance, proceeds in order, and does not overstep what is appropriate. If you think this way about demons, you will never fall into that most absurd opinion by which you might think that evil comes from the good or good from the evil. Nor is the discourse only absurd in this way; but many, conceiving the worst opinions about the gods <note>original: *d diis*; a contraction for 'de diis' (concerning the gods).</note> <unclear>from this</unclear>...

<summary>Porphyry distinguishes between good demons, who act as orderly messengers and guardians of nature, and malicious demons (malefici) who are driven by passion and cause sudden harm. He explains that understanding this distinction prevents humans from mistakenly attributing evil to the gods.</summary>

Thus, they try to clear themselves from being known as the cause of calamities, and by plotting this, they first strive to hide their own injustice from us.

Subsequently, they turn us toward supplications and sacrifices suited for beneficent gods, as if those gods were angry with us. They do these and similar things because they are eager to lead us away from the right understanding of the gods and toward themselves. For they delight in everything done in such an unjust and discordant manner.

And putting on the masks of other gods, trusting in our ignorance, they take the crowds into their company. Because of such desires, they set human minds on fire with habits and cravings for wealth, power, and pleasures. Again, they involve us in new and foreign opinions from which seditions and wars arise, and other things of the same kind. But what is most serious of all: they persuade us that such things are done by the heavenly powers and by God, so that they even subject the Great God to such accusations—claiming he throws everything into turmoil, from top to bottom. 

This happens not only to uneducated people but to many students of philosophy <term>philosophiæ</term> <note>The study of wisdom; for Porphyry, this was not just academic but a way of purifying the soul to return to the divine.</note> as well. The cause of the error proceeds and is confirmed mutually. Indeed, those philosophers who never separated themselves from the common filth fell into the same errors as the common people. Conversely, when the crowds hear opinions similar to their own from praised writers, they are even more confirmed in this view of the gods. 

For poetic art has further excited the suspicions of such men more sharply, because it uses a style of speech that is powerfully suited for astonishment and a kind of magical attraction. It can easily soothe and entice souls, and therefore bring us to believe in things that are utterly impossible. But surely we must firmly believe that the good never harms, nor does the evil ever benefit. For it is not the nature of heat (as <term>Plato</term> <note>Porphyry refers here to Plato’s *Republic*, where Socrates argues that the nature of a good thing is to benefit, not to harm.</note> says) to make things cold, but of its opposite; likewise, it is not the nature of the just to do harm. Now, the most just of all things by nature is divinity itself <term>diuinitas</term>. Otherwise, nothing would be divine.

Should we not, therefore, distinguish this power and lot of the beneficent demons? For that which is naturally inclined toward opposites is contrary to the beneficent; and opposites never occur naturally regarding the same thing. Since, therefore, demons of this kind...

## ON OCCASIONS. ##

In many ways, they harm human nature, and sometimes in great matters. Certainly, **good demons** <note>In the Neoplatonic tradition, "demons" (daemones) are not necessarily evil; they are intermediary spirits between gods and humans. "Good demons" act as guardians and messengers.</note> meanwhile never abandon their duties, but they signal imminent dangers from evil ones everywhere as best they can, sometimes showing them in dreams, and sometimes through minds inspired by the divine. They do this through many other means as well. And if someone could discern these signs, they would detect and avoid all the machines of the wicked; for these spirits give signs to everyone, but not everyone recognizes the signals, just as not everyone is able to read what is written, but only the one who has previously learned his letters.

Through the contrary demons, however, universal **sorcery** <term>veneficium: literally "poisoning," but used here to describe the harmful spiritual influence or "witchcraft" associated with malicious spirits</term> is enacted. For those who insert evils into sorceries are accustomed to honoring these spirits and their leader most of all. These demons truly abound in all kinds of forms and images, and they vigorously deceive with a machine of wonders. By their labor, the wretched manufacture **phantoms** <gloss>eidōla (original: εἴδωλα); these are illusory images or ghosts used in deceptive magic</gloss> and love-potions; for all intemperance and the hope for wealth and glory gain strength through them, and especially deception. For lying is the particular property of such demons.

They wish to be seen as Gods, and the power itself presiding over them wants to be considered the greatest god. These indeed are the only ones who delight in libations and the **smell of roasting meat** <note>original: nidor; Neoplatonists believed that lower, material-minded spirits literally fed on the greasy smoke and vapors rising from animal sacrifices</note>. For by these, their spiritual body is accustomed to grow fat; for this body lives on vapors and fumigations and—as is fitting—takes in strength in quite varied ways through the various smells of blood and flesh.

Therefore, a wise and temperate man will be careful not to use such sacrifices, through which he might attract such demons to himself. He will instead strive to purify his soul perfectly, for they never attack a pure soul because of its total dissimilarity to them. Furthermore, if it is perhaps necessary for cities to reconcile these demons to themselves, such a practice pertains nothing to us. For in a city, wealth and external and bodily comforts are held as "goods" among the citizens, and their opposites as "evils," and they have almost no concern for the perfection and purity of the soul.

We, however, will not need the comforts that demons provide, as much as that is possible; instead, both through our soul and through external things, we will strive with every effort to become like God himself and those close to him. This is surely accomplished through tranquility of mind, through a clear understanding of the truth of things, and a life directed entirely toward these goals. On the other hand, we must become entirely unlike wicked men, and demons, and everything that takes pleasure in the mortal and material. For this reason, following what **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle who wrote extensively on piety and the history of sacrifices</note> handed down, we ourselves will offer sacrifices, which the theologians have also agreed upon—recognizing, clearly, that as much as we neglect to purge the soul from disturbances, so much are we joined to a wicked power. From this, we are rightly compelled to further soothe this power so that... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the next page would likely complete the word "theologians" and the argument about placating lower spirits when the soul is not yet pure.</note>

### On sacrifices to evil demons and on abstinence and caution regarding evil demons.

Therefore, if theologians ever permit the slaughtering of animals to wicked demons for the sake of avoiding the evils they might inflict, they forbid the tasting of such sacrifices at the same time. Meanwhile, they command that before you sacrifice in this way, you must purge the mind by fasting, and especially by **abstinence from animals** <note>Specifically, the practice of vegetarianism, which Porphyry argued was essential for maintaining spiritual purity and avoiding the "heaviness" of material existence.</note>. For they believe that the holy purity of the mind is like a symbol and a **divine mark** <term>character: a spiritual seal or imprint that identifies the soul as belonging to the divine realm, acting as a protective badge</term> by which you are guarded, so that you suffer nothing from those spirits to whom you draw near while reconciling them through sacrifice. For when you are of a different disposition than those to whom you perform sacrifices—and you are purer, and therefore more divine—you remain the same in both body and mind, protected by pure sanctity as if by a fortress. 

For this reason, such caution seemed necessary even to **enchanters** <term>fascinatores: those who use the "evil eye" or spells to bind others through fascination</term> and **sorcerers** <term>venefici: literally "poisoners," referring to practitioners of harmful magic who use potions and herbs</term>, so that they might be safer from danger. Yet they cannot be entirely safe, for wicked demons are accustomed to answer to various kinds of wantonness. Therefore, purity and sanctity are not the property of sorcerers and incanters, but certainly of divine men and those who contemplate divine things. 

Indeed, **chastity and abstinence** <note>In Porphyry’s Neoplatonism, these are not just moral choices but ontological tools that elevate the soul above the influence of the lower, material spirits.</note> protect their observers everywhere against evil demons through a familiarity with the divine. Thus, if enchanters had decided to use this purity entirely, they would certainly never dare to practice enchantment at all; for they would have been called away by this purity from the very lusts for the sake of which they pollute themselves in their displays of piety. Thus, being full of disturbances and scarcely or only a little abstaining from impure foods—and being themselves entirely impure—they pay the penalty for their unjust transgression against the universe: partly under the power of the demons whom they themselves provoke, and partly under divine judgment, which thoroughly inspects all the works and counsels of mortals.

But the divine man will fortify his mind with both divine wisdom and with abstinence from foods that incite disturbances in men, as well as by his very likeness to God. He will consider his uncontaminated mind to be like a temple of God within this universal temple of God the Father.

# ON SACRIFICES

...[done] <note>The text begins mid-word, "cta", likely concluding a word like "facta" (done) from the previous page.</note> on account of a very close similarity and property. For this reason, all theologians rightly applied themselves first of all to abstinence, and the Egyptian <note>Likely a reference to an Egyptian priest or the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, whom Porphyry frequently cites as an authority on sacred mysteries.</note> revealed these causes to us, bringing forward a most natural explanation which experience had confirmed. 

Namely, because a depraved and irrational soul which has left its body by violence, being stripped of it, then moves itself toward that very body and prolongs its stay there. From this, it follows that the souls of men who have died by violence also linger and remain around the body. This very fact warns us not to force the soul out of the body by violent means. Therefore, since the violent slaughter of living things compels their souls to cherish the bodies they have left, nothing hinders a soul from being present wherever anything kindred attracts it. This is why many souls have been seen lamenting everywhere, and why the souls of men who lack burial linger around their corpses. 

Sorcerers truly often abuse these souls to carry out their service, compelling the souls by placing the body nearby, or by taking some part of it <note>A reference to necromancy or "sympathetic magic," where physical remains are used to bind a spirit.</note>. Since these facts were discovered in this history, and they recognized the base nature of the soul and its kinship to the body—and the pleasure by which it is affected toward the body from which it was torn away—they rightly fled from and condemned nourishment from animals. They did this lest they should thus summon to themselves foreign souls, torn away violently and impure, which are drawn to what is kindred to them. They also wished to ensure they would not be prevented from approaching God alone and pure, for they might be driven away from God by the presence of disturbing demons. 

That the nature of a kindred body acts as a certain incentive for attracting the soul is something experience has taught theologians in many instances. For those who desired to introduce into themselves the souls of <term>prophetic animals</term> <note>Animals believed to have natural divinatory powers, such as hawks or crows.</note>, by swallowing the principal members of those creatures—such as the hearts of stags, or moles, or hawks—received immediately the present soul prophesying in the manner of a god. This soul, along with the inward taking of its own body into the human body, insinuated itself deeply within. 

Rightly, therefore, the philosopher and the priest of the God who rules over all things abstains from all animals. Such a man strives by himself to approach the one God alone, so long as no crowd of companions <note>Here, "companions" refers to the lingering, irrational souls of slaughtered animals or low-level spirits.</note> diverts him. By this communion, he himself then understands the natures of things and prophesies. He has God within himself; from this, he possesses the confidence and the pledge of eternal life. Being entirely translated to God, he now emerges as an intimate of Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis"; used here to denote the supreme Deity or the Demiurge in a Neo-Platonic sense.</note> in the place of a seer. 

Hence, if any necessity presses, good demons are not lacking to this intimate of divinity, meeting him everywhere and foretelling future things through dreams, signs, and voices, from which he may learn what it is necessary to avoid. For one must only depart from evil and recognize what is best and most venerable in the universe, and the whole, which is entirely good, friendly, and affable. But wickedness and ignorance of divine things compel a person to despise what he does not know...

Indeed, the wise man knows that wicked <term>demons</term><note>In Porphyry’s Neoplatonic worldview, demons are intermediate spirits between gods and men; "bad" demons are those tied to the material world and blood.</note> delight in animal sacrifices and foretell the future through them. ## From the third book.
### That souls are sentient, rational, and immortal.

IN the third book, he states that he brings forward the true and <term>Pythagorean opinion</term><note>Followers of Pythagoras believed in the transmigration of souls between humans and animals, which led them to practice vegetarianism.</note>: namely, that every soul endowed with senses and memory is rational. He argues that animals possess reason and speech—both internal thought and external expression—by which they speak among themselves. That their words are not understood by us is no wonder, since we often fail to understand the speech of "barbarians" <note>To a Greek or Roman writer, a "barbarian" was simply anyone who did not speak their language.</note> and many other peoples, yet we do not assume they are merely making indistinct noises. He adds that if we are to believe the ancients and those who lived in the time of our fathers and our own time, there are some who say they can hear the speech of animals and understand it. This was said of the ancients such as <term>Melampus</term> and <term>Tiresias</term> <note>Mythological seers famous for their ability to understand the language of birds.</note> and others like them. More recently, it was said of <term>Apollonius of Tyana</term> <note>A famous philosopher and traveling sage of the 1st century AD often credited with supernatural powers.</note>, of whom they say that while in a circle of friends, he heard a swallow announcing to other birds that a donkey laden with wheat had fallen near the city and the grain was scattered on the ground.

He then argues that animals possess reason: first, because they communicate their needs to one another; second, because they look after themselves with diligent skill and provide for future use; and third, because they learn many things both from one another and from humans, and teach each other in turn. He adds that Aristotle, Plato, Empedocles, Democritus, and others who investigated the truth about animals found that they participate in reason and speech. However, it appears in this diversity—as Aristotle also said—that they differ very little in essence, but rather by a degree of "more or less." Just as many believe the difference between gods and men lies in this—not in their fundamental nature, but according to the perfect or imperfect habit of reason—so we consider the nature of reason to be common between us and the animals, differing only by degree. Aristotle says those animals are more prudent (that is, more clever) which excel in the sharpness of their senses. Indeed, differences in physical bodies make the soul more or less "passive" <note>Meaning how easily the soul is affected by physical sensations or emotions.</note> or more or less ready to use reason; however, these physical differences cannot change the soul according to its fundamental essence.

->ON SACRIFICES<-
K ii

# ON SACRIFICES

Neither senses nor passions make <term>them</term><note>Referring to the various species of animals.</note> differ fundamentally from one another, nor do they cause the perfect state to be overstepped. Let it be granted, therefore, that there is a difference of degree in their faculty of reason, according to "more and less"; yet the rest of the animals are not entirely deprived of reason. Nor should we, because we understand more than the animals, deprive them of all understanding—just as we do not deny that partridges fly simply because hawks fly faster. One might indeed concede that the soul suffers along with the body, and is affected for better or worse when the body is affected; yet the nature of the soul itself is by no means changed by this. If the soul only suffers with the body and uses it as an <term>instrument</term><note>A key Neoplatonic concept: the soul is the user, and the body is the tool or "organon."</note>, it will indeed perform many things differently through it depending on how that instrument is disposed, just as we are limited by our own physical states. Thus, the soul suffers according to the body's condition, yet it does not change its own essential nature. 

Those who call animals "brutes" even when they act rationally, claiming they do so merely "by nature," fail to realize they are actually saying these animals are rational by their very nature. It is as if reason were not innate to us by nature as well. Our own perfection grows according to how we are naturally constituted; however, that which is <term>divine</term><note>Porphyry suggests that innate reason is a spark of the divine that does not require "schooling" to exist.</note> does not become rational through instruction. For there was never a time when the divine was not rational; it existed and was rational simultaneously. Nor is a being prohibited from being rational simply because it did not receive its reason through schooling—though even among other animals, just as among men, nature itself has taught many things, while instruction has provided others. 

Not without reason have some attempted to show that many animals are even more prudent than we are, depending on the regions they were allotted. For just as those inhabiting the <term>ether</term><note>The "highest" and purest element, where the gods and celestial beings were thought to reside.</note> are rational, so they say those inhabiting the regions closest to them—that is, in the air—possess reason. Then come those in the water, and finally those on the earth; they differ among themselves by the degree of their reason. For if we measure the dignity of the gods in some way by their locations, so too do we weigh the dignity of animals. 

Socrates and, before him, <term>Rhadamanthus</term><note>A mythical king of Crete and judge of the underworld, known for his absolute justice.</note> used to swear by animals. The Egyptians even regarded certain animals as gods—whether they truly believed them to be gods, or whether they deliberately painted the forms of the gods with the face of an ox, the countenance of birds, or other creatures. They did this so that people would abstain from harming animals just as they abstain from harming men, or perhaps for some other more secret reason. Similarly, the Greeks placed the horns of a ram upon the statue of <term>Jupiter</term><note>original: "Iouis"; specifically referring to Jupiter-Ammon.</note>, and the horns of a bull upon the statue of <term>Dionysus</term>. As for <term>Pan</term>, they composed him of a man and a goat. They gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens, and they say that <term>Cupid</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Jupiter</term> took the forms of a bull, an eagle, and a swan. By these things, the ancients testified that animals ought to be honored. And Socrates was not joking when he said that the swans were his "fellow servants." Indeed, the <term>Table</term><note>Likely referring to the "Table of Cebes" or similar Pythagorean allegorical texts regarding the descent of souls.</note> indicates that animals share a common soul with us, saying that by the indignation of the gods, souls pass from men into animals, and when they have passed through, the gods finally take pity. By these and similar signs, it is signified that animals are rational; though their reason is in many cases imperfect, it is nonetheless not entirely absent.

It cites ancient Egyptian and Greek religious iconography—where gods take animal forms—as evidence of the traditional respect and spiritual status afforded to animals.</summary>

## It is wicked to kill animals.

It is unjust to kill animals since they are not entirely alien to us. Yet we, as if we were wanton and insolent, frequently kill a great many animals everywhere for sport in the <term>theaters</term><note>Porphyry refers to the Roman practice of "venationes," or staged animal hunts, which were held as public spectacles in amphitheaters.</note> and in hunts. The result of this is that the savage and cruel beast-like power within us has grown more intensely powerful, while our humanity and gentleness have withered away. The <term>Pythagoreans</term><note>Followers of Pythagoras, who were famous in antiquity for their belief in the transmigration of souls and their consequent practice of vegetarianism.</note>, however, cultivated gentleness and clemency toward wild beasts as a model of humanity and mercy.

Everything that is inanimate, since it lacks reason and mind, is the opposite of that which possesses a soul, reason, and a certain intelligence. For every animate creature that possesses sensation also possesses <term>imagination</term><note>Original: "phantasiam." In ancient philosophy, this refers to the ability to receive and retain mental impressions from the senses.</note> as a kind of reason. Nature, which does and has done all things for the sake of something and toward some end, did not create the sentient animal simply to feel and be acted upon, but rather so that it might perceive what things are beneficial to it and what are harmful—and that it might pursue the former and flee from the latter. Sensation, therefore, brings the knowledge of both to individual animals. However, those things that follow sensation—namely, the pursuit and apprehension of the useful, and the avoidance of the harmful—must be considered absent unless they possess a certain power of <term>reasoning</term><note>Original: "rōcinationé" (ratiocinationem). Porphyry argues that simple reflex is not enough to explain how animals navigate their environments.</note>, judgment, and memory. And if <term>Strato the Physicist</term><note>Strato of Lampsacus (c. 335–c. 269 BCE), a Peripatetic philosopher who argued that all perception is a form of thought, noting that if our mind is distracted, our eyes may see but we do not "perceive."</note> says that sensation does nothing without intelligence—since we do not perceive things present to our senses while we are intently thinking of something else—then it must be that the senses do not act without the mind. When sensation directs itself toward what is its own and what is foreign by its action, and places a distinction between these two, and flees from the one while pursuing the other, and sagaciously finds the means for pursuing and fleeing, we can conclude that reason is present within it. These things are proper to reason, and they are present in all animals—that is, in all those capable of movement.

## He who lives content with little and is innocent is like a god.

Since the goal of the soul is to become like God, and God stands in need of nothing and harms no one, he is certainly the happiest and most like God who so prepares himself that he requires the fewest external things and causes the least harm. Such a man, therefore, will feed only on the fruits of the earth, so that he does not harm men, nor harm animals; and as much as it is possible, he will even spare plants and herbs. For the ancients even lamented this: that we should need the fruits of trees at all. The cause of this <term>need</term><note>Original: "egestatis."</note> is <term>generation</term><note>Original: "generatio." In Neoplatonic thought, "generation" refers to the descent of the soul into the physical world of birth and matter, which is inherently a state of "poverty" compared to the spiritual realm.</note>, because in that very state of want we are placed through birth, having already been removed from a state of abundance. Indeed, poverty seeks its preservation from external things. Therefore, he who needs more external things is more closely joined to poverty, and is thus more distantly separated from God. For he who is like God possesses true abundance through this very likeness. The rich man who enjoys his riches brings injury to no one; for as long as he brings injury, even if he possesses all the money and all the...

<summary>Porphyry argues that killing animals for sport corrupts human character and that animal behavior proves they possess a degree of reasoning. He concludes that the most godlike life is one of vegetarianism and minimal consumption, as it reflects divine self-sufficiency and harmlessness.</summary>

->ON SACRIFICES.<-

# ON SACRIFICES.

Whoever clings to the earth must be considered poor, for he is a friend to want. Therefore, a <term>just man</term><note>In this Neoplatonic context, a "just man" is one who seeks to align his soul with the divine order.</note> who is uninitiated is polluted by all depravity—a vice brought upon us by a certain fall of the soul as it descends from the good into matter. All things are therefore trifles if one fails from the beginning. The soul is in need of everything as long as it does not look up toward that very fullness. However, that which is mortal in its nature yields to the soul as long as the soul does not truly know itself. But he who, having already become like God, is content with the smallest things for his sustenance, enjoys that prosperity of the <term>Golden Age</term><note>A mythical primordial era of peace and harmony where humans were said to live without toil or violence.</note>.

## A certain reason is also present in animals.

Reason indeed exists naturally. However, <term>right and perfect reason</term><note>Original: "ratio uero recta perfectāq;". This refers to the Stoic and Platonic ideal of reason fully developed through philosophy.</note> is formed through meditation and instruction. Therefore, a certain participation in the rational faculty belongs to all animals. Yet one cannot find even a human who has fully attained perfect rectitude and wisdom; and just as there are differences in sight itself and in flight itself—for <term>hawks</term><note>Original: "Astures," likely referring to the northern goshawk or similar birds of prey.</note> and <term>cicadas</term><note>Original: "Cicadæ." Ancient authors often compared the "voices" and sensory lives of various creatures to highlight natural diversity.</note> do not see in the same way, nor do eagles and partridges fly in the same way—so too is every rational being not equally a participant in sharpness and cunning.

### From the fourth book.
## The ancients abstained from animals.

<term>Dicearchus</term><note>Original: "Icearchus" (an OCR error for Dicearchus), a Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle.</note> the <term>Peripatetic</term><note>A member of the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle.</note> says that the ancient Greeks, as if born closest to God, were the best by nature and lived the best life, so much so that their generation was judged to be of "gold." He adds that they killed no animal. Truly, they found nothing better for health than to minimize the accumulation of superfluities. Therefore, they did not wish to take in nourishment that was more powerful than nature, but rather that by which nature might be made more powerful. The ancient priests of the Egyptians, also devoted to the study of wisdom—whom <term>Chaereon</term><note>Original: "Cheremon," an Egyptian Stoic philosopher and priest of the 1st century AD.</note> the <term>Stoic</term><note>A school of philosophy that taught the development of self-control and fortitude as a means of overcoming destructive emotions.</note> treats most diligently—abstained for the most part from animals. Indeed, they even venerated many things as divine, some of which they said were suited to various gods, such as the hawk, the beetle, the ram, and the crocodile to the Sun. For they understood that the soul of every animal is rational when it has been separated from the body, and is foreknowing of the future, divining for us, and the maker of all things, just as the soul of a man is when released from the body. Therefore, they did not honor animals without reason, and they restrained themselves from them as much as possible.

## The sober life of the Essenes.

He then narrates from the history of <term>Josephus</term><note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> the life of the <term>Essenes</term><note>A Jewish sect known for their asceticism, communal property, and ritual purity.</note>, a religious and philosophical sect among the Jews. They held all things in common, practiced mutual charity, and practiced abstinence...

PORPHYRY: WHY THE ANCIENTS
