# PORPHYRY: WHY THE ANCIENTS

...restraint and patience above all things. They were always intent on divine worship; they were so strong in spirit that they preferred to be killed rather than deny God. And in the midst of their very tortures, they were accustomed to laugh openly; those who were tortured for this reason emitted their souls cheerfully, as if they were to receive them back again. For this opinion is established among them, he says, that souls are immortal and, descending from the thinnest ether, are attached to bodies by an <term>impulse</term><note>Original: ῥυμῇ (*rhymē*), meaning a rush, force, or natural instinct that draws the soul into a physical form.</note>, drawn to bodies by natural instinct. But after they have emigrated from the prison of the body, they exult as if now free from a long servitude, through which they raise themselves to the heights. They abstained then from many animals, and from all incontinence entirely. Finally, from a life that was most temperate, most studious of truth, and most devoted to God, many among them predicted future things; therefore they were called prophets.

-> The ancient sages held the present life in contempt in hope of the future. <-

The sages of the Indians are named <term>Gymnosophists</term><note>Literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greek writers to describe ancient Indian ascetics who practiced extreme self-denial.</note>; among them, those who proceeded in the study of religion and wisdom by a certain succession of lineage are called <term>Brahmans</term><note>The traditional priestly and scholarly class of India.</note>. Those, however, who professed the same by choice alone were called <term>Samaneans</term><note>Derived from the Sanskrit *Shramana*; these were wandering ascetics, including early Buddhists and Jains, who entered the religious life by personal vow rather than birth.</note>, whose life <term>Bardesanes of Babylon</term><note>A 2nd-century Syrian Gnostic scholar known for his descriptions of Indian religions.</note> describes at length. The Samaneans bore the time of this life unwillingly, as if it were a certain necessary servitude serving nature, and they studied how to release their souls from the body. And when they felt the body was faring well, they often departed from life with nothing urging them to do so; therefore their households considered them blessed in death and wept for those who survived them as unfortunate.

-> Sobriety and contemplation join the mind to God. <-

The Gymnosophists, besides their other temperance and holiness, abstained from animals.

Indeed, holiness that abstains from mortal things contains eternal life. But a fattened body forces the soul to starve, falling away from a happy life; and it increases that which is mortal, expelling and hindering eternal life, it contaminates us and renders the soul corporeal, turning it aside toward that which is different. The <term>lodestone</term><note>A naturally magnetized mineral (magnetite).</note>, however, delivers as if a certain soul to the iron whenever it approaches it. Whence iron, by nature most heavy, becomes light and is lifted up by the spirit of the magnet, bringing itself to the magnet. If anyone, therefore, has lived suspended toward God in a non-corporeal and intellectual way, he rightly ought not to seek nourishment by which the body is fattened, which hinders the path to the mind. But he will reduce the body to the minimum and entirely necessary food. And he himself will be nourished by divinity, joined to God more naturally than iron to the magnet. Now indeed, if we did not even require the smallest nutrients, we would be so much happier as we would be more immortal. But now, living in this mortal state, we even (so to speak) secretly make ourselves more mortal

# THEY ABSTAINED FROM ANIMALS.

While we build up the body and—as Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was the successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school.</note> says—while it becomes <term>subject to passion</term><note>Original Greek: ἐμπαθῇ (*empathē*). This refers to the soul becoming "passive" or "affected" by the physical sensations and disturbances of the flesh.</note>, the soul, through its familiarity in dwelling with the body, contracts a great many bonds and moreover gives itself over entirely to it. But if only we could have lived our lives completely without food or drink, so that by restraining the body’s <term>outflow</term><note>The philosophical idea that the body is in a constant state of flux or "leaking" energy and substance, which forces the soul to focus on maintenance rather than contemplation.</note> we might be joined immediately to the highest things, in which God, being as He is, exists as God. 

But why do we shout and weep over these things in vain to men who are so blinded? They constantly nurture their own misfortune; they hate first themselves and their true Father <note>In Neoplatonism, the "Father" or "Generator" refers to the divine source or the One from which all souls originate.</note>. Next, they even hate those who warn and encourage them to finally wake up from their <term>drunkenness</term><note>A common ancient metaphor for the soul being dazed or "intoxicated" by material pleasures and forgetful of its divine home.</note>. 

Democrates <note>Likely referring to Democritus the "laughing philosopher," or a Pythagorean source; Porphyry often quotes such aphorisms to emphasize moral discipline.</note> says that to live without wisdom, without restraint, and without piety is not so much to live poorly as it is to die for a long time.

# THEY ARE CLOTHED FOR SOULS.

Since our body overflows with blood and humors, and is governed by the motion and powers of its soul, it must be that there is a seat for the soul and spirit within this body. But since the soul is <term>incorporeal</term><note>Meaning it has no physical substance or "body."</note>—and is reason itself—how can it exist within a physical body? Certainly, it is because a dwelling place had to be found for it, in which the soul might be carried as if in a <term>vehicle</term><note>Original Latin: *vehiculo*. This refers to the *ochema*, a "soul-carriage" or "astral body" in ancient philosophy that allows the divine soul to interact with the heavy, material world.</note>. 

And that dwelling is most suitable which is closest to the soul's own nature, while also being closest to the nature of the body—that is, something that acts as a **medium** between the two. This medium is indeed air, and a thin, warm spirit. For Paul <note>The Apostle Paul; the author is likely referencing 1 Corinthians or similar Pauline epistles regarding the "spiritual body."</note> cries out: "In which also your spirit dwelt." Furthermore, Solomon <note>Traditionally referring to the Wisdom of Solomon or Ecclesiastes.</note> and Democritus <note>The "laughing philosopher" (c. 460–370 BC) who proposed that the soul was composed of fine, fiery atoms.</note> assert that the soul is governed and moved by spirit, air, and heat. This matter—and it is a wonder—is especially affected; it is the one thing belonging to all living beings, as long as it is, and when it is not... <note>The final sentence of this section appears truncated or corrupted in the original transcription.</note>

<note>The vocabulary list suggests this text is related to or influenced by **Hieronymus Cardanus** (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath. His work *De subtilitate* ("On Subtlety") explored the intersections of medicine, physics, and the soul, often citing the authorities mentioned here.</note>

## MARSILIO Ficino the Florentine to the Magnanimous LORENZO de' Medici. Health and greetings.

->SYnesius, along with Psellus, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Porphyry the Platonists <note>These are the core philosophers of Neoplatonism, a school of thought that merged Plato's ideas with mysticism. Ficino was the primary figure responsible for translating their works into Latin during the Renaissance.</note> long ago entered your most ample house and greeted your noble sons. So far, they seem to have acted quite correctly. However, because they left you un-greeted, they have neither acted prudently nor escaped without misfortune. Recognizing their imprudence at last, so that they might be more fortunate, they now revisit your threshold to acknowledge the father, and once again to recognize the sons together with the father. Thus, they will live more happily from now on. Indeed, they have recently discovered that not even our own books *On Life* <note>Original: "de uita nostros." This refers to Ficino's famous three-part treatise *De vita libri tres*, which dealt with health, longevity, and astral magic.</note> wished to live without your protection. In addition to these five philosophers, Priscian the Lydian and Theophrastus <note>Late ancient commentators who bridged the gaps between the philosophies of Aristotle and Plato regarding the soul and perception.</note> accompany them. Since they have long said "health" to my well-being and desired it ardently, today they approach you eagerly, so that they might achieve their vow with great effort: that first they themselves may be safe with you, and then they may keep my own well-being safe, which desires to be healthy through you especially, after God. Farewell before all others, our best patron, and listen happily to such great philosophers conversing in your presence.<-

## MARSILIO Ficino the Florentine to PIERO de' Medici, the magnanimous man. Health and greetings.

Although you read many things every day that are better than ours, I believe almost none please you more than ours—if indeed one’s own things are usually most pleasing, and those things are most especially one’s own which have been possessed as the oldest of all. Certainly, these **Marsilian** works are possessed by you as the oldest. I hope, therefore, that these will always be most dear to you, so that even if I send dreams, these too might be held as if for truths among you first, and through you, held as true among others. Since, therefore, I desired the book of Synesius the Platonist *On Dreams* <note>Synesius of Cyrene was a 4th-century philosopher-bishop. His work *De Insomniis* (On Dreams) argues that the "spirit" is the organ of dreams and a gateway to divine knowledge.</note>—which we have recently translated from the Greek—to have authority and trust especially with the first reader, and through him with others, I have sent it specifically to you. You are now the fourth generation <note>Piero was the son of Lorenzo, grandson of Piero the Gouty, and great-grandson of Cosimo "the Elder."</note> after the great Cosimo to read our works, and you will immediately prove these to everyone by your approval. I have joined to the book *On Dreams* the book of Michael Psellus the Platonist *On Demons* <note>Michael Psellus was an 11th-century Byzantine scholar. Ficino pairs these two works because Neoplatonists believed that "daemons"—spiritual intermediaries—often communicated with humans through the medium of dreams.</note>—not without merit, since the ancients believe that dreams are sent by demons. Farewell. April 15, 1489.

# SYNESIUS

->**Synesius on Dreams, translated by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine for Piero de' Medici.**<-

<margin>u</margin> It is an ancient custom, and especially a Platonic one, to hide the more serious mysteries of philosophy under a certain more humble pretext, lest by chance those things which were discovered with the greatest labor might perish, or meanwhile be defiled if they were openly exposed to the common people. <note>Ficino is referring to the "Esoteric" tradition, where philosophers used allegories or difficult language to protect sacred truths from those who might misunderstand or disrespect them.</note> Therefore, we have followed this custom in this work to the best of our ability. Whether we have indeed achieved this, and whether we have treated the rest in the manner of the ancients with abundance, those who read these things with a philosophical mind will be able to judge.

->**The prophecy of those things which humans pursue is the best.**<-

<margin>s</margin> If dreams are prophets, and if the things seen in dreams provide humans with the <term>shrouds</term> <note>Original: "inuolucra," meaning coverings or allegorical veils.</note> of future events, they will certainly be wise, yet they will not be certain, insofar as the wisdom of dreams consists in that very uncertainty. For the gods have hidden the [true] life from men. For to achieve the greatest things without labor is a good proper to divinity alone. Among us, however, not only virtues but all other excellent things are sought through sweat. Indeed, <term>Prophecy</term> <note>Original: "Vaticinium," refers to the art of foretelling the future or divine inspiration.</note> will be seen as the greatest of goods. For by its very information, and by the faculty of knowledge itself, God excels man, just as man excels the beast. But for God, nature itself suffices for knowledge. For man, however, prophecy brings far more than common knowledge provides. For the common people know only present things, but only guess at future ones. Only **Calchas** <note>The famous seer of the Greeks during the Trojan War, mentioned in Homer's Iliad.</note> in the assembly of all the Greeks knew those things which are, which were, and which are soon to be drawn into the future. For this reason, in **Homer**, the affairs of the gods depend upon the very judgment of **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>, since he existed before and knows more, by the very fact that he is more ancient. Indeed, I believe age is emphasized in the poems because it happens that one knows more through the benefit of time, since knowledge itself is truly the most honorable thing. If anyone, however, led by other poems, should think that the empire of Jove consists in the power of his hands because the poet says "he is superior in strength," that person interprets the poem poorly. He does not understand the philosophy within it, which says the gods are nothing other than <term>Minds</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, gods were often identified with "Intellects" or "Minds" (Noes) rather than physical beings.</note>. Thus, he again adds to the statement that he "excels in strength" the fact that he is also "prior in birth," since he calls Jove an older Mind. But what else is the strength of the Mind itself than **Prudence**? Whoever, therefore, is a god and is deemed worthy to preside over others, since he is Mind, he commands by the excellence of his wisdom. Therefore, when he says, "he is more excellent in strength," it signifies the same to us as "he knows more." And for that reason...

# ON DREAMS
<sig>L ii</sig>

## ON DREAMS

Therefore the wise man is also said to be like God, because he strives to be closer to the divine mind and exercises himself in that intelligence which constitutes the divine essence. By these reasons, let it be demonstrated that the prophecy concerning the things humans strive for is the best.

<margin>In the world, as in a single living being, some things provide signs for others.</margin>

Through all things, all things are signified. Indeed, since all things in the single world-animal are related, these are like letters of all forms, marked in the universe as in a book—partly Phoenician, partly Egyptian, and partly Assyrian. <note>Synesius uses the metaphor of different ancient scripts to explain that the "language" of nature is varied and requires specific knowledge to read.</note> The wise man reads these himself. The truly wise man is one who has learned the nature of things; one man reads some signs, another reads others; one reads more, another less. Just as one person reads slowly, syllable by syllable, another reads the whole word at once, and yet another understands the entire speech similarly. In this way, the wise look into the future: some by looking up at the stars, others at flames (whether they are still or moving), others by searching for the future in the <term>entrails</term> <note>Original: "visceribus," referring to hepatoscopy, the practice of reading animal livers and organs.</note>, and others in the chatter of birds, observing meanwhile where they fly or where they land. There are also those who interpret clear signs of the future from voices, and from meetings, or from chance events happening to another. Indeed, since all things signify all things to everyone, if birds were wise, they would surely have gathered the art of prophecy from humans, just as we have accumulated skill from them. For we encounter them, just as they encounter us, recently and long ago, on the right and on the left.

<margin>Such is the harmony of the world that some things are drawn by others and breathe together.</margin>

For since this universe is sympathetic to itself and "conspires" <note>Original: "conspirans," which in a Neoplatonic context means "breathing together" or acting in total harmony.</note>, it is necessary that its parts agree harmoniously among themselves, as parts of a single whole. It is worth considering whether the <term>lures</term> or the <term>wagtails</term> <note>Original: "motacillae." In ancient magic, the wagtail or wryneck bird was used in spells to "draw" or attract people or things.</note> of the magi tend toward this. For just as worldly things are signified by each other in turn, so they are mutually soothed. Now, the wise man is he who understands the kinship of the parts of the world. For he draws one thing through another, holding present things as pledges of those far away—namely voices, materials, and shapes—just as in us, when something suffers internally, another part suffers with it. The pain of a finger often results in a <term>nasal discharge</term> <note>Original: "emunctorium," referring to the body's cleansing organs or passages, like the nose.</note>, while many things in between suffer very little. For both are members of a single living creature and have a closer kinship with each other than with the rest. Moreover, this stone or that herb corresponds to a certain god among the number of worldly gods, to whom it yields as if sharing in its nature, and is as if enchanted. Just as he who strikes a deep note suddenly moves not the nearest <term>major second</term> <note>Original: "sexquioctavam," the musical ratio 9:8.</note> but the <term>perfect fourth</term> <note>Original: "sexquitertiam," the musical ratio 4:3.</note>.

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic concept of "cosmic sympathy," where the universe functions as a single living organism where every part reflects and affects every other part. This interconnectedness allows the wise man to predict the future through various signs in nature, such as astrology, bird flight, or musical resonance.</summary>

<keywords>cosmic sympathy, divination, astrology, augury, musical harmony, magic, Neoplatonism, Synesius, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the world as a unified living organism. Having previously described how the wise man reads the "letters" of the universe, the text now moves into the musical harmony of these parts and why prophecy must remain "obscure" or hidden from the common crowd.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>SYNESIUS</header>

...and the sharp tone named the <term>nete</term>. <note>The "nete" was the highest-pitched string on the ancient Greek lyre. Synesius is using a musical metaphor to explain how different parts of the universe vibrate together.</note> For these things agree more closely with each other. For just as there is a certain concord among the parts, so there is also discord. For this world is not simply one thing, but a "one" made of many. And in it, parts are sometimes in agreement and sometimes in disagreement; yet in such a way that their disagreement contributes to the agreement of the whole, just as the structure of a lyre consists of dissonant and consonant tones. This "one made of opposites" belongs to harmony, the lyre, and the world itself.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Only that which is connected to the world can be influenced by worldly things.
<margin>a</margin> Archimedes the Sicilian used to wish for a certain place outside the earth, hoping that he could thus balance a lever against the entire earth. <note>This refers to Archimedes’ famous boast: "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth."</note> For he said that while he was upon it, he had no power against it; but he who is wise in any matter concerning the nature of the world, if he were placed outside of it, would no longer have any way to use this wisdom. For he uses it toward himself. Therefore, if the continuity is interrupted, this wisdom is in vain, and the signs observed by it lack a soul. But as much of the divine as exists outside the world, all that cannot be enchanted. He who is released from the world is like this; he cares for nothing, for charms and allurements do not touch the nature of the mind. But that which is passive is soothed by charms and drawn in. The multitude of things in the world, and the knowledge of distant things, provide the scope and breadth for prophecies and purifications—the multitude of things for those that are separate, and kinship for those that are united. Regarding expiations and solemnities, let this discourse move nothing at present, yielding faith only to civil law; but it is safe to receive prophecy, for the whole of it is proven through the things contained within the world. As far as the present is concerned, one may choose the best and dwell more intensely on its consideration, while meanwhile we have a natural obscurity in all prophecies, so that no type of it should be rejected for the very reason that it is equally present in the whole and complete nature. Now indeed, reason has declared that this too is to be revered: just as there is a secret in sacred rites, so too oracles are not open to all. Hence he who gives responses in the Pythia <note>The Pythia was the priestess of the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi.</note> is called <term>Loxias</term> <gloss>that is, he is called "oblique" and "twisted,"</gloss> <note>original: "λοξίας." This title for Apollo refers to the ambiguous, "slanting" nature of his prophecies, which were notoriously difficult to interpret.</note> because the common people would have heard in vain about the "wooden wall" which Phoebus <note>Apollo.</note> brought to the Athenians for their safety, unless Themistocles had understood the meaning of the oracle. <note>In 480 BCE, the Oracle told the Athenians they would be saved by a "wooden wall." Most thought this meant a hedge or fence, but Themistocles correctly interpreted it as a fleet of wooden ships, leading to victory at the Battle of Salamis.</note> For this reason, the prophecy of dreams should not be rejected because it is obscure, since it shares this obscurity with all other oracles.

->On Intellect, Reason, and Imagination.<-

<margin>s</margin> One must study this most of all, beyond other disciplines, since it is from within us, and internal, and proper to each individual soul...

-># ON DREAMS<-

<note>L iii</note>
<meta>image quality: high; catchword partially visible as bleed-through</meta>

...proper things. For the <term>Intellect</term> <note>In Synesius’s Neoplatonic philosophy, the "Intellect" (Intellectus) is the divine level of reality containing the eternal patterns of all things.</note> possesses the forms of all beings, just as ancient philosophy teaches. We can also add that, just as the Intellect possesses the forms of things that *are* (eternal beings), so the <term>soul</term> <note>The "Soul" (Anima) is the bridge between the eternal Intellect and the changing physical world.</note> possesses the forms of things that *become* (changing things). Indeed, the Intellect stands in relation to the soul as "Being" stands to "the Generated." If, therefore, we swap and match the first to the third, and the second to the fourth, and exchange them in turn, we shall nonetheless speak the truth according to the rules of knowledge. Thus it will be demonstrated, as we hold, that the soul possesses the forms of things that "become." It has all these forms, but it brings into action primarily those that are most fitting, and it illuminates the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiam"</note> like a mirror. Through this mirror, the living creature notices the things that remain within itself. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as we do not notice the actions of the Intellect itself until that presiding power announces them to our common sense—and whatever does not reach that sense remains hidden from the living creature—so too we do not usually notice the things in the "primal soul" until their impressions reach the imagination. And these impressions seem to exist as a certain kind of life that has slipped down a little from that higher place, subsiding into the specific property of nature. The powers of sensing are certainly within this imagination. For indeed we see colors, and hear voices, and perceive the strongest impact of touch while the instrumental parts of the body <note>The physical eyes, ears, and skin.</note> are doing nothing. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Perhaps nothing prevents this kind of sensing from being more sacred than our physical senses. For through this, we sometimes draw near to the gods as they warn us, foretell the future, and simply advise us. Therefore, if someone happened upon a treasure through the gift of a dream, I would not be very surprised. Nor would I wonder if someone went to bed unskilled in the **Muses** <note>The goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note> and, while sleeping, encountered them and emerged as a fit poet—partly speaking and partly hearing his verses. This very thing has happened in our own age, and it does not seem entirely unbelievable. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I will pass over for now the well-known benefits of dreaming, by which people are often freed from traps, or the many times sleep has acted as a doctor and expelled ill health. But when a dream opens a way for a soul—even one not hoping for it or thinking of it—toward the most perfect contemplation of eternal things, this is the most eminent gift in the order of the universe. It allows the soul to transcend nature and finally to join with the **Intelligible** <note>The realm of pure thought and divine reality.</note> itself—even a soul that had wandered so far away that it no longer noticed where it came from.

If anyone considers the ascent into eternal things to be a great matter, yet does not trust the faculty of imagination...

...ion to be available for that blessed communion, let one listen to the sacred oracles, which show various paths to this end, and after the whole order of the narrative, provide occasions from our innermost depths for ascending, through which it is granted to increase the inner seed. They say that God has given to some the ability to learn the concept of light thoroughly, while He has made others participants in the vigor and fruit of the divine even in sleep. Do you not see the eloquence of instruction divided here: while it is said that one is taught in wakefulness, another in sleep? 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But in wakefulness, the teacher is a human being; however, for the one dreaming, God Himself makes them a participant in His own fruit and vigor, as if learning and attaining were not the same thing—for to feed upon the fruits is far more than to teach. Indeed, this was taken up by us to assert the dignity of the <term>imaginative life</term> <note>original: "vitae phantasticae". This refers to the life of the spirit centered on the internal "phantasia" or imagination.</note> against those who despair of even the smallest parts of it. Now, it is no wonder they feel this way due to their unnecessary wisdom—those who have busied themselves with things condemned by the sacred oracles, where it is taught that sacrifices and observations of entrails are vain and to be fled far from. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Yet those men, as if superior to the common people, accepting various arts of divination and approving operations of this kind, neglect dreams alone, as if they were something placed before the eyes of their own accord, of which the ignorant and the wise are equally participants everywhere. But what if, for this very reason, there is greater wisdom here, because it is held as a more common gift? Are not other good things, especially the greatest of all, also the most common? There is nothing among all things seen more divine than the sun, and nothing more common than the sun. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If, then, it is a blessed gift to behold God Himself, certainly to perceive through the imagination is the gift of a more ancient and specific inspection. For this is the <term>sense of senses</term> <note>original: "sensus sensuum"</note>, because the <term>imaginative spirit</term> <note>original: "phantasticus spiritus". In Neoplatonic thought, this is the "pneumatic vehicle" or subtle body that acts as the interface between the soul and the physical body.</note> itself is the most common sensory organ and the first body of the soul. This spirit lies hidden, acting within, and holds the principle of the living creature as if from a citadel. For nature constructed the entire framework of the head around it. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Hearing and sight are not themselves senses, but instruments of sense, serving the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "communi sensui". The faculty that unifies data from the five external senses into a single perception.</note>, acting like porters and doorkeepers of the living creature, announcing to the master the sensible things occurring from the outside, by which the external sensory organs are struck. Meanwhile, the inner sense is a whole sense in all its parts; for it hears with the whole spirit, sees with the whole, and is similarly capable of the rest. It distributes some powers to some parts and others to others, each of which is derived separately from the living creature. They are like straight lines flowing from a center and converging toward the center—all from one common root, though many in their outward procession. Therefore, the sense that occurs through the instruments placed openly is most characteristic of the living creature, though it is not a sense until it returns...

# ON DREAMS

...regarding the first point. For a sense that is produced without an external medium is both closer to the soul and certainly more divine.

->Imagination is more perceptive than the external sense.<-

But if you, while honoring the bodily senses for the sake of knowledge—since we know most clearly those things which we see—nevertheless reject <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia". In this context, it refers to the internal faculty that processes images and visions, not just "make-believe."</note> as being less reliable than the senses, we seem not to notice sufficiently that even the eye itself does not truly show us all things. It fails to show some things and even lies about others, both due to the nature of the things seen and the nature of the organs of sight. Indeed, the same objects appear smaller or larger depending on the distance, and things seen through water appear larger to us; likewise, an oar appears broken in the water. Furthermore, there is the weakness of the eye itself. For a bleary eye presents things as confused and indistinct. Therefore, whoever suffers in their <term>imaginative spirit</term> <note>original: "phantastico spiritu". This is the 'pneuma' or 'subtle body,' a vaporous substance that Neoplatonists believed connected the physical body to the immortal soul.</note> should not demand clear and distinct visions. 

As for what its disease is, the causes for which it languishes and grows dull, or by what means it may be purged, purified, and restored to its natural purity—these are things you must learn from secret philosophy. Once purified by its mysteries, the spirit becomes divine. Moreover, external influences are shut out before the spirit admits the presence of God; and whoever preserves this spirit in a state of purity through a natural way of life uses a faculty prepared by God. In this way, such a gift is made most universal. For a spirit of this kind also perceives the affections of the soul itself and does not lack sympathy for it, just as the earthly body surrounding it does. For the earthly body often has conditions opposite to the soul’s more excellent affections. 

But the soul’s first and proper <term>vehicle</term> <note>original: "vehiculum". A technical Neoplatonic term (ochema) for the subtle body that carries the soul during its descent from the stars into the physical world.</note>, when the soul is in a healthy state, is thinned out and acquires an ethereal condition; but when the soul is in a bad state, the vehicle grows dull and becomes earthly. In general, this is the bridge between reason and irrational nature, between the incorporeal and corporeal levels, and it serves as the common boundary between both. Through this medium, divine things are joined to the lowest extremes. For this reason, it is difficult for philosophy to fully grasp its nature.

->The imaginative spirit is the first vehicle of the soul.<-

For this spirit claims for itself something unique, as if drawing from the neighborhoods of both extremes; things so widely separated meet here in a single nature. Moreover, nature extends the breadth of the <term>imaginative essence</term> <note>original: "essentiae phantasticae"</note> through many classes of beings. It even descends to animals that do not possess a higher intellect; in those cases, it is not the vehicle of a divine soul, but instead presides over the lesser powers and serves as the animal's own form of reason. Indeed, many things through this imaginative...

The previous page argued that internal imagination is more perceptive than the external senses. # SYNESIUS

...the living being partakes of essence and acts with decorum; it is purified even in irrational animals, to such an extent that something more excellent may be introduced. Indeed, entire classes of <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "daemonum". In Neoplatonic thought, these are intermediate spirits—neither purely divine nor purely human—that can be good or bad.</note> derive their very existence from this kind of life. For they are entirely imaginary in their being, and are formed from those things which are imagined within. Furthermore, man performs many actions through this faculty alone, or if he uses another, he does so more through this one. For we are not accustomed to produce acts of intelligence without <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia".</note>, unless perhaps someone should touch upon the immaterial form for a brief moment; however, to transcend imagination is no less difficult than it is a blessed state. Hence that famous Platonic saying: "It is above all things to be wished for and sufficient, if mind and wisdom should come to someone even in old age," <note>A reference to Plato's *Laws* (653a), suggesting that true intellectual clarity is a rare achievement of a lifetime.</note> signifying an intelligence that shines without the need for imagination. This is because the preceding and common life is the proper domain of imagination, or at least of an intelligence that makes use of imagination.

->**The imaginative spirit stands midway between eternal and temporal things, and it is in this that we live most of our lives.**<-

**A**ccordingly, this animal spirit—which the blessed ones have also called the spiritual soul—becomes a god, an all-shaping daemon, and a reflected image. In this state, the soul also undergoes its punishments. On this point the oracles also agree, comparing the life of the soul in this state to the visions of those who dream. Philosophy also confirms that previous lives serve as certain preparations for the lives that follow immediately after, while the best disposition or habit in souls makes this kind of spirit lighter and wipes away the depth of a baser, sluggish nature.

By natural inclinations, therefore, the spirit is either lifted on high due to heat and dryness—which is symbolized in Plato by the "growing of wings," <note>In the *Phaedrus*, Plato describes the soul's attempt to grow wings and return to the divine realm.</note> and in Heraclitus by the saying "the dry light is the wisest soul" <note>Heraclitus believed that a "dry" soul was virtuous and wise, while a "wet" soul was lost in drunkenness or ignorance.</note>—or the spirit becomes thick and moist, whereby it is submerged into the recesses of the earth, hiding away by its natural weight and being driven into the subterranean region. For this place is most suited to moist spirits. There, a miserable life is led, subject to punishments. However, through time, effort, and other lives, it is possible for the purified soul to emerge once more; for it runs its course through two kinds of lives, and by turns draws near to better or worse things. The soul, when first descending, borrows such a spirit from the celestial spheres, and mounting this as if it were a <term>small boat</term> <note>original: "cimbam". This refers to the *ochema-pneuma* or "astral vehicle," the subtle body the soul acquires as it descends through the planetary spheres toward Earth.</note>, it enters into commerce with the corporeal world. Yet it wages a struggle of such a kind that it either leads the spirit along with it, or they do not remain together. Indeed, though it is difficult, it can happen that the spirit is dismissed and follows no further, for it is a sin to disbelieve the sacred signs. However, the return to the realms above would be shameful if souls did not return what was borrowed, but instead left scattered around the earth that which they received from on high.

<summary>Synesius explains that the 'imaginative spirit' is a middle ground between the eternal and the physical, acting as the soul's vehicle. He describes how the soul's 'dryness' or 'moisture' determines its fate—rising to the heavens or sinking to the underworld.</summary>

## ON DREAMS

And this indeed would happen as a gift from God and the mysteries to the one and the second <note>Likely referring to the union of the soul and its "spirit-vehicle."</note>. For it is so arranged by nature that the soul, once implanted in this [spirit], either makes an impulse together with it, or pulls it, or perhaps is pulled by it; but it is entirely joined together until it ascends again to the place from whence it came. Therefore, when the spirit becomes heavy due to depravity, it drags down the soul with it—the soul which had permitted it to become thus burdened. And this is the state in which the <term>Oracles</term> <note>original: "eloquia". Synesius refers to the Chaldean Oracles, a collection of mystical texts central to late Neoplatonism.</note> terrify the <term>intellectual seed</term> <note>original: "semen intellectuale"; the divine spark or innate capacity for reason within the human soul.</note> within us with these words: "Do not decline into the dark world, beneath which lies a depth that is always an unfaithful foundation, and a black hell, filthy on all sides, rejoicing in a mindless <term>phantom</term> <note>original: "idolo" or "simulacro". This refers to the 'eidolon,' the lowest aspect of the soul that clings to the material world.</note>; in what way is a stupid and mindless life profitable to the mind?" But for the phantom—that is, the image—a lower place is appropriate because of such a state of the spirit. For like rejoices in like.

<margin>The imaginative spirit can become purer or more impure, lighter or heavier.</margin> Consequently, if one single thing is fashioned from both through their union, the intellect also sometimes immerses itself because of the pursuit of pleasure. This, however, is the extreme of all evils: not even to notice the present evil. Those who are oppressed by this state do not attempt to emerge, for the disease has already covered them with a very hard callous. And therefore, since they feel no more pain, they rightly do not strive for a cure. For this reason, repentance has a peculiar power that leads one back to the things above. Indeed, as long as one simply endures their present state, one hardly thinks of escape. Therefore, the greatest part of <term>purification</term> <note>original: "purgationis". In this context, it is the process of stripping away material attachments to allow the soul to ascend.</note> is the will. For by the gift of the will, both deeds and words stretch out a helping hand; but if the will is taken away, the soul lacks every instrument of purification. Since it lacks the greatest pledge of reconciliation, for this reason—both in this life and the next—punishments bring the greatest help to the order of things, for they oppose pain to pleasures and purge "stupid joy" from our soul.

Furthermore, those misfortunes which are said to happen "undeservedly" contribute greatly to uprooting the affection we feel for these worldly fortunes. Certainly, in this way, <term>Providence</term> <note>original: "prouidentia". The divine care or guidance of God over the universe.</note> is confirmed among those who possess a mind, though those who are out of their minds usually distrust Providence because of these same events. For no place is left for the soul to escape from matter if it should fall into no evil here. Therefore, it must be thought that the governors of the lower province <note>Refers to the material or sublunary world.</note> have devised common prosperities as if to set traps for animals. Thus, while one might say that forgetfulness happens to souls departing from here by means of a drink <note>A reference to the River Lethe from classical mythology, where souls drink to forget their past lives.</note>, for the soul entering this life, it is a sweet and charming condition that brings the drink of forgetfulness. For when the soul descends to its first life to labor for a wage, it willingly escapes its own divine nature, acting like a hireling. This descent indeed...

<meta>This page continues Synesius of Cyrene's discourse on the soul's descent and ascent. Having previously discussed how the "spirit-vehicle" can be weighed down by material desires, Synesius here uses the metaphor of a contract or "secret book" to describe the soul's entanglement with matter and the difficulty of breaking free. He references the labors of Hercules and Homeric imagery to explain the soul's struggle.</meta>

<page-num>211</page-num>
<header>SYNESIUS</header>

[The soul] was tending toward fulfilling the mystery of universal nature, so ordered by the rules of inevitable law. But fascinated by the gifts of matter, she is affected much like those who, though they are free, are hired for a set time for wages; yet, captivated by the beauty of some servant-girl, they wish to linger there, deciding to serve the master of the one they love. Now indeed, when by a deep-seated opinion external things related to the body seem to be "good" to us and we take pleasure in them, we seem to agree with the nature of matter that she is beautiful. She, however, marks our agreement as a secret contract <note>original: "libello", literally a small book, here referring to a legal document or binding agreement.</note>, and if ever we decide to depart from there as free people, she cries out that we are fugitives, tries to recall us, and seeks us back like runaway slaves, bringing that contract into the open. Then truly the soul has the greatest need for courage and divine help. For it is no light struggle to renounce one's own confession and pact. It even happens that force is applied. For material avenging punishments are then set in motion according to fate against those who rebel from the laws of fate. And this is exactly what is signified by the <term>labors of Hercules</term> <note>Synesius interprets Hercules’ twelve labors as an allegory for the soul’s struggle to free itself from material entrapment and return to the divine.</note> and the dangers which the sacred words testify that Hercules had to endure, as well as anyone else who bravely contends for freedom, so that he may lead his <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritum"; the 'pneuma' or 'spirit-vehicle' that carries the soul.</note> to that place where the hands of nature can no longer reach. But if its leap happens within the boundaries of nature's domain, the soul is confined into a narrow place and needs even more serious struggles. For then nature does not spare us, as if we now appear as aliens; and if she despairs of our ascent, she exacts punishment for the attempt, and she brings forth lives no longer from both of the jars which <term>Homer</term> <note>Referring to the *Iliad* (24.527), where Zeus has two jars on his floor—one containing blessings and the other containing evils.</note> secretly signifies—teaching that there are two portions of matter and distributing a double condition of fate, from which no good is ever pure. Now indeed, someone may also suffer a moderated, yet worse, lot.

### How useful is repentance for sins, and how ruinous is the love of mortals.

**T**ruly, all lives are entirely involved in error—an error, I say, where after the first descent, a return does not happen immediately. Consider indeed with what a great interval this spirit deals with us. For when the soul is inclined downward, the sacred word teaches that the spirit also becomes heavy and is submerged until it enters a region dark on all sides. But when the soul rises again, the <term>spirit</term> also accompanies it as far as it is able to follow. It is able to follow until it reaches a completely distant level. Hear now what the [sacred] words teach on this matter: "Nor indeed shall you abandon this most cast-down thing in the precipice of matter; but even for the phantom <note>original: "simulacro", referring to the 'eidolon,' the lowest shade or image of the soul that remains attached to the physical world.</note> there is a portion in a region radiant on all sides." This region indeed is completely

to the region dark on all sides.

<meta>This page continues Synesius of Cyrene's argument regarding the soul’s journey. Having discussed the "contract" the soul makes with matter, he now explores how the soul might reclaim its higher nature by gathering the subtle elements (fire and air) it collected during its descent and carrying them back to the celestial spheres.</meta>

-># ON DREAMS <-
<meta>bleed-through text visible from the verso page</meta>

is opposed, even if in this place no one has interpreted it too sharply. For the sacred word seems to recall not only the nature proceeding from there back to the spheres. But also, if the soul—descending from on high before it was clothed in an **earthly shell** <note>original: "cortice terreno"; Synesius uses the metaphor of a "shell" or "bark" to describe the physical body as a temporary, rough covering for the soul.</note>—contracted anything from the sublime fire or air into its **imaginal nature** <note>original: "naturam simulacralem"; this refers to the soul's capacity to hold images, which serves as the "vehicle" for dreams.</note>, it says that this very highest part from the air and fire is called back to the heights along with the better part of the soul. For what is said to signify the most debased of matter cannot be a divine body. Now indeed, reason dictates that those things which communicate and contribute to one thing cannot lack a certain mutual relationship, joining, and perseverance among themselves, especially those whose regions are neighboring, just as fire is closest to the **circular body** <note>original: "orbiculari corpori"; the Neoplatonic term for the celestial heavens or the Fifth Element (Aether), which moves in circles.</note>, and not like the earth which holds the extreme end of things. But if better things, sometimes yielding to worse things, enjoy a communion, they form an indissoluble body in matter, as if formed by that which was permitted to rule in the meeting. Perhaps even the worse things—not struggling against the act or action of the soul, but rather being gentle, obedient, and following—show forth a middle nature that cannot be dissipated; by the guidance of the first soul, they are reduced together into the ethereal lot, and by a common pull are raised to the heights. If not to the summit of the universe, then at least to the summit of the elements; thus they pass the height and reach the **region shining on both sides** <note>original: "regionem utrinque lucentem"; likely referring to the boundary between the material world and the purely intellectual or divine realm.</note>. For it has (as he says) a certain portion in itself, that is, it is received into a certain order of the circular body. But let these things said about the part and lot of the elements be sufficient. Which things one may believe or not believe; yet it is not permitted to deny that the bodily essence, proceeding from there, is naturally lifted up at the same time as the soul flies back from the lowest depths and is fitted to the spheres—that is, it is poured back, as it were, into its own nature.

The soul has a celestial as well as an aerial body with which it flies back to the heights. And indeed, these are the two extreme regions and lots. One is entirely dark to both, the other is glowing from every side; these have been allotted the extremes of happiness and unhappiness. But how many **middle regions** <note>These "middle regions" are the intermediate levels of the cosmos (the planetary spheres) where the soul resides while it is neither fully enlightened nor fully trapped in dark matter.</note> do you think exist in the vastness of the world, which are dark on one side but glowing on the other? In all of these, the soul spends its life together with this **spirit-vehicle** <note>original: "spiritu" (pneuma); in Neoplatonism, the *pneuma* is a "spirit-body" or "astral body" that acts as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note>, changing its forms, habits, and lives in turn. Therefore, when it withdraws into its own nobility, it is a storehouse of truth; for it is pure, translucent, and altogether immaculate. It is even a god, and a prophet if it so pleases. But when it slides down, it is darkened, and it becomes a wanderer and a liar. For that which is misty in the spirit cannot grasp the clarity of true things. Finally, when it holds the middle ground, it partly wanders, and partly attains...

<summary>Synesius discusses the "spirit-vehicle" (pneuma) of the soul, explaining how it gathers subtle elements like fire and air during its descent and can carry them back to the celestial spheres if it maintains its purity. He describes the soul's varying states of truth and deception based on its proximity to the divine light versus material darkness.</summary>

<meta>catchword: How</meta>

...follows. You could also, by this reasoning, explore the **demonic nature** and its order. For in all things, to follow truths or to stray only a little is divine, or nearly divine. However, the condition of straying in foretelling necessarily belongs to those who are constantly inclined toward nature, whose condition is subject to passion and is utterly ambitious. For in this way, the soul enters the subterranean regions and lets go of God and the **older demon** <note>original: "antiquioremque dæmonem"; In Neoplatonic thought, a 'daemon' is often a guiding spirit or a rank of being between gods and men, rather than a "demon" in the modern sense.</note>. But by another means, it receives this guide, approaches it, and attains the region dedicated to a more excellent nature.

### On the Region Altogether Bright and Altogether Dark, and on the Middle Region, and How the Spirit is Revolved Everywhere.

**P**rosequently, one may detect the order of the living soul in man from this: in whomever the **imaginal spirit** <note>original: "phantasticus spiritus"; This is the "spirit-vehicle" or *pneuma*, which Synesius believes acts as the mirror for dreams and the bridge between the physical and the divine.</note> is pure, composed, and receives true images of things whether waking or sleeping. Such a person certainly possesses a pledge by which he can assert that the very form of his soul is gaining a better lot. Nor can we hunt lightly for what the primary affection of the animal spirit might be from the imaginations it produces and in which it dwells, when it is struck by nothing from the outside. Philosophy, supplying its judicial and warning role, urges us to nourish and care for this spirit most diligently, lest it ever go astray. 

The best education, however, is to always act according to the power that contemplates and perceives, and to ensure that the principal act of the soul itself is always entirely intellectual. As much as possible, we should always anticipate the absurd and rash impulses of the fantasy's concepts. This means turning toward the best first and not entering into commerce with the worse, except as much as extreme necessity compels. 

**Intellectual intuition** is a thing that, most of all, separates the things that are thickened within the spirit. For it thins the spirit itself more than can be said and directs it toward God. When the spirit is made fit for this, it draws the divine spirit to the commerce of our soul by a certain kinship. Just as by some condensation it is restrained and becomes narrower—too narrow to fill the seats assigned to it by the providence that fashioned man, which are in the **ventricles of the brain** <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the brain's ventricles were thought to be the "seats" or chambers where the animal spirits and the faculty of imagination resided.</note>. 

Then indeed, since **nature does not tolerate a vacuum** in things, an evil spirit is introduced. Then what does the soul not suffer, being constantly pressed by an execrable evil? For thus has nature prepared it: that the seats of the spirit itself, disposed for this very purpose, are full of either something worse or something better. And that evil is the punishment of those who ignore the divine spirit implanted in them; but that good is either the end of piety itself or, without doubt, very near to that end.

<summary>Synesius explains that the purity of the "imaginal spirit" determines whether the soul connects with divine truths or falls into "subterranean" errors. He argues that intellectual discipline thins the spirit, allowing it to house divine rather than evil influences within the brain's ventricles.</summary>

### How someone may detect the purity or impurity of their spirit, and by what means they may purify it.

**W**hen we decided to discuss the divination that occurs through dreams, we did so lest men should despise it; rather, they should cherish it as something remarkably profitable for life. To this end, we have carefully examined the **imaginal nature** <note>original: "phantasticam naturam"; This refers to the *phantasia* or the faculty of the soul that produces images.</note>. However, from that previous discussion, the immediate benefit was perhaps less apparent. But the more excellent fruit of a healthy spirit is its return to the higher realms. Truly, it is a sacred gain for the soul, so much so that it is a kind of religious meditation to strive to render such a spirit fit for divination. Now, some, captured by the desire for prophecy, have preferred a sacred and simple table to a gluttonous one, and they have loved a bed that is pure and entirely unstained. It is certainly far from the case that those who lingered at the Pythian tripod <note>The tripod at the Oracle of Delphi where the priestess delivered prophecies.</note> or the seat of Phoebus <note>Apollo.</note> for the sake of prophecy would spend their nights there in self-indulgence; rather, they would pray to God and devote themselves more intensely to their vows. What is accumulated little by little eventually becomes much, and what is achieved through another means finally grows into something greater, provided we proceed to love God more vehemently and encourage those who did not love Him before.

<margin>First of all, one must strive to keep the imaginal spirit pure and fit for divination.</margin>

**T**herefore, one must not despise divination, which leads us to divine things and remains close by, for it is the most excellent power of the soul. Nor is the utility of the soul—when so joined to God—any less because it has been admitted into divine commerce. For it does not meanwhile abandon the **living being** <note>original: "animal"; in this Neoplatonic context, it refers to the composite of soul and body.</note>; indeed, from its watchtower, it surveys lower things much more fully than if it were mixed with inferior matters. Therefore, remaining unshaken, it will provide images of things that happen to the living being. This is what is meant by the saying that "one who descends does not descend," <note>A Neoplatonic paradox suggesting the higher soul can care for the body without being corrupted by it or truly "falling" into the material world.</note> when a more excellent nature cares for a lower one without being held captive by it. This kind of prophecy I wish for myself and would offer to my children—a kind for which we are not compelled to undertake long journeys or sail outside our borders, as one would for the oracle of Pythian Apollo or **Jupiter Ammon** <note>An ancient oracle in the Libyan desert.</note>. Instead, it is enough to give oneself to sleep with "joyful hands" and after celebrating divine praises. Such a soul, having first performed these joyful acts and clothed itself in a garment of pure color, makes its vows to **Minerva** <note>The goddess of wisdom (Athena).</note>. Thus we shall desire a dream, just as Homer perhaps once desired. For if one is prepared, the God who is said to be "far off" will be present instantly; since for us, even if we have performed no such rituals but are merely sleeping, He is present everywhere; and these things indeed...

<summary>Synesius argues that purifying the "imaginal spirit" through a simple, temperate life is a form of religious practice that enables prophetic dreams. He contrasts the accessibility of dreams with the difficulty of traveling to famous ancient oracles.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s defense of dream-divination. Having previously established the "imaginal spirit" as the medium for these visions, he now argues for the democratic and accessible nature of dreams compared to the expensive, elite, and cumbersome rituals of external oracles.</meta>

->SYNESIUS<-

The entire treatment of the mysteries is one for which no one has ever blamed poverty, as if for that reason it followed the wealthy less than others. Most states choose their overseers of sacred rites from among the most noble and the richest, just as the Athenians choose their naval commanders <note>original: "classis gubernatores"; Synesius refers to the *trierarchy*, a "liturgy" or public service where the wealthiest Athenian citizens were required to out-fit and command a warship at their own expense.</note>. Among them, there is a need for magnificent expenditures and a no small fortune, so that Cretan herbs, Egyptian feathers, Iberian bone <note>original: "ósq́ue hibericum"; likely a reference to an exotic animal part or mineral used in external theurgic rituals.</note>, and by Jove, whatever prodigious thing is born and nourished in the deep sea—whether in the setting or the rising sun—may be imported. For certain things of this kind and many others of the same sort are recounted concerning those who contrive prophecy obtained from without <note>original: "forinsecus"; referring to external oracles like Delphi or Claros that required physical travel and expensive offerings.</note>. The means of no private citizen suffice to provide such things. 

A dream, however, is seen by the man of small means just as much as by the man who possesses a great estate, and by him who labors under the extreme lack of food. The lookout sees it as well as the hireling, and the citizen no differently than the foreigner; indeed, before God, in the matter of prophecy, the herdsman, the slave, and the madman differ not at all from the rest. Because the condition of this prophecy is quite accessible to all peoples, it is surely the most humane; because it is simple and ready-at-hand by itself, it is quite philosophical; because it is not forced, it is undoubtedly pious; and because it is present everywhere—and we are not compelled to employ water, or a rock, or a chasm in the earth <note>References to physical oracles: water (Castalian spring), rock/chasm (the Delphic fissure).</note>—it is deservedly judged most divine. 

It was also fitting to praise it first because, for the sake of this kind of prophecy, we are not distracted from even a single business of life, nor do we waste any time. For no one, having set aside necessary and present business, goes home to bed for a scheduled dream; rather, it is that very time which is necessary for a living creature to spend for the sake of restoring nature <note>i.e., sleep.</note>. Since our substance cannot suffice for perpetual waking action, this time, I say, it grants us freely—the very thing which is often called "leisure greater than business" <note>original: "ociũ negocio maius"; a play on the Roman concept of *otium* (leisure/study) versus *negotium* (business/public life).</note>, uniting, of course, the desirable with the necessary, and well-being with simple existence. 

On the contrary, regarding those foretellings which are accustomed to come by various instruments, we must consider ourselves well treated if, while claiming the greater part of our life for themselves, they meanwhile grant something to the other uses and actions of life. In these, if you direct your mind entirely to any part, it will be very difficult for you to be helped by such prophecy. For it is not possible at any time or place to take up the apparatus and furniture serving sacred rites, nor is it easy to carry around with one the instruments necessary for solemn rites. And to pass over other things: where punishments were recently heaped up, there is a certain harsh heaviness of the hollow ship <note>An allusion to the logistical difficulty of transporting the heavy "baggage" of ritual religion by sea.</note>, to which other parts of the sacred rites are added—namely listed men and witnesses—for so it is more truly said, since this age of ours is accustomed to announce many things through the ministers of the laws.

<summary>Synesius argues that dream-divination is superior to external oracles because it is free, requires no expensive exotic materials, and is available to all people regardless of social class. He emphasizes that while traditional oracles are burdensome and elitist, dreams utilize the necessary time of sleep to provide divine insight without interrupting daily life.</summary>

->ON DREAMS<-

Through their works, sacred rites—already made public—have come into the sight and hearing of the profane common folk. For besides being troublesome and wretched, it is (in my opinion) undoubtedly hateful to God to impose these things upon men. To move someone who is unwilling by force and compulsion is nothing other than to commit an act of violence, a deed which even the founder of laws himself <note>likely a reference to Solon or Minos, or a general legal principle in antiquity</note> would not leave unpunished among men. Therefore, in addition to all these things, which are very difficult for those who search out the future in such a way, there is also the frequent interruption of the ritual itself, and the loss of the art while we wander as outcasts. For it is no light task for those wandering about to carry with them the heavy baggage <note>original: "sarcinas"; referring to the exotic herbs, bones, and equipment for external theurgy mentioned on the previous page</note> required for such a journey. 

But in the prophecy that comes through dreams, each person is his own instrument. Thus, even if they wished, they could not abandon such an oracle; rather, it remains with those who stay at home and migrates with those who travel abroad. It serves alongside the soldier, handles civil affairs with the citizen, goes to the fields with the rustic, and engages in trade with the merchant. Neither do the laws of a jealous city forbid this prophecy, nor could they forbid it even if they wished. For they have no way to prosecute such a prophet. How, indeed, do we do any injury while sleeping? Even a tyrant could not prohibit us from seeing dreams, unless perhaps he banished sleep itself from the city—and yet it would be the mark of a madman to wish for the impossible, and an impious man to command things contrary to nature and to God.

### How useful and desirable prophecy is, especially through dreams.

<margin>a</margin> **I**t is fitting, therefore, for women and men, the old and the young, the poor and the rich, private citizens and princes, rustics and city-dwellers, the refined and the common, to approach this prophecy. It rejects no race, no age, no fortune, and no specific craft. To everyone everywhere, there is a prophet at the ready, a good and silent advisor, a teacher and a disciple of sacred things. It predicts good things so that, by anticipating them, we may enjoy their pleasure longer. It also predicts evil, so that we may guard against the inconvenience and drive it away. For whatever nourishes the human race—offering the best and most alluring things—or whatever provides prudent and useful warnings through fear, all these are found in dreams. Indeed, we are persuaded by no one so much as by our own hopes, even though the gift of hoping is so great and healthy a part of nature that elegant <term>sophists</term> <note>professional teachers and rhetoricians in the Greek world</note> declare that men would not have wished to live if they were affected only by their original state. They would have refused to live, driven by the difficulties of life, had not Prometheus <note>In Greek mythology, Prometheus gave humans "blind hope" so they would not see their own deaths, encouraging them to persevere</note> implanted hope itself in our nature as a remedy for persevering in life. Entangled by its charms, men believe more faithfully in what they expect in the future than in their present condition. Hope itself possesses such great power that if ever the conquered are permitted to hope according to their wish, their chains (so to speak) are loosened...

<summary>Synesius argues that dream-divination is superior to external oracles because it is free, portable, and impossible for tyrants to suppress. He emphasizes that dreams are a democratic form of prophecy available to all social classes and serve as a vital source of hope for humanity.</summary>

...[if he has once] begun, he suddenly profits twofold. Soon after he rules a company, presently leads an army, conquers, slays, is crowned, hosts banquets, and prepares a table—a luxurious Sicilian one if it pleases him, or even a Median one if he likes. Meanwhile, he has forgotten his own feet, until he is now about to lead the army. Yet this is truly the way of one who dreams, or of one awake who has fallen into a dream. For both are concerned with the same subject, namely the <term>imaginative nature</term> <note>original: "naturam phantasticam"; Synesius uses this term to describe the "spirit-vehicle" of the soul, which we would call the imagination. It acts as a mirror between the senses and the higher mind.</note>. Whenever we decide to shape this faculty with images, it brings this one utility above all others: it soothes our life with joy and flatters the soul with wandering hope, and thus recalls us from the perception of troublesome things.

### An exhortation to obtain the prophecy of dreams, and concerning the efficacy of the imagination.

When, however, the imaginative nature—presiding over us by its own proper function—stirs hope within us (which happens to those who dream), we hold the promise of the dream as a pledge from God. Wherefore, a person now eagerly readying his mind—as if about to enjoy the greater gifts he had envisioned in the dream—reaps a double profit: first, because he rejoices before the event itself, and second, because when the things are eventually obtained, he uses them with knowledge. This is because he has already meditated on these things for a long time as being entirely suitable for his life. 

Now indeed, consider the hope which Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet (c. 518–438 BC)</note> praised when speaking of the happy man, saying: 

> "Nurturing a sweet heart, 
> life-giving hope accompanies him, 
> she who chiefly rules the wavering 
> mind of mortals everywhere." 

I say it is this kind of hope that was sung by him. One might say that this hope is not the deceptive kind that deludes those who are awake—which we fashion for ourselves—but that all this pertains rather to the appearance of dreams, and that Pindar spoke thus to celebrate a small portion of the world of dreams.

Therefore, he who pursues the prophecy of dreams along with the <term>art</term> <note>Synesius suggests that dreaming is not just random but a skill or "art" that can be refined through philosophy and observation.</note> shows a firmer appearance in what is seen, so that it does not seem to be of a baser kind. But Penelope, in Homer’s work, introduces two gates of dreams and asserts that half of them are deceptive; this was because she did not possess the wisdom of dreams. For if she had possessed a skillful art regarding these things, she would surely have guided everything through the gate of horn <note>In the Odyssey, Penelope describes two gates: one of Ivory (for false dreams) and one of Horn (for true dreams). Synesius argues that the "deception" is actually the dreamer's fault for not knowing how to interpret them.</note>. 

Thus she is brought in there to be refuted, and she will confess her ignorance concerning that very vision which she did not believe, though she ought to have believed it. The "Geese" were indeed the suitors; "I, Odysseus, am the eagle." But he was a companion <note>referring to Odysseus appearing as an eagle in Penelope's dream to comfort her</note>, and she was speaking nonsense to him regarding the vision. 

Indeed, I seem to hear Homer saying here that it is not fitting to distrust dreams, nor to transfer the weakness of the users to the nature of the visions. In his work, even Agamemnon does not justly accuse his dream as being deceptive, since he had poorly received the oracle concerning victory, which said: 

> "I command you to arm the helmeted Achaeans with breastplates; for now" <note>This refers to the "False Dream" sent by Zeus in the Iliad, which Agamemnon misinterpreted as a promise of immediate victory without further struggle.</note>

# ON DREAMS

...[you will take] a most vast city. Agamemnon therefore hastens as if he were suddenly about to storm the city by his own strength, when he had misheard what was spoken by the oracle and did not keep its conditions. For the oracle said that he would indeed conquer if he armed the entire army of the Greeks. But truly, neither Achilles then, nor the phalanx of the Myrmidons <note>Achilles' elite band of warriors; their absence from the battle led to the Greek defeat described in the Iliad.</note>, went out into battle—and they were surely the most excellent part of the army.

->How much hope the prophecy of a dream offers us.<-

**I** have certainly heaped up many praises, yet I have acted almost foolishly. For I have said just before that the prophecy of dreams sails with us, dwells with us, fights alongside us, trades with us, and serves everyone in everything. However, I have not yet mentioned the benefits bestowed upon me from that source, even though it is accustomed to communicate with men in nothing more than the pursuit of <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophia"; Synesius views philosophy not just as academic study, but as the lived pursuit of divine wisdom.</note>. Many things are truly doubtful while we are awake. After we have gone to sleep, the dream partly reveals things entirely, and partly debates with us; and now indeed, the one who dreams seems to ask questions and to learn, and now even to discover. 

To me indeed, it has often brought books; it instructed my mind and composed my speech. It would partly describe the day’s activities and partly change them. Sometimes, this prophecy—sent by God—would even correct the entire dull disposition of my tongue, which was swollen with the novelty of names due to an excessive love of the older and harsher <term>Attic Greek</term> <note>original: "attheæ linguæ"; Synesius is referring to "Atticism," a literary trend where writers imitated the ancient Greek of 5th-century BC Athens. He admits here that his dreams helped him avoid sounding overly pretentious or archaic.</note>. By dictating some parts and showing what others should be, it smoothed out those innate "swellings" of the tongue, drove out the puffiness, and brought a sense of moderation. 

Moreover, when I was hunting at times, it supplied me with strength and strategies against wild beasts that ran or hid with a certain cunning. Sometimes, even when I was exhausted and breaking camp, it commanded me to persevere and promised "Fortune" as my mistress, so that it was sweet to linger in the hunt with eager confidence. When such divination was lacking, that mistress and Fortune appeared; she clearly showed me the swarms of beasts caught and ensnared. To me, indeed, life consists of books and the hunt. 

For I never desired to perform embassies, thinking it of no benefit to see three ill-omened years of one's life. Yet even then, I was most helped by this prophecy. For it rendered powerless the plots of the <term>sorcerers</term> <note>original: "magorum"; Synesius often complained about the "magicians" or corrupt courtiers who conspired against him during his time at the imperial court.</note> who were gasping for my soul, both by revealing their secrets and by freeing me from all dangers. And so it also arranged public affairs for me, so that the cities might be governed in the best way. It even reconciled me to the Great King <note>Likely a reference to the Emperor Arcadius in Constantinople, whom Synesius visited to seek tax relief for his home city of Cyrene.</note> with greater confidence than any Greek ever had before.

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s exploration of dream prophecy, transitioning from his personal anecdotes to the philosophical mechanics of how dreams work. <meta>catchword: clear</meta>

# Dreams provide us with prophecy in abundance.

<margin>While other [arts] care for others, this one is a good guiding spirit <note>original: "daemon"; in this context, it refers to a personal guardian spirit or divine intermediary rather than a malevolent entity.</note> present for everyone, and it meets as a teacher even those who have studied diligently while awake to discover something by skill.</margin> The soul is so wise when it rests from the confusion of external senses—those things which bring in foreign natures from every side. For whatever forms the soul has, and whatever it is accustomed to receive from the mind, it displays itself clearly to those who have turned toward their inner self, and it transmits those things which come from the divine. For to a soul in such a state, the God of the world <note>original: "Deus mundanus"; Synesius refers here to the divine intelligence that governs the physical cosmos.</note> also joins himself, because the nature of that soul flows from the same source as He does. These kinds of dreams, therefore, are considered more divine, and are either entirely or almost completely whole and clear, needing very little help from the interpretative art. But these happen only to men living virtuously, acquired either through wisdom or through habit. If they ever happen to someone else by chance, it is rare. Truly, a noble dream will not happen to just anyone in a small way; the remaining type, however—the manifold and most common kind—is entirely hidden, for which reason it is necessary to apply an art. For it has an absurd (so to speak) and monstrous origin. And since it sprouts from such things, it proceeds as something very obscure. This is how the matter of dreams stands, as I shall say.

## The prophecy of dreams is available to all.

<margin>From all things that are contained in the nature of the universe—whether they exist in the present, or were done in the past, or are said to be in the future (for these too are certain modes of existence)—images flow out and are constantly shaken out from their substance.</margin> For if any sensible thing is a <term>form</term> <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos); the essential shape or blueprint of a thing that exists in the mind or in nature.</note>, that is, a species in matter, it is extended along with that matter. We perceive from the compound that matter flows outward. Reason certainly dictates that the nature of forms is also derived from the outside through "idols" <note>original: "idola"; these are the thin, film-like images or "simulacra" that ancient philosophers believed objects shed, which then travel through the air to be perceived.</note>, so that on both sides those things involved in generation <note>the world of physical birth and change</note> degenerate from the dignity of Being itself. Of all the images we have mentioned that flow from things everywhere, the <term>imaginative spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus phantasticus"; the "pneuma" or subtle body that acts as a mirror for the soul's thoughts and external images.</note> is certainly the clearest mirror. Otherwise, these things that circle about and fall from their state—both because of their indefinite existence and because they are known by none of the beings—as soon as they are caught in the life-spirits (which are themselves images, but have their seat in nature), they rest entirely upon them and settle as if in dwellings. Therefore, of those things that have been done, as they have already proceeded into the act of being through...

<summary>Synesius explains that while clear, divine dreams are reserved for the virtuous, most dreams are obscure and require interpretation. He introduces a physical-metaphysical theory of "idols" or images that flow from all objects and are captured by the soul's imaginative spirit.</summary>
<keywords>divine dreams, daemon, mundane God, virtue, interpretive art, idols, imaginative spirit, eidos, forms, soul nature</keywords>
