<meta>This page continues Synesius’s discourse on the mechanics of dreaming. Having established that clear, divine dreams are for the virtuous, he now explains how "idols"—the images of things—flow into the human imagination (the "phantastic spirit") and why future events appear blurry or "monstrous" compared to the present.</meta>

->ON DREAMS<-

# ON DREAMS

...clear images are sent out everywhere, until through the passage of time they eventually turn out weak and small. However, those which belong to the present, insofar as they still consist in themselves, arrive as much stronger and most manifest likenesses; but the images of future things are indefinite and, in a manner, indistinct. For these are certain "pre-rollings" <note>original: "praevolumina"; Synesius envisions events unfolding like a scroll; these are the first glimpses of the scroll before it is fully open.</note> of things not yet present and a kind of blossoming of a nature still imperfect, as if leaping and dancing forth, and like the obscure signatures of hidden seeds. For this reason, there is a need for art <note>Synesius uses "art" (ars) to mean a systematic skill or technique of interpretation.</note> regarding future things, for from them come shadowed idols and obscure images—certainly not manifest like those from the present. From all things flow likenesses, whose mirror and receptacle is the phantastic <term>phantastic</term> <note>From the Greek 'phantastikon,' referring to the faculty of imagination which receives and stores sensory impressions.</note> form itself.

<margin>m</margin>The nature of images is indeed wonderful, being so constituted as to be produced by things not yet accomplished. Therefore, something must now be said regarding this art, and by what means it may be acquired. First and best is to have so prepared the divine spirit <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus" (pneuma); in Neoplatonic thought, this is the "spirit-vehicle" of the soul, a subtle, airy body that mediates between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note> that it becomes worthy for the intellect and God to become known to it and to preside over it. Let it no longer be a receptacle for indefinite images. The best education of the spirit, however, is twofold: first, to calm the disturbed movements of the mind through the study of philosophy—for when these are excited, the spirit itself is occupied like a territory under siege—and second, through a moderate and tempered diet, to so affect the living creature that it is as little prone to agitation as possible, and so to compose the physical body that it moves the waves as little as possible; for the wave overflows even to the primary part of the soul. It is necessary to always keep that primary part unshaken and undisturbed. But since to wish for this is easy for anyone, yet to achieve it is more difficult than most things, and since we desire that no one find dreams useless: come then, let us seek some boundary even in indeterminate things. That is, let us establish an art concerning these idols—that is, the images. They behave in this manner:

## How we may be able to interpret dreams.

<margin>q</margin>Those who frequently sail the seas, if they encounter a certain rock and, upon climbing it, look out and see a city, whenever they see that same rock again, they understand it to signify the same city. Indeed, we often realize that army leaders (whom we do not yet see) are about to arrive by seeing their scouts; for in the past, the leaders always followed when those same scouts ran ahead. By the same reasoning, we are accustomed to signify future things everywhere through idols. For the precursors are the same for the same things, and similar for the similar. Just as, therefore, it is a pilot's ignorance not to recognize the rock when it appears, or to fail to predict which shores he is approaching.

<summary>Synesius explains that future events send out "idols" or images that are naturally blurry because they haven't happened yet. He argues that by purifying the "spirit-vehicle" through philosophy and diet, one can better perceive these signs, using the analogy of a sailor recognizing a landmark to predict a destination.</summary>
<keywords>imagination, phantastic spirit, pneuma, dream interpretation, divination, philosophy, Neoplatonism, precursors, idols</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument that dream interpretation is a skill (an "art") that can be learned through systematic observation, similar to how a pilot learns to navigate the sea or a farmer learns to read the weather. He moves from the general principle of observation to the specific reason why "dream dictionaries" fail.</meta>

->SYNESIUS<-
<meta>catchword: threefold</meta>

...and such a navigator is without the aid of conjectures. So too, the person who frequently experiences the same vision, unless he has already determined what specific outcome it portends for him—whether a passion, a fortune, or an action—uses his life foolishly, no differently than a navigator of that sort. We are also accustomed to noting signs of Jove <note>original: "iouia ſigna"; signs of Jupiter, the god of the sky and weather. Synesius is comparing dream-reading to meteorology.</note> in the surrounding air; thus, looking at the circular halo around the moon, we prophesy that there will be storms, since winds have frequently followed for those who observed the same. That poetic saying tends toward this: "from here, indeed, the storm is designated, and from here the circular tranquility." For a broken halo portends winds, while one that vanishes portends tranquility. Two circles indeed precede a storm; but a tripled circle <note>original: "circulus triplicatus"; a rare atmospheric phenomenon where multiple halos appear.</note> portends a more violent tempest, even more so if it appears black, and still more if it is broken. So it is in all things, as both Aristotle and reason dictate: that from sense comes memory, from memory comes experience and expertise, and through this, finally, an art <term>art</term> <note>Synesius uses "art" (ars) to mean a systematic, teachable discipline or science, rather than just a creative endeavor.</note> is proven. In a similar way, we ought to proceed regarding dreams.

## A common and identical rule for interpreting dreams cannot be applied to individuals.

Many have composed many such books on the observation of dreams. However, I laugh at all these, judging them to be of very little use. For it is not as if this final body—that is, the union of harmonized elements—can receive a universal art and a discourse that follows nature equally. For the most part, the body suffers the same things from the same causes, since there is little discrepancy among similar physical things, and that which is in them contrary to nature (the state of being sick) does not usually remain hidden. Therefore, we do use a certain guiding rule [for medicine]; however, I say the phantastic spirit <term>phantastic spirit</term> <note>The "spirit-vehicle" (pneuma) of the soul, which Synesius believes is the organ of imagination and the canvas upon which dreams are painted.</note> is not like this. Rather, from its very first origin, one has differed from another. For one spirit corresponds with one celestial sphere, and another with another, insofar as in its tempering, this sphere or that one prevails. 

Hence that poetic saying: "especially the most blessed souls flow from heaven to earth, and those most wealthy beyond the rest, having obtained inestimable threads." Whatever souls have obtained a gift from the Splendid King, and those which come from Jove <note>Jupiter, representing the highest providential power.</note> himself by the thread of powerful necessity; this was further what he <note>Likely a reference to Plato, specifically the Timaeus.</note> hinted at secretly and with fear, where he assigned to each soul a companion star or cluster. Indeed, souls having fallen from their own nature because they dwell more willingly around matter—this one less, but that one more—insofar as each has used a kind of inclination of the scales, has unhappily defiled the spirit. Therefore, being thus affected, they inhabit bodies, and their whole life is spent in the appearance of transgression and disease, certainly...

<summary>Synesius argues that while general rules work for physical medicine, dream interpretation must be individualized because every person's "phantastic spirit" (imagination) is uniquely tuned to different celestial spheres and stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument from the previous page, where he established that "art" (systematic knowledge) is derived from experience. He now explains why universal dream dictionaries fail: because the human "spirit"—the medium of dreams—is uniquely shaped by each individual's nature and habits, requiring personal rather than general observation.</meta>

->ON DREAMS<-

# ON DREAMS

...beyond nature, as far as the nobility of the species is concerned, but according to nature regarding the animal nature; for the soul is animated by a spirit affected in this way, unless there is an order in its nature into which it is arranged by itself, using both vice and virtue—for nothing is as easily moved and changeable as the spirit. In what way, then, can the same things appear from things so dissimilar to one another—dissimilar in nature, law, and passions? Certainly, it does not happen this way, nor can it. For how can water that is simultaneously turbid and clear, or agitated and still, be affected similarly under the same form? But if the turbid condition is different in one person compared to another according to the differences in colors, and the motions themselves occur in various configurations, then the result will certainly be a generic deviation from a completely clear image, but different in its specific appearance. Whether it is Phemonoe <note>Phemonoe was a legendary Greek priestess of Apollo at Delphi, credited with being the first to deliver oracles in hexameter verse.</note>, or Melampus <note>Melampus was a famous mythical seer and healer who was said to understand the language of animals.</note>, or anyone else who professes to define a common rule for such things and to organize them thoroughly, we shall ask them: can a mirror—whether straight or warped, or made of dissimilar materials—return a similar image of an object? But those people have not, from the beginning, philosophized at all regarding the spirit. They consider their own particular spirit, however it may be disposed, to be the rule and the test for everyone. And for my part, I do not deny that some agreement can be found between things that are entirely different; but indeed, that which is obscure and scattered becomes even more obscure. From the beginning, the phantom <term>phantom</term> <note>original: "idolum"; in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the 'eidolon' or the representative image that the spirit perceives in a dream.</note> of a pre-existing thing was difficult to recognize. It is even more difficult to perceive something in each person’s individual mode or character that is exactly like a common vision and perfectly suited to it.

->Each person observes their own dreams, and the events following from them.<-

<margin>h</margin> For these reasons, one must in no way hope that laws of dreams can be established that are equally common to all; rather, each individual ought to treat himself as the material for this art, and he can record in memory what kind of visions he had and what events followed. Indeed, it is not very difficult for a habit to form around a matter that one contemplates out of practice or necessity; for use or necessity suggests contemplation to the memory. Especially since the material is available everywhere; for in dreams, nothing is more abundant, nor is there anything that draws minds toward itself more strongly. For dreams compel even the foolish to contemplate and care about them to such an extent that it would be shameful <margin>•</margin> for men who have completed a decade beyond puberty to still require another prophet, and not to have already accumulated many rules of this art for themselves. It would certainly be worthwhile to commit to writing one's visions and the things that happen, both in waking and in sleep, if only the customs of civil life did not [disdain] the novelty of this...

<summary>Synesius argues that because the "spirit" (the medium of dreams) varies between individuals like different types of mirrors, universal dream-books are useless. He concludes that every person must become their own interpreter by keeping a personal record of their dreams and subsequent life events.</summary>

--- Page 180 ---
<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument regarding the personal nature of dreams. He transitions from criticizing universal dream books to proposing a personal practice: the keeping of "night-journals" or dream diaries to track the movements of one's own "spirit-vehicle" (pneuma) and to refine one's rhetorical skills.</meta>

SYNESIUS

...he would dread thinking. With this allowance, we judge that nightly notes should be joined daily to our daytime records, and in this way, we can keep the actions of both states of human life recorded in commentaries. For reason has established that a certain life is situated in the imagination—sometimes better than our average life, and sometimes worse—depending, clearly, on how much health or disease the spirit <note>original: "spiritus" — referring to the *pneuma*, or "spirit-vehicle," which Neo-Platonists believed mediated between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note> possesses. 

Thus, if we pursue this kind of observation with diligent effort, from which a systematic art is gradually accumulated, nothing slips from the memory. Besides, this will be a refined delight and an exercise of the mind; for while we honor the history of both our waking and sleeping hours, this exercise will also contribute to our eloquence. For those who care for the training of the tongue, there is (I believe) no invention better suited than this to exercising the faculty of speech in all matters. For if the Lemnian sophist <note>Likely Philostratus the Elder (c. 170–250 AD), who advocated for the daily practice of writing to develop a flexible and powerful rhetorical style.</note> teaches that daily writings are the best instructors for speaking aptly on every occasion—because not even the smallest things are neglected, but it is necessary to express everything, both the grave and the light—why should we not also cultivate nightly notes for the sake of interpretation?

->How varied, deceitful, and playful the imagination is in dreams.<-

<margin>n</margin> Surely someone might ask how great a task he has undertaken who wishes to match his speech to his visions, in which things that are naturally joined are separated, and those naturally distinct are joined. Indeed, there is a need for reason and discourse for these things, so that the vision which does not usually occur to the mind may occur; nor is it a light task to translate the monstrous and absurd emerging motions of the soul into another mode of expression. 

When, through imagination, those things that actually exist are expelled from their office of being, and in turn, things are brought into existence that are nowhere and could in no way naturally exist, what method is there to provide a truly nameless nature to those unthinkable visions from within? This imagination shows these things, bringing forth many hopes—and indeed all of them at once—and almost without the passage of time, even if the dream presents and offers them as if they were real. 

For we believe that whatever the soul wishes will occur to it; in expressing all of which, to linger longer is a task for the most perfect orator, and even then, one must avoid foolishness. Indeed, this boastful matter exults in the dream against the very nature of discernment, bringing in something more than simple judgment can bear. For we do not deal with visions without passion; rather, powerful states and affections occur, great hatreds arise, and frequent charms <note>original: "veneficia" — can refer to sorceries, magical potions, or enchanting delusions</note> loom over those who sleep. Pleasure, indeed, then most prevails, and this state of life is quite readily subject to the most flattering allurements—to such an extent that loves and hates may sprout in the soul that will endure even into the waking state.

<meta>This page continues Synesius of Cyrene's treatise "On Dreams," specifically moving from the theoretical nature of the "spirit-vehicle" (the pneuma) to the practical, almost magical, variety of experiences found within the dream state. He begins to advocate for the practice of "Night-journals" to complement daytime records.</meta>

->ON DREAMS<-
<a>a</a>

# ON DREAMS

### How extraordinary the variety of imagination is in dreams.

**H**ow extraordinary the variety of imagination <note>original: "phantasiæ" — the faculty of the soul that produces mental images, central to Synesius's psychology</note> is in dreams. If one intends to speak not of trivialities, but of things for which a complete discourse has been established, they will certainly need words that stir the listener, placing them within this very state of being—its perceptions and its judgments. For in dreams, a person may simultaneously conquer, fight as a gladiator, fly, and capture; for the imagination seizes all things. But where can speech seize such things? Someone sleeps a dream, and within that dream sees another, and meanwhile, the sleeper "wakes up," as he thinks, and while still lying there, shakes off the dream. He philosophizes and knows something about the appearing dream—both that it is a dream and that it is "double." Then he loses faith in it and believes that what is present is serious and that the things appearing are living realities. From this point, he struggles with all his might, and someone dreams a contest against himself, at times letting go, at other times waking himself up. He puts himself to the test and catches the deception. 

They say indeed that the Aloadae <note>original: "Aloadas" — Otus and Ephialtes, twin giants from Greek mythology who attempted to storm Olympus by piling Mount Ossa on top of Mount Pelion</note> pay the penalty because they built the Thessalian mountains up against the gods. But no law of inevitable judgment ever forbids the sleeper from lifting himself high above the earth, more fortunately than Icarus <note>The son of Daedalus who flew too close to the sun with wings of wax and feathers</note>, and surpassing the eagles in flight. Indeed, you may fly over the celestial spheres, where one may contemplate the orb of the earth from afar—and this does not merely signify the moon's perspective. It is permitted to dispute with the stars and to meet with the hidden gods in the world. For when something is most difficult to do in reality, it becomes easiest there; then the gods clearly and openly meet us, and there is no envy or begrudging in this. 

Shortly thereafter, he resides on the earth, nor has he even traveled, but is present there instantly; for nothing is more characteristic of dreams than to intercept the middle distance and to act without the passage of time. Thus, he immediately speaks with little sheep <note>original: "ouiculis" — small sheep or lambs</note> and believes their bleating to be speech, and understands what they say. Thus, the material of things is so new and so broad a subject, providing a province of inquiry if anyone strives to adapt their speech to dreams. I believe even fables <note>Synesius refers to Aesop-style fables where animals speak</note> received their license and abundance from dreams, in which the peacock speaks, as do the fox and the sea—even if these are small things when compared to the license of dream-states. And although fables are but a tiny part of dreams, they are nevertheless cultivated by the sophists <note>original: "sophistis" — professional teachers of rhetoric and philosophy in the Roman Empire</note> and deemed worthy of interpretation. It would be fitting for those whose art begins with the fable to have the dream as their goal. This is especially true since the faculty of speaking is not exercised in these matters in vain—just as it is not done blindly in fables—but some deeper meaning lies hidden there.

### That it is useful for life and eloquence alike to note daily what you have dreamed, what you have done, and what has happened to you.

Therefore, let everyone who has leisure and the means of life girt themselves to write down everything that happens, whether waking or sleeping. Let him spend some time on this, which is indeed a most excellent pursuit...

<summary>Synesius describes the limitless, surreal power of the imagination in dreams—such as flying past the stars or talking to animals—and argues that dreams are the source of fables and a vital tool for rhetorical training.</summary>

--- Page 182 ---
<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument that recording one’s dreams is not merely a spiritual exercise but a way to sharpen the intellect and the soul. He now transitions into comparing this "art of divination" with the formal disciplines of philosophy and rhetoric, arguing that recording personal experience is superior to the hollow exercises of contemporary public speakers.</meta>

->SYNESIUS<-

Intelligence is what acquires divination—that is, the art of gathering which we have praised. Indeed, nothing could be more useful than this. Furthermore, no system of public speaking will be hindered by it, because of the great consistency of the matters involved. For a philosopher, a treatise of this kind will be a game and a solace, relaxing the mind’s intensity just as archers are accustomed to unstringing their bows. For the rhetorician, however, we shall establish such a work as the very summit and peak of their demonstrations. 

Indeed, they do not seem to exercise their eloquence and passion opportunely when they speak of Miltiades or Cimon <note>original: "Milciadi... atq; Cimoni" — famous Athenian generals from the 5th century BC who became standard, often clichéd, subjects for rhetorical exercises in schools</note>, or even of certain obscure men, the wealthy and the poor, or those who hold civil life in hatred. Regarding these subjects, I have even seen ancient men in the theater sharply competing, although they were venerable in the name of philosophy. Each of them (as it appeared) had grown a talent of beard <note>original: "barbæ talentum" — a talent was a heavy unit of weight; Synesius is humorously suggesting their beards were so long they were burdensome, mocking the "philosopher's look" which often masked a lack of true wisdom</note>. Yet the reverence for their profession did not prevent them from breaking out into insults and brawls, or from immodestly waving their hands about while arranging their speeches with all their strength—speeches which I then considered suitable. 

But as it was later reported to me by those who taught me, they were not suitable then, nor had they ever been, nor were they even suitable by nature from the beginning. For in what way can there be a civil society that gives a prize to a victor for killing a citizen who holds a different view of the Republic? Now, whoever still meditates and contends upon a ninety-year-old fiction <note>original: "nonagenariū figmentū" — a reference to the repetitive, ancient rhetorical themes that had no relevance to contemporary life</note>, in what time shall he distinguish the truth from words? They seem to me not to understand the very name of "meditation" <note>original: "meditatiōis" — in this context, it refers to the Greek *melete*, the practice of preparing and delivering practice orations</note> when they say they study for the sake of something else; yet they have considered the preparation to be the end itself, and have worshipped the very road one must travel as if it were the finish line. 

For they have made meditation itself the contest. It is as if someone, having vigorously exercised his hands in the wrestling school, should then profess to be a master of the <term>Pancratium|An ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling, known for its extreme intensity and lack of rules</term> in the Olympic games. To such an extent, therefore, has both the dryness of the mind and the flow of words occupied men, that some appear to be powerful in speaking, yet have nothing that actually needs to be said. 

However, they ought to have conducted themselves like Archilochus and Alcaeus <note>original: "Archiloc⁹ & Alcæus" — early Greek lyric poets known for writing personal, emotional poetry about their own lives rather than epic myths</note>, both of whom bestowed the sweetness of their singing voice upon their own lives. Thus, posterity remembers the things in which they took pleasure and the things for which they grieved. They did not pour out empty speeches on fabricated arguments, as this recent breed of "wise men" is accustomed to do. Nor did they grant their own excellence to others, as did Stesichorus and Homer, who rendered the heroic race more illustrious by their poems—from which we also have made progress in imitating virtue. But those poets themselves seem neglected as far as their own lives are concerned; we have nothing more to say about them, except that they were vigorous poets. 

Therefore, whoever desires to be remembered by posterity and trusts that they can commit immortal things to letters, let them follow the method of writing approved by us at present, though it is outside common custom. Let him boldly entrust himself to Time. For Time is a faithful guardian when something is entrusted to it according to the will of God.

**THE END**

<summary>Synesius criticizes rhetoricians who waste their talents on stale historical themes, urging instead that writers follow the example of lyric poets by recording their own lived experiences and dreams for posterity.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded Synesius of Cyrene’s treatise on dreams, where he argued for the value of recording personal spiritual experiences. This page marks a transition to a new text: Michael Psellus’s "On Demons," as translated and interpreted by the Renaissance Neoplatonist Marsilio Ficino. The focus shifts from the psychology of dreams to the physical and metaphysical nature of spiritual beings.</meta>

# From Michael Psellus on Demons, translated by Marsilio Ficino.

<margin>n</margin>
The nature of demons is not without a body, but rather possesses a body and occupies itself around bodies, a view which our venerable fathers <note>This refers to the "Church Fathers," the influential early Christian theologians.</note> also held. There are also those who assert that demons have appeared to them in their own presence with bodies. And even the divine Basil <note>original: "Baſilius" — St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), who discussed the "airy" bodies of demons.</note>, the inspector of mysteries hidden from us, attributed bodies not only to demons but even to pure angels, as if they were certain thin, airy, and pure spirits; he brings forward as a witness David, who says: *Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire* <note>original: "qui facit angelos eius ſpiritus ac miniſtros eius flāmeos" — a quote from Psalm 104:4.</note>. Indeed, this is necessary. For as the divine Paul <note>St. Paul the Apostle.</note> asserts, it is necessary that the ministering spirits who are sent forth have a body by which they are moved, by which they stand in rank, and by which they clearly appear; for they know that these ministries cannot be performed in any other way than through a body. 

If you should read anywhere in Scripture that they are called <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Without a physical body.</note>, I respond that both our writers and others are accustomed to naming thicker bodies "corporeal," while frequently labeling "incorporeal" those thin bodies which escape sight and touch. However, the same type of body is not common to both angels and demons. For the angelic body, pouring forth certain rays, cannot be sustained by the eyes of others, as it vanishes completely from them. Whether a demonic body was ever like that, I cannot say; however, it seems that such a thing once existed, since Isaiah names the angel who fell "Lucifer" <note>original: "luciferū" — the "Light-bringer."</note>. But now, on the other hand, the demon exists as something obscure and dark. If it is presented to the eyes stripped of its joined light, it appears troublesome to us. 

The angelic body is indeed entirely devoid of <term>matter</term> <note>In this context, "matter" refers to the heavy, "sludge-like" physical substance of the earthly realm.</note>, and for this reason, it penetrates and passes through every solid thing. It is even less subject to <term>passions</term> <note>External influences or suffering.</note> than a ray of the sun. For as a ray of the sun proceeds or enters through diaphanous and translucent bodies, earthly and opaque obstacles hold it back so much that it undergoes a "breaking" <note>refraction</note>, insofar as it has a kinship with what is base. But nothing of this sort obstructs an angelic body, as it suffers no opposition from anything, since it does not agree with any of these things in rank or nature. 

Demonic bodies, however, although they are invisible due to their thinness, are nevertheless in some way material and subject to passion, especially those that have entered subterranean places. For these have been "thickened" by God so that they may be subjected to touch and may grieve when struck, and may be burned when brought near to fire—so much so that some of them even leave behind ash. History relates that this indeed happened among the Etruscan people of Italy. I do not speak these things as if I were bringing forth a poetic fable or monsters after the manner of the Cretans or Phoenicians, but I affirm these things having been persuaded by the very words of the Savior, which hand down the teaching that demons are tortured by fire.

<summary>This page introduces Michael Psellus’s theory that angels and demons possess subtle bodies of varying density, explaining that while angels are radiant and impassive, demons are dark, material, and capable of feeling physical pain.</summary>
<keywords>demonology, Michael Psellus, Marsilio Ficino, angelic bodies, materiality, St. Basil, St. Paul, Lucifer, subtle bodies, fire</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physical nature of demons. While the previous page established that demons must have some form of "airy" or "fiery" body to act as ministers or to experience sensations, this page explores their physical needs, such as nutrition and reproduction, and begins a classification of their types using geometric metaphors.</meta>

PSELLVS.
<meta>catchword: Scalene</meta>

# PSELLVS.

...precisely because they are corporeal, they are able to suffer <note>In this context, "suffer" (Latin: *pati*) means to be acted upon or affected by external physical forces.</note>. For in what way could they suffer if they were incorporeal? For that which is incorporeal cannot even be imagined to suffer from a body.

<margin>Six species of demons; how they transform themselves, how they insinuate themselves into us, and how they move us.</margin>
<margin>a</margin>
Indeed, I have received much information about these beings from those who have devoted themselves to the study of summoning them into sight, even if I myself have never seen such a thing, nor do I wish to see demons. However, I spent time with a man who lived a solitary life in the Chersonese <note>A peninsula, likely referring to the Gallipoli Peninsula near Greece.</note> bordering Greece, named Marcus. This man traced his lineage back to the region of the Mesopotamia river, and he had progressed more than anyone else in the cult of demons and had witnessed their apparitions. At first, he used to despise and detest these things as vain and false; later, however, he sang a <term>palinode</term> <note>original: "palinodiā" — a poem or song in which the author retracts something said in a former poem; a formal recantation.</note> and adhered to the true dogmas and to our own. This man revealed many wondrous and demonic things to us. To me, when I occasionally asked whether demons were capable of suffering, he replied: "Very much so, to the extent that some demons even cast forth seed, from which certain tiny animals are born." Then I said, "It is unbelievable that demons have excrement and genital members." "They do indeed have members," he replied, "but not like ours. A certain excrement does emanate from them." Then he added, "Believe me." But I said, "They are in a grave state if they are nourished in our manner." "They are indeed nourished," said Marcus. "Some by inspiration <note>Breathing in or absorbing vapors.</note>, just as the spirit thrives in the arteries and nerves; others by moisture, but not through a mouth as we do, but rather like sponges and oysters, sucking up the moisture lying around them from the outside. Furthermore, they secrete that which is more solid within the moisture. However, not all of them experience this; only those genera of demons closest to matter, and the genus of demons that hates the light, as well as the aquatic and the subterranean types." To this I asked: "O Marcus, are there many kinds of demons?" "Many," he said, "and diverse, both according to their forms and according to their bodies, so much so that the air which is above us and around us is full of demons; the earth, the sea, and the hidden and deep places are also full." "Unless it is a burden," I said, "list them." "There are generally six kinds of demons," he said, "though I do not know whether it is better to divide the demons by the places in which they dwell, or rather by the fact that the entire race of demons is affected by a love for the body. I know, however, that the number six is corporeal and worldly. For within it are the corporeal circumstances, and the world is composed through this number; or perhaps because this is the first number that can compose a <term>scalene triangle</term> <note>A triangle with three unequal sides. In this Neoplatonic allegory, the lack of equality symbolizes the instability and "evil" of the material realm.</note>. The <term>equilateral</term> <note>A triangle with all sides equal.</note> is proper to the divine and celestial, insofar as it is equal to itself and is difficult to move toward evil. The <term>isosceles</term> <note>original: "æquicrurii" — a triangle with two equal sides.</note> is proper to the human race; for it wanders from its purpose in one way, yet through repentance, it becomes better."

N ii

# ON DEMONS

The <term>Scalene</term> <note>original: "Scaleni" — referring to a scalene triangle with unequal sides, a geometric metaphor used here to represent spiritual imbalance or imperfection.</note> is truly the proper demonic trait, as it is unequal and in no way approaches the good. Whether the matter stands in this way or another, he used to enumerate six distinct types of demons. And first indeed, in the primary barbaric tongue, he named them **leliureon**, that is, **fiery**. He said these wander about the higher air. For every demonic thing is cast out from the lunar regions as if something profane is cast out from a temple. The second type is that which wanders in the air close to us; this is specifically named **aerial** by many. The third is the **terrestrial**, which dwells mostly upon the earth and opposes men with many schemes and machines. The fourth is the **aquatic** and **marine** type, which immerses itself in moisture, and freely lives around lakes and rivers; it destroys many in the waters, stirs up waves and tempests in the sea, and completely sinks ships laden with men, burying many under the waves. The fifth is the **subterranean** type, which indeed dwells under the earth; it attacks those who dig wells and mines. It causes chasms in the earth, shakes foundations, and stirs up fire-vomiting winds. The sixth and last is the **light-fleeing** <note>original: "lucifugum"</note>, which is inscrutable, entirely dark, and violently responding with cold passions. He used to say that all these types of demons are so disposed that they both hate the gods and oppose men; but some are worse than others. For the aquatic, the subterranean, and especially the light-fleeing types are exceedingly malicious and <gloss>destructive</gloss>. For these do not merely corrupt and harm souls through phantasms and thoughts, but like wild forest beasts, they hurry to the physical destruction of men. Thus, the aquatic indeed suffocate those wandering in the waters, and vex them with the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "morbo comitiali" — a historical term for epilepsy, often attributed to demonic possession or lunar influence in antiquity.</note> and madness. The aerial and terrestrial types, however, attack by a certain art and through thought, and thus they deceive human minds and turn them toward the most foul, wicked, and ruinous disturbances. Then I asked: "In what way and by doing what do they accomplish these things? Do they dominate us and lead us around like slaves wherever they please?" "They do not dominate us," he said, "but they suggest things to us secretly. For they approach the <term>phantastic spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritui phantastico" — in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the "spirituous vehicle" or the part of the soul that processes sensory images and imagination.</note> within us. Inasmuch as they themselves are spirits, they sound within us words of disturbance and pleasure. They do not emit a voice by a certain striking or sound, but they instill their speeches without sound." "But in what way," I asked, "can they instill speeches into us without a voice?" "Is it any wonder," he said, "if you consider this: how a person who speaks, if he speaks from far away, needs a louder shout; but if he is closer, he speaks into the ear of the listener by whispering. If he were able to be joined with the very spirit of the soul, he would need no sound at all, but his speech, conceived by his will, would flow into the listener without any sound whatsoever. They say this happens even to souls that have departed the body. For these converse among themselves without noise. In this very way, demons converse with us, so secretly indeed that it is not even permitted to know from where the war is being waged against us."

...but to perceive. No one who considers what happens to the air will doubt this. For just as the air, when light is present, receives colors and shapes and transmits them into things that can naturally receive them—as is seen in mirrors and other mirror-like objects—so too do demonic bodies receive shapes and colors from their inner <term>imaginative essence</term> <note>original: "essentia phantastica" — the faculty of the soul that produces and manipulates mental images</note>. They transmit whatever forms they wish into our animal spirit, providing us with much trouble by suggesting desires and counsels, indicating shapes, and arousing memories. They frequently stir up images of pleasures and passions in both those who are awake and those who are sleeping. 

Sometimes, indeed, by tickling our thighs and groins, they incite and sharpen insane and wicked loves—especially if they find hot and moist <term>humors</term> <note>original: "humores" — the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) once believed to control health and temperament</note> conducive to this. But these demons, putting on the **Helmet of Pluto** <note>original: "Plutonis galeam" — a mythological artifact that grants invisibility to the wearer</note>, disturb souls through a certain art and sophisticated fraud. 

The other kinds of demons do not devise anything wisely, nor do they accomplish anything easily through cunning, except for things that are bothersome and truly foul; they cause harm in the manner of the **Charonean breath** <note>original: "charonei spiritus" — poisonous volcanic vapors associated with Charon, the ferryman of the dead, which were said to kill instantly</note>. For just as they say this breath corrupts whatever comes near it, whether it be a four-legged beast, a man, or a bird, so do these terrible demons suddenly destroy whatever they meet by their encounter, agitating bodies and souls and perverting natural habits. Often they even destroy not only men but also some beasts by fire, water, or falling from heights.

At this, I asked: "Why do these demons invade beasts?" For the sacred scriptures testify that such a thing happened to the swine near **Gergesa** <note>original: "Gergesam" — a reference to the biblical miracle where Jesus cast demons out of a man and into a herd of swine</note>. To this he replied: "Since demons are enemies of mankind, it should not seem strange that they harm them. Indeed, they even insult some beasts, not so much out of a desire to do harm, but out of a greed for **life-giving heat** <note>original: "vivifici caloris"</note>." 

For since they dwell in the deepest places, which are extremely cold but lacking in moisture, they contract a great deal of dry coldness. Being thus constrained and compressed, they long for moist and vital heat; and to obtain this, they rush into animals and irrational creatures, and fly toward baths and pits. For they flee the heat of fire and the sun as if it were burning and drying. But they love the heat of animals as something moderate and mixed with a pleasant moisture—especially human heat, because it is more temperate. 

Therefore, by insinuating themselves into men, they disturb them greatly, specifically by filling the passages and filling those areas where the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus animalis" — the subtle fluid believed to travel through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation</note> resides. Once the spirit itself is compressed by the thickness of the demonic bodies and shaken within, it happens that the bodies vibrate and are convulsed, the principal powers of the body fail in their actions, and stupid or erratic movements occur. And if the demon that rushes in is **subterranean**, it shakes and destroys the person it has occupied, and they cry out through the sufferer, using the victim's [voice/limbs]...

...the spirit as its own instrument. For this reason, it is rightly called "mute and deaf" by many, nor does it depart from those it has occupied unless driven out by divine power—specifically by the prayer and fasting of the person treating them. 

But I said, "O Marcus, some more cautious observations lead us followers of doctors to assert that passions of this sort are not the effects of demons, but of <term>humors</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids like bile or phlegm whose imbalance caused disease.</note>, vapors, and wind behaving badly. Therefore, they usually attempt to cure these things with drugs and diet, not with the songs of enchanters and purifications." 

Then he replied, "It is no wonder that doctors say these things, for they know nothing beyond the senses, but have brooded only over the knowledge of bodies. Perhaps they ought to attribute to bad humors the discomforts of a heavy sleep in the head, the distress of black bile, or the ravings of <term>frenzy</term> <note>original: "phrenesis" — an acute inflammation of the brain or its membranes, often involving delirium</note>, which they are accustomed to soothe with baths, potions, evacuations, or plasters. However, as for the inspirations and possessions in which the one who is possessed can do nothing through intellect, reason, imagination, or sense—there is something else that moves and leads them, which speaks through the possessed about things they do not know and sometimes predicts the future. How, I ask, can we say these are merely the erratic motions of matter?"

### *How demons occupy a person, speak, move, and transform themselves.*

I therefore give credit to Marcus, especially since I hold in my memory what the divine Gospels tell us about demons, and what happened to the man of Corinth at Paul’s command, and finally the many and deeply wonderful things read in the writings of our fathers concerning demons. It remains for me to report those things of which I was an observer and present as a witness. I traveled to **Elasonia** <note>original: "Elasoniam" — Elassona, a town in Thessaly, Greece.</note>, where a certain man, driven by a demon, poured forth many oracles to many people. Meeting him, I asked from where he had obtained the faculty of prophesying. When he refused to reveal it, having finally suffered <term>Laconian necessity</term> <note>original: "laconicam necessitatem" — a classical idiom referring to extreme pressure or torture used to extract a confession.</note>, he at last confessed the truth. He reported that he had been initiated into the works of demons by a certain man named Aletus.

## ON DEMONS

...had perceived me. Wherefore, after these things, I began to doubt in this way: by what means could a demon appear as a woman while tormenting a woman? Nor was it wrongly questioned whether some demons are indeed male and others female, in the manner of mortal animals <note>original: "animalium caduco"—referring to beings that are subject to death and decay</note>, and so on. Furthermore, how could a demon use the Armenian language? For it is greatly to be doubted whether some demons speak Greek, others Chaldean <note>referring to the language of ancient Babylon, often associated with magic</note>, others Persian, and others Syriac. Next, how did that demon shrink himself at the threats of that magician and fear the drawn sword? For what could an indivisible and immortal demon suffer from a sword?

Then Marcus, noticing my doubt, said: "No demon is by its own nature male or female. For such passions <note>in the philosophical sense of "passions," meaning attributes or things acted upon</note> belong to composite beings <note>beings made of multiple elements, like humans who have both physical matter and spirit</note>. The bodies of demons, however, are simple; they are easy to lead and bend, and naturally suited for every configuration. For just as we look up at the clouds and see them present now the shapes of men, now of bears, now of dragons or other things, so it is with the bodies of demons. 

But there is this difference: clouds are driven into various shapes by external winds, whereas demons, by their own counsel and according to their own will, vary the forms within their bodies. At one moment they are contracted into a smaller mass, and then again they extend themselves into a longer one. This is similar to what is seen to happen with earthworms, because of their finer and very pliable substance; and not only does a diversity in size occur in them, but they also vary multiform shapes and colors. 

For the body of a demon is prepared by nature for both. For by whatever reason it is naturally yielding, it is thus transformed into various species of shapes; and because it is airy, it takes on various colors like the air. But while the air is colored from the outside, the body of a demon receives the appearances of colors from the internal action of the imagination <term>imagination: translated from "phantasia," referring to the internal power of a spirit to manifest mental images into physical reality</term>. 

It is just as our cheeks turn pale when we are terrified, but redden when we are affected by shame. As the soul is affected in this or that way, it transmits such passions into the body; we must think of demons by the same reasoning. For these also transfer appearances of colors from within into their own bodies. Wherefore, each demon transforms its own body into whatever shape it has chosen, bringing a certain appearance of color all the way to the surface of the body; thus it appears as a man, and soon meets one as a woman; it roars in the manner of a lion, leaps like a leopard, or barks like a dog. 

Sometimes it even transfers itself into the shape of vessels or containers. And while it changes through all such forms in turn, it retains none of them as stable. For the body of demons is not solid, such that it could retain the shapes it has received. But just as usually happens in air and water—namely, whether you pour in color or imprint a shape, it is soon diffused and dissolved—something similar happens to demons. For in these, the shape, color, and appearance of things...

# PSELLUS

...it glides away just as quickly. Therefore, Marcus taught that these differences of male and female are not inherent in demons, but only appear so, and that no such form remains stable within them. But if you should hear from many that a demon in female form appears to all women in childbirth <note>original: "puerperis"</note>, know that not all demons have the same power and will, but that they also differ greatly in this regard. Indeed, this is in a similar proportion to how composite and mortal <note>original: "caducaque"—referring to beings that are subject to death and decay</note> animals are constituted. 

For just as among these, man is an intellectual being and a partaker of the power of prudence, having in addition a **power of phantasy** <term>phantasticam uim|The "phantastic" power refers to the ability to create mental images or, in the case of demons, to physically manifest those images by shaping their own airy bodies</term> that is more general, explainable, and diffused toward almost all sensible things—both toward celestial things and those which are around the earth and in the earth itself. The horse and the ox, however, and others of the same order, have that power in a more particular way, operating toward certain recognizable images, such that they recognize their manger and their owners. Gnats, however, and mice and similar creatures, have a narrower and indistinct version of this; they do not even recognize the hole from which they emerged, nor the place to which they traveled or where something is to be brought, but they have only a single imagination: if it is for food, it is so.

In the same way, many and diverse kinds of demons differ among themselves. Indeed, among these, the fiery and airy ones have an imagination that is quite varied, distinct, and discrete, whatever imaginable form they might choose; for they shape themselves to this. On the other hand, the **light-shunning** <note>original: "lucifugum"—describing demons who avoid the light, often associated with the deep earth or underworld</note> race of demons is different; for its imagination is very narrow. Therefore, it does not change into various forms, since it does not have many species of imaginable things, nor does it possess bodies that are agile for movement or suited for bending. 

But the aquatic and terrestrial demons, holding a middle ground between these, are indeed able to change into many forms, but they remain longer in those in which they take the most delight. For those who live in moist places and keep a softer way of life make themselves similar to birds and women. For this reason, they name these **Naiads**, **Nereids**, and **Dryads** <note>These are types of nymphs from Greek mythology: Naiads (water), Nereids (sea), and Dryads (trees)</note> using the female gender. However, those who live in drier places and have somewhat parched bodies—such as those said to be **mountain-legged** <note>original Greek: ὀροσκέλους (oroskelous)—ancient folklore described these as wild, mountain-dwelling spirits</note>—transform themselves into men. Sometimes they also show themselves as similar to dogs, lions, and other animals, in which a masculine character is evident. It is therefore no wonder if a demon invading women in childbirth takes on a female form, especially since it is corrupt and delights in impure moistures; for it takes on the form suitable to the life it finds pleasing.

<margin><unclear>faded annotation</unclear></margin>
Marcus indeed did not explain by what logic they might speak harmoniously <note>original: "harmenice"—likely referring to the Pythagorean idea of the music of the spheres or a structured, musical form of speech</note>, nor was it asked of us. I believe, however, that this will be manifest from the following: that a specific language proper to demons cannot be found, even if someone were to say they preserve the Hebrew language, or Greek, or Syriac, or some other barbarian tongue. For what need is there for a voice for demons, who live together without speech? Yet, just as lower angels preside over lower ranks and others over other nations, so do demons assist various peoples. Indeed, individuals practice the languages of individual nations. For this reason, demons who dwell among the Greeks issued oracles in the heroic style, while among the Chaldeans they used the Chaldaic language, just as among the Egyptians they held conversations in the Egyptian voice. Furthermore, if demons inhabiting Armenia happen to move elsewhere, they use the voice of the natives.

## *Why demons fear threats and suffer.*

<margin><unclear>faded annotation</unclear></margin>
But it is asked why demons fear threats and swords. Truly, all kinds of demons are full of both audacity and, conversely, timidity, especially those more closely joined to matter. For the aerial ones, being partakers of circumspect thought, know how to distinguish whether someone is rebuking or honoring them if they are scolded; nor do they depart from the possessed unless the one adjuring <note>original: "obtestator"—an exorcist or one who calls upon God to witness</note> possesses holiness before God and chants the name of God and his terrifying word with divine power. These are certainly the demons closest to matter, fearing lest they be cast down into deeper places and the abyss <term>abyssúmque|The "abyss" refers to a bottomless pit or a place of confinement for rebellious spirits</term>. Likewise, they fear angels, who hurl them there whenever someone threatens them with that precipice and brings forth the invocations of angels appointed for this purpose; for they fear them greatly. Yet, out of ignorance, they do not always distinguish who is threatening them. Indeed, if some little old woman or a rather proud old man should direct threats of this kind in a rustic manner, the demons often depart because they are unable to tell the difference. Therefore, they are easily enslaved even by certain superfluous things—namely, by nails and hair by the polluted race of sorcerers <term>magorum|Magi or practitioners of ritual magic who used physical components like hair or lead to bind spirits</term>. Likewise, they are bound by lead, wax, and thin thread, and are thrown into confusion by wicked adjurations. Therefore, poisoners <term>venefici|Those who use potions, herbs, and "veneficia" (malicious magic) to control spirits</term> and the wicked tame these subterranean demons. Those who abstain from wicked ministries mostly cultivate the aerial ones, taking care lest a subterranean demon intervene. For if any such thing should intervene, besides the fact that it strikes terror, it is also accustomed to throwing stones; for it is characteristic of the subterranean demon to throw stones at those it encounters, though with ineffective blows. Reason dictates that the aerial demons are intrepid; nevertheless, they bring nothing of good, since they are both proud and boastful, and full of deception and empty phantasy. ->**PSELLUS**<-

...[inferior] demons can have light within them. But all these things are the deceits and illusions of hidden things. There are many who are commonly called the **Euchetae** <term>Euchetae: from the Greek 'Euchetai', meaning 'those who pray'. This group, also known as the Messalians, was a sect frequently accused by Byzantine authorities of heretical beliefs regarding the nature of God and demons</term>, whose fraudulent doctrine flowed from a certain insane Mani <note>original: "Manente"—referring to Mani, the 3rd-century Persian prophet and founder of Manichaeism, whose dualistic teachings influenced many later medieval sects</note>. 

They teach several principles; indeed, following Mani himself, two principles of all things were proposed: so that for the God who is the maker of good, a god who is the architect of evil is set up, and for the God who is the lord of the heavenly, a god is set up as the lord of the sub-celestial <note>the "sub-celestial" refers to the region below the heavens, often associated with the material world and its perceived corruption</note>. From this, the wretched Euchetae added a third principle to these. Specifically, among them, there is one Father, but two sons—the older and the younger. Three principles in total. But they attribute only the super-mundane <note>realms beyond the physical universe</note> to the Father, the heavenly to the younger son, and the sub-celestial to the older son, as if they were lords. This doctrine seems to differ in no way from Greek myths, following that poetic saying: "Rewards are distributed in a threefold number" <note>A reference to the classical myth where the universe was divided by lot among the three brothers: Zeus (heavens), Poseidon (seas), and Hades (underworld)</note>. 

But among the Euchetae, some worship both sons. For even if they say they are now at odds with each other, they nevertheless believe both should be worshipped, because both were born of the same father and are destined to be reconciled to one other in the future. Others, however, worship only one—that is, the younger son—as he rules over a better and more excellent province. They do not despise the older one, but they observe him with caution, namely to ensure he does not do harm. 

The worst among them, however, separate themselves entirely from the heavenly deity. They welcome only the terrestrial **Satan** <note>original: "sathanam"</note> into their borders, and they extol him with names they consider superior, calling him the "first-born" and "the one separated from the father." Likewise, they call him the maker of trees, animals, and all other composite things, though he is pestilential and hostile. 

But those who introduce these doctrines are blind and deaf in their minds. For they do not see from the mutual kinship of things that there is one author of all, nor do they hear Holy Scripture teaching this, nor do they reflect on it with reason. Specifically, if there were two makers of things at odds with each other, there would not be that single harmony and union that binds all things together. And if demons promise us riches and glory, they can deliver nothing of themselves, since they have no power; rather, they bring only empty visions to their worshippers—entirely varied and unstable—which the impious nevertheless think are divine spectacles. 

The Euchetae, so that they might receive demons into their whole hearts, perpetrate unspeakable sacrifices. They gather on the evening of the day when the Savior suffered <note>Good Friday</note> in a designated place together with girls known to them. After certain rites, with the lights extinguished, they engage in promiscuous intercourse, whether with a sister, a daughter, or anyone else. In the ninth month, they return again and summon the girls, snatching away the infants now born from them. They cut the boys over their whole bodies and, with the blood poured around...

# ON DEMONS

## ON DEMONS

...they fill phials. They burn bodies. They mix the ash with blood. With this seasoning, they flavor feasts and drinks, both for themselves and for any other famous people they can. For they believe that through this kind of sacrifice and nourishment, as if they were the most profane of things, the divine mark <note>original: "caracterem diuinum"—referring to the seal of baptism or the image of God within a person</note> impressed upon us is completely abolished and demons are kept far away. Thus, the demons may enter more freely.

**How mages enchant and draw forth demons.**

Sorcery and magic have not earned empty names; rather, they possess a certain power. For sorcery <term>sorcery: translated from 'veneficium', which in Latin implies both poisoning and the use of magical drugs or potions</term> is an art concerned with material and terrestrial demons. It calls the images of demons into view; some it rouses as if from the underworld, while others it draws down from on high. For our discipline <note>the Christian theological perspective</note> considers every demon to be evil, fallen from the angelic state and order because of an excess of pride and vanity. 

However, the Greek opinion <note>referring to Hellenistic or Neoplatonic philosophers like Porphyry or Iamblichus</note> judges only a small portion of demons to be evil. They believe these are not evil by choice, but were affected this way by the primary division of things, acting as a sort of torturer against delinquent souls. It is this portion of demons that the illusionist <note>original: "præstigiator"—one who performs wonders or deceives the eyes</note> calls into an imaginary appearance through sorcery. He presents these imagined visions to spectators; for some, they bring out certain overflowing streams from that realm into the open. For others, they promise the loosening of bonds, delights, and favor. Indeed, they bring such demonic powers through certain knots and chants; in most things they lie, but in some they speak the truth. 

Magic <term>magic: translated from 'magia', which the author distinguishes from 'veneficium' (sorcery) as a more "scientific" or priestly study of nature</term>, on the other hand, was seen by the Greeks as a faculty composed of the greatest power. For they hand this down as the highest part of the priesthood. It often brings certain visions into view that falsely display some form of divinity. For this faculty thoroughly investigates the nature, power, and quality of every single thing created under the moon—the elements and their parts, all animals, plants, seeds, and fruits, as well as stones and herbs—and, in short, the substance and virtue of every single thing. 

From this, therefore, the magician performs his effects, creating statues that bring health—evidently fashioned with all kinds of shapes—and he is skilled in other devices that induce diseases. He knows which things differ and which agree with one another. For the joining of many materials brings a "union" to that art, while distance from one another brings "distinction." Now, among them, eagles and dragons are said to contribute to health, while cats, dogs, and crows contribute to wakefulness. Likewise, wax and clay are often used by them to form certain shapes of body parts, since they possess certain properties within their own powers. Frequently, the drawing down of celestial fire to this place is attempted; then the statues seem to smile, and lamps are spontaneously lit with fires. Magic is heavily equipped with much astronomy <note>in this context, "astronomia" includes what we now call astrology, or the study of the influence of stars on earthly materials</note>.

# PSELLUS

...acts through many faculties and through itself. There is also a certain divination in a basin <term>basin: "peluis" in Latin; the practice is known as lecanomancy, where water is used as a medium for scrying</term> by which even country-folk often prophesy. Indeed, just as a kind of prediction is made in the air and through leaves, so a kind of prediction is made in a basin, frequently used and named among the Assyrians <note>The Assyrians and Chaldeans were often cited in Renaissance texts as the ancient masters of magic and astrology</note>. This practice indeed has a certain compatibility with demons who are closely bound to matter. 

Therefore, those divining take a basin full of water, which is suitable for demons creeping in the depths. Now, that basin full of water seems in some way to even breathe because of the sound. The water itself poured into the basin does not differ in substance from external waters, but it excels greatly due to the power infused by incantations <note>original: "carminibus"—referring to rhythmic chants or spells used to "charge" the water</note> and thus is made more fit to receive the prophetic spirit thereafter. This spirit is indeed particular to demons and of the earth, attracted by compositions. When it first glides into the water, it soon emits a certain small sound, devoid of meaning, signifying its descent to those present. Then, in the now-swelling water, certain thin sounds whisper some prediction of the future. 

Moreover, a spirit of this kind is found everywhere through the earth <note>The OCR reads "ras", likely a fragment of "terras" (lands/earth)</note>, since it has obtained a solar rank; and this kind of demon purposefully emits a thin voice so that, because of the indistinct obscurity of the voice, its lies may be less easily detected. 

But can the bodies of demons be struck? Indeed, they can, and they feel pain when struck by some solid body. But in what way, since they are spirits, neither solid nor of a composite nature? For sensation belongs to composite things <note>According to Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought, "composite" things are made of matter and form; simple "spirits" were often thought to be above physical sensation</note>. But surely in those things which feel, it is not the nerve itself that feels, but the spirit that is within them. Wherefore, if a nerve is rubbed or chilled, or if it suffers anything else, pain occurs—namely, by spirit being sent into spirit. To be sure, a composite thing would never feel pain by itself, but only when it participates in the spirit; once deprived of that spirit, it is also deprived of sensation. 

Thus, the demonic body is naturally sensual throughout its whole self; according to its individual parts, it sees, hears, touches, and suffers by touching without any medium. It feels pain when divided, just as solid bodies do. But there is this difference: when solid bodies are divided, they are restored either with difficulty or never. But the body of demons, when it is cut, is soon recreated within itself and grows back together, just like the parts of water or air when something solid falls between them. But the demonic spirit returns to itself faster than can be told. It feels pain, however, while it is being divided, which is why it fears the edge of iron. Those who strive to put demons to flight take note of this, and they set up spears and swords upright in the places where they do not want the demons to approach. They also devise other means, now repelling them with opposing passions, now soothing them with a certain compatible affection.

# ON DEMONS

-> **MARSILIO** Ficino the Florentine to the noble and magnanimous man Filippo Valori, sends many greetings. <-
-> P. S. D. <note>An abbreviation for "Plurimam Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin greeting meaning "Sends many greetings" or "Whishes much health."</note> <-

He who commands "know thyself" seems to admonish us to know the soul, which, since it is the medicine of things <note>original: "medicina rerum." Ficino frequently describes the soul as the "copula mundi" or the bond of the world; here he suggests the soul is the "medicine" or restorative element that allows us to understand the universe</note>, is certainly also all things. Thus, once this is known, we will easily come to know all things. I, therefore, so that I might first attain knowledge of the soul through which I would attain all things, have for a long time studiously applied myself to philosophers—not those common ones, but the most excellent. When, indeed, I anxiously questioned the Platonists <note>The followers of Plato, who emphasized the spiritual and ideal world</note> on one side and the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who emphasized observation and the physical world</note> on the other, and their answers seemed to disagree with one another, I despaired from the beginning that I would ever be master of my wish. But not long after, Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for reconciling the ideas of Plato and Aristotle</note> provided me with the best hope, asserting that such great philosophers do not disagree in their opinions, but only in their words; and that the opinion of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus concerning the soul is the same under different words. I finally fell, by a certain divine fate, upon a book by Theophrastus <term>Theophrastus: Aristotle’s successor as head of the Peripatetic school</term> concerning the soul, explained briefly but nevertheless diligently by a certain Priscianus Lydus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist who wrote a commentary on Theophrastus</note>, primarily using that reasoning by which Plutarch and Iamblichus, distinguished Platonists and Peripatetics, had explained the Aristotelian opinion on the soul. When, therefore, in reading these I noticed that the Platonists and Peripatetics were in agreement, I possessed almost everything that my mind sought. And so that others might have this book as soon as possible, I have translated it from the Greek language into Latin. We have furthermore added certain brief expositions devised by us during the reading and translating. Nor, however, did I think I should labor too much or wander too widely in this matter for the present. For Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Renaissance polymath and friend of Ficino</note>, a man certainly to be wondered at, is already attending to this at the highest level, where he most diligently discusses the minds of all philosophers on any matter whatsoever. And he wonderfully shows that Plato and Aristotle are in agreement regarding the soul. 

Indeed, my Valori, I decided this book should be dedicated to you above all. For you, together with me, have for a long time vehemently desired the harmony of philosophers on this matter. Our Medici patrons, to whom we are accustomed to give—indeed, to return—everything as to patrons, will undoubtedly agree that this one little gift out of many be dedicated to my Valori, who is the dearest friend of the Medici house above all others, and always the most ready helper of Platonic works. Moreover, although we found only a single Greek manuscript, and that one indeed full of errors and mutilated, nevertheless read it with confidence, and thus offer it to others to be read; for I have studied most diligently to correct and repair it. And our Angelo Poliziano <note>A brilliant humanist scholar and poet</note>, a man of the sharpest judgment and great learning, has approved this diligence of ours.

-> Farewell, and read happily, and offer it to others to be read. Farewell. <-

The header "PSELLVS" likely refers to Michael Psellus, another philosopher whose works were often bound with these texts, though the immediate text concerns Priscian and Ficino.</meta>

<header>PSELLVS</header>

## The interpretation of Priscian of Lydia on Theophrastus's *On Sense*, translated and explained by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine: how the instrument of sense becomes like the things perceived.

## Chapter One. OF MARSILIO.

<a></a> For sense to occur, its instrument must become similar to the things being perceived. Not in a material or natural form, but in a certain species <term>species: in this context, an immaterial "likeness" or formal image of an object that allows the mind to perceive it without the object's physical matter entering the eye or ear</term> and an immaterial, purely representative principle. The form of a sensible object, which is "extended" <note>meaning it occupies physical space</note>, is not sufficient for sense, because the act of sensing happens suddenly and all at once regarding the whole object, which can then be understood.

### OF PRISCIAN.

Next, it is Theophrastus’s purpose to discuss sense. Since Aristotle believes that the instruments of the senses, moved by sensible things, are made similar to them through a certain "passion" <note>original: "passione." In ancient philosophy, a "passion" is not an emotion, but a state of being "acted upon" or undergoing a physical change from an external source</note>, Theophrastus rightly inquires what kind of similarity this is by nature. For it seems absurd that in the instruments of the senses—and much more so in the soul itself—any assimilation should occur through colors, liquids, flavors, sounds, forms, or shapes. Therefore, he himself also says that such a similarity is established according to species and principles without matter. We must therefore discuss whether the species falls upon us from the outside, what its nature is, and exactly where it appears; and whether a species extended and divisible around the body is sufficient for cognition, if indeed such a species falls upon us in an uncollected way. For all cognition consists of a certain gathering into one, and of an indivisible grasping of the whole thing to be known.

## Chapter 2. That which senses already possesses an immaterial species of the thing it senses as a representation; but before it possesses this, the instrument of sense must be moved by and undergo a change from the sensible object.

### OF MARSILIO.

Insofar as <note>original: "Vatenus," likely a typo for "Quatenus"</note> the substance of the soul accommodates itself to the spirit <term>spiritus: a subtle, vapor-like substance believed to bridge the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term> through a kind of inclination, that which is the instrument of sense is unfolded into act from the power of sensing that lay hidden in the soul. This power, once unfolded, runs together like one part with such a body to complete the living being. Thus, the substance of the soul is more separate [from the body], while this power is more closely joined to the body. Nor does it act without the body. The "phantasia"—that is, the imagination—affects the spirit in various ways with its sharper movements, through which it then affects the rest of the body; for the imagination directs its gaze inward toward its own images. Sense, however, is directed toward external things, and does not perceive the physical change of the instrument, or the species which they bring to the sense; but through these two it perceives what is outside. Therefore, by its acts, it does not alter the spirit; for its act is not terminated at internal things, but external ones.

### OF PRISCIAN.

It is necessary, therefore, for that which knows to act according to the species of the knowable thing, and to have taken on its character; and this is called assimilation. Now, the "passion" <note>the physical reception of a stimulus</note> occurs in the instrument of sensing.

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic theory of perception, arguing that the soul does not physically become the object it senses, but rather takes on its immaterial "species." Ficino and Priscian explain how the soul and body cooperate through the "spirit" to perceive external reality without the soul itself becoming material.</summary>
