-># ON DEMONS<-
<note>original: "DE DAEMONIBVS." While this header appears at the top of the page, the text continues the philosophical commentary on the soul and perception. In early printed books, such headers often refer to the title of the overall work or the next major section.</note>

...becomes [the act] of sensing, and it is necessary for this to precede the sense. For the power of sensing is not entirely separated from bodies, but in the very inclination of the soul, or its nod toward the instruments of the senses, it receives its essence, and is required for the completion of the animal <note>the "animal" refers to the living, sensing creature (from Latin "anima," soul)</note>. Nor can it act without instruments. Yet these instruments are not like the imagination, which, being primarily excited, moves at the same time; this is because [the sense] is very widely extended and is directed entirely toward external things, and always requires the presence of sensible objects. Therefore, imaginable things are not from the outside, although they are (so to speak) likenesses of external things. But sensible things are external. For sense occurs around these, not around the "passions" <term>passions: from the Latin "passio," meaning the state of being acted upon or undergoing a physical change from an external force</term> of the instruments, even if the sense itself perceives the species <term>species: the formal, immaterial "likeness" or "image" of an object that allows the mind to recognize it</term> which are in bodies along with such passions.

### Chapter 3.

<margin>e</margin> <margin>Of Marsilio</margin> A thing to be sensed moves the instrument of sense in a certain way—that is, the living spirit <note>in Renaissance philosophy, "spirit" was a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note>. This motion is called a "passion" because the spirit is a body; it is also called an "action" because the spirit is living, and the efficacy of life applies a continuous action from itself to the passion it has received.

Such motion is similar to the objects, both because it is inflicted by them, and because a continuous action is applied to this motion by the life of the spirit; when the spirit itself is already excited toward the objects, such a motion—because it is more a "passion" than an action, and is divisible in time and place, and does not have the nature of a species but of a motion—is therefore not the sense itself. For sense, which acts indivisibly and suddenly through a species, comprehends the whole object. It is clear that such motion is not sense; otherwise, whenever we are moved, we would also sense, and a more violent motion would not offend the sense <note>Ficino argues that if sense were just physical movement, a strong blow (violent motion) would be a "strong sense" rather than a cause of pain or damage that stops sensation</note>. It is necessary, after the motion and passion, to arrive at some species through which sense occurs; for sense attains the species and thus perceives through a species. This species is not in the instrument; otherwise, it would be a motion and passion rather than a species, and it would be equally co-extended with the physical instrument. But one must proceed from this very thing which is physically extended to a species that has been reduced to the smallest quantity, and through this to the "reason" <note>or "rational principle"</note> inherent in the soul, which has no quantity at all. Again, the species itself is not in the "trace of life" which the soul imprints on the instrument; for every action of this trace is mixed with passion. The same motion agitates both this trace and the instrument equally. But the species is devoid of passion and motion. For it is the "term" <note>the end-point or goal</note> of motion. Therefore, it is not in the trace of life, which is a true accident <note>a non-essential quality</note>, but in the life which is like a certain substance—not in the life separated from the body, but in the "animal life," that is, life proceeding from the higher soul. This higher soul is separated or separable, and is a true and complete substance in itself, subsisting; whereas the life diffused from this through the body, although it is like a certain substance, is nevertheless the animal part, and is a certain vital application of the soul to the body, divided along with the body, and like a certain propagation of the soul.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains that sensory perception requires more than just physical motion; it requires the soul to transform physical "passions" into immaterial "species." He distinguishes between the physical spirit that is acted upon and the higher soul that remains indivisible and provides the power of true perception.</summary>

## PRISCIANUS

<margin>p</margin>
**T**he sensory instruments themselves are acted upon <term>acted upon: the Latin "patiuntur" (passions) refers to the state of receiving a physical impression from the outside, like wax being struck by a seal</term> by sensible objects, not as if they were inanimate things, but as an affection <note>original: "passio"</note> of a living body. For this reason, it is neither entirely a "passion" there, nor do all things happen from the outside. Rather, it also occurs according to its own action; it is not even moved first and then acts afterward. Indeed, it is not moved at all without acting at the same time, nor does it act unless it is also moved. Thus, such motion in the instruments is similar to the "species" <term>species: the formal, immaterial "likeness" or "image" of an object that allows the mind to recognize it</term> which are sensed, as it is brought into the instrument both by those objects and according to a certain arousal of a vital manifestation or impression implanted within the instrument.

But this is not yet sensation—that is, this likeness introduced into the sensory instrument for the purpose of sensing. This is because this "passion" is more of a being-acted-upon than an action, and is something corporeal, divisible, and extended in time, striving toward a "species" but not yet established as one, for it is still in motion. Sense, however, grasps the beginning, middle, and end of the thing being sensed as an indivisible whole; it is a completed action and judgment, and it exists all at once in the present moment. It seems to have already established itself according to the "species" of the sensible object. 

For this reason, sensation is not achieved without some "passion" of the instrument; yet this passion is not the sensation itself. This is why we sometimes undergo an impression <note>original: "patiamur"</note>, both while awake and while sleeping, yet we do not actually perceive it. It is necessary, therefore, that after the passion, it is finally perfected and defined into a "species"—a species, I say, similar to the thing being sensed. For sensation is achieved according to a perfected species, since it performs a judgment. This species of the thing being sensed is not placed within the instrument itself. For in the instrument, only passion and motion usually occur. Whatever is here is caught up in "division" <note>meaning it is spread out across the physical organ</note>, and the species does not exist there. Nor, again, is it bound up in the mere "trace of life" which is granted to the instrument by the soul. For the vital action of even this trace is performed along with the passion. And there, a motion occurs that is common to both the instrument and the life-force joined to it. But the species itself, according to which sensation occurs, is placed in the "life"—the life, I say, which is in a state of activity, yet not separated, but as the "animal life" completing the living creature, and in its vital application, which is already divided around bodies.

From Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino, the translator and commentator</note>. Chapter 4. The species produced in the life of the living creature attached to the body, because it is spread out along with this life, is not sufficient for the act of sensing, which is "indivisible"—that is, in an indivisible moment it grasps the whole sensible thing with a single strike.

<margin>f</margin>
**T**herefore, the act of sensing proceeds through some indivisible form, and because it is an act remaining within, it occurs through an internal form, which is called the "exemplary pattern" <note>original: "ratio exemplaris"</note> for representing sensible things; and it is essential...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the soul’s perception. It moves from the physical "passion" of the sense organs to the soul's internal capacity to recognize objects through innate "rational principles" (rationes), emphasizing that the soul does not passively receive images but actively projects them from within.</meta>

...is essential to the soul and lives by itself along with the soul, nor is it only of the composite <note>original: "compositi" – referring to the unified being made of both body and soul</note>. That is, although it communicates in some way with the body, it can nevertheless be separated from the body; indeed, it is separated. Otherwise, it would not be able to act indivisibly. For every species of sensory objects, there is one sensory rational principle <term>rational principle: the Latin "ratio" here refers to a mental blueprint or formal pattern that defines what a thing is</term> in the soul representing all individuals. It represents to us now this, now that, insofar as it is aroused by this or that species <term>species: the formal "image" or "likeness" of an object that the mind uses to identify it</term> formed in the life proper to the body and animal. This is what it means to "sense" properly: to bring forth into action that very rational principle of the sensory thing upon the presence of the species formed in life, when a sensory thing moves its sensory instrument. Note that such a rational principle and the act of sensing and imagination are indivisible, and therefore the substance of the soul in which it exists is indivisible, and therefore separated or separable from the body.

## PRISCIANUS

However, not even this species is sufficient for sensation. For a species that is perfected in action around an instrument, because it is divided across the body and has not been converted into one indivisible thing, is not cognitive. But truly, there is in the soul a certain rational principle <note>original: "ratio"</note> of sensory things existing before the act of sensing and before the species is grasped; this principle lives according to itself and is not only of the composite. Therefore, it also acts indivisibly and as a power over particulars. It does not simply come to be in the soul at some time like a particular, divided species. For the cognitive rational principle of sensory things exists in the soul itself, not lying in the body. It is indeed one, but not like singular things; rather, it possesses one thing in itself that embraces many, and is accommodated to each of them. For through one rational principle of "whiteness," the soul senses individual white things. It is necessary, therefore, that a rational principle of this kind be set forth and produced if sensation is to occur. It is brought forth, aroused toward a vital species as if toward its own familiar one, and is accommodated to this species as a likeness of the external species, acting together with it. For that which judges is the rational principle, and the thought belongs to the sensory soul; and that collection into one indivisible thing exists in a substance separated from bodies.

Chapter five. New forms are not imprinted by sensory things upon the soul; and when the soul is said to "receive" a species from things, it is understood that the soul brings forth into action the species of those things lying hidden within itself upon their presence.

## MARSILIO

Since the act of cognition is intimate and vital, it appears that this is produced from an internal form, just as shining comes from light and heating from heat. This internal form—that is, the exemplary rational principle of sensory things—belongs to the essence of the soul itself. From this essence, which possesses true essential rational principles, depends a certain animal life which is not the true essence, nor the true soul, but like an accident, or like a certain substance and life-giving force hanging from the first, just as light hangs from the lu... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "lumen" (light), consistent with the catchword "O" for the next page's "Oportet" or similar.</note>

<summary>This page argues that sensation is an active power of the soul rather than a passive reception of physical imprints, using the concept of innate 'rational principles' (rationes) to explain how the mind identifies external objects. It establishes that because the soul can unify diverse sensory data into a single thought, it must be an indivisible substance separate from the physical body.</summary>

-># ON THEOPHRASTUS<-

...ce, under which, while it hangs, there occurs a trace of life like a kind of heat. Life of this sort is a part of the animal produced by the soul, insofar as it inclines toward the body, produced into it from the soul through its rational principles <term>rational principles: the Latin "rationes" refers to the innate formal patterns or "blueprints" in the soul used to identify things</term>, both vegetative <term>vegetative: relating to basic biological functions like growth and nutrition</term> and sensory. And therefore, life itself also seems to possess rational principles, sense, and the duty of biological growth. We should not say, however, that there are two separate powers of sensing involved in the same act of sensation. Rather, the power itself, which is enfolded in the soul, is unfolded through life. Similarly, the rational principle hidden in the soul is unfolded through a certain species <term>species: here meaning a formal "image" or mental representation of an object</term> eventually perfected in life. This life is what is called the "limit," the "act," and the "perfection" of an organic body having the potential for life. Finally, in the instrument of sense <note>the physical organ, like the eye or ear</note>, the likeness to the sensible object is imperfect; it is perfected, however, in life, and sensation occurs through the production of the rational principle.

### PRISCIANUS

<margin>a</margin>The soul, therefore, is said to possess the "species" of the thing sensed because it brings forth the rational principle of that thing. It does not do so by receiving any form or shape from the object as if from a seal <note>original: "velut à sigillo" — a critique of the idea that the mind is a passive wax tablet stamped by the world</note>. For judgment and action arise from within and are vital. The rational principle thus remains inside and is essential to the soul. Life, however, which completes the animal, depends on these essential rational principles while hanging from them. Indeed, life exists according to a certain extension toward the body. This life is also sensory, and is the limit and perfection of the animal. Because of this, the likeness of the sensed thing is perfected in this life. In the sensory instrument, however, it is imperfect, and is mixed with both passivity <note>original: "passione" — the state of being physically acted upon</note> and action. Passivity falls upon it from external things, while action proceeds from life. Likewise, the species is in the animal's life, but judgment and thought consist in the very act of reason.

External things affect the instrument of sense in their own way with a certain material affection. But the life present here transfers this affection into an immaterial species, through which the soul is stirred to bring forth the rational principle appropriate to that species.

### MARSILIO. Chapter 6.

<margin>p</margin>Through a production of this kind, the soul shows itself to be similar to the thing sensed. It can, moreover, make itself similar to contrary things at the same time through different productions of rational principles. It would not be able to become similar to contraries if it became so by being acted upon <note>a physical object cannot be hot and cold at the same moment, but the mind can think of both simultaneously</note>. Again, if the soul touched heat with one part of itself and cold with another, it could not compare these two with each other—how they agree or how they differ. For it is necessary that the same judge comprehend both of the opposites to be compared. Therefore, the soul contacts many and contrary things simultaneously in a certain indivisible part of itself. It is, therefore, indivisible. For this very indivisibility suffices for knowledge, and therefore also for life.

### PRISCIANUS

<margin>q</margin>In what way, then, does the soul become like things sensed? Not indeed by receiving anything from them, but because it [acts] upon them according to a rational principle...

...it acts, namely through the impression or appearance of certain exterior species <term>species: formal "images" or mental patterns that represent an object</term>. By what means is the soul made similar to many and even contrary things at once? Certainly, it cannot "suffer" <term>suffer: in philosophy, this means "to be acted upon" or to receive an impression passively</term> contrary things at the same time. It is, however, powerful enough to act upon them. Sensation, then, is a matter of action and judgment, not a matter of some passive reception. For the sensation is produced according to a rational principle <note>Latin: "rationem"</note>, while the passive reception is located in the instrument <note>the physical sense organ, like the eye or ear</note>. Since the instrument is a body and made of parts, nothing prevents it from holding many and even contrary things through its different parts. Yet, the reason <note>the soul’s rational power</note>—being a certain indivisible thing—acts similarly while comprehending different and contrary things, however many there may be. For this reason, it correctly judges their diversity, since it happens that many things reach a single indivisible point.

### Chapter seven. The sensory species which is formed in the first stage of an animal’s life is produced by the innate reason of the soul as the primary cause; it is also produced by "life," in which it exists as if from an instrument. However, the passive reception brought into the instrument of sense by a sensible object provides the occasion for this effect.

->MARSILIO<-

The power of sensing itself is not a "potentiality" waiting to be shaped by external things, but a potentiality for producing its own acts regarding external things. The soul becomes like the things being sensed insofar as it brings forth the "reasons" <term>reasons: the Latin "rationes" refers to the innate blueprints or formal patterns the soul uses to identify objects</term> of those things from within itself into an active state. The instrument of sense, however, becomes like those objects insofar as it is a body affected by them, and as a living thing, it performs an action agreeable to them.

->PRISCIANUS<-

When, therefore, even Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> says that the sense becomes like the things being sensed—according to species and rational principles without matter—we shall admit this in such a way that the species are not simply brought in from external things. Instead, they are established by internal reasons within "life" <note>the "trace" of the soul in the body</note> according to the act of sensation. Now, because the sense is extended toward external things and becomes like them, it is rightly called a certain "potentiality," as if it were carrying acts or actions. In the soul, assimilation <note>becoming like the object</note> occurs according to the act of reason; but in the instrument, it occurs partly through the "passion" <note>passive reception</note> brought in by the sensible object, and partly through a simultaneous vital act or life-giving action.

### Chapter eight. Because the instrument of sense is extended <note>meaning it has physical dimensions</note>, it can "suffer" <note>be acted upon by</note> one contrary thing in one part and another contrary in another part. But the instrument cannot compare these things to one another. The soul, however, is indivisible; if it were to suffer from contraries simultaneously, it would suffer entirely through the same point, which is impossible. Therefore, when it perceives contraries at the same time, it does not "suffer" from them, but rather acts upon them.

**Chapter Ten. External things do not render the sense similar to themselves, and much less so the rational thought. Instead, the power of sensing makes itself similar through the production of its own principles, and much more so does thought do this.**

## MARSILIO [FICINO]

<margin>a</margin> It belongs to the same sense to judge between opposites, just as hearing judges both voice and silence. If it were pure silence, the external sense would not perceive it; rather, the internal sense would do so through the memory of a voice, noticing that it has fallen into the opposite of a voice. However, for the most part, silence is not pure. In those cases, the hearing exerts itself around a very weak object and, barely perceiving anything, is said to grasp silence, as if it were grasping whatever is missing from the voice there. The sense judges a thing to be congruent, friendly, and pleasant when it agrees with something innate to it. Conversely, it judges a thing as alien when it disagrees, during which time the instrument <note>The physical organ, like the ear or eye</note> is moved perversely <note>In an unnatural or distorted manner</note>.

## PRISCIAN [OF LYDIA]

<margin>p</margin> Therefore, since the instrument is usually struck first and more strongly by the proper sensibles <note>Qualities specific to one sense, like color for sight or sound for hearing</note>, but consequently and more faintly by the common sensibles <note>Qualities like size, shape, or motion that can be perceived by multiple senses</note>, any sense is deservedly accustomed to perceive its own objects under the same condition. Sight, for instance, perceives color first, and consequently perceives magnitude and motion. For this reason, common sensibles can seem to belong more to the soul's domain, being known by the sense as if by accident. But certainly, as has been said, this common sensible becomes known to the sense as a consequence, and is not grasped by rational thought alone. 

Furthermore, it is often asked how the eye perceives darkness and the ear perceives silence. The answer must be that they do not so much "sense" as "consent" <note>original: "consentire"; meaning to feel along with a state or lack rather than actively grasping an object</note>. The sense does not lean or fix itself upon such things; rather, because action is inhibited in these cases, the sense judges by its very effort that something is lacking to them. It grasps what is distant and alien from the fact that the reason <term>ratio: the innate proportion or organizing logic of the soul</term> innate to it does not agree with this at all. Meanwhile, the instrument of sense is moved in a somewhat perverse way because of a passion <note>A "passion" in this philosophical context is an impression or "suffering" caused by an external force</note> brought upon it by some sensible object.

## Chapter Twelve. Since the soul is the mistress of the body, and therefore a far more excellent substance, the body is deservedly made and arranged for its sake.

<margin>i</margin> In the order of providence, therefore, the soul is both prior and was distinct before the body. For the body receives as many instruments as may serve a soul that already possesses so many powers. These powers are formal <term>formales: relating to the "form" or essence that gives a thing its identity</term> and are distinguished formally according to their species—a distinction that does not proceed from matter. Therefore, a single innermost sense derives the fruitfulness of its own unity into five senses. For these five senses, instruments were later adapted within the body.

# ON THE SOUL

<margin>1. master</margin> <note>original: "magi." — likely an abbreviation for "magister," referring to the authority of the text, or a reference to Plotinus</note>
Thus far, we have treated the sense in general. Regarding the individual senses, however, such as sight, hearing, and the others, this must be distinguished by us first of all: namely, that there is not just one sense (as some think) which is distinguished into different types merely by the <term>instruments</term> <note>The physical organs of the body, like the eyes or ears</note> that participate in it. For the diversity of the instruments does not precede the differences in the powers of the soul, nor does it have the authority to divide those powers. Rather, the sense itself is both one within itself, and from its own nature is divided into five for the purpose of discerning individual sensible things. Now indeed, the difference in the instruments also followed this distinction of the senses, being appropriately accommodated to each; for the <term>formal</term> <note>The essential or conceptual structure</note> or specific division precedes the material and instrumental division, and the diversity in the "users" <note>The powers of the soul that "use" the body</note> relies on a greater authority.

### Chapter thirteen. The act of sensing is not brought about as if either the sense naturally touches the sensible object, or the sensible object naturally forms the sense, but rather by a certain logic in a spiritual manner.

->MARSILIO [FICINO]<-

<margin>Note</margin>
Neither does sight emit from itself anything natural and as if corporeal by which it might touch color as if with a trunk <note>original: "proboscide" — a trunk or feeler, a common metaphor used to critique the theory of extramission</note>, nor does anything natural flow out from the color to be imprinted upon the sight; nor, again, does the color itself color the air, and the air the sight. <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "species" — the immaterial images or qualities of things that allow them to be perceived</note> separated from matter, because they are entirely released from location and are excluded from the limits of matter, are therefore able to act upon all things and to act equally at any distance. However, forms determined within matter and place, according to the mode of their nature, do act upon something and up to a certain distance, and similarly receive impressions by undergoing action. There are, moreover, many natural actions of the <term>composite</term> <note>The combined unit of the physical body and the soul</note> itself, such as heating and similar things, and naturally affecting something by smell and taste. There are, however, besides these, certain actions of forms of this kind, attributed not so much to the composite bodies as to the forms themselves—namely, following specifically from the excellence and property of the form itself. These actions are indeed, as it were, <term>spiritual</term> <note>original: "spiritales" — in this context, meaning immaterial, refined, or relating to the "pneuma" that carries information</note>, and they extend further than the actions which are proper to the physical body, and they sometimes occur suddenly, yet only up to a certain distance, because these forms are in matter and contained by place. Actions of this sort are not only in the soul acting upon things, but also in the forms of things reaching out in a certain way toward the soul; in such action and reception, the sense is produced. The soul, since it is a living and sensory form, acts upon those things which are offered to it in a vital and sensory manner; and because it is in the body, it operates up to a certain distance.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

The specific forms of things, insofar as they are the formal images of divine forms, act formally and, as it were, spiritually upon a thing that is primarily formal and spiritual—namely, the instrument of sense, which is to say, the living being itself. And such action properly and directly leads to sensation, but only when the action of the soul is added, as I mentioned shortly before. However, the action of the <term>composite</term> <note>The "composite" refers to the unified being of body and soul acting together in a purely physical or biological way</note> that is specific, material, and natural either hinders, or does not assist, or is not sufficient for the effect of sensing. The Soul of the Heavens, because it possesses all sensible things through their causes within its own body, therefore looks into all sensible things through a certain inner sense, using its body as both an instrument and a cause. Conversely, because the principles of sensible things are not in our body, our sense is forced to look outward. From this it is clear that this Priscianus is a Platonist; for what he touches upon regarding the sense of the celestial soul belongs to Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus. Indeed, both from what precedes and what follows, it is everywhere evident that he is a Platonist and a diligent follower of Iamblichus.

## PRISCIANUS.

But what exactly is seeing, hearing, or smelling? And are all the senses brought about through a certain medium? Just as sight occurs through the <term>diaphanum</term> <note>original: "diaphanum"; a technical term in Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy referring to the transparent medium, like air or water, that allows light to pass through</note>—that is, that which is clear and passable for the eyes—or do certain senses rather touch the things to be sensed without a medium? Likewise, what exactly is this "diaphanum"? For my part, I believe that vision is completed neither through some reception from external things (as if the soul were formed by the objects of sense through some flow of matter out of them), nor by an emission from the eyes (as if some physical body were sent out to touch the objects of sense). Nor do colors move the transparent medium as if they were physically molding it, nor does the transparent medium move the sight in a similar way. But the specific forms themselves possess an effective power, through which each one acts upon that which is most exposed to such a <term>passion</term> <note>In this context, a "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving a sensory impression</note>. This happens not only by touching, but also upon things that are at a distance, provided there is a certain proportionate distance: for the former to act and for the latter, in turn, to receive. For since a natural form is corporeal, and is contained in something, and is circumscribed by a certain place, it does not act upon just anything positioned anywhere. But it acts only upon that which is at a distance, according to a certain proportion—one that is measured against the effective power of the agents, the fit and exposed power of the recipients, and the measure of the impression itself. Indeed, the visible object acts upon the instrument of sight from a certain interval, which must be proportionate both to the one seeing...

...both the visible object, for the former [the object] to act and the latter [the eye] to undergo the impression. Since, however, the mere passive impression of a visual nature from a visible object does not simply create sensation—for a more violent impression actually hinders it, because it is <term>incommensurable</term> <note>original: "incommensurabilis"; meaning out of proportion or lacking a common measure</note> to the measure of the impression through which sense occurs—surely distance is also necessary. This is why very bright things, if they are brought closer than that measure requires, hinder vision and ultimately prohibit it altogether. 

Since, however, sensation is produced not only through the passive impression of the [physical] instrument, but also through a certain action (as has already been said), that which sees also acts upon that which is seen by it. It does not act by altering the object or inflicting some passive change upon it, but by acting upon it through judgment. For the soul does not act like a [mere] body, but like something vital and capable of seeing. But since this vital and cognitive power exists within a body, it does not comprehend sensible things according to their cause—as does that celestial life and power of knowing—but rather its work is perfected according to a certain distance and extension toward sensible things. It is for this reason that this proportion requires a distance to adapt these things to one another.

## Chapter 14. How among the other senses, sight alone uses light—a truly celestial thing—and must use it.

### BY MARSILIO <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the philosopher and priest who translated and commented on these works, blending Platonic philosophy with Christian theology.</note>

<margin>5</margin> From light come things that are *luminous* and things that are *luminal*. <note>original: "luminosa" (light-giving) and "luminalia" (light-receptive or light-like)</note> The first **luminous** thing is the celestial. The second is fiery. The third is found among composite things, which shine like fire. 

The first **luminal** thing is the eye—especially the radiant eyes of animals that see at night. But other eyes, though less so, are nonetheless luminal. The second **luminal** thing is color, which is clearly created from a certain dominance of light in naturally composed bodies. The third **luminal** thing is the <term>diaphanum</term> <note>The transparent medium, such as air or water, which allows light to pass through</note>, which we can call transparency or "perspicuity." For this transparency seems to be so easily passable for incoming light that it is a kind of beginning of light, having the highest aptitude for receiving the fullness of the remaining light. 

Since, therefore, sight, color, and the transparent medium naturally possess some small portion of light, they rightly seem to strive toward a fuller light. Through this, the "luminal" things may finally become "luminous," and having achieved a perfect degree in 그at category, they may be joined to one another: namely, color to the eye through the transparent medium. The necessary medium between the eye and color is not "air"—for if it were air, we would not see through water and similar things—but rather it is the <term>diaphanum</term>, that is, the transparent, which is passable to rays from every side and friendly to them, like a welcoming host and something naturally...

...light-like <term>luminal</term> <note>original: "luminale"; meaning having the nature or properties of light</note>. This is truly required: mostly so that, having already been filled with light, it may illuminate both the eye and the colors. It is always necessary that there be a proper distance <note>original: "debitum interuallum"</note> between these; for when either the eye or the object near us is exceptionally bright, a third light is not necessary besides these to complete the medium, through which these things are then perfected. Color is said to be the "limit of the <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: "diaphani"; the transparent medium (like air or water) through which light and color travel</note>" in a bounded body, primarily in two ways: first, by reason of the transparent medium itself; second, by reason of the object. You look at white snow; know then that this white color is the boundary of the transparent medium—namely, the surrounding air, for the whiteness is at its edge where it touches the snow—and also of a certain transparency that we understand to be inherent in the snow. However, this whiteness appears in actuality not in just any part of this transparency, but only at the limit—that is, always on the surface of the snow, however many times you might cut into the snow. Through these points, it is confirmed that color is something "light-like."

### BY PRISCIANUS <note>Priscian of Lydia (6th century AD), a philosopher whose paraphrases of Aristotle and Theophrastus were central to Renaissance theories of the soul.</note>

<margin>h</margin>
These things are indeed common to both hearing and sight, and even to some of the other senses, if any other sense is not forced to touch its own proper sensible object. But in sight, the use of light is most excellent and unique, as light perfects both sides: both the one who will see (so that they may see) and the visible object (so that it may be seen). For neither will the visible object itself act upon the seer without light, nor will the seer act upon the visible object. For that which is within us as the "visual power" is in a certain way naturally light-like, which is clearly shown by certain animals that first illuminate the things they must see <note>A reference to the ancient belief in "extramission," where the eye emits its own light or fire to perceive the world.</note>. For this reason, they can even see at night. Similarly, colors are in a way light-like, as they are observed around the boundaries of the transparency of bounded bodies. For these reasons, therefore, both are rightly perfected by light, since by their own nature they possess a small light-like quality insofar as it pertains to their perfect mutual action. Therefore, they additionally require external light: both the sight itself, as something light-like, and the colors—or "certain lights," as their appearance surely indicates. For colors are the boundaries of the transparent; the transparency is indeed a certain (if I may put it this way) aptitude for receiving light, or perhaps it is a trace of light so faint that it cannot yet complete the middle distance for vision. Yet even this distance itself is adapted for vision—not merely as air or water or something else, but as a transparency already made perfect by an illuminating source, perfecting both that which sees and that which is seen.

### Chapter fifteen: whether vision happens through the emission of a ray from the eye, or by the reception of a certain image from the object. Likewise, concerning three rules generally pertaining to the senses.

## BY MARSILIO <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated and commented on Plato and Plotinus.</note>

<margin>V</margin>ision is an action that remains in the seer, just as shining and heating remain in a fire. Therefore, if vision were in some way located in the external object, the seer itself would be there—namely, through the presence of a certain emitted visual ray. Vision also seems to occur around the visible object located outside; first, because otherwise distance could not easily be judged. Second, because no "natural" substance <note>meaning physical matter</note> from the object to be seen comes to the eye, as seems to happen from other objects to other senses <note>Unlike smell, which was thought to involve physical particles, sight was seen as more "spiritual" or "mathematical."</note>. There are also those who think, in turn, that something does come to the eye from the object. For the eye undergoes some effect from there: thus, vision is surely contracted by black and dilated by white; and now it is dazzled by brilliance. This kind of "undergoing" <note>original: "passio"; the state of being acted upon by an external force</note> is also perceived by the eye, but more on these things elsewhere. There are three primary rules handed down by <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) whose mystical and systematic approach to the soul deeply influenced Ficino.</note> to be firmly held regarding every sense. 

First: something happens from the sensible object to the "instrument" of the sense <note>the physical organ, such as the eye or ear</note>. It is necessary for the organ to be affected from that source in some way. This affection is partly a "passion" <note>original: "passio"</note> brought in from the outside because this instrument is a physical body; yet it is also an "action" resulting within the instrument because the living thing’s affection of this kind becomes, in a way, similar to the thing being sensed. 

The second rule: after this affection in the instrument of the living thing, a certain <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; in this context, a non-physical "image" or "form" that represents the object</note> is formed. This is of a more spiritual kind within the animal's life itself, and is now more suited to the sense, yet still remains similar to the sensible object. 

The third rule: at the presence of this "species," a certain "reason" <note>or "ratio"</note>—which was previously hidden in the soul—is awakened concerning the thing to be sensed. Once awakened, it corresponds to the species, and through the species to the affection, and through the affection to the sensible object placed outside. This awakening and correspondence is, in a general sense, what it means "to sense."

## BY PRISCIAN <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher whose "Paraphrase on Theophrastus" is being commented upon here.</note>

<margin>M</margin>uch variety, therefore, occurs in vision, for it seems to go out beyond itself. This is because it acts around the sensible object located outside; yet it also receives something from the object to be seen, because it clearly undergoes some effect from there. Now indeed, the <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: "diaphanum"; the transparent medium, such as air or water, that facilitates sight</note> and the medium seem to transmit for both as if...

## Chapter sixteen: how a medium is necessary between the sensible object and the sense, and concerning the color of the transparent.

->BY MARSILIO<-

The sensible object itself is excessively material, while the sense is quite spiritual. ## BY PRISCIANUS.

But let us now return to Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was Aristotle's successor; Priscianus Lydus wrote a famous "Paraphrase" of his works on the soul.</note>. He further brings up this point regarding the transparent <note>original: "diaphano"</note>, which might indeed disturb some people on account of its novelty: in what way is this "visible" thing said not to exist through itself, but to be made manifest to the eyes because of a foreign color? It is as if one were to say that something "tastable" becomes so through a foreign flavor. 

Indeed, such a doubt is easily resolved. For that foreign color is called "light," as if it were proceeding from elsewhere—that is, from a source of illumination. For light is so familiar to things that are to be seen that it perfects them and leads them into <term>act</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" is the state of being fully realized or functioning, as opposed to just having the potential to be seen.</note>. Therefore, the transparent medium itself, whether it has its own color or not, is nonetheless perfected by light, just as the colors of other things usually are. For light does not take away the properties of a thing; on the contrary, it leads them to their full expression. Or, as I said, if the transparent is by itself devoid of light, it is certainly perfected by light as if it were "colored," and thus it emerges as something to be seen.

### Chapter seventeen on the transparent and light.

## BY MARSILIO.

Transparency <note>original: "diaphanitas"</note> or clarity is not a physical body. Otherwise, it could not be infused into other bodies without scattering them; nor is it a mere disposition brought upon other bodies by some body through a kind of passive state. Rather, it is a specific <term>species</term> and form in its own right, just like light, color, and heat. Truly, the "species" of forms do not arise primarily from physical matter or from bodies (which are ineffective on their own as matter), but they are created and formally distinguished by the "First Form," which is simultaneously uniform and "all-formed"—that is, by the Divine Mind. 

Moreover, Priscianus proposes this from the mind of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized the divine hierarchy of reality.</note>, just as Julian <note>Likely Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363 AD), whose Neoplatonic "Hymn to King Helios" discusses the metaphysics of light.</note> asserts from the same mind in his book on the Sun. The transparent exists not only in the ether, fire, air, water, and glass, but in the earth itself and in all composite bodies. Certainly, a kind of intellectual soul is infused into all these things. From this soul, insofar as it is a kind of "life," heat proceeds through all things (though it may be hidden); and insofar as it is "intellectual," light is diffused through all things. Although it may be hidden in some places, the transparent is displayed alongside light as the proper "receptacle" for light. Furthermore, Julian says—following the mind of Iamblichus and the Phoenicians—that light is a pure <term>act</term> extending through all things from the activity of the Divine Intelligence. The transparent, however, is the vehicle for an act of this kind, and it is indeed incorporeal—

...and not mixed with the qualities of bodies, although it is diffused through all these things. Therefore, the transparent <note>original: "diaphanum"</note> is a necessary receptacle for light. 

If anyone, relying on the rules of the astrologers, considers how much power the innumerable rays of the immense machinery of the heavens have to penetrate the earth—the central point of the world—he will recognize that through this power and through composite things, celestial light and the transparent are diffused everywhere, even if these things are not apparent to us on the surface of the earth. However, they may perhaps be apparent to certain animals living there <note>A reference to the belief that some creatures can see in what humans perceive as total darkness.</note>. They also say that just as cold relates to heat and blackness to whiteness, so does darkness relate to light; thus darkness is not a "pure privation" (a total nothingness), but is the "least light," or an opaque light. For the light of the celestial bodies is so powerful that a place for pure, absolute darkness is nowhere allowed to exist.

## BY PRISCIANUS.

<margin>Question</margin> What, then, is the nature of the transparent—that is, what is clear and passable to the eyes? For it is not enough to say that this quality belongs to air, water, the ether, and some solids. He says it is necessary for the transparent to be either a certain <term>passion</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, a "passion" (passio) is not an emotion, but a state of being "acted upon" or receiving a quality from an external source.</note> or a disposition. For this quality exists deep within a body; yet one body cannot occupy the same space as another body in that way. 

But if it is a passion or a certain disposition, we shall investigate from what source it arises. For it seems to come perhaps from one or from several of the simple bodies. Yet, if this cannot be the case—for these simple bodies, namely air and water, are naturally transparent—then earth is also transparent through fire. Indeed, all composite bodies are transparent to the extent that they are all colored. For color is the boundary of the transparent. 

I assert, therefore, that the transparent is not a "passion" or a disposition brought upon bodies from the outside, but is a certain reconciling <term>form</term> <note>original: "speciem"</note> of those things that exist in the "generation" (the physical creation) of bodies, meant to receive the perfection of light. Likewise, it offers them a certain aptitude for receiving light and for undergoing darkness, whether it participates in either of these through its very essence, or takes each in turn, or holds both at once through some mixture. Indeed, the transparent that is found in fire has "essential light." But the transparent that is found in the earth has "essential darkness." For this reason, just as fire is light-making, so the earth is darkness-making; for darkness itself (if we may put it this way) is not merely the privation of light, but is itself also an <term>act</term> <note>An "act" (actus) or "actuality" refers to the active presence or realization of a quality, suggesting darkness is a positive force here rather than just an empty absence.</note>. But have we perhaps erred just now in placing it also in the earth...

We ought not, therefore, to inquire from which of the simple bodies the transparent arises. For species are produced neither from elements nor from any bodies at all. Instead, the bodies themselves participate in species, and according to them, they obtain their own proper characters. For this reason, things that do not claim a luminous species for themselves according to their essence require light in order to be seen. Fire and similar shining things, however, do not require it at all, since they are participants in a luminous species that is sufficient for this very thing by its own essence.

Chapter nineteen. That light is not in the transparent as a quality of it, but is present rather as an act of the illuminator itself. BY MARSILIO. <note>original: "MARSILII." Referring to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the head of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>

<margin>The</margin> Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world was composed of physical atoms.</note> think that light is a body: but most of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who walked while teaching</term> indeed think it is not a body—otherwise it would not penetrate bodies so easily—but they want light to be in the transparent things that receive it from time to time as their passion <term>passion: here meaning an "undergoing" or a state of being acted upon (passio)</term> and quality. Priscianus <note>Priscianus Lydus, a 6th-century Neoplatonist whose work Ficino translated.</note> rejects this as alien to the Platonists, whom he venerates above others. He therefore brings forward for this the arguments of Iamblichus, which he also received from Plotinus <note>Plotinus and Iamblichus were major figures in Neoplatonism; they viewed light as a spiritual or metaphysical radiation rather than a mere physical change.</note>. A quality that comes into a body and is properly captured by it, becoming its form, has six conditions. First, it approaches through the parts of the body little by little. Second, it introduces a "passion" into the subject and changes its natural disposition; first indeed an accidental one, and finally a substantial one. Third, because it is propagated only up to a certain distance. Fourth, because when the thing that formed it departs, it remains for a while in the subject, just as heat remains in water when the fire is removed. Fifth, it is itself moved when the body is moved from its place. Sixth, it can be stained by the impurity of the body and there be confused and mixed with other qualities into one, and thus be composed. Light, on the contrary, comes suddenly; it does not change the nature in the subject; it is propagable through the immense <note>original: "per immensum" — suggesting light can travel across vast or infinite distances instantly</note>, provided that something is present that is able to receive it. When the thing that illuminates withdraws, it leaves nothing of itself behind in that which seemed to have it. It is not moved when the air or water is moved; it is not stained when the transparent medium is stained, but either remains pure in itself or departs immediately, always continuous with the illuminator. Moreover, many lights are not composed into one; this is apparent from the fact that if you walk toward two lamps, twin shadows will result. If you walk toward more, there will similarly be more shadows. Likewise, if a huge board is placed against three lamps, with a hole in the middle, they will transmit three lights through this to the opposite side. Finally, light is present to the transparent as separately as the intellectual soul is present to the body.

->BY PRISCIANUS.<-

<margin>Therefore</margin>, following Iamblichus, I do not think light is a body, nor—as the Peripatetics think—a passion or quality of some body. For light does not have its being in the air. For when the air is moved, the light remains; when the air is changed in manifold ways, light departs by its own impulse into itself, and meanwhile keeps an indissoluble connection with its cause. Indeed, its entire presence simultaneously [reaches] through all things capable of receiving it...

It transitions from a general discussion of the "transparent" (diaphanum) to Marsilio Ficino’s specific metaphysical conjectures about light as an incorporeal force originating from the heavens.</meta>

-># ON THE SOUL<-
->P<-

...happening suddenly, clearly in the presence of that which illuminates. And again, when it departs, the sudden disappearance of light—leaving no trace of itself behind—can serve as an argument for us that light is not a passion <term>passion: a state of being acted upon or a physical change (Latin: *passio*)</term> of the air. For passions, such as heat, do not arrive suddenly; and even when the fire is removed, its heat leaves at least some small lingering trace of itself in the subject that underwent the change. It is clear, moreover, that the very act of light is separate from bodies, because it does not arrive through a gradual succession of steps, nor by a total transformation of the subject, nor is it confined within a certain fixed limit. Rather, it spreads itself until it strikes something capable of receiving it. Nor are different lights ever confused or mixed together into a single substance. 

In what way, then, is light called the "act of the transparent"? <term>transparent: the medium, such as air or water, that allows light to pass; Latin: *diaphanum*</term> Certainly not as a kind of passion, nor as a perfection produced within it as if in a physical subject, but rather as something that perfects the medium while remaining separable from it. This luminous act does not at any point truly "belong" to the transparent medium; instead, it brings it about that the medium becomes its permanent dwelling, while the light itself remains continuous with the source that illuminates it. Thus, the light is carried around everywhere along with that source. Let this, therefore, be mentioned briefly, so that we do not suspect that light is produced or received in a subject in the same way that a physical effect is usually produced in other "patients" <term>patient: the object or substance that receives an action or change</term>.

### Chapter 20. On light again and the transparent.

### BY MARSILIO <note>original: "MARSILII." Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the philosopher and head of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>.

Since it is clear from the above that light is something incorporeal and unmixed with bodily things, we can conjecture three things from this. First, that the heavenly body—the first receptacle of light—is ruled in its bodily life and intelligence by a higher power, from which it receives light and hands it on to others. For light, being incorporeal, cannot be produced by a physical body alone. Second, that the heavenly body does not possess the kind of matter that would allow it to be mixed with other elements. Third, that light is a most powerful cause in acting. For if it does not mix with the subjects it acts upon, it acts more freely because it is unhindered, and it is most powerful by its very nature. 

Therefore, wonderful actions proceed from light. Light does not flow from a luminous source through a kind of physical dissolution, like a scent coming from an apple, nor like heat from a fire (which becomes the property of the one receiving it and is not always connected to the giver). Instead, light is like the "visual ray" from the eye—provided that vision happens through emission <note>Ficino refers to the "extramission" theory, popular in antiquity and the Renaissance, which held that the eye sends out rays to "touch" the objects it sees.</note>. This ray is perhaps nothing other than sight itself extended toward external things, or the very act of sight acting at a distance; it does not leave the one who sees, but remains always continuous with them and unmixed with the external things it touches. It is capable of doing harm, as is seen in the basilisk <note>original: "regulo." A mythical serpent believed to kill or wither things merely by looking at them.</note>, and it is capable of doing good, as is established by training. If we say that light consists of the visual rays of the heavenly eyes living within themselves, and that through such rays all things...

<summary>Ficino argues that light is an incorporeal act, not a physical quality, comparing it to "visual rays" that remain connected to their source. He suggests light is a powerful, unmixed force originating from the heavens that can influence the world without being corrupted by it.</summary>

<meta>catchword: and so</meta>

...of those seeing and those acting, and if we do not wander from the Platonists, we will see that the gaze—whether favorable or unfavorable—does not fail. Therefore, there is in a luminous body a form and an act so excellent that it extends itself very far; it is not separated from the agent, nor is it mixed into the recipient. This very extension of the light is what we call the ray proceeding from the light source.

## PRISCIANUS

<margin>P</margin> After these things, Theophrastus asks: if light is incorporeal, why is it produced by the presence of fire or some other body? For in this way, light might seem to be a certain corporeal outflow, or a body itself that dissolves over time. He says this must not be understood in such a manner, but only according to its natural state. Here he certainly declares that the act of light itself exists as something specific or formal, since even heat comes from a form <note>original: "species"; in this philosophical context, it refers to the essential form or defining nature of a thing</note>. Therefore, light is not a body. For light does not consist of a division, a cutting away, or a physical outflow, but rather exists as the very act of the luminous form—or whatever other name one wishes to call the form which is the cause of light. Furthermore, if darkness is seen without light, then light would not be the cause of all things being seen. But indeed, as Theophrastus says, darkness is not "visible." For we do not perceive darkness by any firm foundation of sight, but rather by the deprivation of seeing and by the fact that we do not see at all. Then indeed fire, and anything similar that is seen in the dark, acts as the cause of the perfected transparent medium <term>transparent medium: the "diaphanum," such as air or water, which allows light to pass through it</term>. And for that reason, fire does not entirely need that medium in order to be seen. Fire, therefore, in order to be perceived, does not require a medium that is already "in act"—that is, a medium already illuminated. However, since it is necessary for there to be some medium (for vision does not occur through direct contact), this medium must be transparent. Otherwise, if it were solid or resistant, it might block—with its opaque and dark properties—the mutual action between luminous things, namely the fire and the instrument of the senses.

### Chapter 21. Other senses do not require a perfected medium like sight.

## MARSILIO

<note>Large indent in the original for a missing initial V</note> [V]ision appears to be the most excellent of the senses, since it perceives more quickly, further, more broadly, and more distinctly than the others. Likewise, the movement of apprehension and progression is more perfect than that of descent. Just as the soul and many instruments are needed to perform this more perfect movement, whereas they are not needed for an imperfect one, so for the more perfect act of sensing, there is a need for a much more perfect medium. For this reason, for the act of hearing and the rest of the senses, a material path, a sensible interval, and a suitable medium are sufficient. To see, however, there is required not only a medium of this kind, but one that is perfected—perfected, I say, by light as if by some celestial power. This light can indeed be called a certain "color" of a luminous body...

...and so through the first color, the other colors are sensed.

## OF PRISCIANUS
<note>Priscianus refers to Priscian Lydus, a 6th-century Neoplatonist who wrote a famous commentary on Theophrastus's work "On Sense Perception."</note>

It happens, moreover (as Theophrastus says), that the very cause of seeing colors is color itself; or simply, that the cause for any visible things being what they are is "the visible" <note>original: "visibile"; here used as a technical term for the quality that allows something to be seen</note>. Indeed, light, being a kind of color, is the cause of transparency <note>original: "diaphani"; the medium, like air or water, through which light travels</note> and of the visible. He adds again that this is not absurd, but is found in other cases as well; for instance, taste also occurs through flavor. But perhaps someone will say that flavor—which is the proper object <term>sensibile: the specific thing perceived by a particular sense</term> of taste—and sound—which is the proper object of hearing—require no external thing at all by which the sensory organ may be moved; unless, perhaps, one were to say that sound requires a sounding object, just as color requires transparency. But indeed, sound is suddenly perceptible as soon as the intermediate air has been proportioned. We know, however, that color requires an external illuminator if it is to be visible at all. This is perhaps a unique property of sight: namely, to require light. This is not because sight is less perfect than the other senses (which require no other external "perfecter"), but because it has a more excellent and sublime action for which mere sensory power is not sufficient. Rather, it requires some more divine form <note>original: "speciem"</note> in addition. For just as our body does not require a soul in order to be heavy and to descend, but does require a soul for the motion of progression and apprehension—because of the excellence of that motion, which exceeds the natural downward movement of the physical body—and this higher movement, caused by the impulse of the imagination, is not for that reason worse than natural movement, but better; so also sight, being more excellent than the rest because it operates more excellently, uses a certain other perfecter.

### Chapter 22. Sight, as the most perfect of the senses, and the visible, as the most perfect of sensible things, have an order from the many to the one, which the other senses and other things to be sensed do not have.

## OF MARSILIO
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Florentine Platonic Academy, who translated and commented on these works.</note>

Neither are all tastes reduced to one single taste through which they are tasted, nor are all tastable things reduced to one tastable thing through which they are tasted. And the same is true for the other similar senses. But visible things become visible through the "first visible thing"—that is, light—and therefore all acts of sight occur through a "first sight." Because, indeed, those things which are separate and distinct among lower things are united among higher things, we can conjecture that the "first visible thing" and the "first sight" are the same: namely, specifically the light of the sun. Hence Orpheus calls the sun the "eye of the world" <note>original: "oculum mundi"</note>. Similarly, all intellects are referred back to the first intellect, and all intelligible things are referred back to the first intelligible thing. That indeed is the first intellect and the first intelligible thing. Likewise, just as from the very center of the heavens, as most confirm—that is, the sun...

ON THEOPHRASTUS

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

...universal life is diffused through all things, without any dissolution, or thinning, or mixture of that life itself. Similarly, light is diffused from that point through all things, which indeed, coming from the life of all things, becomes the life-giver for all. And here is a marvelous order in that very category of things seeing and things seen: they are brought back from a multitude into the one from which they had also previously proceeded. There is also a marvelous abundance of that first visible thing <note>original: "primi visibilis"; referring to light as the primary object of sight</note>, so that all things are seen by its power. Finally, there is a singular efficacy of sight, such that it perceives innumerable things through one act. Since, however, the other senses and the rest of the things to be sensed should not be entirely lacking in some order, it is likely that both the other senses and the other sensible objects are contained within the power of the first sight and the first visible thing, so that if they are not ordered by themselves, they are at least ordered through its order.

## OF PRISCIANUS
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century philosopher whose "Paraphrase on Theophrastus" was a key source for Renaissance thinkers like Ficino.</note>

Perhaps someone might say it is worth considering whether that which is bright, and light itself, is the primary visible thing, which of itself moves the eye and upon which sight acts, needing no other external thing to complete the process. Colors, however, as if they were certain tiny lights, cannot be seen by themselves, but require the primary visible thing itself to perfect them immediately. But someone will say furthermore: if it were so, it would not be necessary for light to contribute to colors so that they might be seen; on the contrary, it would confound them. Just as a greater light is accustomed to overwhelm a smaller one, and in the objects themselves, that which shines more occupies the place of that which shines less. Thus, under the sun, the light of a lamp <note>original: "lychni"; a portable lamp or candle</note> is seen very little. However, the comparison of the greater to the lesser is not the same as that of the preceding to the following. For the color is not compared with light simply as a visible thing; for indeed, nothing is visible at all without light. Therefore, color is compared to light as a "consequent visible" <gloss>a secondary object of sight that follows after the first</gloss> insofar as it is perfected by light and becomes visible through it. But light itself is by its own nature sufficient for this: to be seen. And if in the other senses a similar proportion is not found—through which one thing is primarily and another consequently "audible" or "tastable"—this is certainly a kind of wealth, both of that which is first visible of all (which we say is light), namely, that it perfects the other things to be seen, and of the power of seeing itself; for the sense perceives not only light, but also certain other things by the benefit of light itself.

This medium must moderate the action and passion by distance and, by a certain property, adapt the acting agent to the receiving subject. A medium of this kind cannot be a vacuum. <margin>p iii</margin>
<note>This "p iii" is a signature mark used by early printers to guide the binder in assembling the book's pages in the correct order.</note>

...are the affections of the body. Furthermore, so that the eye (which is a body) may be adapted to the visible thing (which is also a body, or located in a body), a certain continuity must be established through a body. This continuity cannot be achieved through a deprivation of body, which is a vacuum <note>Aristotelian physics argued that a vacuum was impossible and that sight required a physical medium to transmit information.</note>.

Let the medium, therefore, be a body of this kind, and certainly not an opaque one. For sight and color are, in a way, "luminal" <note>original: "luminales"; meaning they are of the nature of light or related to it</note>, and they further require a fuller light. Therefore, that which brings darkness is not a medium, but an impediment to seeing. Let the medium then be the <term>diaphanum</term> <note>The "diaphanum" or "transparent" is the substance—like air, water, or glass—that allows light and color to pass through it.</note> which, being situated between the eye and the color, contributes to the process—not by being luminous itself, but by providing the space for the mode of action and reception <note>original: "actionis, & passionis"; "passion" here means the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression</note>, and by its transparency, which allows it to receive and then display a more abundant light. 

Indeed, where either the eye or the color is intensely luminous, the medium helps by providing at least an interval to temper the action and reception. It even helps to bind these two together by a certain shared property; for through its transparency and light, the medium matches both the luminous color and the transparent, shining eye. Remember, meanwhile, that the transparent is in itself something of the nature of light.

->PRISCIANI<-
<note>Priscianus Lydus, a 6th-century Neoplatonist whose commentaries on Aristotle and Theophrastus were influential in the Renaissance.</note>

Since, however, the transparent medium appears to be "moved" by colors, we seek the answer to this question: namely, how is it moved? Is it by a certain flow <note>original: "defluxu"; referring to the theory that objects "shed" thin layers of themselves that travel to the eye</note>, or is it because the colors act while the medium receives the action? We must extend this inquiry even to those who think vision happens without a transparent medium (with colors merely brought directly to the eye), and also to those who believe something is emitted from the instrument of the senses itself <note>This refers to the "extramission theory," the ancient idea that the eyes shoot out rays to "touch" objects.</note>. 

Therefore, it is worthwhile to investigate how the transparent medium is moved, since it truly is moved. Colors certainly seem to be visible through a transparent medium, yet they are not seen when placed directly against the eyes. Regarding this, we have said that the transparent requires a medium so that the things to be seen may be illuminated. But when the spectacle itself shines on its own, is there still a need for some transparent medium? 

Indeed, there is still a need, as we have said, so that there is a suitable distance. It is also necessary that the medium not be solid and opaque, lest it hinder the action with its darkness-bearing property. But does the transparent medium contribute only by not hindering anything? As if the interval were a vacuum? This is not consistent with reason. Rather, it must contribute something, for a medium body does not exist by chance. Now, it clearly helps with colors, which we could not see unless the medium were illuminated. It follows, therefore, that in the case of glowing things as well, the medium contributes something to the process.

¶ Furthermore, if in hearing and in smelling the air is moved in some way, and also in touching when the air is the medium between the thing providing heat and the thing being heated, and similarly in tasting if some liquid should intervene—even though in these latter senses the medium acts through a kind of mixture rather than pure action—if the matter stands thus in these senses, it follows that in seeing the medium is also moved. Again, everything that illuminates acts clearly upon the transparent; such is the case with that which is very bright. Therefore, even that which shines less exerts some action, although not so much as to illuminate. Thus, colors perfected and illuminated by light also stir the transparent.

## Chapter 25. How color moves and acts upon the transparent medium and the eye.

# MARSILIO
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the celebrated Florentine philosopher who revived Platonism in the Renaissance.</note>

The fire of the <term>thermae</term> <note>Ancient Roman-style hot baths.</note> acts upon the air, and the air acts upon the person. Here there are two agents and twin actions: for the fire imparts heat to the air, which then becomes a quality of the air itself. The air, thus boiling, warms the person even if the fire is removed. The sense of touch can feel the boiling air, or at least the lukewarm air, even if it does not perceive the fire itself. ¶ Not so with an illuminated color or a luminous color, such as that of the heavens or of fire. It does not "format" the transparent medium by mixing a certain light through it in such a way that it becomes a permanent quality of the transparent—to the point where the transparent, once "formatted," would become its own agent forming the eye through its own action, independent of the act of the color itself. Otherwise, we would perceive the colored transparent medium rather than the color of the object. ¶ In reality, we clearly perceive the color because its "lucid act" reaches us, and it does so in an instant, and entirely within every portion of the air. For we see the whole thing suddenly and everywhere, from which it is clear that this is not mixed into the air...

...nor a quality produced in the air, but rather (so to speak) sitting upon the air like a rider on a horse <note>original: "insidere sicut eques equo"</note>, not like a shape in a horse. ### OF PRISCIANUS
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century Neoplatonist; here he explores how color "shapes" the air without actually changing its physical nature.</note>

<margin>n</margin> Is it then the case that colors move the transparent medium, and this medium in turn moves the sight, as if the medium itself were formed by the colors to no purpose? Otherwise, we would perceive the transparent medium having been affected in this way, but we would not perceive the color at all. But if we perceive the color itself, it certainly moves the sight. Nevertheless, we also perceive the transparent medium. This medium also moves our intuition through itself—specifically when it has already been illuminated—not through another thing, and as if moved by the colors. 

What then is this motion, so that we may understand how the things themselves which are to be seen move the vision through the medium? I assert, therefore, that just as the illuminating object perfects the transparent medium—while the act of the illuminating object is separately present to the transparent and to the eye through the transparent—not because the transparent medium has properly suffered anything from it, but because it itself has also been separately perfected through the act of light; so the illuminated color acts upon the transparent medium. That is, the action sits separately upon the transparent, or rather is "carried upon" it. For this reason, it does not occur by a succession of parts <note>The author argues that light and color fill the space instantly, rather than traveling through points in space over time.</note>, but is made present everywhere at once, as a whole and to the whole, and as it were forms the transparent separately. Along with this medium thus "formed," it moves our sight at the same time. So much so that the color itself also acts upon the vision, but in such a way that it meanwhile uses the transparent medium as a subject for its own action—not indeed as a passive thing, but as something formed separately through an action of this sort.

**Chapter 26.** The transparent medium is not the subject of light as if it were its own quality, but is the vehicle of light <note>original: "uehiculum luminis"</note>, as if light were separable from it and always continuous with the luminous body.
