That which is material in a voice—that is, the "broken air" <note>original: "aer fractus"; a traditional Aristotelian definition of sound as air being physically struck or broken.</note>—is not present as a whole everywhere, but that which is spiritual in it—that is, the meaningful content or at least a specific quality—is impressed upon the voice both outside of us by the "life of the world" <note>The *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, a common Neoplatonic concept suggesting the universe itself is alive.</note>, and inside us in the organ of sense by the life of that organ. This spiritual quality is said neither to suffer on its own along with the air, nor to be mixed with the air, yet it is present as a whole simultaneously to all who are hearing.

### OF PRISCIANUS
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century philosopher whose work was rediscovered and translated by Marsilio Ficino in the 15th century.</note>

<margin>q</margin> What then does the <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphanum"; the substance, like air or water, that allows light to pass through.</note> contribute to seeing? If the activity of color falls upon it without being physically mixed, it is useful for the very reason that it transmits and leads the color through. For the activity of color reaches the sight, carried by the transparent medium separately (as we have said) and present to the whole indivisibly. Therefore, whoever watches in a theater, no matter how many there are, they all behold the same spectacle as a whole everywhere, just as everyone there hears the voice equally. For the activity of the voice is indivisible; it is whole everywhere in a divisible space, yet remains the same thing present to all, inasmuch as it is neither carried along physically with the air nor altered in the same way the air is. For the proof of its "absolute presence" is that it exists within each and every listener as a whole, filling everyone similarly according to the logic of a single form.

### Chapter 27. What contributes most directly to sensing is not something material, but rather something spiritual.

### OF MARSILIO.
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the head of the Florentine Academy, who added his own Platonic interpretations to these texts.</note>

<margin>m</margin> Remember that what is immaterial, indivisible, and free from a physical subject—and therefore present as a whole everywhere around those who are sensing—cannot proceed from a material source. And therefore it is clear that not only in our senses, but in the entire universe, there is something spiritual and vital in its vigor. By its power, spiritual activities, <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the non-physical "images" or "forms" of things that the mind perceives.</note>, and images are brought forth whenever a material <term>affection</term> <note>original: "passio"; the state of being acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> occurs in the air, whether from a sounding object, or from a coloring object, or from other objects of the senses. Yet, in the meantime, something immaterial results in the organ of sensing, or even in the air itself. This is necessarily required for the act of sensing. That act does not properly arise from the material "suffering" or vibration of the air or the organ, but from a certain spiritual form which results in them through a certain power of life. However, a "species" of this kind is not enough for sensation and judgment, unless the soul, prompted by it, immediately brings the innate principles of sensible things—which are born within the soul—into action.

### OF PRISCIANUS.

<margin>d</margin> Say then: is not the air and the organ of hearing struck and changed passively by the sounding object? Certainly, there is indeed affection and motion...

### Chapter XXVIII. 

Regarding sight, material disturbance appears least of all, while the spiritual form appears most; regarding hearing, however, both appear almost equally. Regarding the three remaining senses <note>Smell, taste, and touch.</note>, the physical disturbance is most evident, but the spiritual form is least.

<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the celebrated Florentine philosopher who translated and commented on these works.</note>

Every kind of sensible object affects the medium and the sensory instrument through its own nature by a certain natural and, in a way, material disturbance. For **light** thins and warms things by the very fact that it is light. **Whiteness** scatters the sight, **blackness** draws it together, **greenness** tempers it; a **sound** breaks, thins, and thickens the air. A **fragrant thing** impresses a quality similar to itself, naturally affecting things in this way; likewise for things that can be **tasted** and **touched**. Because this disturbance, being material, is far removed from the soul which is entirely spiritual—and because if this physical impact increases too much, it diminishes and eventually destroys the sense—it is necessary that besides this, there be a certain **spiritual form** <note>original: "speciem... spiritualem"; the non-physical "information" or "image" of the object that the soul can actually perceive.</note> involved, which is in a way indivisible. This form may result only within the instrument (as in touch and taste), or it may also begin outside (as in sight, hearing, and smell); otherwise, these three senses would not be able to perceive things from such a distance. Certainly, the natural form of the visual organ is the least material, and the natural form of hearing and sound is almost similar. Therefore, in the presence of the smallest material disturbance, the spiritual form results most easily, which is necessary for sensation. But in the three remaining senses, the form of both the instrument and the object is judged more materially; therefore, that form which contributes to sensation results from a greater material disturbance, since it is itself almost material. Nevertheless, these objects can move the sense without a physical **flow of their matter** <note>original: "effluxu materiae"; the idea that objects don't have to physically shed pieces of themselves to be perceived.</note>; therefore, colors can do so much more easily.

### Chapter XXIX. The sensible object contributes to the sense not by outflow, but by action.

## MARSILIO’S COMMENTARY

<margin>e</margin>
**A**n outflow, by dragging something of the matter and nature of the object with it, affects the medium and the sense organ in the same way. Thus, it tends toward changing their very nature. If this change grows too strong, the sensory nature is destroyed. Therefore, a natural outflow from an object does not properly result in sensation; rather, it is the simple **activity** itself. This activity follows the **form** <note>original: "speciem"</note> of the thing to be sensed rather than its matter—a form, I say, not just because it exists in matter, but because it is a form derived from an **Idea** <note>Ficino, a Neoplatonist, refers here to the divine archetypes or "Ideas" from which all physical forms originate.</note>. Therefore, this kind of activity, having reached the organ, settles there—if it has not already been converted into the sort of **spiritual form** necessary for the senses. Light itself, which becomes visible in a simple way, does not get this power from the <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphani"; the air or water through which light travels.</note>; rather, the transparent medium clearly gets its power from the light. But light is carried to us by the transparent medium as if by a vehicle. Consequently, light is visible to us *within* the transparent medium rather than merely *through* it. It can be said that nothing is visible to us except color. Likewise, nothing is visible except light, for light is itself a kind of color: it is natural to the stars and fire, but "foreign" <note>original: "peregrinus"; meaning it is not innate to the air but borrowed from a light source.</note> when in the transparent medium. Conversely, color is light: it is an instrument in complex and opaque objects, but exists in its pure state in the heavens and transparent things.

But certainly, it is not just color, but (as has been said) the very fact of being a sensible object that moves the sense through its own **activity**. Color, however, does not act at all times, but only when it is already illuminated, and when (as Theophrastus says) the transparent medium

# ON THE SOUL

<meta>catchword: air</meta>

The transparent medium <note>original: "diaphanum"; the clear substance, like air or water, that allows light to pass through.</note> underlies it like matter, which indeed simultaneously perfects colors through light and is, in a way, shaped by them—specifically by a separate **activity** <note>original: "actu"; the active expression or reality of a thing as opposed to its mere potential.</note> flowing from that source. Moreover, light is not seen *through* the transparent, but rather *in* the transparent; and according to its own nature, it becomes visible to us, just as the transparent itself is made manifest by light. Perhaps, indeed, they should not be divided (as Theophrastus says, and says rightly); for neither is light perceived by the senses without the transparent, nor the transparent without light. And yet, if light is the "color" of the transparent, then surely this very thing which is called "visible" will be nothing other than colors.

### Chapter XXX. The intermediate air contributes to sight, hearing, and smell, not properly because it receives a form from the thing to be sensed, but because it translates the activity emanating from that form to the sense.

-> MARSILIO FICINO <-

<margin>r</margin> A visible thing does not imprint any form or figure upon the air, but from that thing—once illuminated—there proceeds from its **likeness** <note>original: "specie"; the non-material image or "species" that represents an object to the mind.</note> a certain luminous activity. This activity is special and specific; it is not mixed with the air and therefore does not "shape" the air. Instead, as soon as it touches the **luminous spirit** <note>original: "lucidum spiritum"; in Renaissance medicine, a subtle vapor that carries sensory information to the brain.</note> within us, it emerges again as a likeness matching the likeness from which it came. From a sounding or smelling object—which is more material than the object of sight—the air and the spirit are more evidently affected <note>original: "patitur"; meaning the air undergoes a physical change or "passion."</note> than they are by color. Nevertheless, the sense is not produced by that kind of physical affection, but by a certain special and specific **activity** which, proceeding from the likeness of the thing, lies hidden beneath the physical affection. This activity returns into a likeness within the spirit by the power of our life, which is remarkably specific. And if perhaps it should emerge into a spiritual likeness even before it reaches us, this happens by the power of the **World Soul** <note>original: "mundanae uitae"; the "World Life" or Anima Mundi, a Neoplatonic concept that the universe is a single living organism.</note>. For the single life of the world as a single animal, being inherent in individual things, connects them to one another—especially those that are otherwise similar in form. It brings it about that even things that seem to be far apart act upon each other easily and share in each other's experiences, to which the magnets bear witness.

-> PRISCIAN THE LYDIAN <-

<margin>q</margin> From where, then, does the transparent produce vision by "undergoing" an effect? Some people think that the medium is properly "figured" or "formed," but it should not be thought of in that way. Rather, as we have said, it produces vision by receiving, in an absolute sense, the **activity** emanating from visible things and joining it to the sensory instrument. Now, not only are colors visible, but also magnitudes and figures, although in a secondary degree, as we have already distinguished. Smell, however (as he says), occurs through the air as if the air were mixed and affected <note>original: "patientem"; undergoing a change.</note>, as is apparent. Hearing, meanwhile, occurs through "figured" air. Yet it has been said that sensation does not happen according to physical affection, and that a voice is not a shape made in the air, but a certain perfect **likeness of action** or activity. Furthermore, a smellable thing is not a physical affection, but a **likeness** <note>original: "species"</note>. However, the air is more prone to being affected...

**Chapter XXXI. That which is less material enters the immaterial sense more powerfully; and the sense that is more remote from matter receives the immaterial object more effectively.**

### MARSILIO FICINO

There are four causes through which a sensible thing reaches the sense more fully and is sensed more strongly. First, when the object is more effective for this purpose. Second, when the sense is purer. Third, when the quality of the medium is more conformed to both, so that it more aptly transmits the **activity** <note>original: "actu"; the active expression or reality of a thing</note> from the object into the sense. Fourth, if a shorter distance is added. Sight and the visible object, because of their spiritual nature, act upon each other across a longer distance. The other senses, descending step by step into action, because the material nature in the instrument <note>the physical sense organ</note> and the object gradually increases, act upon each other more poorly and sluggishly, nor do they proceed as far in the act of sensing as sight does.

### PRISCIAN

<margin>p</margin> After these things, Theophrastus asks whether any object to be sensed reaches the sense equally, or rather if this one reaches it more, and that one less. I certainly think that without doubt they do not reach it in a similar way, but rather according to whether that which has the power of sensing has a greater or lesser capacity for action. Again, according to whether the instrument of the sense has a more or less pure **sincerity** <note>original: "sinceram"; here meaning clarity or lack of physical contamination</note>. Furthermore, according to how much the medium itself is more or less fit for the action to be transmitted between the object and the sense. Finally, according to the distance, longer or shorter, by which the sensible object is far off or nearby; a certain difference in the reaching occurs.

**Chapter XXXII. Between the sensible object (because it is too material) and the immaterial sense, there is always need for a certain medium that is, in a way, spiritual.**

### MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>q</margin> When you see a spark from a very long distance, or hear the faint sound of a locust, or even the tiniest animals; likewise, when bees and ants smell honey from very far away, and even shellfish taste at a distance, and the **torpedo fish** <note>original: "torpedo"; a species of electric ray known in antiquity for its ability to numb its prey or fishermen through their tools</note> often numbs you through a long rod just as if it were touching you: do you think (especially in the higher senses) that the vast distance is broken through and materially affected by such a tiny object? Not at all. Instead, something "spiritual" <note>original: "spiritale"; referring to a non-physical, life-force-like transmission that bridges the gap between matter and soul</note> in a certain way intervenes, which acts upon the sense through such a long distance. That is, a certain special and specific activity proceeding from the species of the thing to be sensed—whether this occurs within us, as in touch and taste, or even outside of us, as in sight, hearing, and smell—which also belongs to the common power of life. By its benefit, all things are bound together so easily from distant objects, and the sense is moved and...

# ON THE SOUL

A similar body is affected by something similar, which has been discovered through magic <note>original: "magicen"; here referring to natural magic or the study of hidden sympathies in nature</note>. Although the medium and the instrument <note>the sense organ</note> are more violently affected by an object that is more material—as in touch, taste, smell, and often hearing—nevertheless, a safer and more unhindered sense results from that which comes from what is less material. Regarding sight, the spiritual act proceeds immediately from the object, by the benefit of light itself, I believe. Thus, we see in the same moment that the act proceeds; but sound, near the thing sounding, is a certain material impression <note>original: "passio"; a state of being acted upon by an external force</note> of the air and a fracturing made in time. To this, there soon succeeds a formal <note>original: "specialis"; pertaining to the 'species' or immaterial form of a thing</note> and, in a way, spiritual act, reaching the hearing all at once, which results in the air thus fractured by the duty of a more hidden power. Therefore, you do not hear the one striking at the same moment you see them. However, the formal act proceeds into voices, insofar as the air's impression is not an impression that breaks it, but one that affects it; for it proceeds far beyond the point where the air is broken.

### PRISCIAN

Moreover, it has been sufficiently defined by Aristotle and not doubted by Theophrastus—even if he judged it necessary to insist on it more studiously here—that in all the senses, some medium falls between the sensible object and the sense. Although the medium of external objects appears more clearly, while the medium of those things which are in some way within us is least apparent. But first, one might investigate this: if the presence of a voice (as we have said) suddenly arrives all at once, how is it that those who are closer to the sound hear it better and more swiftly? Or how is it that when someone cuts down an oak tree, we see the strike before we hear the sound? For it is clear that the effect and the hearing of the sound do not happen at the same time as the strike.

It must be said that this happens because it is necessary for the air to be affected and moved first. Once the air has been moved in this way, the form <note>original: "species"</note> of the voice itself soon becomes present all at once. The impression and the motion happen in time, but the Form comes afterward, though it reaches what has already been done all at once. Regarding the voice, therefore, the form of the act itself happens later within the impression, and it reaches as far as the impression proceeds through the continuity of the air. For this reason, those who are closer to the object hear more quickly and better, since those who are closest to the sound-maker are affected more swiftly and more strongly. But as for what is to be seen, it does not act upon the transparent medium <note>original: "diaphanum"; the substance, like air or water, that allows light to pass</note> through a physical impression, since even that which illuminates is not a physical impression. Therefore, it acts without time, and meets all those by whom it is seen at once. Even so, it does not reveal itself to all in the same way, but reveals itself more clearly to those who are closer. For it acts more powerfully upon those things that are more ready; and these are the things that are nearby in space, because both the things that are seen and those that in some way see are bodies.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

### Chapter 33. On the reflection of light, and images. BY MARSILIO.

Light falling upon a body that is somewhat dense, smooth, and shiny stays itself, gathers together, and immediately grows stronger—specifically within a body that is both firmer and more compatible with it than others. Once gathered and made powerful, it acts from there again in the opposite direction; specifically, when it hits mirror-like bodies, it leaps back <note>original: "resultat"; to bounce back or reflect</note> toward the opposite wall and produces a glow there. It likewise leaps back toward other things and into the eyes. Therefore, it is never "broken" <note>original: "frangitur"; here Ficino argues against light being physically fractured, suggesting instead a fluid movement</note>, but first unfolds itself, then folds back, and applies itself. In both cases, the act of light is seen as a single, continuous movement.

Similarly, the visual ray reaching any mirror-like body is strengthened, gathered, reinforced, and folded back. Having slipped back from the mirror in the opposite direction, it sees things that were hidden from the mirror. There are also those who wish for the illuminated forms of things to produce rays toward the mirror, which are then reflected from there into the sight that sees the object. Theophrastus and Plato add that certain images, which are called **Idols** <note>original: "Idola"; from the Greek "eidolon," meaning a phantom or likeness</note>, proceed from the illuminated shapes of things. For **Idos** <note>original: "Idos," from the Greek "eidos"</note> means "form," and from this the name **Idol** is derived as a diminutive <note>a "little form"</note>, as if it were a sample or a thin form coming from a more perfect form. These idols, therefore, being very weak, do not move the sight until they have fallen upon a mirror-like body. There, having been stabilized, restored, and reinforced, they offer themselves to the eyes—whether the idols themselves proceed from there to the sight, or whether the visual ray itself leaps out toward them. However, the manner in which these idols—not only spiritual but also material—flow out of things through light (or sometimes without light) toward the sight or sometimes toward other senses, and how they grow strong especially in our **imaginal spirit** <note>the "spiritus imaginalis," a subtle substance in the body that Ficino believed acted as the bridge between the physical senses and the soul's intellect</note> as if in a mirror, showing themselves to us and acting upon us in wonderful ways, we discuss at length in our commentaries on Plotinus.

### THE WORDS OF PRISCIAN.

Theophrastus says that we must next treat refractions or reflections. For it is common to say that a certain "expression" <note>a pressing out or printing</note> of the presented form occurs in the air, as if struck back. Perhaps Plato himself feels the same when he says that a certain phantom-like appearance of bodily forms <note>original: "idolarem"; image-like or illusory</note> is created in the gentle light spread around a smooth body. We, therefore, ought not to admit "breakings" or "strikings" here in a physical sense. For such a thing is a "passion" <note>original: "passio"; a state of being acted upon or suffering an external force</note> which is inconsistent with what is naturally an "action." This is especially true when we deal with the light of the sun alone; rather, we must accept these reflections as active and effective. This is because both the thing that illuminates and the person who sees act more effectively around a dense, polished, smooth, and bright body—to such an extent that the illuminating source itself further illuminates other things through this, and the person seeing...

...by the same [power] it may look back at another. For the **second act** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "first act" is the possession of a capability, while "second act" is the actual performance of it—like the difference between having the ability to see and actually looking at something.</note> belongs to this. Indeed, since a subject of this kind is smooth and somewhat shimmering, it assists in the action. For this reason, it has an affinity with light. Plato, however, maintains that a certain "imaginal" appearance of bodily forms <note>original: "species"; the outward appearance or formal essence of a thing</note> is produced in the very act of the vision coming forth. This happens around a certain smooth and bright body, not indeed through a physical flowing out from the bodies, but through a certain shadowy shaping of the forms in the process of appearing and seeing. Perhaps this is also what Theophrastus indicates when he says that through reverberations, a certain expression or shaping of the form occurs in the air.

### Chapter 34. There must be a communion between the agent and the patient.

### BY MARSILIO.

<margin>u</margin>Where a destructive action <note>original: "actio peremptoria"</note> is to occur, a communion between the **agent** (the one acting) and the **patient** (the one being acted upon) is sufficient in their matter alone, as is the case between fire and water. If a communion in some quality is added, the action will proceed more easily, such as that which occurs between fire and air. 

However, where a "perfecting" action <note>an action that completes or improves the receiver</note> is imminent, a communion in a certain property of nature is necessary. Thus, the rational teaches the rational; thus, the luminous illuminates the "luminal" <note>something capable of receiving or holding light</note>. For the former perfects the latter above all others because there is a certain unfolding property within the latter that matches the form of the former. 

Therefore, there is a "proportion" in a certain property of this sense toward the sensible object itself. The eye is something <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: "diaphanum"; a Greek-derived term for a transparent medium like air or water</note> and luminal; and in that which it naturally began to possess, it is perfected to the highest degree by light through the transparent medium. Similarly, the **spirit** <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried signals between the soul and the body.</note> serving the hearing has an airy property, already in a sense sounding within itself or easily made to resonate when "broken" air <note>sound waves</note> approaches and sounds more perfectly. In the same way, a vapor is smelled in the spirit; it is most ready for the vapors of odors, and is, as it were, already odorous. In the sense of taste, a certain natural saliva is most ready for liquids similar in flavor. In touch, a more solid nature is present, better suited to the primary qualities of the elements. Everywhere, the one "suffers" <note>is affected</note> by the other, not because it is equal in likeness to it, but because it is in some way similar, and through this, it is a ready and obedient follower toward a complete likeness, just as that which can be shaped obeys the one who shapes it.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains that reflection is an active process rather than a passive one, and establishes the philosophical rule that sensory organs must share a "nature" with the objects they perceive (e.g., the eye is light-like).</summary>

# ON THEOPHRASTUS:

<note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle; this text is a Renaissance commentary on his theories regarding how we perceive through our senses.</note>

...their own powers agree with the objects of sense in that property which we have mentioned. Sense, however, exists within the innate proportions of the things perceived. The intellect agrees with the intelligible <note>Things that can be understood by the mind rather than just felt by the body.</note> much more so. For the intellect penetrates the intelligible by resolving it—something the senses are unable to achieve.

## OF PRISCIANUS.

<margin><unclear>Of Priscianus</unclear></margin>
He adds, truly, after these things, that in certain cases the instrument of sense appears to be kindred to the things being sensed. For the tongue, through a certain moisture of its own, tastes the moisture of flavor. Hearing also hears an airy voice through the movement of the air enclosed within the ear. He asks, therefore, for what reason things are not similarly situated in the other senses as well. Likewise, he asks how like is affected by like—specifically, how the internal air is affected by the external air, and the innermost moisture by external moisture. On the contrary, the principle is similar in the rest. Indeed, in any sense, the instrument is of the same nature as its object, since the instrument is subject to the actions of those objects. Thus, there is something transparent <note>original: "diaphanum"; a technical term for a medium like air or water that allows light to pass through.</note> in vision, and something resonant in hearing. For the ear does not drink in sound simply because it contains air, but because it contains something specifically capable of resonating. Similarly, something "smellable" lies hidden in the sense of smell. For this reason, there is also something here that is watery, or airy, or rather a middle substance. For a watery moisture exists in the sense of taste. Finally, in touch, there is a certain faculty capable of appropriately receiving tangible qualities. Nor is "like affected by like" in a simple way; rather, that which is "in potential" <note>The capacity to become something or receive an impression.</note> is affected by that which exists "in act" <note>A thing currently performing an action or possessing a quality.</note>. Nor, again, does air suffer from air, but rather as something *potentially* resonant is affected by that which is *actually* resonating.

### Chapter 35. Doubts concerning vision, hearing, and smell.

## OF MARSILIO.

<margin><unclear>illegible scribble</unclear></margin>
The medium necessary for seeing is not specifically air or water, but simply the transparent itself, wherever it occurs. However, a watery transparency is placed in the eye for this purpose: so that the watery moisture may restrain the thin spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; in Renaissance medicine, these were "vital spirits," a subtle vapor that traveled through the nerves to carry sensory information.</note> of vision itself, which would otherwise fly away entirely. The object of hearing is sound itself, whether it occurs in pure air or in water. However, air is naturally enclosed within the hearing apparatus above all others. Since air is moved more easily than water, and it is necessary for the instrument of hearing to be moved in order to hear, it follows that because this "airy spirit" is the instrument of hearing, in no way can anything be heard unless that enclosed air is moved. And perhaps for this reason, someone will think that nothing external is heard unless air is poured into it or even surrounded by it. Nevertheless, something can be smelled <note>original: "adorari"; likely a transcription error for "odorari" given the context of "olfatum" (smell).</note> without breathed air—namely, by animals having an unimpeded sense of smell and by men of a similar nature.

->DE ANIMA<-
<note>Latin: "On the Soul." This is a commentary on the nature of perception.</note>

Living creatures and humans who have their nasal passages for smelling blocked follow two main processes through respiration: for they both draw in a more abundant scent and, by the air being violently drawn in, they immediately open up the passages.

## OF PRISCIANUS.
<note>Priscian of Lydia was a 6th-century philosopher who wrote paraphrases of the works of Aristotle and Theophrastus.</note>

<margin>c</margin>
**W**hy then is a somewhat watery moisture placed in the eye? And why not rather a moisture common to both water and air, since indeed transparency <note>original: "diaphanum"; a technical term for a medium like air or water that allows light to pass through.</note> is common to both? Again, why is there not something common to air and water placed in the sense of hearing? Since sound occurs in water as well. A similar doubt arises concerning the sense of smell, but surely one of the two is enough; for in external things there is no need for a mixture, but whether it be water or air which is the medium, we see by a similar logic. Why then is the pupil located in water? Namely, because water contains and preserves much more than air. For what reason, again, is hearing placed in the air? Surely because air is more mobile. Indeed, motion contributes to the perception of sound. But if smelling can happen without breathing, what prevents (as Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle.</note> says) something from being heard without air? This certainly: because sound cannot be produced within without the striking of the air innermost to the ears. For the instrument of hearing is air, but the instrument of smell itself is not that breath <note>original: "spiritus"; here referring to the inhaled air or pneuma.</note> drawn in by respiration; rather, that breath is useful for opening the passages that lead to the sense of smell—specifically in those creatures that have blocked passages. In those where these passages are open, they smell even without breathing at all.

### Chapter 36. Concerning sound and the motion which is perpetual in hearing.

## OF MARSILIO.
<note>Marsilio Ficino, the renowned Renaissance philosopher and translator of this work.</note>

<margin>p</margin>
**T**he Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, known for walking while teaching.</note> believe that audible sound itself—that is, sound which comes to the ears from external sources—is created by a certain violent collision and breaking, where a less dense body striking a denser one is violently blunted and shattered. Moreover, they believe there is an air kindred to the sense of hearing which is perpetually moved and makes a sound. But they hold that its motion is naturally removed from all violence, and is a certain act of the vegetative life <note>The most basic level of the soul responsible for growth and involuntary movement.</note> constantly exercising itself in that air, and from there generating a local motion in some way—namely, an action in a certain circle. This motion of the air, touching the denser parts of the head all around, produces a continuous sound with wonderful ease, yet so faint that it does not rouse our awareness, especially because we are always accustomed to it. Whenever we block our ears, however, that sound—previously diffused and able to dissipate—is compressed, grows stronger, reverberates, and is heard. Before, when it was not being heard, it did not confuse other sounds at all, nor did that motion interfere with the movements coming from outside; for it is both gentle and of a different kind <note>original: "specie"</note> than external motions.

->ON THEOPHRASTUS<-
<note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; this text is a commentary on his theories of perception.</note>

## PRISCIANUS.
<note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher.</note>

<margin>i</margin>
**A**mong these matters, Theophrastus asks whether sound requires some solid object at all, or whether it can also occur without a solid, as the sound of the winds seems to be. But in truth, these winds also resonate by striking the earth. Moreover, even the thunders themselves only occur when a spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; here referring to air or breath in motion.</note> is broken against a cloud as if against something solid. Furthermore, if air is innate to the sense of hearing, and hearing occurs whenever the external air touches this internal air by a pulsation—and since this internal air is also always in motion and always sounding—it follows that motion perceives motion, rather than sound itself perceiving sound. This remains true even if the air within, whether agitated or resonating, prevents sensation, as usually happens in other cases. But that innermost sound is not "sensible" in a simple way <note>Meaning it is not an object of perception that we are consciously aware of.</note>, which is why we do not perceive it as a sound unless we block our ears. Indeed, its motion is vital <note>Belonging to the life-force of the living being.</note>, and not like the motion of air that is beaten and struck from without. However, when the air that is innermost to us is affected by a striking, and has already received the very form of the sound, then indeed hearing occurs in actuality. Therefore, the prior sound, because it is not sensible, does not confuse the hearing. On the contrary, that vital motion not only does not hinder it, but even contributes to the sensing of the struck and broken air.

### Chapter 37. How in seeing, hearing, and smelling there is a medium between the object of sense and the sense organ.

## MARSILIUS.
<note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance Neoplatonist who translated and commented on these works.</note>

**I**t is well enough established that between a colored or luminous thing and the sight, there is some medium—that is, the transparent <note>original: "diaphanum"</note>—and a certain act or spiritual form <note>original: "speciem spiritalem"; an image or likeness of the object that lacks physical matter.</note> without which the sight would be offended and overwhelmed. Moreover, when we hear or smell things from a great distance, it is clear that they are sensed through a tempered medium. But when the broken air from a nearby sound-maker rushes into us, or a vapor flowing from nearby incense enters, does not the sensible nature itself finally touch the sense without a medium? Answer: as much as pertains to the material nature of the sensible object, if it glides into the instrument of sense, it either hinders the sense (if it enters too sharply) or it is not necessary for the sense at all, even if it flows in gently. But that which is both safe and necessary for sensation is not anything material, but rather a certain specific act, or a highly spiritual form of action, coming from the thing to be sensed to the instrument of the sense. The sense, however, senses in the same way it is moved; but it is moved not by the medium as such, but through such a medium by the sensible object. It does not, therefore, sense this medium—meaning this act or this form—but through these it senses the sensible object itself. That which properly moves the sense is the object that moves it through a medium of this kind.

## PRISCIANUS.

**A**nd even if the sound coming from external things penetrates all the way to the hearing, we have discovered that no sensation occurs when the sensible object touches the sense organ directly. For even in smelling, we draw in the odor by breathing. If that which is primary in us...

Regarding things that cannot be brought directly to the senses, if they are to be known by the senses, it is necessary that an "image of action" <term>species actionis</term> <note>A technical term in medieval and Renaissance philosophy referring to the likeness or power of an object as it travels through a medium to the sense organ.</note> be produced by them in the middle [the medium], and the instrument of the senses must be present. In what way it is so affected has been distinguished to the best of our ability in the preceding sections. 

Yet we do not perceive the medium, but the object itself which acts. The effect is not the same as the efficient cause, nor is the action the same as the agent; rather, the efficient cause acts according to the effect, and the "patient" <note>The 'patient' is the entity receiving the action, in this case, the sense organ.</note> receives from the agent, but according to the action proceeding from it, and it does not properly "suffer" from the affection itself. We perceive, therefore, not the action itself coming from the sensible object, but the sensible object itself, according to the action that proceeded from it. For this reason, we do not perceive the medium, but through a certain image of action produced in the medium, we perceive the object itself which produced it.

### Chapter 38. The nature of light is more excellent than the nature of sound.

->MARSILIO<-
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Florentine philosopher who translated and commented on these works.</note>

Sound itself, as a genus, is not properly said to be distinct from high pitch and low pitch <note>original: "acumine & grauitate"</note>, which are its "differences," or from high and low sounds, which are its "species"; for the genus itself is included within its species along with these differences, and it does not surpass them in reality, even if it might seem superior in some rational sense. Light, however, is properly said to be distinct from colors. Colors are neither the "differences" nor the "species" of light, but are certain participations, images, and effects of it; light itself surpasses such things in reality. And because of its causal excellence, light is no less necessary for establishing and declaring colors in nature than sound and any other genus are for their own differences and species.

->PRISCIAN<-

He <note>Aristotle</note> says that the differences of sounds, such as low and high, are revealed within sound in its actual state. He further suggests that just as colors are not seen without light, so neither are low and high pitches designated without sound—as if to say that light stands in a similar relation to colors as sound does to high and low pitch. Here, someone might perhaps contradict Aristotle. For it is not light, but color, that stands in a similar relation to white and black as sound does to high and low pitch. A response can be made on Aristotle's behalf: if these two are considered insofar as they belong to a genus, certainly color itself, as a genus, can be compared with sound as a genus in the present comparison, but light cannot. Nevertheless, because colors are not discerned without light, just as high and low pitch [are not discerned without sound]...

### Chapter thirty-nine: On the nature of taste and how it perceives.

->MARSILIUS FICINO<-

<margin>a</margin> Dry nourishment must be liquefied in the mouth so that it does not cause harm and may slide down more easily; for this reason, the instrument of taste [the tongue] should not be dry, nor entirely unfit for moistening, but very easily moistened. The tongue possesses a spongy nature so that it may be irrigated by the "drippings" <note>Referring to the Renaissance anatomical theory that fluids (catarrhs) flowed from the brain and upper organs to the lower ones.</note> of the stomach, lungs, and brain, and may drink up the liquids of the food. However, it was not appropriate for it to have a viscous moisture within itself, or at least not much of it. Otherwise, it would dull the sense, and it would not perceive the incoming liquid as being moist, since a moist thing does not alter another moist thing <note>This follows the Aristotelian principle that a sense organ must be in a state of "potentiality" or neutrality regarding the quality it perceives.</note>; yet it is necessary even here to perceive the moisture. For moisture pertains to touch, and taste is a certain kind of touch, or very close to touch. Therefore, nature did not give this organ a certain and manifest flavor of its own, lest the discrimination and judgment of flavors be confounded by this one taste; however, nature did give it a certain moisture so disposed and tempered that it is almost every flavor, and is most easily shaped by the flavors flowing into it.

->PRISCIANUS LYDUS<-

<margin>f</margin> But why indeed does Aristotle think that the instrument of taste ought neither to be moist, nor of such a kind that it cannot become moist, since (as he says) that which is to be tasted will be moist? Perhaps someone will respond with this very point: that which is "tastable" is not moisture simply, but moisture that is properly flavorful. It was necessary, therefore, for the instrument of taste not to have a flavored moisture within itself. Or rather, because taste perceives its own proper sensible object by a certain touch, it must not be affected by it as if by something merely "tastable," but also as something "tangible"; for which reason it is necessary that its instrument not be previously submerged in its own proper humidity.

### Chapter 40: On the instrument of taste and touch.

->MARSILIUS FICINO<-

<margin>s</margin> The soul <term>anima</term> is the source of life and sense; it delivers these two things first and more abundantly to the spirit <term>spiritus</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the "animal spirits," a thin, vaporous substance believed to act as the intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note> as if to something closer to itself. Through the spirit, indeed, it communicates them to the nerves and the flesh. Thus, the spirit is the primary instrument of the soul, both for imparting life and sense to the limbs, and for perceiving those things which come from external sources. It is necessary, however, that this instrument, if it is to be affected by the objects of sense, be affected very gently. For a more violent "passion" <note>In the sense of 'passio' or being acted upon by an external force.</note> both dissolves the spirit and occupies the soul and disturbs its judgment. Truly, the affection of the spirit is tempered in the cases of sight, hearing, and smell by distance and the medium of the air. But regarding taste and touch, where there is no such medium, how then is it tempered? By the tongue and the nervous flesh, which two things exist here as a kind of medium between the sensible object and the spirit, which is the primary instrument for sensing. Nevertheless, these two can also be called instruments insofar as they are participants in life and sense.

...they are. To the extent that they either temper the passion <note>In ancient and Renaissance philosophy, a "passion" is an impression or effect produced on the soul by an external object.</note> coming from the sensible object, the media are named. Remember that in these two senses [touch and taste], the act of sensing does not arise from a material nature flowing in from the sensible object, but from a certain special act of it and, moreover, from a sensory form <note>original: "specie sensuali"; the mental image or representation of the object perceived</note> resulting from the internal life, which completes the act of sensing.

->FROM PRISCIAN<-
<note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher whose commentary on Theophrastus was influential during the Renaissance.</note>

**P**roportionately, Aristotle—as Theophrastus also thought later—believes that neither the tongue is the true instrument <note>By "instrument," the author means the primary organ where the soul actually "meets" the sensation.</note> of taste, nor the flesh the true instrument of touch. Instead, he believes these two have a certain proportion or comparison to those things which act as "media" for us in seeing or hearing [such as air or water]. For indeed, in touch and taste, some medium is required, since a sensible object placed directly upon the sense never moves that sense; however, the medium in these cases is not external. For even when an external medium intervenes, taste or touch is not achieved through it alone, but rather together with it. This is like a shield: if a shield is placed in between, a stone does not strike through the shield in the same way that color moves the sight through the air; rather, the stone strikes the hand *together* with the shield, so that both are struck at once. Therefore, since the medium serving touch and taste is not external, it follows that it must be internal. This internal medium is, in a way, the flesh and the tongue. It is clear that the flesh "suffers" <note>original: "pati"; meaning it receives an impression or is acted upon.</note>. Furthermore, it is clear that it does not suffer in the same way as things that lack a soul. Therefore, it suffers vitally <note>meaning as a living, biological entity.</note>. And since the life of the flesh is sensory, it also suffers sensually. In what way, then, does it suffer thus, unless there is something in it that judges? For even if there is something else that is the more primary and perfect instrument of touch—such as the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; the subtle, vaporous substance believed to travel through the nerves to communicate between the soul and the body.</note> itself—the flesh itself is nonetheless sensory. It stands in the same relation here as the air does to sight, insofar as it is a medium close to the primary instrument. Because the flesh is not something added from the outside but is born as part of us, it is rightly a participant in the sense. Why then, if the flesh is sensitive, is it necessary to introduce another more primary instrument of touch? Clearly, it is because the flesh suffers too violently when a sensible object falls upon it from so close; the bitterness of the suffering would destroy the act of sensing. For this reason, Aristotle also judges that there is a medium in touch and taste. Since he establishes that this medium is innate to animals, he rightly concludes that this medium is of a vital and sensory nature.

### Chapter 41: The instrument of sense must be a medium between its sensible contraries, so that it possesses neither one nor the other, nor is a mixture of both.

If it were a mixture of both, it would similarly fail to discern mixed flavors and would confuse the extremes on both sides. <meta>Catchword: airy</meta>

...Furthermore, because it also participates in a life that contains within itself the formal principles <note>original: "rationes"; in this context, the conceptual patterns or "reasons" the soul uses to recognize things</note> of sensible objects, through which the judgment of those objects occurs. In the body there are accidents—namely its qualities and quantities—underlying which is the substance. The external sense perceives only these accidents. Substance, however, is perceived by "opinion"—that is, reason using the imagination, or imagination relying on reason.

<margin>FROM PRISCIAN</margin>
<note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who commented on the works of Aristotle and Theophrastus.</note>
**H**e [Aristotle] also rightly thinks that the instrument of sense must consist in a certain middle state <note>original: "medio"; a balanced mean or neutrality</note> between that opposition found in things that are to be sensed. In this middle ground, it is not mixed from the extremes; otherwise, it would have already suffered a change <note>original: "passum"; in ancient philosophy, to "suffer" or have a "passion" means to be physically altered by an external force</note>. But it is necessary that it not be changed, but rather act as a judge of these "passions" or impressions. For that which is already a mixture of extremes cannot be a judge of the midpoints, because "like" is not accustomed to be affected by "like" <note>This refers to the principle that a sense organ must be neutral (colorless, odorless) to accurately perceive its opposite</note>. He adds, furthermore, that the instrument of sense is indeed a body and a magnitude. However, it is not to be considered sensory because it has size, but rather through a certain formal principle and power. For this instrument consists in a certain proportion looking toward sensible things, and it is characterized by a certain judging form of life over bodies. Accordingly, since all sensible things are impressions or differences of bodies—for they are the qualities and quantities through which each whole is knowable—the sensory instrument also consists in these same things. It may indeed seem to someone that the entire body consists only in these impressions and differences. But in truth, the body is usually known not by sense alone, but rather by "opining reason" <note>original: "ratione opinatrice"; the faculty of the mind that forms beliefs or "opinions" about what the senses report</note>. For according to Plato, the body is known through opinion together with sense. Therefore, "opinion" perceives the corporeal essence.

### Chapter 42. Concerning the Number and Quality of the Senses.

<margin>FROM MARSILIO</margin>
<note>Likely Marsilio Ficino, the famous 15th-century Florentine philosopher who translated and commented on these Greek texts.</note>
**S**ince an animal is defined by the capacity for sensation, it follows (according to Aristotle) that man, as the most perfect animal, has as many senses as can be found in the entire genus of animals. Therefore, in the whole genus of animals, there are no more than the five senses which man possesses. Perhaps it is also probable that there are five categories of sensible things, if indeed whatever is sensible properly belongs to the body. Moreover, there are five elements in the nature of bodies: namely, the four [earth, water, air, fire] and the heavens. Aristotle further thinks that there is very little fire and even less earth within the instruments of the senses. But there is a great deal of air and water, so that these instruments can be called both airy and watery. Likewise, if something is tasted and touched through the tongue, whatever animals have a tongue possess taste in addition to touch. Again, if motion is known through sight, hearing, and touch, whatever animal possesses any of these will in some way know motion. Theophrastus adds that where it is said that an "airy nature" contributes to several senses, "nature" is not to be understood there in a simple way...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

...airy. On the contrary, it is by a certain formal property <note>original: "proprietate formali"; a specific defining characteristic belonging to the soul's nature</note> that the soul contributes to hearing, while with another property it contributes rather to smell.

### PRISCIAN'S COMMENTS
<note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher whose paraphrases of Theophrastus were translated and commented upon by Marsilio Ficino.</note>

Aristotle seems to have convinced himself that there are no more than five senses, primarily because all things are sensible to us. Tangible things are perceived by touch, but those perceived through a medium are detected because we possess the specific elements through which that medium is known. This medium is known through only two of the simple bodies: namely, air and water. Our sensory instruments are composed of only these two simple elements. For fire is either not present at all, or it is common to all the senses; nor is earth used, except insofar as anything detected by touch is mixed with it in some way. Furthermore, he maintains that if several sensible things become known through a single sensory instrument, then whoever possesses that instrument is sufficient for perceiving many things. But if the same thing is perceived through multiple instruments, he believes that whoever has either one of them is able to sense that same thing. 

Since Aristotle stated these things, Theophrastus consequently inquires into them. First, he asks on what basis it is confirmed that a sense is perfected only through these two—air and water. Is it because these alone happen to suit us, since our instruments are composed of them? Sight is attributed to water, and hearing to air; but smell might belong to either one. Next, he asks whether, if many things are known through the same medium, it follows that whoever has that medium necessarily knows all those things. For example, if odors and sounds are both perceived through the air, it does not necessarily follow that both are known through it by every creature; for not all animals that smell can also hear. Indeed, air does not immediately become capable of smelling and hearing simply because it is air—for the air in a person's throat, like a pipe, possesses neither sense. Rather, air becomes capable of sensing through a specific "ratio" <note>original: "rationem"; here meaning a functional proportion or organizing principle</note> rather than through its mere material. Therefore, it is necessary for the organ to possess a certain internal "ratio" for each type of sensing. Thus, one who does not possess the "ratio" for both will not sense both.

## Chapter 43. What the sensory instruments are like.

### MARSILIO'S COMMENTS
<note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Florentine priest and philosopher who translated this text.</note>

**AND** if in the other senses besides touch it is necessary that there be no quality formally similar to the objects—for there is no flavor in the sense of taste, nor any odor in the sense of smell—nevertheless, in the sense of touch, it is necessary for tactile qualities to be present. This is because the body is necessarily composed of these qualities. However, it will be sufficient if there is no "excellent" <note>original: "excellens"; meaning an extreme or overpowering degree of a quality</note> elemental quality in the nerve of touch that would prevent it from discerning a sensory quality it encounters. Therefore, the instrument of touch will be composed of the four elements. But water will exceed earth, and air will exceed fire; and finally, air will also surpass water, so that this instrument can be called "watery" in one sense, and "airy" in another. But no one would say that simple air is an instrument of sense for the sole reason that it is simple.

->PRISCIAN'S COMMENTS<-
<note>Priscian of Lydia was a 6th-century philosopher. His paraphrases of Theophrastus were a primary source for Marsilio Ficino’s understanding of ancient psychology.</note>

Theophrastus furthermore insists, doubting whether that Aristotelian view is perhaps less than true—namely, that the instruments of the senses are so simply "media" <note>intermediary substances like air or water</note> that they are not mixed from external elements. Instead, they should perhaps be defined by us according to the quality that prevails within them. Now indeed we say that heat is common to all things, and moisture is present in several. Furthermore, if we desire a sensory instrument that is entirely unmixed, it will follow directly that whatever is most unmixed is also most sensitive. If that were true, then anything separated from a living animal would be capable of sensing. Added to this is the fact that if a specific ratio <note>or "organizing principle"</note> is the cause of sensation—for sensation is lost where the ratio is dissolved—and since a ratio consists in the very mixing of several things, then surely any sensory instrument will be composed of several elements. Finally, why should senses exist from only two elements? For living consists more in heat, and sensation pertains to life.

### Chapter forty-four: on spirit, life, and sense.

# ON THE SOUL
<meta>The text discusses the hierarchy of light and the necessity of "tempering" elements to support life and sensation.</meta>

Heat prevails in the eye, but its nature is rather light-like, which is apparent from its transparency, its luster, and its ray. Now light is a certain species <note>original: "species"; here meaning a visible form or an image that carries information to the senses</note> among all sensible species that, above the rest, represents the intellectual species. Indeed, light exists in the intellect as a cause, in the heavens through fullness of form, and in fire through the fullness of participation; from there it is derived into smaller portions. That specific tempering of air and water is most suitable for all the senses. However, it is not the case that wherever this mixture exists, all the senses also exist—unless all the formal properties for perceiving all things are present in this temperament, and all the instruments of the senses are present in the body. It is probable, indeed, that all such properties and all instruments exist in the most perfect type of living being, which is the kind that possesses intellect in addition to sense; such is the nature of man. Life itself, since it is the mistress of corporeal generation and motion and an eminent form, does not sprout from a corporeal mixture but depends upon an incorporeal substance. Therefore, all the mundane spheres—both the celestial and the elemental—being the simplest among bodies and the primary members of the world, and thus closest to the life-giving substance, are the first to live in the same way; they are endowed with an exuberance of life and sense. But the portions of the elements separated from their universal wholes are mixed with foreign things and do not properly live unless they are tempered within some animated body. Thus, sensation exists in a simple body, not because it is a body, but because it is near to life; and in a mixture, not because it is mixed, but because it has been reduced to a harmony close to life. Sensation does not exist in portions separated from the elements because they possess neither simplicity nor harmony. Yet as long as they remain within their universal wholes, they are endowed with simplicity, life, and sensation.

# ON THE SOUL

...flees from boundaries, and drives out foreign limits. Air and water, on the contrary, since they are easily bounded by other things, deservedly and easily admit anything into themselves. They are affected for slight cause and are easily formed, which results in the instruments of the senses <note>the physical organs of perception</note> being in us from these two elements. 

How then is the instrument of sight considered among the Pythagoreans <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who often associated natural phenomena with numbers and elements</note> to be both fiery and solar? Clearly, it is because it is a vessel for light, both because of its thin, very shiny, and purest membranes, and because of the humors <note>the fluids within the eye</note>, transparent to the highest degree, which are enclosed by such little skins <note>original: "panniculis"; referring to the delicate layers or membranes of the eye</note>. For light is a fiery form <note>original: "species"; here meaning a visible image or quality</note>, not as if it were a fiery body, but as a certain form shared from fire. 

In these two elements [air and water] alone, therefore, is the medium for sense placed, because of their nature which is most easily formed and bounded. Hence, if several things are known through the same medium, the living being possessing that very thing will also know several things—provided that living being has been neither mutilated nor imperfect. Rightly, then, does Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> judge that through one and the same thing, several effects are produced according to reasons <note>original: "rationes"; meaning the underlying principles or proportions</note>, and according to different reasons directed toward several things. 

That which is truly perfect, however, must necessarily hold all reasons within itself if it is to be perfect. A perfect living being is one which, besides sense, is also a participant in higher sensory powers, just as man is also a participant in intellect. But animals that indeed smell, yet do not hear, are judged imperfect. And if heat is common to all, and moisture to some, the instruments of the senses are not for that reason to be judged as mixtures <note>complex compounds of elements</note>; for neither should external air or water be called mixtures on this account, just because they are the principles of heat. For as long as a substance does not change its essence, they remain simple. 

Even if they were proven to be mixed, the dominance is still held by those two elements which were mentioned. Moreover, even if they are simple, the "sensing" power is not to be called such simply because it is separated. Since they are sensitive not as simple things, but insofar as they are marked by a certain kind of life—if they were deprived of this life, they would also be deprived of sense. Unless, perhaps, I wish to think more in the Platonic way: namely, that those things which are truly simple possess sense most of all. Truly simple things, however, are those which remain in themselves and in their own proper wholes—or (if I may say so) in their "universalities," lest I be forced to say "totalities" <note>original: "totalitatibus"; a technical term for the state of being a complete whole</note>.

->OF PRISCIANUS<-
<note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher who wrote paraphrases of Aristotle and Theophrastus</note>

In what way then is reason the cause of sense? For reason seems to consist in a certain mixture of several things and in their mutual relationship or proportion; but even **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle’s successor in the Peripatetic school</note> solves this where he defines reason itself not in the mutual relationship of the elements, but in the proportion of the sensory instruments for sensing. But I think it more probable that Theophrastus does not primarily place sensory reason in any relationship or proportion, but in the **vital essence** and the judge of sensible things. And he defines the "dissolution" of reason in this way: insofar as the instrument becomes unfit to receive reason. He considers unsuitability to occur even when the thing to be sensed strikes the organ incongruously, and by this very incongruity, it dissolves the fitness which the instrument requires to receive reason. Therefore, if sense indeed pertains to life, and living is situated rather in heat, there will also be heat in the simple things that are within us according to their participation in life itself, arriving through a certain condition. But if the instruments of the senses are found to be mixed, mastery nonetheless is held, as we have said, through two elements alone <note>referring to air and water, mentioned on the previous page</note>.

### Chapter . 46 . Proper, common, and accidental sensibles.

->OF MARSILIUS<-
<note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century scholar who translated and commented on these works</note>

A **proper sensible** is that which is known by a single sense. Color by sight, sound by hearing, smell by scent, flavor by taste, heat by touch. A **common sensible** is that which is known by several: magnitude <note>size</note> indeed by sight and touch; motion, however, by sight, hearing, and touch. The proper sensible, because of its greater suitability with the sense, moves and is felt first; the common sensible second. Thus, you see honey as **yellow** first, and then as **large**. Hence, color is less deceptive at a distance than size. You do not see **sweetness**, however, unless perhaps you are said to see sweetness *by accident* <note>original: "per accidens"; perceiving a quality not directly through that sense, but by association—e.g., seeing the color of honey and "seeing" its sweetness</note>. For the eye is not moved by sweetness; it is moved, however, by the quality of color and the quantity <note>the size or extension</note> of the object.

<margin>In the path of generation</margin> The approach is not made from motion to form, but from the form of the agent, through motion, to the form in the patient <note>the "patient" is the entity receiving an action or sensation</note>. Therefore, in the path of knowledge, we do not perceive form through the knowledge of motion, but vice versa. 
<margin>The quality of a natural thing</margin> inflicts a greater passion <note>original: "passionem"; here meaning the impression or effect made upon a sense organ</note> upon the one sensing than quantity does, because it is more effective. Both quality and quantity are known by some greater passion of the sensing subject than is form—that is, the species, specimen, or character <note>original: "indoles"</note>. This character is something resulting from the proportion of colors and lineaments; it is neither the composite body itself, nor the composition itself, but is granted to the harmony of the composition as if it were some special and celestial gift. Because it arrives last, it is thought to stand far apart from the crudeness of matter, and it corresponds to the higher forms contained in the upper world <note>the divine or intelligible realm</note>. For that which is first to the informer <note>the soul or formative principle</note> is given last to the matter. Since violence pertains to material things, and a form of this kind stands furthest from matter among these things, the sense and its instrument exercise themselves more effectively in its presence, rather than being violently acted upon, as if strengthened like by like.

<margin>OF PRISCIAN.</margin>

Again, Aristotle shows that regarding the common sensibles <note>original: "communia sensibilia"; properties such as size, shape, motion, and number that can be perceived by more than one sense</note> no proper sense exists in us <note>i.e., there is no single organ dedicated exclusively to "size" the way the eye is to "color"</note>. Instead, we perceive common sensibles by motion, and for this reason, we recognize them through multiple senses—such as magnitude by sight and touch alike. 
<margin>Theophrastus says it seems absurd</margin> if one arrives at the notion of form through motion; he says this, I believe, because he does not distinguish how that ought to be understood. 
<margin>It is necessary therefore that we do not</margin> say that we know common sensibles by motion in such a way that we primarily sense motion and the rest only by chance or as a consequence. Rather, we should say that we sense all common sensibles similarly; but we must say that all these things are sensed entirely through motion—that is, we sense because we are changed <note>original: "permutemur"</note> in some way by them. 
<margin>But if sight is moved by</margin> magnitude, it does not sense it by accident <note>incidentally</note> as it does sweetness; for the sight is not affected, nor is the vision altered in any way by sweetness. But if magnitude also belonged to some specific sense, it would be sensed by the others by accident, as sweetness is. But now it is not so; rather, it presents itself to be sensed by moving the sense. There is, therefore, no sense proper to perceiving magnitude. Similarly, among other common sensibles, shape or form also moves the sense; but the passion <note>the physical impression</note> brought from here is less apparent. Instead, a certain action of the sense itself shines forth more strongly because of the nature of the form or shape, which is more specific than the others. Consequently, it moves the sense in us more specifically or more according to its stable action.

## ON THE SOUL

### MARSILIO.

That the five senses must be reduced to one common sense, and that this sense is indivisible, we have sufficiently proven in our theology along with Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, a philosophy that deeply influenced Ficino</note>. The common sense perceives the objects of the five senses, as well as their actions and their cessations <note>original: "vacationes"; the state of a sense being inactive, like hearing nothing in silence</note>. To this faculty properly belongs **attention**—that is, when we notice that we are seeing or hearing something. This is why it often happens that we see or hear things but do not perceive that we are sensing them, because the common sense and the imagination are meanwhile occupied with other things. Sight, hearing, and the rest are contained within this sense. But here, they are a single form and power. From here, however, just like lines drawn from a center to a circumference, the proper forms and powers of the senses are derived toward the five instruments <note>the physical organs like eyes and ears</note>. These forms differ from one another on the circumference (like the lines), but in the center, they are one. Therefore, the common sense is formally something different from the five senses that proceed from it. But as a power gathering them into one, it is the same. Insofar as this central faculty pays attention, it can in a way be said that "sight sees" and "hearing hears," and that sight and hearing then "notice" these things, because the common sense itself is, within itself, both sight and hearing. However, insofar as sight and hearing are separated from that center—with one flourishing in the eye and the other in the ear—the eye does not see itself seeing, nor does the ear hear itself hearing. For to turn back upon oneself and to double one's action <note>self-reflexive awareness</note> does not belong to powers located so far from their source and which are, for that reason, weak. Furthermore, if hearing could perceive its own action, it would also detect its own absence. Therefore, when placed in silence, it would sense that it is not sensing. It would thus be acting and not acting at the same time. Such a contradiction at the same time regarding the same object does not belong to a sense that is already divided at the extreme and utterly weakened. Instead, it belongs to the common form and faculty. Because this faculty turns back upon itself and acts even when the physical instrument is not being affected, it is rightly judged to be **separable from the body**.

### PRISCIAN.

Regarding those things in which we somehow sense that we are sensing, he <note>Theophrastus or Aristotle</note> walks the same path as Aristotle, concluding that a common sense exists there which judges in this way. This sense perceives the activity and the rest of each individual sense. For the same power perceives opposites <note>such as sound and silence, or white and black</note>. The common sense is neither the individual senses on their own, nor is it something entirely different from them. For it seems to be the apex of all of them, according to the collection of all the senses and their elevation into a single indivisible point. For this reason, each individual sense will also somehow perceive itself sensing—not by the logic of it being already divided, but by the logic of it being joined to the one common sense. Now, it is the property of a power separated from bodies to be able to turn back upon itself and to recognize itself. Each individual sense is more corporeal <note>physical/material</note> insofar as it is divided. It progresses, however, toward that faculty by which a thing distinguishes itself according to a certain indivisible vision relative to the other senses. For this indivisible union belongs to **species** <note>the mental images or forms of things perceived</note> that are separated from the body. But if, as he himself rightly thinks...

It is within the power of this same faculty to judge contrary things, and for that reason to perceive even when there is no active "business" <note>original: "negocium"; here meaning a physical stimulus or external object</note> being processed. In the same way, there will certainly be a state of "leisure" <note>original: "otium"; a state of rest or inactivity for the senses</note> where each individual sense is, in a way, separated from its physical instrument. Otherwise, sight would not be able to perceive darkness, since in that state the physical instrument <note>the eye</note> undergoes no sensation. Thus, sight seems to act even when the instrument is not being affected at all. This is even more true for the **common sense** itself, which perceives when the individual senses are at rest.

### Chapter 48: A Confirmation of the Superior Power. BY MARSILIO.

Numenius, Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus <note>These were all prominent Neoplatonic philosophers who argued that the soul exists independently of the body</note> believe that the **sensual soul** can be separated from the body, a point which the author also touches upon here. Priscian <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher</note> offers this conjecture for the present: that a single, indivisible soul possesses a most diverse faculty that acts all at once. I will set aside the function of "vegetation" <note>the vegetative soul, responsible for basic biological growth and nutrition</note> and speak instead of the one **imagination**, which imagines such different things simultaneously. Through this, the soul is turned back into itself, where it notices the actions of the senses. Through this faculty, it acts in a certain way without a bodily instrument, since it perceives darkness, silence, and the cessation of sensing. At such a time, the sense is not moved by the physical organ, and therefore it does not move the imagination; thus, the imagination then acts as if it were somewhat separated from the instrument. Therefore, this **common sense** flourishes in the soul as something eternal, according to its own form and power. When the bodily instruments are applied to it, it produces powers within them that were already flourishing within itself—distinct in their formal logic but not separated by physical location or by their own specific actions. Therefore, when the body fails, the senses do not entirely cease to be; rather, they simply cease to be "unfolded" or expressed. Remember these things as we have recounted them according to the Platonists.

## FROM PRISCIAN.

It is not, therefore, each individual sense that truly notices itself and its own action, but the **common sense** itself. For if any specific sense were to recognize its own action, it would also have to notice the lack of that action. If it recalls its own cessation, it would be resting and acting at the same time, as if it were sensing itself. Does it not, therefore, rest insofar as it is divided and individual? Yet meanwhile, it acts insofar as it remains free from its own specific action and cessation. For this reason, it acts according to the **common sense**, by which each individual sense also acts—not by the logic that makes them single and divided, but by the logic that makes them united through the single unity of all. The duty of this common sense is to comprehend the objects of all the senses toward the same end, even while it acts through principles that differ from one another. For this reason, the "judge" <note>the common sense acting as the evaluator of sensory input</note> remains one and indivisible in number, but it is considered divisible insofar as it carries out different functions.

However, it is said to "sound consonant" to the hearing if it is agreeable. We consider the efficacy and quality within the instrument of the sense; therefore, when the thing to be sensed <note>the "sensible" object</note> of efficacy...
