## PRISCIAN.

<gloss>p</gloss>ollowing this, where <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The famous Greek philosopher whose "De Anima" is the foundation for this text.</note> says that the voice is a "consonance" <note>a harmonious sounding-together</note>. It must be understood that this occurs where it is already active as something sensible, or placed in sensible action—namely, while it is already being heard. But it is heard when both the voice and the hearing are made into one through mutual accord, provided they are thoroughly tempered with one another. For an excessive intensity of the thing being sensed destroys or ruins the action of the senses; the sense itself exists through a certain <term>commensuration</term> <note>a state of being in exact proportion or "measured together."</note>. For this reason, we say that objects are "pleasant" when they are tempered to the senses. Ask yourself then: when the sense is doing nothing, is it placed in no commensuration within itself? Certainly, since a sense is not accustomed to acting within itself alone, but consists in a certain extension toward external things and in a certain relationship to things that are to be sensed. When it is at rest, it will not possess an active or effective commensuration within itself, but will only possess a commensuration according to its potential. For the power itself pre-existed and is considered in itself. But let us proceed to the things that follow next, starting now from another principle, to treat the remaining matters pertaining to the book.

The interpretation of the philosopher <term>Priscian</term> <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher who wrote a commentary on Theophrastus.</note> the Lydian on the book of <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note> regarding <term>phantasy</term> <note>The mental faculty of imagination or the ability to form mental images.</note> and the intellect, translated by <term>Marsilio Ficino</term> <note>A central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated many Greek philosophical works into Latin.</note> the Platonist and explained by the same man chapter by chapter.

## Chapter one.

<gloss>i</gloss>n sense and imagination, there are innate "reasons" <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning internal principles or templates that allow the mind to recognize things.</note> that resemble sensible objects. In the senses, these are provoked into action by the "passions" <note>the physical impressions or experiences</note> of the sensory instrument. In the imagination, however, they are provoked by the actions of the senses. <term>Phantasy</term>, being the middle ground between sense and reason, is a certain action within the sense. <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who emphasized the soul's role in mediating between the divine and the physical.</note> says regarding phantasy: phantasy is born along with all the powers of the soul. It shapes everything within itself, and translates forms from some powers into others; it emulates the acts of all powers. Phantasy does not receive forms from external things, but brings them forth from within itself.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS.

### BY PRISCIAN.

<note>Capital initials for the start of major sections (P, I, V) were intended for illumination or rubrics and were not printed.</note>
**P**hantasia <note>often translated as "imagination," though in this Neoplatonic context it refers more broadly to the faculty that creates and stores mental images</note>, which Theophrastus discusses next, following **Aristotle**, must be admitted from his books to be a power distinct from the senses. Furthermore, it differs from opinion and every kind of rational perception. Moreover, just as the sense is moved in a vital way by <term>sensible species</term> <note>the "forms" or "mental images" of physical objects received through the senses</note> and acts upon them according to the production of its own internal proportions, so too is **Phantasia** stirred by these sensible forms. It uses them as its immediate subjects and acts upon them; for this reason, this too is a "corporeal life" and does not act without physical instruments. This is because the sensible forms that move it are perfected from those impressions that appear in the instruments of the senses.

However, the following doctrines of **Iamblichus** <note>a hugely influential Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who integrated Greek philosophy with mystical theology</note> should be added to these: **Phantasia** is innate to all the powers of the soul; it figures them all and molds the likenesses of forms and appearances, and it transmits the "visions" or impressions of some powers into others. Those that flash from the senses, it stirs up in opinion; those that come from the intellect, it offers in a secondary place to opinion. It receives images from all sources into itself, and through its own nature, it is characterized by its ability to create likenesses—both in acting and in receiving. These likenesses appear in the activities of the intellect, in the processes of <term>generation</term> <note>the physical world of birth, change, and death</note>, or in the middle ground between both.

Indeed, this faculty shapes and expresses all the actions of the soul. It accommodates external things to internal ones, and it imposes the impressions descending from the intellect onto the "stains" or traces extended through the body. Since **Phantasia** is, by its very nature, the power of making other things like itself, it is deservedly joined to the other powers, preceding them and providing the starting points for their actions. It is neither a passive "passion" nor a mere motion, but an *unaffected* and definite action. It is not molded by receiving things from the outside like wax; rather, it is awakened from within according to the production of its "assimilative proportions" <note>its internal capacity to create representations</note> to provide a sign for the phantasms <note>mental images</note>. These are the words of **Iamblichus**.

-> Chapter Two. <-

### BY MARSILIO.

**I**magination shapes the actions of reason under the condition of sensible things, and it can bring forth "phantasms" more broadly than the acts of the senses can. Imagination agrees with the senses because it perceives particulars. It surpasses the senses because it produces images even when nothing is moving it. Imagination is like **Proteus** <note>the shape-shifting sea god of myth</note> or a **chameleon**.

**B**ut if it expresses other "lives," as found in **Iamblichus**, and if it shapes intellectual and rational actions themselves, how can that **Aristotelian** principle still be true—namely, that **Phantasia** is stirred by sensible forms? Perhaps, even if it performs all the more excellent actions...

# ON PHANTASIA AND THE INTELLECT

...images, and it shapes them; at the same time, however, it imagines according to <term>sensory species</term> <note>original: "species sensuales"; the mental forms or "fingerprints" of objects received through the senses</note> and assimilates them through a certain formative condition. It is broken and fashioned in a divisible way according to a certain relation to sensible things. For this reason, it shapes more excellent actions by the same logic with which it is stirred by sensory species. 

In what way, then, is **Phantasia** moved even when the sensible objects are not present? For even if it is moved by sensibles, these movements are produced into action when the sensibles are present, or they fail when they are absent. Perhaps it is not the case that phantasia is always moved only when sensibles are present, in the way that the sense usually is. Instead, after it has been moved once, it can now awaken by itself and bring forth "phantasms" <note>mental images or representations</note> according to a certain relation to the species that first moved it. 

Sometimes, however, it must be moved not just once or twice, but even more often, for this very purpose: so that it may offer up within itself things similar to the original movers. Now, this faculty perhaps communicates with the sense through its formative, shapeable, and divisible nature; yet, by the power through which it brings forth phantasms from itself—even if no external movers are any longer present—it surpasses the sense. Again, because it always refers its own condition to other things and is assimilated to different actions of the soul, it is truly innate to all the powers of the soul. It is judged to be a "defining" power according to the soul's ability to assimilate or be assimilated.

## Chapter Three. BY MARSILIO.

Just as in the same substance of the soul, **sense** and **imagination** are formally different, so the same substance of the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; the subtle, vaporous substance that medieval and Renaissance thinkers believed acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note> acts as the instrument for both imagination and sense according to different qualities. Likewise, from the actions of sense and imagination, certain "marks" representing them are impressed upon the spirit. 

Imagination holds sensory species as its objects, to which it refers innate rational principles. If the motions of reason and imagination produce manifest signs in the <term>humors</term> <note>the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, bile) thought to govern health and temperament</note> and the solid body, how much more so do they do so in the spirit? Through these marks, note how <term>demons</term> <note>original: "demones"; in this Neoplatonic context, these are "daemons" or intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil, who were thought to be able to perceive the physical traces of human thoughts</note> grasp the thoughts of men. Regarding the same object, the sense can be truthful while the imagination is lying, and vice-versa. Once awakened, the imagination can proceed further even while the sense is at rest.

## BY PRISCIAN.

Meanwhile, **Theophrastus** asks in what faculty **Phantasia** should chiefly be placed. For it should not be placed in the sensitive power itself, since even when the sense is truthful, phantasia itself sometimes lies. Nor, again, should it be placed in the physical instrument of the senses. For a "passion" <note>an impression or physical effect</note> produced in the instrument occurs only when a sensible object is actually present. 

However, "phantasms" or "imaginings" (for one may interpret *phantasia* as imagination)—phantasms, I say, occur even when the sensible object is absent. I assert, therefore, that **Phantasia** is a power other than sense, but very close to sense; for that reason, it is moved in a certain way by the sense, and in some way uses sensory species as its underlying subjects. From these it is awakened, and toward which [it directs its] phantasms...

...reports phantasms. And yet it varies these phantasms in many ways because it surpasses the sense; and from itself, after it has been moved once toward formation, it searches out whatever it has begun. I believe, moreover, that the indications or impressions of <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the formal mental images or "blueprints" of objects</note> and of phantasy emerging within their boundaries can be received by the instrument of sensing. This is just as formal and divisible figures testify, which do not indicate something separate from bodies. Often, indeed, while the body is moved toward phantasms and is affected according to them, I believe phantasms appear in the instrument itself, but not as if in a sensory way.

This is because they do not fall upon us from external things, nor are we changed as if by some finite bodies acting upon us; rather, it is as if we are in something receiving phantastic species. Nor should this seem strange, since certain indications and marks of our rational action also descend into the body. This is clearly seen when the eyes and eyebrows are contracted during sharper investigations. Now, if these solid members of the body are affected according to the movements of the soul, it is even more necessary that the instrument of the senses—being more vital—receive certain traces of life. In those things where life is only sensory, the instrument is also only sensory. But in those where phantastic and appetitive life, or even rational life exists, the instrument is similarly suited to receive that kind of life.

Therefore, it will receive phantastic marks as a phantastic instrument, even false ones if the phantasies are false. And just as we sometimes perceive true things, we can nonetheless simultaneously produce false imaginations. Consequently, just as we feel, the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; in Renaissance medicine and philosophy, this is a subtle, vaporous substance that acts as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note> itself receives true marks from the sensory powers; but insofar as it is phantastic, it receives false marks from the senses, and true ones from the phantasy. 

This is like when we see the sun as being a foot wide, while meanwhile we imagine it to be much larger than the earth, compelled by geometric demonstration. Nor, however, is there any sense of the phantasm itself within us, even though the phantasm exists in the instrument of sense; for sense properly pertains to sensible objects and depends on them. 

Phantasms, however, emerge from the phantasy. Hence, it is not impossible for the underlying spirit to receive true and false appearances of the same things simultaneously, as happens to us, as we said, regarding the sun. This is because it receives them from different powers and according to different forms of life; nor does anything prohibit a phantasm and the act of sensing from occurring together in the same thing, even if they are opposites, seeing as they are not of the same order or combination, nor are they works of the same power. Since indeed opinion and sense regarding the size of the sun are opposed to one another in the same subject. 

To this, therefore, a response is made by reason; moreover, it has been said that the presence of sensible things is not always necessary for the phantasy (that is, the imagination) to be moved. But after it has once been awakened and is now striving in the birth of such a form, it is sufficient unto itself. Let us proceed to the rest.

# ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

Our intellect is something belonging to the soul itself, and a certain <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning a formal mental image or the "blueprint" of a thing</note>, and is intellect in act. Through its own essence, it contains within itself all the species of things that can be understood; but because it has declined from the First [Intellect], it therefore requires the nourishment of the First for three things. First, so that it may be most clear-sighted. Second, so that its species may be most bright. Third, so that it may be most united with them. Sensation also is a certain species, and according to its essence it contains the <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; the underlying patterns or logical structures</note> of sensible things, which it brings forth when sensible objects move its instrument. The intellect of the soul, because of the nature of the soul declining toward things that are divisible and changeable, is far removed from the unity and state of the First Intellect and of the first objects of understanding. <margin>Note here that everywhere he means the "active intellect" acting upon ours is the First Intellect.</margin> These things are similar to those in Plato’s *Republic*, where the light of the Good itself joins the intelligible species with the intellects. There are those who write letters on paper with onion juice, but these are not seen unless the paper is heated. The so-called <term>possible intellect</term> <note>original: "possibilis intellectus"; the part of the mind that has the potential to receive and hold forms</note> holds the forms of things in such a way; they come into view by the presence of the divine fire, just as colors [appear] by the light of the sun. Our intellect is not in <term>potency</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to become something</note> for the purpose of becoming intellect and the things understood, but for the ultimate perfection of understanding and of the things understood.

**THEOPHRASTUS**, where the discussion concerning the intellect follows after this, says: "It must not be taken by us quite in that way, nor by the same logic. For it would be contentious to take these things so simply—namely, that the intellect is a certain potency entirely subject [to change] in the way material potencies usually are." And proceeding a little further, he adds: "Perhaps it will appear absurd if the intellect has the nature of matter in such a way that it is nothing, but only the potential for all things. It should not, therefore, be explained this way, nor should this be accepted similarly concerning every intellect. But a distinction must be used; what kind is it then, and what is the distinction? Matter indeed is not 'a this' <note>original: "hoc aliquid"; a specific, individual thing or substance</note>, but if the intellect is not 'a this,' what else will be 'a this'?" Thus far the words of Theophrastus.

**W**hen <note>The OCR shows "Vando," likely a decorative initial "Q" for "Quando" (When).</note> therefore the intellect is compared with nature, it must be understood according to a certain comparison of proportion. And insofar as one intellect is in a certain potency relative to another—for thus the intellect of the soul is related to that which is always intellect in act and separate—it is rightly said to be all things in potency. Even sensation is said to be matter, or like matter, not properly but by a certain metaphor. For matter is thought of as the last of things; however, sensation is not the last like the matter of all things. For sensation is a certain species, and it is said to contain the rational principles of sensible things according to its essence. Moreover, for another reason, sensation is said to be sensible things in potency, insofar as it is incited by them to perceive, and it needs them to be both present and acting upon its instrument for its own action. But the intellect of the soul is neither like matter nor like sensation; for it is the species of all those species, being the grasper [of them] according to its own essence. It also acts from itself, and indeed contains the intelligible things within itself, although through [their] kinship to it...

[conjoined] with the soul, and because of its essential relationship to the soul, and finally because of its certain inclination toward what is divisible <note>referring to the physical world, which can be broken into parts, unlike the indivisible realm of pure thought</note>. For these reasons, it has, in a sense, fallen away from that intellectual essence and action which is entirely indivisible and completely unified. Meanwhile, the <term>intelligible things</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; the pure concepts or forms that the mind grasps</note> within it seem to have degenerated from that substance which is super-radiant, self-illuminating, and the primary source of all intelligible things. In the same way, the connection between the soul's intellect and its intelligible objects has been somewhat loosened; it is no longer entirely intact, unlike that unity which thrives constantly in the <term>separate intellect</term> <note>original: "separato intellectu"; the higher, divine Mind that exists apart from the human body</note>.

For this reason, the soul's intellect requires a "perfecter"—the intellect that is always in act <note>the Active Intellect</note>—to achieve a cognitive state that is entirely indivisible. Likewise, the intelligible forms within it require the illumination that shines forth from the separate intelligibles, so that these too may become perfected objects of thought. Hence, Aristotle says these intelligible objects are like colors that require the brilliance of the sun. The contact between this intellect and its objects is joined into an indivisible whole by the most precise unity of the higher intellect and its objects. 

For this reason, the soul's intellect is said to be "in potentiality," insofar as it relates to the separate intellect. This is because the higher intellect is entirely indivisible and is a pure unity with the most excellent, primary, and perfect lights of understanding. It is also called "in potentiality" insofar as it is perfected by such an intellect. 

Therefore, when the intellect is described as being like a tablet devoid of writing <note>original: "tabella litterarum expers"; the famous "blank slate" or *tabula rasa* metaphor</note>, this should be understood as a proportional comparison. This is not said as if the intellect has no <term>species</term> <note>mental forms or blueprints</note> at all. Rather, just as the intellect itself is "in potentiality"—not in the sense that it is not an intellect at all, but that it is the kind of intellect that must be perfected by the First Intellect—so too the intelligible forms placed within it are indeed intelligible, but they are the sort that must be illuminated by the separate forms to become purely understood. This is why they are compared to colors; and the "tablet" itself is said to be empty of writing only in respect to receiving those perfected forms. 

Rightly, therefore, Theophrastus exclaims that it is absurd to give a material nature to the intellect. He prevents us from interpreting the texts to mean that the intellect is nothing in "act" <note>actually existing or functioning</note> but everything in "potentiality," like matter is. He commands us instead to investigate in what other way the intellect may be said to be "in potentiality." Truly, we have now sufficiently explained how it is said to be in potentiality for our present purposes; we have also distinguished that not every intellect is in potentiality, but only one of a specific kind.

# ON PHANTASY AND THE INTELLECT

[The intellect] is turned, and to that extent it turns toward the primary intellect and its <term>forms</term> <note>original: "species"; the mental patterns or archetypes of things</note>. Note here and below that our intellect is always coupled with the divine. The sense itself, however, for the sake of such formations, leads forth into act from within itself the forms or actions that conform to those external things. When we say that the <term>possible intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectum possibilem"; the mind's capacity to receive and store knowledge</note> is formed by the <term>agent</term> <note>original: "ab agente"; the Active Intellect that illuminates the mind</note>, we do not mean that it receives forms from the outside, but that in the presence of that agent, it uses its own forms more effectively and more closely. In the possible intellect, there is no motion and no <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passio"; in this philosophical context, it refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing change by an external force</note> in the proper sense of the word.

### PRISCIANUS

After these points, Theophrastus wonders how either our intellect becomes <term>intelligible things</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; the abstract concepts or truths that the mind grasps</note>, or how those intelligible things themselves are made, and what it means to "suffer" or be acted upon in that process. For it is necessary that the mind itself, in a certain way, both becomes the intelligible things and undergoes a certain "passion" there, if indeed the intellect proceeds into action in the same way the senses do. Nevertheless, it remains ambiguous what kind of "passion" could be transferred from a corporeal nature into an incorporeal thing, or what change occurs between them, and whether the starting point is given by that external object or rather by the mind itself. It does indeed seem to "suffer" from that object, for of all things that are acted upon, none is acted upon by itself. Yet now, it is also fitting for this mind to be the principle of all things, and it is appropriate for it to understand from within itself; nor is "knowing from itself" attributed to the mind in the same way as it is to the senses, but in a certain more excellent manner. Thus far the words of Theophrastus.

Yet, meanwhile, the intelligible things [remain] here; nor is the thing itself like an intellect that is entirely separate, because its unity has been somewhat loosened, as we have said. And it is more fully adapted to the intelligible things. For this reason, it "suffers" in a sense when it has fallen away from that pure and altogether indivisible and separate union of intelligible things. It is as if it has departed from that state because it was born together with the soul, being surely one thing distinct from others. It is perfected both by that intellect which is "in act" <note>the fully active, thinking mind that is currently engaged in thought</note> and by the intelligible forms that exist within it. Nevertheless, the mind also perfects itself, insofar as it awakens from within itself and accommodates itself to that intellectual act, receiving perfection from that action through its own power. This is especially true because it has not entirely withdrawn from that intellect which is in act; rather, although yielding to it, it remains joined to it, as something that is itself also an intellect. Therefore, it is not distracted by external things, but having entered into itself and turned toward itself, it is joined to itself as much as its power allows. Thus, finally, by that very intellect in act...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

[The intellect] is perfected by the intellect. For this reason, it undergoes <term>passion</term> <note>original: "patitur"; in this philosophical context, "passion" or "suffering" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force, the opposite of "action."</note> in a different way than the senses do. Indeed, it does not do so in the strict sense, but equivocally; rather, it acts more than it is acted upon, because it receives perfections from higher things through its own action, and does not receive the things it understands from the outside. For here the thing itself exists in a second degree, insofar as the intellect is perfected while it is coupled with its own <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibilibus"; the abstract objects or truths that the mind can grasp, as opposed to physical objects</note> and is simultaneously adapted to higher things, because its own objects are not severed from those higher ones.

Hence, intelligible things act upon the intellect just as <term>sensible things</term> <note>original: "sensibilia"; things perceived through the five senses</note> act upon the sense, with this exception: that the intelligibles do not come from the outside to act. Since they are not separate from the intellect, there is a single action for both: for the intellect regarding the intelligibles, and for the intelligibles toward the intellect, insofar as these are not merely joined together, but the intellect *is* those very things which are offered to be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the sense, "passion" happens to the physical organ. Since the primary sensing power is perfected according to its own action, it does not receive movement from sensible things passively, but actively. Therefore, the intellect acts much more from itself, and receives perfection from the things to be understood not by passion but by action—if indeed it should be said to "receive" at all, and not rather to produce from itself. For beginning from itself, it is perfected. 

Now, "passion" properly happens to those things moved by another, such as those incited from the outside. But in things that operate entirely from within and are active through and through, we cannot suspect any "passion" unless perhaps we use the word "passion" in an equivocal sense. For the intellect—even that which is called the **potential intellect**—is indeed an **act** according to its **essence**, though in a certain second degree. This act is therefore opposed to passion, and it can never be affected passively.

In general, regarding incorporeal things that are separate or separable from the body, **Theophrastus** says that neither passion nor change can happen to them. He says that passions usually come from external things, whereas the intellect is a principle and, moreover, exists from itself. Therefore, it can have the appearance of a "passive" thing, although in truth it is not passive at all. For if one excluded all passion, he says, the intellect would be nothing. In this case, he certainly calls the perfection conferred by the intelligibles "passion," because he thinks it necessary to keep the intellect entirely pure. 

Meanwhile, because the intellect is perfected by the intelligibles according to its own action, he uses the word "passion" here not in its proper sense, but in a more common way. For the intellect (as Theophrastus says) is devoid of passion, unless perhaps it is called "passive" in a way different from common usage. Not indeed as something movable—for motion is "imperfect" action—but rather as a complete action. These two differ from each other, even if it is sometimes necessary to use the same names for them. These are the words of Theophrastus.

You see, therefore, that "passion" is accepted in the intellect not according to some defect, transformation, or movement, nor even from external things, but rather according to a certain action belonging to the intellect. He thinks it must be forgiven again

But Theophrastus commands us to define what "passion" <note>original: "passio"; in this philosophical context, being acted upon or receiving an impression from an external source.</note> is in the mind. And according to his opinion, it is said here that "to suffer" <note>original: "pati"; to be the recipient of an action.</note> is to receive a certain perfection from a higher source, while that which is lower is perfected by its own action from that source. Thus, the <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibile"; an object of thought rather than of sense.</note> is in some way acted upon by the intelligible, since it is like a secondary and effective intelligible in the second place; and as something beginning and obtaining a certain primacy, it is shaped by its own action from that which is more excellent. Yet in some way this intellect perfects itself. For, as has been said, it receives the gifts of the superior through its own specific action.

### Chapter six.

->MARSILIO<-
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated and commented on Plato and Neoplatonists.</note>

There is a twofold intellect in the soul, and both are called "possible." The first is an individual essence <term>participated</term> <note>original: "participata"; the Neoplatonic idea that a lower thing shares in or derives its nature from a higher thing.</note> by the soul. The second is a power that moves through reason, which is properly called the "soul." The former always understands in <term>act</term> <note>original: "actu"; actually or currently performing its function, as opposed to being in a state of potential.</note>, having been formed by the divine mind. The latter understands when it is turned toward the former. But it ceases when it is turned away from there toward the senses. In both, the act is one's own and is free. Sometimes the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty of forming mental images.</note> is named "intellect"; for this is the final trace of intelligence. The rational soul, because it is a particular life, acts by turns upon different things. At times it is turned toward divine things, at other times toward falling <note>original: "caduca"; fleeting, transitory, or earthly things.</note> things. <term>Free will</term> <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note> exists in the intellect, both the intellectual and the rational. The intellect—whether intellectual or rational, both of which are within us—begins its act from itself, nor does it have anything prior to it; that is, in terms of time. For if something had recently moved our intellect (which would otherwise be sluggish on its own), two absurdities would follow: first, something would be prior to this in time; second, it would not have its own proper action.

->PRISCIANUS<-
<note>Priscianus of Lydia (6th century AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on Theophrastus.</note>

Following this, it is asked why our intellect does not always receive from the higher intellect, nor does it always seem to understand. But certainly the intellect is always acting. Yet the soul does not always use the intellect, even though it is always present to it, because the soul is clearly turned toward bodies. Indeed, Aristotle and Theophrastus (as has already been said) seem at times to call the whole rational life "intellect" throughout one's entire life, where they extend the name of "intellect" even to the imagination. And so, not without reason, one might ask regarding the soul why it does not always understand. Surely intelligence is never interrupted because the power of understanding is lacking; rather, it is because the soul is distracted toward subsequent things, corporeal things, and things entirely outside itself, due to the condition of a particular life that acts by turns toward both. For the entire perfection of the soul consists in a clear return to itself and a conversion toward the intellect. Conversely, a fall from the intellect occurs through an inclination toward bodies. Nor indeed only the intellect...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS
<margin>Catchword: intellect</margin>

As we have said, but moreover, the soul is perfected by itself, insofar as it originates some act from itself, applies itself to the intellect, and by its own action grasps perfection from the intellect. Since Theophrastus says that the action of the intellect itself is incited by another mover. Otherwise, it is absurd, and it is nothing other than introducing something else prior to the intellect. Likewise, there will not be an act or faculty of understanding in it in this way, unless there is someone else who moves the intellect; and these things are indeed true, whether he calls the intellect an individual essence which is <term>participated</term> <note>original: "participatur"; the Neoplatonic concept where a lower entity shares in the nature of a higher one without diminishing the source.</note> by the soul, or the rational soul itself.

### Chapter seven. MARSILIO'S.

**I**n our intellect, there are <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; things that can be understood by the mind, as opposed to "sensibilia," things perceived by the senses.</note> in the form of things known by reason, which are innate to us. But that [higher intellect] acts concerning those things by a certain eternal act; this [rational soul] acts concerning its own through a temporal action by means of the same action of the intellect, namely, through intelligence. In that state, it is most especially the intellect, and the intelligibles are most especially intelligibles, and vice versa. Therefore, the intellect is the very things understood. Our intellect also, according to its <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentiam"; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</note>, is act. Therefore, in it, being is the same as acting; for that reason, it always understands. But in the soul—that is, in the rational power—essence is one thing and action is another. Therefore, it does not always understand, and it does not always know. Just as our intellect is the intelligibles, so the rational power is the things to be known, although it does not have these always in act, as the higher intellect does. Reason brings the things to be known into act through its own action, when the essence of the soul returns into itself. Where the soul is most individual, it is intellect, and to "be" there is to understand; where it is no less individual, it has an annexed action of reasoning distinct from its essence, as well as the power of <term>discursive thought</term> <note>original: "discurrendi"; the process of the mind moving from one idea to another to reach a conclusion, rather than grasping truth instantly.</note>. The essence of the soul is both stable and mobile, and similarly its action. Stable action accompanies stable essence, and mobile action accompanies the mobile. The whole soul remains and is moved at the same time; likewise, the mobile power revolves around the stable one. Likewise, in the permanent essence of the soul, a certain eternal action lies hidden. The attention of the soul is mostly turned toward things of the imagination and senses; but when it returns into itself, it finds things to be known in the rational power, through which it is finally joined to the intelligibles, which always flourish in the intellect, even in the soul of a living being. The rational power, having returned to the intellect, does not act concerning all things at once, but by a certain succession because of its divisible nature.

For if, he says, the intellect in acting becomes the things themselves—and this is most true of both—then certainly the thing itself will be the intellect. # ON FANTASY AND THE INTELLECT

The objects of the intellect are most fully present when the intellect understands. For this reason, he says both: if when the object itself exists, then the intellect also exists, surely the intellect will be the very things that are understood. Therefore, when it understands nothing, since the object is not there, will the intellect likewise not exist? But indeed that which is truly the intellect—and even that which is called the <term>intellect in potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia dicitur intellectus"; the capacity of the mind to understand before it actually does so.</note>, namely that which is <term>participated</term> <note>original: "participatus"; a Neoplatonic term for a lower soul sharing in the nature of a higher divine Intellect.</note> by the soul—certainly understands, seeing as it is itself an <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; the state of being active or fully realized, as opposed to "potentia."</note> by its own essence, albeit at a second degree. However, in the individual soul itself, there is room for doubt, for this soul does not always understand.

But is the soul nothing at all before it understands? Or is it something indeed, but like a kind of matter, which is formed when it knows things falling upon it from the outside? But truly the soul itself is something before it knows, and it begins not from external things, but rather from itself. It produces the things that are to be known—things it finds within itself—insofar as it enters into itself. Therefore, the soul is itself the things within it before it knows them. Since, however, the soul is in a way divided by this reasoning—because it is clearly not an act by its essence, but possesses an act of knowledge proceeding from its essence—it follows that just as it exists even when it does not know something in act, so too the things themselves exist within it, namely not according to act and action, but rather through essence. For one must take the things in the soul in exactly the same order as the soul itself. This is not because they are always being understood, but because the mind acts in a way that is capable of knowing, and these objects of knowledge are produced according to an action following and proceeding from the essence.

Indeed, in the soul, neither being nor acting is simple and uniform. But this part is permanent, while that part is mobile, while a mobile power proceeds around the permanent power; and meanwhile the whole soul is weighed according to both, and therefore the soul simultaneously remains and is moved. At the same time, it also always acts according to a hidden action innate to its permanent essence, and according to a life that progresses outward and is changeable, when it turns entirely toward sequential and divisible things and works upon them. Then it uses opinion along with sense, and is not turned toward those things which (if I may say so) are called <term>knowables</term> <note>original: "scibilia"; things that can be known through reason or science.</note>. These things are indeed within the soul, and even less is it turned then toward those called <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; the highest truths perceived by the pure mind.</note>, to which it is joined through those very knowables as if by a single continuum or marriage.

Now, however, when it recalls its action—which had been produced and at some time had gone forth—back to those things that remain within its life, it does not act upon everything at once, but now upon these, then upon those, clearly on account of its divisible nature.

## Chapter Eight. [By] MARSILIO.

The **rational power** is said to proceed from <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity or possibility for something to happen or be known.</note> into <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "actu"; the state of being fully realized or active.</note>, not because it receives new forms (for it always possesses all of them), but because it now exercises those which it did not exercise before. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle; Ficino is commenting on his views via the later philosopher Priscianus Lydus.</note> says that if the intellect were like <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"; here meaning a "blank slate" or raw material that has no shape of its own until something else acts upon it.</note> simply in potentiality, it would undergo a certain essential change whenever it understands by receiving new <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formas"; the essential structures or concepts of things.</note>. This is absurd. Theophrastus says this regarding our "intellectual" intellect. Priscianus extends this also in a way to the rational intellect; therefore, that intellect neither receives new forms, nor is it moved in its essence here; it does not indeed receive new ones, but it is moved around the forms it already possesses.

### [By] PRISCIANUS.

Therefore, when we say things are in the soul "in potentiality" and "in actuality," we understand this according to a transformation, or certainly when that proceeding action is not present. When knowledge is possessed, we say that the permanent essence is the producer of such action in potentiality; this essence exists even then as the things themselves, yet it does not act according to a "proceeding" or outward action. Therefore, although the soul does not know all things at once, but rather some at one time and others at another, it is not for that reason one thing now and another thing then. Nor is it ever anything other than the same, since it is not changed in every respect, but there is also something in the soul meanwhile that is permanent; and according to this very permanence, the things themselves have always remained in the soul. 

Theophrastus says it would be absurd if the intellect were in potentiality in such a way that it exists as nothing in actuality, but when placed in actuality, it became some other thing—and yet another thing again when it does not understand itself. For in that case, because it understands one thing and then another, it would never be the same. Indeed, a nature of this kind—becoming indistinct and devoid of order—clearly refutes those who think the intellect is all things in potentiality but nothing in actuality. First, indeed, when it does not understand, it would be nothing. Then, even if it understands, when it understands other things and does not understand itself, it would be something else and not entirely the same, but different at different times, and so it would be perpetually changed. Wherefore he says that potentiality and actuality must not be understood in the intellect in that material way, but (as was said before) where he judged that these two must be positioned according to a certain comparative proportion. In no way are these to be affirmed in the intellect in the same way they are in matter.

<header>ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT</header>

## ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

The rational nature includes the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formas"; the essential blueprints or archetypes of things.</note> of all knowable things within the formal principle of its own essence. Although the soul moves from <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to know something.</note> into <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "actum"; the state of actively thinking or knowing.</note>, it does not thereby become something else, because it does not take on a new form, but rather displays a new action.

->PRISCIANUS<-
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century philosopher who wrote a commentary on Theophrastus's work "On the Soul."</note>

Accordingly, when Aristotle or Theophrastus says that the intellect is "this particular thing," he adds a qualification: that the senses are not equal to it in this regard. For the sense, as he points out now, does not exist without a body, whereas the intellect is separated from the body. Therefore, for its own perfection, it does not require those things that proceed from the outside. Thus, even when the soul is in the process of knowing, nothing new exists in its actual state at that moment; all things exist according to an essential and permanent perfection, even if the action of producing and applying those forms—the active "doing"—is temporarily lacking. Therefore, regarding this action, the soul is judged at that time to be in potentiality. But in truth, since the soul is born together with knowable things, when it does know something, it exists in "actuality" as that very thing which is known; it is not then something "other" than itself. Indeed, the soul determines its own essence according to all knowable things. Nevertheless, it seems to "become" in a certain way, for when it acts in this manner, it is called "knowing in actuality" regarding individual things. We say this happens when it can act according to its own nature; surely it is then still in potentiality in a certain way, but not in the same way as before, when it had neither learned nor discovered the knowledge.

### Chapter Ten.

->MARSILIO<-
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and the likely author or translator of this manuscript.</note>

<margin>1</margin> In the intellect, nothing new is born; in the soul, however, there is born at least a new action and a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition or skill acquired through repeated action.</note> formed through that action. For the intellectual nature is uniform and stable. The nature of the soul, besides these two qualities, also possesses their opposites. For it is, moreover, <term>multiform</term> <note>original: "multiformis"; having many shapes or aspects.</note> and mobile; indeed, motion belongs to the very definition and nature of the soul. The rational soul, because it stands in the middle of things and is mobile by its own nature, shifts its roles toward the extremes, especially because it is a "particular life." The rational power sometimes turns itself toward the intellect, and sometimes toward the senses.

->PRISCIANUS<-

<margin>1</margin> Among these points, Theophrastus asks from what source "generation" <note>Coming into being or being created.</note> occurs in the soul, and in what manner—whether it is the generation of the habit and the power itself, or if the essence itself is being introduced. It seems rather to be a habit, and this habit and its generation move toward the completion of its nature. Thus, the soul "becomes" in a certain way, because it is not as uniform and simple as we judge intellectual things to be, nor is it entirely stable like them; rather, it remains constant while simultaneously possessing an innate change and...

<summary>This page discusses how the soul transitions from a state of potentiality to active knowledge without changing its core essence, distinguishing the stable intellect from the mobile, "multiform" rational soul.</summary>
<keywords>potentiality, actuality, Priscianus Lydus, Marsilio Ficino, Theophrastus, rational soul, habit, uniform vs multiform, intellectual nature</keywords>

--- Page 258 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the soul's transition from potentiality to actuality. The previous page concluded with the idea that the soul possesses all forms essentially but may lack the active "doing" or expression of them. This page explores how the soul's essence itself might be considered changeable to account for the variety of human actions.</meta>

<header>ON THEOPHRASTUS</header>

[The soul] plays both roles, since it is at the center of things and has a life defined by movement. For this reason, it is sometimes carried toward ignorance insofar as it inclines toward the worse, and at other times it is perfected by the gift of knowledge insofar as it turns toward the higher. Thus, it becomes imperfect at one time and perfected at another in turn. For as often as it is ignorant, it is considered imperfect and is therefore said to be in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to know or act that has not yet been realized.</note>, because even then it possesses the power of knowing. But as often as it knows, it is judged to be perfect.

But then, insofar as it acts, it claims perfection for itself from the act itself. However, insofar as it does not always act even when it knows something, it is judged even then to be in potentiality. Yet this is not in the same condition as before it learned or discovered, since it already possesses a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitum"; a stable disposition or acquired skill, like knowing how to speak a language even when one is silent.</note> and has perfected that power which is accustomed to produce acts of knowledge. Therefore, when Theophrastus asks from what source the generation of habit, power, or essence occurs in the soul, he should be understood to ask whether the change in the soul occurs only according to habit and potentiality, or also according to its very essence.

<margin>MARSILIO'S COMMENTARY</margin>
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who sought to harmonize Platonic philosophy with Christianity.</note>

### Chapter eleven.

Our soul is also changeable in some way according to its <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentiam"; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</note>. Otherwise, if its essence were completely unchangeable, it would not produce actions so diverse and changeable that they tend toward opposites. Likewise, there is one soul in us in essence. If it were entirely unchangeable in itself, it would not produce actions that are sometimes right and sometimes perverse. If there were two essences of souls in us, separated from each other, and one did not depend on the other, there would not be one single living being. The intellectual soul would not be the leader of the bodily life unless the latter depended upon it. There is a single essence in which there is an intellectual and rational power, as well as a power that wanders in whatever way <note>original: "quomodocunque discurrens"; referring to "discursive" reasoning, where the mind moves step-by-step from one premise to another.</note>. Here he seems to place the intellect, reason, and imagination within the same essence of the soul; because of this union, the living being is one, and the lower powers are referred to a single principle in the soul. In each of us, the essence of the soul is unique, and it is simultaneously unchangeable and changeable; in whatever change of the soul occurs, the life proper to it—namely, the rational life—remains.

<margin>PRISCIAN'S COMMENTARY</margin>
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century philosopher whose interpretations were used by Ficino to understand the older Greek texts of Theophrastus.</note>

Since, therefore, habits and acts come from the essence, it is impossible to posit a certain essence that is entirely permanent, separated from change, and always maintaining itself in the same way, while it nevertheless sometimes produces perfect and good actions, and at other times imperfect and perverse ones. ->## ON THE IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT<-
<page-num>103</page-num>

...and we rightly conjecture that the form of its essence is the same. But if someone were to imagine a twin essence within us, along with twin powers and actions—some always perfect in themselves, others sometimes imperfect and sometimes perfect—if he understands these as being disjointed, he would turn one animal into many animals. Furthermore, he would set aside the more excellent essence as if it neither governed life nor had anything in common with it, <margin>a</margin> if indeed it is through the second essence that the alternation between the imperfect and the perfect is brought about—which is precisely how human life is defined. 

But if the one who has devised such double aspects in us describes them as two dispositions, or double reasons, or twin lives, let him not break the union of the two in this way, lest our nature become like a <term>choir</term> <note>original: "choro"; a common Neoplatonic metaphor for a collection of distinct individuals moving together, rather than a single unified being.</note> or some other multitude. Instead, let all things come together into one, and let them harmonize, fused into a single principle. We will immediately ask about this "one": whether it is uniform, always immutable, and whole. For if that is admitted at the outset, it would follow that there is never any imperfection in living beings, whether in their essence or their action, nor any depravity or passion. For actions follow essence. However, it must not be granted that this "one" is completely changeable either; for life itself remains throughout its changes.

### Chapter Twelve.
### MARSILIO'S COMMENTARY.

<margin>a</margin> Our soul, because it is the middle point between things that are entirely stable and those that are mobile, therefore possesses both a stable essence and a mobile one. By turns, it acts out the lives of all things that dwell in the world. Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced how later thinkers like Ficino understood the soul's descent into the body.</note> says regarding the composition of the soul and the alternation of its lives: there is a certain change in the soul, not only according to its dispositions but in some way even according to its essence, insofar as it varies its species by its **intellectual or rational fire**. Thus, it lives now as an earthly man, then as an aerial one, and at other times as an ethereal one. To me, Marsilio, it does not seem that Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle's successor; here his views are being filtered through Neoplatonic commentators.</note> places any change in the soul that actually touches its essence. Iamblichus, however, admits the smallest possible amount of change.

...is changed not only according to its <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "habitus"; referring to a stable state or quality a person possesses, like knowledge or virtue.</note>, but also in some way according to its essence. This is indeed what Theophrastus (as I believe) intended to signify when he said: "Generation in the soul seems rather to happen according to disposition." For a change according to disposition and perfection is quite manifest, which is why he says "rather." And by saying this word "rather," he clearly signifies a perfection pertaining in some way to the essence; for this reason, he adds: "this, however, perfects the nature"—namely, the nature of the one who is acting—as if it were not previously perfect. For if the essence were entirely perfect, then surely an imperfect disposition or action would not proceed from that essence alone.

## Chapter Thirteen.
->MARSILIO<- <note>Refers to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the famous Renaissance Neoplatonist who likely provided this summary or commentary.</note>

Immaterial things have nothing in themselves except what necessarily pertains to their essence. Material things, besides their essential qualities, undergo many <term>accidents</term> <note>Features that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color, size, or location.</note>. Our intellect knows both through innate forms; these forms represent immaterial things as being kindred to them, but they represent material things as their causes. Aristotle and Theophrastus wrote about things separated from matter and things joined to it. Iamblichus and Plutarch <note>Plutarch of Athens (c. 350–430 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher, not the more famous biographer Plutarch of Chaeronea.</note> were commentators on Aristotle. The <term>possible intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus possibilis"; the capacity of the human mind to receive or become all things through knowledge.</note> in us is twofold: one is primary and always in a state of activity; the other is secondary and passes from potentiality to activity—that is, human reason. Reason, when it does not wander through the imagination and the senses but is turned toward itself, finds the innate "reasons" or blueprints of things. These innate reasons are siblings to the <term>separated substances</term> <note>Purely spiritual beings or forms that exist without physical bodies.</note>, and they are either the causes of material things or are similar to those causes. The <term>active intellect</term>, seeing itself, beholds all things according to their cause.

->PRISCIANUS<- <note>Refers to Priscianus Lydus, a 6th-century philosopher whose paraphrases of Theophrastus are a primary source for this text.</note>

Next, however, Theophrastus—just like Aristotle—posits two kinds of <term>species</term> <note>original: "specierum"; here meaning "forms" or "intelligible types."</note>: some are indeed immaterial, while others are material. Regarding species separated from matter, he says that "the thing itself" and "its very being" are the same. When he says "its very being," he designates the formal reason and the species; but when he says "the thing itself," he signifies the whole substance. In species that exist without matter, he thinks the whole substance exists according to the formal reason and species alone. However, in material species, he maintains that "the thing itself" is one thing, and "its very being" is another. For the first of these is understood according to both matter and form as a composite whole, while the latter is understood according to the species alone. Since, therefore, the intellect which is called "in potentiality" contemplates both kinds of species, Theophrastus inquires (along with Aristotle) how it contemplates both: and how it knows species existing in matter, even by a certain process of abstraction. So too the potential intellect, at the next level, perceives material things through those proximate causes that are within itself. It does this by contemplating the immaterial principles of material things that are implanted in its own nature.

### Chapter Fourteen.

-> MARSILIO <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the scholar providing this summary or commentary.</note> <-

The sense knows only <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentia"; non-essential features like color, size, or temperature that can change without changing what the thing is.</note> and particulars. The intellect, however, knows universally and knows the accidents following from them through essential principles. Likewise, it knows all things through implanted principles: immaterial things as if they were joined to these principles, but material things as if they were effects produced by them. The principles implanted in the soul regard material things as causes [regard] immaterial things—either as kindred or as effects. Natural <term>species</term> <note>The essential form or "definition" of a thing.</note>, although they do not exist outside of individual objects, are nevertheless truly thought of even when the individual accidents are not being considered. Likewise, if reason thinks of mathematical figures without specific matter, it does so even though it knows they can never exist in reality without matter.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS
30

...in this way, each soul perceives both kinds of forms: those that are material as well as those released from matter. Certainly—as has been said—it perceives both according to the <term>principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; these are the innate blueprints or inner "formulas" the soul uses to organize knowledge.</note> implanted within the soul. However, it perceives immaterial things as if they were joined to these internal principles, or as something even more excellent. In contrast, it perceives material things as if they were mere effects, or through <term>abstraction</term> <note>original: "abstractione"; the mental act of separating a quality (like "roundness") from a physical object (like a ball) to think about it on its own.</note>. By removing the material aspects, these thoughts become, in a sense, the same as the material species themselves; yet, we think of them as they are in themselves—that is, they are not thought of alongside matter. Since they do not exist in a separate state, nor are they understood as if they claimed their essence in a separate way, we call them "material" when we think of them together with matter. But when we recognize them as knowing only the species—while acknowledging meanwhile that they exist in matter and cannot subsist otherwise—then we perceive them by abstraction.

## Chapter Fifteen.
->BY MARSILIO<-
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance philosopher who translated this work.</note>

The same intellectual power in us knows both immaterial and material things, and the latter both universally and individually. It performs all of this through its innate principles, which it uses toward immaterial things as if they were its own kin (or as their effects), and toward material things as if they were their causes.

->BY PRISCIAN<-
<note>Priscian of Lydia (6th century AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentary on Theophrastus is being translated here.</note>

Does the soul, then, judge material and immaterial things by some other power, or by a power acting in a different mode? And does it judge those things found entirely in matter differently from those perceived by abstraction? Or is it rather by the same power acting in a similar way? Perhaps both are true. For the same judge can distinguish between different things. Indeed, the intellectual faculty itself—being the same and acting in the same way—achieves this. It acts according to its own principles, and yet meanwhile it acts through a different faculty, or at least one acting in a different mode. This is because it contemplates its own principles either as causes (when it thinks of material things from them), or as being joined to immaterial things, or as being effects produced from intellectual species. In this way, while contemplating through its own principles, it is turned toward God, so that these principles are meanwhile made different, or at least behave differently.

...they are imperfect; however, those that are immaterial are perfect. That which is separated from matter immediately becomes "intelligible" <note>Capable of being understood by the mind rather than just felt by the senses.</note> as well as an intellect itself. The intellect appears to be indivisible because it turns back into itself; likewise, it is full of <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formarum"; in this context, "forms" are the essential blueprints or ideas of all things.</note> because, by turning inward, it finds all things within itself. There are three orders of separated substances, and three types of intellects: first, there are the "super-mundane" <note>Beyond the physical universe.</note> intellects, which are solely contemplators. Second, there are those that are indeed super-mundane but serve as the rulers of celestial souls. # OF PRISCIDIAN
<note>Priscian of Lydia was a 6th-century philosopher who wrote paraphrases of Aristotle and Theophrastus.</note>

In every way, just as things themselves are separate from matter, so Aristotle and Theophrastus believe the matters concerning the intellect are arranged. Perhaps, then, their opinion should be explained in this way: just as material <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the mental images or "looks" of things.</note> are separated from matter by thought alone. And so they are judged by a different faculty and in a different manner—as if they had been apprehended and distinguished through thought alone—so too the species innate to the potential intellect are set apart by it through intelligence alone. Since, according to its essence, the intellect always exists together with these species, we do not even notice how it is called an "intellect in potential" and is "nothing in act"—namely because it acts through intelligence alone. Either those words of Aristotle and Theophrastus signify this (for this is how Plutarch <note>Plutarch of Athens (c. 350–430 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher, not the famous biographer.</note> explains it), or rather it is as I shall soon add. Just as those things said to be "separated from matter" are in one sense truly separate (as if not in matter at all), while others are separate through intelligence (like things perceived by <term>abstraction</term>), so both are understood. Some are understood as truly detached; others, even if they are detached by some act of thought, nevertheless exist in no other way than (so to speak) materially. But perhaps we might explain it better this way: just as we arrange things that are entirely separate from matter, so it is fitting to arrange the things concerning the intellect. Let us not perhaps posit these according to thought alone, but as properly and primarily separate. For just as those immaterial species are in reality detached from matter, so also the intellect is entirely segregated from matter.

->IN THEOPHRASTUS<-

Indeed, before and above material <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the essential forms or blueprints of things.</note>, it is necessary that immaterial ones exist and subsist within themselves in an <term>intelligible</term> <note>perceivable by the mind rather than the senses.</note> way (if I may put it that way). For these are indivisible, and are entirely full of life and knowledge united through the whole of them; for the emptiness of life and ignorance are said to exist according to <term>privation</term> <note>The absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present.</note>, and privation usually occurs in the mixture with matter. 

Since, therefore, species devoid of matter are immediately intellectual, it is established that they exist in the intellect, and that the intellect itself is entirely devoid of matter and has obtained its essence together with the immaterial species. This is because life and knowledge, which turn back upon themselves, are indivisible—especially since the intellect, by entering into itself, finds beings that are both internal and true. 

But because among things that are truly separate and devoid of matter there is a certain difference according to a "descent" <note>A hierarchy from the highest divine mind down to human reason.</note>: some are entirely indivisible; others exist with a certain <term>unfolding</term> <note>original: "explicatione"; the process of discursive reasoning where the mind moves from one thought to the next, rather than grasping everything at once.</note>; and finally, others are intermediate between these, acting as indivisible things that merely define those that are unfolded. 

The intellect itself behaves in this same way. In the first degree, that which is called the <term>intellect according to act</term> <note>original: "secundum actum"; the intellect when it is actively thinking or "turned on."</note> is separate. In the second degree is the intellect designated according to potentiality, which is shared by the soul, and the rational soul itself. For although the soul exists with "unfolding" [reason], it nevertheless gathers both itself and other things back into that which is indivisible. This soul begins its own work from itself; it finds things—and true ones—within itself; therefore, it is separate and full of separate <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "rationum"; here meaning the formative principles or logical blueprints of reality.</note>.

# ON FANTASY AND THE INTELLECT
<sig>S ii</sig>

Having been illuminated from that source, and united from there with its forms, the <term>potential intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus possibilis"; the capacity of the human mind to receive and understand universal truths.</note> sees with a simple and stable intuition, while the <term>rational power</term> <note>original: "potentia rationalis"; the faculty of reason that processes information step-by-step rather than all at once.</note> acts through a moving and composite action. Therefore, reason is less united to the things it must perceive, but it is made one with them by the intellect, toward which it exists in a state of potential. Reason also gathers itself into a unity and finds all things within itself. The potential intellect is always and everywhere united to the <term>agent</term> <note>original: "agenti"; referring to the "Agent Intellect," the active force that illuminates the mind to allow understanding.</note> and is formed by it. But because it is formed from that source through its own proper and free action, the potential intellect rightly "forms itself"; in this way, it is all things in a "second degree," just as the agent [intellect] is all things in the "first degree."

->FROM PRISCIAN<-

<margin>Theophrastus</margin>Theophrastus again reminds us in a very philosophical way how we ought to properly understand this claim: that objects of the intellect exist both in the intellect according to potentiality and in the intellect according to act. We must be careful not to take "in potential" to mean a state of <term>privation</term> <note>original: "privationem"; the total absence of a quality, like a blank slate or raw matter.</note>, as we usually do when discussing matter. Nor should we suspect that what is called "in act" refers to a <term>passive perfection</term> <note>A state where something is "completed" by being acted upon by an external force.</note> brought in from the outside. Furthermore, it is not like what happens in the senses, where the production of <term>rational forms</term> <note>original: "rationum"; the mental patterns or concepts derived from sensory input.</note> occurs through the movement of physical organs, and the sense itself perceives things placed outside of it. Rather, he says that we must understand "intellectually" that things exist in the intellect itself, both in potential and in act.

For that which is called "in act" must be judged according to an indivisible unity, a pure boundary, and a thoroughly united perfection. For the intellect in act is, in truth, the very things themselves—not by participating in them, nor divided from them, nor as if they belonged to others, nor as if it were limited by them or made imperfect by them. Rather, it exists as the thing itself, and as the boundary and perfection of all things. 

However, we use the term "in potential" to describe a contact made alongside "otherness." This happens through a certain "descent" toward that which is limited and perfected from elsewhere, while that very otherness appears more clearly in the rational soul. Indeed, the soul’s own contemplation makes this clear through a certain "unfolding" and "evolution" <note>original: "evolutione"; here meaning the step-by-step process of thinking through a problem.</note> united to the things to be known. Yet, the soul is not entirely divided or distant from these things; otherwise, it would never have been gathered back to that indivisible unity, nor would it have ever contemplated things known from within itself and in itself. But because it has a "relaxed" union with things, and for that reason depends constantly on that which is thoroughly united, it is said to be "in potential." Now, this relaxation appears more clearly in the soul, and from there in the intellect...

acted upon by the soul through a kind of submission. This <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus"; here referring specifically to the human capacity for thought.</note> surely depends entirely on the unified and indivisible limit of the higher intellect; it remains suspended there and is perfected by it according to its <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentiam"; the fundamental nature or "what-it-is" of a thing.</note>. For this reason, it is said to be **in potential** <note>original: "in potentia"; the state of being capable of knowing something but not yet actively thinking about it.</note> in itself. However, because this intellect is also indivisible—lacking both spatial distance and total difference from the first intellect—it is not moved by an external force or perfected by another at a specific time. Instead, it perfects itself, even though it achieves this perfection through the boundary of that higher intellect. In a secondary degree, it becomes the very thing that the higher intellect is in the first degree; it is united to it through the immediate union that follows and looks back toward it. Thus, the term "potential" should be understood in the intellect in the specific way that is proper to its nature.

## Chapter Eighteen.

### MARSILIO.

The <term>potential intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus possibilis"; the part of the mind that receives and stores knowledge.</note>, when it first exists, is itself all <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the formal mental images or concepts of things.</note> according to its essence; therefore, it does not receive them from the <term>agent</term> <note>original: "agente"; the "Agent Intellect" which acts as a light to make things understandable.</note>. Rather, it receives its perfect union to those species, and their union among themselves. This union it possesses in that realm from **eternity** <note>original: "ab euo"; referring to *aevum*, a state of existence between time and eternity, often associated with the soul's permanent state.</note>. But human **reason** receives this union from the intellect within the realm of **time**. The potential intellect is said to be "empty" of forms in the sense that, unless it is united to its forms by the agent, it behaves as if it did not have them; for it does not "see" them unless it is perfectly united to them. Note here and below that the potential intellect assumes perfection from the agent through its own free act, and thus perfects itself. The potential intellect is always joined to the agent and always formed in **actuality**. Reason, however, is not always joined to the intellect; reason similarly joins itself to the intellect through its own proper and free act, and thereby perfects itself.

### PRISCIAN.

But it seems to me that Theophrastus also signifies here that the state of being "in potential" in the intellect ought to be understood properly, in a way consistent with the nature of the intellect. For the example of the **tablet not yet written upon** <note>original: "tabella non-dum scripta"; a reference to Aristotle's *tabula rasa*, the idea of the mind as a blank slate.</note> was introduced by Aristotle to signify how the intellect is in potential. Priscian understands and notes it thus: we admit a "emptiness of letters" in the intellect only insofar as it is consistent with the intellect—that is, as a faculty that already possesses the species according to their essence and possesses them in a perfected state. But it is "potential" in the sense that its perfect act is "written" or activated by the first intellect. For the very individuality and unity of perfection here—
