### OF PRISCIAN <note>Priscian of Lydia (6th century AD), a philosopher who wrote a famous paraphrase of Theophrastus’s works on the soul and perception.</note>

After these things, where Theophrastus explains Aristotle saying that separate and immaterial things are the same as the intellect, but that in material things, each of the intelligible objects exists in a certain **potentiality** <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity for a thing to be understood, even if it isn't being thought of right now.</note>. And he distinguishes point by point such sayings—that the mind is not present in these things—and directs them, though in the meantime he expresses certain doubts. So that we may also grasp these things more clearly, we shall first arrange Aristotle’s words point by point and as briefly as possible according to our abilities. Since, he says, some things are in matter, while others are without matter—such as incorporeal and **separate substances** <note>Substances that exist independently of physical bodies, such as the Divine Mind or celestial intelligences.</note>—in separate things, the one understanding and the thing understood are the same. For the intellect is not stretched out toward external things, but remaining **within itself** <note>original: "in se manens"; a key Neoplatonic concept where higher minds do not need to look at the physical world to find truth, but find it within their own essence.</note>, it understands the things themselves. Therefore, it is the same as the things to be understood. Moreover, since all immaterial things are indivisible and full of life and knowledge, they are certainly judged to be intellectual. For sensible things, because of their material separation, are to be felt by others, but for the most part, they cannot feel themselves at all. But things entirely devoid of matter, since they are intelligible, differ from sensible things also for this reason: they are not separated from the one understanding, nor are they perfected by external things. Instead, by perfect reason, they are intelligible of their own accord. For this reason, they are also understanding beings, and since they are **indivisible** <note>original: "impartibiles"; things that cannot be broken into parts, unlike physical matter.</note>, they are indivisibly united to the one understanding. And since they are furthermore entirely intelligible throughout, they are rightly united to the intellect entirely throughout. They are not intelligible by accident, but according to their very **essence** <note>original: "essentiam"; their fundamental nature or what they truly are.</note>. And they are perfect according to their essence; and for this reason, existing as perfect according to their own essence, they are certainly those same intelligible things. And at the same time, they are understanding beings, so that according to themselves they are both intelligible and most perfectly intelligible. Therefore, Aristotle also reminds us through the nature of knowledge itself that in separate things, that which understands and that which is understood are the same. For **theoretical knowledge** <note>original: "scientia speculativa"; knowledge sought for its own sake and for the contemplation of truth, rather than for practical application.</note>, he says, and that which is knowable in such a way, are the same as each other. That is, knowledge not at all stretched out toward external things, but remaining...

But the difference is this: it neither comes from the outside, nor is it placed outside—that which is principally knowable—as happens in the case of physical sensation. If, therefore, knowledge and the knowable are the same thing at once, and even more so the understander and that which is understood are united, then certainly the intellect is judged to be the same as the things understood.

### Chapter Twenty. BY MARSILIO. <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance philosopher who sought to harmonize Platonic philosophy with Christianity.</note>

That which is material is not intelligible in itself, but only insofar as it is released from material conditions by the intellect. Therefore, it does not become intelligible to itself, but only to the intellect that abstracts it. On the contrary, a thing that is by its nature separated from matter is both intelligible in itself and to itself. In things that are **separated** <note>original: "separatis"; referring to immaterial entities like the soul or God, which do not need a body to exist.</note>, the intellect and the understood object meet in the same form. 

The intellect knows material things, not through the things themselves, but through their innate principles within the intelligence, as if through causes. According to **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school.</note> and **Aristotle**, the intellect is immaterial, and yet it is a certain "potentiality" for material things. This is explained in three ways: two active ways, and one as if passive. 
1. First, the intellect is the productive power of its own acts or actions concerning material things. 
2. Second, not by an equality of nature, but by a surpassing power, it knows material things through its own forms as if through causes. 
3. Third, it also knows material things insofar as it has been formed by the light of the **active intellect** <note>original: "intellectus agentis"; the part of the mind that illuminates sensory data to turn it into abstract concepts.</note>. 

Immaterial things are always naturally present in the intellect. Material things, however, become present only insofar as they are resolved from matter by the intellect. Knowledge "in act" becomes one with the thing "in act" that is known, even in the very discourse of reason. Much more so, in the state of intelligence itself, the understander and the understood are the same. Indeed, the intellect itself, according to its **essence** <note>original: "essentiam"; the fundamental nature of what a thing is.</note>, is those very forms which are understood by it. <sig>iiiii 2</sig>

...the intellect knows immaterial things as if they were conjoined with it. But it notices material things as inferior, insofar as it observes the causes of forms—acting as material causes—that are innate within itself. The **active intellect** <note>original: "intellectus agens"; the part of the mind that actively produces thought and makes things understandable.</note> is in no way "made." The **first possible intellect** <note>original: "intellectus possibilis primus"; the capacity for thought that is always present in a state of readiness.</note> in us never "becomes," but has always been "made"—that is, it is formed by the active intellect. The **second possible intellect** <note>original: "intellectus possibilis secundus"; often identified with human reason or discursive thought.</note> in us—that is, reason—is always "becoming"; that is, it is formed daily into **act** <note>original: "actu"; the state of being active or fully realized, rather than just a potential.</note> through the higher intellect and its own movement toward it, or at least it brings forth innate forms from a state of idleness into action. This opinion concerning a threefold intellect and a certain eternal act of intelligence within us is frequently approved by **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> and **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's relationship to the divine.</note>.

<margin>OF PRISCIAN <note>Refers to Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle and Theophrastus.</note></margin>
Since these things are so, he [Theophrastus] rightly signified the same point in the opportune middle of his discussion with these words: "Why then," he asks, "do we not always understand, since both that which understands and that which is understood are within us? For both are the same." Therefore, we must consider this with all our strength as soon as possible: in those things that are separated from matter, that which understands and that which is understood are indeed the same, as we said above. But in those things that exist with matter, each of the **intelligible things** <note>original: "intelligibilium"; things that can be grasped by the mind rather than just the senses.</note> is so only in **potentiality** <note>original: "in potentia"; having the capacity to be understood, but not yet being actively understood.</note>. For material things are not intelligible according to themselves, nor according to their essence, nor do they obtain the same rank as the intellect, nor are they known as if conjoined to it. 

How then are they said to be "intelligible according to potentiality"? For if they are such in potentiality, they will also be intelligible in act at some point. They will certainly be so at some point, but perhaps not as things conjoined [to the mind]; rather, they will be known according to their causes placed within the intellect. And because they share the same property as their causes, they themselves are also named "intelligible," but they are intelligible by a certain potentiality; because the intellect understands them, it towers above them, and they are understood by it according to a surpassing cause, but they are not intelligible to themselves or by themselves. For they do not understand themselves. Wherefore he next adds: "Therefore, intellect is not in them"—namely, in material things. For this reason, they are not intelligible to themselves or by themselves, because these things are material, while the intellect exists as immaterial. For the intellect of such things (as he says) is itself "potentiality without matter." Of these things, the phrase "without matter" shows the nature of the intellect to be entirely devoid of matter. 

But the intellect of material things is "potentiality," either as a cause of actions—for so **Plutarch** <note>Refers to Plutarch of Athens, a Neoplatonist teacher.</note> explains it—or as things not conjoined, but understanding these by a certain more eminent condition, since it contemplates them from their cause. Or, the intellect itself in potentiality is also the "potentiality" of such things, as if also understanding these according to perfection from a higher rank...

# ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

...so. Therefore, the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus"; the highest faculty of the human soul capable of understanding universal truths.</note> does not reside in material things, but that which can be understood resides within the intellect, distributing these things in an articulate way. **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle; Ficino is here interpreting his views through a Neoplatonic lens.</note> adds this: but when they come into being and are understood, then the intellect will possess them. For such an intellect is preeminent; he says that the intelligible things—that is, the immaterial things—are always present to the intellect as the same things, since the intellect exists essentially together with them. And the intellect is that very thing which the intelligible objects are said to be. 

Material things, however, are present to the intellect only when they are understood. They are not to be understood by it as if they were of equal rank or order; for material things are never truly joined with the immaterial intellect from which they receive their union. But when the intellect perceives the things within itself—not merely as the things themselves, but as the **causes of material things**—then material things are also present to the intellect according to their cause. I would not affirm, however, that these things were said of the intellect considered in the state of act. For that intellect is not a potentiality, nor can it ever "become" something else.

### Preface of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the short works of Alcinous, Speusippus, and Pythagoras translated by him from the Greek language into Latin. To Giovanni Cavalcanti, Florentine citizen and unique friend.

We also think that their society will be stable only when that which they have proposed to pursue through a common duty is not only one thing, but also stable and firm. But since every human pursuit and social exchange usually strives toward that which is thought to be good—and there seem to be three types of goods for mortals: those of the soul, those of the body, and external ones—either the virtue of the soul, or the pleasure of the body, or an abundance of wealth is sought. Of these, the first is certainly certain and perpetual; the other two are fleeting and mortal. For this reason, the union of a stable life, which is true friendship, can only exist between those who neither strive to accumulate wealth, nor to fill...

->IN THEOPHRASTVM<-

...the lusts of the body, all of which are fleeting and perishable, but they set out with a certain common zeal and with all the ardor of the mind to grasp and cultivate the one stable <term>virtue</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" (Latin: virtus) refers to the excellence or perfected power of the soul, specifically its ability to align with reason and divine truth.</note> of the soul. Our **Plato**, that master and leader of all philosophers, wanted this virtue of the soul to be called **wisdom**. Indeed, he considered wisdom to be the knowledge of divine things. Furthermore, in his books on the *Republic*, he demonstrates that divine things cannot become known to our mind in any other way than by God illuminating us, just as the forms of bodies are seen by the eyes in no other way than by the sun illuminating the eyes. 

Therefore, it is God Himself whom we desire to see, who illuminates the sharpness of the mind so that we may look upon Him, and who finally shows Himself to the brightened mind. By showing Himself, He delights us; likewise, God is for us the **Way**, the **Truth**, and the **Life** <note>original: "uia... ueritas... & uita"; a direct reference to the Gospel of John 14:6, which Ficino here integrates into a Platonic framework.</note>. He is the Way, because He turns us toward Himself with His rays, and leads and seizes us. He is the Truth, because He shows Himself as true to those of us who have turned toward Him. Finally, He is the Life, because He perpetually feeds and delights our soul—the contemplator of Himself—with that blessed vision. 

Therefore, all who desire to taste the sweetest liquids of wisdom must thirst for this perennial fountain. Indeed, it is necessary for all who desire to attain the virtue of the soul to pursue wisdom, from which it follows that whoever resolves to <term>cultivate</term> <note>original: "colere"; this Latin word can mean both to "cultivate" (like a garden) and to "worship" (in a religious sense). Ficino uses this double meaning to link self-improvement with religion.</note> their soul is compelled to worship God. 

Moreover, we defined those as friends to one another in the preceding parts who strive toward virtue with a similar and equal zeal, and who cultivate their souls with mutual favor. The cultivation of the soul consists in virtue alone; virtue is wisdom; wisdom is the knowledge of divine things; and divine light grants us knowledge of this kind. Thus, the cultivation of the soul is the worship of God Himself. Therefore, since **friendship** strives toward cultivating the soul through virtue by the agreement of two people, it seems to be nothing other than the highest concord of two souls in worshipping God. 

Furthermore, all those who worship God with a pious mind are loved by God. Therefore, not only two, but three are necessarily always friends: namely, two human beings and one God. God, I say—**Jupiter, the Patron of Guests**; **Jupiter, the Friend**; **Jupiter, the Savior of human life** <note>original: "Iupiter hospitalis. Iupiter amicabilis. Iupiter humanae uitae seruator"; Ficino uses these classical titles for Jupiter to describe the various ways God protects human relationships and society.</note>—whom Plato always worshipped and whom **Socrates** always honored. He is the leader of human life; He reconciles us into one; He is the indissoluble knot of friendship and its perpetual guardian. 

With this God acting as the reconciler, those ancient theologians whose memory we venerate are said to have entered into a holy bond of friendship among themselves. Among the Persians, **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary Iranian prophet, whom the Neoplatonists considered the first of the "Ancient Theologians" (Prisci Theologi).</note> is said to have chosen **Arimaspes** as his constant companion in the very mysteries of religious philosophy, with the divine power breathing upon him. Similarly, **Hermes Trismegistus** among the Egyptians chose **Asclepius**; **Orpheus** in Thrace chose **Musaeus**; there also **Aglaophemus** chose **Pythagoras** of Athe- <meta>Catchword: niensis (Athenian)</meta>

# ON THE TEACHING OF PLATO

...the Athenian Plato took first Dion of Syracuse <note>Dion of Syracuse (c. 408–354 BCE) was a disciple of Plato and a political figure in Sicily.</note>. Then, after Dion had died, he took Xenocrates <note>Xenocrates (c. 396–314 BCE) was a student of Plato and later the leader of the Academy.</note>. These men, so wise, believed that for the heavenly journey to be completed safely and calmly, both a divine leader and a human companion would be necessary. Although I am confident that I can hardly follow their footsteps, which are impressed high above in the regions of heaven, I nevertheless seem to have already achieved this one thing in abundance: that in the study of sacred philosophy—for the sake of exercising virtue and investigating truth—I do not lack the helpful and pleasant society of an excellent man. 

Indeed, I believe that the friendship of **Giovanni Cavalcanti** <note>original: "Ioāis caualcantis"; Cavalcanti was Ficino’s closest friend and "unique" companion, often described as the "heroic" lover of his soul.</note> and **Marsilio Ficino** should be placed in that number of those whom we mentioned just before. With God as our guide, who happily established and forged this bond for us, I believe it will be of great benefit to both of us for conducting our affairs, for the tranquility of our lives, and for the investigation of divine matters. I have decided at other times to leave behind even greater monuments of this singular benevolence for posterity; for now, here are certain short works recently translated by me from the Greek language into Latin, which seem most likely to contribute to that Platonic school of ours, into whose sacred mysteries you have been initiated. 

Receive, therefore, my one and only friend, the book of **Alcinous the Platonist** <note>Alcinous was a Middle Platonist philosopher; this work, the *Didaskalikos*, was a standard textbook on Plato's thought in the Renaissance.</note> concerning the conclusions of this school. Furthermore, a book on the **Definitions of Plato** composed by his nephew, **Speusippus** <note>Speusippus succeeded Plato as the head of the Academy.</note>. Finally, the laws and symbols of **Pythagoras**, whom Plato followed above all others. By reading these, as one educated in the secret mysteries of divine philosophy, you will despise the empty dreams of this shadow-like life, for which the anxious common people gape. You will lift your mind to celestial things, and by contemplating them, you will obtain tranquility in this present life and blessedness in the future.

## The book of Alcinous the Platonic philosopher, on the doctrine of Plato.

### Chapter one: what philosophy is, and the nature of the philosophical mind.

**T**his is the doctrine of the principal teachings of Plato. **Philosophy** is the pursuit of wisdom. Or, it is the release of the soul from the body, and a certain turning toward those things which are true and divine. **Wisdom** is the knowledge of divine and human things. A **philosopher** is one who takes his name from philosophy, just as a musician does from music. And he who is to be a philosopher must be so fashioned by nature itself that, in the first place, he is apt and ready for all kinds of learning...

...to be obtained. Next, he must apply his mind not to those things which are in a state of flux <note>Referring to the physical world of change, as opposed to the eternal world of Ideas.</note>, but to those which always remain the same. In the third place, he must be truthful by nature and completely foreign to every lie. Furthermore, it is necessary that he be born temperate in a certain way, and that those parts of the soul which are usually carried away by passions be received from nature as already tamed. For whoever is greedy for truth and turns his mind to the contemplation of divine things thinks little of bodily pleasures. 

It is necessary, furthermore, for a philosopher to have a generous soul <note>original: "liberali animo"; implying a noble or free-spirited mind, as opposed to one focused on petty, narrow gains</note>. For the high estimation of worthless things is an obstacle to a man who is to contemplate the truth of things. In addition to this, his will shall love justice, since he is a student of truth, temperance, and generosity. Add to this that he has need of sharpness of intellect and a good memory. For these things make a man a philosopher. And indeed, when those natural gifts are combined with discipline and a decent education, they make a man perfect in virtue. But if they are neglected, they are the causes of the greatest crimes. And Plato is accustomed to signify these qualities by the more common names of temperance, fortitude, and justice.

### Chapter Two. The philosopher prefers contemplation to action.

Indeed, since there are two lives—namely, the contemplative and the active—and since the duty of the contemplative consists in the knowledge of truth, while the active consists in the performance of those things which reason dictates, the contemplative life must indeed be honored. However, that life which is engaged in acting is a handmaid <note>original: "pedissequa"; literally a female servant who follows her mistress, symbolizing that action serves the higher goal of contemplation.</note> and a minister of necessary things. That this is so will be declared from these points. 

Contemplation is the operation of the divine mind while it is understanding. Action, however, is the operation of the rational soul completed through the body. For the soul, contemplating the divine and divine intelligence, is said to be affected in the best possible way. And this affection of the soul is called wisdom <note>original: "sapientia"; in this context, it refers to the highest philosophical wisdom (Sophia) rather than mere practical prudence.</note>, which indeed ought to be called nothing other than a likeness to God. For this reason, an operation of this kind is principal and venerable, and most to be desired of all things; it is also most proper to man, for no obstacles stand in its way to prevent it from remaining within our power. It is also the cause of the goal we have set for ourselves. 

The active life and its action, however, since they use the service of the body for the most part, are frequently hindered; and those who observe the contemplative life desire to transfer its insights to the duties of morals. For indeed, a man who is a student of learning only then betakes himself to the administration of civil affairs when he perceives those affairs to be handled poorly by other men. He considers certain things to be, as it were, external aids: military service, embassies, and the execution of judgments. But the principal and greatest duties of all things to be done are to establish laws for the republic, to prescribe order, and the discipline of those to be educated...

# ON THE DOCTRINE OF PLATO

...to instruct the manners of young men. For this reason, it is necessary for a philosopher never to cease in the pursuit of truth, but to nourish it always and to act upon it, although human actions are sometimes touched upon as something inferior. <note>Platonists often viewed the physical world and human politics as "inferior" to the eternal world of ideas, yet necessary for the soul's development while inhabiting a body.</note>

### Chapter Three. The philosopher is engaged in three things: namely, the contemplation of things, moral action, and the art of discourse.

Plato certainly intended for the philosopher’s study to be focused on three main areas: the speculation of things, the practice of virtues, and the consideration of speech. The knowledge of things is called **contemplative**; the study of behavior is **active**; and the care of speech is **dialectic** <note>original: "dialectica"; in this context, it refers to the logic and methods of reasoning used to uncover truth through dialogue and analysis.</note>.

Dialectic, moreover, is divided into many forms: division, definition, induction, and reasoning. This last category of reasoning is further divided into:
*   **Demonstration**, which is necessary reasoning.
*   **Ostension**, which is called probable reasoning <note>A method of proving something by showing its results or likely outcomes rather than through absolute logical necessity.</note>.
*   The **rhetorical enthymeme**, that is, a cautious opinion, which is called imperfect reasoning <note>An argument where one part of the logical structure is implied rather than stated, often used in persuasive speaking.</note>.
*   And finally, **sophisms**, to which the legitimate philosopher will give his attention—not because he approves of them as primary, but because he deems them occasionally necessary to understand <note>A sophism is a clever but false argument; the philosopher learns them to avoid being deceived by them.</note>.

Furthermore, of that philosophy which is concerned with action, the first part cares for the character of the man himself. The second governs the home, and the last protects the state. The first is called **moral**, the second **domestic** <note>original: "domestica"; equivalent to what we now call economics or household management.</note>, and the third **civil** <note>original: "ciuilis"; equivalent to political science or the governance of a republic.</note>.

And of that philosophy which focuses on contemplation, one part investigates the immovable and divine, and the primary causes of things; this we call **theology**. Another part looks up to the movements of the stars, the orbits and returns of the celestial bodies, and the order of the world; this is called **natural knowledge** <note>This refers to "physics" in the ancient sense—the study of the natural world and the cosmos.</note>. This is followed by **mathematics**, which contains geometry and arithmetic. 

Since philosophy is distributed into these three main types—contemplative, active, and dialectic—we must first treat dialectic itself, what Plato thinks of it, and specifically the faculty of judgment.

### Chapter Four. Concerning the faculty of judgment, and the powers of the soul pertaining to judgment.

Since there is something that judges and something that is judged, it is necessary that something also arises from both, which we can properly call a **judgment**; thus, the faculty of judgment itself is named. More commonly, however, that which judges is also called the judgment. 

Furthermore, the judging element appears to be twofold: one **by which** and the other **through which** judgment is made. The former is our **intellect**, while the latter is a **natural organ** <note>A "tool" or faculty of the mind.</note>; and this organ distinguishes true things in the first place and false things in the second. This is nothing other than **natural reason**. If we wish to explain this even more clearly, the **judge** should be called the philosopher, by whom the things themselves are judged. Likewise, the judge is **reason**, through which the truth is determined, which is why we have called it an organ.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the divisions of philosophy, moving specifically into Alcinous’s explanation of epistemology—the study of how we know things—based on Plato’s "Theaetetus" and "Timaeus."</meta>

-># ALCINOUS<-

Reason is of two kinds: one is entirely beyond our grasp and belongs to truth itself, while the other is infallible regarding the knowledge of things. The first belongs to God; it is not for man at all. The second, however, is suited to man. But this human reason is also twofold: one part looks toward **intelligible things** <note>original: "intelligibilia"; these are non-physical realities or ideas that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note>, and the other looks toward **sensible things** <note>original: "sensibilia"; physical objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>. The first of these is **knowledge**, while the second is **opinion**. Knowledge possesses stability, as it is concerned with stable things; opinion possesses only likelihood and imagination, as it tends toward things that are constantly changing. Intellection and sensation are the foundations of knowledge regarding the intelligible and opinion regarding the sensible.

Sensation is surely an affection of the soul through the body, first reporting a stimulus to the perceiving power. After an image of the thing perceived is impressed upon the soul through the sense organs—so that it remains firm and cannot be erased—the preservation of this image is called **memory**.

**Opinion**, however, is the joining together of memory and sensation. For when a sensible object first meets us, a sensation is produced within us from it, and from that sensation comes a memory. When that same object is later presented to us again, we join our previous memory with the current sensation; in these instances, we say, "This is **Socrates**," or "This is a horse," or "This is fire," and other things of this kind. This is called opinion—our act of joining a prior memory with a fresh sensation. Whenever these things that are gathered together agree with each other, it is a true opinion; if they disagree, it is a false opinion. 

For example, if someone keeps the image of Socrates in their memory but happens upon Plato, and thinks because of a certain resemblance that they have met Socrates again, they take the sensation of Plato and apply it to the memory of Socrates as if they were drawing it from Socrates himself. In this case, a false opinion results. 

Plato compares that place in which sensation and memory occur to a **wax tablet** <note>A famous metaphor from Plato's "Theaetetus" suggesting the mind is like a block of wax that receives "stamps" or "impressions" from our experiences.</note>. Furthermore, when the soul, through thought, reshapes what it has conceived via opinion, sensation, and memory, it looks upon these images as if looking at the very things from which they flowed. Plato calls this a "picture," and also **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"; in ancient philosophy, this refers to the mind's ability to represent images of objects even when they are not present.</note>. 

He calls **thought** the soul’s own internal discourse and reasoning with itself; **speech**, however, is the flow from that thought out through the mouth by means of the articulate voice.

**Intellection** <note>original: "intellectio"; the direct, intuitive grasping of a truth by the mind.</note> is the operation of the intellect as it contemplates the primary intelligible things. This, too, appears to be twofold. One kind exists before the soul descends into the body, for then the soul gazes upon the intelligible truths themselves. The other kind occurs after the soul has been plunged into this body. Of these, the first is "intellection" properly so-called; the second, which exists as a natural intelligence within the soul, is referred to as a kind of intellection. Therefore, whenever we call intellection the principle of knowledge, we do not mean the human kind, but rather that which belongs to the soul when it is freed from the body, which, as we have said,

...is then called intellection, and now natural intelligence. And Plato calls this same intelligence sometimes "simple knowledge," sometimes the "wing of the soul" <note>original: "animæ alá"; a reference to the *Phaedrus*, where the soul's ability to ascend to divine truths is likened to growing wings.</note>, and also "reminiscence" <note>original: "reminiscentiam"; the Platonic theory that learning is actually the soul remembering truths it knew before birth.</note>. Finally, from these simple types of knowledge, reason—which is naturally inherent in the soul—is forged for the sake of natural science. Since, therefore, reason is capable of both knowing and forming opinions, and involves both intellection and sensation, it is necessary that certain subjects exist for these faculties, namely **intelligibles** and **sensibles**. 

And since some intelligibles are primary—such as the **Ideas** <note>original: "ideae"; the eternal, perfect archetypes or blueprints of all things in the mind of God</note>—and others are secondary—such as the forms inherent in matter which cannot be separated from it—intellection will also be twofold: one focused on primary things, the other on secondary things. Again, among the sensible things themselves, some are primary, such as qualities—for example, color or whiteness. Others are "accidental," such as something being "white" or "colored." After these comes that which is compounded from these qualities, such as fire. 

In the same way, primary sensation is of primary things, while secondary sensation is of secondary things. Intellection judges primary intelligibles, not without scientific reason <note>original: "scientifica ratione"; a form of logic based on certain knowledge</note>, through a certain comprehension and mental discourse. But scientific reason judges secondary intelligibles not without "opinionative" reason <note>original: "ratione opiniatiua"; the level of reasoning that deals with the physical world where things can change, unlike the eternal Ideas.</note>. 

However, opinionative reason judges the concrete <note>original: "concretum"; a physical object composed of both matter and form, like a specific chair or a specific person.</note> not without the help of sensation. And since the "intelligible world" is the primary object of intellection, while the "sensible world" is a concrete thing, intellection judges the former with reason—that is, not without reason—while opinionative reason judges the latter not without sensation. 

And since right reason consists of both **contemplation** <note>pure thought and study</note> and **action**, it does not discern the things subjected to contemplation and those subjected to action in the same way. Furthermore, in contemplation, reason considers what is true and what is false; in action, it considers what is one's own, what belongs to another, what is to be done, and what is to be avoided. For because we possess a natural intelligence of the beautiful and the good, by using reason and referring back to these natural intelligences as if to predefined standards <note>original: "normas"; the innate moral benchmarks we are born with</note>, we judge whether individual things are good or evil.

### Chapter Five: The Elements and Duties of Dialectic

Plato intends the first element of the **dialectic** faculty <note>the art of investigating the truth of opinions through logical analysis</note> to be the consideration of the "essence" or "being" of each thing, and afterwards to observe what follows from it. Now, one considers what each thing is either by "dividing" and "defining" from higher categories downward, or by "resolving" or breaking down compounds in the reverse order. 

As for things that are contingent <note>properties that might change without changing the essence of the thing</note> and adjacent to essences, one considers them either from those things that are contained through **induction** <note>original: "inductionem"; reasoning from specific examples to reach a general rule</note>, or from those that contain them through **reasoning** <note>original: "ratiocinationem"; logical deduction from a general rule to a specific case</note>. Thus, the "members" or branches of dialectic are rightly: **division, definition, resolution, induction, and reasoning.**

Furthermore, among types of division, there is the distribution of a **genus** into **species** <note>e.g., dividing "Animal" into "Human" and "Horse"</note>, and the distribution of a **whole** into its **parts**—as when we divide the soul into the rational part and the part lacking reason, and then further distribute the latter into the powers of desiring and anger. Moreover, there is the division of a voice into its various meanings...

<meta>This page continues Alcinous’s introduction to Platonic logic and dialectic. Having previously discussed sensation and simple knowledge, the text now turns to the systematic methods of "Division," "Definition," and "Resolution" (analysis), which allow a philosopher to categorize the world and ascend to higher truths.</meta>

-># ON THE DOCTRINE OF ALCINOUS<-

The name **being** <note>original: "ens"; refers to the concept of existence or anything that exists.</note> is a single term but signifies many different things. To this is added the division of "accidents" <term>accidents (qualities that can change or be absent without changing the fundamental nature of a thing, such as being tall or being in a certain place)</term> according to their subjects. For example, when we say that among "goods," some concern the soul, others the body, and some are external things. Nor is there a lack of division regarding the subjects of these accidents; as when we say that among men, some are good, some are bad, and others are in between.

Therefore, we must first use the **division of a genus into species** whenever we wish to distinguish what a specific thing is. This, however, cannot be achieved without a **definition**. A definition is constructed through division in this manner: one must first grasp the "genus" <term>genus (a broad category, like "animal")</term> of the thing to be defined—for example, the genus of "man" is "animal." Then, one must divide that genus according to its "proximate differences" <term>proximate differences (the specific traits that distinguish a sub-group from the rest of the category)</term>, descending all the way to the species. We divide "animal" into rational and irrational, and into mortal and immortal. Thus, if these proximate differences are added to the genus, the definition of "man" will be established <note>i.e., "Man is a rational, mortal animal."</note>.

There are three types of **Resolution** <note>original: "resolutionis"; in this context, it means "analysis" or the process of breaking a complex idea down into its primary principles.</note>:
1. The first is the ascent from sensible things <note>physical things perceived by the senses</note> to the first "intelligibles" <note>pure concepts understood only by the mind</note>.
2. The second is the approach through things already demonstrated or partially demonstrated toward those propositions that are "indemonstrable" <note>self-evident truths that do not require proof</note> and exist without a middle term.
3. The last is the movement from a "supposition" <note>hypothesis</note> toward principles that are not supposed at all but are certain.

The **first type of resolution** is like this: if we transcend from the beauty of physical bodies to the beauty of the soul; from there to the beauty of duties <note>original: "officiorum"; referring to moral obligations or virtuous actions</note>; then to the beauty found in laws; and finally to the very source of beauty itself. In this way, ascending step by step, we may behold the "Beautiful" as it is in itself.

The **second type of resolution** works as follows: we must suppose the thing being sought, then consider the things that come before it. These must be demonstrated by moving backward from later effects to higher causes, until we arrive at the "first principle" which is fully granted by everyone. Starting again from that principle, we may then return to the original question by way of "composition" <note>the reverse process of building the argument back up</note>. 

For example, if someone asks whether the soul is **immortal**, they first suppose this and inquire: "Is the soul always in motion?" They then demonstrate that, and ask further: "Is that which is always in motion self-moving?" They show this to be true by considering whether that which moves itself is the "principle of motion" <note>the starting point or source of all movement</note>. Finally, they demonstrate and ask whether the "principle" is **unbegotten** <note>original: "ingenitum"; something that was not created or born but has always existed</note>. This is accepted by everyone as a clear truth. Indeed, that which is unbegotten is also "incorruptible" <note>indestructible</note>. From this manifest truth, one may then collect the demonstration: the principle is unbegotten and incorruptible; the principle of motion is that which is self-moving; the soul is that which is self-moving; therefore, the soul is incorruptible and unbegotten.

**Resolution from supposition** is of this kind: whoever investigates something first supposes it, then observes what follows from that supposition. Afterward, if it is necessary to give a reason for the supposition itself, they assume another supposition and ask whether that which was previously supposed is indeed...

...follows to the second hypothesis. And let him always observe the same method until he ascends to a first principle that is not hypothesized <note>original: "principiū, quod non supponatur"; Alcinous is describing the "Upward Path" of dialectic mentioned in Plato's Republic, where one moves from assumptions to a self-evident truth.</note>. **Induction** <term>Induction (a method of reasoning where one moves from specific examples to a general rule)</term>, however, is any process of reasoning that passes from like things to like things through probability, or from particular cases to universal truths. This form of argumentation contributes greatly to awakening our natural understandings.

### Chapter VI. Types of Propositions and Argumentation.

Of the kind of reason which we call a **proposition**, there are two species: **affirmation** and **negation**. An affirmation is like this: *Socrates walks.* A negation is like this: *Socrates does not walk.* Furthermore, among affirmations and negations, some are "universal" and some are "particular." A **particular affirmative** is: *Some pleasure is good.* A **particular negative** is: *Some pleasure is not good.* A **universal affirmative** is: *All that is shameful is evil.* A **universal negative** is: *Nothing shameful is good.*

Of these propositions, some are **predicative** <term>predicative (simple statements of fact, such as "A is B")</term> and others are **suppositional** <term>suppositional (also known as "hypothetical" or "conditional" statements, such as "If A, then B")</term>. Predicative propositions are simple, such as: *All that is just is good.* Suppositional propositions are those that imply a consequence or a contradiction.

**Plato** makes use of reasoning both for **refutation** <note>original: "redarguēdo"; the process of proving an opponent's claim is false.</note> and for **demonstration** <note>original: "demonstrando"; the process of proving a truth through logic.</note>. He uses refutation through questioning to expose what is false, and demonstration through instruction to reveal what is true.

**Reasoning** <term>Reasoning (here used to mean a "syllogism," which is a logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two or more premises)</term> is a form of speech in which, once certain things are established, a conclusion necessarily follows from them. Some types of reasoning are predicative, some are suppositional, and others are a mixture of both. **Predicative reasonings** are those in which both the premises <note>original: "assumptiones"; the starting points of the argument.</note> and the conclusions are simple propositions. **Suppositional reasonings** are those formed from suppositional propositions. **Mixed reasonings** use both.

Plato uses **demonstrative argumentations** in those dialogues that pertain to the explanation of truth. He uses **probable** and **apparent** arguments against the **Sophists** <term>Sophists (professional teachers in Ancient Greece often accused by Plato of using clever but fallacious arguments)</term> and young men. He uses **contentious** arguments against those who are specifically called "litigious" <note>original: "litigiosi"; those who argue merely for the sake of winning rather than finding truth.</note>, such as in his dialogues with **Euthydemus** and **Hippias**.

Furthermore, since there are three "figures" <term>figures (the different ways a syllogism can be structured based on where the "middle term" is placed)</term> of predicative reasoning:
1.  The **First Figure** is that in which the common term <note>The "middle term" that links the two premises.</note> is the predicate of one premise and the subject of the other.
2.  The **Second Figure** is that in which the common term is the predicate in both premises.
3.  The **Third Figure** is that in which the common term is the subject in both premises.

By "terms," I mean the parts of the propositions; for example, in the statement "man is an animal," we call "man" and "animal" the **terms**.

Plato disputes mostly according to the **First Figure**, though he also uses the **Second** and **Third**. Specifically, in the *Alcibiades* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato concerning the nature of man and politics.</note>, he argues according to the first figure as follows:
*Just things are beautiful; beautiful things are good; therefore, just things are good.*
In the *Parmenides* <note>A complex dialogue by Plato regarding the nature of the "One" and the "Many."</note>, he argues according to the second figure:
*That which has no parts is neither straight nor round. But...*

# ALCINOUS

Whatever shares in shape is either straight or round. Therefore, that which has no parts does not share in any shape; this is according to the third manner <note>original: "ad modum tertiæ"; referring to a specific logical mode or figure</note> as stated in that same book. That which shares in shape has a certain quality; that which shares in shape is finite; therefore, that which has a certain quality is finite. Furthermore, one may find frequent arguments in Plato that are woven together through suppositions <term>suppositions (hypothetical or "if-then" statements)</term>, especially of the following kind in the *Parmenides*: "If the **One** <note>original: "ipsum unum"; the central, indivisible principle discussed in Plato's Parmenides</note> itself has no parts, it has neither a beginning, nor an end, nor a middle. But if it has no beginning, middle, and end, it will have no limit. If it has no limit, it shares in no shape. Therefore, if the One itself has no parts, it shares in no shape." 

Now, according to the second figure of the **suppositional argument** <term>suppositional argument (a hypothetical syllogism where the conclusion follows from a condition)</term>—which many call the third figure, in which the "common term" <note>original: "cōmunis terminus"; in logic, the middle term that links the two premises</note> follows both extremes—he reasons in this manner: "If the One itself has no parts, it is neither straight nor round. If it shares in shape, it is either straight or round. Therefore, if it has no parts, it will not even share in shape." 

Furthermore, according to the third figure (which some wish to call the second), in which the common term precedes both, he argues in a certain way in the *Phaedo*: "If, having acquired knowledge of **Equality** <note>Plato’s theory of "Forms" suggests we know concepts like "Equality" before birth</note> itself, we have never surrendered it to oblivion, we surely know it. But if we have forgotten it, we **recollect** it." 

He likewise uses mixed arguments, which proceed by consequence, in this way: "If the One is a whole and finite, this [One], having a beginning, middle, and end, also shares in shape. The antecedent <term>antecedent (the "if" part of a logical statement)</term> is true, therefore the consequent <term>consequent (the "then" part of a logical statement)</term> is true." 

The differences among those things which occur by consequence are considered in this way: whenever someone has diligently observed the powers of the soul and the various natures of men, as well as the different species of arguments—and then, having considered the opportunity of the time, adapts the proper arguments to specific human emotions by which they may be moved—he will be a **perfect orator**, and his rhetoric will rightly be called the "science of speaking well." <note>This definition of the perfect orator is heavily influenced by Plato's Phaedrus, which argues that true rhetoric requires a deep understanding of psychology and logic.</note>

Let us now also look more clearly into the snares of **sophisms** <term>sophisms (clever but false arguments used to deceive)</term> and "captions" <note>original: "captionúmque"; logical traps or fallacies</note>; we shall perceive them suggested by Plato in the *Euthydemus*. For there, one finds both the sophisms that occur according to words <note>original: "secundum uoces"; verbal fallacies like ambiguity</note> and those that occur according to the things themselves, and their solutions besides. Moreover, he handed down the **ten categories** both in the *Parmenides* itself and in other dialogues. He also embraced all the "topics" <note>original: "Locos"; standard categories of argument</note> derived from **etymology** in the *Cratylus*. And without a doubt, our Plato stood out as a man to be admired above all others in the arts of **division and definition**, which two things most greatly testify to the power of **dialectic** <term>dialectic (the art of investigating the truth of opinions through logical discussion)</term>. Those things which were handed down in the *Cratylus* aim at this: he discusses whether names [derive] their power from nature or from convention <note>original: "positiōe"; the debate over whether words naturally fit their objects or are merely human inventions</note>...

->## ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT<-

...have their own [correctness], and it pleases him that the correctness of names consists in a certain imposition <term>imposition (the act of assigning a name to a thing)</term>; yet he judges that this was not done rashly or by chance, but that the imposition itself followed the nature of things. Thus, the correctness of names is nothing other than an assignment of a word that is in harmony with the nature of the thing itself. For not just any assignment of a name is sufficient for correctness, nor on the other hand is it merely nature or the first utterance of the voice, but it is a composition of both. Thus, the correctness of every name is according to an assignment fitting the nature of things. For it does not mean a name is "correct" if any word is applied to anything at random—as if, for example, we were to assign the name "horse" to a "man." 

Indeed, speaking is one of our human operations. Therefore, a person does not speak correctly by speaking in just any way, but by speaking as the nature of the things themselves requires. Since, however, naming is a part of speech—just as a name is a part of a sentence—naming correctly or incorrectly would not happen through just any random assignment, but through the natural kinship of the name to the thing itself. He will be a correct **founder of names** <note>original: "nominum conditor"; referring to the "Nomothetes" or Lawgiver who first named things in Platonic theory</note> who signifies the nature of the thing through the name. 

For a name is an **instrument** <note>original: "organum"; a tool or functional device</note> of a thing—not just whatever chance provides, but what is suitable to nature. And through this tool, in turn, we indicate things to ourselves and discern their nature. Thus it happens that a name is a certain instrument that indicates and distinguishes the substance of each thing, just as the **weaver’s comb** <note>original: "pecten"; the tool used by a weaver to separate and press the threads of the warp</note> is to the weaver. It will therefore also belong to the **dialectician** <term>dialectician (a master of logic and the nature of reality)</term> to use names correctly, just as the weaver uses the comb: recognizing its proper work, even though the craftsman <note>original: "faber"</note> was the one who made it. In no different way, the dialectician will use a name, which the founder of names shaped, in the way that is fitting. Indeed, it is the craftsman's job to build a tiller <note>original: "temonem"; the pole of a carriage or a ship's rudder/tiller</note>, but it is the pilot's duty to use it correctly. In the same way, the establisher of names will set names correctly if he establishes them as if a dialectician were present, since the dialectician understands the natures of those things that lie hidden under the names. Let these things said about dialectic suffice.

### Chapter 7: The Distinction of Speculative Science.

First, we must speak about **speculative philosophy**. We say its branches are **theology**, **physics**, and **mathematics**. 

The goal of the **theologian** is the knowledge of primary <note>original: "supernarum"; literally "above" or "celestial"</note> causes. 

The goal of the **physicist** is to learn thoroughly what the nature of the world is: what kind of animal man is, what province in the world he has been allotted, whether God provides for all things, and whether other ministers <note>original: "ministri"; referring to lesser deities or spiritual forces</note> are subject to Him, and also how men relate themselves to the gods. 

The goal of the **mathematician** is to know nature as it is planar and extended into three dimensions, and to observe the motion and progress of the celestial bodies. And thus, in a certain summary, the mathematician’s speculation...

...be proposed. This was certainly undertaken by Plato for the sharpening of thought, reaching into the soul and sharpening the mind’s edge for the intuition of divine things. 

Moreover, that part of the mathematical faculty which looks to numbers provides no small power for perceiving divine things; indeed, it frees us from the error and ignorance that revolves around these sensible <note>Meaning physical things perceived by the senses.</note> objects, offering help toward the knowledge of essence and making a person ready for the contest because of their skill <term>peritiam</term> <note>Latin: *peritiam*</note> in the order and consequences of things. 

Geometry also seems to contribute very much to understanding the Good itself: provided that one does not pursue it for the sake of mechanical measurement, but uses it so that by its aids one may ascend to higher things, and does not persist only in measuring things that arise and perish. 

Furthermore, stereometry—that is, the measurement of solids—is extremely useful. For after the second dimension <note>literally "augmentation"; referring here to 2D planes</note>, its consideration follows, taking up the third dimension. 

Moreover, astronomy is useful as a kind of fourth discipline, through which we behold the movements of the heavens and stars, and the Author of day and night, months and years. From these, as if from a neighboring region, we investigate the Author of all these things; and from these disciplines—as if from certain benches, elements, and steps—we proceed to higher things. 

We must also learn music, applying our hearing to it. For just as the eyes were created for astronomy, so the ears were created for harmony. Indeed, just as by applying ourselves to astronomy we are led from those things perceived by the eyes to an invisible essence, so too by drinking in the harmony of voices with our ears, we gradually approach intelligible things from those that are heard. 

Therefore, unless we pursue mathematics for the sake of this end, the curiosity for these things is surely considered crippled and mindless, and of no value. For it is proper to cross over immediately from those things perceived by the eyes and ears to those things which reason alone discerns. 

For the study of mathematics is a kind of prelude to the contemplation of divine things. Indeed, arithmetic and geometry, and those who cultivate them, desire to see essence itself. Nevertheless, they dream about it in a way, yet cannot truly discern it; they are ignorant of the principles and those things which are constituted from the principles. 

But they nonetheless contribute to those things we have mentioned. Therefore, Plato did not think that disciplines of this kind should be called **sciences** <note>original: "scientias"; here referring to absolute, certain knowledge (episteme) rather than mere technical skill</note>. However, the faculty of dialectic rises from geometrical suppositions to the first principles, which are not "supposed" <note>meaning they are self-evident or foundational, not assumed for the sake of argument</note> at all. Therefore <term>Quapropter</term> <note>Latin: *Quapropter*</note>, he rightly called dialectic a science.

### Chapter 8: On Prime Matter.

<margin>Plato 8</margin> After these things, let us briefly discuss the principles and those matters that pertain to theology, beginning from the primary things and descending from there to the generation of the world itself, and finally even to the birth of humans. 

<margin>Plato</margin> In the first place, therefore, matter must be treated. This he [Plato] indeed names the mold <note>original: *effigiem*; in this context, the receptacle that takes an impression</note> of all things, the receptacle, the nurse, the mother, the place, and the subject. He asserts that it is "touched" without the use of the senses and is comprehended by a kind of bastard reasoning <note>original: *adulterina ratiocinatione*; a translation of Plato's *logismos nothos*, referring to how we "see" matter not through our eyes or pure logic, but by a sort of indirect mental deduction</note>. 

<margin>Plato</margin> He maintains that the proper nature of matter is to receive all generations and to cherish them like a nurse. Likewise, it takes on all forms, although by its own nature it is devoid of all form, quality, and appearance <term>species</term> <note>Latin: *species*; here used to mean the specific "look" or "type" of a thing</note>. Furthermore, he asserts that it is sprinkled and shaped by forms like a mold, though it shares in no shape or quality by itself. Nor indeed would the subject be suitably prepared for the various impressions of forms unless it completely lacked every quality it was about to receive. For we see those who strive to make sweet-smelling ointments from oil seek out an oil that is tainted by no scent at all; and those who are about to impress forms into wax or clay first polish and smooth the material itself completely, until the former shapes are erased. For it is appropriate for universal matter—if it is to receive all forms—to have none of their natures, but to be subjected to the forms without any quality or appearance of its own. And since it is of such a kind, it will be neither a body, nor even incorporeal, but a body in potential <note>original: *potentia*; it has the capacity to become a physical thing but has no dimensions or weight on its own</note>, just as bronze is a statue in potential, because once it receives the form, it will become a statue.

### Chapter 9: On Ideas and the Efficient Cause.

<margin>Incipet</margin> Since matter truly possesses the character of a certain principle, Plato introduces other principles besides matter: namely, the exemplary principle <note>the model or blueprint of the world</note>, to which the Ideas themselves are reduced; and the paternal principle, which pertains to God, the cause of all things. 

<margin>Plato</margin> An Idea, moreover, is—in relation to God—God’s act of understanding <note>original: *intellectio dei*</note>. In relation to the sensible world, it is the Model <term>exemplar</term> <note>the "blueprint" or eternal pattern for physical things</note>. In relation to itself, it is Essence. For whatever is made by intelligence must necessarily refer to something, which will indeed be the model of the work; just as if something were made by someone—for instance, an image of myself made by me. <margin>L iii</margin>
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

...the pattern is not entirely separate from the agent, just as every craftsman, conceiving the patterns of his crafts within himself, then unfolds their forms into matter. They define the Idea <note>original: *Ideam*; in Platonic thought, these are the perfect, eternal templates of which physical objects are mere copies</note> as the eternal pattern of those things that are created according to nature. For most of those who followed Plato, it was not at all pleasing that there should exist an Idea of man-made things, such as a shield or a lyre; nor, again, of those things that are contrary to nature, such as a fever or an imbalance of bile; nor of individuals, such as Socrates or Plato; nor even of any of those things that are imperfect, such as filth or chaff; nor of relations, such as "greater" or "exceeding." For they say that the Ideas are the eternal thoughts of God, perfect in themselves. 

That Ideas truly exist, they prove in this way: Whether God is Intellect <note>original: *intellectus*; referring to the divine Mind or *Nous*</note> itself, or is something intellectual, eternal and unmoving notions are present within him. If this is the case, then Ideas exist. For indeed, if a measure by its very nature lacks matter, it must receive its measures from something higher and entirely detached from matter. The premise is true, therefore the conclusion is true; and if this is so, Ideas are certain measures existing without the mixture of matter. It follows that if the world is not as it is by some rash chance, it was made not only *from* something, but also *by* someone; and not only that, but it was also fashioned *according* to something. Now, what else exists as that according to which it was made besides the Idea? From which it follows that the Ideas themselves exist. Likewise, if intellect differs from true opinion, the intelligible <note>original: *intelligibile*; things that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note> will also differ from the opinable <note>original: *opinabili*; things known through "opinion" or sensory perception, which can be deceptive</note>. If this is true, there will exist intelligibles different from opinables, such that there are also primary intelligibles, just as there are primary sensibles. From this it is concluded that Ideas exist.

### Chapter 10: How God is Described, and by What Reasons He is Investigated.

Next, we must speak of the third principle, which Plato asserts is almost inexpressible. Nevertheless, let us attempt to show it in this way. If there are intelligibles—and these are neither sensibles, nor connected with them, but there exist primary simple intelligibles among the primary intelligibles, just as there are primary sensibles—then the premise is true, and therefore the conclusion follows. Indeed, humans—being occupied by the disturbance of the senses—whenever they decide to contemplate something intelligible, they soon fall back into the imagination of some sensible thing, to such an extent that they often apply either size, or shape, or color to that which is to be understood. Because of this, they are unable to understand that thing purely <note>original: *sincere*; meaning without the contamination of physical sensory data</note>. But the gods, without the mixture of bodily things, understand with extreme purity and clarity. Since indeed the intellect is better than the soul, and that intellect which is "in act" <note>original: *in actu*; a philosophical term meaning "actualized" or "currently functioning," as opposed to "potential"</note> is better than that which is "in potential," that intellect which always understands all things at once is finally the most beautiful...

...because he is the cause of it, and because he stands above all things, he indeed exists as the first God himself. He is the cause that the mind of the world <note>The *Nous* or World-Intellect, a secondary divine principle that organizes the cosmos</note> always acts, while he himself remains always unmoved, just as the sun acts upon the eye when it is presented. He moves things in the same way that an object of desire, though itself unmoved, stirs the one who desires it. In this way, the supreme mind itself leads the mind of the entire heaven. And since this first Intellect is the most beautiful thing possible, it is necessary that the most beautiful object of thought be subject to it. But nothing is more beautiful than God himself; therefore, he always understands himself and his own notions. And this operation of his is the "Idea." 

Moreover, God himself is supreme, eternal, ineffable, and perfect in himself. He is in need of nothing, and is always and everywhere absolutely perfect. He is the Divinity, the very reason of essence; he is Truth, he is Harmony, and he exists as the Good. Yet I do not number these attributes in such a way as to separate them from one another; rather, I contemplate them all together as one. 

He is called "the Good" for this reason: because he fills all things with benefits according to the capacity of each, and is the cause of all good things. He is "the Beautiful" because he is, by his very nature, fullness itself and all harmony. He is likewise called "Truth" because he is the principle of all truth, just as the sun is the principle of all universal light. He is also the "Father" because he is the cause of all things, and he adorns the mind of the whole heaven and the soul of the world according to his own pattern. For by the gift of his will he has filled all things with himself, awakening the soul of the world and turning it toward himself, since he is the cause of its mind. And that mind, adorned by the Father’s favor, in turn fully adorns the whole nature of this world. 

Furthermore, God is called "ineffable" <note>original: *ineffabilis*; meaning that which cannot be expressed in words</note> and perceivable by the mind alone, because there is no genus surrounding him, nor species, nor any difference, nor does anything happen to him by "accident" <note>technical term for a non-essential quality</note>. For he is not evil—to say so would be a sacrilege. Nor is he even "good" in the sense that he exists by participating in some external goodness. Nor does any "difference" happen to him, for that cannot occur according to his nature. Nor does he have quality, for he is not a "qualified" effect. Yet he is not formless, for he is not deprived of any quality belonging to him. He is not a part of anything, nor is he a "whole" as if composed of parts. He is not the "same" as anything else, nor "different" from others; for nothing happens to him by which he might be distinguished from others. He neither moves, nor is he moved. 

Whence, the first way of understanding him is through "removal" <note>original: *ablationem*; also known as the *via negativa*, a theological method of defining God by what He is NOT (e.g., "immortal" = "not mortal")</note> of all these things, just as we think of a mathematical point by way of removal: considering first the surface, then the line, and finally the point. The second way of understanding him is according to the principle of proportion <note>or analogy</note> in this manner: just as the sun stands in relation to sight and to the things seen—not being sight itself, but providing the one with the power to see and the others with the quality of being seen—in exactly the same relation does the primary Intellect stand to the understanding of the soul...

->T<-
<meta>catchword: third</meta>

...is in them, and those things which are understood; for he is not the same thing as the intellect itself. Nevertheless, he extends the power of understanding to the soul so that it may understand, and to the objects of thought <note>original: "intelligibilibus" — things that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses</note> so that they may be understood, illuminating the truth that resides within them. 

The third mode of understanding is as follows: A person noticing the beauty present in physical bodies directs themselves to the beauty of the soul, then to that beauty found in duties and laws, and finally to the very fountain of beauty itself. Above this, they perceive that the Good itself is to be loved and sought after—shining like a sudden brilliance upon the soul that has flown upward to that height. Because of its excellence, one recognizes this light to be God himself.

Furthermore, one acknowledges him primarily as being without the magnitude of quantity. For a part, and that from which something is constituted, always precedes that of which it is a part; for a plane is prior to a body, and a line is prior to a plane. Since he has no parts, he will be moved neither according to place nor according to alteration. For if he undergoes change, he must be transformed either by himself or by someone else. If by another, that other would surely be stronger. If by himself, he would transition either into something worse or something better. Yet both are impossible. From all these points, it is clear that he is himself incorporeal <note>lacking a physical body or material substance</note>. 

However, the same will also be clear from what follows. If God were a body, he would consist of matter and form, because every body is a certain composition of matter and form together, which is rendered similar to the Ideas <note>The eternal "Forms" or blueprints in the mind of God</note> while it participates in them by some ineffable reason. But it is absurd for God to be constituted of matter and form. For he would then be neither "simple" <note>In philosophy, "simple" means "not made of parts" and therefore indestructible</note> nor a "principle" <note>The primary source or starting point of all things</note>. Therefore, God is incorporeal. 

Moreover, if he were a body, he would consist of matter. Therefore, he would be either fire, or air, or earth, or water, or something forged from these. But in whatever way he existed, he would not be a principle at all, and matter itself would be prior to him, if indeed he were made from matter. Since these ideas are impious, it is necessary that God be incorporeal. For if he were a body, he could be destroyed, he would have been born, and he would be subject to change. Yet none of these things apply to God.

### Chapter XI: Qualities are incorporeal.

Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that qualities <note>The properties of a thing, like color, heat, or virtue</note> are incorporeal in this manner. Every body is a "subject" <note>The underlying thing that possesses traits</note>, whereas a quality is not a subject at all, but an "accident" <note>A property that exists only within a substance; for example, "whiteness" cannot exist without a white object</note>; therefore, quality is not a body. No body exists *in* a subject, but every quality exists *in* a subject; therefore, quality is not a body. Likewise, quality is contrary to quality, but no body—as a body—is contrary to another body. Therefore, qualities are not bodies. Moreover, it is most consistent with reason that just as matter is devoid of quality, so too should quality be devoid of matter. And if it lacks matter, it cannot be a body...

<meta>This page transitions from the "theological" discussion of the First God (the Good) to "physics," or the study of the natural world. It concludes the argument that God must be incorporeal because active forces must be non-physical, whereas bodies are passive and changing.</meta>

...would perish. <note>The text continues from the previous page's final word "be..." to complete the thought that if God were a body, he would be subject to destruction.</note> For indeed, if bodies were merely qualities, then two or three bodies could occupy the same location at once, which is far from reasonable. But if qualities are incorporeal <note>not made of physical matter</note>, then the craftsman who makes them must also be incorporeal. Furthermore, nothing can be an active force except for that which is incorporeal; for bodies are passive and in flux, never remaining in the same way or staying in the same state. Even in those instances where bodies might seem to cause something to happen, they will be found to be much more affected by others. Therefore, just as there is something that is entirely passive, so there must necessarily exist something that is entirely active. We shall find that this active thing is nothing other than the incorporeal. Let this discourse on the principles of things, which is called "theological," now reach its end here. For next, it seems we must descend into that discussion which is called "physics" <note>original: "physica" — in the ancient sense, this means the study of nature and the physical universe</note>.

->ON IMAGINATION AND INTELLECT<-

### Chapter 12: On causes, generation, elements, and the order of the world.

It is necessary that there be certain pre-defined patterns—called Ideas <term>Ideas: eternal, perfect blueprints or "Forms" that exist in the divine mind</term>—for all bodily things that are created as distinct entities according to nature. Scientific knowledge and definitions should be referred back to these Ideas. For beyond individual men, it is right to understand "Man" itself; and beyond individual horses, "Horse" itself; and generally, beyond all living creatures, a "Living Creature" that is immortal and unbegotten. Just as many images are impressed from a single seal, or many images are made of one man, the Idea itself is the cause for all these things being of the same kind as the Idea is. 

Therefore, this entire world—the most beautiful work of God—must have been fashioned by God himself in such a way that he looked toward a certain Idea as a pattern for this world during its construction. While God equipped himself for the construction of this "machine" with a wonderful providence <note>divine care or foresight</note> and the best of rules—that is, his own goodness—he brought it forth from the whole of matter. Indeed, before the generation of the heavens, this matter was in a state of chaotic turmoil without any order; God called it back from this formless confusion into a beautiful order. He decorated its parts on all sides with fitting numbers and figures, so that the world might be woven together with that same proportion which fire and earth still maintain toward air and water. 

At that time, only the traces of these elements lay confused within the receptacle <note>the "receptacle" is a Platonic term for the space or "womb" in which matter is formed</note>, without reason or measure; they shook the matter and were in turn shaken by it. For he fashioned the world from the entirety of the four elements <term>four elements: fire, air, water, and earth—the fundamental building blocks of the universe in ancient science</term>—namely, from all the fire, air, water, and earth—leaving no part or power of them remaining elsewhere. For he foresaw that the world was to be a body, and therefore must be perceptible through touch and sight. But without the presence of fire and earth, nothing can move the senses of sight or touch. For this reason, following a congruent logic, he constructed the world from fire and earth; since, however, by a certain bond of both...
