...<note>original: "rectum" — This is a catchword from the previous page, likely completing a sentence about "rightly" or "correctly" ordering the world.</note> it was necessary to bind the middle to the extremes. For a divine bond is one that is formed according to proportion, which makes both itself and the things it binds into a single unit. Since the world was not intended to be a flat plane—in which case a single middle term would have sufficed—but was destined to be spherical <note>referring here to a three-dimensional solid</note>, it required two middle terms. For this reason, air and water were placed between fire and earth according to a harmony of proportion. Thus, as fire is to air, so air is to water; and as air is to water, so water is to earth. Conversely, as earth is to water, so water is to air; and as water is to air, so air is to fire. 

Furthermore, because the Creator left nothing outside of the world, He made it unique, corresponding in number to its own Idea <term>Idea: the eternal, perfect blueprint in the divine mind</term>, which is also unique. Moreover, neither disease nor old age could ever affect it, since nothing remains outside that could exert force upon it. Instead, it would remain self-sufficient, lacking nothing, and preserved in safety. He gave it a spherical shape, as it is the most beautiful of all shapes, the most spacious, and the easiest to move. And since it had no need of hearing, sight, or the other senses, He added no sensory organs at all for the purpose of perception. He likewise commanded all other types of motion to be far away, granting it only circular motion, as this is the proper movement for the mind and for wisdom.

### Chapter 13: On the compatibility of shapes with the elements of the world and the world itself.

**A**ND since there are two things from which the world is constructed—namely, body and soul—the former is visible and subject to decay, while the latter is invisible and intangible; thus, the power and constitution of each is different. Indeed, the body of the world is compacted from fire, earth, water, and air. The Architect of the world Himself, encompassing these four, gave them shape—observing no prior order among the elements—using the pyramid, the cube, the octahedron (that is, a shape of eight faces), and the icosahedron (that is, a shape of twenty faces). Upon the whole, He impressed the dodecahedron (that is, a shape of twelve faces). 

Therefore, insofar as matter took on the shape of a pyramid, fire shone forth. This shape is indeed thin and more suited for cutting than the others, composed of fewer triangles, and therefore the lightest of all shapes. Insofar as it took on the octahedron, it assumed the quality of air. But when it first took the icosahedron shape, it obtained the nature of water. Finally, He bestowed the cubic shape upon earth, which is the most solid and stable of all the elements. Lastly, He used the dodecahedron shape for the fabric of the universe. The nature of planes <note>two-dimensional surfaces</note> is more ancient than all of these, for planes precede solids. Of the nature of planes, there are two primary origins for right-angled shapes: the scalene and the isosceles. A scalene triangle is one...

...having a right angle, another of two-thirds of a right angle, and another of one-third. Therefore, let the <term>scalene triangle: a triangle where all three sides and angles are unequal</term> be the element of the <term>pyramid: here referring to the four-sided tetrahedron, representing fire</term>, the <term>octahedron: an eight-sided solid representing air</term>, and the <term>icosahedron: a twenty-sided solid representing water</term>. Since the pyramid is constituted of four equilateral triangles <note>original: "æquilateris" — triangles with all sides equal</note>, each of which is distributed into six scalene triangles. The octahedron figure, however, consists of eight similar ones, each of which is divided into six scalene triangles. The icosahedron figure similarly consists of twenty. But the <term>isosceles triangle: a triangle with two equal sides</term> is the element of the cubic figure <note>the cube represents earth</note>. For four isosceles triangles coming together complete a square; and from six such squares, a cube is fashioned.

But God Himself adopted the <term>dodecahedron: a twelve-sided solid</term> figure for the construction of the universe <note>Plato associated the dodecahedron with the shape of the entire cosmos</note>. Whence also the twelve forms of animals are seen in the circle of the <term>zodiac: the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</term>, each of which is cut into thirty parts <note>the 30 degrees of each zodiac sign</note>. Similarly, in the dodecahedron figure itself, one may observe twelve <term>pentagons: five-sided shapes</term>, each divided into triangles in such a way that each exists divided by six triangles. Thus, in the entire dodecahedron, three hundred and sixty triangles are found, exactly as many portions as exist in the zodiac. 

By these shapes, matter—having been formed by God Himself—began to be stirred. At first, it moved in traces without order, but then it was reduced into order by God, with each part tempered with one another according to proportion. Yet these elements do not remain separate in one place; they possess a constant agitation and bring that motion into matter. For they are kept constricted by the circumference of the world and are carried along, agitated by mutual alternating pulses, the thin particles being driven into the province of the solid ones. For this reason, no empty space remains at all, and the inequality, persisting continually, provides the cause for this pulsing. For by these shapes matter is shaken, and these shapes are in turn shaken by matter.

## Chapter 14: On the World Soul, the Spheres, and the Stars.

<margin>e</margin>
Thus, he allowed us to investigate the powers of the soul starting from physical bodies. For since we discern individual things by means of the soul, God rightly bestowed the principles of all things upon it, so that whatever we might ever encounter, we might recognize it through a certain kinship and apply the soul’s essence in harmony with those things. 

Therefore, while he said that there is a certain intelligible and indivisible substance, he also taught that there is another substance dispersed around bodies. He found that the soul is able to perceive both substances through intelligence. And because he recognized that there is "the Same" and "the Other" <note>original: "ipsum idem, atq; ipsum alterum" — these are the Platonic categories of Sameness and Difference used to explain how the soul can understand both eternal truths and changing physical things</note> both in things pertaining to intelligence and in those pertaining to sense, he rightly constituted the soul out of all these. For either "like is known by like" (as pleases the <term>Pythagoreans: followers of the philosopher Pythagoras who emphasized mathematics</term>), or, as it pleases the physicist <term>Heraclitus: a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine of change</term>, "unlike is always known by unlike." 

Furthermore, when <term>Plato</term> says that the world was "generated" <note>created or born</note>, it is by no means to be believed that he meant that a period of time once preceded the world. Rather, he says this because the world always persists in a state of "becoming" and indicates a cause for its existence that is more excellent than itself.

# ALCINOUS

Furthermore, God did not create the <term>World Soul: the animating spirit of the universe</term>—which has always existed—but rather adorned it. In this sense, He is sometimes said to "make" it because He awakens it and turns its mind toward Himself, as if from a certain deep sleep <note>original: "somno" — the soul is awakened from a state of potentiality to active intelligence</note>. Thus, by looking toward those things which are understood by God and desiring divine concepts, the soul receives the species and forms from Him. It is clear, moreover, that the world was granted a soul and a mind by God himself. For since He wished for it to be the most excellent work, He rightly made the world both animate and intellectual. For a living creation is entirely superior to a non-living one, and that which possesses a mind is superior to that which is void of mind. Perhaps a mind could not even approach the world without a soul. And since the soul poured itself out from the center of the world to its furthest extremities, it embraced the entire body of the world in a circle, covering the whole and communicating itself to its individual parts. In this way, it connects the world with an unbreakable bond and preserves it in safety. And that power of the soul which remained on the outside precedes its innermost parts. For that outer part remained undivided; but the inner portion was divided into seven circles, distributed everywhere from the very beginning by <term>double and triple intervals: harmonic ratios used in Platonic music theory and cosmology</term>. And indeed, that part which is contained by the indivisible sphere remains related to that which is called **the Same**; but that which is dispersed is related to that which, conversely, is called **the Other**. For the motion of the heaven which encompasses all things is one, since it never wanders, and it maintains a principal order. But truly, the progress of the subjects below is varied, changed by their rising and setting. Hence it is called a "wandering" or an "erratic movement." The outermost circle indeed runs across to the right from the rising to the setting. But the inner circle, conversely, resists the upper one, moving to the left from the west to the east. Furthermore, God himself fashioned the stars and constellations: those which do not wander at all, for the adornment of the heaven and the night. And the number of such stars is innumerable. But those which do wander are seven in number, serving for the origin of number and time, and for the illumination of all things. Time clearly made the interval of the world's motion, like a certain <term>image of eternity: a famous Platonic definition of time</term> <note>original: "æternitatis imaginem"</note>. Indeed, eternity is the measure of the eternal world's state. Also, the power of the wandering stars is certainly not the same for all. For the **Sun** is the leader of all the rest, both illuminating and revealing the universe to our eyes. Next, the **Moon** holds the second rank for the sake of her power. The other planets each follow according to their own proportion and lot. Indeed, the Moon indicates the limit of a month, running through her circle in that space and overtaking the sun. The Sun, however, is the measure of the year, for running through the circle of the zodiac it completes the seasons of the year. Each of the other stars is also carried in its own circuit. And indeed, these circuits are known not to just any men, but to the learned.

Each of these stars is a living and intelligent being, and they are moreover called gods; their shapes are round.

## Chapter 15. On daemons and elements.

**T**here are also others, who are called <term>daemons: intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not to be confused with modern "demons"</term> within the individual elements. We may call these "intelligible gods"; some are visible, while others escape the sharpness of our sight. They dwell in the ether, fire, air, and water, so that no part of the world should be left void of soul or of a nature superior to living creatures. All earthly things and those beneath the moon are subject to these beings. For the God of the whole world is the author of the gods and daemons, and by the gift of the divine will, this universe shall never hereafter be dissolved. However, His sons <note>original: "filii" — referring to the created celestial gods/planets</note> preside over the other works, transforming individual things according to the Father’s command and imitation. From these come the stirring of those in a frenzy, divine raptures, dreams, oracles, and whatever else happens to mortals through <term>prophecy: the art of foretelling the future through divine inspiration</term>. 

The Earth is situated in the very middle of everything, pressed together around the axis <note>original: "discordiam agitationémue" — likely a corruption or variant of "discursum" or "axem," referring to the central axis of the universe</note> that extends through the whole. It is the guardian of day and night, and the most ancient of all the gods that are within the heavens. And after the Soul of the whole world, the Earth provides us with sweet nourishment. The heaven revolves around it, and the Earth itself is a kind of star; for this reason, it remains immovable, as it is balanced in the center like those things which contain it. The ether, however, has been allotted the outer province, distributed into the spheres of the wandering stars and the non-wandering stars. After these follows the air. In the middle, the Earth has settled down together with its moisture.

## Chapter 16. The younger gods are the craftsmen of man. On the transmigration of the soul.

When all these things had been fashioned, three types of mortal living beings remained: those that fly, those that swim, and those that walk. The <term>World-Maker: the Demiurge or divine craftsman</term> entrusted the generation of these creatures to his sons <note>The "sons" are the younger, celestial gods or stars mentioned in the previous chapter</note>. For if he himself had brought these to life, they would have been born immortal. Therefore, borrowing particles from the primary matter—to be returned once certain fixed cycles of time had passed—the younger gods fashioned the mortal types of living beings. However, because he cared for the human race as one more closely related to both the Father God and his offspring, the Architect of all things himself sent down souls for this race, equal in number to the stars.

But when he had placed each soul upon a related star as if upon a chariot, he explained the laws of fate to them like a legislator, so that he himself might remain free from the blame of any future sins. He taught them that mortal disturbances would arise from the body: first, sensory perception; then pleasure and pain; and fear and anger. He declared that those who overcame these passions and did not allow themselves to be led by them would live justly and finally return to their kindred star. However, the soul that was overcome by injustice would, in its second birth, migrate into the life of a woman. And those who still did not cease from wickedness would finally degenerate into the nature of brute animals. He taught that the end of their labors would only come when they had expelled the physical passions born within them and returned to their own proper state of being.

## Chapter 17. On the body, the limbs of man, and the powers of the soul.

These younger gods first fashioned man out of earth, fire, air, and water, borrowing certain portions from matter—to be returned eventually—and binding them together with hidden links to create a single body out of them all. Next, they placed the more excellent part of the soul <note>The rational part of the soul</note> in the head, having first prepared the brain as if it were a cultivated field. Around the face, they arranged the organs that serve as the instruments of the senses. They also composed the marrow from smooth and straight triangles <note>original: "triangulis" — Alcinous follows Plato's theory that the four elements are composed of microscopic geometric shapes</note>, from which the elements had been generated, to be the future source of the generative seed.

Furthermore, they fashioned bone out of marrow and earth, after they had repeatedly moistened these two with fire and water. They made the nerves from bone and flesh. Flesh, however, was compacted from a certain salty and sharp fermentation. They surrounded the bones with marrow, and used nerves for the sake of joining the bones together. From this arrangement, the bending of the joints and the knots of the limbs were produced through the service of the nerves. Finally, a covering was added to them by means of the flesh, which was rendered both white and abundant for the sake of the living creature's beauty and utility. Beyond these, the internal organs were entwined, including the belly and the intestines coiled all around it. From the mouth above...

They assigned the power of anger to the heart, and the power of desire to the belly and those parts around the navel, which we shall discuss in later sections.

### Chapter 18. On sight, light, and mirror images.

But after they carved light-bearing eyes into the face, they kindled a fiery light within them. Because this light was gentle and somewhat dense, they considered it a kinsman of the divine light. This light flows out everywhere through the eyes, but it runs through the pupils more purely and abundantly. When this light is mixed with and strengthened by an external brightness of a similar nature, it provides the sense of seeing. Therefore, when night comes or the light is shadowed, this ray of ours no longer mixes with the nearby air. Consequently, it withdraws into the interior, smoothing and loosening our internal motions, and soothes the limbs with sleep. For this reason, it closes the eyelids once it has been retracted. If it induces a great deal of rest, sleep creeps in almost without dreams. But if some agitations still remain, frequent <term>phantasms: mental images or apparitions</term> occur to us. In this way, imaginations—whether true or false—are born through a direct path. Following these are the images seen in mirrors or other translucent and smooth bodies, which result in no other way than through <note>original: *reuerberationẽ*</note> reflection. According to whether the mirror is concave, convex, or oblong, different sights will appear to those looking. For the lights will be reflected in other directions, being repelled and dispersed by a convex mirror, but coming together in a concave one. For this reason, in some mirrors, right and left appear reversed; in others, they appear the same; and in some, the upper parts are turned to the lower, and vice versa.

### Chapter 19. On the other senses and their objects.

**H**earing was indeed created for the perception of the voice, arising from a movement that is produced around the head and descends all the way to the <term>liver: *iecur*; in Platonic thought, the liver was the seat of the lowest part of the soul</term>. The voice, however, penetrates through the ears, the brain, and the blood to the soul. A high pitch is that which moves faster, a low pitch moves slower; a loud voice is composed of much movement, a small voice of little.

After this follows the power of the nostrils, brought forth for the perception of smells. Now, an odor is a certain <term>passion: *passio*, meaning a physical sensation or state</term> flowing through the veins of the nostrils as far as the regions of the navel; its types have no names at all except for two general ones. And indeed, these are called nothing other than "good smell" and "bad smell," which are the names for sweetness and nausea. Certainly, all odor is thicker than air but finer than water. This kind of odor specifically occurs in those things which have not yet undergone a complete transformation, but consist of a certain mixture of air and water, such as those made of smoke and mist; for from the alternation of these, the sense of smelling is produced.

Next, the gods fashioned taste as a judge of very diverse <term>juices: *succorum*, referring here to the flavors or "saps" of substances</term>, extending veins from the tongue to the seat of the heart, by which various liquids might be examined. Indeed, as these veins are variously dilated and contracted according to the impact of the juices, they discern their variety. There are seven differences of flavors: sweet, sharp, <term>puckering: *ponticus*, literally "from the Black Sea," used here to describe a specific astringent flavor</term>, harsh, salty, pungent, and bitter. And indeed, the nature of the sweet is contrary to all the rest; for it bathes and soothes the moisture absorbed by the tongue. The sharp disturbs and disperses it. The pungent inflames and flies upward. That which violently wipes away and liquefies is called bitter. But that which purges more gently and softens is salty. Among those flavors that block the passages of the tongue and contract them, those that act more harshly are called "puckering"; those that do so more gently are called harsh.

Finally, the sense of touch was created by the gods so that it might distinguish hot and cold, soft and hard, light and heavy, and smooth and rough. We call those bodies "yielding" which give way to the touch, and "resisting" those which do not yield at all. This happens because of the foundations of the bodies themselves. For those that have broad, stable, and solid foundations are hard; those, on the contrary, which use a small foundation, are yielding, soft, and slippery. That which is unequal and hard is surely rough; that which is level and <term>oily: *pinguem*, literally "fatty," describing a smooth or sleek texture</term> at the same time is smooth. Since, however, the sensations of hot and cold are quite opposite, they are brought about by different causes. For that which cuts with the sharpness and velocity of its parts produces the sensation of heat. Cold, however, is produced by that which is slower in its entry, while the thinner parts are expelled and the thicker parts are forced to penetrate into their places. Then indeed, a shaking and trembling occurs, and the sensation that arises in bodies from this is called <term>shivering: *rigor*, referring to the physical contraction and trembling of being cold</term>.

# ON IMAGINATION AND INTELLECT

### Chapter 20. On the heavy and the light.

<margin>g</margin>It is not proper to define "heavy" and "light" by "upper" and "lower" locations. For nothing is truly either "up" or "down." Since the heavens are entirely spherical and smoothed equally across their convex surface, it is not right to declare any part as "higher" or any part as "lower." Rather, "heavy" should be said of that which is moved with difficulty into a place outside its own nature, while "light" is that which is moved easily. Likewise, the "heavy" is that which is composed of very many parts, while the "light" is that which is composed of very few.

### Chapter 21. On respiration.

<margin>r</margin> We breathe in this manner: the vast air surrounding us on all sides flows in through the mouth, the nostrils, and other hidden passages of the body. Once warmed, it strives to flow back out toward the external, kindred air. But from the part where it has flowed out, it pushes the outer air back into the internal parts. And so, through such a never-ceasing cycle, inhalation and exhalation follow. <note>This refers to the Platonic theory of *periphesis* or "circular thrusting," where air expelled from the lungs pushes surrounding air back into the body through the pores of the skin.</note>

### Chapter 22. On the causes of diseases.

<margin>m</margin>He taught that there are many causes of diseases. The first is an excess or deficiency of the elements, and the movement of these elements into regions of the body that are not at all suitable to their nature. The second is the mutual transformation of related substances. For instance, if blood, bile, or <term>phlegm: *pituita*; one of the four humors of ancient medicine</term> is produced from the flesh; for all these are nothing other than a melting and a decay. Indeed, phlegm is the liquefaction of fresh flesh. Sweats and tears are a certain discharge and the remains of phlegm. Furthermore, when phlegm is expelled externally, it induces white <term>skin-eruptions: *insectiones*; likely referring to conditions like vitiligo or leprosy</term>. But internally, when mixed with black bile, it produces the "comitial disease" <note>original: *morbum comitialem*; an ancient name for epilepsy, so called because a seizure was seen as a bad omen that could halt the *comitia* or Roman assemblies</note>, which is called "sacred." Moreover, sharp and salty phlegm is the cause of those sufferings which occur through a flux (a discharge of fluid). For all who are burdened by both phlegm and bile must necessarily suffer this. Indeed, bile combined with phlegm produces innumerable and various diseases. He believes that a continuous fever happens from an excess of fire; a daily fever from air; a tertian fever from water; and finally, a quartan fever from earth. Next, we must speak of the soul, taking our beginning from here, even if we seem to be returning to the same subject.

For they willed its dwelling place to be the head, fashioned in that same shape in which the world was elaborated <note>referring to the spherical shape of the head as a microcosm of the universe</note>. They placed the rest of the body beneath it as a servant, like a vehicle. To those [parts...]

...to the mortal parts they assigned individual provinces. Specifically, they assigned the chest to anger. They engineered the lungs for the sake of the heart, making them soft and airy, hollow like a pipe and similar to a sponge, so that the heart—lest it boil over with the heat of anger—might be cooled by some measure of refrigeration. The liver, however, was given both sweetness and bitterness to excite and then soothe the soul's desire. Furthermore, it was so designed that divinations occurring through dreams might shine within it <note>The liver was historically viewed in Platonism as a "mirror" for the irrational part of the soul, reflecting images from the rational mind.</note>. Indeed, because of its smoothness, solidity, and luster, he believed that a power flowing from the mind reflects there. The spleen, moreover, exists for the sake of the liver, both to purge it and keep it bright, so that corrosive impurities <note>original: "putredines corrodentes"</note> which flow around the liver during certain illnesses might drain away into the spleen.

### Chapter 24. On the distinction between the parts of the soul.

<margin>q</margin> That these three parts of the soul are separated into their own specific locations can be learned from the following. First, those things which are distinct by nature are separate. Now, nature distinguishes that which possesses reason from that which is subject to reason. For the former is concerned with the intelligible <note>Intelligible: Things that can only be understood by the mind, rather than perceived by the senses.</note>, while the latter is concerned with pain and pleasure. Furthermore, reason belongs to humans alone, whereas the part of the soul that obeys the emotions is common to all other living creatures as well. Therefore, since the rational and irrational portions of the soul are distinct by nature, they must also be separated by location. For these two are often found to conflict with one another. Nothing, however, can be in conflict with itself, nor can things that are contrary to each other exist in the same place, in the same respect, and at the same time. 

In the character of Medea <note>Medea: A figure from Greek mythology who, in Euripides' tragedy, kills her own children to take revenge on her husband, Jason. She is a classic example of the conflict between passion and reason.</note>, anger is seen to struggle against reason; she says, "I understand that the things I am about to do are evil, yet anger overcomes my better judgment." <note>original: "intelligo... quæ factura ſum eſſe mala, ira tamen conſilium ſuperat"</note> Likewise in the case of Laius <note>Laius: The father of Oedipus, whose abduction of the youth Chrysippus was considered a foundational act of hubris in Greek myth.</note>, while he was abducting Chrysippus, desire fought too strongly against reason; for he says, "Alas, alas, this is a divine evil for men, when one knows what is good but does not practice it." Likewise, it is clearly evident that the rational power is a distinct thing from the fact that the treatment for each is different. For the former is refined through instruction <note>term: "disciplina" — academic or philosophical study</note>, while the latter is trained through habit and exercise.

### Chapter 25. On the immortality of the soul.

<margin>a</margin> Plato demonstrates that the soul is immortal by the following arguments. To whatever the soul is present, it brings life, as life is naturally inherent to it. However, that which provides life can by no means admit death.

Whatever is of this nature exists as immortal. If it is immortal, it is the soul; it will also be incorruptible. For an incorporeal essence is, according to its substance, immutable, <term>intelligible</term><note>Capable of being understood by the mind rather than the physical senses.</note>, invisible, and uniform. Will it not, therefore, be both simple and indissoluble? The body, on the other hand, is sensible, visible, dissipable, composite, and multiform. Furthermore, when the soul descends through the senses of the body to those things which are sensible, it is distressed and disturbed. Nor can it be similar to that thing whose presence causes its disturbance. Therefore, it is more similar to the intelligible than to the sensible. The intelligible, by its very nature, is always incorruptible. 

Added to this is that the soul, by its own nature, rules the body. That which by its nature governs and commands is akin to divinity. Wherefore the soul, being closest to God, will be immortal. Likewise, whatever opposites exist without a middle ground—not according to themselves, but according to a certain accident—are so established by nature that they are able to be made from one another in turn. Indeed, that which men call "to live" is the opposite of that which is called "to die." Just as death is the separation of the soul from the body, so life is the union of the soul with the body—of the soul which existed before the body. If it both existed before and will exist after death, it seems consistent that it is eternal, for one cannot devise anything further that might destroy it. 

Add that if learning is a kind of <term>reminiscence</term><note>original: "reminiscentia"; the Platonic theory that learning is actually the soul "remembering" knowledge it possessed in a divine state before birth.</note>, it is necessary that the soul be immortal. We argue that learning is reminiscence thus: we cannot learn anything except by the recollection of those things we once knew. For if we understood <term>universals</term><note>General concepts or categories, like "Beauty" or "Equality," that exist beyond individual physical examples.</note> from individual instances, how could we run through all individuals since they are infinite? Or how did we perceive those common qualities from just a few individuals? We would be deceived and lying, just as if we judged every creature that uses respiration to be the only kind of animal. Or how would those very intelligences be the primary things within us? 

Therefore, we understood by remembering, recollecting from small perceptions of certain partial occurrences those things which we had known long ago. We first suffered the forgetting of these things when the souls first descended into bodies. Furthermore, if the soul is in no way corrupted by its own evil, it will never be corrupted by the evil of another. Nor will it be destroyed simply by any evil whatever. Since it is of this nature, it will remain uncorrupted. 

Likewise, that which is moved by itself, being the <term>principle of motion</term><note>The starting point or source of all movement.</note>, is always moved; and what is of this nature is immortal. Now, the soul is moved by itself, and that which is moved by itself is the principle of all motion and generation. Moreover, a principle remains unbegotten and incorruptible. The souls of other living beings perhaps exist in such a way. Furthermore, from the fact that they are rational, it follows that they enter into bodies from the outside, attaching themselves to already formed fetuses, and are able to <term>transfigure</term><note>original: "transfigurare"; refers to the process of metempsychosis or the migration of the soul into new forms.</note> into many bodies, both human and others, always maintaining the same number. This occurs by the will of the gods, or through a lack of restraint in life and a love for the body. For the body and the soul have a certain kinship between them, such as fire and <term>bitumen</term><note>A naturally occurring petroleum-based substance like tar; the analogy suggests the soul and body are drawn together and "ignited" or bound as easily as fuel and flame.</note>. Moreover, the souls of the gods have obtained the power of discerning, which can also be called the faculty of recognition. Besides this, they possess a nature of "approaching" <note>original: "aggrediendi"; the active or spirited part of the soul.</note>, which we can call the vigor of assistance. After these, they have a certain power by which they unite and govern. These natures, while they exist in the souls of men, are changed after they have entered into bodies. For the faculty of uniting and governing is transformed into <term>concupiscence</term><note>original: "concupiscentiam"; the part of the soul driven by physical desire or appetite.</note>, while the vigor of "approaching" is transformed into anger.

## Chapter 26. On virtues and vices, and the distinctions between them.

<margin>q</margin> Since the soul is divided into three parts according to its rational and irrational powers, Plato considers this to happen to man: that he can never be <term>prudent</term><note>In this context, "prudence" refers to practical wisdom (phronesis), the highest virtue of the rational soul.</note> as long as he remains either fearful or intemperate. And therefore, the absolute virtues are inseparable from one another. Virtues are also spoken of in another way as "natural gifts" and good inclinations; because of a certain similarity, they have acquired the same name as the "perfect virtues." For this reason, we sometimes call soldiers "brave," even though they may be unwise or reckless, and we occasionally proclaim certain people to be "brave"—speaking not indeed of perfect virtues, but of natural gifts. Absolute virtues certainly never increase nor decrease. Vices, however, are intensified and also diminished; for one person may be more imprudent or more unjust than another. Nor can anyone be found who is stained by the marks of every vice, just as a body cannot be afflicted by all corruptions of disease at the same time. For it is not necessary that all men be either good or wicked; for those of that kind are the ones who have already reached perfection. It is certainly not easy to progress from vice to virtue in a single step, for the extremes are separated from each other by a long distance.

Moreover, some virtues are "leaders," while others are "attendants." The leaders are those in the rational part of the soul, by which the other virtues are perfected. The attendants, however, are those concerned with the part devoid of reason. These indeed perform honorable deeds, though not according to a reason inherent in them (for they have none), but according to a rule imposed on them by <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudentia"; in this context, it refers to *phronesis* or practical wisdom, which directs the moral virtues.</note> through habit and exercise. For they do not possess their own intelligence.

Nevertheless, Prudence, which is itself a science, assigns to each its own task, just as a pilot sometimes indicates to sailors things they have not seen at all. They, in turn, follow. The same logic applies to the soldier and the general of the army. Since evils are both intensified and relaxed, sins will by no means be equal, but some will be greater and others smaller. For this reason, the makers of laws punish some things more leniently and others more harshly.

And although the virtues themselves are certain "summits" because they are perfect and compared to the right, yet in another way they are called <term>middle states</term> <note>original: "mediocritates"; this refers to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," the idea that virtue is the perfect balance between two extremes of behavior.</note>, because around each—or at least most of them—two vices are seen on either side, one of which comes from excess and the other from deficiency. For example, regarding <term>liberality</term> <note>original: "liberalitatem"; the virtue of being generous and balanced in spending money.</note>, greed is seen on one side and prodigality on the other. For in the passions, intemperance follows either from the fact that one goes beyond what is decent, or from the fact that one does not reach it at all.

Nor, indeed, is he moderate who is not moved at all by his parents' rage, nor he who is carried away by even the smallest things. Likewise, he who feels no grief when his parents have passed away is senseless; but he who destroys himself with sorrow is unrestrained. But he who grieves moderately is called moderate. And he who trembles at everything is fearful, while he who fears nothing at all is fierce; but the brave man is he who maintains a middle state between fearing and daring. The same reasoning applies to all other things. Since, therefore, the middle state in the passions is best, and a middle state is nothing other than the mean between excess and deficiency, for that reason such virtues...

### Chapter 27. How Virtue is Voluntary, and Vice Involuntary.

**S**ince indeed, if anything else lies within our power and is not coerced, virtue is especially of this kind; for it would not be considered worthy of praise if it occurred either by nature or by divine chance. It follows that virtue exists voluntarily, and this through a certain burning, noble, and perpetual disposition <note>original: "affectionem"; a state of mind or psychological inclination.</note>. From this, finally, because virtue is voluntary, it is concluded that vice is involuntary. For who would ever willingly choose the extreme evil for the most excellent part of himself? But if someone falls into vice, they are first inclined toward it not as an evil, but rather as if it were a good. And if they rush into evil, they are entirely deceived, as if avoiding a greater evil through a lesser one. Thus, they are driven involuntarily. For it is not possible for anyone to turn toward evils with the intention of desiring them as evils, nor without some hope of good or fear of a greater evil. For this reason, all things that a wicked man does are involuntary. Since injustice is involuntary, it will be much more involuntary to act unjustly, to the extent that the actual practice of vice is worse than its idle habit. And because crimes are involuntary, criminal men must nevertheless be punished. Yet there must also be different kinds of punishments, just as the damages caused by injury are different. Furthermore, the involuntary consists in a certain ignorance or disturbance. These can certainly be shaken off through reason, civil custom, and diligence.

### Chapter 28. On Injustice, and on the Distinction of the Passions.

Both are indeed shameful. Nevertheless, to inflict an injury is worse to the extent that it is more shameful. A passion is a movement of the soul without reason, for the sake of some good or evil. It is called an irrational movement because neither judgments nor opinions are passions, but are movements of the irrational parts of the soul. There are two primary and simple affects: namely, pleasure and pain. Others, however, are composed of these as if from certain elements. Nor should we number fear and desire among them as if they were simple and primary. For one who fears is not entirely deprived of pleasure; indeed, if he utterly despaired of the repelling or lightening of evils, he would fear no more, but rather, afflicted by a sharper passion, he would grieve rather than fear. But one who desires, since he hopes for the attainment of what he seeks, is in a certain way delighted. And when he does not have certain hope, he is distressed. 

If, then, desire and fear are by no means simple, it will be granted without controversy that none of the remaining affects is simple—such as anger, longing, emulation, and others of this kind. For in these, pleasure and pain are seen as if within these composites. Furthermore, some disturbances are civilized <note>original: "domesticae"; literally "domestic" or "tame," meaning they are natural to the human condition and can be managed by reason.</note>, while some are wild <note>original: "agrestes"; meaning savage or beast-like.</note>. The civilized ones are those which are naturally within humans. But when they are carried beyond measure, they surely fall into fault. Of this kind are pleasure, pain, anger, mercy, and shame. For it is appropriate for humans to be delighted by those things that happen according to nature, but to grieve at the contrary; and anger is indeed necessary for repelling and avenging injury. Mercy is characteristic of humanity and charity. Shame, moreover, provokes us to turn away from disgraceful things. But wild and beastly disturbances are produced beyond human nature from a perversion of life and the worst habits. Of this kind are excessive laughter, exultation in the misfortunes of others, and hatred of the human race. It is also always encountered mixed with its opposite, pain—which certainly would never happen if pleasure could be an absolute good and pain an absolute evil.

### Chapter xxviii. On fate and free will.

Regarding fate <term>destiny</term>, certain views of this kind were held by Plato. He says that "all things are within fate," yet not all things are "decreed by fate." For fate is like a law <note>original: "fatum enim legis instar"; Alcinous is explaining that Fate acts as a general rule or conditional law, rather than a script for every specific action.</note>. It by no means says: "this man will do such things" or "this man will suffer such things." For then the progression would be infinite, since those who are born are infinite, and the things that happen to them are innumerable. Furthermore, no freedom would remain, and praise and blame would be entirely abolished. Rather, he pronounces fate in this way: "Whichever soul chooses such a life and commits such acts, these specific consequences shall follow." Therefore, the soul is free, and it is placed within its own power <term>free will</term> either to act or not to act, nor is it forced to do this by anyone. However, that which follows the action will be fulfilled by fate itself. Just as from the fact <note>original: "q̃" (quod)</note> that Paris will seize Helen—which will indeed be within his own power to choose—it will follow that the Greeks shall fight over Helen. In this same way, Apollo predicted to Laius <note>In Greek mythology, Laius was the King of Thebes and father of Oedipus.</note> himself: "If you father a son, that son will slay you." In this law, both Laius and the fathering of a son are included together. But what follows from the fathering of the son is instituted by Fate. Moreover, the nature of the "possible" itself <note>original: "possibile"; referring to contingent events that may or may not happen.</note> falls in the middle between the false and the true; and because it is undefined by nature, the free power of the rational soul is carried over it from every side. But that which is brought about by us choosing is immediately either true or false. This differs greatly from that which is "in potential"—that is, what will at some time exist in habit and in act. For "potential" signifies a certain faculty and fitness for things which have not yet obtained their specific order...

...just as a boy is said to be a grammarian, a flute-player, or a blacksmith in *potentiality* <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to become something before it is realized.</note>, he will then be established in the habit of one or two of these once he has learned them and attained that specific skill. For by its own nature, the "possible" is indeterminate and indifferent; it is by our own freedom—as if we were tilting the balance of a scale in whichever direction we please—that the possible soon becomes either true or false.

## Chapter XXX. On Goods, and the Highest Good, and Virtues.

<margin>d</margin> Next, let us briefly survey what pleased Plato regarding ethics <note>original: "moribus"; referring to moral philosophy or character.</note>. He believed that the most venerable and supreme good is neither easily found, nor, once it has been found, can it be safely revealed to just anyone. Therefore, he communicated the contemplation of this "Highest Good" to only a very few people, and specifically to those who were most intimate and properly chosen. However, if anyone diligently examines his books, they will find that he placed our own human good in the contemplation of the "First Good" itself. This good may rightly be called both God and the "First Mind." For he maintained that all things which are called "good" by men are named so for the reason that they participate, in some way, in that First Good. This is just as all things that are sweet or hot are granted those names through a certain participation in a "First Sweetness" or "First Heat." Furthermore, among the things that exist within us, only the mind and reason attain a likeness to that Good. For this reason, our good is called by him something beautiful, venerable, divine, lovable, proportionate, and happiness <note>original: "beatitudo".</note>. But of those things commonly called goods—such as health, beauty, strength, as well as riches and high status—none is at all a "good" unless it is used in the service of virtue. For if these things are separated from virtue itself, they perhaps hold the status of mere "matter" <note>In this context, "matter" refers to raw potential that has no moral value until shaped by a higher form or purpose.</note>, and for those who use them badly, they are undoubtedly evils. Nevertheless, Plato sometimes refers to these as "mortal goods." He holds that true happiness is by no means found in [merely] "good" men, but in divine and holy ones. Therefore, he proclaims that the souls of legitimate philosophers are filled with certain admirable and divine goods. After the death of the mortal body, they feast upon divine banquets and survey the "plain of truth" <note>A reference to a famous passage in Plato's *Phaedrus*, describing the place where souls behold true reality.</note> together with the gods. They merit this especially because, throughout their whole lives, they burned with a desire for divine knowledge <term>scientia divina</term> <note>Referring to *Episteme*, or certain knowledge of eternal truths, as opposed to mere opinion.</note> and cherished it above all other things as something most precious. By the gift of this knowledge, the eye of their mind—having been awakened and revived from its previous blindness—is yet more precious than countless physical eyes, making them masters of all rational nature. For igno... <meta>catchword: igno</meta>

## ALCINOUS

...[Plato] compares these wandering men to those who have spent their entire lives in a subterranean cave, where they never look upon the bright light of the sun, but only at the small and empty shadows of those bodies which we see above the earth. Looking at these, they thought they saw true bodies. For just as it is fitting that these people—if they ever emerge from the darkness into the light—would disparage everything they had seen before, and would much more despise themselves as being entirely deceived; so also it is reasonable that those who turn from the darkness of this life toward divine things should despise what they once valued most, and love only the blessed contemplation of divine things. 

From these points, it follows that the only good consists in the knowledge of the "First" <note>original: "primi"; referring to the First Principle or God</note>, which is also the "Beautiful." This is shown throughout all of Plato’s books, yet it is always asserted according to that very participation <note>This refers to the Platonic idea that earthly things "participate" in or reflect divine Forms.</note>. In the first book of the *Laws* <note>original: "de legibus"</note>, he speaks in this way: "There are indeed two kinds of goods: the human and the divine," and so forth. But if anything is possessed without virtue and lacks the essence of the "First," it is called "good" only by the ignorant. In the *Euthydemus*, Plato testifies that such a thing is actually a great evil to the possessor. 

That he considers virtues to be chosen for their own sake is clear from the fact that he judges only the beautiful and the honorable to be truly good. While this is demonstrated in many of his dialogues, it is seen most clearly in those he published concerning *The Republic* <note>original: "de re. p." (de res publica)</note>. 

For this reason, he considers the man who has achieved the knowledge of God to be the most happy and blessed. He does not call him blessed for the sake of the honors that follow such a man, nor for the sake of any other reward; rather, even if he remains hidden from all men, and even if those things commonly thought to be evils—infamy, exile, and death—should befall him, he will nonetheless be blessed. Conversely, he does not think a man who lacks the knowledge of God is any more blessed for possessing all those things the common people call "goods": riches, kingdoms, health, strength, and beauty. 

To all these things, he introduced a consistent and harmonious goal: that is, **to become like God** <term>likeness to God: "similitudo dei"; the concept of *homoiosis theo*, or striving to emulate divine perfection</term>, as far as the human race can attain it. He attempts to establish this in various ways. Sometimes he says that the "likeness to God" consists in being prudent, just, and holy, as he declares in the *Theaetetus*. From this, he warns that one must strive to flee from here to divine things as quickly as possible; but this "flight" is the likeness to God, and becoming like God means becoming prudent, just, and holy. 

Sometimes he also demonstrates that we can become like God through justice alone, as in the last book of *The Republic*. For he says: "No one is ever neglected by God who strives to become just, and through the duty of virtue, renders himself as much like God as is possible." In the *Phaedo*, he asserts that the likeness to God is acquired through temperance and justice, saying: "Are they not blessed and holy, and [passing] into the best place..."

...move to a [better] place, those who have practiced popular and civil virtue, which they call temperance and justice. Sometimes, therefore, [Plato] says the end of life is to become like God; at other times, he says it is to follow God, as when he says: "God indeed, as the ancient word testifies, holding the beginning, middle, and end of all things, completes each thing in a straight path according to nature, encircling everything." Judgment always follows him, the judge of those who have departed from the divine law. He who is to be happy, voluntarily submitting himself to this law, obeys mildly and modestly. Sometimes he mentions both, as when he says: "The soul following God and made similar to Him," and other things that follow. For the very principle of utility is the Good itself; and this is said to proceed from God. Therefore, the end will be in harmony with the principle: to be made like God—namely, the celestial or undoubtedly the super-celestial God <note>Alcinous distinguishes between the God of the heavens (the World Soul or Demiurge) and the "First God" who is above all being.</note>. This God does not possess virtue, yet He is superior to virtue. For this reason, someone might rightly say that <term>misery</term> <note>original: "κακοδαιμονίαν" (kakodaimonian); literally "having an evil spirit."</note> is the depravity of the "demon," while <term>happiness</term> <note>original: "εὐδαιμονίαν" (eudaimonian); literally "having a good spirit."</note> is the good state of the "demon" <note>In this context, the "demon" refers to the highest, rational part of the individual soul, which guides the person.</note>.

Finally, we shall approach the very likeness of God if we utilize a suitable nature, habits, and way of life, and if we use our senses according to law and reason, and especially through doctrine—so that, being far removed from human business and devoted to divine contemplations, we may live forever. Moreover, the preliminary cleansings and, as it were, the purifications of the inner "demon"—if greater expiations are required—will be the mathematical disciplines themselves: music, arithmetic, astronomy, and geometry. Care for the body must also be maintained through gymnastics, by which the body is made more ready for the works of both peace and war.

### Chapter 31. The Definition and Distinction of Virtue.

**Since** virtue is a kind of divine treasure, it is itself a certain perfect and optimal state of the soul, making a person orderly, harmonious, and stable, both in acting and in speaking, and toward himself as well as toward others. Among the virtues, some concern the rational part of the soul, while others concern the part devoid of reason. For since the nature of the rational part is one thing, the power of anger <note>original: "irascendi"; referring to the "spirited" part of the soul (thymos) that deals with courage and indignation.</note> is another, and the power of desire <note>original: "concupiscendi"; the part of the soul responsible for physical needs and lusts.</note> is yet another, the perfections of these parts must also be different. Hence, <term>prudence</term> pertains to the first, <term>fortitude</term> to the second, and <term>temperance</term> to the last. Prudence is the knowledge of things that are good, evil, or indifferent. Temperance is the order regarding pleasures and lusts, making them obedient to reason. When we attribute order and obedience to temperance, we wish it to be understood that there is a certain power by which desires become the followers of their natural master [reason]. Fortitude is the preservation of lawful instruction...

...arduous, whether it be easy to preserve—that is, the power that preserves and executes the legitimate aim. **Justice** is a certain consensus of all the parts of the soul; indeed, it is a kind of power through which the three forces of the soul harmonize with one another, and each performs its own duty according to its dignity. Thus, justice is a kind of common and complete perfection of these three virtues: **prudence**, **fortitude**, and **temperance**, while reason leads and commands, and the remaining parts remain subject and obedient, each according to the duty of its own nature. For this reason, it must be understood that the virtues follow one another in a certain bond. For since fortitude is the preservation of legitimate instruction, it will be the preserver of right reason. Moreover, right reason proceeds from prudence. Furthermore, prudence stands with fortitude, as it is surely the knowledge of good things; for no one can discern the good while they are blinded by fear and the disturbances that follow it. And in the same way, a prudent man has no commerce with intemperance. Generally speaking, whoever is stirred by disturbance and acts in any way contrary to reason always goes astray through ignorance. Prudence, however, administers personal affairs, domestic affairs, and the affairs of the state. When it governs the state, it is called **civil science**. Its duties are two: to establish laws and to execute those that have been established. The first is called <gloss>nomothetikē</gloss> <note>original: "νομοθετικὴ"; the legislative branch or the art of law-making</note>, and the second is called <gloss>dikastikē</gloss> <note>original: "δικαστικὴ"; the judicial branch or the art of judging</note>. Finally, civil expertise considers those things which pertain to peace and those which pertain to war, and in this, among many other things, it especially considers whether a war should be entered into or rather refused.

# Chapter XXXII. On Friendship.

**Friendship** is properly nothing other than mutual benevolence. This truly exists when each person desires the good for the other just as much as for himself, and this equality is maintained in no other way than through a similarity of character. For "like is friend to like" and to the moderate. Those who are intemperate can agree neither with each other nor with the moderate. There are also said to be other kinds of friendship, though they are not truly so, which are colored in some way by virtue. Such is the natural benevolence of parents toward their children and of kinsmen toward one another, as well as those called civil and rhetorical friendships; for these do not always involve a reciprocal exchange of benevolence. Furthermore, a certain species of friendship is the affection of a lover. Honorable love belongs to a noble soul; base love to a vile one; and intermediate love to an intermediate soul. Indeed, just as there are three dispositions of the rational soul—namely good, bad, and intermediate—so there are three effects of love, differing from one another in kind. That there are three types of love is declared by their diverse ends. **Base love** seeks only the pleasure of the body...

...pleasure follows. <meta>Completing the word "voluptatem" (pleasure) from the catchword of the previous page.</meta> And therefore, this is the passion of beasts. The noble man, however, looks toward the naked soul, ready for the duties of virtue. The intermediate man loves both the beauty of the body and the beauty of the soul. Moreover, he who is chosen in this middle way is neither purely virtuous nor wicked. For this reason, it is more fitting to call love that declines toward the body in some part a **spirit** <note>original: "dæmone"; referring to a 'daemon' or intermediary spirit between gods and humans, as described in Plato's Symposium</note> rather than a god; for it is never submerged in earthly bodies, but instead conveys divine things to humans and human things back to the gods. 

When the movement of love is distributed into the three forms we have mentioned, the love of a good man is free from passion and is, in a way, practiced as a craft. Thus, it resides in the non-rational part of the soul, and its thoughts are of this nature: to discern who is worthy of goodwill based on the gifts of their soul, and to win them over. Then, if the thoughts and desires of the one he loves are noble and directed toward the good with a certain fervor of the soul, he praises and approves of them. But if they are the opposite, he will not flatter that person, nor will he charm them with sweet words and obedience; rather, he will deter them and teach them that they should by no means live in such a state. He will always promise and provide those things by which the beloved, through practice, may attain the best character. The ultimate goal of this love is that it should turn into **friendship**.

### Chapter 33. On the Forms of the State

He says <note>Alcinous is referring to Plato's teachings</note> that certain forms of the state must be presupposed, which he handed down in his books on the Republic. In those books, he described the first form as harmonious and the second as discordant, inquiring which of these were superior and how they were established. According to him, the Republic is divided into three members, mirroring the division of the soul: into **guardians**, **assistants**, and **craftsmen**. 

To the first, he assigns consultation and leadership. To the second, he assigns defense whenever it is needed; he compares these to the "spirited" <note>original: "iracundiæ"; the 'thumos' or spirited part of the soul</note> part of the soul, as if they are bringing aid to reason. To the last, he assigns the arts and other services. He believes that the leaders should be **philosophers** and devoted to the contemplation of the Good itself. For only in this way will they govern all things correctly. Indeed, the human race will never find rest from evils unless either philosophers rule, or those who govern happen to philosophize by some divine lot. 

For the state is administered best and with justice when each portion of the city performs its own duty: the leaders consult and decree for the people; the military obey them and protect them; and the rest willingly obey their superiors. He introduced several forms of the state: the first is the **rule of the best** <note>original: "optimatum gubernationem"; aristocracy</note>, when the best men are in charge; the second is the **ambitious** form <note>original: "ambitiosam"; timocracy</note>, in which men inflated with pride dominate; and the third is the **popular** form <note>democracy</note>.

...the fourth, the power of the few <note>An oligarchy</note>. The last is tyranny, the worst of all. He also describes other forms of the state based on certain suppositions: such as the one established in the books of the *Laws*, and that which exists by way of correction in his *Letters*. Thus, according to the diversity of their natures and regions, a proper discipline is shown to be necessary regarding imports, exports, and weaponry. Its specific role is also to command; hence, it holds all military arts as subject to it.

### Chapter 34. Concerning the Sophist.

<margin>h</margin> Thus far, we have described what kind of person the philosopher is. The **Sophist**, however, differs from the philosopher in both method and matter. In method, because he chases after the wages of the youth, and prefers to seem good and famous rather than to actually be so. In matter, because the philosopher is concerned with those things that are always the same and remain in the same state <note>Eternal truths or Forms</note>; the Sophist, on the other hand, contends and labors over that which "is" the least, retreating into a province that is difficult to perceive because of its darkness. For to him, "that which is" is by no means opposed to "that which is not" as a simple contrary. For [absolute non-being] neither exists, nor shares in any substance, nor can it even be understood. If anyone were forced to utter or think it, he would wander and waver, because he would be fighting against himself and distrusting himself. But "that which is not," insofar as it is heard as a pronouncement, is surely not a bare negation of being itself, but is heard with a certain suspicion and under the insinuation of **the Other** <note>original: "alterius"; drawing from Plato's "Sophist," Alcinous explains that "non-being" is actually just "difference"—being something other than something else.</note>, which in some way accompanies "that which is." If things did not participate in "that which is not," they could not be distinguished from one another. But as it stands, "that which is not" is expressed in as many ways as there are things that exist. For that which is not one specific thing is, in fact, the "non-being" of that thing.

### The Final Chapter. Concerning the Epilogue.

<margin>h</margin> Let these things suffice as a certain introduction to the **Platonic discipline** <note>original: "platonicam disciplinam"; the systematic study of Plato's philosophy</note>. Some things have been treated in their proper order; others have been introduced out of order and scattered. Nevertheless, they have been handed down in such a way that, by following these tracks, one may also hunt down the remaining meanings of Plato.

## ## ¶ The Book of Speusippus, a disciple of Plato, on the Definitions of Plato.

<margin>s</margin> ¶ **Everlasting**, that which existed through all time, both previously and now, subject to no corruption. ¶ **God**, a living, immortal being, sufficient in itself for happiness, an everlasting essence, the cause of the Good itself. ¶ **Coming-into-being**, movement toward essence, the receiving of essence, the process into existence. ¶ **The Sun**, celestial fire, which alone can be seen from its rising to its setting by the same observers; an everlasting living being, an ensouled star, diurnal <note>Active during the day.</note>, and the greatest. ¶ **Time**, the movement of the sun, the measure of progression. ¶ **Day**, the journey of the sun from rising to setting, light contrary to night. ¶ **Dawn**, the first beginning of the day, the first light from the sun. ¶ **Noon**, the time in which the shadows of bodies are shortest. ¶ **Sunset**, the end of the day. ¶ **Night**, the shadow contrary to day, the deprivation of the sun. ¶ **Fortune**, movement from the hidden to the hidden, the cause of a fortunate action by a certain chance. ¶ **Old Age**, the decrease of life brought about by time. ¶ **Wind**, the agitation of the air around the earth. ¶ **Air**, the element whose every change of place is according to nature. ¶ **The Heavens**, the body embracing all bodies except the highest air itself. ¶ **The Soul**, that which moves itself, a vital motion, the cause for living things. ¶ **Power**, that which is effective through itself. ¶ **Sight**, the faculty by which bodies are discerned. ¶ **Bone**, marrow consolidated by heat <note>original: "Os, medulla calore consolidata." In ancient Platonic biology, bones were thought to be composed of marrow that had been "cooked" and hardened by internal heat.</note>. ¶ **Element**, that from which things are composed, and into which composed things are dissolved. ¶ **Virtue**, the best disposition or habit of a mortal living being, praiseworthy in itself; the habit according to which that which possesses it is called "good." ¶ **Social Fellowship**, a just institution of laws, by which that which is endowed with it is called upright; a habit providing harmony <note>original: "Communio." In this context, it refers to the social bond or community created by shared laws.</note>. ¶ **Prudence**, a power which leads by itself to human happiness; the knowledge of good and evil things, providing a fortunate disposition, by which we judge what should be done and what should not. ¶ **Justice**, the agreement of the soul with itself, and the mutual order of its parts with one another; a habit distributing to each according to their dignity; the habit by which one who is endowed with it always chooses what appears just; the habit of a life obedient to laws; communicative equality; a habit that always obeys right laws. ¶ **Temperance**, moderation of the soul regarding natural desires and pleasures; the composition and order of the soul regarding natural pleasures and pains; the harmony of the soul for commanding and obeying; the voluntary action of those things that are according to nature; the conduct of the rational soul regarding honorable and shameful things; the habit by which [one] chooses what is fitting—

## Speusippus

...we lead and preserve. ¶ **Fortitude**, an intrepid habit of the soul; military boldness; skill in those things which pertain to war; constancy of the mind against those things which usually terrify. Boldness that follows prudence. Fearlessness in the expectation of death. A burning affection for a rational purpose in the face of dangers. Strength that resists danger. Skill in military affairs; a habit persevering immovably in the law. ¶ **Constancy**, the power of enduring trouble resulting from what right reason has ordered; a power that is never cast down from the purpose of reason. ¶ **Self-sufficiency**, the perfect possession of goods; a habit by which each person becomes their own master. ¶ **Equity**, a softening of what is strictly just or advantageous <note>In Greek philosophy, this is 'epikeia'—the idea that a person should follow the spirit of fairness rather than the rigid letter of the law when the law is too harsh.</note>. Moderation in dealings; the rational order of the soul regarding what is honorable and what is shameful. ¶ **Endurance**, the suffering of hardship for the sake of what is honorable; the suffering of labors for the sake of what is honorable. ¶ **Boldness**, a sense of security, in which one neither expects future evil nor dreads present evil. ¶ **Freedom from Pain**, a habit by which we never fall into pain. ¶ **Perseverance**, a disposition that perfects whatever it has chosen; that is, voluntary endurance. An unshakable habit against labors. ¶ **Shame**, a relaxation of boldness; the spontaneous and willing acceptance of what appears best; the dread of true reproach. ¶ **Liberty**, mastery over one's life; absolute dominion and own license in all parts of life; a disposition that is not stingy in the possession and use of things. ¶ **Generosity**, a habit that preserves decorum in seeking and spending money; the decent acquisition and accumulation of money. ¶ **Gentleness**, a constitution of the soul that is immovable against the impulse of anger; a moderate tempering of the soul. ¶ **Modesty**, a voluntary concession to that which is judged best; a refinement in the posture of the body. ¶ **Happiness**, a good accumulated from all goods; a power sufficient in itself for living well; perfection according to virtue; a sufficient convenience of life. ¶ **Magnificence**, an estimation according to right and honorable reason. ¶ **Industry**, the natural talent of the soul by which a person, being so equipped, easily guesses what is fitting in individual cases; sharpness of mind. ¶ **Frugality**, the simplicity of a rational life; the study of good character. ¶ **Goodness**, a disposition by which we choose the best things. ¶ **Magnanimity**, the moderate use of life's chances; polite conversation with people. Magnificence of the mind combined with reason. ¶ <note>original: "Philanthropia"</note> **Love of Humanity**, that is, humanity; a disposition that fosters human friendship; a habit beneficial to people; the returning of thanks. Beneficial gratitude.

# On the definitions of Plato

¶ **Piety**, justice toward God; an affection that worships God; a voluntary veneration of God; the right knowledge of divine honor. ¶ **The Good**, that which is to be sought for its own sake. ¶ **Fearlessness**, a habit through which we are moved by no terrors. ¶ **Health of the soul**, a habit that does not succumb to the passions <note>original: "affectibus" — in this context, the irrational impulses or "affects" that disturb the mind's peace.</note>. ¶ **Peace**, a state of rest by which we cease from the enmities of war. ¶ **Mildness**, a flexibility of the soul entirely free from anger <note>original: "humilitas" — while often translated as humility, in this philosophical context it refers to the Greek "praotes," the virtue of being even-tempered or gentle.</note>. ¶ **Astuteness**, an affection by which we aim for our own specific end. ¶ **Friendship**, agreement in honorable and just things; the choice of the same way of life; agreement in deliberating and acting; harmony in the sharing of life with goodwill; communion in giving and receiving benefits. ¶ **Nobility**, the virtue of a well-born character; a readiness of the mind for both speaking and acting. ¶ **Choice**, right approval. ¶ **Benevolence**, a pleasing and welcome choice made by one person toward another. ¶ **Kinship**, communion within the same kind. ¶ **Agreement**, the communication of all things; a harmony of thoughts and suspicions. ¶ **Charity**, an entire declaration of the mind; the civic science of honorable and useful things; the science that introduces justice into the republic <note>original: "rem p." (republica). Here, "charitas" refers to social love or "philanthropia" that binds a city-state together.</note>. ¶ **Society**, friendship forged from the long-standing habit of equals. ¶ **Sagacity**, an innate virtue for reasoning. ¶ **Faith**, a right presumption that a thing is exactly as it seems to be; stability of character <note>original: "fides" — signifies trust, reliability, and good faith as much as belief.</note>. ¶ **Truthfulness**, a right habit in affirming and denying; knowledge of the truth. ¶ **Will**, an appetite according to right reason; a rational affection; an affection with reason tending toward nature. ¶ **Counsel**, the advice given to another regarding the method of things to be done. ¶ **Opportunity**, the imminence of a time in which it is necessary either to act or to suffer anything. ¶ **Caution**, the avoidance of evil; diligence in guarding. ¶ **Order**, the harmony of operations with one another; the proportion of communion; the cause of reciprocity in all things; a tempering suitable for perception. ¶ **Attention**, the stretching of the mind toward learning. ¶ **Natural Talent**, speed of learning; a good birth of nature; an innate virtue within nature. ¶ **Docility**, the talent of the soul for perceiving quickly. ¶ **Judgment**, a settled pronouncement concerning that which has come into dispute. ¶ **Law**, the standard by which it is asked whether someone has inflicted an injury or not. ¶ **Lawful Citizenship**, obedience to good laws. ¶ **Joy**, gladness found in the works of temperance. ¶ **Honor**, the bestowal of goods on account of the duty of virtue; esteem and dignity acquired by virtue; a figure of veneration; the preservation of dignity. ¶ **Readiness**, the open execution of a purpose toward acting. ¶ **Grace**, voluntary beneficence; the returning of a good service at an opportune time <note>original: "gratia" — encompasses both favor given and gratitude returned.</note>. ¶ **Concord**, the agreement of those ruling and those being ruled.

->## Speusippus<-

...in the method of commanding or obeying.

¶ **The Republic**, a gathering of many people sufficient for happiness in itself; a lawful agreement <note>original: "conspiratio" — in this context, it refers to a "breathing together" or harmony of the citizens rather than a modern "conspiracy."</note> of the multitude. 
¶ **Providence**, preparation for things to come. 
¶ **Deliberation**, the consideration of future things and the manner in which they might be brought together. 
¶ **Victory**, a force that prevails in a contest. 
¶ **Eloquence**, insight and the faculty of obtaining what is proposed. 
¶ **A Gift**, a mutual grace and exchange. 

¶ **Opportunity**, the very flower of time that contributes to things being done; time bringing a certain helpful aid. 
¶ **Memory**, a disposition of the soul that guards the truth inherent within it. 
¶ **Intelligence**, the concentration of thought. 
¶ **Understanding**, the beginning of knowledge. 
¶ **Holiness**, a caution that turns away from sins committed against God; the diligent observation of divine worship according to nature. 
¶ **Divination**, a prophetic knowledge of things without the need for demonstration. 
¶ **Prophecy**, the knowledge that distinguishes what is present or what is to come for a mortal living being. 
¶ **Wisdom**, a knowledge that assumes absolutely nothing; the knowledge of things that always exist; the science that contemplates the cause of all things. 
¶ **Philosophy**, the appetite for wisdom; the contemplation of truth as it is; the care of the soul according to right reason. 
¶ **Knowledge**, the soul's comprehension of immutable reason; a power capable of grasping one or several things through immutable reason; a true reason in thought that is unchangeable. 
¶ **Opinion**, a perception held with belief through the discourse of reason; a thought that falls into truth or falsehood through reasoning. 
¶ **Perception**, the progress of the soul; the movement of the mind; a report from the soul through the body regarding the forms of men, from which the irrational power of the soul comes to know things through the body. 
¶ **Habit**, a disposition of the soul according to which we are said to be of a certain quality. 
¶ **Voice**, an utterance from the mouth according to thought. 
¶ **Speech**, a voice that can be written, expressive of any matter; a composition of word and name, without the harmony of song. 
¶ **A Name**, a simple word signifying that which is predicated according to its essence, and of everything which is not spoken of as being "of itself" in the least degree. 

¶ **Expression**, the voice of a man that can be written, and a certain common sign signifying without the harmony of song. 
¶ **A Syllable**, an articulation of the human voice that can be written. 
¶ **Definition**, a speech composed of genus and difference. 
¶ **Conjecture**, an indication of a hidden thing. 
¶ **Demonstration**, true reasoning; a speech showing something through things already known. 
¶ **An Element** of the voice, a simple voice, and the cause by which other voices are made to be voices. 
¶ **The Useful**, the cause by which each thing is well-affected; the cause of a certain good. 
¶ **The Conducive**, that which leads toward the good. 
¶ **The Beautiful**, that which is good. 
¶ **The Good**, that which is the cause of safety in all things that exist; the cause of everything that tends toward itself; that from which all things to be chosen proceed. 
¶ **Temperament**, the ornament of the mind. 
¶ **Law**, an institution of the statute from which justice proceeds. 

¶ **The Voluntary**, that which leads itself; that which is to be chosen for its own sake; that which completes a thought. 
¶ **The Free**, that which is master of itself. 
¶ **The Moderate**, the middle between excess and deficiency, sufficient according to art. 
¶ **Measure**, the middle of excess and deficiency. 
¶ **The Palm**, the reward of virtue to be desired for its own sake. 
¶ **Immortality**, a living essence and everlasting perseverance.
