## On the definitions of Plato

¶ **Holiness**: the worship of God, which is pleasing to God.
¶ **A Festival** <note>original: "Celebritas"</note>: a time made sacred according to the laws.
¶ **Man**: a wingless, two-footed animal with broad nails; the only being among those who breathe that is a participant in the knowledge of things through reason. <note>This is the famous "featherless biped" definition, often mocked by Diogenes the Cynic.</note>
¶ **Sacrifice**: the gift of a victim offered to God.
¶ **A Vow**: a prayer of men to God, by which they demand either good things or those things which seem to be good.
¶ **A King**: one commanding according to the laws, subject to no one, and an irreproachable establisher of the civil order.
¶ **Leadership**: providence <note>original: "puidẽtia" — used here in the sense of foresight or care</note> for the whole.
¶ **License**: a concession of the law.
¶ **A Legislator**: the author of the laws by which a state ought to be governed.
¶ **Law**: a civil institution of the multitude, without a fixed time limit.
¶ **Supposition** <note>original: "Suppositio," translating the Greek "hypothesis"</note>: an undemonstrable principle; the brief summary of a discourse.
¶ **A Decree**: a civil institution regarding a certain fixed time.
¶ **A Statesman** <note>original: "Ciuilis homo"</note>: one skilled in those things which pertain to the administration of the republic.
¶ **The State**: a habitation of many men using common laws; a gathering of men subject to those same laws.
¶ **Civic Virtue**: the right constitution of the republic.
¶ **Military Virtue**: experience in war.
¶ **Safety**: a defense secure from all harm.
¶ **A Tyrant**: one commanding a state according to his own opinion.
¶ **A Sophist**: a mercenary hunter of noble and wealthy youths.
¶ **Wealth**: a possession of things so moderated that it contributes to happiness; an abundance of things contributing to bliss.
¶ **A Deposit**: a giving [of goods] with faith and trust.
¶ **Purification**: the segregation of the worse from the better.
¶ **To Conquer**: to overcome an adversary.
¶ **A Good Man**: one who is of such a character that he returns good things to man.
¶ **Temperate**: one who has moderate desires.
¶ **Continent**: one who restrains the parts of the soul that fight against reason.
¶ **Upright**: one who is perfectly good, possessing his own proper virtue.
¶ **Conscience**: a sorrowful thought without reasoning. <note>In this context, conscience is defined as the instinctive "pang" or regret felt after an action, rather than a process of logical deliberation.</note>
¶ **Unteachableness**: slowness in learning.
¶ **Dominion**: a just leadership, subject to no one.
¶ **Anti-philosophy** <note>original: "Aphilosophia," also known as misology</note>: a habit by which one hates reasons and arguments.
¶ **Fear**: a shaking of the soul in expectation of evil.
¶ **Spiritedness**: a violent, irrational impulse of the soul without reason or the order of the mind.
¶ **Dread**: a trembling in expectation of evil.
¶ **Flattery**: an association for the sake of pleasure without regard for the good; a habit tending toward the delight of social custom and overstepping moderation.
¶ **Anger**: a provocation of the irascible part of the soul toward avenging.
¶ **Insult**: an injury inflicted through contempt.
¶ **Incontinence**: an affection drawing one toward those things that seem pleasant, contrary to the judgment of right reason.
¶ **Laziness**: a flight from the labors that come from governing.
¶ **Timidity**: the primary <note>The OCR "pría" likely represents "prima."</note> cause of a retreating impulse.
¶ **Calumny**: a dissension among friends caused by words.
¶ **Opportunity**: the time in which each thing is fit either to be suffered or to be done.
¶ **Iniquity**: a habit that despises laws.
¶ **Indigence**: a lessening of goods.
¶ **Modesty**: a dread in expectation of infamy or disgrace.
¶ **Boastfulness**: an affection that claims for itself those goods which are not present at all.
¶ **Sin**: an action contrary to right reason.
¶ **Envy**: sadness resulting from the goods of friends, whether present or past.
¶ **Impudence**: a habit of the soul undergoing disgrace for the sake of profit.
¶ **Ferocity**: an excess of boldness, not fearing those things that ought to be feared.
¶ **Ambition**: a habit of the soul accepting all expenses for the sake of honor, beyond the norm of reason.
¶ **Degeneration**...

### The Golden Verses of the Philosopher Pythagoras.

<margin>1</margin> First, honor the **Immortal** gods, as the laws command; respect your oath; then the blessed heroes <note>In the ancient sense, "heroes" were semi-divine figures or departed souls of great merit.</note>. Next, honor the earthly spirits <note>original: "dæmones" — referring to guardian spirits or intermediaries between gods and men, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>. Observe what has been established by law. Honor your parents and your relatives. Of other men, make him your friend who is most excellent in virtue. Yield to mild words and useful deeds. Do not turn against your friend for a slight error; bear with them as much as you can. For power dwells near necessity. Consider these things well. 

But abstain from these: first from your belly, then from sleep, lust, and anger. Commit nothing shameful, neither in the presence of others nor by yourself. Above all else, respect yourself. Practice justice in word and deed alike. Accustom yourself to do nothing without reason. Know that death is ordained for all by fate. Learn to accumulate money in season, and again, when the situation demands, to spend it. 

Of those things which happen to men by chance and are adverse, whatever lot you have, bear it without agitation. It is right to heal it as much as you can. Know that fortune does not bring many of these things to good men. Many and various discourses, partly good and partly bad, are spread among the common people; do not be moved by these, nor allow yourself to be restrained by them. If anything false is said, bear it moderately. 

What I tell you now, fulfill entirely: let no one, by word or deed, lead you to do that which is not best for you. Deliberate before the deed, lest you act rashly. For it is the mark of a miserable man to say or do anything rashly. Do not do those things which might later cause you regret. Do not do what you are ignorant of, but learn as much as is necessary. And so you will lead a most pleasant life. 

Do not neglect the health of the body, but use measure in food, drink, and exercise; by "measure," I mean that which will cause you no distress. Accustom yourself to a pure and simple way of life. Avoid those things which stir up envy. Do not scatter the goods of fortune beyond what is appropriate, nor be stingy. For moderation <note>original: "mediocritas" — the classical ideal of the "golden mean"</note> is best in all things. Do not do things that can harm you. Consider before the deed. Do not surrender yourself to soft sleep until you have turned over the day's works three times in your mind...

# The Golden Verses of the Philosopher Pythagoras
<sig>X iii</sig>

Where have I passed? What have I done? What that ought to have been done did I omit? <note>original: "Quā transiui: qđ egi: qđ quod agendū fuerit, prætermisi" — This refers to the famous Pythagorean daily examination of conscience.</note> Beginning from the first, run through the rest. When you have done something shameful, torment yourself. But when you have performed good deeds, congratulate yourself. It is necessary for you to practice these things, to meditate on these things, and to love these things: these will place you in the footsteps of divine virtue through him <note>Referring to Pythagoras himself, or possibly the master-student relationship.</note> who delivered to our soul the fourfold fountain <note>original: "quadruplicē fontē" — The Tetractys (1+2+3+4=10), a central symbol in Pythagoreanism representing the source of all nature.</note> of ever-flowing nature. Go forth to the work, having prayed to the gods. For if you hold to these things, you will understand the condition of the immortal gods and mortal men, how all things proceed and are contained. You will understand, as far as is lawful, nature to be similar in all things: so that it may not happen that you hope for things that are not to be hoped for; nor let anything be hidden from you. You will understand that men are wretched, since they are the cause of their own evils. They neither see nor hear the good things which are near. But very few understand the release from evils. Such a fate harms the minds of men, who are carried by certain revolutions from some things to others, subject to infinite evils; a deadly discord implanted within works harm secretly. You, by yielding, avoid it, and after it has come, do not increase it. O Father Jupiter, either free men from evils, or show them what spirit <note>original: "dæmone" — in the Greek sense of a guiding spirit or inner genius, rather than a malevolent entity.</note> they use. But you, take heart, since a divine race is within men. To these, sacred nature, bringing forth all things, demonstrates them. If any of these are revealed to you, you will abstain from those things from which I command you to abstain. But if you apply the medicine, you will free your soul from these labors. However, abstain from those mortal things which we mentioned above in the purification and release of the soul. Consider each thing with right judgment. Then set the best opinion before you as a charioteer.
¶ When, having laid aside the body, you depart free to the heavens,
¶ You shall escape being a man, made a god of the nourishing ether.

### ¶ The Symbols of the Philosopher Pythagoras.

¶ When you have come into the temple, worship; meanwhile, do not say or do anything that pertains to sustenance <note>original: "uictū" — items for survival or common daily business.</note>. ¶ From a journey, one should not enter a temple by the way, nor pray, even if you pass by the very vestibule itself. ¶ Sacrifice and worship with bare feet. ¶ Flee the public roads; walk by the side-paths. ¶ Abstain from that which has a black tail, for it belongs to the gods of the earth <note>original: "terrestrium... deorum" — likely referring to chthonic or underworld deities.</note>. ¶ Restrain your tongue above all, imitating God.
¶ When the winds blow, worship the echo. ¶ Do not poke the fire with a sword.
¶ Remove everything sharp from yourself. ¶ Help a man who is lifting a burden; however, do not help him lay down what he is putting aside. ¶ Put your right foot into your shoes first, but your left into the bath. ¶ Do not speak of divine matters without light. ¶ Do not step over a yoke. ¶ Do not step over a balance-scale.
¶ When you have left home, do not return, for the Furies <note>original: "furiæ" — the deities of vengeance; a metaphor for being haunted by regrets or attachments.</note> will meet you.
¶ Do not urinate facing the sun. ¶ Do not speak facing the sun.
¶ Do not wipe the seat with oil. ¶ Indeed, nourish the rooster, but do not sa- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; it likely intended to say "sacrifice" or "kill" it, as the rooster was sacred to the sun or to Pythagoras.</note>

<meta>This page concludes the list of Pythagorean "Symbols"—metaphorical or cryptic commands for living a philosophical life—and begins a new section: a preface by the famous Renaissance scholar Marsilio Ficino to his translation of a work on death by Xenocrates, dedicated to the Medici family.</meta>

### Symbols of the Philosopher Pythagoras

<note>These "Symbols" or *Acusmata* were short, often enigmatic rules of conduct used by the followers of Pythagoras. While some seem like superstitions, they were traditionally interpreted as allegories for moral and spiritual discipline.</note>

...sacrifices, for it is dedicated to the sun and the moon. <note>original: "erifices" — likely part of "Alectryonem nutriendum ueruntamen non immolandum fore censebat: diis enim sacrum esse uolebat" referring to not sacrificing a rooster.</note> ¶ Do not sit upon a bushel measure. <note>A warning against laziness or resting on one's laurels; the "bushel" represents a day's rations.</note> ¶ Do not nourish animals with crooked talons. <note>Usually interpreted as avoiding the company of greedy or predatory people.</note> ¶ Do not split wood on the road. ¶ Do not wear a ring. ¶ Do not engrave the image of God on a ring. <note>This reflects a prohibition against treating the divine as a common or material object.</note> ¶ Do not look at yourself in a mirror by the light of a lamp. ¶ Concerning the gods and divine things, say nothing so wonderful that you should not believe it. ¶ Abstain from immoderate laughter. ¶ Do not cut your nails during a sacrifice. ¶ Do not offer your right hand too easily to everyone. <note>A warning not to share secret or sacred knowledge with the uninitiated.</note> ¶ When rising from your bedding, gather it together and disturb the shape. <note>A symbolic act of leaving no trace of the physical self behind.</note> ¶ Do not eat your heart. <note>A famous metaphor: do not consume yourself with grief or anxiety.</note> ¶ Do not eat the brain. ¶ After you have cut them, discard the trimmings of your hair and nails. ¶ Do not look up at anything red. ¶ Disturb the trace of the pot in the ashes. ¶ Do not cling to one who has gold for the generation of children. ¶ Honor first the figure and the altar; the figure and the price of three denarii. <note>original: "figuram ac pretium denariorum trium" — This refers to the Pythagorean study of geometry and mathematics (the "figure" on the abacus) as being more valuable than material wealth.</note> ¶ Abstain from beans. <note>A famous Pythagorean taboo, possibly for spiritual or biological reasons.</note> ¶ Sow the mallow plant, but do not eat it. ¶ Do not receive a swallow into your home. ¶ Abstain from [eating] animals. ¶ It is fitting to flee with all zeal and by every device, and to cut away with iron and fire: disease from the body; luxury from the diet; ignorance from the soul; discord from the home; sedition from the city; and finally, intemperance from all things.

->The End.<-

### Preface of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the translation of the book of Xenocrates the Platonist, concerning death, to the most illustrious man Piero de' Medici.

<margin>c</margin>
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a key figure in the revival of Greek philosophy.</note>

Cosimo <note>original: "Cosmus"</note>, the glory of Italy, Piero de' Medici, was happy both in his achievements and in having such a son as you; he gained for himself a wonderful glory not only through kingly and human prudence, but truly through divine wisdom. Although he passed no time of his life, even in his greatest business, without the company of the Muses <note>A metaphor for the arts and scholarly study.</note>, in his old age especially he gave himself over entirely to the study of philosophy and sacred letters. So that he might be initiated into the first mysteries of philosophy, he wished for several books of Aristotle to be translated by Johannes Argyropoulos <note>A Greek scholar who helped bring ancient learning to Italy.</note>, a most learned man, and he read them most diligently. Then, so that the intimate secrets of wisdom itself should not be lacking to him, he ordered ten books of the divine Plato and one of Hermes <note>original: "mercurii" — Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> to be translated by us from the Greek language into Latin, in which all the precepts of life, all the principles of nature, and all the holy mysteries of divine things are laid open. Cosimo both read all these things accurately and understood them perfectly. And when he had already finished Plato's book *On the One Principle of All Things and the Highest Good*, on the twelfth day thereafter—as if about to return to that very principle and to enjoy that good—he was called back from this shadow of life and approached the light above. While both his fatherland and the Academy might grieve heavily at his departure, Piero remains, a man most like his father, in whose prudence and piety the fatherland might strengthen its hope and the Academy might find rest. On the twentieth day before his pure spirit was released from the bonds of the body, with the sun already setting...

...as his life was setting, he began to deplore the misery of this life. And he so railed against the errors of mortals that he said death was actually a kind of gain. In that place, he discussed the contempt of this life very acutely and at great length, as one who was already aspiring to heavenly happiness. When he had finished speaking, Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the Renaissance.</note> said: "Xenocrates, that holy man and beloved disciple of our Plato, treated these same matters in his book on death." ### The Platonic philosopher Xenocrates’ book on death, translated from the Greek language into Latin by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, for the most illustrious man, Piero de’ Medici.

->Socrates, Clinias, Axiochus<-

**W**hen I was setting out for the Cynosarges <note>A gymnasium and public park outside the walls of Athens, famously associated with the Cynic school of philosophy.</note> and had already reached the Ilissus <note>A small river in Athens, often used as a setting for philosophical walks in Plato's dialogues.</note>, I heard the voice of someone calling me by name. Turning around, I saw Clinias the son of Axiochus, running toward the Callirrhoe fountain <note>A famous natural spring in Athens; the name means "Beautiful Flow."</note>, and with him Damon the musician and Charmides the son of Glaucon. Of these, one was a teacher of music, while the other was joined to him by a certain mutual goodwill. It seemed right to me to turn back and meet them, so that we might gather together more quickly and easily. Clinias said, "Socrates, the present time demands that you show us that wisdom which you always preach. For my father has been oppressed by a sudden and intolerable disease, and seems to be near death; he appears to take it hard, even though he once used to mock those who dreaded death as if they were shivering at the sight of masks of ghosts <note>original: "larvarum vultus" — referring to the frightening masks worn by actors to represent spirits or bogies.</note>. Come, I beseech you, and rebuke him as you usually do, so that he may bear necessity easily. Join us then, and together with the others, perform this pious work." Socrates: "Honest Clinias, your wish shall be fulfilled as much as is in my power, especially since the work you command is a holy one. Let us hurry then. For if he is in such a state, we must make haste." Clinias: "As soon as he sees you, O Socrates, he will recover. For it has often happened that he would somehow come to his senses." Thus we proceeded toward him through the fields along the Peritonian walls. For he lived near the gates, toward the Amazonian column <note>A monument in ancient Athens supposedly marking the burial place of an Amazon.</note>. We found him strong and robust in his joints and body, but weak in spirit and greatly in need of consolation, breathing frequently and drawing sighs, with many tears and the beating of his palms...

## The Platonic Xenocrates

When I saw these things, I said, "What is this, O Axiochus? Where now is that former and boastful constancy of yours? Where are the perpetual praises of the virtues? Where is the wonderful greatness and boldness of your soul? For like a cowardly wrestler who appears noble in the **Gymnasia** <note>The training grounds for Greek athletes; Socrates is comparing Axiochus's philosophical talk to an athlete who looks good in practice but fails in a real fight.</note>, you have succumbed in the actual contests. Why do you not consider the order of nature itself? Since you are such a great man, and imbued with so many disciplines, and if nothing else, at least an **Athenian** <note>To be a citizen of Athens carried an expectation of intellectual and civic bravery.</note>. Do you not hold that common and worn-out sentiment, which says that this life is a kind of **pilgrimage** <note>original: "peregrinationem"; a metaphor for life as a temporary journey away from one's true home.</note>, and that it is necessary for us, journeying rightly and with an even mind, to approach that which is owed and necessary with a joyful rather than a sick mind? This softness is not suitable for a mature age, but for an infant."

**Axiochus**: "These things, O Socrates, seem to be said rightly. But I do not know how it is that when the danger is imminent, those very speeches about endurance, however abundant, secretly vanish and are neglected. Instead, a certain opposing fear rises up, shaking the soul from all sides. Alas, I shall be deprived of this light and these goods. I shall lie in obscurity; captured in taste and sight, I shall rot. I shall be turned into worms and wild beasts."

**Socrates**: "O Axiochus, you join the deprivation of sense with the possession of sense without the examination of reason, and you contradict yourself in both speaking and grieving. You do not notice that you are simultaneously complaining about the deprivation of sensation and mourning over rot and the loss of goods, as if you were about to pass into another life, rather than migrating into the deprivation of all sense—a deprivation, I say, such as preceded your birth. Just as in the Republic of **Draco or Cleisthenes** <note>Draco (7th c. BCE) and Cleisthenes (6th c. BCE) were famous Athenian lawmakers; Socrates argues that Axiochus suffered no 'evil' before he was born during their eras because he did not exist.</note> no evil happened to you—for you were not there, around whom evil could exist—so after death no evil will be against you. For you will not be there, around whom evil might be.

Therefore, drive all trifles of this kind away from you. Consider this: when that which was composed is dissolved, and the soul departs to its own proper place, this which remains—the earthly and irrational body—is in no way the 'man.' For we are the soul, an immortal animal enclosed in a mortal dwelling. And nature constructed this shelter for us for evil. The things that are sweet to it are adulterated, fleeting, and mixed with many troubles; but the things that are truly troublesome are whole, long-lasting, and devoid of sweetness. Added to this are the swellings of **bile and phlegm** <note>Refers to the 'humors' or bodily fluids that pre-modern medicine believed caused disease when out of balance.</note>, as well as diseases of the senses and the corruption of the internal organs. The soul must necessarily suffer with these, spread through every passage so that it may bind them together. Thus it happens that it already longs for its celestial and kindred ether, and thirsts for the life and the heavenly choir. For the loss of this life is a transition from evil to good."

**Axiochus**: "Since you judge this life to be evil, O Socrates, why do you remain in it? Especially since you meditate on these things most of all, and you exist as a curator for others, and you surpass the rest in mind?"

**Socrates**: "Axiochus, you are not a sufficiently true witness to me. For you think that..."

<summary>In this opening of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes the dying Axiochus for his fear of death, arguing that the soul is immortal and the body is merely a burdensome "dwelling" that hinders true life. Socrates uses the logical argument that death cannot be an evil because the person will no longer exist to experience it.</summary>

-># On Death<-

...certainly the Athenian people, because I am a researcher of things, believe that I know something. I, however, would wish indeed to know those common things, rather than being skilled in superfluous matters. What we have been saying, however, are the declamations of **Prodicus** <note>Prodicus of Ceos was a contemporary of Socrates known for his "Choice of Hercules" and his pessimism about the human condition.</note> the wise; some bought for two-thirds of a coin, some for two drachmas, some for four—truly, he teaches nothing for free. He always has that saying of **Epicharmus** <note>A Greek dramatist and philosopher.</note> in his mouth: *Hand washes hand* <note>original: "Manus manum lavat"; meaning favors are reciprocal.</note>. *Give something, receive something.* In recent days, he brought so many arguments against life that I was very nearly ready to end my own life. Since that time, my soul has been continually dying, O Axiochus.

**Axiochus**: What, then, were the things that he said?

**Socrates**: I will recount everything that remains in my memory. For he said: "What part of life is not full of evils? Does the newborn infant not wail immediately, beginning life from sorrow? Nor is any pain absent. For he cries because of either want, or cold, or heat, or a blow; he cannot yet explain in words what he suffers, but he weeps and screams, and this one voice is the sign of his distress. 

When he has completed his seventh year, he is burdened with many labors. There arise, of course, **pedagogues** <note>Slaves who escorted children and supervised their behavior.</note>, **grammarians**, and **gymnastics masters** <term>paedotribae</term> <note>Technical term for a physical trainer in ancient Greek education.</note>. These rule over him no differently than tyrants. When he has grown a little older, he is overseen by censors of arithmetic, geometry, and distributors of tasks, and innumerable masters besides these. 

When he becomes a youth <term>ephebus</term> <note>A young man aged 18–20 undergoing military and civic training.</note>, fear surrounds him and enslaves him; the **Lyceum** and the **Academy** <note>The famous gymnasia and schools of Athens.</note>, the governorship of the gymnasium, the rods of authority, and an immoderate amount of evils rush upon him; and all the distress of the adolescent stands under the censors of character and the council of the **Areopagites** <note>Members of the high court of Athens, who supervised the morals of the youth.</note> chosen for this purpose. 

When he is released from the jurisdiction of these men, cares and deliberations creep in, while he debates which path of life it is proper to enter. It is such that, in comparison to the following labors, those preceding ones seem light and to be feared only by infants. Military expeditions, wounds, and frequent struggles arise. Finally, **old age** itself creeps in secretly, into which every foul and incurable evil of nature flows. And unless one immediately pays back life as a debt, nature, like a **usurer** <note>original: "quaestuaria"; one who seeks profit or rents.</note>, presses in and demands her pledges: sight from one, hearing from another, or both from another. But if anyone resists, she dissolves, infects, mutilates, and cuts him off. Some live all the way to extreme old age, but they become decrepit, being twice children in their minds. 

Therefore, God, providing for the affairs of men, recalls those whom He loves from this life to Himself in a short time. Thus **Agamedes** and **Trophonius** <note>Architects of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note>, when they had built the temple for the **Pythian God** <note>Apollo.</note> and prayed for whatever might be best for them, were immediately weighed down by sleep and never rose again. The same also happened to the priests of **Argive Juno** <note>Referring to the story of Cleobis and Biton, though the text here calls them priests; usually they are the sons of the priestess.</note>, when their mother requested some gift from Juno for the piety of her sons. For when the yoke-oxen were slow, they themselves went under the yoke and transported their mother to the temple...

...truly. And when they had made their vows to the god, they departed from life in the night <note>This likely refers to the story of Biton and Cleobis, two brothers who died in their sleep after their mother prayed for them to receive the greatest gift possible.</note>. It would be tedious to relate the opinions of the poets, who deplore the calamities of human life in their divine poems. I will cite one most famous poet <note>Homer, in the Iliad.</note> who says: "The gods have decreed that wretched mortals should live in perpetual sorrow. Nor is there anything on earth more miserable than man." 

Thus they say that **Amphiaraus** <note>A legendary seer and hero who was swallowed up by the earth; in some traditions, this was seen as a divine favor to spare him from a worse fate.</note> was loved with the highest affection by **Jupiter** and **Apollo**, and yet he did not reach old age. What, moreover, do you think of that man <note>Likely a reference to the poet Euripides.</note> who commands us to mourn the misery of a life just beginning at birth? But I will stop now, lest I seem to wander further beyond what was proposed. 

Who is there, however, who does not complain greatly about the pursuit and the craft they have chosen? Let us consider hired laborers and craftsmen <term>mechanicos</term> <note>Manual laborers or those working with machines/tools, often looked down upon by the upper classes.</note>, working from night to night, and barely acquiring those things necessary for food. Furthermore, they live complaining, and fill their nightly watches with weeping and tears. 

What shall I say of sailors? To how many dangers are they subjected? Rightly indeed did **Bias** <note>Bias of Priene, one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> say that he counts a sailor neither among the dead nor among the living. For a man of the earth, as if a sharer of both a double and uncertain life, plunges himself into the water, entirely subject to fortune. 

"But agriculture is pleasant." Granted, but does it not always find—as they say—an occasion for sadness, just like an ulcer? Now indeed the farmer blames the drought and groans; now the rains; now the heat and scorching; now the worms; now the warmth, now the untimely cold. 

The pursuit of public affairs <term>rei publicae</term> is indeed honorable; yet, to skip over much, with how many evils and hardships is it twisted! It possesses a joy that is as unstable, swollen, deceitful, and turbulent as phlegm or burning bile. Its loss is sad and worse than a thousand deaths. Who, moreover, can be happy while living at the whim of the crowd, mocked and hissed off stage, as if a kind of game and a tale for the common people—shaken, hissed at, fined, wretched, and ruined? 

Where, O statesman **Axiochus**, did **Miltiades** die? Where is **Themistocles**? Where is **Ephialtes**? <note>Famous Athenian leaders who all met tragic or ignominious ends despite their service to the state.</note> Where are the rest of the leaders? I have never yearned for these things myself. For it does not seem honorable to me to hold office among a demented people. 

Consider those who, around **Theramenes** and **Callixenus**, the next day as presiding officers, drove on the schemers and condemned men to death in a single lot <note>A reference to the illegal trial of the six generals after the Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE, where the assembly condemned them all at once rather than individually.</note>. You, along with **Euryptolemus**, resisted them before three thousand assemblymen.

**Axiochus**: You speak the truth, O **Socrates**. Indeed, from that time until this very day, I have avoided the tribunal; nothing has seemed more difficult or harsher than the governing of the state. This is clear to those who handle civil affairs themselves. But you speak of these things as if you had observed them from a lookout point far off. We, certainly, understand those things more clearly, being involved in the work itself. For the people, O friend **Socrates**, are ungrateful, irritable, hostile, cruel, envious, and unrefined...

<summary>Socrates argues that every profession—from manual labor and seafaring to farming—is filled with misery, focusing specifically on the fickle and cruel nature of Athenian politics. Axiochus agrees, citing the historical mistreatment of great leaders and his own disillusionment with the public assembly.</summary>

# On Death

## On Death

...overflowing with a crowd and heaped up with trifles; and whoever familiarly accommodates himself to this is far more wretched than that man. **Socrates.** Since, O Axiochus, you judge the most liberal discipline <note>This refers to statesmanship or public life, which was considered "liberal" (fitting for a free man) but is here described as exhausting and full of trivialities.</note> above all others as the one most to be avoided, what must be thought of the rest? Should they not be fled from with the utmost effort? I once heard **Prodicus** <note>Prodicus of Ceos was a famous 5th-century BCE philosopher known for his focus on the correct use of words and his pessimistic views on the human condition.</note> saying that death pertains neither to the living nor to the dead. **Axiochus.** By what reasoning, O Socrates? **Socrates.** Because death does not exist regarding the living, and the dead simply do not exist. For this reason, it is not around you now, for you are not yet dead. Nor, if you pass away, will it be around you. For you yourself will not exist. Therefore, it would be an empty sorrow if Axiochus were to mourn that which is neither around Axiochus now, nor will be in the future. For you would be acting just as if you were terrified of **Scylla** or a **Centaur** <note>These are classic mythological monsters used here as metaphors for non-existent things that cannot actually harm a person.</note>. Since these monsters are neither around you, nor will they ever be. For that which is to be feared and is horrible happens to those who exist. But for those who do not exist, there is nothing to be terrified of. **Axiochus.** You indeed gather those things from that superficial talkativeness that is now spread everywhere. For from there comes this abundance of empty words, composed for the sake of young men. But I mourn because I am being deprived of the goods of this life, even for <gloss>pro</gloss> <note>The Latin abbreviation "p" stands for "pro," meaning "for" or "on behalf of."</note> the sake of which you might bring forward stronger reasons than the ones before. For a wavering mind does not understand the ornament of words, nor does it grasp the colors of speech. It ignores the pomp and splendor of a sermon, even if it hears it, and remains far from the truth; it by no means tolerates the little traps of **Sophisms** <term>sophismata</term> <note>Clever but fallacious arguments used to deceive rather than to find the truth.</note>. It pays attention only to those things which can completely <gloss>omnino</gloss> strike and penetrate the soul. **Socrates.** Without reason, Axiochus, you join the feeling of evils with the deprivation of goods, and it escapes your notice what it is to be dead. Clearly, the contrary suffering of evils afflicts one who is bereaved of goods. But one who does not exist does not even notice the bereavement itself. In what way, therefore, where the knowledge of things that cause affliction is absent, can there be affliction? For at the start, unless through ignorance you assumed a certain sense of feeling, you would not dread death. But now you pervert yourself, fearing lest you lose your soul. Yet you grant a soul to that very loss. You dread being deprived of sense, and you think that a non-existent sense can be perceived by sense, even though there are many and famous discourses concerning the **immortality of the soul**. For mortal nature would never have risen to such excellence as to despise the violence of savage beasts, cross the sea, build cities, prescribe order for the republic, look up into heaven, and measure the circuits of the stars, and notice the progress of the sun and moon, their risings and settings, and furthermore eclipses, and the swift meridian returns, the double turnings of the **Pleiades** <note>A prominent star cluster. In antiquity, their rising and setting were vital for marking the change of seasons for agriculture and navigation.</note>, and winter and summer alike. The blowing of the winds, and the force of the rains, the throwing and flash of lightning, and finally, it would wonderfully establish the phenomena of the world in eternity, unless some divine spirit were present in the soul, through which...

<summary>Socrates comforts the dying Axiochus by arguing that death cannot harm the dead because they no longer exist to feel it, while also beginning a counter-argument based on the soul's divine capacity for high science and astronomy.</summary>

<header>Xenocrates the Platonist</header>

## Xenocrates the Platonist

...he had attained the understanding of such great things. For which reason, O my Axiochus, you are not migrating into death, but into immortality itself. You will not be deprived of good things, but you will enjoy the full possession of goods. Nor will you perceive pleasures mixed with the mortal body any longer, but those entirely free from all sadness. To that place, I say, you go forth, free from this prison <note>The "prison" of the body is a classic Platonic metaphor (soma-sema), suggesting the soul is trapped in the physical form until death.</note>, where all is quiet and removed from sadness and old age; where there is holy exultation and a life ignorant of evils, nourished by tranquil peace, beholding the nature of things and contemplating the secrets of philosophy—certainly not for the favor of a crowd or a theater, but for the sake of the object of clear truth. 

**Axiochus.** Your speech has led my feelings in the opposite direction. For I no longer dread death, but I desire it. To express something overflowing in the manner of orators, right now, O Socrates, I am carried on high, and I traverse the divine circuit and the throne. Rescuing myself from this weakness, I have been reborn. 

**Socrates.** I will relate to you moreover, if you please, what Gobrias the Magus <note>Gobrias is presented here as a Persian sage or "Magus." This reflects a Renaissance and late-antique interest in "Oriental" wisdom as a supplement to Greek philosophy.</note> handed down to me. For he said that at the time when **Xerxes** <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> crossed the Hellespont, his grandfather, named Gobrias, was sent to **Delos** to guard the island where the two gods <note>Apollo and Artemis, who were born on the island of Delos.</note> appeared. There he says he learned from certain bronze tablets, which **Opis and Hecaergos** <note>Mythical maidens from the far north who served Apollo.</note> brought from the **Hyperboreans** <note>A legendary people living "beyond the North Wind" in a land of perpetual sunshine and peace.</note>, that upon the release of the body, the soul migrates to a hidden place beneath the earth, in which is the palace of **Juno**, a court no narrower than that of **Jove**. <note>The text uses Roman names (Juno/Jove) for the Greek deities Hera and Zeus. In this underworld context, Juno likely refers to Persephone.</note> 

Since the earth holds the middle of the world and the sky is spherical, one hemisphere of which the celestial gods have obtained by lot; the other, the infernal ones—partly brothers of the sky-dwellers, partly sons of brothers. The vestibules of **Pluto’s** province are bound on all sides by enclosures and bronze chains. The river **Acheron** first receives the one who arrives there, then **Cocytus**. Having crossed these, one must be led to **Minos** and **Rhadamanthus**, to that region which is known as the Plain of Truth. There sit the judges examining the life of each who comes. Here, no one can protect himself with lies. 

Whomever, therefore, a good spirit <term>daemon</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, a 'daemon' is a guiding spirit or a person's inner divinity, rather than an evil entity.</note> favored in life, these pass over into the place of the pious. There, eternal spring overflows with all kinds of fruits, and fountains of shining waters gush forth; moreover, pleasant meadows are painted with various colors. There is no lack of gatherings of philosophers and theaters of poets. There are circular dances and musical songs, and sweet harmonies. Joyful banquets and holy and abundant gatherings of those drinking; inviolable joy and sweet companionship. There is no excess of cold or heat there, but the nature of the air is healthy, tempered by the gentle rays of the sun. Here are the seats of purified souls, where they celebrate divine mysteries. What therefore prevents the first honor and reward from being given to you there, since you derive your origin from God? Also those who were around **Hercules** and **Dionysus**, when they descended <note>original: "descendunt"</note> there...

<summary>Socrates comforts Axiochus by describing the soul's transition from the "prison" of the body to a paradisiacal afterlife. He cites a story from Gobrias the Magus about the geography of the underworld, the judgment of souls by Minos and Rhadamanthus, and the eternal spring enjoyed by the virtuous.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue. Following the previous page’s introduction of the Persian sage Gobrias, Socrates describes the divergent paths of the soul: the punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the virtuous. The dialogue ends with Axiochus fully reconciled to his passing, no longer fearing death but welcoming it.</meta>

# On Death

...descend, reason dictates that those who have been purified go forth, and they receive the hope of a happy journey from the worship of Ceres <note>original: "Cereris cultu"; Ceres is the Roman name for Demeter. Her "cult" refers to the Eleusinian Mysteries, ancient secret religious rites that promised initiates a blessed afterlife.</note>. On the contrary, those who have defiled their lives with crimes are suddenly snatched through Tartarus <note>The deepest, darkest abyss of the underworld used as a dungeon of torment.</note> by the Furies into Erebus and Chaos. There lies open the province of the wicked, and the fruitless labor of the daughters of Danaus <note>The Danaides were forty-nine sisters condemned in the underworld to eternally fill a perforated tub (or sieves) with water as punishment for killing their husbands.</note>, who strive in vain to fill sieves with water. There is the thirst of Tantalus, and the entrails of Tityos <note>A giant whose liver was perpetually pecked out by vultures, only to regrow.</note>. There is the rock of Sisyphus, which must be perpetually rolled back up. There, biting beasts coil themselves inseparably around bodies; there, unquenchable torches burn their flesh. There the impious, tortured by every form of suffering, are plagued by perpetual punishment. 

These things I indeed learned from Gobrias. But you, O **Axiochus**, may judge these matters for yourself. For I, compelled by reason, know this one thing clearly and firmly: that every soul is immortal, and that soul which departs pure from these places shall live without sadness. Therefore, whether you go upward or downward, **Axiochus**, you must be blessed, provided that you have lived piously and holily.

**Axiochus.** I blush, my **Socrates**, and I am afraid to speak further. So much has the dread of death departed from me that I now vehemently long to die; your previous speech has persuaded me like a heavenly oracle. Now, therefore, I despise this life, as one who is about to pass happily into a better place. Wherefore, for the present, I shall silently reflect upon what has been said. You, however, O **Socrates**, shall return to me after midday.

**Socrates.** I will do as you say. But in the meantime, I shall return to the **Cynosarges** <note>A public gymnasium outside the walls of Athens, dedicated to Heracles, where Socrates was known to frequent.</note> for the sake of a walk, from where I was first brought here to you.

->The End of Xenocrates on Death.<-

# ¶ The Preface of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, written while still a youth, for his Book on Pleasure, addressed to Antonio Canisiano, citizen of Florence.

## THREE GENRES OF DISCUSSION

<margin>m</margin>
I remember when I was with you at your estate in Campolitano <note>A villa near Florence where the Florentine elite gathered for intellectual retreats.</note>. While we were being drawn in by the particular loveliness of that region and the sweetness of the various fruits in which that villa especially abounds, we fell into a discussion about pleasure. You requested this [discussion] from me, and asked that I commit it to writing as soon as leisure was granted. Therefore, as soon as I returned to Figline <note>Figline Valdarno, Ficino’s birthplace and family home.</note>, I composed this little work on pleasure for you with the greatest pleasure myself. 

¶ To begin from the most important point, there are three genres of discussion among philosophers. The first is that by which we defend and prove a certain specific side of a question through debate, as the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their systematic and scientific approach to philosophy.</note> and the **Stoics** <note>Philosophers who taught that virtue is the only good and that one should remain indifferent to external pleasures or pains.</note> have done. The second is that by which, once a question is proposed, we bring forward various opinions and arguments regarding the matter being sought. By proposing many views and comparing them in turn, we may choose which of them appears most probable and likely; this was the method used by the **Academics** <note>Members of the school founded by Plato; in Ficino's time, "Academic" often referred to a style of skeptical or investigative inquiry.</note> and nearly all the **Socratics**. The third genre is most characteristic of the **Sceptics** <note>A school of philosophy that argued human beings cannot reach certain knowledge; Ficino views them negatively here for creating confusion.</note>, who—since they think all things are indifferent and hold no certain or probable path to follow—confuse and mix together those things which are separated and distinct by the order of nature. These are rejected by all the more excellent philosophers. 

¶ I, therefore, have decided at this time to adopt the method of the Academics and Socratics from among all these options. For indeed **Plato**, whom we follow and venerate as the "god of philosophers," forbids those who are still of a tender age to offer their own opinion on any matter. This is because, as often happens among the young, what we most approved of in our early years must later be revoked in a more mature age and with weightier judgment, and changed to a contrary opinion. I have judged it better, therefore, to run through the opinions of other philosophers on pleasure in a brief discourse, rather than to express my own. I do this so that I do not impudently assert something against what we are taught by our Plato, and so that I might satisfy your desire, which I know to be most burning for the study of philosophy. But enough on these matters; let us now come to the opinions of the philosophers.

## ¶ Chapter One. On the parts of the soul.
### ¶ Likewise on gladness, joy, and pleasure, according to Plato.

<margin>**P**</margin> **LATO**, then (to begin with the prince of philosophers), since he divided the soul into two parts—namely, the **mind** <note>original: "mente" — the higher, intellectual part of the soul.</note> and the **senses**—attributed **gladness** <note>original: "laetitiam"</note> and **joy** <note>original: "gaudium"</note> to the mind, and **pleasure** <note>original: "voluptatem"</note> to the senses. Indeed, he thinks these first two differ from one another because all *joy* is worthy of praise, whereas *gladness* is partly to be praised and partly to be blamed. For he defines *gladness* as a certain elation of the mind regarding the possession of some good, which can either preserve or exceed the bounds of modesty. *Joy*, however, he defines as that specific delight which is taken from contemplation or from some other use of the virtues. 

Therefore, in his *Phaedrus* <note>One of Plato’s most famous dialogues, dealing with the soul, beauty, and love.</note>, when he spoke of that first and true life which the soul enjoys in its heavenly seats, he says that "it is nourished and **rejoices** in the contemplation of truth." For this reason, he frequently calls joy "the sustenance of the mind." For he wishes truth itself to be like a field, and the contemplation of that truth to be the crops. Then, he considers *joy* to be the nourishment taken from those two things, by which the mind enjoys the contemplation of truth. 

For this reason, in that same *Phaedrus*, when he discussed those shadows into which the soul has been cast and submerged from the highest and true light, he said: "where there is much effort to see where the **plain of truth** <note>original: "veritatis campus" — a metaphorical place where the soul perceives true reality before birth.</note> lies; for the fitting food of the soul comes from there, and the nature of the **wings** <note>In the *Phaedrus*, Plato uses the myth of the winged chariot to describe the soul’s ability to ascend to the divine.</note> by which the soul is raised up is nourished by this." Plato calls those things "wings" by which the soul flies back to the heights from which it had descended due to the contemplation of earthly things. Since it can achieve this through two virtues—namely, the **contemplative** and the **moral**—Plato (as I interpret it) understands those virtues to be the "wings" of the soul, which it recovers through the contemplation of truth and divine things, just as it had lost them through the desire for these earthly things. 

When the soul has flown back to the heavens, having recovered its wings through the exercise of both natural and moral philosophy, he thinks that two rewards are given to the returning soul. One is the contemplation of divinity; the other is a certain perfect and absolute **joy**, which the soul enjoys in that very knowledge of God. Plato calls the former <term>Ambrosia</term> <note>The food of the gods in Greek mythology, granting immortality.</note> and the latter <term>Nectar</term> <note>The drink of the gods.</note> in the *Phaedrus* with these words: "The soul which has truly looked upon [the truth] and been nourished by it, returns again to its home within heaven. But when it has returned, the **charioteer** <note>In Plato's metaphor, the 'charioteer' represents the rational part of the soul.</note> stands the horses at the manger and sets before them ambrosia, and upon that, nectar to drink." Following the school of **Pythagoras** <note>An earlier Greek philosopher whose ideas on the soul's immortality and reincarnation heavily influenced Plato.</note>, he calls the charioteer "Reason," and the horses the other parts and natures of the soul which Reason leads. The rest...

## ¶ Chapter .ii. What pleasure is, and why it is not a good in itself, by many arguments, according to Plato.

**P**LATO <note>The woodcut initial 'U' (for *uoluptatem*) marks the beginning of the new chapter.</note> intends for **pleasure** to be a certain sweet motion in the senses, which proceeds from the replenishment of a deficiency. For he holds that deficiency and its replenishment are, in a certain way, in conflict with one another; from the former come desire and pain, while from the latter, pleasure reaches our senses. 

Nor does he think that this pleasure of which we now speak should be numbered among "the goods." Although he has demonstrated this with many very true arguments, this one is the first and most powerful of all: 

¶ Just as by the presence of heat, the things to which heat arrives are made hot, so too by the presence of that which is "good," all things become good in which goodness itself is present. However, no one is made better by the possession of pleasure. For even beasts possess pleasure—and indeed to a greater degree than men—yet they are not made better by it, nor are they even "good" at all. Furthermore, women, children, and fools—and finally, all those who are cowardly—pursue pleasure and embrace it with all their might, much more so than men who are good and of excellent character. Yet it would be absurd if that which is "good" belonged more to the wicked and the cowardly than to honest and excellent men. 

¶ Nor can contraries be mixed with one another, as he believes. Yet pleasure is undoubtedly found even where there are evils, since it is not lacking in the wicked and the unjust. Therefore, in no way is it a "good," for it joins with that which is evil. But "the good" can in no way join with "the evil," because they are fundamentally opposed. 

¶ Add to this what is said by Socrates in the *Gorgias* <note>One of Plato's dialogues focusing on ethics and rhetoric.</note>: good and evil are never found at the same time in the same person. Yet the same person, at the same time, is frequently affected by pain and pleasure equally. Indeed, he calls every deficiency painful, and every replenishment of that deficiency delightful to the senses. He calls thirst a "deficiency of nature," and drinking a "replenishment." Therefore, the former is troublesome, while the latter—drinking—is on the contrary pleasant.

# ON PLEASURE

Furthermore, it happens that one hungers and thirsts at the same time; from this, he [Plato] wishes to show that it is possible for someone to experience pain and pleasure simultaneously. Indeed, desire, anxiety, suspicion, envy, and pity—all of which contain pain within themselves—are the constant companions of pleasure. Therefore, "fearing desire," he says, is permitted to both pain and pleasure alike, proceeding from the senses; thus it happens that pleasure is joined and confused with pain. And since the **good** is never mixed with **evil**, he denies that pain (an evil) and pleasure (a good) can be defined as such <note>If pleasure and pain are always mixed, and the "Good" cannot be mixed with evil, then pleasure itself cannot be the "Good."</note>.

¶ Besides, since every **good** ought to be stable and permanent, who would say that pleasure—which has no stability—is the good? And yet, this cannot be denied. If anyone considers its definition, they will find pleasure to be unstable and uncertain; for in its definition (as we reported above), it was called a <term>motion</term> <note>original: "motio" — In Platonic philosophy, "motion" refers to any process of change or becoming. Because pleasure is a process of "filling a lack," it is always moving and never arrives at a state of permanent being.</note>. Nothing, however, is more contrary to stability than motion. Nor is there anyone who has tasted any bodily pleasure who does not know how fragile it is, how brief, with what speed it slips away and flows off, and how quickly it turns into its opposite. 

Moreover, that which is good can never be contrary to the good. But since pleasure hinders many of the greatest goods, who could doubt that it is contrary to the good? For pleasures hinder **prudence**, pour darkness into the **mind**, and corrupt **judgment**. With their charms and allurements—like certain little harlots—they entice and ensnare the minds of men, prostrating the entire nature of man in the mud and filth of vice and crime. For the divine Plato, in his letter to Dionysius, says: "Pleasure brings detriment to men, giving birth to ignorance, restlessness, foolishness, and insolence."

¶ Besides, there is no **good** that is not worthy of either praise or veneration. Yet no one of sound mind praises pleasure, nor is anyone judged worthy of honor and glory simply because he enjoys the greatest pleasures. Rather, he is honored who is of such a character that he spurns and neglects them with a high and unconquered spirit.

¶ Added to these points is the fact that no good seems rightly able to be called "ours" unless it is either inherent in our very nature or proceeds from our own selves. And we are nothing else besides **mind** and **reason**. The **body**, however, is a **prison** and a **tomb** for us <note>original: "carcer, & sepulchrum" — This reflects the famous Platonic pun "soma sema," suggesting the physical body is a grave that restricts the immortal soul.</note>. The **senses**, indeed, are like certain guards and ambushers, who seem to care for and strive for this above all: to submerge and bind us deeper in the darkness of this prison, so that our souls might not fly back to their own place and celestial fatherland.

...nor do they look back at the breezes, shut as they are in darkness and a blind prison <note>A reference to the Platonic "Allegory of the Cave" or the "prison of the body," where the soul is trapped and cannot see the light of truth.</note>. The result is that only those things seem to be ours, and to exist within us, which proceed from the soul and reason. Everything else, however, arises from fortune or from that prison which is hostile to us; these things are not so much "ours" as they are the property of the body and of luck. Just as **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a Roman scholar and writer.</note> rightly said: **"No one should call his own what is outside of himself."** Therefore, since pleasure is inborn and implanted in the body and the senses, anyone who counts it among our true "goods" will undoubtedly seem to be out of his mind. 

To these points, add if you please what **Socrates** says in **Plato’s** *Gorgias*: that all goods of the soul proceed from art, rectitude, order, and <term>choice</term> <note>original: "electione" — In this context, it refers to deliberate, rational selection rather than an impulsive act.</note>. Furthermore, the entire discipline of moral philosophers agrees on this point: that the whole power of virtue and the goods of the soul consists in choice. But who would say that pleasure proceeds from choice? Must not those things which fall under choice first have had a place for counsel and deliberation? For nothing is "chosen" unless it has first been consulted and judged. Yet no one deliberates in order to have pleasure within himself, for it is innate to us.

For this reason, **Socrates** thinks there are two "ideas" <note>original: "ideas" — Here used in the sense of guiding principles or inner drives.</note> in each of us which we follow, wherever they may lead. One is the <term>opinion</term> <note>original: "opinionem" — A rational judgment or belief about what is best.</note> that pursues the best; the other is the desire for pleasures. The former principle he calls "acquired," while the latter he calls "innate." Thus, pleasure follows neither art, nor reason, nor any order at all. Rather, it is stirred up within us by a certain sudden and reckless impulse of nature and the senses, rather than by any certain judgment or counsel. It fawns upon the senses, soothes and titillates the body with a certain ruinous sweetness, weakens the soul, and displaces the mind and reason from their proper state.

¶ Furthermore, it is the nature of all true goods that, while they are still in the future, they raise a person’s hope; but when they are present, they make the soul of the possessor tranquil, quiet, and rendered content by that which is at hand. They fulfill the person by their possession, so that he requires nothing further, seeks nothing, and desires nothing—as if he possessed that one thing which is by its nature sufficient and perfect. Even if he who enjoys the possession of some good should desire something beyond it, he nevertheless seems to be entirely free from anxiety and distress.

Future pleasures, however, affect the senses with a certain intolerable burning of desire; they kindle worry, burden the soul with anxiety, and (to put it briefly) drive one into a kind of madness and rage. But when someone embraces those present pleasures for which they had burned with desire, they immediately bring fear and suspicion along with them. They blind us while we enjoy them and reduce us to the savagery of wild beasts. Nor are they yet drained—or rather (to speak more truly), not yet...

...even when tasted with just the edge of the lips, they affect the soul with an incredible kind of regret, shame, weariness, disgust, and listlessness. Thus, that saying of **Socrates** in the *Phaedo* <note>In Plato's *Phaedo*, Socrates remarks on the strange relationship between pleasure and pain—how one often follows the other—as he rubs his legs after his shackles are removed.</note> is most true: that **pain** and **pleasure** are both connected from the same head, and nature has joined their peaks into one. For this reason, it happens that whichever of them is present, the other follows afterward. From this, the fires of desire arise again; and the more greedily pleasures are drunk down, the more numerous and fertile the seeds and sprouts of lust grow back. Hence (I believe) the poets in the underworld introduce **Tityos** <note>A giant in Greek mythology punished in Tartarus for attempting to rape Leto; his liver was eternally devoured by vultures.</note>, whose body

> Is stretched across nine whole acres,
> And a huge vulture with a hooked beak,
> Pecking at his immortal liver and his vitals
> Fertile for punishment, searches for his feast, and dwells
> Deep within his breast; nor is any rest given to the fibers as they grow back. <note>original: "Porrigitur, rostróque immanis uultur adunco / Immortale iecur tondens fœcundáque pœnis / Viscera rimatur epulis..." — A quotation from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, lines 596–600.</note>

Therefore, the divine **Archytas of Tarentum** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician, and a friend of Plato.</note> and **Plato** held that a soul of this kind is like a **perforated vessel** <note>original: "perforato uasi" — This refers to the "leaky jar" metaphor in Plato’s *Gorgias*, representing a soul that can never be satisfied because its desires leak out as fast as they are filled.</note>, because of the insatiable and infinite abyss of wanting, which can be filled by no pleasures. **Epicharmus the Pythagorean** and **Socrates** compared the lustful soul not only to a broken vessel, but even to the **Euripus** <note>The Euripus Strait in Greece is famous for its violent and unpredictable tidal currents that change direction many times a day.</note>. For just as the water in the Euripus flows and ebbs, and is tossed up and down, so too in a soul of this kind, desire or pleasure now enters, now ceases, flows away, and is born again and flows back. At one moment the lustful soul rejoices and hopes, raised up as it were; at another it grieves, distrusts, fears, is anxious, and falls downward. Now it wants this, then it does not; indeed, at the very same time, reason wants one thing while the senses affect another. Thus it happens that such a soul not only aims now at this, now at that, but is even pulled apart at the same time into contrary passions and diverse opinions. Therefore, **Socrates** used to say he would rather his lyre be out of tune, or the chorus he led, and that many other men should contradict him, than that he himself, being one, should be contrary to and out of harmony with himself. Hence **Pythagoras** reasonably calls virtue a certain **harmony**.

Next follow Plato's remaining three arguments against pleasure. For he considers the nature of good and evil to be opposites, such that we attain the good with difficulty. But into the evil we slip easily, as if down a slippery path. Therefore, evils would grow so much that the entire nature of the good would necessarily be destroyed and uprooted, unless nature had applied a most suitable remedy to this so destructive a plague. For it is so ordained that individual goods, because of their great kinship with nature, [support] one another...

And the **virtues** <note>The "Unity of the Virtues" is a classic philosophical doctrine suggesting that if you truly possess one virtue, like courage, you must possess them all, like wisdom and temperance, because they all stem from the same rational foundation.</note> follow one another with such a close connection that he who has acquired one already enjoys the possession of all virtues.

However, the person who ascends with the greatest difficulty necessarily attains the whole and entire summit. 

Since, therefore, this is the condition of evils and goods, it is concluded by necessary reason that those things which do not follow one another cannot be "goods." **Pleasures**, however, not only fail to come together, but they seem to conflict with one another and more often bring about an impediment. For while one of the bodily senses is moved by the greatest sweetness, the remaining senses hardly perceive the delight of the things then offered to them. It also happens that one person perceives more and greater pleasures than another, and not all living creatures are delighted equally. 

**Virtues**, however—and everything that is truly good—are so coupled together for the reason we mentioned just a moment ago, that they are all present at once in the same person; nor can more of them be present in one person than in another. Since, therefore, it is clear that the natures of "goods" and "pleasures" are different from each other, surely no one would call bodily pleasure "good," unless they were too much a friend to it.

¶ Next, a second argument of **Plato's** <note>original: "platonis"</note> proves that it is the property of **goods** to tend toward the common utility and salvation of the human race. He says, however, that **pleasure**—which he calls **lust** <note>original: "libidinem"</note> and **love**—begets a private interest. He who is subject to this always focuses only on his own desire; he has no care for anyone else, provided he may more watchfully obey his own **whirlpool** <note>original: "uoragini" — a metaphorical term for a bottomless pit of desire or greed.</note> of appetite. Everything he does, he refers back to that sweetness and delight perceived by the senses.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of "The End" (the ultimate goal of human life) and the nature of pleasure. ...they say it is, but they define the **End** <term>finis: the ultimate goal or "highest good" toward which all human actions aim</term> as that to which a desire is referred as its final point. Therefore, since the natural desire of man seeks pleasure only for the sake of something else, who of sound mind would think that pleasure is the End, or even a good at all? Indeed, they believe that nature granted this kind of sweet perception to living things for this reason: so that they might acquire and prepare the things necessary for living. For a living being especially requires two things: to reject and repel what can cause harm, and to take in and adopt what is beneficial. 

However, because repelling the former and pursuing the latter is laborious and difficult, nature has woven a certain pleasure into every action of this kind, lest living things be too slow to provide what they need because of that very difficulty. Thus it happens that, enticed and thoroughly captured by this sweetness—just like **bait** <note>original: "esca". Ficino uses the metaphor of pleasure as a lure or hook used by nature to ensure survival through "baiting" the senses.</note>—they do not flee from any dangers or labor, nor do they feel the difficulty of preparing their food, and they are rendered more ready to provide the necessities of life. They demonstrate that pleasure was given to us by nature for these reasons by this sign: that all animals are moved by this sweetness (which we have already mentioned so often) when they either expel something from the body that is superfluous or take in what is necessary. And the more they act toward that purpose, the greater the delight they perceive. 

Yet, once they have fully satisfied nature’s need, they feel no further pleasure. But we see them moved as long as they are filling a deficiency, as if nature directed the pleasure of the senses toward attaining life's necessities and filling what is lacking. Therefore, pleasure was handed down for the sake of preserving life and **propagating the species** <note>original: "generis propagandi". Referring to reproduction.</note>; it is not to be sought for itself, nor is it the End, and therefore, as we have demonstrated many times, it should not even be called a "good."

**Archytas the Pythagorean** <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 435–360 BC) who was a contemporary of Plato and a key figure in the Pythagorean school.</note> also used this argument against the pleasure of the body: that causes must always be related to the things that follow from those causes. Therefore, he thinks no one should doubt that something from which so many evils follow cannot be a good. It is clear that for the sake of pleasure, all the plague-like disturbances of the soul are born—adultery, debauchery, homicide, theft, dissension, and finally all crimes. From these things it follows (as he believes) that pleasure appears not only to be no good, but a certain supreme and detestable evil. 

By the same reasoning, **Antisthenes the Socratic** <note>A pupil of Socrates and a founder of Cynic philosophy, known for his emphasis on virtue and his rejection of luxury.</note> proves that bodily pleasure is the extreme and highest of evils. For whatever is the cause and origin of all evils can also be rightly judged as the worst of all things; and since all sins proceed from **ignorance** <note>original: "ignorantia". A Socratic theme suggesting that we only do evil because we do not truly know what is good.</note>, and nothing can be as much of a...

<summary>Ficino argues that pleasure is merely a biological "bait" designed by nature to ensure survival and reproduction, rather than a moral good. He supports this by citing Archytas and Antisthenes, who viewed pleasure as the root of all social and moral evils.</summary>

...pleasure corrupts judgment and counsel, it is necessary (as he concludes) that both ignorance and all evils originate from it. Hence, he was accustomed to say that he would rather be seized by madness than by pleasure. <note>original: "insania dicere solebat potius, q̃ uoluptate corripiar". This sentiment is famously attributed to the philosopher Antisthenes, emphasizing that the loss of reason in pleasure is worse than mental illness.</note> 

Furthermore, **Hermes Trismegistus** <term>Mercurius Trismegistus: a legendary Hellenistic figure seen as a "thrice-great" Egyptian priest and philosopher who provided the foundation for all human wisdom</term>, the wisest of all the Egyptians, attempts to root out this wicked plague from the souls of men for two primary reasons. He judges that something is "good" for a person only if it either contains the essence of that person’s true nature or leads them toward a better state of being. We see that virtues of the first kind are those placed in action; for their specific purpose is to render the soul free and tranquil from all the tumult of disturbances. Indeed, the removal of disturbances and a certain serenity of mind is the natural property and essence of every soul. 

It is well-established that virtues of the second kind are those engaged in contemplation. Truly, when these virtues lift up and exalt the soul through the study and understanding of divine matters—somewhat beyond human nature itself—the soul seems to approach most closely to the life of God, which consists solely of contemplation. However, it is clear that the condition of pleasure is the opposite of both these states. For pleasure agitates the soul with countless and most burning passions, as if by certain **furies** <note>In mythology, the Furies were deities of vengeance who drove people to madness; here used to describe the chaotic effect of physical desires.</note>, so that it remains far from that tranquility which nature so greatly requires. 

Since the human race holds a middle position between God and the beasts, and for that reason rightly appears to share in the qualities of both, **Trismegistus** believes it is possible for a person to migrate and be "converted" into either one. And indeed, he who primarily uses his mind surely leads the most blessed life of the immortal gods, while he who uses the body and the senses leads the life of beasts. Therefore, since the use of pleasure exists within the body and the senses, he who is most devoted to it not only fails to ascend to those things which are better and more divine, but he does not even retain the status and dignity of his own nature. Instead, he slips, as it were, from soul to body, from mind to the senses, and from man to the beasts. 

**Socrates** speaks divinely on this in **Plato’s** *Phaedo*: pleasure, he says, holding a sort of **nail** <term>clauum: a pin or nail used to fasten things together</term>, fastens and joins the soul to the body. It causes the soul, infected by the appearance of the body, to believe that whatever the body suggests is true. For since the soul is moved by the same things and feels the same things as the body, it is forced (as I believe) to take on the same habits and the same way of life.

From these points, another argument is woven by **Trismegistus**. In every category of things, he wishes there to be one thing that is greatest and highest, through participation in which all other things in that same category are classified. For example, all things that are hot become hot through the nature of fire, in which the highest heat resides. In the same way, whatever things are "good" follow after that which is the **highest and first good** <term>summum bonum: the ultimate source of all goodness in the universe</term>, and...

# Chapter 3. Objections of the Peripatetics against the Platonic definition of pleasure.

This, then, is Plato's divine opinion on pleasure, in which **Hermes Trismegistus**, all the **Pythagoreans**, and the most excellent **Socratics** agree without any doubt. But the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, who traditionally taught while walking in the shaded walkways (peripatoi) of the Lyceum</term>, who are certainly sharp men—though perhaps more eager for argument in this matter than for the truth—strive to subvert and corrupt this most excellent and divine opinion of Plato with certain subtleties of theirs. 

There are three points on which they attempt to criticize the Platonists. The first is that Plato called pleasure a "motion" in his definition; for they say every motion is either fast or slow, yet no pleasure can be called fast or slow. Instead, it must be called either brief or long-lasting. Furthermore, they argue that no motion can exist as a whole all at once; rather, one part of a motion always follows another, so that as one part ceases, another is born, and two parts of a motion cannot exist at the same time. Pleasure, on the contrary, occurs all at once as a whole, and all its parts together (as so... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

...to remain (as I might say). For when the soul knows it is enjoying the possession of some good, they think it immediately perceives pleasure. Thus it happens that the pleasure of the soul follows cognition and perception, and just as the perception of that which seems good is completed in an instant by an external object, so too pleasure, which follows such an apprehension, is perfected in an instant. Those things which happen in this way occur all at once and equally, consisting of a certain indivisible and simple nature. From these things, they wish to conclude that pleasure is born in the senses at a simple point in time, and is whole and perfect right from its first beginning, not requiring another part to make it more complete; hence, it cannot be a **motion**. 

Next, they reject **Plato** for calling pleasure the "filling of a lack" <note>original: "repletionem indigentiæ". In his dialogue *Philebus*, Plato argues that many pleasures, like eating, are merely the process of returning a body from a state of "lack" (hunger) to "fullness."</note>. They think this is false because pleasure resides in the soul, whereas "filling" occurs in the body. Nor do they agree that all pleasure is of such a kind that it corresponds to the filling of a lack. For instance, the pleasures perceived by the eyes, ears, and nostrils—derived from forms, sounds, and smells—do not fill any prior lack. Furthermore, they argue there is an ineffable pleasure in contemplation which fills nothing lacking. Indeed, they claim this is proper to the mind, and the mind neither needs any physical support nor can it be filled in any way. For being filled or conversely emptied belongs to bodies, which can be both full and empty. But since the soul is simple and incorporeal <note>meaning: without a physical body</note>, these things can in no way happen to it.

In the third place, they argue against the fact that Plato said no pleasures are good, and most are bad. But they [the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who famously walked about while teaching.</note>] judge many to be excellent and most worthy of praise, such as those arising from honorable actions. For such actions seem most pleasant, and the pleasure within them exists as the best and purest.

### Chapter 4: Responses to the Objections.

These are the arguments of the Peripatetics, which I would despair of being able to answer, if the very man against whom they fight did not defend himself by his own "warfare" <note>original: "suo marte", a Latin idiom meaning by one's own efforts or strength.</note> (as they say). Therefore, the first argument, by which they conclude that pleasure can in no way be a motion, even if it happens to be true, nevertheless has no weight against the Platonists. For Plato himself taught that there are two kinds of motion: one of bodies, the other of souls. And the motion of those bodies, in which it is the nature of a body to follow, cannot be gathered into an individual and simple state. He focuses on whether pleasure is a "motion" and clarifies the distinction between the soul's instantaneous acts and the body's time-bound movements.</meta>
