<meta>Catchword: to happen</meta>

...it must. However, that which remains undivided now sheds the nature of a body. Because every body is extended and divisible, it is necessary—if it ever acts or suffers anything, or is moved from one place to another—that the nearer and front parts suffer, act, or turn before the others. Thus, every motion of bodies requires a span of time and is stretched out in a sequence from what is prior to what is posterior. The soul, however, is indivisible and simple, having no internal division or distance between parts. Therefore, the soul’s motion is indivisible and simple, and is completed entirely at a single point of time. Hence, **Thales of Miletus** <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, often called the first philosopher.</note> says nothing is faster than the soul. 

Therefore, since pleasure was defined by **Plato** not as a motion of the body, but of the soul, nothing indeed prevents it from being a motion and also existing entirely all at once. This is especially true since in Platonic books, "motion" <note>original: "motio"</note> signifies not only flow and succession (as the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note> maintain) but also every operation and act. 

Next, as for their claim that **Plato** called pleasure the "filling of a lack" <note>original: "indigentiæ repletionem"</note>, and lack itself "pain," this may perhaps seem less than true. For in the *Gorgias*, he even wants pleasure to consist in filling. But that pleasure consists "in pleasure," or that any other of those things that occur naturally consists "in itself," no one would say except those most unlike **Plato**. Furthermore, in that same book he says that "filling" is pleasurable, but "lack" is mostly painful. But who speaks so absurdly as to call pleasure "pleasurable" or pain "painful"? Who likewise would say "beautiful beauty" or "just justice"? In the same way, **Plato** would not have called pleasure "pleasurable" nor pain "painful." Therefore, he did not intend for pain to be lack, nor pleasure to be filling. 

Moreover, he says that pleasure comes *from* filling, and pain *from* want <note>original: "egeſtate"</note>. Yet he himself thinks nothing can be made from itself. How then could pleasure, if it is filling, be made from filling itself? Or pain, if it is want, be born from want? Furthermore, the same man in the *Timaeus* places pleasure in the senses and calls it a motion and an affection <note>original: "affectum"</note>. A man so great would never say that an affection or a motion of the senses is "filling." 

If anyone reads in the *Gorgias* that pleasure is the filling of the body, let him consider that passage more carefully; he will eventually find that **Plato** himself does not hold that opinion, but rather that it is the opinion of **Callicles**—a most pleasure-seeking man—against whom **Socrates** disputes most sharply. 

Indeed, the **Peripatetics** grant us these points. However, some deny that all pleasure comes from the actual filling of a lack; especially since that pleasure which contemplation brings to us, and which [exists] in the mind...

...consists, and that it occurs from no filling of a lack. Even if I could show more clearly than light that even that delight of the mind, which is captured from contemplation, takes its origin from that very filling, let us nevertheless grant this to them, lest we perhaps seem too argumentative. Let it be exactly as they wish. What then? Did not **Plato** (as we also said above) place pleasure in the senses and joy in the mind? If therefore the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> also place it in the mind, what is that to us? For this is not what **Plato** believes. Therefore, that which is perceived in contemplating, we call not *pleasure* <note>original: "voluptatem"</note>, but *joy* <note>original: "gaudium"</note>. If it is born less from a "filling," it is nothing against **Plato**, who said that it is not joy (which is in the mind) but pleasure (which resides in the senses) that is created from the filling of a lack.

But **Aristotle** insists more sharply in his tenth book on Ethics, proving that even that pleasure which occurs in the senses does not always proceed from the filling of a lack. For he maintains that this is true regarding touch and taste. But in those pleasures which we take from smells, forms, and sounds, he argues it happens in no way at all. For he who rejoices in sounds or forms is not, by any reasoning, "filled" by these very things in which he takes delight, nor did he previously lack them.

And yet, even if these arguments perhaps seem plausible, they are not of such a kind that they can detract from **Plato** in any part. For those words of **Plato**, in which he says pleasure is born from the filling of a lack, we can interpret (as it seems) in two ways. For these two things—**lack** <term>lack: original "egestas," the state of being without something</term> and **desire** <term>desire: original "appetitio," the reaching out for something</term>—are so connected to each other that one cannot be separated from the other. For we desire those things which we lack, and we do not desire anything which we did not lack before the longing; nor is anyone in a state of lack without desiring, nor does anyone ever desire who does not lack. Thus, it happens that both seem to be so joined together that one always accompanies the other.

Therefore, among all the most excellent philosophers, it is the custom to frequently signify *desire* by the name of *lack*, and in the same way, they wish *lack* to be understood by the name of *desire*. Hence **Cicero** <note>The Roman statesman and orator, much admired by Renaissance humanists.</note> rightly says, "He does not lack, who does not desire." **Socrates** also denied that he lacked our riches and luxuries (for which others most ardently strive) because he did not desire them at all. **Epicurus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure is the highest good, though he defined it as the absence of pain.</note> also said that it was not the man who had little who was in a state of lack, but the man who craved more. Therefore, if anyone wishes to drive away lack, he must not add to his money, but rather take away from his desire. 

And in the same way, when **Plato** says "the filling of a lack," he wanted the "filling of desire" to be understood. For desire is filled when it attains that which it was wanting. The filling of desire is nothing other than a certain attainment of that which had entered into one's longing. From these things, therefore, which I have said...

# ON PLEASURE

...thus we interpret **Plato**. The "filling of a lack" <note>original: "Repletio indigentiæ"</note> stands as the cause of pleasure. This occurs when the appetite, which lacks something and which we call "indigence," has attained that which it longed for and enjoys its presence, and is, as it were, filled. That movement is immediately born in the senses, which we call sweetness, delight, and pleasure. Hence the Delian epigram <note>An ancient Greek inscription found on the island of Delos, often cited in ethical philosophy.</note> says that the most pleasant thing is "to possess the thing loved." This interpretation has a place in all the senses, and even in the mind (if one wishes). For indeed, when all the senses have attained the very thing they previously desired, they are charmed by a certain ineffable pleasure. 

And this is the first way of responding, by which the **Platonists** can escape the snares of the **Peripatetics** <note>Ficino uses "snares" to describe the logical traps Aristotle's followers set for Plato's theories.</note>; and if this interpretation perhaps seems too harsh to anyone, come, let us try another, lest our side seem to have fallen under their arrows. What else, then, is "filling a lack" but achieving that which you lack? But what do we lack, except those things which can either protect our health while it is present, or restore it if it is lost, or bring us some other utility in some way?

Now, we are men. But "man" is, as the **Peripatetics** and **Stoics** <note>The Stoics believed in living according to reason and virtue, viewing the soul and body as a unified organism.</note> believe, that which consists of a rational soul and a body. The **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**, differing slightly from the others, think that man is a certain divine mind bound in earthly chains. The result is that among other philosophers, the soul has the nature and name of a "part" of the man, while among the **Platonists**, our soul is the *whole* man.

For this reason, when **Socrates** was asked by **Crito** how he ordered himself to be buried, he said: "However you like, if only you can catch me, and I do not escape you." <note>A reference to the *Phaedo*, where Socrates argues that his true self—the soul—cannot be buried in a grave.</note> And the same **Socrates**, disputing with **Alcibiades** in **Plato's** writings, proves by many arguments that man is nothing else besides the soul. The body, however, is not the man, but belongs *to* the man. External things belong not to the man, but to fortune. 

Yet he does not call our soul "man" always and everywhere. Rather, as long as it leads its life in the celestial seats, it is called now a "god" and now a "daemon" <note>term: daemon (a divine or semi-divine spirit that acts as an intermediary between gods and men, or the higher guiding part of the soul)</note> by the **Platonists**. But when it is enclosed in earthly dwellings, it receives the name of "humanity" from the very nature of the ground <note>original: "humus" (soil/earth), a common Renaissance etymology linking 'homo' (man) to 'humus'.</note> in which it is submerged. Therefore **Origen** the **Platonist**, a most noble man, asserted that a man can be transformed into a daemon and a god, and sometimes even migrate into beasts. **Seneca** likewise, being very studious of **Plato**, called our soul "a god guest-hosting in a human body." But all these, and **Plato** himself, imitated **Heraclitus**, **Empedocles**, and **Pythagoras**. For **Pythagoras** asserts that our soul is transferred from man into god with these verses:

> Having left the body behind, when you go free into the heavens,
> You will escape being man, made a god of the nourishing air.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the nature of pleasure. Having previously discussed Plato’s definition of pleasure as the "filling of a lack," Ficino now transitions to defining the human being and how the different senses correspond to the physical elements.</meta>

# BOOK

¶ Since therefore (to return to our purpose) man is, in the opinion of the **Aristotelians**, a being that consists of a rational soul and a body—whereas **Plato** holds that man is a certain divine soul that makes use of the service of an earthly body—it follows that we must certainly undertake the care of two things: namely, the soul and the body. The care of the soul (as Plato commands) is for its own sake alone; however, all care of the body ought to be referred to the soul, just as a servant is to a master. 

There are, therefore, two kinds of things that we need. We require those things which will benefit the soul, and those which will benefit the body. Those things benefit the body which either restore or preserve life, health, strength, beauty, and its own proper nature. To the soul, however, belong all those things which contribute to the best character <term>mores: refers to moral conduct and the habits of the mind</term> and to the knowledge of reality. Add to these, above all, that those things benefit both soul and body which seem similar and related to either one. For like things (as it is said) are preserved by like things, and each individual thing seeks its own well-being. 

These, then, are the things that humans need. For this reason, when these things are present—or at least those things which have a certain appearance and similarity to them—we are affected by pleasure. Indeed, if things that seem good to us are present, they bring pleasure. From this it follows that opinion precedes pleasure; for as the **Stoics** <note>A school of philosophy that emphasized reason and the belief that our internal judgments, rather than external events, determine our happiness.</note> believe, nothing can be pleasant to anyone unless he has judged it to be related to himself and good. 

¶ Now, since bodily pleasure is perceived by the senses, and since there are five types of these, there will similarly be five kinds of pleasures. One is perceived by touching, another by tasting; smells provide another, and the ears and eyes supply the remaining ones. And these senses relate to one another in such a way that they maintain a specific order, both of location and of nature. 

For the eyes are the purest and—as the Platonic **Timaeus** <note>Referring to the character Timaeus in Plato’s dialogue of the same name, which discusses the creation of the universe and the human body.</note> discusses and proves—are related to the nature of fire and light. The ears hold the second rank of purity and are compared to the air. The nostrils then possess the third degree of refinement <note>original: "tenuitatis"</note>, and being composed of a certain thicker nature, they occupy a middle ground between air and water. Next, the organ of tasting is thicker and very similar to the nature of water. Finally, in the [lowest] degree of refinement, those parts with which we touch are distributed; for these approach more closely to the nature of the body and are assigned to the density <note>original: "crassitudini"</note> of the earth. 

You see these five senses arranged step by step, relating to each other so that those located in the higher part of the body also obtain a superior rank of purity, and each is related to different things. Because we have discussed this more extensively in the commentaries we published on Plato's *Timaeus*, let it suffice to have touched upon it briefly in this place. Here, he applies this principle to each of the five senses to explain how they experience pleasure as a "filling" of a lack.</meta>

When denser bodies are brought near <note>original: "crassiora corpora"; Ficino is likely referring to the objects of Touch here, as the other four senses follow sequentially.</note>, endowed with the same nature of moisture and heat as the sense itself is affected, their presence—because they are kindred and share the same nature, protecting its own composition and quality—causes the sense to exult in a way and leap for joy, being completely bathed in sweetness. 

**Taste**, indeed, is refreshed by more liquid bodies (as is evident); for it is delighted by those flavors that have the nature of a ripened and matured moisture. Indeed, since **Taste** itself (as the **Platonists** believe) is composed in the same proportion, it happens that when a similar and, so to speak, familiar object approaches, it rests most sweetly with it. 

Furthermore, the power of **Smelling** is greatly restored by those odors which are a mixture of the natures of water and air—which is perceived in fruits and flowers—provided that the sense itself has been granted that same nature from its origin. 

Moreover, the **Ears** are delighted by sounds of the kind made from the purest air and consisting of the same harmony <term>armonia: the mathematical proportion or "tuning" that allows a sense to perceive its object</term> as the ears themselves; thus we see that, due to the diversity of nature, some people are delighted by softer harmonies, others by more vigorous ones, some by deeper sounds, and others by clearer ones. 

As for the **Eyes**, because they are most familiar with light, those things seem most pleasing whose nature is tempered most similarly to light. Indeed, such things are all those that result from a most beautiful blending of colors, all of which originate from light. 

We do not only need these things, which we draw in through the senses, for the sake of increasing life and restoring our nature, but also for attaining the skill and expertise of the mind. From this it follows that the senses, for two reasons, require certain excellent things offered from the outside: first, because they are kindred and similar to themselves (for it is necessary that individual things be preserved and perfected by things similar to them); and second, because they can provide instruction for the knowledge of things and arts, which is what we most greatly desire. 

Whenever, therefore, those things of which we have spoken are offered to the senses and admitted deep within for enjoyment, that lack <note>original: "indigentia"; the state of being empty or lacking something necessary</note> of the senses—which previously gave birth to desire—is filled. And that pleasure which we seek occurs from this refilling <term>repletio: the act of filling up a void or deficiency</term> of a lack. 

This is, therefore, the second interpretation of the **Platonic** definition, which I believe no one, provided they are of sound mind, will find fault with. Therefore, enough on these matters; let us proceed to the rest. 

¶ There are three questions proposed by the **Aristotelians** against **Plato**: 
1. First, that he falsely called pleasure a "motion." 
2. Another, that neither a "refilling" nor pleasure itself can entirely arise from refilling. 

To all of these, I believe I have already responded sufficiently—not indeed by my own meager wit (for I do not claim so much for myself), but by those arguments which were most extensively discussed by **Plato** himself. But the final objection of **Aristotle** was that many pleasures exist, contrary to **Plato**, who had denied it <unclear>...</unclear>

Therefore, we will grant to Aristotle that what is mixed with virtue is a good; yet we will not grant that "pleasure" is the good, but rather **joy**. For everyone uses his own vocabulary according to his judgment; and while Aristotle differs from Plato in name, he agrees in reality. Indeed, the **Pythagoreans**, **Stoics**, and **Cynics** <note>These were major schools of ancient Greek philosophy; Ficino often tries to show they are in underlying agreement.</note> agree with our views both in reality and in name.

### Chapter 5. Various opinions on what pleasure is. The first opinion, that of Aristotle.

<margin>a</margin>
Aristotle, however—to come to his opinion—uses the name of **pleasure** more broadly. By it, he wishes to signify not only 그 sweetness that clings to the senses, but also that which consists in the mind. Yet, what pleasure itself actually is, he seems to hint at rather than explicitly define. Nevertheless, what he discusses concerning this in the seventh and tenth books *On Morals* <note>original: "de moribus"; this refers to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>, we can interpret in the way I shall describe. 

There are (to use Aristotle’s words) three powers of the soul. One is common to us and the plants, which they call the **vegetative power** <term>vegetandi vim: the basic biological force of life found in all living things</term>. Its duties are three: to nourish its own body, to increase it (growth), and finally to produce another similar to itself (reproduction). Next, he calls the second nature of the soul the **sensitive power**, which exists in us in common with the other animals. Of the senses, some are internal and others are external. The external ones, which are more relevant to our purpose, are five in number, most well-known by the common division. 

The third power of the soul belongs to humans alone out of every kind of mortal living thing, and this he calls the **intellect** or **mind**. To these, he adds the power of movement; but let us set that aside, as it has no bearing on our purpose. Regarding the first nature of the soul, which belongs to plants, the ancient philosophers held diverse views. Indeed, **Plato** thinks that the souls of trees and herbs have a certain silent appetite, which he calls the "striving of nature." **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who believed all things were made of four elements.</note> maintained that not only a natural inclination, but even sensation is present in plants. **Anaxagoras**, moreover, and **Democritus** believe they are affected by pleasure and pain; and they judge them to have the power not only of sensing, but also of thinking and understanding. But Aristotle judges that they are endowed neither with reason nor with sensation at all, nor do they participate in any pleasure. Thus, it follows that the power of nourishing and growing has no relevance to Aristotle's opinion on pleasure.

...might offer his opinion. Therefore, the remaining powers of the soul to which he attributes pleasure are two: one of which (to use his own words) he calls **intellect**, and the other **sense**; to these he assigns their own actions, which he calls **cognitions**. He wishes, therefore, the operation of the intellect or—to speak in Latin—the **mind** <note>original: "mentis"</note> and **reason** to be called intelligence, thought, and contemplation. 

Truly, he calls the operation of sight "vision," of hearing "audition," of smell "odoration," of taste "gustation," and finally of touch "taction" <note>Ficino is methodically listing the Latin technical terms for the act of using each sense.</note>. Thus, sight itself is the power and nature of the soul by which one is able to see, whereas vision is the action itself—that is, the act of seeing. The same applies to the other senses. 

Regarding vision (to follow one example for all), it has two primary principles from which it arises as if from certain causes: namely, the faculty of sight itself in which it resides, and the external thing which is perceived, by which the sight is stimulated to see. Aristotle calls the faculty of sight a "power" and "potentiality" of the soul. That which is perceived by sight is the **object**, and the vision itself should be called "perfect" when the power of the soul is in its best state and the object to be seen is by its own nature the best and, moreover, harmonious with the nature of the soul. If either of these is lacking, the vision will be imperfect; but when both concur as one, it will be perfect. 

Indeed, whatever vision is perfect is also pleasant; the more perfect it is, the more pleasant; and the most perfect is the most pleasant. Therefore (to repeat the same point often), because vision is perfect, it is pleasant; thus the perfection of vision seems to be a certain pleasantness. For this reason, conversely, the pleasantness of vision is its perfection. Since pleasantness and pleasure—as far as our purpose is concerned—mean the same thing, he concludes that **pleasure is the perfection of vision**. 

And what has been said of sight, we wish to be understood also of the other senses and of the mind itself. For in all things there is a proper operation: in hearing, audition; in smell, odoration; and similarly for the rest. Therefore, according to the common definition in Aristotle, **pleasure is nothing other than a certain perfection of the operation of the soul**, which is the same as the perfection of cognition. Since pleasure dwells in all the senses, the pleasure of sight will be the perfection of vision; of hearing, the perfection of audition; of taste, the perfection of gustation; and so on for the others, so that the pleasure of each is the perfection of its own proper operation.

There is, however, in Aristotle a twofold perfection: one is "primary," the other is "annexed." The primary perfection is that which exists as a part of the nature of that thing which it completes—for example, the soul of a human being. For this is the human's perfection and a certain part of the human substance. But we call that "annexed" perfection which, although it is no part of the substance, nevertheless follows the substance itself and, as it were, ac-

### Chapter VI. Opinions of the Peripatetics regarding pleasure.

Aristotle, however, seems to call none of these things "pleasure." Rather, he views it as a certain perfection of the perception itself. Thus, the primary perception is of sweetness, and from this something else is born as its companion and its annexed perfection; this very thing is pleasure. But what this kind of "perfection" is, which he calls pleasure, he never (so it seems) sufficiently explained. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkway in the Lyceum where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note>—those who descended from Aristotle—wished to explain and bring to light what had been obscurely stated by their leader, and so they were divided into various opinions. 

For some placed pleasure in the senses, while others placed it in the appetite <term>appetitus: the faculty of the soul that moves a person toward a perceived good</term> which follows the senses. Even those who placed it in the senses interpret Aristotle in different ways. Indeed, some think there are two perceptions in the senses. The first seems to proceed and flow into the mind from things offered from the outside. The second, however, having proceeded more from the mind itself, is extended toward those things which are outside. 

For example, the mind first perceives sweetness, and this first perception seems to arise from the pleasantness of the object presented. Then, the mind considers that it has attained that sweetness—that it perceives it, holds it, and enjoys it. They judged that this second perception—be it thought, meditation, or notice—was what Aristotle called pleasure. Thus, pleasure is that very consideration by which one thinks to oneself that they are enjoying the presence of good things.

¶ Some, however, think it is not the sense itself, but that when the mind notices it has attained sweetness, it is uplifted and conceives a certain cheerfulness and carries it within itself; they believe this is what Aristotle meant by pleasure. Therefore, pleasure is the elevation or cheerfulness of the mind having already obtained the good it desired.

¶ But those who placed pleasure in that part of the soul by which we desire <note>The "appetitive" part of the soul.</note> think there are two properties of appetite. One is the state of being moved and inclined toward those goods which are far from us and which we have not yet attained. The other consists in that which we have already acquired and attained. They call the first "desire" <term>cupiditas: a longing for what is absent</term>; the second they call "rest" <term>quies: the state of being at peace once a goal is reached</term>. 

They maintain that the former (desire) is full of trouble, solicitude, care, and anxiety. But they believe the latter (rest) is infused with a certain ineffable sweetness, and that this is what is called pleasure by the leader of the Peripatetics. In this view, pleasure is nothing else but a certain limit or "rest" of the appetite in a good that has already been attained. Whence Lucretius says: "the rest of men and the pleasure of the gods." <note>original: "requies hominum divumque voluptas." This is a variation of the opening line of Lucretius’s *De Rerum Natura*, usually "hominum divumque voluptas" (the delight of men and gods), here modified to emphasize "rest" (requies).</note>

¶ However, as to what this "rest" itself is, not all explain it in the same way...

...have explained. For some define it as that very cessation and, as it were, a certain end of seeking—a state of rest. For the appetite <term>appetitus: the soul's faculty of desiring or striving toward a goal</term>, once it has attained the good it desired, ceases from its seeking. Therefore, to be free from worry and anxiety—which freedom is rest itself—is what Aristotle called pleasure. And so, as these men define it, pleasure is the freedom from all the worry and anxiety of seeking, once the good that was desired has been acquired.

¶ But some Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle, named after the Greek word for "walking," as they often held discussions while walking.</note> added something else to this freedom. They argue that to be without any trouble is not yet to possess the full and perfect nature of pleasure. It becomes whole and absolute only if every desire comes to rest in that state in such a way that it not only seeks nothing further, but clings to this good which it enjoys with all its nerves and strength, assents <note>original: "affentiatur"; a philosophical term for the mind giving its internal agreement to a sensation</note> that it is enough for itself, and is thoroughly spread through it. Therefore, as these men believe, pleasure is the **assent** and the **diffusion** <note>original: "diffuſio"; a "spreading out" or expansion of the soul toward an object</note> of the appetite into the good which it possesses, whereby it happens that in the midst of pleasures the whole body seems to melt and flow away. This occurs when every power and movement of the soul and body leans toward that which is presented from the outside and is utterly carried away. 

But this kind of spreading out should not only be in the members and parts of the body, but also in the appetite and the nature of the soul. For the body is not spread out toward anything unless it is driven by the appetite and the power of the soul. For this reason, it is necessary that the appetite and the soul themselves be spread out, and most greedily fixed and clung to that which seems to agree with its own nature. Therefore, every such effort of the soul and appetite to join, to cling to, and to be fixed to the good which is already possessed contains pleasure; and pleasure seems to be nothing else, as these men please, than to assent, to cling, and to be fixed to a present good, and to flow into it and be thoroughly spread through it. Provided you understand that these things happen in the soul, and in that part of the soul which is called the power of desiring. 

For a movement of this kind is also found in the heat, the blood, the spirits <note>In Renaissance science, "spirits" were subtle substances that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note>, and the whole body, which is nonetheless neither pleasure itself nor any part of pleasure. But from that spreading and assent which is in the soul—which they call pleasure—those meltings and flowings of the body proceed, like certain footprints of the innermost pleasure. For just as these things are in the body, such pleasure also exists in the soul.

...our Plato's opinion does not differ, except that Aristotle speaks more broadly using the same name of "pleasure" <note>original: "uoluptatis"</note> for both the delight that is in the mind and that which is in the senses. Plato, however, calls that which happens to the senses "pleasure," whereas he names that which is in the mind "joy" <note>original: "gaudium"</note>. Indeed, sometimes even Plato himself confuses the names of pleasure and joy, using either term to signify both. Therefore, in name they differ either not at all, or only slightly and in the smallest degree; that they agree in the actual reality, several of Plato’s books can bear witness, as can many Platonic philosophers who are by no means to be looked down upon.

For Apuleius, Chalcidius, Contius, and the noble Platonist Ptolemy <note>These are prominent commentators and scholars who translated or interpreted Plato’s works, particularly the *Timaeus*, for Latin-speaking audiences.</note> interpret Plato’s opinion—which was set down in very obscure words in the *Timaeus*—in the manner that I shall briefly report. They say, indeed, that Plato understands **sensation** <note>original: "sensum"</note> to be the soul’s first perception which arises from the "passion" or experience of the body itself. For they believe that certain "species" <term>species: the outward forms or appearances of things that flow toward the observer</term> of all things that are to be known flow toward us, are drawn in through the openings of the senses, and are imprinted and sealed upon the "spirit" <term>spiritus: a very thin, vapor-like substance believed to reside in the brain's ventricles and act as a bridge between the physical body and the non-physical soul</term> which is in the ventricles of the brain. 

The forms of things of this kind, being shaped within the spirit—which is itself a very thin and transparent body—strike the soul and cause it to gaze upon and perceive those very external objects whose images these are. We see that this perception of the soul arises from the very "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon by an outside force.</note> and impulse of the body. Since the spirit is moved by external bodies, it strikes the soul with a matching image and gives it shape. Since, therefore, a perception of this kind arises from the impulse of the spirit, it follows that it proceeds from a bodily "passion"—that is, from a strike and a motion. 

Aurelius Augustine, a good Platonist, imitated this in the book titled *On the Quantity of the Soul*. He says: "Sensation is a passion of the body which is, by itself, not hidden from the soul." <note>This is a famous definition from St. Augustine's *De Quantitate Animae*, emphasizing that the soul must "notice" what the body undergoes for it to count as a sensation.</note> That is to say, through the very form of the body drawn in by the senses, the "passion" of that same body is perceived by a certain primary and proper image.

From these things it happens that we feel through a twin "passion" of the body. For by the impulse of the brain and the spirit, we apprehend the "passions" caused by external bodies. However, the Platonists divide that "passion" which one's own body receives from the outside into two parts: one of which eases and soothes the body, not so much striking the limbs and organs as stroking and tickling them; the other, however, shakes them more roughly and harshly. When the soul consents to that first motion of the body, whose nature is to soothe, **pleasure** is created. When it shrinks from and abandons the other motion, which we call harsh, they say it brings **pain**. 

The soul "assents" to the motion of the body when it willingly clings to it, is fastened to it, joined with it, drenched in it, and rests most sweetly within it...

Indeed, they differ in nothing even here; for the soul never rests unless it consents, nor does it consent unless it also rests.

## Chapter 8. How the Peripatetics divide pleasure, and regarding the powers of the soul.

**W**hat the Platonists and Peripatetics handed down regarding the definition of pleasure, and how the discussions of both groups agree on the same point, has now, I believe, been sufficiently declared. Let us now examine what the Peripatetics thought regarding the division of pleasure. The Peripatetics believe that the whole nature of man consists of a soul and a body. Regarding the soul, as it pertains to the question at hand, they divide it into two parts: the mind <note>original: "mentem"</note> and the sense. In turn, they hold that the mind has a twin power and nature. One of these is engaged in the investigation of truth, the other in deliberation and action. To use their words, they call the former the **contemplative intellect** and the latter the **active intellect**. They say the property of the former is to search out the causes, properties, and progressions of those things contained within the order of nature, and that it is content with the contemplation of truth alone. The work of the latter, they claim, is to discern through deliberation what things are to be done or avoided. 

Of the senses, they call some "internal" and others "external." The internal senses (as Averroes <note>original: "Auerois." Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, the most acute of the Peripatetic interpreters, maintains) are divided into four types. The first of these collects and perceives all the images <note>original: "imagines"</note> that are drawn in through the five external senses; for this reason, they call it the **common sense**. The second power is named **imagination** by them; its duty—since it perceives nothing itself—is to retain the images accepted from the prior senses and bring them to the third nature of sensing, which they call **phantasia**, or the power of judging and thinking. They believe the work of this power is to judge and perceive, once those images are received, what or of what sort the thing is whose images they are. Finally, those things which it has discerned—whether it has joined, or conceived of them by judging—it commends to be saved in the last part of the brain and the sense, which they call **memory**. As for those external senses...

Therefore, sight is seen as purer than hearing, hearing purer than smell, the power of smelling purer than taste, and this finally purer than touch. For light and colors pertain to sight; sounds to the ears; odors to the nostrils; flavors to taste; while solidity, softness, heat, and cold pertain to the power of touch. Because light and color are purer than sound, sound than odors, and these than flavor—and because flavors are purer than those things subjected to touch—it follows that sight excels hearing, hearing excels the sense of the nostrils, this sense excels taste, and taste finally excels touch in purity and dignity. To these five powers of sensing, five corresponding organs (as they call them) are attributed in the body as subjects and foundations. These seem to be nothing other than certain affections <note>original: "affectiones"; in this context, physical states or impressions</note> of the body, which some call "dispositions," others "qualities," and some "complexions" <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, a "complexion" was the specific balance of the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) within a person or organ.</note>. These arise in different parts of the body through various mixtures of the elements and serve as the foundations for the different senses. For there is one affection of the body by which the power of seeing is sustained and thrives, and another by which the power of hearing does so; the same must be judged regarding all the rest. In addition to these five affections—or subjects—five corresponding instruments and more solid members of the body have been established as "receptacles" in which both the senses and the affections themselves reside. For the eyes, like small vessels, receive the affection and the power of seeing, and the other members of the body, as is evident, are assigned in a certain order to the other qualities and senses. Furthermore, certain internal movements are innate to these members and instruments, which seem to demonstrate the innermost feeling <note>original: "affectum"</note> of each. Thus, in the very disturbances of the soul, we see the body now turn red, now grow pale, and at times contract and stiffen, while at other times it flows abroad and, as it were, melts. ¶ Aristotle thinks that pleasure <note>original: "uoluptatem"</note> pertains to all these things we have now listed in a long sequence, such that in that mind which he calls "contemplative," there resides a certain perfect and absolute pleasure. In the other parts of man, pleasure then gradually degenerates. For (as he thinks) for seven reasons, that first pleasure seems to be more perfect than the second pleasure, which is placed in the "active" mind. ¶ For every pleasure which comes from the investigation <note>original: "indagatione"; the text cuts off at "inda"</note> of truth...

# BOOK <note>original: "LIBER"; the OCR metadata suggests this is the fourth book of the treatise.</note>

...investigation <note>The text begins mid-word; likely "investigatione" (investigation).</note> and contemplation is honorable and most worthy of praise. However, when the other part of the mind deliberates on things to be done or avoided and delights in such choices, not every pleasure of that kind is usually praised. That which arises from those plans and actions that oppose the best laws is justly blamed—for instance, if the mind should rejoice in a plan undertaken against the safety of one's homeland or parents, or against what is right. When the mind is delighted by honorable actions, the pleasure is honorable. But when it is delighted by neutral <note>original: "mediis"; referring to actions that are neither inherently virtuous nor sinful, but intermediate.</note> things, that pleasure is also neutral. Thus, in the primary mind, there exists only one kind of joy, and that is worthy of praise. In the second part, however, three types are found (as we have said): the honorable, the base, and the neutral.

¶ That reasoning which he <note>Aristotle</note> uses in the tenth book *On Ethics* <note>original: "decimo de moribus"; referring to Book 10 of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, which discusses the superiority of the contemplative life.</note> is of no small importance to our subject. For he says that we are able to contemplate for a longer time than we can perform any other kind of action. Since the search for truth is more firm and stable than any duty of action, it follows that the pleasure arising from it must also be more stable and more perfect.

¶ Add to this that the life and contemplation of a wise man requires fewer things than a civil <note>The "civil" or "active" life refers to public service, politics, or business.</note> life. For this reason, his pleasure—since it is content with few and minimal things—will undoubtedly be more self-sufficient and be judged more perfect.

¶ Furthermore, that part of the mind to which we attribute the contemplation of nature is (as no one would deny) the more perfect part, and therefore it brings a pleasure more excellent than all the rest.

¶ And since the movement and agitation of the active mind is directed toward something else—either to be chosen or rejected—while the contemplation of the primary mind is content with itself and desires nothing else at all besides itself, it is established by necessary reason that the pleasure proper to contemplation is desired for its own sake alone. The other kind, however, seeks something else beyond itself as an end, and therefore that first kind must be judged much more excellent.

¶ In addition to these points, the primary and more perfect part of anything acts as the representative and namesake for the whole. From this, it follows that although each human being is composed of many parts, the part devoted to contemplation—because it excels the others in dignity—embraces almost the entire nature of man. And man, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose system of thought dominated medieval and Renaissance science and ethics.</note> says, exists primarily as that part. For this reason, its action is especially suited to us and contains an ineffable pleasure; for those things which are more closely related by nature usually bring greater pleasure.

->¶ The last<-

-># ON PLEASURE<-

¶ Finally, Aristotle’s argument proves that the unique activity of the immortal gods consists solely in contemplation. Therefore, nothing in us appears to be related to God except for the "primary mind" (as we have said), contemplation, and the pleasure that arises from it. If pleasure of this kind is the most divine because it alone is suitable for the immortal gods, it will rightly be judged more excellent than all other pleasures. 

¶ Aristotle used these arguments, then, to place the pleasure of contemplation above the pleasure found in action. But let us now turn to those pleasures that, as it were, tickle the senses; they flow toward and glide into the senses with a certain sweetness. We find that Aristotle divided these into two types: some are natural, while others appear to be against nature. He calls those "natural" which, because they restore our nature, are sought by all or most people. He further divides these natural pleasures into two equal groups: some are equally common to all living creatures, while others are, in a way, specific and innate to individuals according to the diversity of their nature. For example, the fact that all creatures seek food, drink, and <term>sexual intercourse<note>original: "veneris usum"; literally "the use of Venus," a common euphemism for sex.</note></term> is a characteristic of common and natural desire and pleasure. However, the fact that individuals are variously delighted by specific and certain things according to the diversity of their nature—and that different things are more pleasing to some than to others—belongs to natural but "specific" pleasure. Since that which is pleasurable to each person is what fits their nature, and since the tendencies and natures of different living beings are diverse, it follows that those things which are suitable for different animals must also differ. And for that reason, a certain and, as it were, specific desire and pleasure belongs to each individual living creature, as <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine of change.</note> **Heraclitus** says: "Each is delighted by what is fit for its nature; his own pleasure draws each person." These are the ones he calls natural. 

¶ On the other hand, he maintains that pleasures "against nature" are those from which almost the entire human race shrinks. He divides these into three types: some arise from a certain shameful and corrupt nature, others from the worst habits, and some from diseases and unfortunate circumstances. Aristotle writes that it happens through a perversity of nature—for instance, that a certain woman was driven by a burning desire to cut open the wombs of pregnant women to devour the infants, or what they say of certain savage tribes around the <note>original: "Pontum"; referring to the Black Sea region, which in antiquity was often associated with "barbarian" or "savage" customs.</note> Black Sea. For some of them are said to delight in raw meat, others in human flesh; some are said to trade their children to be eaten at banquets. The **Troglodytes** <note>A term used by ancient geographers for various "cave-dwelling" tribes, often depicted with exotic or primitive customs.</note>, indeed, feed on the flesh of serpents. It also happens to many through long-standing habit, such as the pulling out of hair or the eating of nails... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

-># BOOK<-

...they are delighted. Often, this also happens through diseases of either the mind or the body, such as in the case of the man who sacrificed and ate his mother, or the one who boiled down the flesh of his father and daughter so that he might feed on both, and the man who ardently craved the liver of his fellow servant, and having killed him, devoured it with the greatest pleasure. We too have seen those affected by a certain physical disease <note>This refers to the medical condition known as pica, where individuals crave non-nutritive substances.</note>—some indeed chewing pebbles, others plaster, many earth, some charcoal, and others lime—grinding them most greedily with their teeth, as often happens to pregnant women. These three types of pleasures are contrary to nature; Aristotle considers them to belong not to a human character, but to a wild and <term>monstrous</term> <note>original: *immanis*—this term describes behaviors that fall outside the boundaries of human nature, often translated as "brutish" or "bestial" in modern editions of Aristotle.</note> disposition. For this reason, in his seventh book on ethics, he calls such pleasures "monstrous."

¶ From those which we have recounted so far, there appear to be three kinds of pleasures according to Aristotle. The **first** consists in **contemplation**; the **second** is occupied with **deliberation and action**. Both of these certainly reside in the mind, but (as we have said) in different ways. The **third** we have placed in the **senses**, and this we have divided into two species: namely, the **natural** and the **contrary to nature**. Of the natural pleasures, we call one "common" and the other "specific." Furthermore, we find that the monstrous pleasures occur in three ways: through a **corrupt and wicked nature**, through **vicious habit**, or through **disease**. 

The first pleasure, therefore—that which is born from contemplation—he calls **divine**, because it is most like God; it falls to us not insofar as we are humans, but insofar as we are like gods. However, that pleasure which is proper to the active mind he calls **virtuous** <note>original: *honesta*—denoting moral beauty and social excellence.</note>, though not divine. For virtue itself is not divinity, but a certain perfect likeness and image of divinity. Thus, the second level of mind and pleasure is a step down from the first, because the first is attributed to divinity itself, while the other is attributed to the image of divinity. 

As for those pleasures which soothe the body, they can no longer participate in divinity, nor any more in virtue. Indeed, virtue exists as the grace, beauty, and adornment of the mind alone. Yet this adornment and the harmony of all parts is called "virtue" in the state of the mind, "moderation" in the passions, "modesty" in actions, and "order" in one's works. Among most <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato who often emphasized the mathematical and aesthetic harmony of the soul and body.</note>, it is called "beauty" in the body. Nevertheless, even those pleasures which move the senses possess a certain small image of virtue. For those among them that obey the laws of mind and reason, and for that reason become moderated, seem to imitate the nature of the virtuous and the graceful by this very moderation. And while they are not entirely worthy of the name "virtuous," they are called "good" by the followers of Aristotle. But those that are more unbridled...

...and they are less partakers of reason; these he deems neither divine, nor honorable, nor finally even good, but rather worthy of blame and evil. And when they do not exceed the bounds so far that they seem utterly abhorrent to human character and nature, he calls them "vicious" yet nonetheless **human pleasures**. He divides these into two parts: for some only corrupt the **appetite** <note>the "appetite" or *appetitio* refers to the desiring part of the soul that should ideally listen to reason</note>, so that he who is affected by them indeed desires against reason and acts, yet he does not do so by deliberate choice, nor does he think—when established outside of his agitation—that he ought to act so. Instead, as a certain heat of passion grows, he is inclined and dragged against that which his right mind had previously chosen. He considers the pleasures of the **incontinent soul** <term>incontinent soul</term> <note>original: *incontinentis animi*—refers to a person who knows what is right but lacks the willpower to resist their impulses.</note> to be of this kind. 

Others, however, deprave not only the appetite but even the judgment of the mind; so that one both lusts against what is proper, and the mind judges that very thing as something to be done and good. By deliberate choice, such a person chooses to indulge the pleasures of the body to the best of their power. He proves these to be the pleasures of the **intemperate man** <term>intemperate man</term> <note>original: *intemperantis hominis*—unlike the incontinent man, the intemperate man has a corrupted moral compass and believes his vices are actually good.</note>. 

Nevertheless, all these which we have so far placed in the senses appear human. But when pleasures alien to human custom and nature dominate a person—whether they were born or raised very poorly, or set apart by disease—since they belong to **beasts** <note>original: *bestiarum*</note> rather than to the human character, he calls them **slavish** and **monstrous** <note>original: *immanes*—this refers to behaviors that are "brutish" or fall outside the natural limits of human behavior.</note>. 

But all these pleasures which the senses offer us are arranged by the **Aristotelians** into five levels, as it were, according to the number of the senses. They believe these pleasures hold the same order as the senses themselves: so that the pleasure of **seeing** and that which the **ears** provide is purer and worthier. The others, in the same way, excel one another in the same order of purity and dignity.

...they do not only charm the ears and eyes, but they also move the mind and reason by those very **traces of reason** which they contain within themselves. Since these senses have the greatest natural kinship with the mind, they occupy it deeply, seize it, and fill the soul with a certain ineffable pleasure. From these two images and pleasures, two species of **divine madness** <note>original: *diuini furoris*—Ficino refers to a state of being "possessed" by a higher power, such as poetic inspiration or religious ecstasy, which he explored in his work *On Divine Madness*.</note> arise, as we have discussed more extensively in the little book on divine madness. 

¶ But indeed, smells, tastes, heat, and cold, and other things of this sort which pertain to smell, taste, and touch, seem to possess or display neither harmony, nor proportion, nor order—and much less any similarity to reason. Therefore, they soothe only the nature of the senses and the body. They agree with the mind in no way at all, or only with great difficulty. For this reason, the pleasures that proceed from these possess neither reason nor dignity, nor do they provide any nourishment—so to speak—to the mind. 

¶ Added to those things about which the **Peripatetics** <note>the "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they discussed philosophy</note> were just now debating is the fact that the power of sensing is common to more living beings the "thicker" or coarser it is. Hence, the power of **seeing** <note>The Latin text reads *uiuendi* (living), but in the context of the list of senses—hearing, smelling, tasting, touching—it is almost certainly a scribe's or printer's error for *uidendi* (seeing).</note> or hearing is not granted by nature to all creatures. To more, she gave the power of smelling; to perhaps all, tasting; and finally, no one would doubt that touching is present in all animals. The pleasures of these senses follow the same pattern, such that some are judged more common and cheaper than others. Indeed, it is established that among all of them, those which are placed in taste and touch are the most common and the lowest. For this reason, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>the famous Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose work formed the basis for medieval and Renaissance science</note> says they are bestial, slavish, and absurd. <term>Plato</term> <note>the Athenian philosopher (c. 427–347 BC) who argued that the physical world is a shadow of a higher, spiritual reality</note> calls them most incontinent and furious. <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> moreover—as we said above—judged one of them <note>Hippocrates famously compared the intensity of sexual pleasure—the sense of touch—to a "minor epilepsy."</note> to be similar to the **falling sickness** <note>original: *comitiali morbo*—an old term for epilepsy</note>. Nor does it carry little weight that nearly all who philosophize about morals wish those who exceed the measure in these two pleasures to be called "incontinent" or "intemperate." But regarding the remaining pleasures <note>namely sight and hearing</note>, because they are more truly **liberal** <note>original: *liberales*—befitting a free person or a gentleman, as opposed to a slave or an animal</note>, philosophers have associated them with neither incontinence nor intemperance. 

¶ Thus far we have recounted the three things to which pleasure is attributed: namely the contemplative mind, the active mind, and the senses. But truly, after the powers of sensing, the affections themselves and the members of the body which lie beneath the senses are arranged. While these perceive neither delight nor distress through themselves, they are nonetheless subject to those very bodily movements and agitations by which either joy or pain is brought to the senses. From this it happens that the members themselves also seem to hold certain traces of inward pleasure. And this very agitation of the viscera and parts of the body, which within...

He cites Aristotle, Plato, and Hippocrates to argue that overindulgence in the lower senses constitutes vice, whereas the higher senses are "liberal" and refined.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the summary of Aristotelian views on pleasure and shifts to the Stoic perspective. It follows the previous discussion where the author distinguished between sensory pleasures (lower) and rational pleasures (higher). The transition "to be rejoiced" connects the bodily senses mentioned previously to the psychological definitions of the ancient schools.</meta>

-># ON PLEASURE #<-

...to be rejoiced and to be grieved, most of the ancient philosophers have used the terms **pleasure** and **pain**. Others, however, have judged that pleasure is the very restoration of nature made manifest to the senses, while pain is the dissolution and weakening of that which is proper to nature. Moreover, beyond these internal motions, certain external gestures follow which provide signs of hidden **affections** <term>affections: here meaning 'affectus' or emotions/states of being moved</term>, and there were some who even called those very signs by the names of pleasure and pain. But the brevity of this little work seems to require that we bring an end to the **Aristotelian** discussion. 

And this will now be done, provided we first give this warning: whenever pleasure is placed by us within the mind in this very discussion, it should be understood as being placed in that part of the mind which desires and wills something. For one part of the mind thinks and considers; another remembers; a third wills—and even if the mind could be divided differently, these distinctions will suffice for the present. Nor is the pleasure of the mind anything else but that very perfect and pleasant **assent** <note>original: *assensio*—in this context, it refers to the mind's voluntary agreement or 'saying yes' to a thought or state.</note>, by which the will rests deeply in that which the mind considers, seeing it as something familiar and its very own.

### Chapter Ten: Opinions of the Stoics and others concerning pleasure and all the emotions.

These things, therefore, should be enough regarding the opinion of **Aristotle**. Let us now come to the **Stoics**. The Stoics, whose leader was **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BCE), the founder of the Stoic school of philosophy in Athens.</note>, define joy no differently than **Plato** does; however, they frequently confuse the names of "pleasure" and "gladness" with one another, and they designate the same thing by both names while disputing. For when we are moved in such a way that we are in some state of "good," they think this happens in two ways. 

Namely, when the soul is moved by reason calmly and steadily, they want that to be called **joy**. But when it exults immoderately and emptily, they call it **exuberant gladness** and **pleasure**. They define this as an irrational elevation of the soul which believes it is enjoying some great good. 

Nevertheless, **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman; the text refers to his work *De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum* (On the Ends of Good and Evil).</note> in the second book of *On Ends* wants us to use these names in Latin such that **joy** and **gladness** reside in the mind alone, whereas **pleasure**, while chiefly attributed to the senses, can also be transferred to the mind. He says that **gladness** is an elevation of the mind thinking it enjoys a great good, but **joy** is a rational elevation of the mind. **Pleasure**, he says, is that sweetness perceived by the senses, and although it can be transferred to the mind, such pleasure in the mind is always to be condemned.

<summary>This page concludes the Aristotelian definition of pleasure as a "perfect assent" of the will and begins an analysis of Stoic philosophy, specifically distinguishing between rational "joy" and irrational "pleasure."</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Stoics, Zeno, Cicero, pleasure, joy, gladness, the will, mental faculties</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definitions of pleasure, transitioning from a general summary to a specific comparison between the views of Cicero, the Stoics, and Aristotle regarding the nature of emotions and the state of the soul.</meta>

-># BOOK #<-

These things he says when he disputes about philosophy, and when he expresses the difference between these matters. In other places, however, he more often uses the name of **pleasure** <note>original: *uoluptatis*</note> for both **joy** <note>original: *gaudio*—often considered a rational or quiet delight</note> and **gladness** <note>original: *lætitia*—often considered a more exuberant or outward emotion</note>. ¶ **Aristotle**, however, seems to differ greatly from **Cicero** and the **Stoics**, since he does not wish for either joy or any pleasure to be called "gladness." For when he enumerated the **affections** <term>affections: *affectus*, the various ways the soul is moved or disposed, often translated as emotions</term> in his second book on morals, he included gladness among them. He then added that those are affections which pleasure or distress follows. From this it follows that, for Aristotle, pleasure cannot be an affection; otherwise, what he had said just before would necessarily be false. For since pleasure cannot follow itself, anyone who calls it an **affection** would seem to deny Aristotle’s premise that pleasure follows all affections.

Furthermore, in that same second book, he called the affections "motions of the soul," yet in the tenth volume of that same work, he demonstrates that pleasure is by no means to be called a "motion." Who, then, would not understand that Aristotle utterly denied that pleasure is an affection? Therefore, since in his opinion pleasure is neither a motion nor an affection, yet he maintained that gladness *is* an affection, it is concluded by necessary reasoning that pleasure and gladness differ greatly from one another. 

Nor is gladness, according to the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle's philosophy, named for the "covered walkways" where they studied</term>, of such a kind that it is present in the soul while it enjoys a present good. For no one among the Peripatetics doubts that gladness is a motion of the soul. Indeed, since affections are defined by them as certain **passions** <term>passions: *passio*, the state of undergoing or being affected by something external</term> of the appetite, and since in their opinion a passion consists of a flow and a motion, then affections must be motions. And so gladness, being an affection, will necessarily appear to be a motion. 

However, the soul, having already attained what it had desired, is no longer moved; rather, all the agitation of desiring ceases, and it rests most sweetly in that good which it has obtained. Therefore, while it enjoys the object of its appetite, one must remove all the affections that are concerned with that very thing which has been attained. Consequently, when the soul enjoys some good, we shall also remove gladness from it.

¶ Someone might perhaps ask: what then is gladness, if it is neither pleasure nor joy, nor consists in the appetite while it enjoys a present good? Even if this has not been sufficiently explained by the **Aristotelians**, I think I shall interpret Aristotle in this way—and not at all absurdly. When something that appears good is presented to us, the mind first judges that it ought to be seized; then the appetite is inclined toward that very thing which has been judged. This we call **desire** or **longing** <note>original: *cupiditatem, ſeu libidinem*</note>.

<summary>This page analyzes Aristotle's technical distinction between pleasure (a state of rest) and gladness (a motion of the soul), contrasting his views with Cicero and the Stoics. It argues that for Aristotelians, gladness is an active emotion that ceases once the desired good is actually achieved and enjoyed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definitions of pleasure, transitioning from a general summary to a specific comparison between the views of Cicero, the Stoics, and Aristotle regarding the nature of emotions and the state of the soul. It focuses specifically on how the soul moves from desire to either despair and sadness or hope and gladness.</meta>

# ON PLEASURE

Then the soul itself inquires within, whether it might easily obtain what it desires; this care we call **anxiety** <note>original: *solicitudinem*</note>. If the soul finds that it is unable to attain its goal, then this very opinion is called **distrust** <note>original: *diffidentia*</note>, which is followed by **despair** <note>original: *desperatio*</note>. This is when the soul no longer expects that it will easily enjoy what it desires. From this arises **sadness** <note>original: *tristitia*</note>—that is, the depression and dejection of a despairing and distrusting soul. This state is reflected in the face no less than in the soul by those who care for speaking Latin correctly.

If, however, someone believes they will easily attain what they desire, this very faith is called **confidence** <note>original: *confidentia*</note>. **Hope** <note>original: *spes*</note> then follows confidence; it is a firm and easy expectation of a future good. From this is born **gladness** <note>original: *lætitia*</note>, a certain lifting up and elation of a soul hoping that it will, without any doubt, possess what it has sought. Indeed, a certain confidence, a most firm hope, and a powerful consideration of the very thing we hope for represents the object of our quest to the soul in such a way that it is not far from appearing entirely present. 

The result is that something very similar to pleasure is born from this hope and thought. I believe **Aristotle** called this gladness a certain "image and appearance of future pleasure." **Lucretius** the Epicurean called it a **drop of Venus** <term>drop of Venus: *gutta veneris*, a poetic expression for the first spark or physical inkling of sexual desire or love</term>, because it is a small and light perception of the beloved thing. **Pleasure** <note>original: *uoluptas*</note>, however, is the perfect and absolute enjoyment of the desired thing (to speak in the **Platonic** manner). For this reason, the same Lucretius, in his fourth book *On the Nature of Things*, when speaking of this first "drop of Venus," says:

> For silent desire foretells pleasure. 
> From this comes Venus to us; from this comes the name of love. 
> From this, that drop of Venus’s sweetness first 
> Distilled into the heart, and was followed by burning care. 
<note>original: *Namque uoluptatem præsagit muta cupido. / Hinc uenus est nobis, hinc autem est nomen amoris / Hinc illa te primum ueneris dulcedinis in cor / Stillauit gutta, & successit feruida cura.*</note>

That is to say, when **desire** <note>original: *cupido*</note> itself—which we call "venereal love"—is silent (that is, still hidden) and considers itself with an internal movement on account of hope and confidence, it perceives in advance and, as it were, "pre-tastes" the future pleasure. In that moment, that first "drop of Venus" arises, which we call **gladness**. 

Therefore, among the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, so named because they often walked while discussing</term>, let gladness be a certain sweet foretaste of future pleasure born from hope itself; just as pleasure exists in the appetite while it enjoys, so gladness exists in the appetite while it hopes. And this is the controversy regarding these names—gladness, joy, and pleasure—between **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Zeno**, and **Marcus Tullius [Cicero]**. ¶ But let them use their own names as they please; let us return to the **Stoics**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of emotions from the previous page, moving from a general description of hope and sadness into a formal categorization of the "disturbances" of the soul according to Stoic philosophy. It follows the previous page's mention of Aristotle and Lucretius by contrasting Stoic definitions with those of the Peripatetics.</meta>

# BOOK

Now, a disturbance <note>original: *perturbatio* — the Stoic term for an irrational "passion" or emotion that clouds judgment</note> is (as the Stoics prefer) a movement of the soul turned away from right reason and contrary to the nature of the mind; they believe such disturbances are born from a mere opinion. For as soon as the appearance of something is presented to us, the mind forms an opinion that it is either a harmful evil or a good. From this opinion, four disturbances of the mind proceed. For those things that are presented to us—whether they be evil or good—seem to be either in the future or in the present. 

If the mind reflects on certain future evils, it immediately tries to turn away from them. If this turning away is done with reason, it is called **caution** <note>original: *cautio*</note>; this is not a disturbance, nor is it foreign to the mind of a wise person. However, that which occurs without reason, and with a lowly and broken loss of spirit, is called **fear** <note>original: *metus*</note>. Fear, then, is a turning away that is averse to reason, or a worried expectation of a future evil. 

But when that which seems to be an evil is already imminent and affects the mind in the present, that disturbance arises which they call either **distress** <note>original: *ægritudo*</note> or **pain** <note>original: *dolor*</note>. Distress is a contraction of the soul that opposes reason; notably, the wise person feels no such affection for a present evil <note>The Stoics believed a truly wise person remains indifferent to external "evils" like pain or loss</note>. 

On the other hand, when the appearance of something that seems to be a future good is offered, the opinion itself impels us to go and get it (to use Stoic phrasing). When this is done consistently and prudently, we call such a desire **will** <note>original: *uoluntatem*</note>. They believe this exists only in the wise person and should by no means be called a disturbance. They define it thus: **will** is that which desires something with reason. But that which is incited in opposition to reason, more vehemently, is **lust** <note>original: *libido*</note> or **unbridled desire** <note>original: *cupiditas effrenata*</note>, which is found in all foolish people. 

When we are moved in such a way that we enjoy some good, it happens in two ways: for the mind is moved either weightily and calmly, which they call **joy** <note>original: *gaudium*</note>; or, when it exults lightly and profusely, they call it **wanton gladness** <note>original: *lætitiam gestientem*</note> and **pleasure** <note>original: *uoluptatem*</note>. They define this as an irrational and wanton elation of a mind thinking it enjoys a great good. On this point, they agreed with those Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> whose opinion I cited in the second place earlier when speaking of **Aristotle**. For both schools agree on this: that pleasure is the very elation of a mind thinking it has attained some supreme good.

The Stoics divide pleasure into many parts. They held that there are five parts in the senses and four in the mind, provided the mind agrees with the senses. The things that move the senses do not have distinct or proper names among the Stoics, except for that which is perceived by hearing; this they call **delight** <note>original: *delectationem*</note>, and they define it as follows: **Delight** is a pleasure soothing the mind with the sweetness of hearing, while the others flatter the remaining senses.

It distinguishes between the rational responses of a wise person (caution, will, joy) and the irrational disturbances of the "foolish" (fear, distress, lust, and wanton pleasure).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Stoic philosophy regarding emotions, moving from "distress" (pain) to the various forms of "pleasure." It then transitions into a new chapter comparing these views with the Cyrenaic school of thought.</meta>

->ON PLEASURE<-

But besides those pleasures by which the body is affected, four have been identified that are also found in the mind after it has been corrupted by desire. These are: **delight**, **effusion**, **boasting**, and **malevolence**.

**Delight** <note>original: *oblectatio*</note> is a softening inclination of the mind toward pleasure. I do not think this is anything other than the very softness of the mind and its assent, by which it most willingly joins itself to, agrees with, obeys, and complies with the sweetness offered by the senses.

**Effusion** <note>original: *effusio* — literally a "pouring out"</note>, however, they define as the relaxation and dissolution of the soul's virtue. For the mind is not only inclined and drawn by a certain softness to obey the pleasures of the senses (as we said occurs through delight); but even more significantly, the entire force and intention of our mind melts away and flows abroad due to the sweetness of a present good. It raises itself up to enjoy it and pours itself out entirely. This is what the Stoics call, I believe, effusion.

Next follows **boasting** <note>original: *iactatio* — a bounding or vaunting pleasure</note>, a pleasure that leaps and carries itself forward quite insolently. This too is a disease of the mind, occurring when it exults and vainly glories in the possession of what appears to be a good.

**Malevolence** <note>original: *maliuolentia*</note> is a pleasure taken in the misfortune of another without any personal gain. For when someone feels pleasure at another's misfortune for their own benefit, it seems they suffer this more out of self-love than any ill-will toward others. Therefore, that detail "without personal gain" was rightly added to the definition.

### Chapter 11. The Cyrenaics on pleasure, and how it is the ultimate goal. ###

<margin>h</margin>
Let these remarks on the opinion of the <term>Stoics</term> <note>A school of philosophy that taught virtue is the only good and emotions are often irrational disturbances</note> suffice. Let us now hear the <term>Cyrenaic</term> <note>A Greek school of philosophy that believed immediate physical pleasure was the highest good</note> philosophers, who descended from **Aristippus**, a disciple of Socrates. The Cyrenaics proposed two disturbances: pain and pleasure. They called the latter a "smooth motion" and the former a "rough motion." They argued that no pleasure differs from another pleasure, nor does one soothe more than another, and that indeed all living things seek the one while they shun the other.

By pleasure, they specifically mean bodily pleasure, which they say is the <term>end</term> <note>original: *finis* — the "ultimate goal" or highest purpose of human life</note>. This is not the kind of pleasure that consists of a steady state or the mere absence of pain, acting as a rest from disturbance—which **Epicurus** <note>Founder of the Epicurean school; he defined pleasure more as the absence of pain (*ataraxia*) than the active stimulation favored by the Cyrenaics</note> later adopted and established as the goal. They believe the evidence for pleasure being our goal is that nature has endeared it to us from childhood, even without the judgment of reason. At an age when the mind's judgment is neither corrupted by habit nor shaped by opinion, we seem to judge pleasure to be the **highest good** <note>original: *summum bonum*</note> by the instinct of nature alone. And when we enjoy it, we seek nothing else beyond it, as if seeking...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Cyrenaic school of philosophy, which emphasizes that pleasure is the ultimate goal of life.
