# BOOK VI

...of all goods, there exists a final, extreme, highest point and end; nor is there anything we naturally flee as much as pain. Therefore, we seek pleasure most of all. Moreover, they <note>The Cyrenaic philosophers, who followed Aristippus.</note> hold that pleasure is a good even if it arises from the most shameful things. For even if a matter is foul, pleasure itself is still to be chosen for its own sake and considered a good. 

Furthermore, that "removal of pain" <note>original: *doloris abiectio*</note> which Epicurus defends does not seem to them to be true pleasure, nor is the mere deprivation of pleasure to be considered pain. For they believe both pleasure and pain consist in motion. They also hold that pleasures belong not only to the body, but also to the mind—namely those perceived from the recollection of past events, the hope of future goods, or the study of various disciplines. Yet, they believe bodily pleasures are far superior to those of the mind, and bodily pains are worse than those of the mind. 

Indeed, they argue that the virtues, and absolutely anything else besides pleasure, are good and to be sought only for the sake of pleasure. Likewise, whatever things are seen as "evils" are avoided only because they cause pain. Truly, pleasure alone is good and sought for its own sake, while pain is evil for its own sake and to be rejected. They also believe that pleasure and pain reach the body through the mind's assent <note>agreement or acceptance</note> and sympathy. For the body is agitated by various and diverse motions; if these are gentle and pleasant, the mind assents, and that is pleasure. But if the body is struck by a harsher suffering <note>original: *passione* — in this context, an external force acting upon the body</note>, the mind contracts, suffers with it, and feels pain. 

For this reason, in this specific definition of pain and pleasure, they agree with most of the Platonists and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note>. However, they disagree in several other matters, as may be clear from what we have reported, and furthermore because they did not think anything was inherently "sweet" or "unsweet." Instead, they believed that some people rejoice while others are distressed by the very same thing, whether due to its novelty, variety, or a sense of satiety.

### Chapter XII: The opinion of Eudoxus that pleasure is the highest good.

The opinion of Eudoxus <note>A famous astronomer and student of Archytas and Plato.</note>, a student of Archytas, is nearly the same. For he proves pleasure to be the highest good by the reasons I shall set forth. He says that whatever is sought is seen as a good; that which is sought *more* is better; and finally, no one would doubt that what is sought *most* of all is the greatest and highest good <note>original: *summum bonum*</note>. 

He judges it to be clear from two reasons that pleasure is sought above all other things. First, because there is nothing among all things that living beings desire more vehemently and ardently than pleasure. Second, because there is no other good besides it that is sought by everyone. Indeed, not only humans, but all other animals, as well as infants as soon as they are born, and then youths and the elderly, all strive for pleasure. Moreover, nothing...

...can be found among the rest of the goods, because it is sought by all of them. Likewise, that which is most in accordance with nature, no one—even the unlearned—would deny to be the <term>highest good</term> <note>original: *summum bonum*; the ultimate goal or supreme end of human life in ethics</note>. That pleasure, indeed, most especially agrees with nature will be evident from this: that living beings are born from it, and it is so necessary for generation itself that most of the ancient philosophers argued that even plants join together by a mixing of both sexes and give birth through pleasure, and sprout shoots. Furthermore, living things, having hardly been brought into the light of day, desire it immediately before they seek anything else or are able to choose what they seek by any deliberate counsel. Moreover, by the charms of pleasure, from the nurse’s milk itself and through all of life, we are nourished, educated, and increased. We are instructed by its delights, we spend our lives in its lap, and it is innate to all our senses. As if by a <term>bait</term> <note>original: *esca*; often used in philosophy to describe how nature lures creatures toward necessary actions like eating or procreating</note>, all the necessary duties of life are completed; for we neither expel what is pestilential nor pursue what is useful without pleasure. Therefore, it seems to agree most with nature and to be (as Aristotle says) most familiar to our kind.

¶ Furthermore, a good is to be considered more divine the more widely it extends; and since pleasure is compatible with all living things and is mixed into all goods, who could doubt that it is most widely open and diffused everywhere? Indeed, there is no virtue that is present in all other virtues, or that belongs to all animals by nature. Pleasure, however, is mixed into all virtues, nor can any of the virtues be found at all without pleasure. Yet pleasure itself is found in many things without virtue, nor can there be any possession of a good without pleasure. From these things, it is concluded that it is infused into all goods, and for that reason, it is the most ample and the best.

¶ Moreover, there is nothing besides pleasure that we do not look for because of something else. On the contrary—which seems more significant—we desire all other things for the sake of pleasure itself. For we do not pursue what is good for any other reason than that we may finally enjoy it once it is acquired, if that is possible by any means. Therefore, for the sake of "enjoyment" (if I may speak so), all goods are sought after. But since pleasure is nothing else but a certain sweetest enjoyment of a good already acquired, who would deny that the rest of the goods are desired for its sake? Nor is there anyone who seeks anything good except to obtain it to the best of their ability; and they do not wish to obtain it except to possess it and to rest most sweetly in it. ## Chapter 13. Aristotle's arguments against Aristippus and Eudoxus concerning pleasure prove that the pleasure of the mind is superior to the pleasure of the body.

<margin>a</margin> And Aristotle weaves together the truest and most approved reasons against both opinions. Especially, by many arguments, he demonstrates that the pleasure of the mind is superior to that of the body. ¶ For of all bodily pleasures, the most intense are those perceived by touch and taste. The nature of these, however, is such that without a sense of <term>lack</term> <note>original: *indigentia*; a state of physical need or deficiency, like being hungry</note>, they can either not move the body at all, or certainly only with difficulty. Hence Socrates used to say that hunger was the seasoning of food, and thirst the seasoning of drink. But every lack, since it is an enemy to nature, brings pain; and since pleasures of this kind cannot occur without lack, they must always be sharers in pain. For that reason, they are considered neither whole nor pure, especially since they produce regret, satiety, and diseases. But the pleasure of the mind has no lack mixed in at all, and for that reason it neither shares in pain nor affects the mind with any satiety or annoyance. ¶ What of the fact that the delights of the senses, the more and more greedily they are drained, the more quickly they fall back into their opposite? But the joy of the mind, the more it is sought, the greater and more perfect it is held to be. ¶ Furthermore, there are two causes, or as it were, "principles" of pleasure: namely, the power of the soul itself which receives such a movement, and that which is presented to us from the outside; they call the former the *subject* of pleasure and the latter its *object*. The subject of bodily sweetness is the sense, while the object is the quality and nature of the body, which the forms drawn in by the senses present. Of that joy which the mind enjoys, however, the subject is the mind, while the object is truth itself—something incorporeal, simple, absolute, and eternal. Therefore, to the degree that the principles of this pleasure are more divine than those of the former, this pleasure is more perfect than that one. ¶ And (as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age, known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> argues) the senses reach only the surfaces of things, or certain properties from the outside,

# ON PLEASURE

...nor are they <note>Referring to the senses mentioned on the previous page</note> joined to the things themselves, but rather to their images. The **mind**, however, inspects the intimate and absolute nature of the object presented to it, and is joined with what it considers in such a way that either one thing is made from two (as <note>original: "Auerrois"; Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> **Averroes** holds), or they cohere in an unbreakable connection (as <note>original: "Aurelius augustinus"; St. Augustine of Hippo</note> **Aurelius Augustine** says). Through this grasping and joining, a much greater pleasure belongs to the mind than to the senses, which are unable to achieve this.

¶ Add to this that the nature of the mind is always one and the same, and therefore remains always similar and consistent with itself. From this it follows that the same thing is always pleasant to it, and the same pleasure is present. The nature of the **body**, however, either never remains in the same state (as <note>original: "Eraclitus, & Plato"; Heraclitus and Plato, both of whom argued the physical world is in constant flux</note> **Heraclitus** and **Plato** argue) or is quickly changed into many different states (as **Aristotle** believes), and its quality varies from one to another. For this reason, the same thing does not suit the body at all times. What seems to agree with its nature now, immediately or shortly after disagrees and conflicts; thus, the same thing is not always pleasurable to it. By these facts, it is understood that the pleasure of the mind is certain and stable, while that of the body is brief, fleeting, and fragile.

¶ Likewise, the **senses** are moved only by the sweetness of present things, nor do they receive pleasure from anything except physical objects. The mind, however, is delighted by the **memory** of the past, the **hope** of the future, and similarly by the **contemplation** of the present; it can take joy not only in things that lack a body, but even in the knowledge of bodies themselves.

¶ Since the soul is the most excellent part of a human being, no one can doubt that what is agreeable to the mind should be judged as more kindred and similar to a human than what suits the senses. Whatever is most kindred to someone is undoubtedly the most pleasant; from this, it is understood that the joy of the soul is greater and more excellent than the sweetness of the body.

¶ Added to this is the fact that the soul is <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "indiuiduus"; simple or "not-divisible," meaning it has no parts that can be pulled apart</note> and simple. The knowledge of truth is likewise indivisible. Therefore, the pleasure of the mind, since it flows from these two as if from certain causes, will be seen as simple, and unable to become smaller or larger than itself, since its principles do not allow for that kind of variation. The senses, however, are scattered and distributed throughout the limbs. Because of this, they are composed of many different parts; the objects of the senses also seem to be nothing other than certain forms and qualities of bodies, which arise from a certain harmony of their parts, such as shapes, colors, sounds, smells, and other things of this kind. And since that very proportion of bodies by which the senses are moved is also harmonious and similar to the proportion of the senses, the senses adopt it as something proper, familiar, and good, and [derive] pleasure...

...are affected. Since the harmony of such bodies can approach the likeness of the harmony of the senses to a greater or lesser degree, it follows that the senses of that same body receive a greater pleasure at one time and a lesser pleasure at another, according to the proportion <note>The author uses "proportion" to mean the mathematical or physical fit between the sense organ and the object it perceives</note>. This can be observed in songs and sounds; for at the same moment of time (if I may say so), the very same delight perceived from a song is made more intense or more relaxed depending on whether the voices are produced more sweetly or more discordantly. Therefore, since the pleasure of the mind remains simple and unchangeable, while the delight of the body is mixed and becomes greater or smaller, no one of sound mind will deny that the former is more excellent and perfect than the latter.

¶ Indeed, Aristotle's final argument on this point is clear: those things which are sought for their own sake (he says) seem more important than those sought for the sake of something else. The joy of the mind is shown to be loved for its own sake primarily because the mind and its activity greatly surpass all other things within us in dignity. From this it follows that there is nothing in us to which we might refer the mind as if to some higher goal; by the same reasoning, we do not desire the pleasure inherent in the mind for the sake of anything else.

¶ We desire bodily pleasure, however, for three main reasons. One of these is surely the mind. The second is the deficiency of nature <note>The state of lacking something necessary, such as hunger or thirst</note>. The last is internal and perpetual pain. For since nature has directed the lower things toward those that are more powerful—so that there might be an inexplicable order of things and a perfect connection of parts among themselves—it is necessary that the senses of the body and their movements be referred to the mind as if to a mistress and queen.

¶ Next (as we also said above), nature implanted such intense pleasure in the senses for this reason: so that we would be more inclined by these enticements to acquire the things necessary for life. This is most clear from the fact that as long as we admit into the body that which nature lacks, we are moved by this kind of sweetness. But after every natural need is satisfied, not only do we taste no further pleasure, but what is more, we are affected by either a sense of regret <note>original: "pœnitétia"; here meaning a physical aversion or "turning away" after over-consumption</note> or satiety. I believe nature established this for the following reason: just as we are lured by pleasure to drive away deficiency, so we are deterred by regret and satiety, so that we do not harm our nature by admitting more than is necessary.

¶ We also seek pleasant bodily movement as a kind of medicine to soothe hidden pain (as Aristotle discusses in the seventh book of the *Ethics* <note>original: "de moribus"; referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*, where Aristotle discusses how pleasure can act as a remedy for the "pains" of natural depletion</note>). For not only obvious pains occur, but also certain hidden and intermediate ones. Indeed, violent movements brought in from the outside cause obvious pain, while the natural agitations that happen within cause a silent and intermediate pain. He believes that the natural spirits and the movements of the senses and mind are perpetually within us. For the soul both contains the body, and nourishes it, and generates it

Furthermore, it has been established by nature herself—the craftswoman and mistress of things—that what long habit has erased from our awareness should be stirred up by a certain necessary and blind instinct, lest the animal perish through such negligence. Thus, that saying of Plato—which we discussed above—is most true: namely, that all pleasure proceeds from the filling of a deficiency <note>original: "egestatis expletione". This refers to the Platonic theory that pleasure is the process of returning to a natural state of balance after a "depletion" like hunger or thirst.</note>. For in those where no open lack appears, an internal and hidden one can never be absent as long as they live.

This very innate deficiency of which we speak occurs most especially in the young and in those of a melancholic temperament. In the young, certainly, because they are driven by many intense movements due to the necessity of the body growing and reaching perfection; it follows that they need a greater medicine, and for this reason, they pursue pleasures most of all. But in those dominated by black bile <note>original: "atra bilis", which the author notes the Greeks call μελαγχολίαν (*melancholian*).</note>, the body (as the author says) is constantly being consumed and gnawed away by the intense dryness of that humor <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed to dictate health and personality. Black bile was considered cold and dry.</note>. For that reason, they too yield greatly to pleasures; hence the young and the melancholic tend to be the most incontinent and intemperate of all.

¶ There is, however, a "middle pain," such as hunger and thirst, and whatever other desire of the body can be named. For this pain is not entirely hidden, nor does it torture the body with open or more violent motion. Thus it is not without merit that it is called "middle," and as everyone can see, we seek pleasures for the sake of driving it away.

<margin>I</margin> We have already declared in a long series Aristotle's judgment that the pleasure of the mind is superior to the sweetness of the body. There remains now another of Aristotle's arguments against Eudoxus <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–337 BCE) was a Greek astronomer and mathematician who argued that because all things, rational and irrational, seek pleasure, it must be the supreme good.</note> and the Cyrenaics <note>A school of philosophy founded by Aristippus that held that immediate, physical pleasure was the only absolute good.</note> by which he demonstrates that bodily pleasure is by no means the highest good. Indeed, by the authority of all philosophers, the **highest good** <term>summum bonum (the ultimate goal or supreme end of human life)</term> must be of such a kind that there is nothing better beyond it, nor can it be referred to any other purpose. However, bodily pleasure is significantly inferior to the joy of the mind (as we showed a little earlier), and it is desired for the sake of the mind and for other things we have discussed. Furthermore, that which is the highest good in itself must always and to all people appear to be a good worth seeking, and it must be approved of in all its parts. Yet, not every bodily delight is sought always, nor by everyone. For what usually provides pleasure to one person often causes distress to another; things that are pleasing to children seem bothersome to men; and what we crave while we are sober, we later find nauseating to even look at once we are full. To this we also add that it is the nature of the highest good that whatever we do, we choose to do it for that good's sake, as if compelled by necessity. Yet there are many very laborious tasks and certain duties full of danger. Even if we know for certain that these will bring us no bodily pleasure, we do not hesitate to undertake them for the sake of honor, or moral integrity, or the joy of the mind. Indeed, many of the bravest and wisest men have committed themselves to certain death for the sake of what is right, for their country, or for their parents. If anyone were to say that they did these things because they were ensnared by bodily sweetness or inflamed by lust—or if one preferred the opinion and impulse of the common rabble and of beasts to the judgment of these men—that person should surely be judged the most foolish of all.

Besides, anyone, even the most lowly person, can enjoy bodily pleasures no less than the best person. But no one would say that "happiness" <note>original: "fœlicitatem". In this philosophical context, "happiness" (eudaimonia) refers to a state of flourishing or supreme well-being, not just a passing mood.</note> belongs to the lowly. Nor is it reasonable to assert that pitiable, half-dead little men are just as blessed as great and wise men. Likewise, the highest good of any nature ought to be unique to it; yet since bodily pleasure is common even to tiny living beasts, it should by no means be judged the highest good of man. Or would you call the "highest good" something that does not even seem to be a good at all? Our Plato has, I believe, already sufficiently persuaded us above how shameful, how wicked, and how pestilential this "exaltation of the senses" is. As for the point on which Eudoxus and Aristippus <note>Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 435–356 BCE), a pupil of Socrates who founded the Cyrenaic school of hedonism.</note> primarily relied—namely, that pleasure [is sought by all...]

...bodily pleasure <note>original: "uoluptas"</note> is sought by everyone. This seems to the followers of Aristotle to have little weight in proving what they [the opponents] contend. For he thinks that there are various dispositions among different bodies. Consequently, those things which are naturally related to these dispositions, and which produce pleasure because of 그very relationship, differ greatly from one another. From this, it is understood that various and differing pleasures occur to different living beings. Indeed, if you were to run through all bodily pleasures, you would find none that is ultimately and greatly desired by all. 

But it is established that the mind <note>original: "mentem"; the author distinguishes between the physical 'body' and the rational 'mind'</note> is either one in everyone, or certainly very similar. And so, what is proper to the mind seems proper and related to all those who possess a mind. Now, the proper work of the mind is the investigation and knowledge of truth. It is therefore clear that this is suitable for all humans, and for that reason, is to be desired. Wherefore all men (as Aristotle says) by nature desire knowledge <note>This is the famous opening line of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. Moreover, that which is sought, if it is absent, usually produces distress, but if it is present, it produces pleasure. Therefore, there is one thing naturally related to all humans, one thing to be sought by all, and finally, one thing most delightful of all. And yet, all of this consists in the contemplation of truth. This (as Plato says) is the food of the mind <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is nourished by the "plain of truth."</note> and it fills the soul with a certain inexpressible pleasure. Therefore, while some bodily pleasures are sought by some and others by others, the joy of the mind is one and the same, loved by all.

### Chapter XV. Why humans are inclined toward bodily pleasure.

<margin>a</margin>
**S**omeone might perhaps ask why nearly innumerable people are more prone to the pleasures of the body. Aristotle certainly thinks the cause of this is that the sweetness of the senses is a certain shadow and image <note>original: "umbra quaedam, atque imago"</note> of that joy by which the mind is nourished. Therefore, from our earliest years, we use only our senses, which can neither grasp the nature of truth nor its joy. In place of that pleasure toward which nature's first intention is directed, we follow that which charms the senses, deceived by this resemblance and embracing it greedily. 

But when age has matured and, with the eyes of the soul awakened, so to speak, we begin to suspect the truth and taste its joy, even then many continue in the course of their past life right up to old age. For they have long been accustomed to trusting the senses and obeying their movements, and that very habit <term>consuetudo (the power of habitual behavior to shape character)</term> has now driven roots deeper and more profoundly, so that it is impossible, or certainly most difficult, to uproot those habits once they are solid and deep. From these things it is clear that there are two principal...

To return to the proposal: pleasure <note>original: "uoluptas"</note> is varied and uncertain according to the diversity of men, but a single joy of the mind <note>original: "mentis... gaudium"</note> is sought by all by nature. And since these two—namely, the **contemplation of truth** and the **pleasure** derived from it—reside in the mind, and the nature of the highest good seems to consist of these, the ancient philosophers doubted which of these is more important and superior for happiness.

**Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and alchemy.</note>, **Theodorus** (the disciple of Dionysius the Dialectician), **Democritus**, **Pyrrho**, **Eurilochus**, **Philotimon**, **Phliasius**, **Nauphiphanes**, **Theius**, **Epicurus**, **Origen**, **Avicenna**, and **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "Algalzel"</note> seem to judge that in the nature of happiness, the **joy** which is the companion of contemplation is the most important.

However, **Thales**, **Bias**, **Anaxagoras**, **Socrates**, **Euclid of Megara**, **Aristotle**, **Herillus of Chalcedon**, and **Averroes** <note>original: "Auerois"</note> prefer **contemplation itself**. This dispute and controversy has flourished even into our own age and is also debated among Christian theologians. But regarding this, I will speak at another time. For now, it will suffice to have warned how Aristotle differs from **Eudoxus** and **Aristippus** in two main points (as we declared above).

He denies that a thing which admits such variety can exist as it appears by its own nature. Instead, they believe things appear varied according to the diversity of the people to whose senses they are applied. Dionysius of Heraclea <note>Known as "the Renegade," he was a pupil of Zeno who famously abandoned Stoicism for the pursuit of pleasure.</note>, however, defended not just this one point, but all the teachings of the Cyrenaics <note>A school of philosophy that believed pleasure—specifically immediate, physical pleasure—was the supreme good.</note>, and stated that the goal of all goods is pleasure. Thus, after he had listened to Zeno the Stoic, he betook himself to the Cyrenaics. Theodorus, however—a disciple of Dionysius the Dialectician—differs greatly from both this man and the Cyrenaics. For he uses the name "pleasure" only to signify that sweetness which touches the senses; he believes that such pleasure is not only not the "highest good," but is not even a good at all. He holds that the highest good is indeed the joy of the mind <note>original Latin: "mentis gaudium"</note>, and the affliction of the mind is the highest evil. He believes the former consists in prudence, the latter in imprudence. Furthermore, he claims that the goods by which we obtain happiness are prudence and justice, while the evils are the contrary habits. Pleasure and pain, however, he considers "indifferent," just as the Stoics do.

### Chapter 17. What the Epicureans thought concerning the origins of things, Pleasure, the affects, and character.

<margin>a</margin> The Epicureans, however, established the name of pleasure as a kind of genus, of which there are two species: they believe one pleasure consists in motion, and the other in a state of rest. The pleasure placed in motion they divide into two parts: one resides in the mind, the other in the senses. They mostly call the former "joy," and the latter "delight." They define joy <note>original: "gaudium"</note> as a sweet commotion of the mind enjoying what it had sought. But they define delight <note>original: "laetitiam"</note> as a pleasant motion by which the senses open up and overflow. They teach that this very pleasantness which is placed in motion arises in the following way. They say that the beginnings of all things—the primary building blocks—are certain very small and entirely indivisible bodies, which they call *atoms* <note>original Greek: "ἀτόμους," meaning "uncuttable" or "indivisible."</note> for the reason that they cannot be cut. These atoms differ from one another in size and shape, so that some of these seeds are larger and others smaller; some are round and smooth, while others are curved, hooked, and rough. All these fly through the immense void in perpetual motions, touching one another, and by chance collisions they cling together to constitute whatever exists in the nature of things. By the gathering together of these atoms, they think three principal types of things are made. Some things are produced by those atoms which are round, small, and smooth, while others are made of larger...

...er and more jagged <note>The text continues from the previous page's description of the different shapes of "seeds" or atoms.</note>. Some things, however, hold a middle ground between these two, being neither smooth nor entirely rough. They <note>The Epicureans, followers of Epicurus who believed the world was made of atoms.</note> maintain that our body and soul are likewise composed of these same seeds, yet with this difference: the body is formed from larger and thicker ones, while the soul is fashioned from those that are minute, smooth, and round. They claim, moreover, that there is a **void** <note>original: "inane"; the empty space through which atoms move.</note> mixed into all bodies and natures, which they call **channels and pores** <note>original: "meatus porosque"; these were thought to be tiny openings in the body that allowed atoms to pass through.</note>. It is through these that bodies are able to receive one another and, as it were, drink each other in.

Therefore, when those first types of seeds are presented to us, because (as we have said) they are very small, they penetrate the body and soul from every side without any offense. Because they are round and smooth, and thus related to the nature of the soul, they immediately soothe it and flatter the senses. They believe that things such as sweet fruits, honey, liquid milk, songs, the most pleasant odors, and other things of this sort are of this kind. For this reason, when the seeds of which the soul is woven are touched by these smooth and flattering little bodies, they indeed agree to this sweet commotion; they spread themselves out with the greatest eagerness into those little bodies that have been drawn into the senses and pores, clinging to them joyfully, binding to them firmly, and embracing them most sweetly. They consider this very agreement, spreading out, joining, and embracing to be **pleasure** <note>original: "uoluptatem"; here defined as a positive physical motion of atoms.</note> consisting in motion.

On the other hand, the opposite happens when that third kind of body, which is constructed from rough and heavy seeds, is brought to the senses. Because the elements of which they consist are large, they are thrust into the openings of the body and soul with difficulty; they strike, break through, and pull apart the particles of the soul with a certain force. Furthermore, because they are rough and hooked, they bite the soul sharply in a way and sting the body. They judge such things to be wormwood, bile, unpleasant colors, sounds, and odors. In short, all other things that touch the senses with some roughness or bitterness cause the beginnings of the soul to be stirred up and pulled apart by these seeds; they shudder, flee, and quickly contract themselves. They define such dispersion and contraction as **pain** <note>original: "dolorem"; defined here as the mechanical disruption of the soul's atoms.</note> following the motion.

The noble Epicurean Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher whose work "On the Nature of Things" is the primary source for Epicurean physics.</note> expresses this in the second book of *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "de rerum natura"</note> with these verses:

> So that you may easily recognize that from smooth and round seeds
> Are those things which can touch the senses pleasantly.
> But on the other hand, those that seem hooked and rough
> Are held more tightly bound together by hooks,
> And because of this, they are accustomed to tear open the paths
> Of our senses and break into the body by their entrance.

> Furthermore, since pain arises when material

But indeed, those things which are joined by certain middle elements are divided into several kinds. For some closely approach the smooth and flattering bodies; others rather approach those which are rough to the senses; while some stand at almost an equal distance from both. The first kind, by a certain silent motion, allure the soul to pleasure; the second seem to incite it gradually and hiddenly toward sadness and pain. Those, however, which are said to be in the middle, produce an ambiguous and doubtful motion. For this reason, the soul grows sluggish and numb by their impulse, and is not excited to action unless some new motion is added. Nor indeed do I think it should be passed over in silence that between those things which are entirely smooth and round, and those moreover which are altogether hooked and rough, a certain middle genus of bodies is interposed. This consists of those **atoms** <note>The fundamental, indivisible particles that Epicureans believed made up all matter.</note> which are neither entirely round nor bent and hooked, but stand out with certain small and soft angles. In this category they wish to place certain wines and fruits which are moderately tempered with a rustic, sharp, and (as they say) acute flavor. These do not soothe the soul, nor do they scatter it, nor do they make it grow more languid; rather, they prick it lightly and moderately, and as it were **tickle** it, and thus produce pleasure. All of this is understood from these verses of Lucretius:
> There are also those which can no longer be rightly 
> considered smooth, nor entirely hooked with curved points, 
> but rather with angles projecting slightly, which can 
> tickle the senses more than hurt them. 
> Of this kind are wine lees and the flavors of wine.
<note>original: "Sunt etiam quæ iam nec leuia..." Lucretius uses the example of wine dregs (fecula) to describe sensations that are pleasant but have a slight "edge" or bite.</note>

Wherefore it happens that there are three types of pleasures that follow from motion in the senses: one indeed is a certain affection toward softness, which he calls "allurement"; the second is a smooth and sweet commotion; and the last is a certain slight pricking and (as they say) a sort of itching and **titillation** <note>original: "titillatio"; a technical term in Epicureanism for a specific, light physical pleasure.</note>. Epicurus also uses another division of pleasures: for he says some are **natural and necessary** <note>original: "naturales, & necessarias"; such as food for hunger or water for thirst.</note>, such as those which settle pain and the vehement longing of nature through food and drink, and all other things to which the vehement motion of nature impels us. <meta>Catchword: freedom from pain [indolentiá],</meta>

...remove pains, but do not increase pleasure. Since nature’s lack is fulfilled and the pain that follows it is removed, **Epicurus** believes that the highest bodily pleasure is reached. After this point, pleasure may be varied or distinguished, but it cannot be increased or amplified. 

Therefore, this second kind consists of those pleasures identified by the Epicureans which are perceived through various seasonings and the exquisite delights of banquets. He then adds a third kind of pleasures: those that are neither natural nor necessary. These include things like the spectacles of external affairs that have nothing to do with sustenance or skill, and absolutely all those pleasures taken from an immense pile of riches and resources. 

The reasoning regarding all these pleasures is that the desire for those which are necessary can be satisfied without much labor or expense. Nor do the cravings for natural pleasures require much, because nature itself provides riches that are both easily obtained and limited in order to be satisfied. However, for empty cravings—which seek pleasures that are neither natural nor necessary—neither limit nor end can be found (as he believes). 

Hence, if you live according to nature, says <term>Epicurus</term> <note>Epicurus (341–270 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the goal of life was to reach a state of tranquility and freedom from fear and bodily pain.</note>, you will never be poor; if you live according to opinion, you will never be rich. Indeed, nature itself enriches the wise person, as its riches are easily obtained. Nor indeed are the pleasures perceived from the simplest and most humble diet any less than those from the most exquisite things for feasting. For nature is content with a few small things. 

Nor does Epicurus follow only that pleasure which moves nature with some sweetness, about which we have already said enough. Rather, he considers that to be the greatest pleasure which is perceived when all pain is removed. He says this is "set in a stable state" <note>This refers to what scholars call "static" or "katastematic" pleasure—the peaceful state of being free from distress, as opposed to "moving" pleasures like eating or drinking.</note>. 

And although the <term>Cyrenaics</term> <note>A rival school of philosophy that believed only "moving" pleasures (like the physical sensation of eating) were real pleasures, and that the absence of pain was merely a neutral state like sleep.</note> denied that this was pleasure, Epicurus, on the other hand, teaches that this must be called pleasure, because when we are deprived of pain, we rejoice in the very liberation and vacancy of all trouble. Everything in which we rejoice is pleasure, just as everything by which we are offended is pain. 

The removal of all pain is rightly named pleasure. For just as when hunger and thirst are driven away by food and drink, the very removal of the trouble brings the attainment of pleasure; so in every matter, the removal of pain brings about the succession of pleasure. Thus, it did not please Epicurus for there to be some middle ground between pain and pleasure. For that very thing which seems to some to be a middle ground—when we lack all pain—is not only pleasure but even the highest pleasure. For whoever feels how they are affected must necessarily be either in pain or in pleasure. 

Furthermore, they divide this pleasure "set in a stable state" into two parts. One they place in the mind, the other in the body; they call the latter <term>freedom from pain</term> <note>original: *indolentia*. This is a Latin translation of the Greek term *aponia*, meaning the absence of bodily pain.</note>,

<summary>This page outlines the Epicurean classification of pleasures into three types—necessary/natural, natural but not necessary, and neither—and argues that the highest pleasure is simply the total absence of pain (aponia).</summary>
<keywords>Epicurus, Cyrenaics, pleasure, pain, nature, freedom from pain, aponia, katastematic pleasure, wealth vs poverty</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Epicurean ethics, specifically moving from the types of pleasures (natural and necessary versus empty desires) to the definition of the "highest good." It explores the distinction between physical freedom from pain and mental tranquility.</meta>

freedom from pain <note>original: "indolentiam"</note>. This they truly call tranquility. Now (as it pleases them), freedom from pain in the body is the removal of all pain. Tranquility, however, is a certain peaceful and constant release of the mind from all disturbance. But sometimes they embrace both kinds of pleasure under a single name, calling it absolute and complete tranquility. Thus it happens that tranquility is twofold: one belongs to the soul alone, the other to the whole person—the latter being that which is entirely perfect and absolute.

## Chapter XVIII. Moderation in pleasures, and that happiness consists not in active pleasure, but in tranquility according to Epicurus and Democritus.

**M**oreover, every pleasure is good by its own nature and to be sought, yet sometimes it is to be avoided for the sake of another thing. For those pleasures which are undertaken from immoderate and shameful actions ought to be avoided for the reason that they are very brief and fragile, and bring with them repentance, care, anxiety, and pain. Likewise, all pains are to be avoided for their own sake, yet they are to be undertaken for the sake of another thing when, although light and very brief, they are likely to provide us with certain very great pleasures and advantages. 

And even if all pleasures are good, nevertheless the blessed life is not situated in all of them. For neither is that pleasure which occurs through motion <note>This refers to "kinetic" pleasure—the active enjoyment of the senses, such as eating or drinking.</note> sufficient in itself for the blessed life, nor is it entirely necessary for living blessedly for its own sake. Furthermore, they think that absolute tranquility—which contains the peaceful rest of the mind and the body's freedom from pain—is the highest good of all. 

For by these two things, the entire nature of the human being—namely, the body and the mind together—is made perfect, and this is the state to which all affairs are referred. Since people undergo all labors so that they may afterwards be in leisure and rest, they follow those pleasures which we have placed in motion in order to drive away pains and satisfy the needs of nature. 

But to drive away pain and satisfy need is done so that we may be released and free from all pain which arises from the poverty of nature. And this is that <term>freedom from pain</term> <note>original: "indolentia"; in this context, it means the physical state of being without pain, not the modern sense of laziness.</note> which they want to be understood as a stable state, and which they consider to occupy one part of happiness; the other part is governed by the <term>tranquility of the mind</term> <note>original: "tranquillitas animi"; a state of mental calm known in Greek as *ataraxia*.</note>, for the sake of which all virtues are sought. 

Since indeed the virtues desire nothing else but to free the mind from all disturbance. That is indeed tranquility itself, for which reason they want all virtues to be sought for the sake of tranquility itself, and much more so all other human actions. 

<summary>This page defines the Epicurean "highest good" as a combination of physical freedom from pain (indolentia) and mental peace (tranquillitas), explaining that virtues are merely tools to achieve this state of rest.</summary>
<keywords>Epicurus, Democritus, pleasure, tranquility, freedom from pain, happiness, virtue, kinetic pleasure, mental peace, ethics</keywords>

# ON LIBERTY

<meta>
catchword: quod
image_quality: good
</meta>

Other human goods are either proper to the mind alone or to the body. That absolute and perfect tranquility alone, out of all things, encompasses the entire nature of man. Therefore, it ought to be judged by right as the most excellent of all goods. 

¶ To these points also, that which is confirmed by the authority of all philosophers carries no small weight: namely, that that appears to be the highest good to which nothing further can be added. But what will you add to tranquility? Or indeed, can you add anything unless it lacks something? But if some good should be lacking, it is necessary that he who lacks it should desire it. He who truly desires, however, can in no way be tranquil. Where, therefore, tranquility is, there is no desire <note>original: "appetitio"</note>. Where truly nothing is desired, there is no want. Where there is no poverty <note>original: "egestas"</note>, there finally is the perfect state, an abundance of things to be sought, and the absolute embrace of all goods. Where therefore tranquility is, there are all goods. Where all things are, there is also tranquility. By which it is understood that nothing is missing from it, nothing can be added at all, and that it contains within itself the nature and reason of all goods. And therefore it is the perfect and ultimate good, to which every desire of nature is directed. 

¶ And since there are many goods, either one of these is happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note>, or all of them gathered together in turn, or rather something which is fashioned from the accumulated possession of all other goods. Truly, any good separated from the others, since many other things can be added to it, can in no way be seen as the highest good. Nor even all [goods] collected together [can be the highest good]. For happiness stands as a certain final and extreme end of human life. However, the ultimate end ought to be one and simple. Wherefore the highest good will be that which has proceeded from the accumulation of all others. That, truly, can be nothing other than tranquility. For the nature of goods is twofold: for they both fill the soul and free it from all distress. Truly, such a filling and liberation is without doubt tranquility itself. 

¶ Since this tranquility follows the possession of other goods, it follows that it should rightly be seen as the end and extreme of them all, and for that reason the highest good. For the mind never rests unless it has attained all goods. Rest <note>original: "quies"</note> and tranquility, however, are one and the same. Therefore, tranquility succeeds the possession of other goods. For its sake, therefore, all goods seem to be sought—as if this were the ultimate and best end to be desired by all. Wherefore <term>Epicurus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher (341–270 BCE) who taught that the greatest good is to seek modest pleasures in order to attain a state of tranquility and freedom from fear.</note> judges that the blessed life consists in tranquility of the soul—or rather, that most blessed life which contains at once freedom from pain <note>original: "indolentiam"</note> for both the soul and the body. 

¶ But lest I seem to assert from my own self those things which have been reported concerning Epicurus, first...

# ON PLEASURE

<meta>The text uses early modern printing conventions: 'u' for 'v', tildes (~) for nasalization (m/n), and ligatures. Catchword 'io-' at the bottom right.</meta>

That pleasure, which accompanies motion, is not the highest good, <term>Epicurus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 341–270 BCE) often wrongly accused of promoting pure hedonism; he actually taught that the greatest pleasure is the absence of pain.</note> himself testifies in his own words in his *Letter to Menoeceus*, saying: "When, therefore, we say that pleasure is the goal, we do not mean the pleasures of the profligate or those consisting in physical gratification—as some who are ignorant and disagree with our views suppose—but rather the absence of pain in the body and the lack of disturbance in the soul." For it is not drinking bouts and continuous partying, nor the company of youths and women, nor the consumption of fish and other delicacies which a costly table provides, that produces a pleasant life. Instead, it is sober reasoning, which searches out the causes of why every thing is to be either chosen or avoided, and which drives out those opinions through which the greatest turmoil occupies the soul. Likewise, in the same letter, he says: "The absence of pain and disturbance are constant <note>original: "constantes," referring to static or "katastematic" pleasures which are stable states rather than fleeting sensations.</note> pleasures; but joy and gladness are considered an action according to motion." Indeed, the highest pleasure is the removal of pain, and the pleasures of the mind are certainly greater than those of the body. For the flesh is bathed only in present sweetness, but the mind rejoices together in the thought of things past, present, and future. 

Also in the same letter: "It is not possible to live pleasantly unless one lives prudently, honorably, and justly; nor to live prudently, honorably, and justly unless one lives pleasantly." From these points, Epicurus shows that the highest good consists neither in pleasures according to motion, nor in those which are taken from shameful actions. Rather, he shows that these two things—namely, the <term>indolence</term> <note>original: "indolentiam," used here in the classical sense of "aponia," or the total absence of physical pain, rather than laziness.</note> of the body and the tranquility of the mind—produce the most blessed life. Lucretius the Epicurean also testifies to this same thing in the second book of *On the Nature of Things*. There, while he censures the vain desires of men and their luxurious delights, he says:

> O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts!
> In what shadows of life and in how great dangers
> Is this span of time, however much it is, passed! Do you not see
> That nature barks <note>original: "latrare," a vivid metaphor suggesting nature has a primal, insistent demand.</note> for nothing else for itself than that,
> With the body separated from it, pain may be absent, and that the mind may enjoy
> A pleasant sense, removed from care and fear?

Here, therefore, by censuring the luxury of men, he calls them blind and wretched because they burden themselves with all sorts of troubles and do not see what nature desires as its supreme end and good. He himself explains what that truly is, saying that nature seeks this: that pain be absent from the body (which signifies that "indolence" of which we spoke) and that care and fear be removed—by which words he certainly wishes the tranquility of the mind to be understood—and that it may enjoy the benefit and sense of these two things.

<summary>This page clarifies the Epicurean definition of the highest good, defining it not as sensory indulgence but as the combination of physical painlessness (aponia) and mental peace (ataraxia). It supports this by quoting Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus and Lucretius's famous poem on the nature of reality.</summary>

...[pleasant] and in the mind; as if to say, that in these things consists the highest joy of body and soul. Since, therefore, the most blessed life consists in these two—namely, <term>painlessness</term> <note>original: "indolentia," translating the Greek *aponia*, the complete absence of physical pain.</note> and tranquility of mind—these testimonies of Epicurus and Lucretius ought to be sufficient. Regarding the fact that he who possesses tranquility of mind remains blessed even if his limbs are tortured, Epicurus is a witness in his letter to <term>Metrodorus</term> <note>Metrodorus of Lampsacus (c. 331–277 BCE), one of the most important disciples of Epicurus.</note>, saying: a man who has once become wise cannot pass into the opposite state, nor can he err by yielding to disturbances; and whether he is tortured or racked, the wise man will nonetheless be happy. Also, in that letter which he wrote to <term>Hermarchus</term> <note>Epicurus's successor as the leader of the Epicurean school.</note> while dying, he says: "While we were spending the last and most blessed day of our life, we were writing these things. Such great diseases of the bladder and intestines were present that nothing could be added to their severity; yet all these things were compensated for by the joy of mind which I received from the memory of our reasonings and discoveries." In these words, he says he is spending a blessed day, and yet he is tortured by the greatest pains. The same is said to have been the opinion of <term>Leucippus</term>, <term>Democritus</term>, and <term>Theodorus</term>: that happiness lies in tranquility of the mind. But if painlessness of the body is joined to this, then in this state, absolute and perfect happiness consists in the disposition of both soul and body.

We have written down these things for you, compiled from various philosophers regarding pleasure. However, as to which opinion you should follow from among these, I wish for you to be persuaded by the authority and reasonings of those who debate here, rather than by my own judgment. For it will have been enough for me to have related the opinions of nearly all the philosophers for the sake of exercising my memory. **THE END**

### Decorative Design
The cover is decorated with **blind-tooled** geometric patterns, consisting of:
*   Vertical and horizontal lines that form a rectangular frame.

<note>The term "blind-tooling" refers to a traditional method of decoration where a bookbinder presses a heated metal tool into dampened leather. This creates a permanent, darkened impression without the use of gold leaf or colored pigments.</note>

<margin>Metal hardware</margin>

<note>Clasps were a standard feature of early books, especially those written on parchment. Because parchment is sensitive to humidity and tends to curl, these metal fasteners were necessary to keep the book tightly closed and the pages flat when it was not in use.</note>
